sections.overview: Heterophasic polypropylene copolymers are multiphase materials combining a polypropylene-rich matrix with an elastomeric ethylene–propylene-rich component. Often called impact polypropylene copolymers, they can be produced by sequential polymerization. The rubber-rich phase can improve impact behavior while the matrix contributes stiffness. Composition and phase morphology determine the balance, and finished compounds may contain further additives or fillers.
sections.history: Heterophasic polypropylene developed as producers combined a polypropylene matrix with an elastomeric phase to broaden the material’s impact performance. It is a reactor-made multiphase material class, with no single first-invention date established by the sources used here. LyondellBasell documents the role of gas-phase copolymerization stages and successive Spheripol catalyst generations in expanding impact-copolymer production. Such process development supported the polypropylene industry’s expansion in automotive parts, appliances and other molded goods. The 2002 Spherizone milestone provides a later example of producers changing reactor architecture to gain additional control over product architecture.
sections.nomenclature: The record covers the heterophasic or impact-copolymer form of polypropylene, also denoted PP-B or HECO. These terms identify a multiphase material with a polypropylene-rich matrix and an elastomeric phase rather than an arbitrary random polypropylene copolymer. A resin designation does not specify the amount or ethylene content of its rubber-rich component. Fillers and additives can further distinguish a finished molding compound from the reactor-produced material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Heterophasic polypropylene copolymer is a reactor-made multiphase polypropylene material, not a simple mechanical blend. It is commonly prepared by sequential polymerization: a propylene-rich matrix fraction is first made, then ethylene with propylene and/or an alpha-olefin is polymerized in the presence of that first fraction to create a dispersed rubbery copolymer phase. Documented multistage routes use stereospecific Ziegler–Natta catalyst systems with titanium-containing procatalyst, organoaluminum cocatalyst, and optional electron donor; slurry/bulk and gas-phase stages can be combined. One recent three-stage example forms initial propylene copolymer fractions then makes a propylene–ethylene elastomer in a further gas-phase stage. Reactor sequence, comonomer feeds, catalyst/donor system, hydrogen use, and phase proportions are composition-specific. Subsequent compounding, filler addition, or molding is outside this synthesis account.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Heterophasic polypropylene copolymers are multiphase thermoplastics in which a semicrystalline isotactic-polypropylene matrix supplies stiffness and yield strength while dispersed ethylene-propylene rubber, commonly with polyethylene-rich inclusions, promotes energy absorption and ductile fracture. Relative to polypropylene homopolymer, the characteristic design tradeoff is higher impact resistance, especially below room temperature, against lower tensile and flexural stiffness. Their response is strongly temperature- and rate-dependent: notches, rapid loading, thick sections, weld lines, or temperatures near and below the matrix and rubber transitions can shift a molding from yielding and plastic deformation toward brittle fracture. The balance depends on matrix tacticity, molecular mass, crystallinity and molecular-mass distribution; rubber fraction, ethylene content, molecular mass and glass-transition temperature; dispersed-particle size, shape, internal core-shell structure, spacing and interfacial adhesion; and any polyethylene, external elastomer, filler, reinforcement, nucleating agent, or peroxide modification. Melt viscosity ratio and deformation during compounding or molding govern the resulting phase morphology, while cooling rate, annealing, orientation, specimen thickness, notch geometry, strain rate and test temperature govern the measured result. Increasing rubber fraction can produce a brittle-to-tough transition but generally lowers modulus; higher-molecular-mass phases and a fine, well-adhered dispersion can improve toughness. Talc or glass fiber can raise stiffness and dimensional stability, but filler loading, dispersion and coupling determine whether strength rises and impact resistance is retained. As one bounded commercial example, SOCAR Polymer reports typical values for its phthalate-free CB 1200 MO injection-molding heterophasic copolymer grade: flexural modulus 1200 MPa by ISO 178 at 2 mm/min, tensile modulus 1100 MPa by ISO 527 at 1 mm/min, tensile stress at yield 23 MPa and elongation at yield 6% by ISO 527 at 50 mm/min, and notched Izod impact strength of 10 kJ/m2 at 23 °C and 5 kJ/m2 at -20 °C by ISO 180. The sheet does not identify specimen molding history, geometry, conditioning, or replicate statistics, and labels these as typical rather than specification values; they therefore characterize CB 1200 MO only, not the family or filled, oriented, recycled, weathered, or differently processed articles.
sections.processing:
Heterophasic polypropylene copolymer is a melt-processable thermoplastic used for injection molding, extrusion, thermoforming, and (for suitable grades) compression molding. Pellets normally need no routine drying when kept dry, but moisture, contamination, and any filler or regrind package should be checked before molding; grade molecular mass, rubber-phase content, filler loading, and mold geometry change the usable window. Compounding or regrinding should provide enough distributive mixing to retain a fine rubber dispersion while avoiding excessive residence time, shear heating, and oxidative degradation.

A bounded supplier example is SCG's EL-Pro P740J impact-copolymer grade: its technical sheet recommends a 230–270 °C melt, 25–70 °C mold, fast injection, 40–70 rpm screw speed, and injection/packing/back-pressure settings expressed as 40–80%/30–60%/10% of machine maximum. Those values apply to that grade and machine/product context, not to every heterophasic PP. A separate PP injection guide gives broader compound guidance (about 200–250 °C mass temperature for PP variants, 20–90 °C mold temperature depending on reinforcement, and residence time below 10 min) and notes that drying, moisture, shrinkage, and cooling depend on formulation and part geometry. These sources support melt conversion; reactor polymerization of the heterophasic material belongs in Synthesis.
sections.structureAndMorphology: A common impact-copolymer structure contains a crystalline polypropylene matrix and dispersed rubber-rich domains. Ethylene-rich compositions can also contain crystalline polyethylene-rich inclusions within those domains. The amount, size and distribution of the dispersed phase affect how deformation is accommodated in the material. The reactor product is therefore more complex than a single uniform copolymer chain, and a filled molded article may have additional structural features.
sections.properties: The rubber-rich phase can improve impact toughness, including low-temperature performance, while the polypropylene matrix contributes stiffness. A review reports that ethylene-rich dispersed phases can improve low-temperature toughness, whereas propylene-rich rubber gives finer dispersion and may improve transparency but is less suitable at very low temperatures. In a study for cable insulation, an impact copolymer with 15% ethylene–propylene rubber phase had approximately 32.4% lower tensile modulus and 64.9% higher elongation at break than the tested isotactic PP. The copolymer with 30% rubber showed a substantial drop in elongation compared with the 15% sample. These are differences among particular prepared specimens, not predictions for every grade or molded part.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Heterophasic PP is used where molded articles require impact toughness as well as useful stiffness. SOCAR identifies its CB1200MO grade for crates, housewares, rigid packaging and automotive battery cases. The polypropylene matrix and rubber-rich phase support different parts of the stiffness–impact balance. The supplier reports a flexural modulus of 1,200 MPa by ISO 178 and a melt flow rate of 12 g/10 min at 230 °C/2.16 kg for this injection-molding grade. Together these illustrate a specific grade chosen for stiffness and processability; they are typical values rather than design limits and do not guarantee finished-part performance.

Purchasing. The CB1200MO supplier sheet lists pellets in 25 kg bags, with 1,250 kg per pallet, or 1,000 kg bulk bags by agreement. A converter should select an impact grade for the molding process and finished part, rather than assuming all heterophasic materials are interchangeable.

Scale and evidence limits. These are delivery package sizes, not annual purchases. No reliable separate global purchased or consumed tonnage was established for heterophasic PP.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In a study of Novatec BC03AD block PP, repeated melt processing changed tensile response and generated signs of thermal damage. The authors proposed that radicals could be consumed through crosslinking in the ethylene–propylene rubber phase, helping explain its different response from a selected homopolymer. The study did not identify a complete small-molecule product inventory.

Timescales: The researchers used up to five extrusion passes, about one minute of barrel residence per pass and approximately 210 °C resin temperature at the die exit. The initial peak tensile stress of the subsequently molded block-copolymer specimens decreased from about 30–32 MPa to about 26 MPa over five passes. In a different study, two recycled heterophasic PP hollow-chamber sheets were exposed for 1,000 hours to cycles of UV light, heat and water spray. Maximum tensile force at break fell by 33.5% for one sheet and 0.9% for the other, while strain at break fell by 20.7% and 17.7%, respectively. Their different geometries, manufacturing histories and compositions prevent attribution of the difference to a single factor.

Environmental persistence: Processing and accelerated-weathering changes do not measure mineralization. Neither experiment establishes an outdoor disappearance time for a finished product.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Re-extrusion and injection remolding were demonstrated for the Novatec BC03AD block PP grade. Its molded tensile response changed with repeated passes, although the selected homopolymer and block copolymer did not change at the same rate. Rubber-phase chemistry, processing history and additive content therefore matter to the recovered grade’s performance.

The experiment used known materials under controlled conditions; it does not establish the composition of a mixed waste stream or a local collection route.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Heterophasic PP melt processing involves hot surfaces, pressurized resin and possible fumes. As polypropylene-family context, HSE lists formaldehyde, acrolein and acetone among products detected when PP is heated above its recommended processing range. The mixture depends on temperature, residence time, stabilizers and other ingredients. LyondellBasell’s polyolefin guide adds guarding, spill control and eye/hand protection for film equipment; the actual grade and operation determine the control measures.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The matrix, elastomer composition and amount and distribution of dispersed phase vary among impact grades. A review describes a tradeoff: ethylene-rich dispersed phases can improve toughness at low temperature, while more propylene-rich rubber can give finer dispersion and improved transparency but is less effective at very low temperatures. Increasing the elastomer fraction can reduce stiffness, so the desired balance depends on the part and service temperature. Fillers, processing and loading rate add further variability; one formulated specimen cannot represent the entire class.

synthesisRoutes.conditions: Sequential matrix and elastomer formation with a Ziegler–Natta catalyst.
synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Sequential polymerization forms a polypropylene-rich matrix and an ethylene/propylene rubber phase. Olefin first coordinates to an active metal site and then inserts into the metal–carbon bond of the growing chain. The longer metal-bound chain can coordinate and insert another monomer; catalyst environment and feed selection govern the resulting sequence and stereochemistry. The staged feeds create different polymer populations and phases; successive reactor stages do not by themselves establish a covalent block sequence.

steps.title: Prepare the reaction
steps.body: Polymerize propylene, ethylene and 1-butene to form the first propylene-rich matrix fraction.

steps.title: Coordinate and insert monomer
steps.body: Follow repeated olefin coordination and insertion at the activated catalyst. Each insertion adds carbon atoms to the chain and regenerates a metal-bound growth site. Apply the catalyst and comonomer choices of this route when interpreting branching or stereoregularity.

steps.title: Form and recover the product
steps.body: Form the second propylene-rich matrix fraction, then add propylene and ethylene in a later reactor to prepare the elastomer fraction.

synthesisRoutes.limitations: This outline does not specify a universal recipe, reagent loading, operating schedule, or conversion endpoint. sections.overview: Poly(1-butene), or PB-1, is the homopolymer derived from 1-butene. Stereoregular material can crystallize and develop more than one crystal form. Poly(1-butene) is used in applications including packaging blends and piping materials. Copolymers of 1-butene with other monomers have a distinct composition and must be identified separately.
sections.history: Poly(1-butene) belongs to the first wave of stereospecific polyolefins. LyondellBasell traces its discovery to Giulio Natta’s research group in 1954 and industrial introduction in Europe to the mid-1960s. Flexible pressure piping became an important early application, with subsequent development directed toward hot- and cold-water systems. The company’s later PB-1 business also developed packaging, polymer-modification and adhesive uses. This history connects an early catalyst discovery to decades of pipe-grade development; the performance of a particular pipe system still depends on its resin generation, fittings and installation.
sections.nomenclature: PB-1 is the abbreviation used for poly(1-butene), also called polybutene-1. This record is the 1-butene homopolymer; copolymers, particular pipe compounds, and their crystallization histories are not alternate names for the base polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(1-butene) (PB-1) is made by coordination polymerization of 1-butene. Stereospecific Ziegler–Natta catalyst systems are used to favor isotactic material, while polymerization medium, temperature, hydrogen, and any alpha-olefin comonomer are route-specific controls of molecular mass, tacticity, and product form. One suspension-process example combines a titanium-based transition-metal component with an organoaluminum cocatalyst and conducts 1-butene polymerization in liquid isobutane; the source notes optional hydrogen for molecular-mass control. A separate catalyst patent describes a MgCl2-supported titanium component, aluminum-alkyl cocatalyst, and optional electron donor, including gas-phase and slurry variants. These are coordination-polymerization examples; they do not imply that copolymer recipes or crystallization histories are intrinsic to every PB-1 grade.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Poly(1-butene) (PB-1) is semicrystalline and polymorphic, so stiffness, stress relaxation, and tensile response depend on crystal modification, crystallinity, molecular orientation, thermal history, temperature, and copolymer content. Open studies of isotactic PB-1 connect mechanical response to crystal-phase composition and the rigid/amorphous physical-network structure; a stress-relaxation study specifically identifies orientation and transformation from crystal form II to form I as part of the response. These dependencies make fresh versus aged or differently processed PB-1 specimens non-interchangeable.

A bounded pipe-system endpoint is Buteline's PB-1 pipe, which is stated to use Basell PB-1 granules: its design sheet lists hydrostatic design stress of 7.6 MPa at 20 °C and 3.5 MPa at 80 °C. These are manufacturer design values for pipe service, not tensile-test values for the polymer family; pipe geometry, extrusion history, pressure-test duration, and compound details limit transferability.
sections.processing: Poly(1-butene) (PB-1) is a semicrystalline thermoplastic processed by extrusion of pipe, tubing, film, and profiles, by melt spinning, and by injection molding with conventional polyolefin equipment when the grade and tooling are appropriate. Pellets should be kept dry and clean; melt temperature, shear, line speed, draw-down, and cooling must be coordinated because freshly formed PB-1 is soft and crystallizes slowly, changing from the initially formed phase II toward the stiffer phase I during aging. In a bounded LyondellBasell pipe-resin guide, small-pipe extrusion uses approximately 180–200 °C melt temperature and 10–12 °C cooling water, with immediate spray quenching, water pre-sizing, vacuum sizing, and controlled draw-down; the guide warns that higher temperature can cause sticking while lower temperature can increase machine-direction orientation. An independent melt-spinning study used commercial homopolymer PB0110M and 4.3 mol% ethylene copolymer PB8220M: pellets were vacuum-dried at 80 °C for 10 h, extruded through a single-screw/spin-pack system with a 110–260 °C barrel range, and wound at 7 or 10 m min−1; hot-pressed films were melted at 180 °C for 10 min and aged one week. These settings are grade- and article-specific, and the ethylene copolymer example is not identical to the homopolymer family. Butene-1 polymerization and catalyst chemistry belong in Synthesis; this section covers pellet handling, melt shaping, spinning, cooling, aging, and post-processing.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Isotactic poly(1-butene) can crystallize from the melt into a form often called form II. That form can slowly transform near room temperature into the more stable form I. The crystal structures differ in the helical arrangement of the chains. In a National Bureau of Standards experiment, one form-II specimen was prepared by holding the melt at 100 °C, while form I was obtained by cooling and storing a specimen near room temperature for a week. The rate and extent of transformation depend on temperature and specimen history.
sections.properties: The crystal forms have different melting behavior and packing density. In a National Bureau of Standards study, a form-II specimen crystallized at 100 °C melted at about 120 °C under relatively rapid heating, while form-I specimens stored near room temperature for a week to several months melted at about 128–132 °C under moderate heating. The values reflect the specified preparation and heating history, not fixed limits for every PB-1 grade. PB-1 is also used as a component of some packaging blends to create peelable seals; blend composition and component distribution influence that application.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PB-1 is used for hot-water pipe systems, fittings, peelable packaging, hot-melt adhesives and polyolefin modification. LyondellBasell identifies flexibility, creep resistance and heat fusion among characteristics relevant to these products. The supplier offers both homopolymer and random-copolymer grades, so a particular pipe or packaging grade should not automatically be treated as the homopolymer covered by this entry.

Purchasing. LyondellBasell offers PB-1 resins through its product-information channel. Specify whether the order concerns homopolymer resin for pipe, film modification or an adhesive formulation; finished piping systems are a different purchase and may use a copolymer grade.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was established in the checked material. The supplier portfolio documents commercial end uses, not industry-wide volume or a standard order size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Isotactic PB-1 film oxidation proceeds through hydroperoxide formation and chain scission, with carbonyl-containing material accumulating. The Toyo Soda study identified acetaldehyde, ethanol, water, acetic acid and propionic acid in collected volatiles; it also reported formaldehyde and tentatively assigned methyl ethyl ketone.

Timescales: Product collection used approximately 2 g polymer under flowing oxygen for 7 h at 170 °C, with a 130 °C comparison. Oxygen-uptake experiments used 130–180 °C and showed a film-thickness effect. These accelerated oxidation conditions are not a service-life or environmental-decay clock.

Environmental persistence: Chain scission, oxygen uptake and volatilization do not establish complete mineralization in soil or water. The study does not provide an environmental half-life for PB-1 articles.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The Polybutene Piping Systems Association describes returning production residues to the process during PB-1 pipe manufacture. It separately describes recovery and reuse of unpolymerized butene during resin production. Neither statement measures recovery of installed, contaminated or mixed-material pipe after its service life.

A post-consumer route would depend on collection, sorting, product composition and the specification for the intended recycled article. The industry statement does not establish a general pipe-collection program.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PB-1 oxidation experiments demonstrate that severe hot-oxygen exposure can generate volatile oxygenated compounds, including aldehydes, acids and water. These laboratory products are not a measured exposure level during ordinary use. For industrial handling, the polyolefin-processing guidance on hot melt, pressurized equipment, ventilation and prevention of prolonged overheating is applicable as family context; the supplied grade’s stabilizers and processing window remain important.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The structure of a PB-1 article can change after fabrication as the crystalline form transforms. In the cited study, form-II and form-I specimens prepared and stored differently had different melting responses, so the article’s age and thermal history are relevant when comparing measurements. The study tested a particular polymer and preparation, not all commercial products. In peelable films, blend ratio and composition also influence performance; pipe and film data should retain grade, age, fabrication and test conditions.

sections.overview: Poly(4-methyl-1-pentene) (PMP) is a polyolefin made by polymerizing the alpha-olefin 4-methyl-1-pentene. Highly isotactic PMP is a semicrystalline thermoplastic with a distinctive combination of low density, transparency and heat resistance. Its gas permeability is useful in membrane applications, while clear articles can be made for laboratory and packaging uses. Commercial materials may also contain comonomer, so a formulation should not automatically be equated with the homopolymer.
sections.history: ICI introduced poly(4-methyl-1-pentene) as TPX in 1965, according to a contemporary UNIDO paper. Mitsui Chemicals subsequently became a major developer and producer of the material. Its commercial development has emphasized an unusual combination of transparency, heat resistance and release behavior. Established uses include laboratory vessels, electrical insulation, rubber-hose mandrels and release films. More specialized applications include hollow fibers and processing aids for electronics. These applications explain its place as a specialty polyolefin rather than a direct replacement for commodity polyethylene or polypropylene.
sections.nomenclature: PMP is the abbreviation used for poly(4-methyl-1-pentene), also called poly-4-methyl-1-pentene. This record is the homopolymer of 4-methyl-1-pentene; copolymers, grades, and downstream molded or drawn forms are not aliases for the base polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(4-methyl-1-pentene) is a coordination/insertion homopolymer of 4-methyl-1-pentene. The sterically demanding alpha-olefin makes catalyst structure important for activity, molecular weight, and isotactic stereoregularity. One documented route uses a single-site bridged imine-amido catalyst to coordinate and insert 4-methyl-1-pentene in toluene; other routes use aluminum-chloride catalyst systems in halogenated solvent. Catalyst/activator, solvent, monomer-to-catalyst ratio, reaction temperature, and termination are bounded experimental or industrial route choices rather than a universal polymerization recipe. The polymer is distinct from a cyclic metathesis-derived material, and extrusion or other final conversion is not treated as synthesis here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Poly(4-methyl-1-pentene) is a semicrystalline thermoplastic polyolefin with a bulky isobutyl side group. The isotactic homopolymer can be comparatively stiff but brittle, while small amounts of other alpha-olefins are used commercially to disrupt packing and improve toughness and elongation. Its response is viscoelastic and strongly temperature dependent around the amorphous-phase transition: modulus and tensile strength can fall markedly as temperature rises even though the crystalline phase remains. Tacticity, comonomer identity and fraction, molecular weight, crystal form and crystallinity, tie-chain and amorphous-chain entanglement density, physical aging, and additives therefore matter. Melt-draw ratio, cooling rate, annealing, film or fiber orientation and thickness, loading direction, strain rate, and test temperature can change yield, strain hardening, recovery, and failure.

An open film study provides a bounded processing example rather than a bulk-material constant. It used a Mitsui extrusion grade with melt-flow index 9 g/10 min at 260 °C/5 kg, number-average molecular mass 180,000 g/mol, and weight-average molecular mass 622,000 g/mol. T-slot films were cast through a 270 °C die onto a 100 °C chill roll. At melt-draw ratio 40 the 50 μm film, tested at 60 °C and 50 mm/min, had 665 MPa tensile modulus, 15.8 MPa yield stress, and 27.8% elastic recovery after the stated 50%-strain hold/release cycle. Raising the draw ratio to 164 produced a 15 μm film with 147 MPa modulus, 7.2 MPa yield stress, and 44.8% recovery under the same method. The opposing changes were attributed to fewer crystalline tie chains but greater amorphous entanglement and orientation; they must remain limited to this grade, extrusion-cast geometry, draw history, loading direction, and elevated-temperature protocol.
sections.processing:
Poly(4-methyl-1-pentene) is a high-melting thermoplastic that can be injection molded, extruded into sheet and profile, melt-cast into film, melt-spun into fiber, and solution-cast for specialized thin films and composites. Melt processing requires equipment capable of its elevated melt temperature and careful control of residence time, oxidation, die and chill-roll temperatures, draw ratio, and cooling. Flow-induced crystallization and drawing strongly alter lamellar orientation, thickness, shrinkage, and film mechanics; blends and filled compounds require separate compatibility and dispersion work.

Yin and co-workers provide a bounded extrusion-casting example for a Mitsui extrusion-grade PMP with melt-flow index 9 g/10 min at 260 °C/5 kg, melting point 234 °C, and reported molar masses. They used a T-slot die at 270 °C and a chill roll at 100 °C, then varied melt-draw ratio from 40 to 164 to make films about 50 to 15 micrometres thick. Increasing draw transformed the morphology from spherulitic toward oriented lamellae and changed crystallinity and elastic response. Those temperatures and draw ratios are specific to that grade, die/roll setup, and hard-elastic-film experiment, not a universal PMP window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The PMP repeat unit carries a bulky isobutyl side group, and isotactic chain segments adopt helical conformations. Ordered crystal regions coexist with less ordered material. The crystal form ordinarily obtained from the melt has a tetragonal unit cell and helical chains, while different crystal structures have been reported for solution crystallization. In the most stable form discussed in a review, the crystal density is lower than the density of the amorphous material, an unusual feature that helps explain why crystalline PMP can remain optically clear. Processing and composition determine which structures are present.
sections.properties: Highly isotactic PMP can combine transparency with a relatively high melting temperature for a polyolefin. Its crystalline and amorphous regions have unusually similar refractive indices, reducing light scattering at their boundaries and supporting transparency. It also has low dielectric loss, and its gas permeability is useful in membranes such as hollow fibers for oxygen transfer. A government technical review summarizes radiation experiments in which electron-beam exposure reduced melting and recrystallization temperatures for the examined high-molecular-weight PMP. Such observations depend on the sample and irradiation dose rather than defining a property of every commercial article.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PMP is used for laboratory equipment, heat-resistant food containers, cosmetic packaging, LED molds and release films for electronics or synthetic-leather manufacture. Mitsui’s TPX examples also include hose-production mandrels and sheaths. Transparency and heat resistance are useful when the contents of a container or laboratory vessel must remain visible. Low adhesion supports release films: Mitsui describes temporary films used when pressing flexible printed-circuit substrates, where the surface must conform to fine features and later separate from the part. These requirements differ from those of an optical LED mold or a food container.

Purchasing. Mitsui supplies TPX in pellet form for molding and extrusion, and its American product page says it does not sell converted rods or sheets. It recommends RT18, MX002 and MX004 for flexible-circuit release film, while listing RT31 and RT18 variants for food containers. A converter selects the resin grade and makes the film or molded part; the finished form has separate manufacturing requirements. The marketed PMP family includes composition-dependent materials, so verify the grade and intended application.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate purchased or consumed tonnage was established from the checked manufacturer page. Its application and grade listings do not provide a quantitative ranking of markets. Pellet availability also does not establish a typical order size or finished-film volume.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A government laboratory review summarizes thermal oxidation experiments on atactic and isotactic PMP powders in dry oxygen. Infrared changes in the isotactic material were consistent with formation of hydroxyl and carbonyl-containing groups, while gas chromatography and mass spectrometry identified volatile products including carbon dioxide and several aldehydes. The conditions and material govern the product mixture. A separate patent reports molecular-mass reduction while melt mixing a specified PMP grade with polypropylene; its measured peak belongs to the mixture, not isolated PMP.

Timescales: The review describes oxidation experiments at elevated temperatures including 145 °C, where the cited researchers followed spectroscopic and volatile-product changes. The patent’s DX820/HP461Y example uses a 4:6 mass ratio, an extruder outlet temperature of 250 °C and 200 rpm; it measures an altered molecular-weight peak rather than an elapsed environmental decay time. These are different accelerated or processing experiments and do not establish an outdoor lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Identification of volatiles during heating in dry oxygen does not establish complete conversion of PMP carbon to carbon dioxide and biomass in natural surroundings. The melt-mixing patent similarly concerns an engineered mixture rather than discarded PMP exposed to soil or water. A material-specific environmental mineralization time remains unresolved.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The patent describes melt mixing virgin PMP and a selected polypropylene to obtain lower-molecular-weight material. In its comparison, PMP processed alone retained a higher molecular-weight peak than the extruded mixture. This demonstrates a specified processing approach to modifying the resin, rather than separation of used packaging or recovery of pure PMP from mixed waste.

Application to post-consumer PMP reclamation and commercial waste recycling remains unverified.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For poly(4-methyl-1-pentene), polyolefin-processing guidance provides useful workplace context: protect against hot melt and equipment, control pressure and moving machinery, and remove processing fumes. HSE stresses actual temperature and residence time when assessing emissions; its polyethylene and polypropylene product lists should not be treated as measured PMP emission compositions.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Highly isotactic PMP homopolymer can be brittle, and incorporation of alpha-olefin comonomers is one approach used to improve toughness. Comonomer identity and amount affect crystallization and must be stated when comparing modified materials with homopolymer. In published radiation studies summarized by a government laboratory, lower- and higher-molecular-weight PMP films differed in their starting elongation, and both became much less extensible at a high electron-beam dose. Catalyst, stabilizers and processing also matter, so the response of one tested film or commercial mixture does not describe every PMP grade.

sections.overview: Cyclo-olefin polymers (COPs) are materials made from cyclic olefin monomers. A common commercial route uses ring-opening metathesis polymerization followed by hydrogenation. Optical grades are used for precision components and medical containers. Their properties vary with the monomer-derived structure and the selected grade.
sections.history: The modern commercial COP history is illustrated by Zeon’s hydrogenated cyclic-polymer materials. Zeon completed its ZEONEX plant at Mizushima in November 1990 and began selling ZEONOR in September 1998. Optical applications were particularly important because dimensional stability and low moisture uptake complemented transparency; medical and industrial molded parts broadened the market. Zeon’s history therefore records a transition from cyclic-monomer chemistry to precision-use plastics. These milestones date specific commercial families, while COP as a broader chemical category can include materials with different research and production lineages.
sections.nomenclature: COP is the abbreviation used for cyclo-olefin polymer in this record. It denotes a family or material class rather than one commercial grade or one fixed cyclic-olefin composition. A common commercial route uses ring-opening polymerization followed by hydrogenation, while COC often denotes addition copolymers of cyclic and acyclic olefins. The distinction helps identify different polymerization routes, but the abbreviation by itself does not specify the monomer, molecular architecture or grade.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cyclo-olefin polymer (COP) is commonly made by ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) of cyclic-olefin feedstocks followed by hydrogenation of the unsaturated polymer backbone. Unlike ethylene/norbornene COC addition copolymerization, ROMP opens the cyclic alkene and leaves backbone double bonds before the hydrogenation stage. A documented academic example uses a ruthenium Grubbs catalyst to ROMP strained bicyclic monomers and then hydrogenates the main-chain double bonds; changing comonomer feed changes the polymer composition. A Zeon patent likewise describes hydrogenating norbornene ring-opened polymer with hydrogen and a homogeneous or heterogeneous hydrogenation catalyst, and identifies vinyl/diene additions as molecular-weight modifiers during ring opening. These route-specific examples should not be read as a specification for every commercial COP grade.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cyclo-olefin polymers (COPs) are amorphous engineering thermoplastics. Their measured tensile and impact response depends on the named grade and test configuration, as well as the molded article geometry; numbers from one resin or tube should not be treated as a family-wide design range.

A supplier comparison of optical ZEONEX COP grades reported ISO 527 tensile moduli of 2530 MPa (K26R), 2570 MPa (K22R), 2650 MPa (T62R), and 2960 MPa (360R), with corresponding tensile strengths of 54, 72, 67, and 37 MPa. These are separate grade values from the supplier table, not a universal COP interval.

For a bounded article-level durability example, an independent study injection-molded Zeonex 690R COP blood-collection tubes (4 and 9 mL) and drop-tested water-filled, stoppered 10 mL tubes vertically onto linoleum. Table 2 reports zero breaks among 24 COP tubes at both 36 and 48 inch drop heights. That result describes this molded tube geometry, fill state, orientation, and visual breakage criterion rather than a standard bulk impact property.
sections.processing:
Cyclo-olefin polymer can be injection molded into optical, medical, and precision articles and hot-embossed or thermally bonded as sheet for microstructured devices. ZEON's molding guide treats the settings as product-specific: ZEONEX grades are preheated for 4–10 h at the listed grade temperature to remove dissolved air rather than simply to remove absorbed water, while overly long heating can discolor the material. For optical molding it recommends excluding oxygen with nitrogen at the hopper and barrel because oxidation at melt temperature can produce burning, discoloration, and contamination. Its listed ZEONEX examples span cylinder and mold settings that change by grade, so those tables should not be read as a family-wide window.

A separate bounded study hot-embossed COP sheet at 180 °C and 103 kPa for 5 min using a powder-reinforced PDMS mold constrained in an aluminum frame. Omitting either reinforcement or the frame produced inconsistent or distorted microscale features; patterned and unpatterned sheets were subsequently thermally bonded into chips. The temperature, pressure, time, and mold constraint are specific to that sheet-scale microfluidic experiment.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Commercial optical COPs are described as amorphous resins containing cyclic structures. In the ring-opening route, cyclic monomers form chains that are subsequently hydrogenated to reduce residual backbone double bonds. The remaining ring-containing groups distinguish these materials from simple polyethylene. Specific monomer structures and processing conditions affect the finished material.
sections.properties: Selected optical COP grades combine transparency with low water absorption and low birefringence. Low birefringence helps a lens avoid unwanted changes in the polarization of transmitted light, while lower moisture uptake can help maintain dimensions in a humid environment. Zeon reports 92% light transmission by ASTM D1003 and less than 0.01% saturated water absorption at 23 °C by ASTM D570 for each of its K26R and T62R optical grades. Their reported glass transitions are 143 and 154 °C respectively by JIS K7121. These are supplier-reported comparisons for named grades and methods, not universal optical or thermal limits for COP.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Optical COP grades are used in smartphone lenses, VR optics and sensors. Zeon identifies high transparency and low birefringence as useful for transmitting images without excessive light loss or polarization effects; low water absorption also helps optical dimensions remain stable as humidity changes. The supplier notes that higher-flow grades help fill thin, highly curved smartphone lenses while reducing the risk of knit lines. These attributes are reported for its optical product family and the finished part must meet its own specification.

Purchasing. Specify an optical COP grade through the manufacturer’s contact channel, matching both optics and molding needs. For example, the supplier reports ISO 1133 melt flow at 280 °C and 21.18 N of 52 g/10 min for ZEONEX K26R versus 16 for T62R; the reported glass transitions are 143 °C and 154 °C respectively. A converter must balance flow and thermal requirements for the article; resin, converted film and finished lenses are distinct purchase forms.

Scale and evidence limits. The two values compare named resins under one test condition; they are neither a universal COP flow range nor proof of a finished lens’s optical performance. No reliable separate purchased or consumed tonnage was established from the checked source, and these examples do not estimate the entire COP market or a typical order.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In a photo-irradiation study, two experimental hydrogenated cyclic polymers developed oxygen-containing groups including ketones, alcohols and esters. Both also formed an insoluble gel fraction; the authors interpreted the results in terms of competing crosslinking and chain scission. These studied materials were hydrogenated poly(cyclohexadiene-ran-butadiene) and hydrogenated polystyrene, not necessarily the composition of a commercial optical grade. A supplier’s separate COP-based adhesive bond test measures assembly performance rather than identifying the breakdown products of these samples.

Timescales: Researchers exposed 85–90 µm films of the two hydrogenated experimental polymers to filtered xenon light at 63 °C without water spray. After 200 hours, more than 90% of the hydrogenated poly(cyclohexadiene-ran-butadiene) and more than 70% of the hydrogenated polystyrene were insoluble in the test solvent. In a separate supplier test of commercial ZEONEX 360R optical COP, light transmission changed by less than 4% after more than 800 hours of irradiation at 400 nm, as reported by the supplier. Optical transmission and solvent-insoluble fraction are different endpoints, neither of which establishes an outdoor lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Formation of an insoluble fraction or retained optical transmission does not establish environmental mineralization. These tests did not measure conversion of polymer carbon to carbon dioxide or biomass in soil or water. A natural-environment lifetime for a particular COP article remains unresolved.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Zeon’s 2024 report records completion of a dedicated COP recycling plant and preparation for operation. That is an industrial-development report at the stated date, not evidence that every COP grade or finished article has a commercial recycling route. Optical cleanliness, additives and contamination can affect the requirements for a recovered material.

The report does not establish general post-consumer COP collection or a closed loop for a particular medical or optical product.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: ZEON’s ZEONEX molding guide describes nitrogen sealing of the hopper to limit oxidation and cautions that the surrounding nitrogen concentration must be monitored with adequate room ventilation. This adds a gas-handling consideration to the hot-melt operation. Processing fume controls should follow the grade and actual temperature/residence history, as set out in HSE plastics guidance.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: COP denotes a family rather than one chemical structure or grade. A supplier's optical data apply to its identified resins and test methods: for example, K26R and T62R have different listed glass transitions and melt-flow rates even though their listed light transmittance is the same. The comparison does not isolate one formulation variable as the cause of the difference. A blood-collection tube study examined a particular injection-molded COP and tube geometry, not all COP products. Monomer structure, processing and article shape must be retained when comparing results.

sections.overview: Cyclic olefin copolymers (COCs) contain units derived from a cyclic olefin and a linear olefin such as ethylene. Ethylene–norbornene copolymers are an important commercial example; random incorporation limits chain packing and produces amorphous grades. They can combine transparency and low water absorption with grade-dependent thermal behavior. Applications include packaging, optical components and microfluidic devices.
sections.history: Cyclic olefin copolymers became commercially important when catalyst advances enabled controlled incorporation of cyclic and linear olefins. TOPAS traces its lineage to Hoechst research in the early 1990s and a commercial plant at Oberhausen in 2000. The business later passed through Ticona/Celanese to Daicel and Polyplastics in 2006. Early development targeted transparent, dimensionally stable products, including optical data storage and lenses; pharmaceutical packaging, diagnostic disposables and barrier films became important markets. These dates describe the TOPAS industrial lineage rather than the first laboratory preparation of every cyclic olefin copolymer.
sections.nomenclature: COC abbreviates cyclic olefin copolymer. The name covers a composition-variable copolymer family, not one defined repeat-unit sequence. Ethylene–norbornene and ethylene–tetracyclododecene are distinct examples studied as COCs. The term should not be silently merged with cyclic olefin polymers made by other polymerization routes, nor treated as a specification for one grade.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cyclic olefin copolymer (COC) denotes addition copolymers in which an acyclic olefin, commonly ethylene, is copolymerized with a cyclic olefin such as norbornene or tetracyclododecene. This is coordination-insertion polymerization: the cyclic olefin double bond is consumed during chain growth while the cyclic ring framework is retained in the chain, distinguishing the route from ring-opening metathesis routes used for many cyclo-olefin polymers. Group 4 molecular catalysts, including titanium- and zirconium-based systems, are documented for ethylene/cyclic-olefin copolymerization; catalyst structure and cocatalyst choice govern cyclic-monomer incorporation, sequence distribution, and molecular weight. A Polyplastics patent route uses a metal-containing catalyst, with aluminoxane or borate cocatalyst options, to copolymerize ethylene and a norbornene monomer while limiting polyethylene-like byproduct. The cited conditions describe particular catalyst systems, not a universal COC formulation.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cyclic olefin copolymers (COCs) are amorphous engineering thermoplastics whose tensile response is grade- and molding-history-dependent. In injection-molded parts, flow-induced orientation and the associated birefringence can vary through the plate; reported tensile values therefore need the grade, specimen location or orientation, and test method rather than being combined into a universal COC range.

A bounded supplier example is TOPAS 6017S-04, an injection-molding COC grade. Its technical data sheet reports an ISO 527-3 tensile modulus of 3000 MPa at 1 mm/min, tensile stress at break of 58 MPa at 5 mm/min, and strain at break of 2.4% at 5 mm/min. These are values for that named grade and test configuration, not for all COCs.

An independent study of injection-molded COC plates measured tensile moduli of 1991–2040 MPa, tensile strengths of 56–58 MPa, and elongations at break of 3.3–3.5% at three plate positions. The position-dependent results reinforce that an injection-molded article's local orientation and geometry affect the measured response.
sections.processing:
Cyclic olefin copolymer grades can be injection molded, extruded as film, sheet, or profile, and converted by blow molding or injection-blow molding; films may also be stretched above the grade's glass-transition temperature. Standard thermoplastic equipment is usable, but melt and mold temperatures, flow, and permitted residence time vary with grade. TOPAS guidance says routine predrying is generally unnecessary, while surface-moist pellets may be dried at 80 °C and high-surface-quality molding may require grade-specific predrying; it also warns that excess melt temperature or residence time can yellow the resin and that undersized gates can cause shear heating.

Hot embossing and thermal bonding provide a separate article route for microfluidic structures. In one bounded example, 1.5 mm mcs-COC-13 sheet with a reported glass-transition temperature of 142 °C was embossed against an epoxy mold for 10 min at 160 °C and 2.3 MPa, then held under pressure for another 15 min while cooling. The embossed substrate was cleaned, dried, and thermally bonded to another COC plate for 30 min at 130 °C and 2.3 MPa. These conditions belong to that sheet, mold stack, and device geometry, not to every COC grade.
sections.structureAndMorphology: In common ethylene–norbornene COCs, cyclic units are incorporated into the copolymer chain. The three commercial TOPAS grades in one calorimetry study were amorphous, as random norbornene incorporation limited crystallization of the ethylene segments. The supplier-reported norbornene fractions of the tested 6013 and 8007 grades were 54 and 37 mol%, respectively. Their molecular masses also differed, so the comparison does not isolate composition from every other variable. Other cyclic monomers and processing histories yield other structures.
sections.properties: COC grades can provide high light transmission and low water absorption. In ethylene–norbornene copolymers the glass transition generally rises as the norbornene fraction increases, reflecting more restricted chain mobility. In a photoaging study, the supplier-listed glass transitions for TOPAS 6013 and 8007 were 140 and 80 °C, respectively; these are grade values rather than results for a single controlled compositional series. Low moisture uptake can help maintain dimensions in aqueous microfluidic uses, while chemical resistance depends on the medium and applied stress.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. COC is used in healthcare packaging, diagnostic components, optical parts and packaging films. Its transparency and low water uptake help explain its interest for microfluidic chips, while a supplier describes stiff, shrinkable COC-based sleeves for PET bottles and grades for clear packaging films. These uses require different material and part specifications.

Purchasing. Buy a named COC grade from TOPAS or its commercial supply channel according to the part, sterilization or barrier requirements. A generic cyclic-olefin label does not specify the grade needed for an application; a resin purchase differs from a finished vial, film or device.

Scale and evidence limits. The September 2019 brochure describes the Oberhausen, Germany plant that started in 2000 with annual capacity of 30,000 tons, as reported in the source. This is historical plant capacity, not present production or annual purchases. No separately verified COC consumption total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A study of cast COC films exposed to UV tracked carbonyl formation, tensile changes and glass-transition behavior. Films with added iron, cobalt or manganese stearates changed differently from the corresponding neat films; the researchers reported a stronger pro-oxidant effect for iron in the tested series. The experiments show formulation-dependent photo-oxidation, not a complete inventory of breakdown molecules. The supplier separately warns that hot water or fats together with stress can initiate cracking in molded articles.

Timescales: Researchers exposed 25 µm ethylene–norbornene and ethylene–tetracyclododecene films to 340 nm UV in an accelerated weathering tester for up to 30 days, removing samples at five-day intervals. They measured carbonyl index and tensile behavior and compared neat films with films containing metal stearate additives. These are laboratory photoaging endpoints for specified films, not a general outdoor lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Carbonyl formation, loss of elongation or stress cracking does not demonstrate complete conversion of polymer carbon to carbon dioxide and biomass. The accelerated film study and supplier guidance do not determine an ambient soil or aquatic mineralization time. Composition, additives and the finished article can affect exposure and must be identified in any environmental test.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The TOPAS supplier describes separating COC-based shrink sleeves from PET bottles by flotation because their densities differ. Separation can help preserve a PET-rich bottle stream; the statement does not demonstrate recovery of the COC sleeve into an equivalent new COC product.

The feasibility of a specific package route depends on labels, adhesives, collection and sorting conditions. This supplier example does not establish closed-loop recovery or local collection for every COC article.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The TOPAS COC brochure identifies dust and volatile exposure during processing as matters for workplace control and refers users to the grade-specific safety data sheet. HSE guidance adds temperature control, avoidance of excessive residence time and suitable ventilation for melt operations. Optical clarity or chemical resistance of a finished COC article does not by itself characterize exposure during manufacture.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The name COC does not specify the cyclic comonomer, its fraction, molecular weight or processing history. A calorimetry study found different glass-transition behavior among three commercial ethylene–norbornene grades and dependence on cooling rate. The TOPAS supplier also warns that hot water or fats combined with molded-in stress can initiate stress cracking. Device geometry, surface treatment and exposure therefore matter as well as resin identity.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Coordination addition incorporates the cyclic olefin while retaining its ring framework. Olefin first coordinates to an active metal site and then inserts into the metal–carbon bond of the growing chain. The longer metal-bound chain can coordinate and insert another monomer; catalyst environment and feed selection govern the resulting sequence and stereochemistry. In this addition route, the norbornene double bond is consumed while its bicyclic skeleton is retained.

steps.title: Coordinate and insert monomer
steps.body: Follow repeated olefin coordination and insertion at the activated catalyst. Each insertion adds carbon atoms to the chain and regenerates a metal-bound growth site. Apply the catalyst and comonomer choices of this route when interpreting branching or stereoregularity.

steps.title: Form and recover the product
steps.body: Control comonomer incorporation during addition polymerization; monomer ratio affects the resulting sequence population.

sections.overview: Ethylene–vinyl acetate (EVA) is a copolymer of ethylene and vinyl acetate whose properties depend strongly on composition. Increasing the vinyl-acetate content changes the balance between polyethylene-like and more flexible behavior. EVA is used in packaging seal layers, including blends with polyethylene. It can also be crosslinked for applications requiring a different response at elevated temperature.
sections.history: EVA developed as an ethylene copolymer offering flexibility and adhesion useful in many formulations. DuPont’s ELVAX was imported by the Mitsui Japanese venture from 1962, followed by domestic EVAFLEX production in 1965. This is an international commercialization milestone rather than EVA’s first synthesis. The subsequent product range served footwear and packaging foams, hot-melt adhesives, agricultural and protective films, electrical-wire coverings and molded goods. Development of different vinyl-acetate contents and processing grades allowed these markets to diverge while retaining the same basic ethylene–vinyl acetate chemistry.
sections.nomenclature: EVA and EVAC are abbreviations used for ethylene–vinyl acetate copolymer. The record is the uncrosslinked copolymer family and its grade variation; polyethylene, ethylene–vinyl alcohol (the hydrolyzed derivative), and a crosslinked or foamed article are related but not aliases for the base copolymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–vinyl acetate copolymer (EVA) is produced by radical copolymerization of ethylene and vinyl acetate. High-pressure free-radical processes are documented in tubular and stirred-autoclave reactors, using organic peroxide initiators; a continuous route separates unreacted monomer from the polymer and recycles monomer to the reactor. A more recent tubular-reactor patent uses staged mixed initiators and reactor-temperature feedback for the same two monomers. These examples show that initiator identity, staged injection, pressure, temperature, and vinyl-acetate feed are process controls that can be varied for a target grade, rather than family-wide constants. EVA crosslinking or curing after polymerization is a separate formulation step and is not included in the synthesis description.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–vinyl acetate copolymer (EVA) spans flexible thermoplastics and elastomer-like grades. Tensile and impact response depend on vinyl-acetate content, melt-flow grade and molecular architecture, specimen form, and whether the material is crosslinked or filled; values for a high-VA adhesive grade or crosslinked formulation are not universal EVA values.

A bounded commercial example is EVATANE 40-55, a random EVA with 38–41 wt% vinyl acetate. Its technical data sheet lists tensile strength at break of 7 MPa and elongation at break of 900–1100%, determined to ISO 527/ASTM D638. These values apply to the named high-VA grade only.

An open study of radiation-crosslinked EVA reports that vinyl-acetate content and crosslinking change dynamic-mechanical behavior. This reinforces the need to identify both composition and crosslink state when comparing EVA mechanical results.
sections.processing:
EVA can be processed on conventional thermoplastic equipment by extrusion, film and coating operations, injection molding, and related routes, but the usable window shifts with vinyl-acetate content and melt index. Celanese's extrusion guide says lower-MFR, higher-viscosity grades generally need higher temperatures, while higher-VA grades melt at lower temperatures and can be run cooler to reduce tack and sticking. Its nominal extrusion examples are about 150, 175, or 205 °C depending on grade and melt index; it recommends a water-cooled feed throat, monitoring head pressure and motor amperage, and generally keeping EVA below 220 °C because degradation can eliminate acetic acid and corrode equipment. These are general starting guidelines, not universal grade specifications.

For injection molding, flexible/high-VA grades can be tacky, so mold-release and ejector design matter, and long residence time or excessive pressure can promote frozen-in strain. SK Functional Polymer's EVATANE 28-800 sheet independently advises conventional thermoplastic equipment, avoiding melt temperatures above 230 °C, and purging after a run; it also calls for protection from heat, humidity, and UV during storage. The 230 °C limit and purge advice apply to that named grade and should be confirmed for other EVA formulations, especially crosslinked or foamed compounds.
sections.structureAndMorphology: EVA chains contain both ethylene and vinyl-acetate units. Incorporation of acetate-bearing units interrupts regular polyethylene-like packing, so crystalline regions coexist with a less ordered phase. In a study of two commercial materials, the untreated grade with 6 wt% vinyl acetate had approximately 39% crystallinity by X-ray diffraction, compared with 35% for the grade containing 12 wt%. Electron-beam irradiation was used to form links between chains in a separate treatment of those materials. These results refer to the studied grades and do not imply that every EVA article is crosslinked.
sections.properties: EVA can provide flexibility and polar interactions in addition to chain entanglement. In differential scanning calorimetry of two untreated commercial samples, the 6 wt% vinyl-acetate grade had a melting peak near 102 °C, while the 12 wt% grade peaked near 96 °C. The materials also differed in measured crystallinity, illustrating how composition and preparation affect thermal response. In packaging, EVA can modify heat sealing and toughness in a blend, while a separately crosslinked network can restrict flow at elevated temperature. Neither the DSC values nor a crosslinked encapsulant describes every EVA grade.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. EVA grades serve packaging, adhesives and photovoltaic encapsulation. Evatane 40-55 is a documented high-vinyl-acetate grade for hot-melt and solvent-based adhesives, inks and foams for the shoe industry. In crystalline-silicon photovoltaic modules, EVA encapsulant bonds the cell and glass layers; this same adhesion makes separation at end of life more difficult.

Purchasing. Purchase a specified EVA grade by vinyl-acetate content and melt flow through a producer or material supplier. SK Functional Polymer offers Evatane resins; the 40-55 technical sheet identifies a particular high-vinyl-acetate grade rather than an interchangeable family specification. A formulated encapsulant or adhesive is a different purchase from resin.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed EVA tonnage was established from the checked sources. Packaging, adhesive and footwear grades cover different formulations, so volume shares cannot be inferred from a product catalog.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Thermal breakdown of EVA can begin with release of acetic acid and formation of an unsaturated polymer intermediate, followed by breakdown of the remaining backbone into smaller hydrocarbons. The cited waste-photovoltaic encapsulant study does not identify every final product. The mechanism and products depend on heating conditions and formulation and should not be treated as an ambient-weathering inventory. In a separate mini-module study, the researchers detected deacetylation markers in EVA exposed to either UV or damp heat. They attributed greater encapsulant degradation in the damp-heat samples to hydrolysis and linked the resulting acetic acid to corrosion of electrical contacts; stabilizer behavior and moisture ingress affected that comparison.

Timescales: Nitrogen thermogravimetry of the studied waste-module encapsulant used heating rates of 0.5–5 °C/min and found two main mass-loss stages spanning approximately 276–372 °C and 372–495 °C. These are programmed-heating results, not environmental lifetimes. In the mini-module experiment, samples containing 26–28% vinyl acetate were tested at 85 °C and 85% relative humidity for up to 2,000 hours; module maximum power began to decline substantially after 1,000 hours. This electrical endpoint includes the behavior of the full module and is not a time to polymer mineralization.

Environmental persistence: Thermal mass loss and delamination do not establish biodegradation. Both the pyrolysis and the damp-heat experiments concern controlled treatment of photovoltaic encapsulants, not discarded material in soil or water. Crosslinking, vinyl-acetate content, stabilizers and module construction limit transfer from the studied encapsulants to other EVA articles; the tests do not establish an environmental disappearance time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Pyrolytic removal of EVA is being studied to enable separation of glass and other components of photovoltaic modules. The kinetic study characterizes degradation of the waste-module encapsulant to inform that process; decomposition of the EVA is not recovery of reusable EVA polymer.

A separate laboratory study removed EVA residues from glass after manual hot-knife separation, reporting extraction within four hours for its tested approach. The target was clean glass, and the result does not establish a commercial route or a closed loop for the encapsulant.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: EVA overheating can release acetic acid as acetate groups are eliminated; the cited photovoltaic-encapsulant thermal study demonstrates that pathway for its particular waste-module material. During extrusion or hot encapsulation, fume assessment therefore needs the actual EVA formulation, curing package and thermal history. HSE recommends controlled temperature/residence time, trained purging and ventilation appropriate to the process.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Vinyl-acetate content is an essential qualifier when comparing EVA materials. In the cited comparison, the 12 wt% grade had a lower initial melting peak and crystallinity than the 6 wt% grade; irradiation produced further changes in both materials. These were two particular commercial grades, so other formulation and processing differences cannot be ruled out. Heat-seal performance also depends on blend composition, substrate and surface treatment. Data from one grade or crosslinked photovoltaic encapsulant do not describe every EVA product.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: High-pressure radical copolymerization incorporates acetate-bearing units. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another.

sections.overview: Ethylene–vinyl alcohol (EVOH) is a family of thermoplastic copolymers containing ethylene and vinyl-alcohol units. Commercial EVOH is commonly made by hydrolyzing an ethylene–vinyl acetate precursor to convert acetate groups to alcohol groups. Strong interactions between hydroxyl-bearing chains and semicrystalline structure contribute to its oxygen-barrier performance. EVOH is often used as a thin layer inside packaging, where surrounding layers help protect the moisture-sensitive barrier and provide other functions such as sealing.
sections.history: Kuraray began the research program that led to EVOH in 1957 while seeking useful plastics derived from its vinyl-acetate and PVA chemistry. Discovery of the copolymer’s gas-barrier behavior was followed by fifteen years of development before EVAL commercialization in 1972. Coextrusion was a major enabling advance because EVOH could be combined with other plastics in multilayer packaging. Food films and condiment containers were prominent early markets. Hollow-fiber artificial-kidney membranes and, from the 1990s, automotive fuel tanks extended its use. This is a company-documented commercialization history, not a claim that a single grade serves all those applications.
sections.nomenclature: EVOH denotes the ethylene/vinyl-alcohol copolymer; it is commonly obtained by hydrolyzing an ethylene–vinyl acetate precursor. It is distinct from EVA, the acetate-containing precursor, and from poly(vinyl alcohol), which does not identify the ethylene copolymer composition. Ethylene content and degree of hydrolysis describe narrower EVOH materials. A grade designation and processing history give additional information that the family abbreviation alone does not.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–vinyl alcohol copolymer (EVOH) is ordinarily obtained by post-hydrolyzing or transesterifying an ethylene–vinyl acetate precursor; it is not made by direct copolymerization of ethylene with free vinyl alcohol. In a BASF route, a high-pressure, free-radical ethylene–vinyl acetate copolymer is contacted with an alkali-metal hydroxide or alcoholate in a C1–C4 alcohol medium, converting some or all vinyl-acetate ester groups into vinyl-alcohol units. A Monsanto example uses an inorganic hydrolyzing agent in an aromatic-hydrocarbon/lower-alkanol solvent mixture and recovers the hydrolyzed copolymer by addition to hot water with volatile removal. Both the degree of hydrolysis and the recovery medium are route-specific controls that leave different residual acetate contents.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–vinyl alcohol copolymer (EVOH) is a semicrystalline thermoplastic whose tensile response depends strongly on ethylene content, grade, crystallinity, orientation, specimen form, and water content. Inter- and intramolecular hydrogen bonding contributes to stiffness and cohesion in dry EVOH, while absorbed moisture increases chain mobility and can plasticize the material; dry injection-molded values therefore cannot be transferred directly to humid or solution-cast films. Drawing direction, cooling and annealing history, film thickness, multilayer constraint, fillers, test rate, temperature, and conditioning humidity can shift modulus, strength, ductility, creep, and cracking behavior.

A bounded grade example is Kuraray EVAL H171B (38 mol% ethylene). For dry injection pieces at 23 °C, its data sheet lists ISO 527 tensile stress at break of 31 MPa, elongation at break of 16%, and Young's modulus of 4.0 GPa; ISO 178 flexural modulus is 3.8 GPa. These values are specific to this dry, injection-molded grade.

For a distinct film example, Luzi and co-workers used an EVOH containing 32 mol% ethylene and a melt index of 3.8 g/10 min at 210 °C. They solution-cast it from 1-propanol/water, dried it at 60 °C for 3 h, and equilibrated the 50–70 micrometre films for two days over silica salt. Five 50 x 10 mm rectangular specimens were tested at room temperature to UNI ISO 527 with a 25 mm gauge length and 5 mm/min crosshead speed. The neat films gave 45 ± 4 MPa strength at break, 265 ± 28% elongation at break, and 440 ± 65 MPa Young's modulus. The study does not report the relative humidity reached during desiccator equilibration, so even this well-bounded film result should not be treated as a general dry-state value. In service, conditioning relative humidity, temperature, ethylene content, orientation, and layer construction should accompany any mechanical comparison.
sections.processing:
EVOH is melt-extruded and coextruded into films, sheets, bottles, and multilayer structures, but moisture control and thermal residence are central constraints. Soarnol's processing note reports that moisture absorbed after package opening can cause bubbles; a few hours in a hopper or circulating-air dryer at 90–110 °C is recommended when needed. It warns that temperatures above 240 °C can cause bubbling or decomposition and that temperatures below about 190 °C can produce high torque and unmelted gels; suitable extruders use L/D about 24–30 with chrome- or nickel-alloy-plated melt-contact surfaces. The guidance is for Soarnol grades and equipment, not all EVOH.

An independently published cast-film experiment used Soarnol AT44 03B (44 mol% ethylene). The grade was dried at 110 °C for 10 h before each extrusion; three twin-screw compounding passes used 80 rpm with a 160 °C feed-to-210 °C die profile, followed by cast-film extrusion from 160 °C to a 220 °C flat die and 50 °C chill rolls at 7 bar. Water was treated as a process-critical variable because it can alter film structure. These values are a bounded E44 research protocol, not a general EVOH production window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: EVOH contains hydroxyl-bearing vinyl-alcohol units as well as ethylene units. Hydrogen bonding between chains contributes to cohesive interactions, while crystalline regions coexist with less ordered material. The ethylene proportion changes crystal organization and the balance between the two kinds of repeat units. For example, researchers electrospun a 44 mol% ethylene EVOH into fibers and annealed the mat at 145 °C to fuse the fibers into a continuous film. That processing history produces a different specimen from an ordinary melt-extruded film, even when the nominal copolymer composition is similar.
sections.properties: EVOH can provide a strong oxygen barrier when relatively dry, but its permeability depends on humidity. At 25 °C, one electrospun and annealed 44 mol% ethylene film had oxygen permeability of 0.10 × 10⁻²⁰ at 20% relative humidity and 4.7 × 10⁻²⁰ m³·m/(m²·Pa·s) at 80% relative humidity. The researchers attributed the high-humidity increase to absorbed water disrupting interchain associations and increasing available free volume. This comparison is for those prepared films, not a universal EVOH value; outer layers in packaging can reduce the barrier layer’s direct exposure to moisture.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. EVOH is used as a gas-barrier component in food and medical packaging, automotive fuel tanks, agricultural containers and films, and heating pipes. In a multilayer food package, the EVOH layer limits oxygen ingress while other layers contribute moisture protection, strength or sealing. In a tray study, a 404 µm PP/EVOH/PP sheet contained a 13 µm EVOH layer with 32 mol% ethylene; thermoforming to a 50 mm deep tray reduced that layer to about 1.5 µm in a measured corner. Oxygen transmission increased with draw depth, illustrating why the final shape and local thinning matter as well as the starting resin. Vacuum-insulation panels are another application listed by Kuraray.

Purchasing. Buy a specified EVOH barrier grade from a producer such as Kuraray through its regional product-inquiry or sales channel. Resin is normally selected as one component of a multilayer product, rather than by the total weight of that product; ethylene content and processing needs matter to grade selection.

Scale and evidence limits. Kuraray reported global EVAL nameplate capacity of 103,000 tonnes per year in August 2023, across Japan, the United States and Belgium. This is historical capacity, not actual production, purchases or the complete world EVOH market. The tray measurements describe the tested construction and forming conditions, not every package.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Heating EVOH in the cited conversion experiments produces water, shorter wax-like chains and unsaturated or aromatic products; catalytic hydrogen treatment can convert intermediates to alkanes and water. Biological tests examine a different route. In one laboratory study, EVOH film incubated with the fungus Phanerochaete chrysosporium showed infrared and thermal changes consistent with alteration of the polymer structure. Those observations do not identify every product or show complete conversion of the film to carbon dioxide.

Timescales: The fungal experiment used a 22 µm film containing 29 mol% ethylene in moist corncob and cornhusk substrate at room temperature. Researchers examined films after 16 and 19 days, observing changes in the infrared spectrum and thermal behavior under the tested conditions. Separately, the Ru-catalyst work used 250 °C, 30 bar hydrogen and 16-hour batch experiments; this is engineered reactor conversion rather than environmental decay.

Environmental persistence: In a different 40-day assay at 45 °C with a bacterial consortium, an EVOH formulation containing 27 mol% ethylene blended 50:50 with thermoplastic starch produced carbon dioxide corresponding to approximately 66% of the theoretical total. That endpoint applies to the whole blend, including starch and its plasticizer, and cannot be assigned entirely to EVOH. The fungal and blended-film tests do not establish a universal lifetime for EVOH in soil, freshwater or seawater, or the fate of a multilayer package.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Laboratory Ru/ZrO2 hydrogenolysis/hydrodeoxygenation converts EVOH and studied EVOH/LDPE blends into alkanes. Aromatic deposits can deactivate catalysts, so pressure and regeneration matter. This is a chemical-conversion experiment rather than widespread collection or closed-loop EVOH recovery.

Mechanical recycling of a seven-layer PE/polyamide/EVOH packaging film was also studied using extrusion into a mixed monolayer film. A maleic-anhydride-grafted polyethylene compatibilizer improved several mechanical properties, while the recycled films had greater haze and did not retain the original multilayer puncture resistance. The EVOH remains part of a mixed material; this is not separation and recovery of pure EVOH.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For EVOH melt processing, temperature and residence-time control matter because thermal reactions can form volatile material and altered polymer. The cited EVOH conversion study identifies water and wax-like/unsaturated products under deliberately severe treatment; it is not an occupational-exposure measurement. HSE plastics guidance supports controlling fumes at extrusion, shutdown and purging, with assessment of the complete multilayer or additive formulation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: A barrier result needs the ethylene content, film preparation, temperature, humidity and test gas. In the electrospun 44 mol% ethylene study, adding 0.5 wt% cellulose nanocrystals increased oxygen permeability at 80% relative humidity from 4.7 to 8.8 × 10⁻²⁰ m³·m/(m²·Pa·s). The filler also changed the film’s crystallinity and other properties, so the comparison is for these particular films rather than all EVOH composites. Thickness, surrounding layers and exposure also influence the performance of a complete package.
