sections.overview: Ethylene–acrylic acid (EAA) is a copolymer containing ethylene and acrylic-acid units. The acid groups introduce polar functionality into a polyethylene-based material. EAA is used in adhesive layers and heat-seal layers in packaging. Different acid contents and formulations serve different adhesion and conversion requirements.
sections.history: Ethylene–acrylic acid copolymers developed as functional polyethylenes whose acid groups improved interaction with other materials. A documented milestone is the Dow patent by John Thomson and George Waples, published in 1970, describing their preparation and coating behavior. It shows that research was already focused on balancing polyethylene-like processability with adhesion, rather than merely establishing that the monomers could react. Coatings and laminated structures became an important direction for the class. This patent provides a dated industrial contribution; it should not be read as proof of the first EAA synthesis or of a universal commercial formulation.
sections.nomenclature: EAA abbreviates ethylene–acrylic acid copolymer. The record covers the acid copolymer itself, whose carboxylic-acid groups are part of the chain composition. Neutralizing some of those groups produces an ionomer, a distinct material whose counterions influence its behavior. Ethylene–methacrylic acid and ethylene–acrylate ester copolymers also have different chemical structures and are not aliases for EAA.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–acrylic acid copolymer (EAA) is defined by incorporation of ethylene and acrylic-acid-derived units; it is distinct from an ethylene–acrylate ester copolymer. A high-pressure free-radical patent example feeds ethylene and acrylic acid to a zoned autoclave, injects radical initiator into the reaction zones, and separately pressurizes the acid feed; the stated pressure threshold is at least 1000 bar. An alternative patent route is deliberately indirect: it first makes an ethylene/(meth)acrylate ester random copolymer with a late-transition-metal complex catalyst, then heats it to convert ester groups to carboxylic-acid groups. The latter is a source-specific post-conversion route, not evidence that all EAA is produced that way.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–acrylic acid copolymer (EAA) is a semicrystalline thermoplastic whose stiffness and tensile response depend on acrylic-acid content and distribution, molecular weight and processing history, crystallinity, and any neutralization to an ionomer. Open experimental work on synthesized EAA shows that changing acid content changes melting behavior, storage modulus, tensile strength, and elongation; a 15 mol% acrylic-acid material had lower storage modulus but greater tensile strength and ductility than its hydrogenated-polybutadiene polyethylene reference, while a 6 mol% EAA had intermediate values. Thus an EAA number must retain composition and material-form context.

A bounded research example is the 15 mol% acrylic-acid pEAA prepared by tandem hydrocarboxylation/hydrogenation: tensile strength 2.61–3.97 MPa, elongation 223–507%, and DMA storage modulus 200 MPa. The authors also report for their 6 mol% material tensile strength 2.19–2.76 MPa, elongation 101–324%, and storage modulus 378 MPa. These synthesized materials are not commercial-grade specifications. For a commercial comparison, the Primacor 1321 EAA data sheet lists molded ultimate tensile strength 20.3 MPa, tensile yield 9.8 MPa, and elongation at break 660%; its separately reported 60 μm film data differ by direction, underscoring that grade and specimen form govern the result.
sections.processing:
Ethylene–acrylic acid copolymer is melt-converted in extrusion coating and lamination, cast or blown film, coextrusion tie layers, hot-melt applications, and formulation-appropriate molding; higher-acid, high-flow grades can also be dispersed for thin coatings. Pellet flow and softening behavior vary with acid content and melt index. Dow guidance advises using the lowest practical fabrication temperature, corrosion-resistant or plated melt-contact surfaces when needed, and purging the machine with polyethylene at the end of a run. It specifically warns against shutting down with EAA left hot in the extruder because crosslinking and gel formation can impair restart.

A bounded research example compounded EAA7 and EAA15 grades with a 40 vol% nanocellulose masterbatch in a twin-screw extruder, diluted the material to 20 vol% nanocellulose, re-extruded it with different screw configurations and pass counts, and finally used a single-screw extruder to form films. The authors found that repeated extrusion reduced aggregate size but treated screw design and number of passes as experiment variables. Those composite operations do not define a neat-EAA window; likewise, the temperatures and corrosion limits in the Primacor guide depend on acid content, grade, equipment metallurgy, residence time, and coating target.
sections.structureAndMorphology: EAA combines ethylene-derived chain segments with units bearing carboxylic-acid groups. The acid groups can form hydrogen bonds with neighboring chains and interact with polar surfaces. A packaging-primer technical guide explains that higher acid content can also interfere with polyethylene-like crystal growth, influencing optical and melting behavior. In a laboratory composite, cellulose nanofibers were dispersed in an EAA matrix by melt compounding; this introduces a separate reinforcing phase rather than a new EAA chain structure. Neutralization of the acid groups produces an ion-containing material distinct from the acid copolymer.
sections.properties: Carboxylic-acid functionality supports adhesion to polar substrates used in multilayer packaging. Hydrogen bonding between acid groups can contribute to cohesive behavior, while wetting and substrate surface condition influence the bond formed at an interface. A technical primer guide describes adhesion to materials such as metal, paper and nylon for a high-acid EAA formulation. In a separate EAA/nanocellulose composite, repeated melt compounding reduced visible fiber aggregates while discoloration increased. The latter result concerns a reinforced blend, not a universal rule for neat EAA.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. EAA is used as an adhesive layer joining foil, metallized film, paper and plastic in flexible and aseptic packaging. Its carboxylic-acid groups contribute polarity and interaction with those substrates, while the ethylene segments retain a polyolefin character. Documented PRIMACOR uses also include toothpaste tubes, carpet backing, wire-cable films and nylon compounding; requirements differ among these applications.

Purchasing. SK Functional Polymer markets PRIMACOR EAA resin. Select an acid-content and flow grade for the substrate and conversion process; EAA resin and metal-neutralized ionomer products are distinct purchasing specifications. A finished multilayer package or formulated adhesive is a different product.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed EAA tonnage was established. The manufacturer identifies products and applications but does not quantify the resin volume used in those markets.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Repeated melt compounding of EAA/cellulose composites can cause discoloration while changing reinforcement dispersion. In one thesis, a longer-residence screw configuration produced more discoloration than a shorter-residence configuration; the author attributed the color in part to the limited thermal stability of cellulose. Individual EAA breakdown products were not separated from changes in the reinforcement. Separately, a historical patent exposed EAA films to ultraviolet light and reported brittleness; that physical endpoint does not identify the resulting molecules.

Timescales: The patent tested approximately 38 μm EAA films under a 1,200 W ultraviolet lamp. A sample described as containing 2% acrylic acid became brittle after 228 hours, while a sample reported as containing approximately 12.5% did so after 144 hours. The samples also differed in reported density, and the patent does not establish an environmental disappearance time. In the separate composite experiment, screw residence was approximately 7–8 or 4–5 minutes per pass for up to three passes; the two observations address different materials and exposures.

Environmental persistence: Re-extrusion, discoloration and brittleness do not establish conversion of EAA carbon to carbon dioxide or biomass. Cellulose degradation cannot be transferred to the whole composite or an unfilled EAA film, and small pieces produced by weathering remain polymer-derived material. The cited experiments do not determine a soil or aquatic mineralization time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A thesis demonstrated repeated melt compounding and shaping of a cellulose-reinforced EAA composite. Increasing the number of passes improved reinforcement dispersion and some measured mechanical properties while also increasing discoloration, illustrating competing consequences of the process for that formulation. The work is an experimental composite-processing example rather than recovery of a pure EAA feedstock.

Post-consumer EAA collection, separation from multilayer packaging and closed-loop reclamation remain unverified by this study.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: EAA is often processed as an adhesive or composite matrix, so workplace assessment needs the complete formulation and its actual extrusion or coating conditions. In the cited EAA/cellulose reprocessing study, discoloration and degradation accompany repeated processing, without a separate molecular emission inventory for EAA. HSE recommends limiting excessive thermal history and controlling fumes, including during purging and recycling of variable feedstocks.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Acid content, formulation and substrate all affect EAA adhesion and film behavior. A cellulose-reinforced EAA study found that screw design and residence time affected both dispersion and discoloration during compounding. The observed color change could involve the reinforcement and cannot be assigned entirely to the EAA matrix. Acid-form EAA and a neutralized ionomer have different structures and should be compared separately.

sections.overview: Ethylene–methacrylic acid (EMAA) is an ethylene copolymer bearing methacrylic-acid units. Its acid groups introduce polar interactions into an ethylene-based chain. EMAA is used in adhesive and heat-seal applications, including multilayer packaging. Partial neutralization creates an ionomer with properties distinct from the parent acid copolymer.
sections.history: EMAA developed within the acid-functional ethylene-copolymer industry. By 1988, a General Electric patent described DuPont NUCREL as an established commercial source and investigated its use in engineering-plastic blends. Dow-Mitsui’s corporate chronology records full Japanese NUCREL production in 1985. Coatings, films, adhesive layers, wire applications and molded articles became outlets for the unneutralized acid copolymer. Its history overlaps with ionomers, but neutralizing acid groups creates a separate material development. These records establish commercial availability and subsequent applications without assigning an unsupported first-synthesis date to the entire EMAA class.
sections.nomenclature: EMAA is the abbreviation used for ethylene–methacrylic acid copolymer. The record is limited to the acid copolymer and its stated composition range; ethylene–acrylic acid (EAA), ethylene–methyl methacrylate (EMMA), a neutralized ionomer, and a finished compound are related but not aliases for the base copolymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–methacrylic acid copolymer (EMAA) comprises ethylene and methacrylic-acid-derived units; it is not ethylene–methyl methacrylate copolymer, which retains an ester group. Japan’s medical-device-material standard defines EMAA as the product of copolymerizing ethylene and methacrylic acid. A Dow patent gives a route example for ethylene with unsaturated carboxylic acids, explicitly including methacrylic acid: continuous, steady-state free-radical polymerization in a well-stirred high-pressure autoclave. Its composition and operating windows are patent-specific; they should not be read as universal EMAA specifications. The same patent distinguishes the acid-comonomer material from other ethylene copolymer classes.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–methacrylic acid copolymer (EMAA) is a ductile thermoplastic whose tensile and flexural response depends on methacrylic-acid content, molar mass and melt-flow grade, specimen history, and whether acid groups have been ionically neutralized. Measurements on an EMAA ionomer or reinforced composite are not values for the unneutralized copolymer.

A bounded unneutralized-grade example is INEOS M21N430, an additive-free EMAA extrusion-coating resin with 1.2% methacrylic-acid content. Compression-molded plaques tested to ISO 527-2 had a tensile modulus of 238 MPa, tensile strength at yield of 9.9 MPa, tensile strength at break of 10.5 MPa, and strain at break of 394%; the same data sheet reports ISO 178 flexural modulus of 209 MPa. These values apply to that grade and plaque test configuration only.

An open EMAA study comparing sodium- and zinc-neutralized ionomers found that introducing ionic groups greatly changed tensile properties and dynamic viscoelasticity. This makes neutralization chemistry and thermal or processing history essential qualifiers when comparing EMAA-derived materials.
sections.processing:
EMAA is primarily converted by melt extrusion coating, coextrusion, extrusion lamination, and melt compounding; the available guidance here concerns extrusion rather than upstream copolymerization. For INEOS M24N430 (3.7% methacrylic acid, MFR 7.5 g/10 min), the manufacturer gives a 260–320 °C melt-temperature range for commercial extrusion-coating equipment and says to use parameters comparable to LDPE of the same MFR. It notes low coating weights at ordinary line rates, corrosion precautions, no extended melt standing, and standard LDPE purging after the run. These are grade-specific starting guidelines, not a family-wide window.

A separate patent gives a bounded extrusion/compounding example for an EMAA containing 10 wt% methacrylic acid. A two-inch extruder used an approximately 158 °C plasticating section and a 270–280 °C mixing section at about 750 psi; another example extruded the copolymer at 30 rpm with a 160–180 °C melt into 60-mil sheets. The temperatures, pressure, screw speed, and sheet geometry belong to those formulations and equipment, and should not be generalized to all EMAA grades or simple coating runs.
sections.structureAndMorphology: EMAA contains ethylene segments and carboxylic-acid-bearing methacrylic units. The acid groups can associate through hydrogen bonding. An experimental study of one EMAA and its sodium and zinc salts found ethylene crystallites in the acid and ionomer specimens. Neutralized groups can also associate into ion aggregates; their interpretation depends on the counterion and material examined.
sections.properties: The acid groups enable interactions with polar substrates and contribute to adhesion. Dow-Mitsui describes its NUCREL EMAA grades as adhesive to aluminum foil and glass, and identifies heat sealing and hot tack as useful in packaging. Its product chart lists N1560 at 15% acid and a melt-flow rate of 60 g/10 min, while N1525 has the same listed acid content and 25 g/10 min; both are supplier typical values measured or converted to 190 °C and 2.16 kg conditions. Thus acid content alone does not select the processing response. The chart values are grade-specific and should not be applied to all EMAA.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. EMAA is used for extrusion coatings, adhesive films, laminated tubes and metal-coating layers, including cable-tape adhesives. Dow-Mitsui describes adhesion to aluminum foil and glass as a consequence of polar carboxyl groups in its NUCREL acid-copolymer grades. A finished multilayer product also depends on surface preparation, grade and processing.

Purchasing. Dow-Mitsui Polychemicals offers NUCREL grades in Japan and directs users outside Japan to Dow. Specify the acid copolymer grade and application; neutralized ionomers should not be substituted solely because they share a precursor chemistry. Resin and converted adhesive film are distinct purchasing forms.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separately reported annual EMAA purchase or consumption total was established. The grade chart and application list document commercial availability without market tonnage or a standard order size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: For NUCREL 0910 acid-copolymer resin, the supplier lists possible thermal-decomposition products including carbon monoxide, organic acids, aldehydes and alcohols, with acrylic acid, methacrylic acid, formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein among the named species. This is an overheating-product list for a specified grade, not an inventory of products released during ordinary environmental exposure.

Timescales: The safety data sheet states that decomposition depends on temperature and residence time and accelerates above its 325 °C condition-to-avoid value. It does not report a general time to failure or degradation lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The supplier data do not establish a mineralization time in soil or water. Thermal decomposition and environmental biodegradation require separate evidence.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A documented recycling example for an EMAA derivative uses sodium-neutralized EMAA ionomer rather than the unneutralized acid copolymer. Barbosa and Souza melt-blended ground Surlyn PC2000 cosmetic-packaging production scrap with LDPE, using 25–75 wt% ionomer, followed by injection molding. The blends remained phase-separated and traded higher tensile/flexural properties for lower low-temperature impact strength as ionomer content increased. This demonstrates re-use of that neutralized derivative in a different product blend; it does not establish the same recipe or performance for an unneutralized EMAA film or adhesive.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For the NUCREL 0910 EMAA grade, the supplier identifies organic acids, aldehydes and alcohols among possible overheating products, including methacrylic acid, formaldehyde and acrolein. The list concerns thermal decomposition of that formulation, not an exposure level from the cool solid. Melt operations need controlled temperature and residence time and suitable fume extraction, including during stoppages and purging.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Acid content, molecular architecture and whether the copolymer has been neutralized are important to comparisons. Dow-Mitsui lists two NUCREL grades with 15% acid but different melt-flow rates, illustrating that grades with the same nominal acid fraction need not process identically. A separate ion-aggregate experiment used one acid composition and separately prepared sodium and zinc ionomers. Packaging adhesion also depends on substrate and seal conditions, and ionomer results should not be assigned unqualified to every unneutralized EMAA grade.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: High-pressure radical copolymerization incorporates methacrylic-acid units. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another.

sections.overview: Polyolefin ionomers are ion-containing materials derived from an acid-functional polyolefin, often an ethylene–acid copolymer. Some acid groups are neutralized by counterions, creating ionic associations between chains that act as reversible physical junctions. The associations can be overcome during heating and reform on cooling, allowing thermoplastic processing. Seal layers, protective surfaces and molded consumer products are examples of applications.
sections.history: Polyolefin ionomers emerged commercially through partially neutralized acid-containing ethylene copolymers. DuPont’s SURLYN reached Japanese imports through the Mitsui venture in 1964. Domestic manufacture began in autumn 1978 under the HIMILAN name, followed by expanded production. Golf-ball covers became a recognizable application, while films and heat-sealing layers supported meat, snack and beverage packaging. Cosmetic-container components and tool grips provided other molded uses. This lineage traces a commercial ionic-polymer platform, whose compositions and neutralizing ions vary; it does not assign one invention date to every ion-containing polyolefin.
sections.nomenclature: The record uses polyolefin ionomer, also called ethylene-acid ionomer, for the neutralized ethylene/acid-polymer family. It is not a synonym for the unneutralized acid copolymer or for one sodium, zinc, or other metal-salt grade; counterion and neutralization level define narrower materials.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: A common polyolefin-ionomer route begins with a random ethylene/(meth)acrylic-acid copolymer made by high-pressure free-radical copolymerization, analogous to low-density polyethylene production. A controlled fraction of the pendant carboxylic-acid groups is then converted to carboxylate salts with a cation source, commonly sodium, zinc, lithium, magnesium, or potassium. The ionic groups associate into reversible multiplets rather than permanent covalent crosslinks, so acid-comonomer content, cation identity, and degree of neutralization define the ionomer architecture. One cited patent explicitly describes high-pressure ethylene/(meth)acrylic-acid copolymerization and partial neutralization. A distinct patent scopes melt blending and neutralization of ethylene/acid copolymers, including highly neutralized variants and staged blending of parent acid copolymers. Ternary parent copolymers may also include an alkyl acrylate to tune flexibility. Sulfonated or grafted polyolefin ionomers are related route variants but are not implied by the carboxylate examples.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyolefin ionomers such as partially neutralized ethylene/(meth)acrylic-acid materials combine a semicrystalline polyethylene-rich matrix with ionic aggregates that restrict local chain motion and behave as reversible physical cross-links. Acid content, neutralization level and cation, crystalline morphology, thermal history, orientation, and any blend or reinforcement therefore govern the strength, stiffness, and large-strain response. A public patent’s typical-property table identifies sodium-neutralized Surlyn 8940 (about 15 wt% acid, about 29% neutralized) with ASTM D638 tensile strength 33.1 MPa and elongation 470%, plus ASTM D790 flexural modulus 350 MPa. These are grade-specific typical values; specimen preparation and conditioning are not given in that table. Separately, an open study of dried, extruded and injection-molded Surlyn PC2000 scrap/LDPE blends found that raising ionomer content increased tensile and flexural strength, stiffness, and strain at break but reduced notched impact strength at −70 °C, illustrating that blend phase morphology and test temperature can reverse an otherwise simple toughness comparison.
sections.processing:
Ethylene-acid polyolefin ionomers are thermoplastically converted by profile, shape, tube, pipe, sheet, wire and cable coating, blown-article, and grade-appropriate injection molding, as well as by compounding, hot compression molding, and gas- or chemically blown foam extrusion. Their reversible ionic associations raise melt strength and make viscosity unusually sensitive to temperature, moisture, neutralizing ion, acid content, and shear history. Sealed resin should be kept dry and allowed to warm above the dew point before opening; exposed material and regrind may require controlled dehumidified or vacuum drying. Screw cooling and geometry, melt-temperature measurement, die streamlining, pressure, cooling-tool or quench capacity, and winding or cutting settings should be developed around the named grade and product geometry. Marginal moisture produces elongated surface bubbles, while excessive moisture can create bubbles through the extrudate. Foams additionally require enough melt strength to resist the evolved gas and adequate cooling to prevent cell collapse; low-density flat sheet may require a circular die, slitting, and flattening rather than a flat die.

DuPont's Surlyn extrusion guide gives grade- and process-specific guidance rather than a universal ionomer window. It says newly opened resin normally need not be dried, but exposed or recycled material may be dried in a dehumidified or vacuum tray oven; it recommends at most 65 °C for most Surlyn grades or 60 °C for softer 9020 and 8020, generally for eight hours in layers no deeper than 50 mm, and warns against hot-air and hopper dryers because of moisture addition or pellet bridging. Dow separately identifies Surlyn 7940 as suitable for conventional polyethylene-type extrusion and injection equipment. In an independent experiment, Tita and co-workers dried Surlyn 8940 pellets at 60–65 °C for 12 h, fed a 5 mL twin-screw microcompounder at 170 °C and 100 rpm, mixed at 350 rpm for 3–5 min, and then hot-compression-molded neat and PZT-filled films by preheating at 175 °C for 10 min without pressure followed by 21.3 MPa for 2 min. Those conditions apply to the named sodium-neutralized grade, composite formulation, microcompounder, and 50 micrometer mold.
sections.structureAndMorphology: In ethylene–methacrylic acid ionomers, acid groups are partially neutralized by metal ions such as sodium or zinc. Ionic groups associate into aggregates alongside crystalline and less ordered polymer regions, restricting nearby chain motion. In an experiment blending sodium-neutralized EMAA scrap with LDPE, microscopy and thermal analysis showed separate phases despite their related ethylene segments. The organization depends on ion, neutralization level and formulation.
sections.properties: Ionic associations and hydrogen bonding can increase melt strength and influence sealing behavior. A supplier identifies hot tack—the strength of a seal while still hot—as useful for packaging processes, alongside clarity and toughness in particular grades. In single-cell photovoltaic modules, researchers found that three tested ionomer encapsulants had lower adhesion energy at glass or cell interfaces than the tested EVA system, both before and after aging. That interface comparison is specific to the module materials and preparation; it does not describe the mechanical strength of every ionomer article. A separate LDPE/ionomer-scrap blend also showed composition-dependent changes in strength and low-temperature impact behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polyolefin ionomers are used in sealing layers for meat, cheese and other packaged foods, cosmetic caps, golf balls and protective surfaces. Dow describes hot-tack strength and seal integrity as attributes of selected SURLYN packaging grades; hot tack matters while a newly formed seal is still warm. Researchers also tested ionomers as photovoltaic-cell encapsulants: the film is laminated between glass and cell, where optical transmission and interfacial adhesion both matter. In their single-cell experiments the ionomer interfaces lost adhesion during aging and could delaminate, illustrating a design tradeoff rather than establishing suitability of every formulation. A cosmetic cap, food-contact seal and photovoltaic assembly need different qualifications.

Purchasing. Dow offers SURLYN ionomer grades through product-selection and specialist-contact channels. It lists SURLYN 1652 for blown and cast film, extrusion coating and sheet extrusion, with a melt index of 5.2 g/10 min at 190 °C and 2.16 kg under ASTM D1238. The grade is described for sealant and packaging applications; that measurement and use list do not specify all ionomer products. A packaging sealant and a golf-ball material require different specifications, and resin is distinct from a finished package.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separately reported annual ionomer purchased or consumed tonnage was established from the checked source. The range of examples does not provide market shares or imply that every ionomer chemistry serves every use. A documented grade and melt index establish a product option, not its sales volume.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A SURLYN extrusion guide states that excessive processing time and temperature can cause degradation and yellowing. The guide uses yellowing as a practical sign that natural resin regrind may have been overheated; it does not identify the individual chemical products. A separate photovoltaic-module study tracked an interface failure rather than polymer mineralization: field-aged ionomer encapsulant delaminated from the glass in the tested miniature modules. Other colorants, stabilizers and component interfaces can change the behavior of a formulation.

Timescales: The extrusion guide describes particular UV-stabilized products used outdoors for more than 10 years. In a different study, researchers exposed three ionomer-encapsulated single-cell modules in Colorado, Florida and Arizona and observed glass-interface delamination after six months of field deployment. That interval is a particular module-adhesion endpoint, not a universal ionomer service lifetime or a mineralization measurement.

Environmental persistence: A loss of adhesion between an ionomer film and glass can make a module fail without establishing destruction of the polymer. Conversely, retained outdoor performance for a stabilized grade does not measure carbon conversion to carbon dioxide or biomass. Neither observation establishes a soil or aquatic mineralization time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The extrusion guide permits 15–20% clean, dry, undegraded regrind in its described operation. This is production-scrap reuse guidance for the named resin family, with quality and thermal history constraints rather than an unlimited recycled-content rule.

In a separate laboratory example, ground sodium-neutralized EMAA ionomer scrap from cosmetic packaging was blended with LDPE and injection molded. Increasing ionomer content increased tensile and flexural strength but reduced notched impact strength at −70 °C for those samples. The recovered ionomer became part of a different blend; this does not prove a closed-loop route for all ionomer packaging.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The Surlyn extrusion guide warns that molten ionomer adheres strongly to skin, making protection from hot melt particularly important. It also identifies high temperature/pressure, processing fumes and spilled pellets as handling concerns. The guide calls for ventilation and eye protection; the actual ionomer grade, neutralizing ion and additive package determine additional precautions.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Polyolefin ionomers differ in parent copolymer, acid content, neutralization level and counterion. In a photovoltaic study, three ionomer formulations and a separate EVA encapsulant had different baseline interface adhesion, and field aging reduced adhesion in the tested modules. The LDPE blend study used one sodium-neutralized EMAA grade, industrial scrap and specific injection-molded specimens. Neither experiment fixes the behavior of all ionomers or all packaging films; article construction, processing and exposure matter.

sections.overview: Poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) is a chlorine-containing thermoplastic made from vinyl chloride. PVC resin is compounded with additives to make materials ranging from rigid to flexible: rigid compounds are used in pipes and profiles, while plasticized compounds serve flexible tubing and cable sheathing. The polymer and the finished formulation must be distinguished when comparing performance or recycling routes. The type and amount of plasticizer, stabilizer and filler vary by use.
sections.history: PVC’s origins precede its useful commercial formulations. Henri Victor Regnault studied vinyl chloride in 1835, and Eugen Baumann reported its light-induced conversion to a white solid in 1872. Fritz Klatte’s early-twentieth-century work at Griesheim-Elektron advanced monomer and polymerization chemistry. At BFGoodrich in 1926, Waldo Semon found that combining the rigid polymer with suitable liquids produced flexible material, opening a practical path to plasticized PVC. Coated fabrics, electrical insulation and other vinyl goods followed. The distinction is between early polymer observation and later formulation and manufacturing advances; rigid and plasticized PVC products subsequently developed different applications.
sections.nomenclature: PVC identifies the vinyl-chloride polymer, while PVC-U denotes an unplasticized compound class. Plasticized PVC contains additives that make the material more flexible; it is not a different polymer backbone. A profile, pipe, tube or other converted product therefore needs its formulation state and relevant stabilizer or plasticizer information in addition to the PVC name. Chlorinated PVC is a separately modified material rather than an interchangeable name for PVC-U.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) is the vinyl-addition homopolymer of vinyl chloride monomer (VCM). Commercial suspension PVC is made by free-radical polymerization of VCM droplets dispersed in water. The German Federal Environmental Agency report identifies monomer-soluble organic peroxide initiators and protective colloids, with agitation and the colloid affecting grain size and resin rheology. It describes stopping at a chosen pressure and recovering VCM as part of resin manufacture. Emulsion and mass polymerization are separate resin-production modes. A patent route similarly identifies initiator, buffer, suspending-agent system, and temperature as process-specific controls. PVC here is the VCM homopolymer; deliberately copolymerized vinyl-chloride materials remain distinct.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PVC ranges from a relatively stiff, notch-sensitive unplasticized thermoplastic to soft, highly extensible plasticized compounds. Mechanical response is governed principally by plasticizer type and level, resin molecular mass and particle morphology, stabilizer/lubricant/filler and impact-modifier package, cellular versus solid form, fusion and cooling history, extrusion or molding orientation, thickness/notch condition, temperature, and strain rate. A PVC-U grade example is Trovidur EN: on the listed ISO test specimens it reports 55 MPa tensile stress at yield (ISO 527), 3,100 MPa tensile modulus (ISO 527-2), 78 MPa compression strength (ISO 3605), and no rupture in the specified unnotched impact test at 0 °C (ISO 179). The data sheet calls these averages on defined test specimens but does not provide rate, conditioning, exact formulation, or finished-article process history, so they apply only to that rigid compound. Independent plasticized-PVC experiments at 25 °C illustrate the formulation shift: their pure-PVC control had 153.87 ± 6.3 MPa Young modulus and 30.33 ± 0.28 MPa tensile strength, whereas plasticized blends had much lower modulus and different strength/elongation; these cast formulations are not values for commercial flexible PVC generally.
sections.processing:
Poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) is converted only as a formulated compound containing the stabilizers, lubricants, impact modifiers, pigments, fillers, and other additives needed for its route and service. This entry emphasizes rigid or unplasticized PVC; plasticized PVC is covered separately. Important rigid-PVC routes include profile, pipe, sheet, and foam extrusion; injection molding of fittings and technical parts; and calendering or thermoforming of sheet. Dry blend or pellets are fused by external heat and shear, shaped through streamlined low-inventory dies or molds, vented, and cooled rapidly and uniformly. PVC has a narrow thermal-stability margin, so melt temperature, shear heating, residence time, stagnant zones, venting, corrosion-resistant metal surfaces, start-up/shutdown purging, regrind temperature, vacuum sizing, and water cooling require close control.

GEON's rigid-vinyl profile guide explains that shallow screws or high speed increase shear heating and recommends matching compound form, screw, tooling, die inventory, vacuum sizing, and cooling to the profile. Teknor Apex gives one supplier-bound injection reference for its rigid PVC pellets: drying is normally unnecessary, though 120 °F for 2–3 h may be used; it lists a 380–395 °F melt, 80–130 °F mold cooling, slow-to-moderate injection, 50–150 psi back pressure, and at least 20% shot utilization, and warns not to leave material hot in the barrel for more than 15 min. A distinct production example is the NOvA detector profile: Talaga and co-workers gravimetrically fed a custom 15 wt% TiO2 PVC dry blend at about 390 kg/h into a counter-rotating twin-screw extruder with four heating zones and a vacuum vent; the melt reached about 188 °C and 180 bar at the die, then passed through water-cooled vacuum calibrators and partial-vacuum tanks. Those values apply only to that 16-cell, 64.1 cm-wide formulation and line.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PVC chains carry chlorine atoms along a carbon backbone. Commercial PVC is largely amorphous but may contain a limited crystalline fraction, and the polymerization method influences the particle form in which resin is supplied. External plasticizers are mixed with the resin rather than chemically bonded to every chain; they can increase chain mobility by changing intermolecular interactions. Other additives such as fillers and stabilizers make a finished compound more complex than the polymer alone.
sections.properties: Unplasticized PVC is generally rigid, while a suitable plasticizer increases chain mobility and flexibility and lowers the formulation’s glass transition. A heritage-materials review summarizes approximate glass-transition values of 80 °C for unplasticized PVC and 5 °C for a formulation containing 30 wt% DEHP; these are literature-based examples, not values for every PVC compound. This flexibility helps explain uses such as tubing and cable coverings, whereas rigid compounds serve pipes and profiles. Thermal stabilizers are used because heating can initiate dehydrochlorination. Electrical and chemical performance depend on the complete compound and exposure.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PVC is used in pipes, fittings, windows, flooring and roofing; cable insulation; medical bags and tubing; and consumer articles. Vynova identifies rigid construction products and flexible medical and cable applications, illustrating how formulation tailors the same resin family to different uses. A flexible tube and a rigid window profile require different compound and product specifications.

Purchasing. Buy a specified PVC resin or formulated compound through a resin producer or compounder. Vynova offers suspension-resin grades; formulation and end-product qualification determine suitability for rigid construction or flexible products. A finished medical device or window profile is a separate purchase.

Scale and evidence limits. Plastics Europe’s preliminary 2023 global fossil-based PVC production is approximately 53 million tonnes. This production estimate is not purchased tonnage and does not split rigid from plasticized PVC.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PVC can eliminate hydrogen chloride during heating and develop conjugated polyene sequences; oxidation can also produce carbonyl- and hydroxyl-containing material. Discoloration can accompany polyene formation, while loss or migration of a plasticizer is a separate change that can leave a flexible article more brittle. Stabilizers influence how the compound responds. A product list from thermal treatment does not describe every UV or environmental exposure.

Timescales: A plastics-pipe industry report describes standard PVC pipe compounds incorporating UV screening, usually titanium dioxide, as suitable for at least one year of outdoor storage. It distinguishes that storage guidance from the formulation needed for long-term exposed service. The period is not a measurement of environmental disappearance and does not apply automatically to a different PVC film or compound.

Environmental persistence: Discoloration, embrittlement and fragmentation leave polymer-derived material and are distinct from complete conversion of polymer carbon to carbon dioxide and biomass. The pipe-storage guidance describes useful performance, not biodegradation. The sources do not supply one transferable soil or aquatic disappearance time for PVC articles.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Mechanical recycling can sort, grind and reprocess suitable PVC waste while retaining polymer material. A review notes that relatively clean feedstocks are needed and that different sources, including construction and medical products, bring different collection and formulation constraints. Heat history and additives affect whether the recycled compound can meet a new product specification.

Solvent-based recycling also aims to retain polymer while separating components; chemical conversion instead changes the polymer into smaller compounds and must address its chlorine content. These routes have different feedstock needs and stages of development. Energy recovery is a separate end-of-life route and does not recover PVC material.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PVC processing must control overheating and excessive residence time because the backbone can eliminate hydrogen chloride. HSE treats PVC as heat-sensitive and emphasizes temperature control, effective ventilation and defined purging/shutdown procedures. Rigid and flexible compounds have different additive packages; an assessment of vinyl chloride monomer or one plasticizer cannot stand in for the complete finished PVC formulation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PVC is a formulation platform rather than one fixed material. Plasticizer type and amount, stabilizers, fillers and processing history affect the finished article. Many external plasticizers are not chemically bonded to the chain and can migrate or leach into contacting materials. Loss of plasticizer can reduce flexibility and contribute to embrittlement or cracking, but the rate depends on the formulation and contact conditions. Measurements on a rigid profile cannot be transferred directly to a flexible formulation.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical chain growth converts vinyl chloride to PVC. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another.

The cited initiator, feed composition and reaction medium determine the particular preparation; transfer, grafting and termination control architecture alongside propagation.

steps.body: Polymerize with controlled agitation, stop at the selected endpoint, and recover residual vinyl chloride.

sections.overview: Chlorinated poly(vinyl chloride) (CPVC) is made by further chlorination of a pre-existing PVC resin. Additional chlorine alters the chain’s local structure and raises its glass transition relative to the starting PVC, supporting use in hot-water and industrial fluid-handling systems. CPVC resin is compounded with stabilizers and other additives before conversion into a pipe, fitting or other article; the finished formulation and service conditions determine its performance.
sections.history: CPVC developed as a way to extend the service range of PVC, particularly in piping. Lubrizol traces its BFGoodrich predecessor’s CPVC development to 1959 and the subsequent commercialization of FlowGuard plumbing systems. Pipe and fittings for hot- and cold-water supply became the defining early market. Continued work involved compound formulation, joining methods and the practical manufacture of complete systems. A later expansion milestone was the 2020 partnership announced with Grasim for resin production in India. These dates describe one major industrial lineage; the original resin, later branded compounds and installed piping systems are separate historical subjects.
sections.nomenclature: CPVC and PVC-C are common abbreviations for chlorinated poly(vinyl chloride). The term denotes a PVC resin that has undergone additional chlorination, not an unmodified PVC or a vinyl chloride copolymer. Chlorine fraction, stabilizers and other additives identify a particular resin or compound more closely than the abbreviation. A formulated pipe, fitting or sheet must also meet its own product and service specifications.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Chlorinated poly(vinyl chloride) (CPVC) is made by post-chlorinating PVC resin; it is not produced by polymerizing vinyl chloride with chlorine present. One aqueous photo-slurry route begins with suspension-polymerized vinyl chloride resin, using poly(vinyl alcohol) as a suspending agent and a chain-transfer agent during the PVC stage. Chlorine gas is then introduced to the aqueous PVC suspension while ultraviolet irradiation initiates chlorination; the cited Kaneka route specifies a mercury lamp and a 40–90 °C reaction range. Particle size and porosity of the parent PVC are treated as route controls in that source. A distinct patented two-stage aqueous route uses an organic peroxide catalyst rather than actinic radiation, illustrating that chlorination initiation and staging are process-specific rather than intrinsic to every CPVC grade. Washing, dewatering, and drying of the resulting slurry are manufacture finishing steps, not article conversion.
sections.mechanicalProperties: CPVC is normally used as a rigid, amorphous thermoplastic, but its mechanical response is strongly dependent on temperature, loading rate, formulation, and the material's fabrication history. Post-chlorination raises the glass-transition range relative to unmodified PVC, while stabilizers, lubricants, impact modifiers, residual orientation, weld lines, notches, and aging can change stiffness, yielding, impact resistance, and fracture mode. A study of specimens machined from commercial Schedule 80 CPVC pipe found brittle fracture below about 25 °C and increasingly ductile behavior above that temperature. For those flattened pipe-wall specimens, tested in tension after the reported thermal preparation, yield strength at 5 mm/min decreased from 59.18 MPa at -20 °C to 18.50 MPa at 90 °C; at room temperature it increased from approximately 46 to 60 MPa as crosshead speed increased from 5 to 500 mm/min. The same study found elastic modulus to decrease with increasing temperature and increase with loading rate. These values describe that pipe product and specimen-preparation protocol, not a family-wide CPVC range. As a separate named-compound example, the Prince FlowGuard Plus CPVC technical manual reports at 23 °C a tensile strength of 55 MPa, tensile modulus of 2.50 GPa, and notched Izod impact strength of 80 J/m for its ASTM D1784 cell-classification 23448 compound. Those manufacturer values are representative product data; the table does not fully report conditioning, molding direction, or specimen preparation, so they should not be transferred to other CPVC grades. Moisture is generally less dominant than temperature and time scale for rigid CPVC, but environmental exposure, stress concentrators, installation damage, and sustained pressure can still govern long-term creep and brittle failure in pipe service.
sections.processing: CPVC (PVC-C) can be converted by extrusion and injection molding; a NASA materials reference additionally lists thermoforming, blow molding, foam molding, slush molding, and calendering. Thermal and shear history require control. A public PVC-C extrusion guide describes a vacuum twin-screw extruder with a low-shear four-stage PVC screw and explicitly notes greater heat and shear sensitivity than PVC-U. Its general guide gives 180–195 °C cylinder and melt temperatures, 25–30 L/D, a 1.7:1 compression ratio, no predrying, and output about half that of PVC-U. These are website-provided starting points for the specified extrusion setup, not a universal CPVC processing window; the NASA reference establishes the broader method coverage without setpoints.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Post-chlorination replaces some hydrogen atoms on the PVC backbone with chlorine, creating a distribution of local structures rather than a single uniformly substituted sequence. In one CPVC sample containing 63 wt% chlorine, solid-state carbon NMR distinguished methylene and chlorine-bearing backbone-carbon environments. The authors reported a higher proportion of chlorine-bearing carbon environments in that specimen than in their PVC comparison. Chlorine placement and the measured composition of that sample do not specify a universal sequence for every CPVC grade.
sections.properties: CPVC generally has a higher glass transition than its parent PVC, which helps formulated products retain rigidity at higher temperatures. Its chemical resistance supports pipe and fluid-handling uses, but compatibility and pressure rating depend on the specific compound, chemical and temperature. In tensile tests on specimens cut from a particular CPVC pipe, yield strength decreased as temperature increased and rose with increasing crosshead speed. Those trends describe the tested product and conditions.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Formulated CPVC is used in hot- and cold-water plumbing and industrial piping, ducting, tanks, sheets and linings. For example, Lubrizol identifies Corzan CPVC components for chemical processing and wastewater treatment, where fluid-contact and corrosion resistance are relevant. Its published compatibility examples are product- and service-specific, so the exact chemical, concentration, temperature and pressure must be checked for a proposed system.

Purchasing. Resin and compound suppliers sell materials for conversion, while pipe and fitting suppliers provide finished systems. Specify the compound or qualified finished component for the intended chemical service and joining method: a resin listing alone does not establish a pipe system’s rating.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual CPVC purchased or consumed tonnage was established from the cited sources. The manufacturer’s industrial-use examples do not quantify installations or worldwide demand.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Heating CPVC can eliminate hydrogen chloride and produce increasingly aromatic, carbon-rich material. In a study of pure CPVC with 63 wt% chlorine, the authors observed rapid mass loss attributed to dehydrochlorination, followed by aromatization and polycondensation. These observations concern the resin used to make the experimental carbon-fiber precursor. Stabilizers and heating atmosphere influence how a finished CPVC product responds.

Timescales: The cited thermogravimetric experiment reports decomposition beginning near 270 °C, with rapid changes through 400 °C. The researchers separately carbonized solution-spun precursor fibers at 1000 °C for five minutes under nitrogen and reported a 26.2 wt% carbonization yield. These controlled heating conditions are neither normal pipe operation nor a natural-environment lifetime.

Environmental persistence: A carbon-rich residue formed during high-temperature treatment does not establish biodegradation or environmental mineralization. The experiment used heat in a controlled atmosphere rather than soil or water exposure. No transferable ambient disappearance time follows from this result.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A laboratory study converted solution-spun fibers made from pure CPVC containing 63 wt% chlorine into carbon fibers. Under nitrogen, the researchers heated the fibers to 1000 °C and held them for five minutes, reporting a carbonization yield of 26.2 wt% from the spun precursor. This is a precursor-conversion experiment rather than demonstrated recovery of contaminated CPVC products or commercial closed-loop recycling. Chlorine-containing degradation products and feedstock formulation would need consideration in any waste-conversion process.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Heating CPVC can release hydrogen chloride and form an increasingly carbon-rich residue, as demonstrated for the 63 wt% chlorine material in the cited thermal study. This is a reason to control overheating and fumes during thermal operations; it is not an ambient emission rate. HSE provides the general plastics guidance on ventilation, temperature/residence-time control and trained shutdown procedures, while CPVC-specific settings must come from the compound supplier.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Chlorine content and distribution, additives and processing influence CPVC behavior. Stabilizers and heat and shear history matter because the resin can degrade during conversion; impact modifiers and fabrication history also affect mechanical performance. Published pipe-manual values describe a particular product, not every CPVC resin or fitting. Comparisons should retain the compound, specimen geometry, temperature and loading conditions.

sections.overview: Poly(vinylidene chloride) (PVDC) is the polymer of vinylidene chloride. Its homopolymer and vinylidene-chloride-rich copolymers are distinguished in commercial barrier materials. The latter have been used as films or coatings on other substrates to reduce gas and vapor transmission. Comonomer content and article processing affect their properties.
sections.history: PVDC’s industrial history is closely associated with Ralph Wiley’s 1933 discovery at Dow Chemical and the subsequent Saran resin business. Early products included insect screens, chemical-plant pipes and fishing line; the Powerhouse museum holds Saran fishing equipment made in 1944. Dow’s national introduction of household Saran Wrap in 1953 made barrier packaging a familiar consumer application. The history therefore extends from industrial and wartime products to food storage and protective packaging. Saran is a trade name whose formulations can change, so a later branded film should not be identified as PVDC solely from its name.
sections.nomenclature: PVDC names the vinylidene-chloride polymer and should be distinguished from a specified VDC copolymer grade. A latex, coating, or oriented barrier film is an article or formulation based on PVDC or a VDC-rich copolymer, not an interchangeable name for the unqualified homopolymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(vinylidene chloride) (PVDC) is the free-radical addition homopolymer of vinylidene chloride (VDC). A documented suspension route charges demineralized water, dimyristyl peroxydicarbonate initiator, and methyl hydroxypropyl cellulose suspending agent to a stirred autoclave, then adds VDC, polymerizes at controlled temperature, strips residual monomer, and washes, filters, and dries the recovered powder. A distinct aqueous-emulsion example uses a sulfosuccinate emulsifier with potassium persulfate and sodium bisulfite initiation. Those route examples establish homopolymer manufacture; adding vinyl chloride, acrylate, or another comonomer instead produces a compositionally distinct VDC copolymer, even where it is marketed within the broader PVDC-resin family.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PVDC materials are usually semicrystalline, vinylidene-chloride-rich copolymers rather than readily fabricated homopolymer. They can form tough films and filaments, but their strength and ductility are highly formulation- and orientation-dependent; drawing can raise tensile strength along the oriented directions, while low temperature, notches, or an unsuitable formulation can favor brittle failure. The identity and fraction of comonomer—commonly vinyl chloride, acrylonitrile, or an alkyl acrylate—alter chain regularity, crystallization, melting behavior, and flexibility. Molar mass, crystalline fraction and crystal texture, plasticizer and stabilizer level, rubber or other modifier content, layer support in a coating or coextrusion, casting or extrusion history, quench and draw ratio, film thickness, test direction, temperature, strain rate, aging, and thermal degradation are therefore consequential. Crosslinking can increase modulus and strength while reducing extensibility, and reported coating or laminate properties must not be assigned to the PVDC layer alone.

One bounded example is an approximately 0.15 mm THF-solvent-cast PVDC copolymer film described in Korean patent KR20160005576A. Unirradiated 100 mm × 5 mm strips, tested with a 50 mm grip separation, 1 kN load cell, and 50 mm/min crosshead speed, gave 8.65 ± 0.15 MPa tensile strength, 67 ± 4 MPa initial modulus, and 469 ± 14% elongation. Electron-beam exposure increased gel fraction and shifted the response: the 8 MeV condition gave 21.77 ± 1.68 MPa, 396 ± 16 MPa, and 264 ± 7%, respectively. The patent does not identify comonomer chemistry or fraction, molecular mass, specimen conditioning, or test temperature, so even the unirradiated result is specific to that cast film and cannot serve as a family range. A separate EPA survey independently documents the wide composition- and orientation-dependent response of commercial VDC-rich copolymers.
sections.processing:
Commercial poly(vinylidene chloride) (PVDC) barrier articles are commonly based on stabilized VDC copolymers rather than unmodified homopolymer. Important routes include monolayer cast or double-bubble blown film, coextruded barrier layers, extrusion coating, and aqueous-latex or solvent coating followed by drying and crystallization. Melt-film lines compound the selected copolymer with its approved plasticizer, lubricant, and stabilizer package, use streamlined low-hold-up screws and dies, quench the primary tube, warm and biaxially orient it, then heat-set and cool it. Latex is transferred with low shear, filtered, laid down by air knife, reverse gravure, or Mayer bar, progressively dried, aged if required, and wound under controlled tension. The narrow interval between adequate fusion and dehydrochlorination makes melt temperature, residence time, metal compatibility, dead spots, purge practice, and rapid cooling especially important; latex shear, foam, skinning, substrate treatment, airflow, humidity, coat weight, crystallization, curling, and blocking are separate controls.

Asahi Kasei's PVDC-latex guidance recommends a lower initial dryer temperature followed by a rise, giving 100 °C to 110–120 °C as an example, and describes 40 °C for 48 h as an example post-coating age. It also calls for low-impact transfer, an approximately 100 µm filter, sealed 3–30 °C storage, and avoidance of iron, aluminum, and copper contact that can promote coagulation. These are supplier examples for its latex products, not a family-wide schedule. A distinct SK Geo Centric patent reports double-bubble trials using named PVDC-VC 2051 and PVDC-MA 32088.00 copolymers. The blends were run in a 3.5 inch, L/D 22.4 single-screw extruder at 120 kg/h and 40 rpm with set values of 175-180-156-153-150 °C, quenched at 10 °C, warmed at 25 °C, stretched at a 3.2 diameter ratio to 34 cm-wide, 1 mil film, and heat-set at 120 °C for 30 min. Those settings apply only to the disclosed compositions and double-bubble equipment.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PVDC homopolymer has a chain derived from vinylidene chloride units. Homopolymer and vinylidene-chloride-rich copolymers can crystallize, but comonomer chemistry and content alter how readily this happens. A historical EPA report notes that homopolymer can crystallize within minutes at 25 °C, whereas some quenched copolymers remain amorphous for much longer. Orientation and processing affect the structure of the resulting coating or film.
sections.properties: Vinylidene-chloride-rich copolymers have been used as barriers to oxygen and water vapor in packaging; a thin coating can improve the barrier of a supporting film or paper. In a historical EPA comparison of commercial films, a 1-mil Saran film at room temperature transmitted about 1 cc of oxygen per 100 square inches per day, versus 400 cc for the polyethylene film in the same table. The report does not identify the individual grades and test conditions sufficiently to make those values a modern product specification. Crystallinity, comonomer chemistry, film thickness and multilayer construction all affect the barrier obtained.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PVDC-based barrier materials are used in pharmaceutical blister packaging and food packaging, with additional industrial coatings. Asahi Kasei distinguishes aqueous Saran latex coatings from resin dissolved in solvent to coat substrates. A coating on a base film supplies resistance to oxygen and water vapor, helping protect moisture- or oxygen-sensitive pharmaceuticals and foods. The substrate and coating work together: a thin PVDC-based layer is not the same product as a free-standing homopolymer film. The supplier lists sausage and confectionery packaging as food examples.

Purchasing. Purchase the required latex dispersion, powder resin or finished barrier film. Asahi Kasei provides quotation, sample and information-request channels; verify comonomer and formulation scope because commercial PVDC-based products need not be pure homopolymer.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was established. The manufacturer documents resin and latex supply forms without quantifying the mass sold or attributing finished-package weight to PVDC.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Heating unstabilized vinylidene-chloride polymer releases hydrogen chloride and forms a discolored, unsaturated chlorinated residue. The historical NBS study includes materials with less than 10% vinyl chloride comonomer; its results are not an inventory of ambient-weathering products.

Timescales: At 176.4 °C under flowing nitrogen, the NBS experiment follows HCl evolution over 1–24 h, with an initial induction period and a changing release rate. The reported HCl evolved was 1.8% of the total theoretical amount after 1 hour, 27.2% after 6 hours and 45.0% after 24 hours. At 130 °C, a separate comparison found a faster HCl-evolution rate but slower discoloration for the tested vinylidene-chloride polymer than for the tested PVC. These are severe thermal conditions, not an outdoor lifetime or a result for every stabilized package.

Environmental persistence: Neither the thermal study nor the recycling announcement measures carbon mineralization in soil or water. Discoloration, HCl release and loss of barrier function are different endpoints from complete environmental disappearance.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Solvay reported a proof of concept using post-industrial, biaxially oriented Ixan PVDC food-packaging film. The company describes potential reintegration and blending with virgin material while retaining barrier performance. This is evidence for the reported feed and a development-stage process, not a complete public process specification.

The announcement does not demonstrate routine post-consumer collection or separation of PVDC from every multilayer package. Feed sorting, coating construction and quality requirements remain material-specific.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PVDC is thermally sensitive: the NBS vinylidene-chloride polymer experiments measured hydrogen chloride evolution during prolonged heating. That evidence concerns severe thermal exposure, while practical coating and film operations require the actual copolymer, stabilizer and latex formulation to be considered. HSE plastics guidance supports preventing excessive temperature/residence time and controlling fumes during processing and cleanup.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PVDC homopolymer is not interchangeable with every commercial vinylidene-chloride-rich copolymer. Comonomer chemistry and content change crystallization and permeability, while formulation balances barrier and film-handling requirements. The historical EPA report also describes laminates combining a PVDC-based barrier layer with polyethylene skins, which contribute flexibility and heat sealing; the multilayer construction must be assessed as a whole. Its film comparisons describe the materials and conditions reported and should not be treated as universal modern grade values.

sections.overview: Poly(vinyl acetate) (PVAc) is a thermoplastic polymer made from vinyl acetate. It is available as a solid resin or as particles dispersed in water and is used in adhesives, paints, and coatings. Related vinyl acetate copolymers are distinct materials whose composition changes their behavior. A commercial adhesive is a formulation: protective colloids, plasticizers, and other ingredients can be present alongside the polymer.
sections.history: Poly(vinyl acetate) became an industrial resin during the early expansion of vinyl chemistry. Wacker traces its PVAc research lineage to Willy O. Herrmann’s work in 1924 and its first Burghausen production plant to 1930. The VINNAPAS product lineage subsequently developed into adhesives and binders, including materials for construction. This history reflects a change from simply making a vinyl resin to controlling how it could be delivered and used in formulations. Dispersion and powder technologies helped manufacturers serve very different markets. Wacker’s milestone dates one major production lineage, rather than establishing the first laboratory preparation of PVAc by any researcher.
sections.nomenclature: PVAc names the vinyl-acetate polymer and is not interchangeable with its hydrolysis product poly(vinyl alcohol). A PVAc-copolymer emulsion, crosslinkable adhesive, or filled formulation is a narrower material system and should retain its copolymer or formulation description.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(vinyl acetate) (PVAc) is produced by free-radical addition polymerization of vinyl acetate. It can be made in bulk or solution, but aqueous emulsion polymerization is a major route: vinyl acetate is dispersed in water with a protective colloid or emulsifier and polymerized with a radical initiator. A classic patent describes stable PVAc latex formation from vinyl acetate in aqueous emulsion. A separate route uses fully hydrolyzed poly(vinyl alcohol) or soluble starch as the dispersing agent and an activated-peroxide initiator system, with staged monomer addition used to control the dispersion. Initiator type, protective colloid, chain-transfer conditions, and monomer-feed profile affect particle size and molar mass; these route-specific choices do not change the identity of the vinyl-acetate homopolymer. Subsequent hydrolysis or alcoholysis converts PVAc toward poly(vinyl alcohol) and is not an alternate PVAc polymerization route.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PVAc mechanical performance is normally measured as a dried adhesive film or a bonded joint, not as a single bulk-resin constant. Copolymer content, protective colloid and plasticizer, crosslinking or grafting, film thickness and drying history, relative humidity, temperature relative to the adhesive glass transition, substrate, bondline geometry, and loading mode all control the observed tensile, shear, peel, or creep response. In a public study of commercial PVAc-copolymer emulsion adhesive films, both crosslinkable and uncrosslinkable free films lost tensile strength and modulus after equilibration above 40% relative humidity; shelf-life had much less effect than humidity over the examined periods. A separate public study of PVAc-emulsion wood joints from −130 to 140 °C found that bond and film strength were strongly temperature dependent, peaked near the PVAc glass-transition region, and could be increased by higher grafting. These sources concern adhesive formulations and free films/joints, not unmodified PVAc resin. A focused search in this pass found no anonymous full-text, condition-complete numerical endpoint for a neat PVAc free film, so no family value is stated.
sections.processing:
Poly(vinyl acetate) (PVAc) is commonly supplied and converted as an aqueous emulsion or organic solution rather than as a pellet molding resin. Important article-forming operations are adhesive coating and bead application, paper or textile coating, binder impregnation, and solution or dispersion casting followed by water or solvent evaporation. Emulsion adhesives are compounded by mixing plasticizer, tackifier, thickener, filler, preservative, wetting agent, or defoamer into the base latex; addition order, moderate shear, foam control, viscosity, substrate wetting, coat weight, open time, drying airflow, humidity, and pressure during bond assembly control the resulting film or joint. Because drying dispersions lose substantial volume, shrinkage and premature skinning or hole formation must be managed.

A SpecialChem starting-point formulation illustrates a practical bookbinding compound rather than a universal PVAc recipe: it combines 90 parts PVAc emulsion with 6 parts dibutyl phthalate and 4 parts toluenesulfonamide-formaldehyde resin, directs the processor to mix liquid ingredients before slowly adding any filler, and notes low-solids application and foaming constraints. Cowan and co-workers provide a distinct bounded film-forming experiment with a commercial PVAc-copolymer emulsion. They cleaned coated-glass plates, applied a release agent, heated the plates at 105 °C for 15 min to remove volatiles, doctor-bladed the adhesive with a 0.072 mm blade setting, and held the coated plates at 72% relative humidity for 24 h. Lower humidity dried their film too rapidly and produced holes, especially with catalyst. The formulation and humidity schedule apply only to the named experimental emulsion system.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The PVAc chain has acetate-containing side groups attached to a carbon backbone. Vinyl acetate may be polymerized into the homopolymer or combined with other monomers to make copolymers, which are not identical to this record's homopolymer. In an aqueous dispersion, the resin occurs as polymer particles stabilized in water. As water evaporates, the particles coalesce to form the adhesive film.
sections.properties: PVAc resins can form clear films and dissolve in suitable organic solvents. Some resins have a glass transition near room temperature, so temperature affects how readily the material flows under load. The dry resin can creep when stressed for a prolonged period. In adhesive dispersions, added plasticizer can lower the temperature needed for particles to coalesce into a continuous film, but it can also increase creep under load. This is a formulation tradeoff: film formation and long-term joint performance need separate assessment. Water-based dispersions can carry higher molecular weight resin at relatively high solids content while retaining a useful application viscosity.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PVAc homopolymer dispersions are used in wood and paper adhesives, bookbinding and textile sizing. In a waterborne bookbinding formulation, the dispersion is combined with other ingredients and applied to paper; evaporation and film formation contribute to the bond. Solid PVAc is also used in chewing-gum base, a different product stream from the vinyl-acetate–ethylene dispersions often sold alongside it.

Purchasing. Purchase an aqueous homopolymer dispersion for adhesive formulation or a specified solid-resin grade for the intended use. TAFAUL identifies adhesive-emulsion grades, while Wacker documents industrial solid-PVAc manufacture; resin and formulated glue have different specifications.

Scale and evidence limits. Wacker’s publicly available China brochure lists 20,000 tonnes per year of PVAc-solid-resin capacity at Nanjing. This undated brochure, checked in 2026, establishes a plant-capacity order of magnitude only; it is not global consumption or adhesive-emulsion tonnage.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Thermal deacetylation of PVAc releases acetic acid and leaves unsaturated polymer; higher-temperature pyrolysis of the tested resin also produced small gases and aromatic compounds. A separate conservation survey reports acetic acid emissions from some dry PVAc adhesive films, with formulation and initial acidity affecting emissions. This emission behavior is not equivalent to the products of analytical pyrolysis.

Timescales: For the Mowilith 50 resin, a 12-second analytical pyrolysis at 400 °C produced a dominant acetic-acid signal. Conservation studies reviewed by the Society for the Preservation of Natural History Collections found that emissions from tested adhesive films were highest in the first three months and decreased almost to zero after two years. The products and conditions differ, so neither time is a general PVAc lifetime.

Environmental persistence: These thermal and adhesive-aging observations do not measure ambient mineralization. No transferable soil or aquatic disappearance time is established.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Manufacturing-stage reclamation is documented for PVAc process streams. A patent describes a vented-extruder process that removes vinyl acetate and methanol from polymerization paste for return to production while retaining PVAc. In one reported devolatilization example with methanol but no vinyl acetate monomer, a 38 wt% PVAc solution yielded an extrudate containing 99.0% PVAc; this is composition, not a polymer recovery yield.

This conserves volatiles during production and does not establish depolymerization of used adhesive or recovery of clean resin from bonded paper, wood or paint. Those end-of-life separation routes remain an evidence gap.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PVAc heating can release acetic acid; analytical pyrolysis of the Mowilith 50 paint binder also produced further fragments at higher temperatures. Those measurements concern heated binder rather than emissions from every waterborne adhesive. For drying, hot processing or thermal removal, assess the full binder formulation and use the temperature control and fume-management measures described in HSE plastics guidance.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Molecular weight, whether the material is a homopolymer or a copolymer, and its additives all influence the properties of a product. Plasticizers can make a homopolymer dispersion more flexible, while fillers, thickeners, and other ingredients alter its formulation. Resistance to moisture and weather is limited for the PVAc resins discussed in a conservation compendium. An adhesive's behavior should therefore be assessed for the specific product, substrate, and service environment rather than inferred from PVAc alone.
