sections.overview: Poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) is a hydroxyl-bearing polymer usually made by hydrolysis or alcoholysis of poly(vinyl acetate). Commercial materials vary in molecular weight and in the proportion of acetate groups remaining after this conversion. PVA can form films and fibers and is used in coatings, membranes, and other water-based formulations. Its response to water is central to the selection of a suitable grade.
sections.history: PVA’s early history reaches back to 1924, followed by extensive development in Japan. Ichiro Sakurada’s research group produced a Japanese synthetic-fiber precursor in 1939, and Kuraray commercialized KURALON PVA-based fiber in 1950. Producing resin for those fibers created the technical foundation for a broader PVA business. Kuraray began merchant PVA resin production in 1958, initially targeting textile sizing and paper treatment; resin sales eventually outgrew the company’s fiber consumption. The story therefore joins polymer chemistry, fiber processing and later water-soluble binder applications, with distinct dates for discovery and industrial commercialization.
sections.nomenclature: PVA, PVOH, and PVAL are abbreviations for poly(vinyl alcohol) in this record. The name distinguishes the hydrolyzed polymer from PVAc; partially hydrolyzed grades and chemically crosslinked films are specified PVA materials rather than alternate names for the base polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) is normally made indirectly because vinyl alcohol is not isolated as a stable monomer for conventional chain polymerization. Vinyl acetate is first free-radically polymerized to poly(vinyl acetate) (PVAc); the acetate groups are then converted to hydroxyl groups by hydrolysis or, commonly, methanolysis/alcoholysis with an alkaline catalyst such as sodium hydroxide or sodium methoxide. The extent of deacetylation is an architecture/composition control: partially hydrolyzed grades retain vinyl-acetate units, whereas near-complete conversion gives highly hydrolyzed PVA. One cited patent lays out the industrial sequence from vinyl-acetate solution polymerization through methanolic alkaline hydrolysis and purification. A distinct patent describes alcoholysis of a PVAc solution in methanol using acid or alkaline catalysts and identifies mixing and catalyst concentration as controls. These examples concern PVA formation and purification; film casting or dissolution conditions belong to processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PVA commonly forms hydrogen-bonded films, fibers, and hydrogels whose strength and ductility depend strongly on degree of hydrolysis and polymerization, crystallinity, water content and humidity, plasticizer or salt, cross-link density, filler compatibility, drying/annealing, and molecular orientation. Absorbed water and low-molecular additives can plasticize PVA, while drawing and crystalline or chemical network formation can raise stiffness; consequently, a dry cast-film value cannot represent a swollen gel or a drawn fiber. In one solvent-cast, desiccator-stored PVA film study, unmodified 100–130 µm films made from a 10 wt% PVA solution had a Young modulus of 670 ± 50 MPa, tensile strength of 39 ± 4 MPa, and elongation at break of 189 ± 17%. Test specimen geometry, tensile rate, and test humidity/temperature were not reported, so these values are bounded to that dry cast-film preparation. The same work showed that glutaric-acid feed level changed modulus, strength, elongation, swelling, and solubility; independent PVA/cell-plastic film data likewise show that added biological particulate phase can retain substantial modulus but sharply reduce tensile strength and strain at break through aggregate failure.
sections.processing:
Conventional poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA or PVOH) is most often converted from water by solution coating, casting, wet spinning, paper or textile sizing, and binder impregnation. Polymer should be dispersed into cold water under agitation before heating for dissolution; hydrolysis level, molecular mass, concentration, water temperature, mixing geometry, foam and skin formation, filtration, deaeration, substrate wetting, drying rate, humidity, and any orientation step control the article. Ordinary highly hydrolyzed PVA has little margin between melting and degradation, but purpose-designed plasticized or modified PVOH compounds can be thermoplastically injection molded, blow molded, extruded into film or filament, and fused-filament fabricated. Numerical settings are therefore grade-specific, and moisture can be either a required solution medium or an unwanted plasticizer in melt processing.

Kuraray's MOWIFLEX guidance supplies one bounded FFF example for its water-soluble, PVOH-based support filament. It recommends sealed moisture-protected storage, optional drying near 50 °C, a 190–215 °C nozzle, 25–70 °C bed, 20–50 mm/s printing speed, 10–20 mm/s interface speed, and an idle nozzle below 170 °C; it says not to exceed 225 °C. These are MOWIFLEX settings, not general PVA limits. For a distinct solution-coating example, Iritani and co-workers coated a highly hydrolyzed PVA solution onto polyimide film, held it at room temperature for three days, and then oven-dried it at 100 °C for 4 h. Their glutaraldehyde-crosslinked and Chlorella-filled variants used the same coating and drying sequence after room-temperature mixing. The crosslink chemistry belongs in Synthesis, while the casting substrate and drying schedule are Processing; the authors also tested immediately after drying to limit humidity effects.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PVA has hydroxyl groups along its carbon backbone, which can form hydrogen bonds between and within chains. The polymer can contain both crystalline and less ordered regions. Partially hydrolyzed material retains acetate groups, which affect chain packing and generally reduce crystallinity compared with highly hydrolyzed material. Molecular weight and processing history also influence how the chains organize in a film or fiber.
sections.properties: PVA is hydrophilic and interacts strongly with water, but dissolution depends on grade and temperature. Extensive hydrogen bonding in highly hydrolyzed material can make it more difficult to dissolve than some partially hydrolyzed grades; Kuraray notes that warmer water speeds dissolution of its resins. In Kuraray’s 30-minute stirred-water measurements, solubility of its approximately 98 mol% hydrolyzed resins decreased substantially as degree of polymerization increased, whereas the 88 mol% series showed much less dependence. These are comparisons for the tested grades and conditions, not a universal solubility rule. PVA can form films and membranes, where crosslinking can limit swelling and dissolution while changing transport. Results depend on the degree of hydrolysis, molecular weight and membrane preparation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PVOH supplies textile sizing, paper coatings, adhesives, ceramic binders and food-packaging formulations; electronics uses include LCD polarizing films. It also serves in water-soluble detergent films: one study describes films formulated from PVOH resins with other ingredients, including plasticizers. Dissolution allows the film formulation to disperse in wash water, but it does not by itself establish biodegradation. Kuraray also identifies a resin that can dissolve in continuous starch-cooking equipment for paper coatings, illustrating how dissolution behavior matters for a particular process. Membrane applications require additional control of swelling and transport.

Purchasing. Industrial users obtain application-specific PVOH resins through suppliers such as Kuraray, specifying viscosity, degree of hydrolysis and purity. Thermoplastically processable compounds and finished films are distinct purchasing forms.

Scale and evidence limits. Kuraray reported 94,000 tonnes/year capacity at Höchst, Germany, in 2021: order 10^5 tonnes/year at one site. This is historical nameplate capacity, not European consumption or a customer order size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Adapted bacteria can mineralize dissolved PVA to carbon dioxide. Disappearance measured by a polymer assay and CO2 evolution measure different endpoints; dissolution in water alone establishes neither complete degradation nor mineralization.

Timescales: After 20 days at 30 °C in dark mineral-medium cultures containing 0.1% PVA at pH 7, isolates identified as Bacillus subtilis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa gave reported CO2-based mineralization of 45.4% and 28.9%, respectively. These are partial endpoints under the study’s conditions. A separate assay used a different medium composition, so its polymer-disappearance values should not be read as the same endpoint.

Environmental persistence: A separate industry-authored study tested an 88 mol% hydrolyzed, 130,000 Da PVOH resin in a laboratory simulation of aerobic wastewater treatment. After an initial lag and growth phase, dissolved-organic-carbon removal averaged 97.4% during a 29-day plateau; a separate adsorption test indicated little retention on sludge solids. The study measured removal from the reactor effluent, not direct conversion of all polymer carbon to CO2. These results and the adapted-isolate cultures do not establish complete removal in every wastewater plant, river or soil: grade, residence time and the microbial community matter.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A patent proposes recovery of selected highly hydrolyzed PVA by dissolution in warm water, removal of insoluble contamination and isolation of the polymer. Its selection relies on solubility differences, and it identifies precipitation as one way to recover polymer from solution and separate some impurities. This is a specified proposed route, not proof of widespread PVA collection or recovery for every formulation.

Biological mineralization of dissolved PVA under appropriate conditions is a separate destructive pathway rather than polymer recycling.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Melt-processed PVA formulations require control of processing fumes and thermal history under HSE plastics guidance. Water solubility is an application and disposal property rather than evidence of harmless exposure. For the polymer in a coating or printing formulation, plasticizers and other ingredients remain part of the workplace assessment; dissolution or partial biodegradation results do not establish suitability for ingestion or medical contact.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: A nominal PVA designation does not specify degree of hydrolysis or molecular weight, both of which affect crystallinity, solubility, and solution viscosity. Water uptake can change the performance of a film or membrane, and crosslinking may limit swelling while changing transport. The glass transition and degradation behavior also influence the conditions under which a formulation can be processed. Test results for a crosslinked or compounded PVA should be interpreted for that formulation and environment.

sections.overview: Poly(vinyl butyral) (PVB) is a poly(vinyl acetal) obtained by reacting poly(vinyl alcohol) with butyraldehyde. The resulting material contains butyral groups and residual hydroxyl groups, and may retain acetate groups from its precursor. PVB is used in coatings and adhesives as well as in laminated-glass interlayers. Interlayer products commonly include plasticizer, so the resin and the finished film are not interchangeable descriptions.
sections.history: PVB became important through the search for better interlayers in laminated safety glass. A National Park Service account of aircraft-cockpit materials identifies a 1939 development effort involving DuPont, Libbey-Owens-Ford, Pittsburgh Plate Glass, Monsanto and Carbide and Carbon Chemical Corporation. The new interlayer addressed limitations of earlier cellulose-based laminates and became an enduring safety-glass material. Automotive and aircraft glazing gave PVB a practical role in holding fractured glass together. This milestone concerns safety-glass development and adoption; it is not a claim that every participating company independently invented the polymer in that year.
sections.nomenclature: PVB denotes the butyraldehyde acetalized PVA-derived material, not PVA itself or every vinyl acetal. Acetalization extent, residual vinyl-alcohol or acetate groups, plasticizer, and a laminated glass interlayer are material-specific descriptors that should remain explicit.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(vinyl butyral) (PVB) is a PVA-derived polyvinyl acetal, not a direct polymer of a butyral monomer. Acid-catalysed reaction of poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) with n-butyraldehyde converts part of the PVA hydroxyl groups to butyral-acetal groups; starting PVA and conversion therefore determine residual hydroxyl functionality. A Monsanto process begins in aqueous acidic medium at low temperature and continues after PVB precipitates; agitation and temperature control particle/granule formation. A Sinopec aqueous example dissolves PVA, then adds catalyst and n-butyraldehyde under stirring; it treats catalyst, surfactant, temperature, and addition rate as controls for acetalization. Dissolution and precipitation are route variants, not direct-polymerization routes.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PVB is commonly used as a tough, highly extensible adhesive interlayer in laminated glass, where the post-fracture response is that of a constrained sheet rather than an unmodified resin. Its large-strain tensile and shear response is nonlinear and viscoelastic, with strong dependence on temperature relative to its glass transition, strain rate and loading duration, plasticizer/residual hydroxyl content, moisture and aging, interlayer thickness, adhesion to glass, and lamination/thermal history. In a dynamic interlayer study, PVB tested at 0 °C and 2 s⁻¹ had reported yield stress 26.4 MPa at strain 0.122, failure stress 34.1 MPa at strain 1.412, and Young modulus 519 MPa. The accessible report does not identify the supplier grade, plasticizer content, thickness, specimen geometry, or conditioning in the quoted table, so these are dynamic interlayer values rather than intrinsic PVB constants. Independent Saflex PVB tensile work documents response through tearing across a broad deformation-rate range and likewise describes pronounced temperature and rate sensitivity; PVB laminate performance must also retain the glass/interlayer adhesion and pane geometry context.
sections.processing:
Poly(vinyl butyral) (PVB) resin is converted principally by solution coating or casting and, when plasticized, by melt extrusion into interlayer sheet. In laminated safety glass, cleaned and matched glass plies are assembled with the PVB sheet, deaired by vacuum or heated nip rolls while preserving surface texture, and autoclaved under heat and pressure before controlled cooling and depressurization. Resin composition, plasticizer and adhesion-control additives, melt temperature, moisture conditioning, sheet gauge and roughness, clean-room handling, glass cleanliness, trapped air, prelaminate temperature, autoclave hold, and pressure-release temperature govern haze, bubbles, edge stability, adhesion, and yellowing.

Kuraray's extrusion patent directly describes feeding PVB resin and plasticizer to a twin-screw extruder, separately metering an aqueous adhesion-control solution, extruding a 0.76 mm sheet through a slit die, winding it, nip-roll prelaminating it between cleaned 2.1 mm glass, and autoclaving it. Its examples used a maximum melt temperature of 210 °C; the patent more generally keeps melt below 260 °C and preferably below 220 °C to limit yellowing and identifies additive plate-out on extruder and die surfaces as a practical constraint. For a distinct article-lamination example, Eastman's Saflex Q-series guide recommends an autoclave hold at 135–145 °C and 12–14 bar for at least 30 min, followed by pressure release only after cooling below 40 °C to avoid edge bubbles. Those extrusion and autoclave values are tied to the patent formulations and Saflex Q-series sheet, respectively, not to all PVB resin or interlayer grades.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PVB chains contain acetal groups together with remaining vinyl alcohol and vinyl acetate units. The relative amounts of these groups vary with preparation and grade. Hydroxyl groups can form hydrogen bonds between PVB chains, while plasticizer changes the local environment of the chains. In one studied plasticized interlayer, researchers observed structural heterogeneity and a larger-scale separation developing during stretching; this observation applies to the tested film.
sections.properties: PVB can produce clear films and adheres to glass and other substrates. Its glass transition and film behavior depend on composition, including hydroxyl content and plasticizer. In laminated glass, a plasticized PVB interlayer can dissipate energy during deformation and help the film remain attached to glass. Stress relaxation depends on the time and deformation history of the material. In tensile tests of two commercial 0.762 mm PVB interlayer sheets, specimens loaded at higher rates showed greater initial stiffness than those loaded quasi-statically. The results belong to the tested films and temperatures; the response of a laminated assembly also depends on the glass and interlayer construction.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PVB is used in laminated safety and architectural glass, specialty films, printing inks, coatings, adhesives and temporary ceramic binders. The interlayer helps glass fragments remain attached after breakage, while resin grades for inks and coatings serve different formulation needs. These applications span construction, glazing, printing and technical ceramics.

Purchasing. Kuraray supplies Mowital PVB as technical resin, including powder grades; finished Trosifol interlayer films are a separate form of purchase. Molecular weight and residual functional-group content distinguish resin grades, and an interlayer includes plasticizer and other formulation components.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed PVB tonnage was established in the checked sources. Powder-resin and finished-interlayer volumes should be distinguished, including any plasticizer or other formulation mass.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Thermal aging of PVB can involve acetal-ring cleavage and oxidation; reported high-temperature products include butanal, butyric acid, acetic acid and butanol. In a separate reprocessing study, heat and shear caused chain scission and increased yellowness in tested PVB. Selected antioxidants reduced changes in melt-flow and color measures under the study’s conditions. Water absorption can also change the performance of a glass–PVB bond, even without demonstrating cleavage of the polymer backbone.

Timescales: One set of in-situ infrared experiments followed cast films at 100–150 °C for 10 days. The reprocessing study used an internal mixer at 150 °C for minutes. In a separate immersion study, laminated glass disks with a 1.5 mm Saflex PVB interlayer were held in distilled water at about 23 °C for 168 hours. Their measured bond/shear strength in the saturated state was 73% lower than the dry control; drying restored some strength. This is an assembly-level response to a specified water test, not an outdoor lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Neither thermal nor immersion study measures environmental mineralization. Glass protection, plasticizer and prior aging can alter an interlayer’s response, and weakening of an assembly does not establish disappearance of the polymer.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Retrieved PVB interlayer can be separated from glass, cleaned and remelted, with added stabilizers to control degradation during reprocessing. In a 2025 pilot extrusion study, high-quality retrieved PVB was blended with virgin plasticized interlayer at a 40:60 ratio and selected antioxidants. The authors tested final-film mechanical performance and reported that it was consistent with commercial specifications.

The researchers used the blend partly to address yellowness observed in wholly retrieved material. Their results concern a defined feedstock and stabilizer system; contamination, glass separation and optical quality can constrain broader reuse.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PVB interlayers and recovered interlayer material need formulation-specific assessment because plasticizer and prior thermal aging alter the material. The cited thermal work reports aldehydes, acids and alcohols from PVB degradation. These high-temperature products support controlling fumes during hot reprocessing or removal; they should not be presented as measured emissions from laminated glazing in use. HSE guidance addresses overheating, ventilation and purge procedures.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Different PVB grades vary in molecular weight and the proportions of butyral, hydroxyl, and acetate groups. Formulation adds another source of variation: plasticized interlayer films do not have the same response as an unplasticized resin. For example, a study of one plasticized film found that the structure formed during stretching depended on the applied strain. A measured interlayer response should be used with its composition, temperature, loading rate, and test geometry, rather than treated as a universal PVB property.

sections.overview: Poly(vinyl formal) (PVFM) is a poly(vinyl acetal) made by reacting poly(vinyl alcohol) with formaldehyde. The material can retain hydroxyl and acetate groups as well as formal-acetal groups. It has been used in electrical insulating coatings and other surface coatings. A specific grade or coating formulation must be identified when comparing performance.
sections.history: Poly(vinyl formal) was already a practical electrical-insulation material during the Second World War. The Powerhouse museum preserves a 1943 specimen made by Australian General Electric and describes its display as an example of a material that could replace rubber in wire covering. That surviving industrial object provides a firm date and named manufacturer for an early application. It also shows how wartime material shortages encouraged the use of vinyl-derived plastics. The collection does not establish the first synthesis or complete international commercialization history of poly(vinyl formal), so 1943 is an application milestone rather than an invention date.
sections.nomenclature: PVFM and polyvinyl formal identify the formaldehyde-derived vinyl acetal, not PVA or the butyraldehyde-derived PVB material. Trade or application-specific coatings based on poly(vinyl formal) are formulations of the base polymer and should not replace its chemical name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(vinyl formal) is a PVA-derived polyvinyl acetal: it is made by formalizing PVA with formaldehyde under acid catalysis, not by polymerizing vinyl fluoride. The PVA can be fully or partly saponified, so retained acetate and hydroxyl groups depend on the precursor and formalization extent. A Kuraray aqueous route uses formaldehyde, acid, and metal chloride; the metal chloride and phase behavior control high formalization while avoiding intermolecular acetal crosslinking in that specific route. A Monsanto source identifies Formvar as formaldehyde condensed with partially hydrolyzed poly(vinyl acetate), retaining acetate and hydroxyl groups. Filled or networked compositions are composition-specific derivatives, not a general assertion about this polymer.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Poly(vinyl formal) is ordinarily a partially acetalized poly(vinyl alcohol), so commercial and experimental materials retain different fractions of vinyl-formal, vinyl-alcohol, and sometimes vinyl-acetate units rather than sharing one invariant repeat composition. At ambient conditions an unplasticized, sufficiently formalized material can behave as a stiff glassy film, with an initial elastic response followed by yielding and plastic deformation; coatings, porous products, plasticized grades, and ultrathin membranes can respond very differently. Degree and distribution of acetalization, precursor-PVA molar mass and hydrolysis, residual hydroxyl and acetate content, plasticizer or solvent residue, water uptake and humidity, porosity, film thickness, orientation, thermal and drying history, and residual stress all affect modulus, yield, toughness, and creep. The retained hydroxyl groups enable hydrogen bonding and make conditioning especially important, while blending or crosslinking changes both interfacial load transfer and mobility.

A bounded numerical example comes from freestanding Vinylec E poly(vinyl formal) membranes only 10–100 nm thick. Films were spin-coated from 0.25 wt% solution in ethyl lactate, baked for 1 minute at 50 °C, released in water, mounted over circular holders, dried overnight under ambient conditions, and indented with a 2 mm sapphire sphere at about 45% relative humidity. For one 100 nm film, finite-element optimization of the indentation response gave a 3.28 GPa elastic modulus, 0.0018 pre-strain, and, in a bilinear fit, a 43.50 MPa yield strength with 100 MPa tangent modulus. These are model-derived membrane parameters under biaxial indentation, not a bulk-resin tensile dataset; the study also shows that neglecting residual pre-strain can produce much higher apparent moduli. An independent melt-blending study confirms that acetalization level, retained hydroxyl interactions, formulation, conditioning, and phase morphology materially change PVFM-containing specimens, but it does not provide a transferable neat-PVFM tensile endpoint.
sections.processing:
Poly(vinyl formal) (PVFM, often encountered in Formvar-type materials) is most commonly article-formed from solution as electrical wire enamel, protective coating, adhesive layer, or free-standing support film. Resin and any curable co-resins are dissolved and mixed to the target viscosity, filtered or deaerated as needed, applied by dies, rolls, dipping, or casting, and passed through staged ovens to remove solvent and, for reactive enamels, cure the coating. Repeated thin passes may be used on wire. Selected PVFM compositions can also be dried, compounded in the melt with a compatible polymer, pelletized or chopped, and compression- or injection-shaped. Resin acetal/hydroxyl content, molecular mass, solvent balance, solids and viscosity, coat concentricity, line speed, oven gradient, volatile removal, cure residence, blend feed dryness, mixing sequence, shear, and melt residence all need formulation-specific control. Network-forming reactions belong in Synthesis; coating, drying, cure schedule, and melt shaping belong here.

A General Electric wire-enamel patent supplies a bounded coating-and-cure example. Its Example 3 used a 50:50 blend of the stated low- and higher-molecular-mass Formvar grades in a specified phenolic/melamine/polyisocyanate enamel, coated a 40.3 mil copper wire to a 3 mil coating at 46 and 54 ft/min, and used a tower reported at 250 °C at the bottom and 500 °C at the top. Those severe oven settings belong only to that historical reactive enamel and line. In a distinct melt-compounding study, Han and co-workers first made a masterbatch containing 70 wt% of their PVFM in PPC in a 60 cm³ Haake mixer at 200 °C and 60 rpm for 7 min with a 55 g charge, cut it into small pieces, then diluted it with PPC to 30–50 wt% PVFM under the same mixing conditions and stored samples in a sealed desiccator. The two-step sequence addressed the components' large melt-flow mismatch and is not a general neat-PVFM molding prescription.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Formaldehyde reacts with pairs of hydroxyl groups on a poly(vinyl alcohol)-derived backbone to form cyclic formal-acetal groups. Unreacted hydroxyl groups and residual acetate groups can remain, so commercial poly(vinyl formal) is not necessarily composed solely of one repeat unit. Scientific Polymer Products describes its catalog 1091 material as approximately 82% formal, 12% acetate and 6% hydroxyl content and reports an approximate weight-average molecular mass of 90,000. These supplier figures describe that material, not the composition of every PVFM resin.
sections.properties: Poly(vinyl formal) can form electrically insulating coatings with useful resistance to abrasion and to certain oils and hydrocarbon liquids. Solubility is selective: Scientific Polymer Products lists acetic acid, chloroform, dioxane and THF as solvents for its catalog 1091 material. Its datasheet reports a glass-transition range of 103–113 °C, while a different Formvar 15/95 product is listed at 108 °C. A wire enamel can also include other resins or plasticizers, so its finished-film response depends on the formulation as well as the PVFM grade.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Poly(vinyl formal) is used for support films on transmission-electron-microscopy grids and for specialty wire-insulation and protective coatings. The laboratory application uses a thin film supporting fragile specimens. The Formvar film spans openings in the supporting grid and holds thin specimens while allowing the electron beam to pass through. A university microscopy protocol notes that film thickness matters: excessively thick or uneven films are unsuitable for its procedure. Wire enamel uses the same family for its film-forming and electrical-insulation behavior, but has different formulation and service requirements.

Purchasing. Polysciences sells Formvar 15/95 as powder, including catalog item 00631-100 in a 100 g package, with online ordering and a separate bulk-quotation channel. The supplier lists a molecular-weight range of approximately 24,000–40,000 and names acetic acid, dioxane, THF and chloroform among solvents for this product. These specifications describe the purchased resin; a laboratory preparing a microscopy support film also needs to choose an appropriate solution and film-preparation procedure. The university protocol describes solution casting under a fume hood for trained users.

Scale and evidence limits. The documented 100 g unit demonstrates a sub-kilogram laboratory purchase scale. It does not measure industrial demand; no reliable separately reported worldwide annual purchase or consumption figure was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In a study comparing synthesized poly(vinyl formal) with PVA, formal-acetal formation reduced the hydroxyl-elimination behavior seen during heating. The same work found that adding the material to poly(propylene carbonate) reduced the blend’s thermal stability; the authors attributed the effect to promotion of carbonate-chain unzipping by residual hydroxyl groups. The study does not provide a complete product inventory for pure poly(vinyl formal).

Timescales: In nitrogen at a heating rate of 10 °C/min, the synthesized poly(vinyl formal) reached 5% mass loss at approximately 296.5 °C. This is a temperature-ramp measurement on one preparation, not an outdoor degradation time or a universal operating limit.

Environmental persistence: The degradable blend partner does not establish that poly(vinyl formal) itself mineralizes. Material-specific environmental timing remains unresolved.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A production patent describes recovering process solvent from poly(vinyl formal) manufacture: vapors from spray-drying the resin solution are condensed and rectified so the acetic acid can be reused. This recovers a manufacturing input; it does not convert the polymer back to its starting materials or reclaim resin from an old coating.

For unused powder, an SPI safety sheet recommends collecting spills without generating a dust cloud and retaining material for recycling or appropriate disposal. A demonstrated end-of-life recovery process for polymer from electrical or protective coatings remains unresolved in the cited sources.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: SPI’s 2015 Formvar powder SDS warns of dust-cloud explosion potential and recommends minimizing airborne powder, controlling ignition sources and using local extraction at open equipment. It lists less than 0.1% residual formaldehyde for that TEM-grid-coating product; that composition is not a specification for all PVFM resins. Eye protection and controls matched to any casting solvent are needed when preparing films.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Formal-acetal, hydroxyl and acetate contents vary with precursor and reaction conditions. Catalog 1091 has approximately 82% formal, 12% acetate and 6% hydroxyl content and an approximately 90,000 weight-average molecular mass, whereas Polysciences lists a molecular-weight range of approximately 24,000–40,000 for Formvar 15/95. The listings describe different products and the latter does not identify the same molecular-weight average, so they should not be treated as interchangeable specifications. Coatings containing phenolic resin or other modifiers are formulated systems rather than neat polymer; adhesion and solvent resistance require testing of the chosen film and exposure.

sections.overview: Polystyrene (PS) is a thermoplastic homopolymer made from styrene. General-purpose PS is a transparent, rigid material used in molded and sheet products; it is also made into foamed articles. The PS name covers chains with different molecular weights and stereochemical arrangements. Rubber-modified high-impact polystyrene is a related multiphase material rather than the unmodified homopolymer.
sections.history: Polystyrene’s history begins with Eduard Simon’s 1839 observation of styrene forming a solid material. BASF developed industrial production in 1930, following styrene work at Ludwigshafen in 1929; Dow introduced Styron in 1937. It grew into solid molded products and expanded materials for packaging, household articles and insulation. The EPA’s 1980 account records an established producer base including Dow, Monsanto and BASF. Copolymers and rubber-modified products became neighboring branches of styrenic materials. The BASF milestone identifies industrial development rather than the earliest observation of styrene forming a solid polymer.
sections.nomenclature: PS and PSt identify polystyrene itself, not rubber-modified high-impact polystyrene, styrene–acrylonitrile copolymer, or an expanded-foam article. Those related materials contain additional phases, comonomers, or processing-defined structures and require their own names.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polystyrene is produced by addition polymerization of styrene. The dominant family chemistry is free-radical polymerization, which can be run in bulk, solution, aqueous suspension, or emulsion. Peroxide or azo initiators generate radicals; heat can also initiate styrene in bulk. In suspension polymerization, styrene droplets are dispersed in water with a protective colloid or suspending agent and polymerize into beads, while staged initiator addition helps manage conversion and heat generation. One cited patent documents aqueous suspension polymerization with peroxides dosed during reaction. A distinct patent demonstrates living anionic polymerization of styrene with sec-butyllithium in a hydrocarbon medium; exclusion of water and other protic impurities preserves active chain ends. Initiator concentration and monomer/initiator ratio control molar mass in the anionic route, and sequential monomer addition can form blocks, although ordinary polystyrene requires only styrene. Chain-transfer agents, regulator feeds, or reactor staging are route controls rather than changes to the repeat unit. Rubber modification and styrenic copolymers are separate compositions or families.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polystyrene (PS) is an amorphous, glassy thermoplastic under ordinary room-temperature service, so its tensile and fracture response is sensitive to molecular mass, thermal and physical-aging history, temperature and strain rate, molding-induced orientation and residual stress, specimen geometry, and crazing. Rubber modification (HIPS), plasticization, recycled content, and mineral or nanoscale fillers create materially different products and must not be collapsed into a single PS value. In one study of unfilled PS film specimens, tensile testing gave strength at break 56 ± 1 MPa, Young's modulus 1.6 ± 0.1 GPa, and strain at break 5.6 ± 0.2%; the same study found that filler identity and loading changed the response. Independently, injection-molded recycled HIPS from electronics waste had room-temperature ISO 527 tensile strength 40.1 ± 0.87 MPa, modulus 3460 ± 49 MPa, and break strain 1.5 ± 0.06% at 5 mm min−1; the study also tested its temperature and tuff-filler dependence. The numerical values are therefore for the named unfilled research material and recycled-HIPS comparator, not universal values for GPPS, HIPS, expanded PS, or filled/recycled grades.
sections.processing:
General-purpose polystyrene (GPPS), high-impact polystyrene (HIPS), and filled PS compounds are melt converted by injection molding and extrusion into profiles, film, and sheet; suitable grades are also blow molded or injection-blow molded and extruded sheet is thermoformed. Grade selection matters because molecular mass, rubber modification, filler, melt flow, heat resistance, and melt strength change filling, drawdown, sag, and cooling. PS absorbs little bulk water, so routine drying is usually unnecessary, but pellets carrying condensation or stored outdoors should be dried; color concentrates and clean regrind should be mixed consistently and contamination from incompatible polymers purged. In injection molding, cylinder/nozzle temperature, screw speed and back pressure, shot size and residence time, injection and hold profile, gate and vent design, and uniform mold cooling govern fill, weld lines, sink, shrinkage, frozen orientation, residual stress, and warpage. Extrusion requires stable melt temperature and pressure, controlled shear, clean streamlined dies, limited drawdown, uniform roll or air cooling, and matched take-up; sheet gauge and orientation then carry into thermoforming. Uniform sheet heating, sag and stretch control, tool temperature, cooling, and demolding govern wall distribution and distortion, while blow-molding grades require sufficient parison melt strength. Excess temperature or residence time can cause yellowing, volatiles, odor, and degradation. Styrene polymerization and rubber-phase formation belong in Synthesis; this section covers compounding and shaping existing resin.

Numerical guidance is bounded to its source. The BASF Polystyrene/Styrolux guide recommends drying outdoor-stored material at 60–80 °C for 2–3 h or using vacuum-vented extrusion, and its route guidance applies to the named BASF GPPS and HIPS grade portfolio rather than every PS. In a distinct open experiment, Moskalyuk and co-workers compounded PS 585 with the study's fillers in a 5 mL twin-screw microcompounder at 220 °C for 10 min and 50 rpm, injected the melt into an 80 °C die, and allowed the removed die to cool in room-temperature air. Their selected 200–220 °C melt-processing range and below-100 °C mold constraint, as well as the strong filler-dependent viscosity and agglomeration behavior, apply only to PS 585 and those nanocomposite formulations and laboratory equipment.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PS has a carbon backbone bearing phenyl side groups. General-purpose, predominantly atactic PS is normally amorphous, whereas stereoregular forms can crystallize. Syndiotactic PS has several crystal forms: in one study described by a structural review, annealing a particular gamma-form sample at increasing temperature decreased its beta-form content, with almost pure alpha form obtained at 150 °C. This illustrates how stereoregularity and thermal or solvent history influence morphology; the observation is not a description of all general-purpose PS.
sections.properties: General-purpose PS is transparent, stiff and dimensionally stable and provides electrical insulation. It is also brittle under many ordinary loading conditions. Its response changes around the glass transition as chain segments become more mobile. For the specified general-purpose Styrolution PS 158K, a supplier data sheet lists an ISO 527 tensile modulus of 3.3 GPa and tensile strain at break of 3% at 23 °C. It also lists ISO 899 tensile creep modulus decreasing from 3.3 GPa at one hour to 2.6 GPa at 1,000 hours, illustrating time-dependent deformation under that method. A foam, unfilled solid and rubber-modified product have different structures and should not be assigned the same property values.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polystyrene is used for packaging, appliances and insulation, including molded or sheet products and foamed articles. General-purpose PS is valued for its clarity and rigidity; INEOS lists transparent GPPS for refrigerator drawers and laboratory ware, and extrusion grades for expanded-PS insulation and packaging. Foam has a cellular structure and lower apparent density than solid resin, useful where light weight and insulation are desired. Rubber-modified high-impact PS is a distinct material choice when additional toughness is required. The polymer grade, foam density and finished construction all influence performance.

Purchasing. INEOS Styrolution offers a polystyrene portfolio through sales specialists and electronic ordering. Its EMEA table identifies PS 153F as a high-heat extrusion grade with good foaming behavior, while PS 124N/L is listed for injection molding and extrusion with good flow. A converter specifies the resin and process; buyers of converted foam or sheet specify the finished product. Those forms are not identical feedstocks, and a grade listing does not guarantee every end-use approval.

Scale and evidence limits. Plastics Europe’s preliminary 2023 world fossil-based PS-plus-expanded-PS category is about 22 million tonnes. This combined production estimate includes expanded material and is not a neat-PS purchase or consumption total. The supplier’s applications and grade portfolio do not divide that global figure by product or industry.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Controlled depolymerization of polystyrene can produce styrene-rich oil that is distilled for monomer recovery. Weathering is a separate route: a laboratory UV-B study of surface-modified PS nanoparticles observed oxidation, decreasing particle size and release of dissolved small molecules. In another study of five commercial PS samples, simulated sunlight produced both dissolved organic carbon and carbon dioxide. The irradiated samples differed in physical form and additives, so their response does not characterize every PS article.

Timescales: The nanoparticle study irradiated 53 nm amine-modified and 62 nm carboxyl-modified PS particles in water for up to 100 days. In the separate solar-simulator experiment, dissolved organic carbon nearly tripled after five days of light exposure for the studied sample. The xenon-lamp exposure was more intense than the natural sunlight used in the authors’ comparison, and neither endpoint is a general outdoor disappearance time.

Environmental persistence: The simulated-sunlight study measured photochemical carbon dioxide production and used carbon isotopes to support its origin in polystyrene; it also detected partially oxidized dissolved organic products. This establishes conversion of a fraction of the tested materials, not complete conversion of an entire article or microbial mineralization. The authors’ long-term estimates depended on modeled light exposure and assumptions about reaction kinetics, so they should not be treated as measured lifetimes for PS in soil, freshwater or the ocean.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Recovery approaches include sorting and mechanical reprocessing, solvent dissolution followed by polymer purification, and thermal depolymerization followed by styrene distillation and repolymerization. These routes recover different outputs and have different feedstock requirements.

In the ResolVe research project, INEOS Styrolution reported depolymerizing post-consumer PS into styrene oil and purifying a fraction for new polymer production. The company reported that contamination affected yield and bromine-containing traces remained when legacy flame-retarded waste was treated. This research result does not establish that every mixed or flame-retarded PS stream is suitable for closed-loop recycling.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For PS heated above its recommended processing range, HSE identifies styrene and aldehydes among the measured fume components. This is an overheating context, not a migration value for a finished article. Extrusion, molding, recycling and purging need control of temperature/residence time and appropriate ventilation, with the actual pigments, flame retardants and other ingredients included in the assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: A reported property depends on the PS grade, molecular weight and stereochemical form, as well as additives and processing history. Syndiotactic PS can crystallize in several forms, and annealing a gamma-form sample changes the proportions of its alpha and beta forms; the predominantly atactic general-purpose material is normally amorphous. Filler-containing specimens and rubber-modified materials are not equivalent to unfilled general-purpose PS. The 158K supplier listing reports different creep moduli at one and 1,000 hours, so a short-duration stiffness value does not describe its response under sustained load. Specimen geometry, temperature and loading conditions also matter when transferring measurements to a product.

sections.overview: High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) is a rubber-modified polystyrene material designed to improve the toughness of a glassy styrenic matrix. A common route polymerizes styrene in the presence of polybutadiene rubber. Phase separation, grafting and phase inversion during production create a dispersed rubber-containing morphology. HIPS grades differ in rubber content and particle structure, so they do not have one fixed impact response.
sections.history: The British Plastics Federation dates commercial high-impact polystyrene to 1949. Rubber modification addressed the brittleness of ordinary polystyrene and expanded molded and sheet applications. By the EPA’s 1980 industry survey, packaging and consumer products were established uses. HIPS is consequently a postwar development branch of polystyrene whose rubber phase and manufacturing details matter, rather than a separate monomer invention.
sections.nomenclature: HIPS names the rubber-modified polystyrene material, not general-purpose polystyrene or the rubber feedstock alone. The rubber type, grafting conditions, and resulting morphology are formulation and grade variables; they should be retained when identifying a particular HIPS product.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) is a rubber-modified polystyrene made by polymerizing styrene in the presence of a dissolved elastomeric rubber, commonly polybutadiene or a styrene–butadiene rubber. The resulting material contains a polystyrene matrix and a dispersed rubber-rich phase with polystyrene grafting; it is not simply a dry blend of the two polymers. During solution or bulk polymerization, homopolymerization of styrene and grafting onto unsaturation in the rubber occur together, and phase inversion changes the morphology from a rubber-continuous to a polystyrene-continuous system. Documented processes control initiators, conversion, temperature, shear, and phase inversion to set rubber-particle morphology. These conditions are process examples rather than a universal HIPS recipe; extrusion and molding occur after the material has been made.
sections.mechanicalProperties: High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) is polystyrene modified with a rubber impact modifier; the commercial record for RP-HIPS specifically identifies a butadiene-rubber modifier.  Accordingly, the stiffness--impact balance is formulation- and grade-specific, and the two commercial records below differ in recycled content and melt-flow range.  As a bounded fresh-grade example, ASCHEM HIPS 825E, identified for extrusion and thermoforming with melt-flow rate 4.0 g/10 min (200 °C/5 kg), reports typical ASTM D638 tensile strength 20 MPa, elongation at break 44%, and tensile modulus 2,090 MPa; its notched Izod impact is 135 J/m at 23 °C by ASTM D256.  The supplier marks these as typical rather than specification values.  Separately, The Plastics Group lists a reprocessed RP-HIPS grade (melt-flow range 3--8) at 73 °F with 3,600 psi tensile strength, 20% elongation at break, 260 kpsi tensile modulus, and 2.0 ft-lb/in notched Izod impact; that product-specific record should not be used to infer values for virgin HIPS grades.
sections.processing:
High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) is converted by injection molding and by extrusion into sheet or profile followed by thermoforming. The rubber-modified amorphous melt is generally easy to process, but feed moisture/volatiles, colorant dispersion, gate size, mold temperature, cooling, and residence time affect molded stress, weld lines, shrinkage, and surface quality. Regrind and additive packages should therefore be kept within the grade supplier's limits.

Americas Styrenics' EB6400 sheet gives a bounded grade example: injection molding uses approximately 199–249 °C barrel zones, 213–243 °C nozzle, 2–12 bar back pressure, and 60–150 °F (16–66 °C) mold-surface temperature; its extrusion guidance gives approximately 193–232 °C melt, 199–232 °C die, 66–104 °C polish rolls, and 10–21 MPa head pressure. The same guide recommends a mixing head or static mixer for colorants/additives and warns that sheet orientation above 30% sharply reduces brittleness/tear performance. Independently, an open thermoforming study used HIPS sheet temperatures of 130–170 °C and mold temperatures of 30, 60, or 80 °C; a plug mold and suitable mold temperature improved wall-thickness uniformity. These are EB6400- and experiment-specific settings, not universal HIPS windows; styrene/rubber polymerization is upstream Synthesis rather than Processing.
sections.structureAndMorphology: HIPS commonly contains a continuous polystyrene-rich matrix with dispersed polybutadiene-rich particles. During bulk polymerization the initially rubber-rich continuous phase can invert as the polystyrene-rich phase grows. Some rubber particles contain multiple occluded polystyrene domains, often called a salami morphology. Graft copolymer at the interface helps couple the phases, and particle size and internal structure vary with production conditions.
sections.properties: The rubber phase improves impact response relative to brittle unmodified polystyrene, while the matrix contributes rigidity and processability. A review of recycled HIPS describes competing changes during reprocessing: crosslinking can stiffen the dispersed rubber particles, while chain scission, grafting and disruption of the particle structure also change melt viscosity and impact performance. For example, a study summarized in that review reported Charpy impact resistance of Kayson 8669 HIPS falling from 74 to 68 J/m after eight regrind/extrusion cycles at 220 °C. This result applies to the specified grade and process, not to every recycled HIPS product.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. HIPS is used for refrigerator liners and parts, yogurt cups, toys and office articles. The dispersed rubber phase improves impact response compared with unmodified PS, helping explain its use in products exposed to handling or knocks. INEOS lists both extrusion and injection-molding grades, allowing sheet-based liners and molded parts to be selected for different conversion processes. Grade selection also considers surface finish and chemical stress-cracking performance.

Purchasing. A converter specifies an extrusion or injection-molding HIPS resin grade, including required gloss or stress-cracking performance. INEOS lists PS 454N as a high-flow injection-molding grade, PS 486N for thermoformability, and PS ESCRIMO for stress-cracking resistance. Recovered electronic-waste plastic is a different feedstock and requires its own identification and quality control. A grade’s listing for a process does not by itself qualify a finished article for food contact.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable HIPS-only annual purchased or consumed tonnage was established. Aggregate polystyrene statistics also cover other PS materials and should not be assigned entirely to the impact-modified subset. Named grades and applications document supply options, not their market shares.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Repeated melt processing of recovered HIPS can change the polymer chains and melt flow. In a study of electronic-waste HIPS, melt-flow rate increased with reprocessing; the authors associated this with chain scission and reduced molecular mass. A separate simulated-sunlight study included a black, rubber-containing high-impact PS grade among five commercial samples and measured conversion of some material to carbon dioxide and dissolved organic carbon. The complete product inventory and behavior of all HIPS grades were not established.

Timescales: Washed electronic-waste HIPS was followed from first-cycle flakes through fourth-cycle material, with filament extrusion at 195 ± 5 °C. From first to fourth cycle, measured melt-flow rate increased by about 20% under the study’s 200 °C, 5 kg test. In the separate light study, the black high-impact grade was the only one of the five samples showing measurable oxygen consumption at 450 ± 26 nm. Its additives changed the absorption and oxidation response; the solar simulator was more intense than the natural sunlight used in the authors’ comparison. Cycle counts and these laboratory exposures are not environmental lifetimes.

Environmental persistence: Simulated sunlight produced carbon dioxide from the commercial PS samples, including the stated high-impact grade, but did not demonstrate complete conversion of an entire HIPS article. Dissolved organic carbon includes partially oxidized material and is not equivalent to complete mineralization. Neither reprocessing nor the light experiment establishes a general soil or aquatic disappearance time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Mechanical recovery by washing, drying and extruding electronic-waste HIPS into 3D-printing filament was demonstrated in a laboratory study. The authors compared specimens printed with different orientations and found that several strength measurements remained comparable to a commercial filament through the fourth cycle; melt-flow rate nevertheless increased, and fourth-cycle printability was slightly worse.

This is a specific sorted waste stream and printing setup. Different contaminants, rubber content, prior use and printing orientation can change the result; four cycles are not a universal guarantee for HIPS.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For HIPS processing, the polystyrene phase makes PS fume guidance relevant as family context: HSE identifies styrene and aldehydes when PS is overheated. The rubber phase and additive package mean that list is not a complete HIPS emission analysis. Temperature/residence-time control, suitable extraction and planned purging are practical controls for molding and reprocessing.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Rubber type, concentration, particle size, grafting and matrix molecular weight influence performance. The morphology formed during polymerization also depends on conditions such as mixing and phase behavior. In studies reviewed by Belblidia and colleagues, rubber-phase crosslinking, changes to grafting and matrix-chain scission could contribute in different directions to viscosity and impact behavior during reprocessing. The balance depends on the material and thermal history, so a property measured for one recycled grade should not be applied to every HIPS article.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Styrene radical polymerization combines matrix formation with rubber grafting and phase inversion. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another. Matrix formation and graft growth remain distinct parts of the staged preparation; this chain-growth description does not imply a uniform monomer sequence throughout the multiphase material.

steps.title: Propagate the radical chain
steps.body: Successive monomer additions convert alkene π bonds into backbone σ bonds while regenerating the radical growth site. The cited initiator, feed composition and reaction medium determine the particular preparation; transfer, grafting and termination control architecture alongside propagation.

steps.title: Form and recover the product

sections.overview: Styrene–acrylonitrile (SAN) is a thermoplastic copolymer made from styrene and acrylonitrile. It combines the clarity and rigidity associated with styrene-containing chains with chemical and thermal resistance contributed by acrylonitrile. Clear SAN is used in household and other molded products; glass-fiber-reinforced compounds serve different stiffness requirements. SAN also forms the matrix of more complex styrenic materials such as ABS, where a rubber phase improves toughness. The styrene-to-acrylonitrile ratio and formulation distinguish grades.
sections.history: SAN was an established commercial copolymer by the EPA’s 1980 survey, which lists Dow Tyril, Monsanto Lustran SAN and ARCO/Polymers Luran. Its later development continued in transparent household components. A specific 2022 milestone is Bear Electric’s selection of INEOS Styrolution Luran SAN C for food processors, yogurt machines and filter kettles. Related grades serve drinkware, blenders and coffee-machine water containers. These sources trace industrial suppliers and sustained application development; they do not establish a unique first laboratory synthesis of SAN.
sections.nomenclature: SAN abbreviates styrene–acrylonitrile copolymer. The name denotes a styrene/acrylonitrile copolymer, not ABS, which additionally contains a butadiene-rubber phase.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–acrylonitrile (SAN) is formed by free-radical copolymerization of styrene and acrylonitrile. Industrial routes include continuous bulk or solution polymerization and aqueous suspension or emulsion polymerization. In continuous bulk manufacture, a styrene/acrylonitrile feed can include a small amount of solvent, a peroxide or azo initiator, and a mercaptan chain-transfer agent; the viscous polymer solution is then devolatilized to recover unreacted monomers and solvent. One cited patent example continuously polymerizes styrene and acrylonitrile in ethylbenzene with a peroxide initiator and n-dodecyl mercaptan before vacuum devolatilization. A distinct historical patent uses aqueous suspension polymerization and adjusts styrene feed during conversion to compensate for monomer reactivity and acrylonitrile partitioning, then strips residual acrylonitrile with inert gas. Monomer ratio and feed profile control incorporated acrylonitrile and compositional drift; initiator level, temperature, residence time, and chain-transfer agent regulate conversion and molar mass. SAN is the ungrafted binary copolymer. ABS, ASA, or other rubber-modified materials add a dispersed elastomeric phase or grafting step and are not synonyms for SAN.
sections.mechanicalProperties: SAN is an amorphous random styrene/acrylonitrile copolymer that is typically stiff but has limited unmodified elongation and notch impact. Acrylonitrile fraction, molar mass, residual stress and moisture, injection or extrusion history, temperature and rate, and rubber, fiber, or alloy modifiers determine the strength–toughness tradeoff. NETZSCH describes unfilled SAN as having an elastic modulus near 4 GPa. For Taitalac 1200 SAN, the producer reports at 23 °C ASTM D638/5 mm min⁻¹ yield and break stresses of 700 and 690 kg/cm² (about 68.6 and 67.7 MPa), 5% break elongation, and ASTM D790/2.8 mm min⁻¹ flexural modulus 34,000 kg/cm² (about 3.33 GPa). These are average values for that named resin and test configuration, not a SAN-family range.
sections.processing:
Styrene–acrylonitrile copolymer (SAN) is an amorphous thermoplastic converted primarily by injection molding; suitable grades are also extruded or compounded as blends, alloys, and glass-fiber-reinforced materials. Pellets should be protected from moisture and dried when storage or handling has allowed uptake. Melt and mold temperature, screw speed and back pressure, injection speed and pressure, gate design, reinforcement, wall thickness, residence time, and cooling determine fill, transparency, surface quality, shrinkage, residual stress, and warpage. High speed can help fill because SAN solidifies quickly, but the machine window must be adjusted for the selected acrylonitrile content, molar mass, reinforcement, pigment, and part geometry. Copolymerization belongs in Synthesis; pellet preparation, compounding, molding, and cooling belong here.

Taita Chemical's injection guide gives a bounded supplier window for its general-purpose TAITALAC 1200(Z) and 1400(N/Z) SAN grades: dry at 80–85 °C for 2–4 h, use a 205–235 °C nozzle, a 40–70 °C mold, 50–70 psi back pressure, and 30–100 rpm screw speed, with moderate-to-moderately-high injection pressure and moderate-to-fast injection. The sheet explicitly calls these reference conditions that require equipment and molding adjustment. Autodesk's independent Moldflow material reference gives broader SAN starting guidance of 80 °C drying for 2–4 h, 200–270 °C melt temperature (230–260 °C for most applications), 40–80 °C mold temperature, 35–130 MPa injection pressure, and high injection speed; it also recommends at least 60 °C molds for reinforced grades. These are separate technical starting windows, not a family specification or a reason to combine their endpoints into one universal range.
sections.structureAndMorphology: SAN consists of chains containing both styrene and acrylonitrile-derived units. Commercial SAN is generally described as a linear, amorphous random copolymer rather than a crystalline polymer with a single repeating sequence. Its composition is not fixed: a public technical report describes commonly used resins with different styrene and acrylonitrile proportions. The copolymer can also be combined with elastomer or other additives for particular products.
sections.properties: SAN resins are typically rigid, transparent and glossy, with chemical resistance and dimensional stability useful in molded articles. Acrylonitrile incorporation changes the balance compared with polystyrene, while reinforcement changes the compound’s stiffness. For example, INEOS lists tensile moduli of 3.8 GPa for its Luran 378P grade and 12 GPa for its glass-fiber-reinforced 378P G7 grade using ISO 527. These are manufacturer data for specified compounds, not universal SAN values; chemical resistance also depends on exposure.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. SAN is used for water tanks, food-storage products, blender components, industrial battery components and cosmetic articles, serving appliance, packaging and electrical markets. Its clarity is useful for visible containers, while compounders can also use SAN as a component of other styrenic systems. Requirements for clarity, food contact and toughness differ between finished products.

Purchasing. Specify a SAN molding or extrusion grade, such as a member of INEOS Styrolution’s Luran range; the portfolio includes glass-reinforced material as well as clear grades. Distinguish SAN from the separately listed alpha-methylstyrene-containing high-heat materials.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable SAN-only annual purchased or consumed tonnage was established. The grade portfolio demonstrates commercial availability but provides no mass-based end-use split or standard order quantity.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Pyrolysis of SAN-dominant printer waste produces oils rich in styrene and toluene, with ethylbenzene, α-methylstyrene, phenol and heavier aromatic products also identified. This waste-specific study characterizes the hydrocarbon oil fraction; it does not provide a complete nitrogen-containing product inventory or natural-weathering leachate profile. A separate laboratory weathering study followed yellowing and gloss loss in SAN containing 3% titanium dioxide pigment. The authors connect gloss loss to surface erosion and exposure of the pigment, and describe oxidation of aromatic rings in styrenic polymers; the visual measurements alone do not provide a complete chemical product inventory.

Timescales: The study treats 2 g cryomilled waste portions in a preheated tube furnace at 800, 1000 or 1200 °C under argon flowing at 1 L/min. Collection continues until emissions stop, about 5 min under that apparatus protocol. In the weathering study, injection-molded chips were exposed at 55 °C under filtered UV at different relative humidities. At lower UV intensity, dry SAN changed color and lost gloss faster than the humid specimens; the authors could not establish a chemical explanation for this difference. The lamp spectrum and lack of rain cycles limit direct conversion to outdoor service time.

Environmental persistence: Neither high-temperature pyrolysis nor accelerated UV exposure measures SAN mineralization in soil, freshwater or seawater. The UV study followed color and gloss rather than the loss of all polymer carbon, while the pyrolysis study deliberately heated waste in argon. Neither experiment establishes an ambient disappearance time; specimen composition, light, oxygen and exposure conditions would need to be specified for a relevant comparison.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Clean production scrap can be ground and remolded, preserving polymer material rather than converting it to a chemical feedstock. In one study of an identified SAN grade, injection-molding runners were milled, separated by particle size and molded into tensile specimens. The unsifted regrind had a tensile modulus nearly 4% lower than the virgin material after one reprocessing step; the smallest and 1–2 mm fractions showed decreases approaching 10%. These results apply to the tested clean industrial scrap and processing conditions, not mixed household waste.

A separate laboratory study converted SAN-rich printer waste to mixed hydrocarbon oils by heating under argon. The oil requires separation or upgrading and the experiment does not demonstrate a closed SAN-to-SAN loop or commercial operation. In another laboratory approach, a palladium-catalyzed reaction transferred nitrile-derived functionality from SAN to ethylene, yielding propionitrile and a modified polymer; the authors measured 96% dehydrocyanation for their SAN sample after 18 hours at 130 °C. This controlled chemical experiment does not establish the collection or commercial processing of SAN waste.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: SAN melt operations need a formulation-specific fume assessment. HSE plastics guidance explains that emissions vary with polymer ingredients, actual melt temperature and residence time, and calls for reliable temperature control, ventilation and trained shutdown/purging procedures. Its polystyrene fume examples provide styrenic-family context, but do not determine the complete emission mixture of the acrylonitrile-containing copolymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The composition of SAN varies, and commercial production routes and additives can differ between grades. A report identifies fillers, stabilizers, colorants and elastomers among materials that can be used in SAN formulations. Optical quality may also depend on how the copolymer is produced and processed. A property value from a supplier's grade should therefore be interpreted for that grade, specimen and test conditions.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical copolymerization forms SAN chains. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another.

steps.title: Propagate the radical chain
