steps.title: Prepare the microemulsion
steps.body: Dissolve CuBr₂, ligand and EBiB in 14.04 g MMA. Combine with the aqueous surfactant solution, transfer to the reactor and purge with nitrogen.

steps.title: Activate and add the second feed
steps.body: At 50 °C, inject the first ascorbic-acid solution portion. After 15 min, add 42.12 g MMA and the remaining reducing-agent portion.

steps.title: Follow polymerization
steps.body: Continue the E4 run to 5 h. The study withdraws samples, quenches them by cooling, and measures conversion and molar mass; methanol is identified for polymer precipitation.

synthesisRoutes.limitations: The paper gives total ascorbic acid but does not quantify its split between the two injections in the methods text. This outline preserves that limit. No crosslinker is included. Oxygen removal, colloidal stability and initiator loss during purging are experimental controls; repeat-unit identity alone does not establish livingness.

sections.overview: Polyacrylonitrile (PAN) is a nitrile-bearing vinyl polymer derived from acrylonitrile. PAN-based materials are used in acrylic fibers and as precursors for carbon fibers. Fiber production develops orientation in the polymer before a precursor is stabilized and carbonized. Many practical precursor formulations include comonomers, so their behavior depends on more than the PAN name.
sections.history: PAN first became commercially important through synthetic-fiber development; the British Plastics Federation records DuPont’s introduction of PAN in 1940. A later, transformative use was as a precursor to carbon fiber. In 1961, Akio Shindo at Japan’s Government Industrial Research Institute in Osaka demonstrated strong PAN-derived carbon fibers, followed by Japanese pilot production in 1964. William Watt’s work at Britain’s Royal Aircraft Establishment provided another major 1964 advance. These developments shifted PAN’s role from a textile polymer to a feedstock for structural carbon materials. Carbonization changes the material chemically, so carbon-fiber history should not be mistaken for the mechanical history of unconverted PAN.
sections.nomenclature: PAN abbreviates polyacrylonitrile. The name denotes the acrylonitrile homopolymer, whereas many commercial acrylic fibers are copolymers and should not automatically be treated as identical to PAN.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyacrylonitrile (PAN) is the radical-addition homopolymer of acrylonitrile. It can be made by aqueous emulsion or precipitation polymerization using a persulfate-based initiator system, or by solution polymerization in a PAN solvent such as dimethylformamide, dimethylacetamide, dimethyl sulfoxide, or thiocyanate-containing media. Radical initiator type and amount, monomer concentration, temperature, solvent composition, and oxygen exclusion determine polymerization rate, molar mass, and whether the polymer stays dissolved or precipitates. The term PAN here means the acrylonitrile homopolymer; acrylic fibers and carbon-fiber precursor copolymers often contain comonomers and have distinct composition and downstream stabilization/carbonization steps, which are outside this entry's synthesis scope.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyacrylonitrile (PAN) mechanics are strongly form-dependent: precursor-fiber molecular weight and comonomer content, spinning/coagulation history, draw ratio, fiber diameter, void content, crystallinity, and orientation must be retained with any tensile value. In one single-fiber study of 97:3 acrylonitrile/methyl-acrylate copolymer precursor, the high-molecular-weight fiber after a total draw ratio of 18 had tensile strength 241 ± 7 MPa and elongation at break 12.49 ± 1.71%; the undrawn counterpart was 126 ± 3 MPa and 62.26 ± 9.36%, respectively. Independent work on ionic-liquid-spun textile-grade PAN likewise reports that draw ratio changes the fiber tensile response. These fiber results do not define bulk PAN or all PAN copolymer precursor grades.
sections.processing:
Polyacrylonitrile (PAN) is normally solution-spun because conventional PAN grades cyclize or degrade before providing a broad, stable melt-processing interval. Established article-conversion routes include wet spinning, dry spinning, dry-jet wet spinning, gel spinning, electrospinning, and phase-inversion casting or spinning of membranes; specially modified copolymers can also be melt-spun. For wet and dry-jet wet precursor fiber, a filtered and degassed spinning dope is metered through a spinneret, coagulated by solvent–nonsolvent exchange, washed to remove residual solvent, drawn in hot water, oiled where required, dried/densified, and steam-drawn. Dope solids and viscosity, spinneret pressure and temperature, air-gap stability, coagulation-bath composition and temperature, solvent diffusion, jet stretch, total draw, washing, drying, and steam stretch control voids, skin–core structure, diameter, orientation, and filament breaks. Stabilization and carbonization that convert PAN to carbon fiber are downstream chemistry, not PAN article shaping, and are outside this Processing account.

Ahn, Yeo, and Lee review wet, dry-jet wet, gel, electrochemical wet, and modified melt-spinning routes and identify dope viscosity, thermodynamic affinity, air-gap jet stretch, coagulation, and drawing as key controls rather than prescribing a family-wide window. Cao and co-workers provide a bounded pilot-line example for their PAN–2 wt% itaconic-acid copolymer in DMSO: a degassed and precisely filtered dope containing 20% polymer was gear-pumped to the spinneret at 60 °C; coagulation-stage draw ratios were 2 for dry-jet wet spinning and 0.7 for wet spinning, followed by washing, hot-water stretching, drying/densification, and steam stretching. Total draw ratios were 20 and 9.8, respectively. These values describe those matched pilot processes and dope, not all PAN compositions or spinnerets.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PAN chains carry polar nitrile groups along the carbon backbone. In precursor fibers the chains and ordered regions can become preferentially oriented along the fiber axis during spinning and drawing. Fiber structure is hierarchical, with molecular organization, microfibrils and larger-scale features all relevant to performance. Subsequent stabilization changes the chemistry as nitrile groups react, so a stabilized precursor is not structurally identical to the starting polymer.
sections.properties: Strong interactions between nitrile groups contribute to PAN precursor processing. Molecular orientation and defects affect fiber response: a review reports that, in one series of wet-spun PAN homopolymer fibers drawn in boiling water, greater chain orientation accompanied an increase in single-filament specific tensile strength from 2.4 to 6.2 cN/dtex. These precursor measurements are normalized by linear density and are not carbon-fiber strength values. Subsequent stabilization and carbonization change both chemistry and organization.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PAN-rich acrylic fibers are used in apparel and household textiles; engineered PAN precursor fibers are converted to carbon fibers for composite reinforcement. Textile acrylic grades commonly contain comonomers and can provide a soft, bulky, wool-like feel in sweaters and other yarns. Carbon-fiber production has a different objective: the precursor is stabilized and carbonized to form the reinforcing fiber, so its spinning history and defects matter to the final composite reinforcement. A related product, oxidized PAN fiber, is used in welding blankets and insulation; Teijin describes Pyromex as produced by heating a stretched PAN precursor in air. The oxidized product has changed chemistry and is not the original PAN fiber.

Purchasing. Textile mills source acrylic fibers such as Aksa Acryluna, while carbon-fiber manufacturers require precursor tow qualified for stabilization and carbonization. Teijin separately lists oxidized Pyromex as a 312,000-filament tow or as crimped staple cut to lengths from 51 to 102 mm. Those are available forms of the oxidized product, not package masses or interchangeable textile and precursor grades. A buyer should specify composition, fiber form and intended conversion.

Scale and evidence limits. Textile Exchange reports just under 1.6 million tonnes of global acrylic fiber production in 2024, order 10^6 tonnes/year. This category is not isolated PAN homopolymer production and does not quantify carbon-fiber precursor demand. The Teijin tow count and staple lengths describe product formats rather than production volume or order size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PAN thermal breakdown can produce nitrogen-bearing volatiles, including hydrogen cyanide and nitrile compounds, while leaving a substantial nonvolatile residue. The relative products depend on temperature and secondary reactions. A separate experiment exposed solution-cast PAN films to mercury-lamp UV in air or vacuum; the films browned and their infrared spectra changed, with oxygen-containing bands more pronounced in air. UV-driven changes are distinct from the high-temperature products and residue formed in the vacuum-pyrolysis experiment.

Timescales: The NBS study compared vacuum-pyrolysis behavior of a high-purity PAN powder with approximately 40,000 number-average molecular weight. Its comparison identified 316 °C as the temperature at which that sample lost half its weight by volatilization within 35 minutes. In the separate UV study, an unoriented PAN film was irradiated in air for 34 hours under a 500 W high-pressure mercury lamp for one reported spectrum. Neither laboratory treatment determines how long an article persists outdoors.

Environmental persistence: Brown coloration, infrared changes and mass loss under heat are not measurements of biodegradation in soil or water. The observations do not show complete conversion of the polymer carbon to carbon dioxide or biomass. The studies therefore leave material-specific environmental mineralization times unresolved.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A laboratory route converts waste acrylic-fiber PAN into a useful hydrolyzed polymer rather than regenerating acrylonitrile. In the micro-water study, mixed acrylic waste was hydroplastized with water at 180 °C for 2 h, then ground and screened to isolate PAN-rich powder. A 20 g PAN portion was treated with 10 g NaOH and 12 g water at 160 °C for 1 h, with evolved ammonia absorbed separately. Conversion of nitrile groups to amide/carboxylate groups produced hydrolyzed PAN sodium salt evaluated as a drilling-fluid filtrate reducer. The study does not establish industrial deployment of this particular process or a closed monomer loop.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: A waste-acrylic-fiber recycling study illustrates a process-specific exposure issue for PAN: alkaline nitrile hydrolysis releases ammonia. Its 160 °C micro-water treatment uses a closed reactor and absorbs the evolved ammonia in an acidic solution. This is a chemical-conversion operation involving alkaline reagent and off-gas; it should not be confused with contact with untreated acrylic fiber. Material and process controls need to include any fiber finishes and mixed-fiber contaminants.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Precursor fibers vary in comonomer content, molecular weight and the way they are spun and drawn. Solvent, coagulation, drawing and stabilization conditions affect orientation and defects. Studies that correlate precursor orientation with the performance of a carbon fiber involve a particular sequence of processing steps. Values for one precursor or carbonized product therefore cannot be assumed for all PAN fibers.

sections.overview: Poly(alkyl acrylates) are a family of polymers made from alkyl esters of acrylic acid. Changing the ester side group produces different members, such as poly(methyl acrylate) and poly(butyl acrylate). Materials can also be copolymerized or crosslinked to create a wider range of products. The family name alone does not specify a single glass transition or mechanical response.
sections.history: The poly(alkyl acrylate) family grew from early acrylic research, including Otto Röhm’s 1901 thesis, into major coating and adhesive technologies. After the Second World War, Harry Neher’s group at Rohm and Haas improved monomer manufacture using work derived from Walter Reppe. Benjamin Kine and Gerald Brown promoted waterborne acrylic emulsions, and the company launched Rhoplex AC-33 paint binder in 1953. Leather coatings and textile finishes preceded the large house-paint market; later products served industrial coatings and adhesives. This is a family history involving many ester monomers and formulations, not a single invention date shared by every alkyl-acrylate homopolymer.
sections.nomenclature: Poly(alkyl acrylate) is used as a family name for acrylic ester polymers, including poly(n-butyl acrylate) and related members. The family excludes poly(acrylic acid), methacrylate polymers, and any one crosslinked or copolymer formulation as silent synonyms for all poly(alkyl acrylates).
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: The poly(alkyl acrylate) family comprises vinyl-addition polymers of alkyl acrylate esters; the alkyl ester substituent and any comonomer identify the particular family member or copolymer rather than a single interchangeable resin. Conventional free-radical polymerization may be carried out in bulk, solution, dispersion, or emulsion, with initiator, solvent, regulator, temperature, feed, and reinitiation determining the resulting architecture and molar-mass distribution. Patent Example 5 uses n-butyl acrylate and 2-ethylhexyl acrylate together with acrylic acid, maleic anhydride and N-tert-butylacrylamide, with AIBN and subsequent initiator additions in acetone under nitrogen and a thioester regulator; it is an acrylic copolymer example, not a synthesis prescription for every neat poly(alkyl acrylate). Plasma-initiated chemical-vapor deposition is a separate thin-film route: short atmospheric-pressure plasma pulses fragment alkyl-acrylate monomers, and the fragments can initiate or terminate competing radical/plasma pathways. Plasma-film chemistry should likewise not be generalized to bulk polyacrylate production.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Poly(alkyl acrylates) span soft, generally amorphous acrylic-ester materials whose tensile response is set by ester-side-chain identity, molar mass, copolymer or hard-segment content, and—when a rubber or coating is cured—crosslink density and crosslink chemistry. Temperature relative to the material's glass transition, strain rate, physical aging, orientation, and fillers or other formulation components also matter; an uncrosslinked liquid or pressure-sensitive adhesive cannot be compared directly with a network elastomer. In one room-temperature tensile study at 100 mm min−1, 6% chemically crosslinked poly(n-butyl acrylate) networks incorporating 6% of a PEG-based crosslinker gave an elastic modulus of 3.82 ± 0.13 MPa, tensile strength of 0.63 ± 0.17 MPa, and strain at break of 0.19 ± 0.05; the corresponding UPy-containing network gave 5.57 ± 0.08 MPa modulus and reached 4.5 MPa and 0.8 strain without fracture before the apparatus load limit. Those values describe the named 6%-crosslinked poly(n-butyl acrylate) rubbers and their particular reversible crosslinker, not the whole poly(alkyl acrylate) family. A separate open study likewise distinguishes viscous poly(n-butyl acrylate) with a low density of UPy groups from higher-UPy materials that could be compression-molded into tensile dog-bones, underscoring the role of physical association and specimen preparation.
sections.processing:
Poly(alkyl acrylate)s are usually converted as soft films, pressure-sensitive adhesive layers, latex coatings, solution-cast sheets, and plasma-deposited conformal coatings rather than as unsupported high-temperature melt articles. Coating and casting require control of polymer concentration or latex solids, viscosity, wetting, wet-film thickness, evaporation rate, coalescence, residual solvent or water, and any crosslinking step. In plasma-initiated chemical-vapor deposition, monomer delivery, discharge power, substrate position and temperature, pressure, and residence time couple film growth to polymer formation; the reaction mechanism belongs in Synthesis, while substrate deposition and film conditioning belong in Processing.

Two open studies bound different routes. Loyer and co-workers deposited several poly(alkyl acrylate) films by atmospheric-pressure plasma-initiated chemical-vapor deposition and showed that monomer structure and operating conditions affected deposition and chain termination. In a solvent-casting example, Fage and co-workers made poly(butyl acrylate)-graft-polystyrene films from 20 mL of a 3 wt% toluene solution in 10 cm Petri dishes, evaporated solvent for 24 h at room temperature in a fume hood, water-immersed the dishes for 2 h to release the films, and vacuum-dried them at 50 °C for 24 h, obtaining about 100 +/- 10 micrometre films. That recipe is specific to the graft copolymers and test-film geometry and is not a family-wide coating window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: These polymers have a carbon backbone bearing ester side groups whose alkyl substituent varies between members. Alkyl group length and structure influence chain motions and packing. Linear chains and crosslinked networks are different architectures; a network joins chains through junctions rather than allowing them to flow independently. In one study, methyl, ethyl and butyl acrylates were each made into networks using a diacrylate crosslinker.
sections.properties: The glass transition and mechanical response depend on side group and architecture. In one comparison of methyl-, ethyl- and n-butyl-acrylate networks made with a diacrylate crosslinker, the methyl-acrylate network had a glass transition near room temperature and substantially higher fracture energy under the study’s conditions. The authors attribute the difference to greater viscous energy dissipation near that transition. Crosslink density, loading rate and test temperature affect this comparison; it is not a universal ranking of all acrylic formulations.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Alkyl-acrylate-based commercial formulations serve pressure-sensitive labels, specialty tapes, protective films, flooring mastics and graphic arts. Packaging, consumer-goods labeling and construction are documented downstream markets. These formulated acrylic products may contain comonomers and additives. For a label, the adhesive must initially grip the surface and also resist peeling and shear during use. Synthomer describes SYNTHEBOND E 2800 as a high-solids acrylic emulsion with high peel strength alongside tack and shear properties, and lists it for permanent labels and protective films. These performance descriptions concern a commercial formulation, not every poly(alkyl acrylate).

Purchasing. Synthomer lists both compounding bases and coater-ready water-based acrylic emulsions. For clear-on-clear labels it describes SYNTHEBOND 7703 as optimized for reverse gravure coating and 7708 for higher-viscosity coating methods such as curtain coating. A converter should select the formulation and coating process together and confirm solids content and substrate compatibility. These catalog emulsions are commercial formulations, not necessarily neat alkyl-acrylate homopolymers.

Scale and evidence limits. No separate purchased tonnage for this broad family is disclosed in the checked portfolio. Wet-emulsion shipments and dry-acrylic-polymer demand require different accounting: emulsion mass includes water as well as polymer and other ingredients. The supplier’s named product examples do not establish the total volume used in labels or other markets.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In vacuum pyrolysis, poly(methyl acrylate) gives carbon dioxide, methanol and a mixture of larger fragments. A separate photochemical study found that room-temperature UV exposure caused poly(methyl acrylate) film to crosslink and become insoluble, while chain scission also occurred; the balance of these reactions changed with methyl methacrylate content in the copolymers. These outcomes describe specified polymers and exposures, not every alkyl ester or crosslinked coating.

Timescales: In an outdoor agricultural-soil study, a cast latex film made from n-butyl acrylate, methyl methacrylate and methacrylic acid lost 1.77% of its measured weight after 12 months. Its surface developed cracks and holes after six months, with more visible changes after a year. Soil adhered to the film and could affect the measured weight, and this one copolymer and soil exposure cannot supply a family-wide lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The soil study measured film mass and surface changes; it did not establish conversion of the polymer carbon to carbon dioxide and biomass. Volatilization during hot vacuum pyrolysis and UV-induced insolubility likewise do not establish ambient mineralization. Ester identity, copolymer composition, network structure and exposure require separate fate studies.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Research on deliberately cleavable poly(n-butyl acrylate) networks demonstrates recovery of soluble polymer fragments and rebuilding of a solid network. Dawson and co-workers used disulfide crosslinks or a thionolactone-derived cleavable comonomer, then recovered thiol-bearing fragments and oxidized them in air with pyridine at 30 °C. Selected RAFT-derived networks underwent repeated degradation/regelation, while network topology and cleavable-group content controlled success. This laboratory design-for-recycling example requires the installed cleavable chemistry; it does not establish the recyclability of an ordinary permanent acrylic adhesive network.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Health assessment of an alkyl-acrylate coating depends on the ester identity, residual ingredients and whether the material is a solution, dispersion or cured network. For hot operations, HSE plastics guidance calls for controlling thermal history and processing fumes. Poly(methyl acrylate) vacuum-pyrolysis experiments identify methanol, carbon dioxide and larger fragments as one bounded family example; that composition is not a measured emission profile for every acrylic adhesive.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The family includes different alkyl substituents, molecular weights and network or copolymer architectures. A tested n-butyl acrylate network is one member, not a representative for every alkyl acrylate. Crosslinker content, composition, temperature and test method must accompany comparisons of mechanical behavior. A glass-transition trend established for a particular series should not be extrapolated without accounting for chain structure and tacticity.

sections.overview: Polyacrylamide is a synthetic polymer with pendant amide groups. Linear polyacrylamide can dissolve in water, while crosslinking produces a water-containing network or hydrogel. High-molecular-weight materials are used as flocculants and viscosity modifiers in water treatment and other applications. Commercial usage of the name also includes acrylamide copolymers and partially hydrolyzed materials whose charge differs from that of the homopolymer.
sections.history: Polyacrylamide was already commercially available when Edwin R. Kolodny filed his American Cyanamid patent in 1958, granted in 1961. His work developed high-molecular-weight materials to control the viscosity of water injected for petroleum recovery, linking polymerization research to a specific industrial problem. Later producers expanded water-soluble-polymer manufacture and applications: SNF, founded in 1978, developed polyacrylamide-based products for water treatment and industrial processing. These milestones document an established polymer’s manufacturing and application history. They do not identify its first laboratory synthesis, and charged derivatives and copolymers should retain their particular composition scope.
sections.nomenclature: PAM abbreviates polyacrylamide. The canonical name refers to the acrylamide homopolymer; copolymer and hydrogel formulations need separate qualification.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyacrylamide is the linear radical-addition homopolymer of acrylamide. Aqueous solution and adiabatic gel polymerizations use water, acrylamide, and a radical initiator system; peroxides, persulfates, azo initiators, and redox couples are documented choices. Monomer concentration, pH, initiator identity and loading, heat removal, and dilution or dissolution after gel polymerization affect conversion, solution concentration, and molecular mass. Mildly alkaline aqueous routes have also used free ammonia or ammonium hydroxide alongside a radical catalyst to produce water-swellable, dispersible polymer. Copolymers containing acrylic acid or sulfonated comonomers, and intentionally crosslinked hydrogel articles, are outside the homopolymer boundary unless separately named.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Reported polyacrylamide (PAAm) mechanics commonly concern hydrated, cross-linked networks rather than a single dry-resin grade. Network cross-linker content, monomer concentration at gelation, entanglement density, equilibrium water content, specimen geometry, and loading mode/rate can all change the response. In an equilibrium-swollen PAAm-gel series tested in tension, the 2% cross-linker specimen (10 × 20 × 3 mm dumbbell) had a Young's modulus of 56 ± 7 kPa, break stress of 22 ± 3 kPa, and break strain of 62 ± 6%; the reported 1–9% cross-linker series spanned 19–157 kPa in modulus. A separate PAAm hydrogel study found that increasing monomer concentration at fixed 5.0 mol% cross-linker raised tensile modulus from 9.6 to 196.7 kPa (1.0 to 5.0 mol/L AAm), while swelling reduced fracture stress and strain. These are gel-network measurements under their stated preparation and test conditions, not general values for all PAAm forms.
sections.processing:
Polyacrylamide is article-processed mainly from water-based solutions, inverse emulsions, or hydrogel precursor mixtures rather than as an ordinary thermoplastic melt. Important operations include emulsion inversion and solution make-up for coating, papermaking, and water-treatment dosing; casting between plates or in molds; photopolymer vat printing of hydrogel articles; and, for selected high-molecular-weight grades or blends, solution spinning and electrospinning. Commercial-emulsion handling requires gentle storage agitation and low-shear transfer, followed by strong localized mixing only where emulsion first contacts dilution water so individual particles invert and dissolve. Water hardness, pH, temperature, concentration, aging time, dissolved iron, oxygen, and order of addition govern fisheyes, incomplete dissolution, viscosity loss, and solution life. Hydrogel shaping additionally requires control of resin rheology, oxygen inhibition, exposure dose, layer release, washing, and swelling after cure.

The SNF handbook's numbers are guidance for its inverse-emulsion products, not for every polyacrylamide. It specifies indoor storage at 5–30 °C, minimal shear during pumping and storage, water below 30 °C for make-up, emulsion addition into water, and about 5 g/L active polymer (10–15 g/L commercial emulsion) as an efficient inversion concentration; harder water above roughly 300–400 ppm as CaCO3 slows inversion. As a distinct shaped-hydrogel example, Wang and Li printed their stated acrylamide/bis-acrylamide, tartrazine, and LAP resin at room temperature by DLP using 100 µm layers, 8 s first-layer and 7 s subsequent exposures, then rinsed the parts and post-exposed them for 10 min under a 15 W, 365 nm lamp. Those settings belong to that formulation and printer, and the article-forming exposure schedule is reported here as Processing even though the underlying network chemistry belongs in Synthesis.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The homopolymer consists of acrylamide-derived units on a carbon backbone and is nonionic. Related anionic materials can contain acrylate groups introduced by copolymerization or hydrolysis. Crosslinking connects chains into a three-dimensional network that retains water rather than dissolving as separate chains. Network composition and crosslink density influence the amount of water a particular hydrogel holds.
sections.properties: Linear polyacrylamide can increase the viscosity of water, with molecular weight an important factor in the response. Long chains are useful for flocculation and for reducing friction in flowing fluids. Crosslinked polyacrylamide hydrogels can be soft and highly swollen, but increasing crosslinker content can make a network stiffer. In one tensile study, Young’s modulus increased from 19 ± 2 kPa for a 1% crosslinker formulation to 157 ± 5 kPa for a 9% formulation; measured elongation at break fell from 66 ± 6% to 30 ± 4%. These results describe the tested hydrogels and tensile method, rather than all linear and crosslinked polyacrylamides.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PAM-based flocculants serve municipal water and wastewater treatment, sludge dewatering, mining, oil and gas extraction, papermaking and agriculture. These industrial families include charged copolymers as well as nonionic PAM. In sludge treatment, polymer chains can bridge small suspended particles into larger flocs that settle and can be dewatered more readily. The appropriate charge and dose depend on the sludge: a treatment plant must select a formulation for the suspension, rather than assume that any PAM grade will perform equally. In high-volume hydraulic fracturing, a commercial PAM formulation is used as a friction reducer: long chains suppress turbulent vortices in the flowing fluid and reduce pumping costs. The same flow can break chains, potentially reducing drag-reduction performance.

Purchasing. SNF offers powders, emulsions, liquids and beads through industrial technical-sales channels. Charge type, molecular architecture and formulation must be specified; a finished emulsion is not entirely active polymer.

Scale and evidence limits. SNF’s undated page accessed in September 2026 reports 1,670,000 tonnes of production capacity across its global network, order 10^6 tonnes. The page does not supply a reporting year or an unambiguous active-polymer/time basis for that figure; it is not a homopolymer consumption statistic.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A sludge-derived Pseudomonas putida strain, HI47, produced an extracellular amidase that converted some PAM amide groups to carboxyl groups. The researchers also observed a reduction in molecular mass and smaller oligomeric products. Side-group conversion, assay removal and complete mineralization are different endpoints. In a separate study of a commercial friction reducer, a sharp capillary contraction broke PAM chains mechanically; the authors observed a narrower molecular-weight distribution and no detectable change in chemical composition, unlike the formation of carbonyl groups in their radical-induced chemical degradation comparison.

Timescales: In the selected-strain culture, PAM-assay removal was 31.1% after seven days at 30 °C and shaking at 100 rpm. With added yeast extract, the authors reported 47.2% removal after five days in a separate nutrient comparison. These values describe specific culture and assay conditions, not the lifetime of PAM in a treatment plant or soil. In the capillary experiment, a single pass at a deformation-rate parameter of 4 × 10⁶ s⁻¹ reduced peak molecular weight from approximately 10⁷ to 7 × 10⁵ Da. This is an extreme flow experiment, not a time for biodegradation.

Environmental persistence: The experiments did not establish conversion of all PAM carbon to carbon dioxide. Dissolution and removal from a measured solution cannot by themselves demonstrate mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The selected-strain experiment demonstrates biological transformation of PAM in culture, including loss of amide groups and reduction in molecular mass. It does not recover reusable PAM, and it is not evidence that every wastewater plant achieves the laboratory result. Material-reclamation routes remain an evidence gap in this entry.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The SNF polyacrylamide-emulsion guide separates the polymer from residual acrylamide, hydrocarbon carrier and surfactants in the delivered product. Its 2013 formulations contain residual free monomer, so a polymer identity alone is insufficient to assess the concentrate. Handling instructions and the safety data sheet should cover the actual emulsion or powder, dilution operation and ingredient package, rather than treating all PAM solutions as compositionally identical.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Polyacrylamide includes linear water-soluble chains and crosslinked, water-swollen networks, which serve different purposes and cannot share a single property specification. In a series of model hydrogels, increasing crosslinker content from 1% to 9% raised tensile stiffness while reducing elongation at break. The same study found that the lower-crosslinker specimens responded differently in tension and compression, illustrating why both network preparation and loading mode matter. Molecular weight, ionic modification, water content and measurement conditions add further variability.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical chain growth forms the water-soluble polyacrylamide backbone. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another.

sections.overview: Poly(acrylic acid) (PAA) is a polymer with carboxylic acid groups along its carbon backbone. It is a weak polyelectrolyte: the groups can ionize in water, and their charge depends on solution conditions. Linear PAA is used in dispersant applications, while neutralized and crosslinked formulations provide distinct material states. The behavior of a solution or hydrogel depends on its composition and environment.
sections.history: Poly(acrylic acid) has a broad history that includes soluble polymers and crosslinked gels, which should not be assigned one common commercialization date. A particularly influential branch is documented by Harold Brown’s BFGoodrich patent filed in 1952 and granted in 1957. It describes lightly crosslinked acrylic-acid polymers that swell in water and function as thickeners, suspension aids and film-forming materials. This research helped establish the formulation-oriented history of acrylic-acid polymers. The milestone applies to those crosslinked compositions; it is not the first synthesis date of linear PAA or evidence that every PAA product has the same gel behavior.
sections.nomenclature: PAA is the abbreviation for poly(acrylic acid). The record denotes the acrylic-acid homopolymer; polyacrylate salts, acrylic-acid copolymers, crosslinked PAA hydrogels, and a particular neutralized formulation are not aliases for the base polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(acrylic acid) (PAA) is the vinyl-addition polymer made from acrylic acid; a common route is free-radical polymerization in water or another appropriate medium. A bounded aqueous example removes oxygen with nitrogen and uses the potassium persulfate/sodium thiosulfate redox pair to initiate acrylic-acid polymerization; this is a low-molar-mass PAA preparation rather than a universal PAA recipe. PAA can also be made indirectly when tert-butyl acrylate is radical-polymerized and its ester groups are acid-cleaved. In one patent example, AIBN and a protected aminoethanethiol chain-transfer agent are used in toluene before acid treatment converts the poly(tert-butyl acrylate) product to amino-terminated PAA. Initiator system, medium, conversion, and chain-transfer-agent amount are route controls for molar mass and end groups. Those linear-polymer routes are distinct from later crosslinking used to make a PAA hydrogel.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Poly(acrylic acid) (PAA) mechanics are especially state-dependent: dry polymer, neutralized aqueous network, and swollen hydrogel are different materials. In hydrogels, crosslink chemistry/concentration, ionization and pH, water content, fillers, temperature, and strain rate control modulus, strength, and extensibility. An open tensile study reports a neat PAA hydrogel at 152 kPa Young's modulus, 119 kPa tensile strength, and 969% elongation at break; adding 0.05% GO-based covalent crosslinker gave 161 kPa, 248 kPa, and 4078%, respectively. A separate open pH-sensitive acrylic-acid hydrogel study likewise reports that network crosslinking and swelling change tensile response. These hydrogel endpoints do not represent dry PAA or a universal polymer value.
sections.processing:
PAA is commonly converted from aqueous solution into hydrogel films, molded gels, superabsorbent networks, patterned or layered actuators, and substrate coatings. For network articles, the shaping operation may be coupled to cure in a flat mold or template; the underlying polymer-forming chemistry belongs in Synthesis, while filling, heat or radiation exposure, demolding, washing, swelling, drying, and patterning belong in Processing. Solution neutralization, viscosity, degassing, crosslinker and initiator distribution, mold heat transfer and exotherm, layer-to-layer interpenetration, residual-sol removal, and hydration history govern cavitation, uniformity, swelling, adhesion, and final dimensions.

Lee and co-workers provide a bounded flat-film example. They degassed an 80%-neutralized acrylic-acid formulation by nitrogen bubbling for 1 h, filled an 11.5 x 15 x 0.1 cm glass template, and heated it on a 55 °C plate for 2 h before demolding a freestanding film; sequentially casting a second formulation made adhered bilayers, and crosslinker loading controlled swelling and curvature. In a distinct PAA/graphene-oxide-crosslinker experiment, the authors sonicated the crosslinker/initiator dispersion for 30 min, mixed it into the formulation, filled a two-plate glass mold separated by a 2 mm PTFE spacer, and held it at 58 °C for 4 h under inert atmosphere before demolding. These conditions apply only to the reported formulations and mold geometries.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PAA chains have pendant carboxylic acid groups that can lose protons in aqueous solution. Ionization changes charge along the chain and thus the balance of electrostatic repulsion and other interactions. In fluorescence and diffusion measurements on a series of labeled PAA samples, chains below about 16.5 kDa number-average molar mass did not show the pH-responsive conformational change observed in higher-mass samples. The authors reported that their short chains remained extended over the measured pH range. Crosslinking connects chains into a network rather than leaving them as independently dissolved molecules.
sections.properties: The ionization of PAA changes with pH, which can alter aqueous chain conformation and interactions. In one series of labeled PAA samples, higher-molar-mass chains displayed a pH-dependent transition between compact and more extended states; samples below about 16.5 kDa number-average molar mass did not show that transition. The threshold and response describe the experimental polymers, solvent and measurement method rather than every PAA formulation. Crosslinking creates a different material state: the connected network can hold water as a hydrogel, whose swelling and response also depend on network composition.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Linear acrylic-acid homopolymers and their neutralized grades are dispersants for detergents, cleaning products, water treatment and industrial formulations. Crosslinked absorbent products are a different material form and cannot be treated as equivalent to this linear acid resin. In water-based cleaning formulations, a dispersant can keep mineral particles from collecting into deposits. Dow identifies ACUSOL 402 as a partially neutralized acrylic-acid homopolymer and lists calcium-carbonate dispersion, scale inhibition and prevention of clay redeposition among its functions. These claims concern a specified low-molecular-weight commercial grade.

Purchasing. BASF’s Sokalan PA range provides an industrial supplier channel: it identifies PA 110 S as a free-acid grade and PA 25 CL PN as partially neutralized. Dow lists ACUSOL 402 at 48% solids and molecular weight 2,000 g/mol. The formulation’s shipped mass therefore includes material other than polymer solids, and its molecular-weight specification should not be assumed for a high-molecular-weight absorbent network. Specify free acid versus neutralized polymer, molecular weight and supply concentration for the intended formulation.

Scale and evidence limits. BASF lists both acrylic homopolymers under Sokalan PA and acrylic copolymers under Sokalan CP. The existence of this multi-grade portfolio demonstrates supply to industrial formulators but does not reveal the mass sold of the acid homopolymer. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was found in the checked open sources.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In a laboratory study, purified monooxygenase PCX02514 with NADPH cleaved low-molecular-weight PAA into shorter chains. Mass spectrometry detected a C6H10O5 product consistent with a hydroxyl-terminated acrylic-acid dimer, although alternative formation mechanisms remained under discussion. A decrease in molecular mass is not complete mineralization.

Timescales: For PAA of approximately 2,000 Da, the researchers incubated enzyme, NADPH and PAA in pH 7.4 buffer for five hours at 30 °C. The number-average molecular mass decreased by about 34% relative to the control in their measurement. This is a short-chain substrate under selected enzyme conditions, not an environmental half-life.

Environmental persistence: In a review of radiolabeled PAA river-water tests, the reported 135-day mineralization to carbon dioxide decreased from 20% for a 1 kDa sample to 7% for a 10 kDa sample. Tests using pre-adapted river water or water mixed with sediment gave different outcomes, illustrating the importance of the inoculum. These are partial results for the stated low-molecular-weight substrates and controlled media, not lifetimes for high-molecular-weight or crosslinked products. The purified-enzyme experiment measures chain cleavage rather than carbon dioxide production.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The enzyme experiment demonstrates cleavage of a low-molecular-weight PAA substrate into smaller molecules. It does not establish recovery of reusable PAA or a commercial recycling process, and its enzyme and cofactor requirements would need evaluation in a practical treatment. Evidence for material reclamation remains to be added.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For the research-grade PAA powder Polyacrylic Acid 250,000, FUJIFILM Wako’s Japanese SDS dated 3 October 2023 classifies suspected carcinogenicity and repeated-exposure respiratory toxicity. This is a dated supplier classification for the identified powder, not a universal assessment of diluted or neutralized PAA formulations. The document recommends containing dust, local exhaust, eye and skin protection, and separation from strong oxidizers; airborne-powder exposure therefore deserves particular attention.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Linear acid polymer, neutralized forms and crosslinked hydrogels should be distinguished when comparing PAA materials. Solution pH and molecular weight influence chain conformation, while network composition affects a gel's response. In one study, adding a functionalized graphene-oxide crosslinker changed the stretchability and toughness of a PAA hydrogel relative to the authors' comparison gel. Those findings describe the tested formulations and are not a general property value for PAA.

sections.overview: Thermoplastic polyesters are melt-processable polymers with ester linkages in their chains. PET and PBT are familiar members, but different diols and diacids give rise to distinct polymers within the family. Their products include fibers, films, molded components and formulated engineering resins. Crystallinity, reinforcement and blending add further variation to the properties of a finished material.
sections.history: Thermoplastic polyesters developed through several distinct inventions. John Rex Whinfield and James Tennant Dickson’s terephthalate-polyester work at the Calico Printers Association, with a 1941 British priority, established a route to useful synthetic fibers. The family subsequently expanded from fiber-forming PET to molding materials. Celanese dates commercial PBT to 1970, when Celanex helped establish a separate engineering-plastics branch. These milestones show how changing the glycol component and developing processing methods created different commercial materials. Fibers, films, packaging and molded parts consequently have related but different histories; there is no single introduction year for the whole family.
sections.nomenclature: Thermoplastic polyester is a family name rather than one fixed composition. PET, PBT, and related linear polyester members fall within the boundary, while segmented copolyester elastomers, wholly aromatic liquid-crystalline polyesters, unsaturated-polyester thermosets, and a single commercial grade are separate scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: The principal thermoplastic-polyester families are linear step-growth polymers made from bifunctional diacids or diesters and diols. Representative semiaromatic members pair terephthalic acid or dimethyl terephthalate with ethylene glycol for PET, 1,3-propanediol for PTT, or 1,4-butanediol for PBT; copolyesters introduce additional diacids or diols to alter crystallization and transition temperatures. Manufacture generally has two reaction stages. Direct esterification of a diacid releases water, whereas ester interchange of a dialkyl ester releases methanol and forms hydroxy-terminated oligomers. Melt polycondensation then proceeds at higher temperature and reduced pressure while excess glycol is removed, shifting the equilibrium toward high molar mass. One cited PET process directly esterifies terephthalic acid with ethylene glycol and uses cobalt-, manganese-, and antimony-containing components during polycondensation. A distinct continuous PBT process transesterifies dimethyl terephthalate with excess 1,4-butanediol using a titanium catalyst, then precondenses and polycondenses under subatmospheric pressure while recovering and recycling butanediol-rich vapors. Monomer purity, near-equimolar functional-group balance, catalyst and stabilizer choice, temperature, vacuum, residence time, and removal of condensates control conversion, molar mass, color, and side reactions. Segmented copolyester elastomers, wholly aromatic liquid-crystalline polyesters, and unsaturated thermoset polyester resins use related ester chemistry but have distinct feedstocks or network formation and are treated separately.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Thermoplastic polyesters cover chemically and mechanically distinct materials, from rigid semicrystalline PET-, PBT-, PTT-, PEN-, and PCT-type engineering resins to amorphous copolyesters and highly oriented aromatic liquid-crystalline members. Rigid semiaromatic grades commonly combine tensile stiffness and strength with dimensional stability and useful creep resistance; depending on temperature, crystallinity, molecular orientation, and impact modification, they may yield and draw extensively or fail in a notch-sensitive manner. Amorphous or heavily comonomer-modified grades generally trade some stiffness, chemical resistance, and high-temperature load retention for transparency or toughness, while wholly aromatic liquid-crystalline copolyesters have a separate, strongly anisotropic response. A single family property range would therefore obscure consequential differences in chemistry, morphology, formulation, and material form.

Mechanical response is governed by backbone rigidity and comonomer sequence, molar mass and chain degradation, crystal fraction and lamellar morphology, physical aging, thermal history, and uniaxial or biaxial orientation. Glass or mineral reinforcement raises modulus and load retention but introduces fiber-orientation, weld-line, and transverse-strength effects; impact modifiers, plasticizers, flame retardants, nucleants, recycled content, and blends can shift the stiffness–toughness balance. Although many engineering polyesters absorb relatively little moisture in service, hot-water aging and moisture present during melt processing can hydrolyze ester chains and reduce strength or ductility. Temperature relative to the glass transition, loading rate and duration, notch geometry, specimen thickness, conditioning, and molding or drawing direction must accompany comparisons.

As one bounded numerical example, BASF reports typical values at 23 °C for uncoloured Ultradur B 4520, an unreinforced PBT standard injection-molding grade. ISO 527-1/-2 measurements give a tensile modulus of 2400 MPa, yield stress of 55 MPa and yield strain of 3.7% at 50 mm/min, with nominal strain at break greater than 50%; ISO 899-1 gives a 1000 h tensile creep modulus of 1200 MPa at no more than 0.5% strain and 23 °C. The same sheet lists ISO 179/1eA notched Charpy impact strength of 5 kJ/m² at 23 °C. These are grade-datasheet typical values, not specifications or representative values for PET, copolyesters, reinforced compounds, oriented film or fiber, or the full thermoplastic-polyester family.
sections.processing:
Thermoplastic polyesters span semicrystalline PET and PBT, amorphous or modified copolyesters, and grades engineered for distinct melt strength and crystallization behavior, so no single processing window represents the family. Important conversion routes include injection molding; profile, pipe, tube, sheet, cast-film and monofilament extrusion; fiber spinning; extrusion coating; thermoforming of extruded sheet; extrusion blow molding; and injection or reheat stretch-blow molding of suitable PET and copolyester grades. Grade selection must match flow, melt strength, crystallization rate, transparency, orientation, heat setting, and the intended cooling or reheating sequence.

Feed preparation is central because moisture hydrolyzes polyester chains in the melt, reducing molecular mass and viscosity even when visible bubbles are absent. Pellets, color concentrate, and regrind should be dried to the grade supplier's limit, moved through a closed dry-air system, and protected from condensation and reabsorption. Processing controls include screw design and speed, shear heating, melt temperature, residence time, back pressure, hot-runner or die stagnation, injection/hold pressure, gate freeze, mold and cooling temperature, extrusion filtration and take-up, sheet gauge, preform reheat uniformity, axial and hoop stretch, parison strength, blow pressure, quench, heat setting, and annealing. Cooling rate and orientation determine crystallinity, clarity, shrinkage, warpage, and dimensional stability. Stoppages require temperature reduction or purging, and regrind should be checked for viscosity loss rather than assigned a universal recycle fraction. Polymerization and solid-state molecular-weight build belong in Synthesis; pellet drying, melting, shaping, orientation, cooling, and heat setting belong here.

BASF's Ultradur guide directly documents injection molding and extrusion of its PBT grades into film, pipes, profiles, sheet, monofilaments, fibers, and coated products, and it ties moisture, residence time, mold temperature, shear, cooling, and regrind history to hydrolysis, degradation, crystallization, and warpage. Eastman's separate guides establish extrusion blow molding for its high-viscosity PET-family copolyesters and thermoforming for named extruded Eastar, Tritan, and Eastalite sheets. For one bounded injection example, Unitika lists its own homogeneous and copolymerized PET molding resins: crystalline material is dried at 130 °C for 8 h or 140 °C for 6 h; its example uses 255–290 °C nozzle/cylinder settings depending on resin type, 150 rpm screw speed, an 8 s injection, 16 s cooling, and 27 s total cycle with chilled molds in the 15–30 °C range. These are supplier examples for those Unitika PET products and mold setup, not family-wide polyester settings.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyester chains contain ester linkages formed from diol and acid or ester-derived components. PET and PBT can develop crystalline regions alongside less ordered material, but their crystallization behavior differs. Cooling and molding conditions influence the morphology of a part. Reinforced grades and polymer alloys add other phases to the base polyester, so their structure is more complex than that of an unfilled homopolymer.
sections.properties: Crystallinity contributes to hardness, stiffness and chemical resistance in the PET and PBT materials discussed in a supplier manual. In the supplier’s processing comparison, PBT crystallizes rapidly enough to permit short molding cycles in cooler tooling, whereas its PET products need warmer molds to develop crystallinity quickly. This distinction concerns the materials and processing context in the manual, not a single cycle time for every polyester. The supplier also offers reinforced, impact-modified and alloy products that change the balance of properties. Temperature and moisture exposure affect the performance of an article, and melt processing requires attention to the material's moisture condition. No one thermal or mechanical value describes the entire family.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Thermoplastic polyesters span distinct markets: PET is used in bottles and packaging, while PBT engineering grades serve automotive parts, electrical connectors and precision components. The family must be selected by polymer and grade rather than treated as one interchangeable material. For molded engineering components, BASF describes its Ultradur PBT grades as combining low water absorption with dimensional stability and chemical resistance. Its HPP grades are designed to crystallize faster and flow readily during injection molding; the intended benefit is shorter processing cycles for dimensionally demanding parts. These claims apply to the named PBT product line rather than all polyester grades.

Purchasing. Purchase the named resin and conversion grade through its producer or material supplier. BASF lists unreinforced and reinforced PBT grades and separately identifies PBT blends; PET resin is also sold directly to large packaging converters.

Scale and evidence limits. Textile Exchange reports about 78 million tonnes of polyester fiber produced worldwide in 2024. This is a fiber-market measure, dominated by textile uses, and excludes the family’s separate bottle and engineering-resin markets; it is not total polyester purchases.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PET is one directly studied family example. In a hydrothermal experiment on milled bottle material, ester-bond cleavage yielded a solid rich in terephthalic acid; potassium hydroxide changed the distribution toward soluble salts and additional decarboxylation products. In another study, an engineered cutinase hydrolyzed low-crystallinity PET microparticles to soluble products under controlled aqueous conditions. Both examples concern PET; other polyester chemistries require separate study rather than assignment of PET’s products.

Timescales: The hydrothermal screening treated milled PET bottle material at 350 °C for a 20-minute residence time in water, with and without added alkali. Separately, an engineered cutinase converted 90% of a PET microparticle substrate with 9% crystallinity in 17.0 ± 3.4 hours at 70 °C, as monitored by the authors’ pH-stat method. The particle preparation, enzyme and elevated temperature are central to that result. Neither engineered treatment supplies a family-wide environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Enzyme-catalyzed depolymerization to soluble compounds is not the same endpoint as conversion of all PET carbon to carbon dioxide and biomass. The controlled reactor experiments do not establish how PET persists in an uncontrolled environment, much less give a shared lifetime for other thermoplastic polyesters. Composition, crystallinity and article form must be identified when comparing environmental evidence.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Reclamation depends on polyester identity and the waste stream. PET provides directly supported examples of several major routes. Industrial mechanical bottle recycling sorts, washes and dries flakes, then uses decontamination, extrusion, melt filtration and pelletizing. Chemical glycolysis yields BHET and oligomers for purification and reuse, while Eastman reports commercial methanolysis operation at Kingsport from early 2024. Laboratory hydrothermal depolymerization is another PET recovery example.

Carbios reports enzymatic PET depolymerization followed by purification of terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol at demonstration scale, with 100 packaging/textile-waste batches reported in July 2026. These PET-specific examples establish a range of recovery technologies; their catalysts, operating conditions, feedstock tolerance and commercial maturity must not be transferred to every thermoplastic polyester.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Thermoplastic polyester family hot processing requires assessment of the actual formulation and thermal history. As an explicitly bounded thermoplastic-polyester example, BASF’s PBT guide warns about fumes from excessive temperature or residence time and recommends extraction over the barrel; its caution about corrosive products concerns halogen-containing flame-retarded grades. HSE supplies the general temperature-control and ventilation framework; PBT-specific temperature settings or emission compositions are not transferred to this entry.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Individual polyesters have different chemical structures and crystallization rates, so PET and PBT data are not interchangeable. Glass reinforcement, impact modifiers and other additives distinguish compounds from their base resin. Part orientation and processing history can affect dimensional and mechanical behavior. A datasheet for one grade or an alloy should therefore be interpreted within its own formulation and testing conditions.

sections.overview:
Poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) is a thermoplastic polyester whose chains contain ethylene and aromatic terephthalate units linked by ester groups. It is made by polycondensation after either direct esterification of terephthalic acid with ethylene glycol or ester interchange between dimethyl terephthalate and ethylene glycol. PET is used in textile fibers, films, and food and beverage packaging, as well as molded products.

PET can be made into largely amorphous, transparent articles or semicrystalline materials, depending on its composition and processing history. Cooling, stretching, and subsequent heat treatment influence the structure and hence the balance of optical, thermal, mechanical, and barrier performance. PET is therefore a material platform rather than a single set of properties: molecular mass, copolymer units, additives, and the intended conversion process distinguish commercial grades.
sections.history: PET emerged from the Calico Printers Association research of John Rex Whinfield and James Tennant Dickson. Their terephthalate-polyester patent has a 1941 British priority and describes polymers that could be drawn into fibers, establishing the textile-oriented beginnings of PET. Packaging later created a second major historical role. At DuPont, Nathaniel Wyeth began investigating beverage containers in 1967 and developed a biaxially oriented PET bottle, patented in 1973, that could withstand carbonated drinks. His work connected polymer processing with container design and helped make PET bottles a familiar alternative to glass. Bottle manufacture was therefore a later application breakthrough, not the invention of PET itself.
sections.nomenclature: PET is the standard abbreviation and PETE is also used. The canonical name identifies the ethylene-terephthalate homopolymer and should not be used as a synonym for all thermoplastic polyesters.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) is a terephthalate polyester made from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid or a terephthalate diester such as dimethyl terephthalate. The ester route performs ester interchange with ethylene glycol to form hydroxyethyl terephthalate intermediates and methanol, then melt polycondenses while removing ethylene glycol. Direct esterification from terephthalic acid similarly forms oligomer before polycondensation, with removal of water needed to advance esterification. Manganese, zinc, cobalt, and antimony catalysts are documented source-specific choices for ester interchange or polycondensation. These route variants produce PET; they do not establish a single universal catalyst package or reactor sequence.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PET is a semicrystalline polyester whose stiffness, strength, and ductility vary markedly with intrinsic viscosity or molar mass, crystallinity and morphology, orientation from drawing or stretch-blow processing, copolymer/contaminant content, and thermal, moisture, and aging history. Test temperature and strain rate are especially consequential near the glass-transition region; hydrolysis, thermo-oxidative processing, physical aging, and repeated recycling can change chain length and the balance of brittle and ductile response. In an open study of filament-based printed recycled bottle-grade PET with no intentionally added HDPE, the batch of three specimens printed one at a time gave a Young's modulus of 1.7 ± 0.3 GPa and maximum tensile stress of 44.8 ± 7.7 MPa, whereas three specimens printed simultaneously gave 2.1 ± 0.1 GPa and 47.9 ± 3.2 MPa. The interlayer cooling delays were 27 s and 85 s, respectively; these labels describe printing schedules, not single-specimen measurements. Those figures apply only to that recycled feedstock, print construction, and tensile protocol—not virgin PET, bottle preforms, drawn film, or fiber. A second open study of post-consumer recycled PET further compares physical aging and crosshead-speed effects, so its results should likewise remain tied to its recycled feedstock and conditioning.
sections.processing:
Poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) is converted into injection-molded parts and bottle preforms, injection-stretch-blow-molded containers, extruded sheet, film, profile and strapping, thermoformed packaging, and melt-spun fibers and nonwovens. Grade intrinsic viscosity, copolymer content, additives, recycled-feed contamination, and thermal history distinguish bottle, sheet, fiber, film, and engineering-molding feeds. PET is hygroscopic: pellets and clean regrind must be dried and protected from reabsorption because melt moisture causes hydrolytic molecular-mass loss. Melt temperature, shear and residence time also affect discoloration and acetaldehyde; rapid cooling retains transparent amorphous preforms or sheet, while mold temperature, reheating, biaxial stretch, draw ratio, cooling, and heat setting control crystallinity, orientation, shrinkage, and barrier performance.

Celanese's polyester manual directly covers injection molding plus profile, tube, monofilament, melt-blowing, and other extrusion routes and emphasizes that Impet PET grades require especially careful drying. The U.S. International Trade Commission independently documents preform injection followed by stretch blow molding, as well as sheet extrusion, thermoforming, and strapping. As one bounded injection example, Unitika's published homogeneous PET-resin setup uses 270-290 °C at the nozzle and front/middle cylinder, 250-270 °C at the rear, a 15-30 °C mold, 150 rpm screw speed, and 16 s cooling; it warns that mold temperatures above 40 °C can prevent complete solidification in that process. Those settings are Unitika's example for its disclosed resin categories, not a universal PET window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PET chains consist of ethylene terephthalate units joined through ester linkages. The polymer can be quenched from the melt into a largely amorphous solid or allowed to crystallize into a mixture of ordered and disordered regions. Crystalline lamellae can grow into larger spherulitic structures, while portions of the surrounding amorphous chains remain constrained near the crystals. Drawing can orient the chains and induce additional ordering or crystallization; cooling, stretching, and heat treatment therefore produce different structures in films, fibers, bottles, and molded articles.
sections.properties: Amorphous PET can be transparent, while the amount and organization of crystals influence optical appearance, thermal response, and barrier performance. The glass transition marks a change in mobility of amorphous chain segments; in semicrystalline PET, segments close to crystallites can remain more constrained than the mobile amorphous fraction. PET also provides a useful barrier to oxygen and water vapor, although permeability depends on the material and its morphology. In the melt, viscosity depends on molecular weight and chain architecture as well as the rate of deformation, which matters when selecting resin for a particular conversion process. A crystallization review reports that incorporating diethylene glycol units can lower both the glass transition and melting temperature, with a reported decrease of about 1–3 K per mole percent of those units. This compositional relationship concerns the copolyesters examined in the cited literature and should not be used as a universal specification for all PET products.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PET is used for beverage bottles, sheet, strapping and thermoformed containers, as well as textile fibers and other molded products. Its transparency and useful oxygen and water-vapor barrier help explain its use in packaging; orientation, crystallinity and the complete container design influence actual performance. The USITC investigation covers a packaging-resin market and does not include the entire fiber market.

Purchasing. Industrial buyers obtain specified PET resin grades from producers, importers or distributors. The USITC describes rail and truck supply and direct importing by larger purchasers. Bottle, sheet and fiber conversion can require different resin specifications, so a polymer name alone does not establish a suitable grade.

Scale and evidence limits. The USITC reports apparent U.S. consumption of about 7.3 billion pounds in 2020, approximately 3.3 million metric tonnes, for PET resin within its investigation scope. This measures domestic shipments plus imports, not actual purchase orders, all PET grades or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Hydrolysis cleaves PET ester chains to terephthalic-acid- and ethylene-glycol-derived products; further reactions depend on treatment severity. Glycolysis with ethylene glycol instead yields BHET (bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate), dimers and oligomers. These deliberate-treatment products are distinct from the chemical and physical changes observed during weathering. In a separate accelerated UV study, PET film developed increased surface roughness and particles, with humidity and temperature affecting the changes.

Timescales: A milled-bottle hydrolysis study used 350 °C water for 20 minutes, with and without KOH. In the separate UV study, PET films exposed at 50 °C for 20 days showed more surface particle formation under saturated humidity than under dry conditions. Neither duration represents a general environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Surface cracking and fragmentation produce smaller pieces rather than establishing mineralization. The controlled hydrolysis and weathering experiments do not provide a transferable time to mineralization in soil, water or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Mechanical recycling of collected PET bottles is an established industrial route: bottles are sorted, reduced to flakes, washed and dried, then decontaminated and reprocessed through extrusion, melt filtration and pelletizing. Commercial vacuum-treatment systems can also restore intrinsic viscosity. The EREMA/Texplast operating example documents this sequence; feedstock quality, decontamination and intended use determine recyclate suitability.

Chemical recovery includes glycolysis, methanolysis and hydrolysis. Glycolysis with ethylene glycol produces bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET), dimers and oligomers. A laboratory study of coloured bottles, trays and polyester textile wastes used biobased ethylene glycol and zinc acetate, followed by filtration, crystallization and activated-carbon purification. Methanolysis has reached commercial operation: Eastman reports its Kingsport polyester-renewal facility became operational in early 2024 and achieved on-spec production and revenue. The separately cited hydrothermal study demonstrates laboratory monomer-derived product recovery; solvent/catalyst management and product purification remain process-specific requirements.

Enzymatic depolymerization is another recovery route. Carbios describes pretreated PET reacting with water and an enzyme, followed by residue filtration, activated-carbon treatment and separation of terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol. Its July 2026 report documents 100 batches from packaging and textile waste at its Clermont-Ferrand demonstration plant and an expanded licensing offering. This establishes demonstration-scale operation; it does not establish widespread commercial deployment. Reactor conversion and material recycling do not imply rapid biodegradation in the environment.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Poly(ethylene terephthalate) hot processing requires assessment of the actual formulation and thermal history. As an explicitly bounded thermoplastic-polyester example, BASF’s PBT guide warns about fumes from excessive temperature or residence time and recommends extraction over the barrel; its caution about corrosive products concerns halogen-containing flame-retarded grades. HSE supplies the general temperature-control and ventilation framework; PBT-specific temperature settings or emission compositions are not transferred to this entry.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PET absorbs moisture, and residual water can promote chain cleavage at melt-processing temperatures; drying and control of thermal exposure are therefore important. Heat and oxygen can also change molecular weight during processing, affecting viscosity and the properties of the finished article. In recycled PET, prior use and repeated melt processing can alter molecular structure, while chain extenders can produce longer or branched chains with different flow behavior. Composition, crystallinity, orientation, and thermal history must also be considered when comparing PET products: a property measured for one grade or article should not be assumed for every PET material. Residual diethylene glycol can enter the chain during manufacture: the review describes commercial PET grades generally containing around 2–5 mol% of the corresponding unit. Its presence also changes crystallization kinetics, so thermal histories cannot be compared without considering composition.
