sections.overview: Thermoplastic polyimides are imide-containing materials designed to be processed from the melt. Their polymer chemistry and molecular architecture distinguish them from other polyimide systems that are cured into networks. A documented route forms a poly(amic acid) intermediate before conversion to the imide. Commercial examples can be injection molded or extruded into components, films and fibers.
sections.history: Thermoplastic polyimides developed through efforts to make heat-resistant imide polymers suitable for melt fabrication. Mitsui Toatsu’s AURUM lineage is documented by a Canadian trademark application filed in 1989 and a declaration of use in 1994. Those are commercial-record milestones, not a claimed first synthesis of the entire class. Mitsui Chemicals’ subsequent technical literature describes injection-molded and extruded materials for precision machinery, semiconductor equipment, electrical connectors, wire coatings and transportation components. Reinforcement and wear-resistant formulations extended this application range. Different thermoplastic PI chemistries have separate histories, and AURUM’s chronology should not be generalized to every melt-processable polyimide.
sections.nomenclature: TPI is the abbreviation used for thermoplastic polyimide. The record denotes linear polyimides selected for thermoplastic processing; thermosetting polyimides, crosslinked polyimide networks, and other named imide-containing families are not alternate names for this subfamily. The processing category can overlap the separately indexed polyetherimide chemistry family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Thermoplastic polyimides (TPIs) are linear polyimides whose dianhydride/diamine structures and controlled molar mass permit melt flow without creating a covalent network. They are commonly synthesized by reacting an aromatic tetracarboxylic dianhydride with an approximately equimolar aromatic diamine in a dry polar aprotic solvent to form a high-molar-mass polyamic-acid precursor. Flexible ether, methylene, or other non-coplanar linkages and asymmetric monomers reduce chain packing and melt viscosity relative to rigid, infusible polyimides. The precursor is converted to imide rings by cyclodehydration. Thermal imidization removes water on heating, while chemical imidization uses a dehydrating reagent such as acetic anhydride with a base catalyst; a one-pot high-temperature solution route can combine precursor formation and imidization. One cited powder process reacts tetracarboxylic-acid and diamine components in an alkylene-glycol-based medium, heats the polyamic acid through imidization, precipitates polyimide powder, and washes and dries it. A distinct process prepares a melt-processable aromatic polyimide in solution and uses either thermal or chemical imidization. Slight stoichiometric offset or monofunctional end cappers control molar mass and stabilize melt viscosity. Monomer purity, moisture exclusion, addition rate, solids content, solvent, end-capper amount, and imidization completeness control chain length, cyclic oligomers, residual solvent, and melt processability. Crosslinked or otherwise infusible thermoset polyimide networks are outside this melt-processable scope. Polyetherimides are separately indexed by chemistry and can also be thermoplastic.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Thermoplastic polyimides are linear, melt-processable members of the broader polyimide family; they should not be conflated with insoluble thermoset polyimide networks. Separately indexed polyetherimides can also be thermoplastic. Aromatic rings and imide linkages give commercial TPI resins high glass-transition temperatures, useful strength and stiffness, dimensional stability, wear resistance and comparatively good creep retention at temperatures where many ordinary thermoplastics soften. An unfilled grade can nevertheless be tough and ductile, whereas carbon- or glass-filled structural grades are much stiffer and stronger but typically less extensible and more direction-dependent; PTFE, graphite and other bearing formulations deliberately exchange some tensile performance for friction and wear behavior. Film, injection-molded, composite and additively manufactured forms therefore need separate mechanical descriptions.

Response varies with dianhydride/diamine architecture and flexible linkages, molar mass, physical aging or crystallization/annealing state, residual stress, and thermal or oxidative exposure. Fiber identity, fraction and orientation, lubricating fillers and interfaces, part thickness, gate or flow direction, and weld lines control filled moldings. Water absorption is modest rather than zero, so conditioning and feed drying matter, especially during the unusually hot melt-processing cycle. In material-extrusion printing, filament drying, nozzle/chamber/bed temperature, raster orientation, layer height, void fraction and interlayer adhesion can dominate the nominal resin response. Test temperature relative to the glass transition, strain rate, loading duration, specimen orientation and notch geometry must be retained with tensile, creep, impact or wear results.

A focused example illustrates both grade and process sensitivity. Mitsui Chemicals lists 92 MPa ASTM D638 tensile strength for natural, unfilled AURUM PL450C TPI in its laboratory-specimen grade table, while warning that the representative values are not product specifications and do not necessarily describe a customer's finished part. Vidakis and co-workers independently melt-extruded this grade into 1.75 mm filament, dried it for 8 h at 120 °C, and printed 3.2 mm-thick ASTM D638 Type V coupons at a 420 °C nozzle, 150 °C build plate and 70 °C chamber with 0.2 mm layers, 100% rectilinear ±45° infill and two perimeters. For five room-temperature replicates per rate, ultimate tensile strength was approximately 82 MPa at 10 mm/min (0.011 s^-1) and approximately 95 MPa at 25 mm/min; at still higher speeds it declined, by about 40% at 300 mm/min relative to the maximum. These values are specific to PL450C and that printed architecture, drying history and tensile protocol, not a family range or a substitute for molded, reinforced or differently oriented TPI data.
sections.processing:
Thermoplastic polyimides selected for stable melt flow can be converted by high-temperature injection molding and extrusion; documented AURUM applications include tube, fiber, wire coating, and film, and unfilled grades can also be extruded into filament for fused-filament fabrication. Grade and equipment selection are unusually important because the melt temperatures are high, reinforced grades are abrasive, and prolonged residence or stagnant material can cause gelation or thermal degradation. Pellets should be dried and transferred without moisture pickup, while cylinder and die temperature, screw speed and shear, shot size and residence time, nozzle design, melt pressure, gate and runner dimensions, mold temperature, cooling, and flow-induced orientation govern fill, surface quality, shrinkage, warpage, and anisotropy. Filled grades require wear-resistant melt-contact hardware. Purging before shutdown and restart, avoiding dead spots such as an inappropriate shut-off nozzle, and using generous gates and runners reduce retained or frozen material. In filament production and material-extrusion printing, filament diameter and cooling, redrying after extrusion, nozzle and chamber thermal capacity, raster orientation, print speed, infill, strand width, and interlayer fusion control porosity, dimensions, surface finish, and directional performance. Polyamic-acid formation and imidization remain Synthesis operations; this section begins with preparation and shaping of an already imidized, melt-processable resin.

Mitsui Chemicals' AURUM brochure gives supplier guidance for that commercial thermoplastic-polyimide grade family, not a universal TPI window. It calls for a high-temperature molding machine, wear-resistant specifications for glass- and carbon-filled grades, pellet drying at 200 °C for at least 3 h with dehumidification recommended, and a residence time within 15 min to limit gelation. Its typical injection settings are 390 °C at the hopper-side cylinder and 400 °C at the center/nozzle with a 170–180 °C mold for natural grades; for filled grades they are 400 and 420 °C with a 190–210 °C mold. The same document recommends PEI purge material, thick gates and runners, and no tunnel gate or shut-off nozzle. A distinct open experiment by Petousis and co-workers provides a bounded additive-manufacturing example for unfilled AURUM PL450C. They extruded filament on a 3devo Precision 450 at 350/375/390/405 °C from hopper zone to nozzle, 7 rpm screw speed, and 30% cooling fan, then dried the filament at 120 °C for 8 h before printing on a high-temperature Intamsys machine. Their 16-run design varied nozzle temperature, print speed, raster orientation, infill density, and strand width; for example, Run 3 used 440 °C, 25 mm/s, 0° raster, 85% infill, and 115% strand width and gave the study's lowest CT-measured porosity. Those extrusion and printing settings apply only to PL450C, the named machines, specimen geometry, and experiment.
sections.structureAndMorphology: These materials contain imide groups in the polymer backbone, with the remaining chain structure determined by the selected monomers. Molecular design can improve melt flow compared with more rigid or strongly interacting polyimides. End groups and molecular weight also depend on the preparation. Filled grades introduce reinforcement or other dispersed materials in addition to the base resin.
sections.properties: The cited commercial thermoplastic polyimide series is marketed for thermal, mechanical and electrical performance. In a Mitsui comparison of AURUM grades, tensile strength changed only modestly over the displayed high-temperature aging interval at 230 °C, while the separately plotted impact strength of AURUM 450 declined with aging at 220 °C. The published plots do not specify all specimen and atmosphere details, and the differing endpoints should not be treated as a universal durability rating. In a separate study of 3D-printed specimens of one thermoplastic polyimide grade, tensile strength rose from about 82 MPa at a crosshead speed of 10 mm/min to about 95 MPa at 25 mm/min, then fell at higher speeds. The test describes printed coupons and specified loading rates; printing history, layer adhesion and specimen geometry can affect the result. Composition and forming history both matter to a finished component.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Thermoplastic polyimide serves washers, bearings, gears, seals, semiconductor equipment, cable coatings and reinforced structural components in industrial, electronics and transport markets. Mitsui describes AURUM’s low, stable sliding friction and low wear as useful for moving machinery parts. Its carbon- or glass-fiber-reinforced grades address structural stiffness, while low outgassing is relevant to semiconductor equipment. These are grade-specific design considerations: wear depends on the mating surface, load, speed and lubrication.

Purchasing. Mitsui lists AURUM neat, glass-filled, carbon-filled and wear-resistant grades. Its 2019 notice documents BIEGLO as a European TPI powder distributor; current regional terms should be confirmed when obtaining a quote.

Scale and evidence limits. No annual TPI purchased mass is given in these documents. This thermoplastic market should not be equated with all polyimide films or thermoset polyimides.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A Mitsui AURUM technical note documents thermally induced weight loss but does not identify the evolved molecular products. It lists 1% and 5% loss temperatures of 520 and 570 °C respectively, without specifying atmosphere or heating rate. A separate supplier comparison plots declining impact strength during thermal aging of AURUM 450; a property change is not the same endpoint as mass loss. These observations apply to the stated thermoplastic-polyimide products and tests.

Timescales: The thermal-loss note reports a temperature ramp but not its atmosphere or rate, so its thresholds cannot supply a transferable degradation rate or duration. The aging guide presents tensile-strength histories at 230 °C and impact-strength histories at 220 °C for particular grades, illustrating why temperature and the chosen failure criterion matter. Those high-temperature supplier tests are not soil or marine persistence measurements.

Environmental persistence: Loss of impact strength and weight loss at high temperature do not show conversion of polymer carbon to carbon dioxide and biomass. Neither supplier note measures degradation in soil, freshwater or seawater. A material-specific environmental mineralization time remains unestablished.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Mitsui reports direct mechanical-recycling trials in which injection-molded AURUM was ground and remolded using 100% reprocessed material. Natural PL450 was followed through ten remolding cycles at a 400 °C molding temperature and 200 °C mold temperature, with relatively small changes in the listed strength/modulus values. A separate 30% carbon-fiber grade, JCN3030, showed substantially declining tensile and flexural properties over five cycles under its different molding conditions. These supplier trials demonstrate clean-scrap reprocessing and the importance of reinforcement; they do not establish performance for contaminated post-consumer material.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Thermoplastic-polyimide molding uses high-temperature equipment and molten resin. HSE’s general plastics guidance supports reliable temperature control, suitable fume extraction and trained purging/shutdown; prolonged residence and residues heated during cleanup are separate concerns from use of a finished part. The AURUM thermal note demonstrates weight loss under severe heating but does not identify a complete evolved-product inventory, so a material-specific safety data sheet remains necessary.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Thermoplastic polyimide is a subfamily, not a unique polymer or property specification. Molecular structure, grade and reinforcement affect flow and final behavior. The cited printed-coupon study used a particular resin and processing sequence, while the supplier brochure describes its own products and test specimens. Comparisons should preserve grade, drying, processing, specimen geometry and test conditions.

sections.overview: Alternating ethylene–carbon monoxide polyketone is an aliphatic copolymer whose chain contains ethylene-derived segments alternating with carbonyl groups. Catalytic copolymerization of ethylene and carbon monoxide provides the regular sequence. The material is discussed as an engineering thermoplastic within a broader family of olefin–CO polyketones. Products containing a third olefin have different chain compositions. The regular backbone places a ketone group between ethylene-derived segments, producing a material that can crystallize. Commercial olefin–CO materials may include propylene, so an application or property report must identify the composition.
sections.history: Aliphatic polyketones developed through efforts to copolymerize carbon monoxide with olefins. A 1951 metal-catalyzed example produced low-melting oligomers; later nickel and palladium catalysts enabled useful alternating polymers. E. Drent and colleagues reported highly efficient diphosphine-palladium catalysts in 1991. Shell commercialized the carbon-monoxide/ethylene/propylene terpolymer as Carilon in 1996, then discontinued production in 2000. Hyosung revived industrial development in the following decade, announcing its polyketone in 2013 and starting its Ulsan commercial plant in June 2015 under the POKETONE name. Application development emphasized mechanical and industrial parts, including gears and vehicle components, together with food-contact and medical equipment. These milestones concern the alternating aliphatic engineering-plastic lineage; later research on non-alternating CO/ethylene polymers has a separate catalyst and application history.
sections.nomenclature: The canonical name is deliberately limited to the alternating ethylene/CO copolymer. It does not silently include non-alternating ethylene/CO chains or ethylene/CO/propylene terpolymers, whose catalyst-controlled microstructure and composition define related but different polyketones; POK is used only in that qualified sense here.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: This record is limited to the alternating ethylene–carbon monoxide copolymer: ethylene and CO are copolymerized by coordination-insertion catalysis to give an alternating ketone-containing backbone. Nickel and palladium systems are established for alternating copolymerization; the catalyst/ligand system is the key control that distinguishes this material from non-perfectly alternating ethylene/CO polymers. The 2024 review notes that the favorable CO insertion chemistry of Ni/Pd systems often produces the perfectly alternating sequence, whereas phosphine–sulfonate palladium systems can promote successive ethylene insertion and thus make a different, non-alternating product.
sections.mechanicalProperties: The alternating carbonyl sequence gives aliphatic polyketone strong interchain dipolar interactions, high crystallinity potential, and engineering-thermoplastic behavior, but molecular mass, cooling, orientation, and comonomer incorporation remain consequential. Open sources available in this pass discuss molded and drawn forms and their mechanical response qualitatively but did not provide a readily comparable, fully specified tensile value for neat alternating ethylene/CO homocopolymer. Fiber and ethylene/CO/propylene data should remain labeled as neighboring materials rather than collapsed into a family range.
sections.processing: Alternating ethylene/CO polyketone has been studied in molding and oriented-fiber forms. Cooling rate and drawing affect crystallinity and hence final response; melt viscosity is also molecular-mass dependent. Because alternating material is distinct from non-perfectly alternating ethylene/CO copolymer and ethylene/CO/propylene terpolymer, temperatures or extrusion conditions reported for those related products must not be assigned to this record. The present open evidence supports melt shaping and drawing as relevant routes but leaves a grade-specific operating-window gap.
sections.structureAndMorphology: In the alternating copolymer, ethylene-derived segments and carbonyl groups recur in a regular sequence along the backbone. The chains can pack into ordered crystallites as well as less ordered regions; cooling and deformation alter the morphology. A review of drawn fibers reports predominantly beta-form crystals in the ethylene–CO material, with alpha-form crystals also present depending on cooling. Introducing propylene changes the chain-unit population, so a propylene-containing terpolymer must be identified separately.
sections.properties: Polar carbonyl groups distinguish this polyketone from polyethylene, while the regular ethylene–CO sequence permits crystallization and a relatively high melting temperature. A review cites 244 °C for an alternating copolymer in one melting study and maximum melting temperatures of 278 °C in another study of low- and high-molecular-weight samples. Those reported values belong to different samples and measurement histories, rather than defining a guaranteed grade specification. Introducing propylene into the related terpolymer lowers melting temperature and can ease processing, but changes the composition of the material.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. The exact alternating ethylene/CO copolymer has been investigated for high-strength fibers and engineering or barrier materials. The reviewed evidence does not establish a major current end-use industry specifically for this two-monomer composition; many commercial polyketone examples instead contain propylene. The regular copolymer has been investigated as a fiber-forming material; processing into a fiber and the orientation produced during drawing contribute to its performance. Reports on commercial propylene-containing polyketones require a separate composition label.

Purchasing. No current catalog purchase channel or standard pack size for the exact two-monomer alternating material was verified. Procurement would require composition confirmation: Hyosung identifies commercial POKETONE as derived from CO, ethylene and propylene, outside this entry’s narrow scope.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased, consumed or produced tonnage was established for exact alternating ethylene/CO copolymer. Commercial POKETONE capacity and sales cannot be substituted because they concern a related terpolymer.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A review of alternating ethylene–CO copolymer experiments reports chain cleavage and cyclization during heating. Products identified in pyrolysis at 500 °C included carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, water, lower-molecular-weight ketones and aromatic compounds. The product mixture depends on conditions and sample history.

Timescales: In the reviewed experiments, crosslinking was reported to begin around 230 °C, while mass loss began around 290 °C and was greatest at approximately 370–410 °C. These are observations from particular high-temperature laboratory tests, not a time or rate for an article to degrade outdoors.

Environmental persistence: Heat-driven volatilization and formation of fragments do not demonstrate complete biodegradation. No transferable environmental mineralization time was established for the alternating copolymer.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A study of mechanically recycled commercial aliphatic-polyketone composites remolded samples containing short glass fibers and found that recycling changed both fibers and matrix. The precise commercial composition must be checked before transferring that result to the strictly alternating ethylene–CO copolymer.

The polymer is a thermoplastic, but repeated melt processing can alter molecular structure and performance. The cited composite work does not establish an exact-composition post-consumer collection system or a closed loop for all neat alternating material.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For alternating aliphatic polyketone, the cited batch-pyrolysis study demonstrates a complex gas and condensate mixture during severe heating, including carbon monoxide and light hydrocarbons. That reactor experiment is not an occupational exposure measurement during ordinary molding. HSE guidance supports controlling actual thermal history and fumes at extrusion, reprocessing, stoppages and cleanup; the particular polyketone copolymer and additives must be included in the assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Alternating ethylene–CO copolymer, non-alternating materials and ethylene–propylene–CO terpolymers should be distinguished. Molecular mass, crystallinity, cooling and drawing affect the performance of a particular sample. The review reports different melting values from different ethylene–CO studies and discusses drawn fibers with both the two-monomer copolymer and propylene-containing terpolymers. A result for one sample or processing history is not automatically a specification for the other compositions or for a finished article.

sections.overview: Poly(tetrafluoroethylene) (PTFE) is a fluoropolymer made by polymerizing tetrafluoroethylene. Its carbon backbone is surrounded by fluorine atoms. PTFE is used in applications such as seals, electrical insulation and low-friction surfaces. Powder and dispersion products are converted using specialized forming and sintering methods. Its fluorinated structure contributes to resistance to many chemicals and to a low-energy surface, useful for non-stick and low-friction applications. Its stability is conditional: strong treatments such as high-temperature pyrolysis or particular mechanochemical reactions can break down PTFE.
sections.history: Roy Plunkett and his assistant Jack Rebok discovered PTFE on April 6, 1938, while investigating tetrafluoroethylene refrigerant chemistry in the DuPont-associated Kinetic Chemicals program. Turning the unexpected solid into usable products required further engineering because it was difficult to shape. Its early wartime application was corrosion-resistant valves and seals for uranium-hexafluoride handling in the Manhattan Project. The Teflon trademark was registered in 1945. Nonstick cookware emerged during the 1950s and reached the U.S. market in 1961 through Marion A. Trozzolo. PTFE’s history thus progressed from an accidental laboratory finding to specialized industrial service and later familiar household coatings.
sections.nomenclature: PTFE names the tetrafluoroethylene homopolymer and is distinct from fluorinated copolymers such as FEP. A filled PTFE composite, a paste-extrusion grade, or a molded and sintered part is a material-specific formulation or article form rather than a synonym for neat PTFE.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(tetrafluoroethylene) (PTFE) is formed by free-radical addition polymerization of tetrafluoroethylene (TFE). Commercially relevant aqueous routes include suspension polymerization, which yields granular resin, and dispersion polymerization, which maintains colloidal particles with a fluorinated surfactant. Both use a deoxygenated, pressure-rated aqueous reactor and a radical source such as an inorganic persulfate or peroxide; monomer feed, agitation, dispersant level, and initiator choice distinguish particle-forming routes and influence molecular mass. One cited suspension process uses an aqueous medium, persulfate initiator, vigorous agitation, and only a small amount of perfluorinated carboxylate dispersant, while a separate dispersion process describes emulsifier, buffer, and radical initiator in contact with pressurized TFE. These are route examples for PTFE formation, not downstream sintering or shaping conditions, and TFE copolymers with substantial comonomer content fall outside the PTFE homopolymer scope.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PTFE is a semicrystalline fluoropolymer with a compliant, highly extensible tensile response and important time-dependent deformation under load. Measured behavior depends on resin grade and molecular mass, powder consolidation and sintering history, porosity/crystallinity, temperature and strain rate, specimen geometry, and fillers; filled PTFE should not be treated as virgin PTFE. One open study reports for its unfilled PTFE reference a tensile breaking stress of 30.0 ± 1.2 MPa, strain at break of 416 ± 20%, and tensile modulus of 766 ± 29 MPa. Those are the study's neat-reference specimens, tested alongside boron- and glass-filled materials, rather than a general PTFE grade range. A separate open cyclic/creep study on a PTFE dog-bone specimen finds that ratchet and creep strain depend on stress level and temperature, including changes across the material's thermal-transition regime; static short-term tensile values therefore do not represent long-term load-bearing performance.
sections.processing:
Conventional high-molecular-weight poly(tetrafluoroethylene) (PTFE) has such high melt viscosity that it is not shaped by ordinary melt injection molding or screw extrusion. Granular molding powders are instead cold-compacted into a preform, removed from the mold, sintered above the first-melt transition, and cooled under a controlled schedule; ram extrusion combines sequential compaction, sintering, and cooling for long rods or tubes. Fine powders are blended gently with a hydrocarbon extrusion aid, aged or conditioned, preformed, paste-extruded into tubing, wire insulation, tape, or membrane precursor, dried to remove the aid, and sintered. Aqueous dispersions can also impregnate or coat substrates before drying and baking. Powder cleanliness, shear damage, preform density, lubricant distribution and removal, sintering uniformity, cooling rate, and machining or skiving allowance are central controls.

Two grade records illustrate why PTFE conditions must remain product-specific. Chemours describes Teflon PTFE 60 X as a fine powder for paste extrusion and reports an extrusion pressure of 8 MPa at a 100:1 reduction ratio. It warns that premature shear irreversibly fibrillates the powder, recommends cooling compacted shipping lumps below 19 °C before screening, and requires clean, condensation-free handling. For a distinct granular route, AGC specifies Fluon G350 and G355 for automatic, isostatic, and compression molding; its sheet gives a compression ratio of 2.7, slow preforming at 4500–5000 psi, heating above the 342 °C gel point, and typical maximum oven temperatures near 371 °C or higher depending on wall thickness. These values belong only to the named grades and processes, not to every virgin, modified, filled, or dispersion PTFE.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PTFE chains consist of repeating tetrafluoroethylene-derived units and can form highly crystalline regions. The fluorinated chain has low surface energy. Processing and cooling affect crystalline morphology and the structure of a finished part. Fillers introduce additional phases in composite grades. The backbone is made of carbon–carbon bonds with fluorine attached along the chain. The fluorine-rich sheath and strong carbon–fluorine bonds help explain why the material resists many chemical reagents.
sections.properties: PTFE combines low friction with chemical resistance and electrical insulating properties. Its very high melt viscosity makes conventional melt processing difficult. Under sustained load it can creep, and its mechanical response depends on temperature and loading history. In a cyclic tensile study of PTFE dog-bone specimens, accumulated ratcheting strain increased with higher mean stress and stress amplitude; substantial strain accrued in the initial cycles. This repeated-load result belongs to the tested material, temperatures and stresses. Filled compounds can behave differently from unfilled PTFE. The low surface energy contributes to non-stick behavior, while the fluorinated structure contributes to chemical resistance. The handling of a powder and the performance of a consolidated component are different matters: Chemours notes that the preform pressure and sintering and cooling cycle affect finished properties of its 7A X grade.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PTFE is used in gaskets, mechanical seals, bearings, electrical insulators and chemical linings. Its chemical resistance is useful for components exposed to aggressive media, and low friction is useful for sliding surfaces. Fine-powder grades are also supplied for hoses, wire and cable insulation and filtration membranes; the grade and method of forming differ among these products.

Purchasing. Chemours lists 7A X granular powder for molding and sintering into billets from which film and sheet may be skived. It is supplied in 40 kg lined drums; the powder, a molded billet and finished sheet are distinct purchasing stages.

Scale and evidence limits. The supplier recommends an eight-drum, 320 kg pallet for shipping convenience. This is one grade’s shipment recommendation, not a minimum annual buyer requirement, global demand or production estimate.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PTFE resists many reagents but can decompose under sufficiently severe treatments. In a vacuum-pyrolysis study of PTFE at 423.5–513 °C, the volatile product was predominantly tetrafluoroethylene. A separate electron-beam study identified oxidized fluorocarbon products and carbon dioxide on heating irradiated powder; heating conditions and prior irradiation affect the products and cannot be substituted for an ambient-weathering inventory.

Timescales: In the vacuum study, a 305.7 mg sample at 423.5 °C lost 0.5% mass in 337 minutes, whereas a 7.05 mg sample at 500 °C lost 93.1% in 445 minutes. These high-temperature tests have different sample sizes and measure volatilization in a reactor, not environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The polymer’s stability makes disposal and environmental persistence concerns, but neither reactor volatilization nor fragmentation establishes complete mineralization in soil or water. An ambient residence time for a particular PTFE article cannot be inferred from these experiments.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Clean PTFE scrap can be reclaimed through specialist powder routes; the resulting material and its properties depend on feedstock and treatment. A high-molecular-weight molded product cannot simply be assumed to be recovered from ground or degraded powder.

A separate research route chemically converts PTFE rather than retaining it as a polymer. A 2026 review describes a laboratory process in which PTFE powder, tape or a seal was ball-milled with potassium phosphate salts at room temperature for three hours, forming fluoride-containing salts that were used in later fluorination reactions. It is a chemical-recovery demonstration, not evidence of municipal acceptance or a general commercial process; handling the other reaction products and scaling the operation require assessment.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PTFE handling guidance distinguishes the supplied resin from fumes generated during heating. The Fluoropolymers Product Group guide covers PTFE, FEP, PFA, ETFE, ECTFE and PVDF and warns that overheated fumes can cause polymer fume fever; higher exposure can be more serious. It calls for effective extraction of fumes and dust, protection from molten material, and keeping tobacco away from resin-handling areas because contamination can create hazardous fumes when burned. Fillers and dispersion ingredients need separate assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PTFE is supplied in different powder and dispersion grades for different processing routes. Molecular structure, sintering, porosity and fillers affect the finished article. A cyclic-creep or composite study describes its tested grade and loading conditions. Those results should not be generalized to every PTFE part. Processing must be qualified by grade: for example, the 7A X supplier specifies powder compaction and sintering rather than an ordinary low-viscosity melt-forming route. Chemical stability under service conditions does not mean the material is inert under every treatment.

sections.overview: Fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP) is a fluoropolymer made primarily from tetrafluoroethylene and hexafluoropropylene. It is melt-processable and can be supplied as pellets, powder or a dispersion. A supplier describes wire insulation, tubing and molded components among the uses of one general-purpose FEP resin. Different grades and finished constructions require separate qualification. Its combination of dielectric performance and melt extrusion helps explain its use as insulation on wire. The same material name covers formulations and finished articles with different histories.
sections.history: DuPont commercially introduced FEP in 1960 as part of the effort to retain useful fluoropolymer characteristics while making fabrication easier than with PTFE. Copolymerizing tetrafluoroethylene with hexafluoropropylene created a melt-processable material suitable for extrusion, molding and films. Electrical-wire insulation, including plenum and network cables, became a major market; chemical-resistant pipe and tank linings, nonstick surfaces and solar-related films provided other applications. By 2012, the industrial literature documented commercial products from DuPont, Daikin and Dyneon. The 1960 milestone is FEP’s market introduction, distinct from Plunkett’s earlier discovery of the PTFE homopolymer.
sections.nomenclature: FEP names the tetrafluoroethylene/hexafluoropropylene copolymer boundary, not every fluoropolymer or a particular FEP grade. Optional fluorinated vinyl-ether comonomer and molecular-weight-control choices describe specific compositions within related manufacturing practice and should not be treated as synonyms for unqualified FEP.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Fluorinated ethylene propylene copolymer (FEP) is the tetrafluoroethylene (TFE)–hexafluoropropylene (HFP) copolymer, despite the historical name. A DuPont process example copolymerizes TFE and HFP in an aqueous medium with water-soluble initiator, dispersing agent, and optional chain-transfer agent; listed initiation systems include persulfates and redox initiators. A separate Chinese process begins with deionized water, emulsifier, an initial TFE/HFP mixture, and initiator, then continuously adds the mixed monomers to maintain pressure. That patent’s feed ratios, temperature/pressure window, and optional chain-transfer agents are specific to its manufacturing example rather than universal FEP conditions.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP) is a semicrystalline, melt-processible fluoroplastic. At room temperature, unfilled FEP is typically relatively soft and tough, with yielding, substantial plastic extension, and high elongation rather than a stiff, high-load-bearing response. Its deformation is viscoelastic and time dependent: creep, stress relaxation, ratcheting under repeated load, and permanent set can matter well below short-term tensile failure. Mechanical performance depends on hexafluoropropylene content and sequence distribution, molecular mass and melt-flow grade, crystallinity, cooling or annealing history, processing degradation, film or molding orientation, thickness, welds and defects, strain rate, load duration, test direction, and temperature relative to the crystalline melting interval. Higher temperature and long load duration reduce useful stiffness and strength, while drawing can create machine/transverse anisotropy. Fillers may raise hardness, modulus, dimensional stability, wear resistance, and creep resistance, but filler agglomeration or a weak interface can sharply reduce elongation and toughness. Radiation, thermal aging, scratches, and repeated flexing can also promote embrittlement or stress cracking. Olifirov and co-workers provide one bounded unfilled example using a finely divided tetrafluoroethylene-hexafluoropropylene powder from HaloPolymer Kirovo-Chepetsk. The powder was dried for 1 h at 140 °C, injection molded at a 380 °C cylinder temperature into 80 x 10 x 4 mm plates, and cut into ISO 527-2 type 1BA dumbbells. After conditioning for 88 h in an ISO 291 standard 23 °C/50% relative-humidity atmosphere, at least five specimens were tested at room temperature and 20 mm/min. The unfilled F0 material gave Shore D hardness 57.5 ± 1, Young's modulus 0.59 ± 0.01 GPa, tensile strength 15.4 ± 0.4 MPa, and elongation 295 ± 11%. These results describe that supplier powder and laboratory molding history, not all FEP grades. As a separate commercial benchmark, Chemours lists typical values for additive-free FEP 100 molding and extrusion resin of 26 MPa tensile strength and 300% elongation at 23 °C by ASTM D638, Shore D 56 hardness, no break in notched Izod impact at 23 °C, and 10,000 MIT folding cycles for 0.20 mm film. The sheet does not state tensile specimen preparation, rate, or conditioning, and expressly treats the values as non-specification data. Finished films, cable insulation, linings, and molded parts therefore require application-specific creep, flex, stress-crack, and elevated-temperature tests.
sections.processing: FEP is a melt-processible fluoroplastic and is converted by conventional extrusion, injection molding, compression molding, blow molding, and film casting. Chemours describes a general-purpose FEP 100 grade supplied as 3 mm pellets for smooth extrusion feeding; equipment in contact with the melt is specified as corrosion-resistant and capable of temperatures up to 400 °C. The same sheet warns that grade values are typical rather than specification data. A separate laboratory study dried an unfilled FEP powder for 1 h at 140 °C and injection molded it at a 380 °C cylinder temperature into plates before machining test specimens. The two examples show that high melt temperature, equipment materials, and feed preparation are important, but neither setting is universal: melt-flow grade, die or mold geometry, residence time, filler, and cooling history must be established for the selected FEP.
sections.structureAndMorphology: FEP chains contain tetrafluoroethylene-derived units and hexafluoropropylene-derived units bearing fluorinated side groups. The comonomer distinguishes FEP from the tetrafluoroethylene homopolymer PTFE; its amount and distribution are not fixed by the family name. The solid contains crystalline and less ordered regions, whose proportions and orientation depend on cooling and thermal history. In a study of 25 µm FEP film, X-ray analysis found a crystalline fraction of about 31.9% in virgin film and 43.5% after the specified UV exposure; the authors related the change to structural rearrangement in that sample.
sections.properties: FEP combines chemical resistance and useful dielectric properties with the ability to be melt processed into wire insulation, tubing and other articles. Chemours describes its FEP 100 as a low-moisture-absorption extrusion resin and recommends testing finished cables for resistance to repeated flexing and temperature cycling. The film study illustrates another influence on response: measured Young’s moduli were approximately 584–589 MPa for virgin film and 652–666 MPa after 72 hours of the specified UV exposure, depending on test direction. After combined heat and UV treatment, the moduli were lower, about 409–499 MPa; these results are for that 25 µm film and exposure, not universal FEP values.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. FEP serves electrical wire insulation, cable jacketing, small tubing and injection-molded parts. Chemours describes its FEP 100 as a melt-extrudable resin with useful dielectric properties for primary wire insulation. For cables that repeatedly bend or undergo temperature cycles, the supplier also discusses stress-crack resistance and uses thin-film flex testing as a comparative guide between resin grades. It recommends testing the completed cable because the resin test alone does not establish cable performance.

Purchasing. FEP 100 is supplied as approximately 3 mm pellets in 25 kg bags; the manufacturer recommends 1,000 kg pallet orders for convenient shipment. Other FEP grades and converted films or tubing have their own specifications.

Scale and evidence limits. The recommended 1,000 kg pallet corresponds to forty of the stated 25 kg bags of FEP 100 pellets. It is a shipment recommendation for one grade, not a mandatory minimum order, annual buyer usage or worldwide FEP consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Daikin identifies hydrogen fluoride and other fluorinated compounds as possible products when its FEP resins are overheated. That warning does not establish an ambient-weathering product inventory. Separately, an experiment found that ultraviolet and heat treatment altered the structure and mechanical response of a 25 µm FEP film.

Timescales: In that experiment, 72 hours of simulated UV exposure increased the measured tensile modulus and yield stress relative to virgin film; heat treatment at 200 °C for 30 minutes produced different changes. The combination of heat and UV lowered the modulus relative to the virgin film, whereas UV treatment alone raised it. These are test-specific responses, not outdoor lifetime or environmental mineralization times.

Environmental persistence: A change in film stiffness or yield stress does not establish biodegradation or disappearance. A transferable FEP mineralization time in soil, water or landfill remains unresolved.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The Fluoropolymers Product Group handling guide explicitly identifies FEP as a melt-processable fluoropolymer whose clean film trim can be returned to extrusion; startup and shutdown scrap can also be reprocessed. This is mechanical reclamation of production waste. The guide cautions that final properties may change and the recovered material will not suit every application. It does not establish broad collection of mixed or contaminated post-consumer FEP articles.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: FEP handling guidance distinguishes the supplied resin from fumes generated during heating. The Fluoropolymers Product Group guide covers PTFE, FEP, PFA, ETFE, ECTFE and PVDF and warns that overheated fumes can cause polymer fume fever; higher exposure can be more serious. It calls for effective extraction of fumes and dust, protection from molten material, and keeping tobacco away from resin-handling areas because contamination can create hazardous fumes when burned. Fillers and dispersion ingredients need separate assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: FEP grades can differ in composition, molecular weight and processing history. A supplier recommends evaluating final cable constructions when thermal cycling and repeated flexing are important. Heat exposure during melt conversion can also affect the polymer, and the cited industry guide notes grade-dependent thermal stability. Results for a particular film, wire coating or molded article do not define every FEP material. For the named cable resin, resistance to stress cracking is a separate performance concern: a resin property table alone cannot establish a cable’s performance under repeated flexing or thermal cycling.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical copolymerization incorporates TFE and HFP residues. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Termination removes active radical ends; transfer and termination pathways depend on the monomer and reaction medium.

steps.title: Prepare the reaction
steps.body: Prepare water, dispersing agent, initiator, and the initial monomer charge.

steps.title: Propagate the radical chain
steps.body: Successive monomer additions convert alkene π bonds into backbone σ bonds while regenerating the radical growth site. The cited initiator, feed composition and reaction medium determine the particular preparation; transfer, grafting and termination control architecture alongside propagation.

steps.title: Form and recover the product
steps.body: Meter mixed monomer feeds to maintain the selected pressure/composition conditions.

synthesisRoutes.limitations: This outline does not specify a universal recipe, reagent loading, operating schedule, or conversion endpoint. Those details must retain the material and process limits of the cited source. Figure notes distinguish exact molecules from representative motifs and variable architectures.

sections.overview: Perfluoroalkoxy alkane polymer (PFA) is a melt-processable fluoropolymer generally made from tetrafluoroethylene and a perfluorinated vinyl ether. The ether-derived comonomer distinguishes its chain from PTFE. PFA is supplied as pellets, powder or dispersion and can be converted into articles such as tubing, seals and stock shapes. The selected resin and fabrication history influence the finished product. Its chemical resistance and ability to be melt-shaped support uses in tubing and stock shapes for demanding fluid-handling equipment. Those uses require a specified grade and finished-part qualification.
sections.history: PFA emerged from efforts to obtain melt-processable fluoropolymers while retaining a fully fluorinated backbone. DuPont commercialized it in 1972. A contemporary patent by William Franklin Gresham and Alfons Franz Vogelpohl, issued that year, describes aqueous copolymerization of tetrafluoroethylene with perfluoroalkyl vinyl ethers and addresses polymer quality. This was a process-development milestone, rather than evidence that every present PFA composition was invented simultaneously. PFA belongs to the subsequent diversification of fluoroplastics into materials that could be shaped by conventional melt conversion; control of the vinyl-ether component and polymerization conditions was central to that development.
sections.nomenclature: PFA abbreviates perfluoroalkoxy alkane polymer. The term names a tetrafluoroethylene/perfluoroalkyl-vinyl-ether copolymer family, not every fluoropolymer or all perfluorinated polymers.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Perfluoroalkoxy alkane polymer, commonly called PFA in polymer practice, is a family of melt-processable copolymers rather than PTFE homopolymer. Its principal monomers are tetrafluoroethylene and a perfluoroalkyl vinyl ether; perfluoromethyl, perfluoroethyl, and perfluoro-n-propyl vinyl ethers are documented examples. Free-radical copolymerization has been carried out in aqueous dispersion or emulsion media and in fluorinated organic solvent/suspension media. The cited aqueous example uses a water-soluble persulfate initiator, emulsifier, and gaseous chain-transfer agent; a separate route controls the tetrafluoroethylene/perfluoroalkyl-vinyl-ether feed ratio in the presence of a chain-transfer agent. These are route examples, not a fixed PFA composition or a claim that every TFE/ether copolymer has the same comonomer content.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PFA is a melt-processable fluoropolymer family, but mechanical values must remain tied to resin grade, additives, finished form, and test conditions. In particular, a conductive PFA grade and a virgin rod made from named commercial PFA resins are different materials; thermal history, crystallinity, orientation, and service temperature also limit comparisons across molded parts, film, tubing, and rod. Supplier data should consequently be read as grade/form benchmarks, not as a single PFA property range.

A bounded rod example is Pexco's ASTM D3307 Type II PFA rod, made from virgin Chemours 350 PFA or Daikin AP-230 PFA resin: the sheet lists ASTM D638 tensile strength of 3,600 psi (about 24.8 MPa), 300% elongation, and ASTM D790 flexural modulus of 85,000 psi (about 586 MPa). Its test temperature, specimen dimensions, conditioning, and statistical basis are not stated. Separately, Daikin reports 25 MPa tensile strength and 300% elongation by ASTM D1708 for conductive AP-230ASL; the sheet labels these as representative, non-guaranteed values, so they are not interchangeable with the virgin-rod data.
sections.processing: Perfluoroalkoxy alkane (PFA) is a melt-processable fluoroplastic converted by extrusion, including wire and cable extrusion, and by injection, transfer, compression, and blow molding. Processing requires high-temperature corrosion-resistant equipment and control of shear and melt residence because melt fracture or degradation can occur when conditions are unsuitable. Solvay's Hyflon PFA guide gives grade-specific packing-temperature ranges of 320–400 °C for P420 and 300–380 °C for M620, with packing pressure of 150–300 bar; its wire-extrusion example uses approximately 390–420 °C melt temperatures, 5 rpm screw speed, and 40 bar pressure. Daikin's NEOFLON brochure independently lists the melt-processing routes and gives 350–380 °C mold temperatures for AP-210/AP-230 grades, with operation below the critical shear rate to avoid melt fracture. These are named-grade guidance values, not a family-wide PFA window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PFA chains contain tetrafluoroethylene-derived segments and units with perfluoroalkoxy side groups. The identity and amount of ether comonomer vary among grades; these units are part of the copolymer chain rather than a separate liquid ether. PFA is semicrystalline, with ordered regions alongside less ordered material, and cooling and processing affect that organization. In a reprocessing study of one resin, adding recycled material increased the measured crystallinity; the authors associated this with shorter chains and easier chain packing. This observation describes the tested material stream rather than every PFA article.
sections.properties: PFA combines chemical and thermal resistance with melt processability, making it useful for tubing, linings and machined components. For a specified virgin-resin rod, Pexco lists ASTM D570 water absorption below 0.03%; that supplier measurement is not a universal PFA specification. In a separate study of virgin PFA and recycled production scrap from the same grade, samples containing more than 50% recycled resin had a reported Young’s modulus of approximately 540 MPa versus 330 MPa for virgin material. The increased stiffness accompanied greater crystallinity and reduced ductility in that particular reprocessed series.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PFA is used in tubing, pipe and vessel linings, seals, fittings and valve components for chemical-processing, semiconductor and other equipment. Pexco supplies PFA stock rod for applications including seals and valve seats and identifies chemical resistance, low moisture absorption and creep resistance as features of that stock. A fabricator can machine rod into components, but a seal’s service depends on its dimensions and the chemical and temperature it encounters. Tubing and linings are separate product forms with their own construction requirements.

Purchasing. Chemours supplies PFA resin grades in pellet or powder form, while Pexco offers rod made with specified virgin resins in standard 6 or 12 ft lengths. A buyer should specify dimensions, length and quantity to obtain pricing and lead time; a stock rod and the pellet used to make it are different purchasing stages.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked product information does not disclose annual PFA sales or consumption. Stock dimensions establish component supply options, not worldwide polymer demand.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A supplier safety sheet identifies hydrogen fluoride, carbonyl fluoride and acid fluorides as hazardous thermal-decomposition products of its PFA resin. These are overheating products, not demonstrated ambient metabolites. In a separate study of recycled PFA, yellowing and lower melt viscosity were consistent with probable chain degradation during reprocessing.

Timescales: In an immersion experiment, virgin PFA tensile strength after 28 days at 23 °C in sodium hypochlorite was 19.4 ± 0.5 MPa, compared with 19.8 ± 0.6 MPa before immersion. The researchers also tested sulfuric acid and blends with recycled resin; those controlled chemical-resistance results do not predict environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Tensile retention in a chemical bath measures the specimen’s mechanical response under that exposure, rather than the conversion of its carbon to carbon dioxide. The immersion and processing studies do not establish complete biodegradation or a transferable mineralization time in soil, water or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A study re-extruded post-industrial PFA waste and blended it with virgin PFA. In its tensile specimens, the 100% recycled sample had a tensile strength of 14.8 ± 0.5 MPa compared with 19.8 ± 0.6 MPa for the virgin sample; the researchers associated lower viscosity and greater yellowing with probable degradation during reprocessing.

These are results for the studied material stream and processing conditions. Waste sorting, contamination and property requirements determine whether a particular article can be reused; the experiment does not establish an existing collection system for all PFA products.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PFA handling guidance distinguishes the supplied resin from fumes generated during heating. The Fluoropolymers Product Group guide covers PTFE, FEP, PFA, ETFE, ECTFE and PVDF and warns that overheated fumes can cause polymer fume fever; higher exposure can be more serious. It calls for effective extraction of fumes and dust, protection from molten material, and keeping tobacco away from resin-handling areas because contamination can create hazardous fumes when burned. Fillers and dispersion ingredients need separate assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PFA grades differ in molecular structure and may be chemically stabilized. A rod made from a specified resin is not equivalent to every PFA film, coating or molded component. Thermal stability can vary with grade and exposure history, and fillers can alter the response. Comparisons should retain resin identity, article geometry, processing and test conditions. Pexco lists rod made from either Chemours 350 or Daikin AP-230 resin and invites customers to specify dimensions and length; those named stock materials do not establish identical behavior in a thin PFA film.

sections.overview: Ethylene–tetrafluoroethylene (ETFE) is a fluoropolymer copolymer of ethylene and tetrafluoroethylene. It is a melt-processable thermoplastic supplied in several grades. ETFE can be made into films and other shaped articles. Composition and processing distinguish particular materials. ETFE foil can form lightweight roof and façade membranes, whereas extrusion grades are also converted into wire insulation and tubing. The foil and a solid component do not necessarily share the same response.
sections.history: ETFE entered commercial fluoroplastics during the early 1970s. Chemours dates the introduction of DuPont’s Tefzel plastics to 1970 and associates the development with wire and cable insulation. An industry-history review instead dates independent DuPont and Asahi Glass commercialization to 1972; these sources therefore support an early-1970s transition more securely than one universal launch date. Cable insulation was a principal early market. Tough, flexible ETFE films subsequently established an architectural use alongside electrical applications. The material’s history reflects industrial copolymer development and conversion into films and insulated conductors, rather than the original discovery of PTFE.
sections.nomenclature: ETFE is the abbreviation for the ethylene–tetrafluoroethylene copolymer. The record covers the ethylene/TFE copolymer rather than PTFE homopolymer, FEP, or ECTFE; optional minor comonomers in particular grades do not make those distinct fluoropolymer families aliases.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–tetrafluoroethylene copolymer (ETFE) is made by free-radical copolymerization of ethylene and tetrafluoroethylene, optionally with a minor third copolymerizable monomer in particular formulations. Documented routes include solution, suspension, emulsion, and bulk polymerization; radical initiator, polymerization medium, and chain-transfer-agent selection provide practical control of molecular weight or melt viscosity. One ETFE patent specifically describes polymerizing the two monomers in a chlorine-free organic medium with chlorine-free chain-transfer agent and peroxide initiator; another gives solution polymerization as a preferred route and documents a gas-feed protocol for holding reactor pressure and composition. These patents define particular ETFE compositions and operating envelopes, not a single obligatory solvent, initiator, or comonomer for every ETFE grade. Pelletizing, extrusion, and article manufacture occur after polymer formation and are not synthesis steps here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–tetrafluoroethylene copolymer (ETFE) is a thermoplastic whose tensile response depends strongly on finished form, processing/orientation, thickness, producer or grade, test temperature, and strain rate. In a multivendor foil study, lower temperature and higher loading rate increased strength and stiffness, while lower temperature reduced elongation capability; temperature had the larger effect over the tested ranges. The investigators also found that a distinct yield point was not common to every foil/test combination, so a foil result is not a general resin design value.

A bounded foil measurement illustrates that limitation: for 250 μm machine-direction foils at 23 °C and 10 mm/min, first yield was 24.5, 21.3, and 23.5 MPa for the study’s three anonymized producers. Separately, Zeus reports for its ETFE extruded-material table an ASTM D638 ultimate tensile-strength range of 48–52 MPa, elongation at break of 382–415%, and ASTM D790 flexural modulus of 890–960 MPa. Zeus explicitly cautions that geometry and processing can substantially change extruded-part properties; the table is therefore a supplier guideline, not a universal ETFE specification.
sections.processing:
ETFE is a melt-processable fluoroplastic used in extrusion, injection molding, blow molding, compression molding, and related operations. A public injection-molding guide gives no pre-drying requirement, an ETFE compound-temperature range of 315–365 °C, mold temperatures of 80–120 °C, and a low injection rate because of shear sensitivity; it also advises avoiding sharp mold bends and abrupt section changes, reheating preforms when after-shrinkage needs control, and using corrosion-resistant contact surfaces. These are broad guide values rather than a grade-universal prescription.

A separate ETFE cast-film patent describes a nitrogen-protected line with nickel-alloy screw/barrel and melt pump. Its six-zone example rises from 240–260 °C at the feed to 330–350 °C at the final zone, with filter and pump at 330–340 °C, die at 330–350 °C, and an 80–180 °C temperature-controlled cooling roll. The line is heated for 30 min, started at low screw speed, and adjusted while observing plasticization; the disclosed film is about 25–300 μm at 5–60 m/min. These settings and controls are specific to that cast-film apparatus.
sections.structureAndMorphology: ETFE contains both ethylene-derived and fluorinated tetrafluoroethylene-derived segments. It is semicrystalline, with crystalline and amorphous regions in the material. Cooling and deformation during film or part production affect crystallinity and orientation. These structural differences influence the behavior of a finished article. In a fabricated foil, molecular orientation and thermal history become part of the specimen description; a comparison of films from different producers therefore also compares their processing histories.
sections.properties: ETFE is valued for chemical and weather resistance and can be processed from the melt. Thin ETFE foils are used in architectural applications. In tensile tests of 100 and 250 µm foils from three producers, lowering temperature or increasing loading rate increased stress at a given strain; the cooler material also had lower elongation capability. The authors found a larger influence from temperature than rate over their tested ranges. Film thickness and thermal history also matter, so their model is not a universal yield rule for all ETFE parts.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. ETFE foils have been used in lightweight roof and façade structures; ETFE also serves wire and cable insulation and specialized extruded components. Structural foil design must account for its temperature- and loading-rate-dependent tensile response, as demonstrated in tests of foils from multiple producers. For converted ETFE products, Zeus identifies abrasion resistance as useful in protective jacketing and low moisture absorption for sensor-protection heat shrink. A building foil and an extruded cable jacket have different design requirements and should be qualified separately.

Purchasing. Zeus supplies ETFE as extrusions or drawn products rather than only as base resin. Specify dimensions, tolerances and service conditions to the converter; finished tubing or coated optical fiber is a different purchase from molding resin.

Scale and evidence limits. The cited converter guide does not give annual ETFE purchased mass or an end-use share. A tubing dimension or length cannot establish family-wide demand.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: For its ETFE products, Bohlender identifies carbonyl fluoride, hydrogen fluoride, carbon oxides and perfluoroisobutylene among possible high-temperature decomposition products. This supplier hazard inventory is not a list of ambient-weathering products. In another experiment, accelerated UV-A exposure reduced tensile strength of a particular ETFE film.

Timescales: Bracciale and colleagues exposed 50 µm Tefzel PV3221 film to six cycles of UV-A and condensation at 25 °C, then tested it in tension. They reported strength falling from about 60 to 42 MPa. A separate conference report examined 60 µm ETFE greenhouse film after 35 years outdoors in Japan: measured breaking strength was 55.5 MPa, compared with 60.0 MPa for the original film, using JIS K7127. These are observations on different films and exposures, not a general outdoor lifetime or environmental mineralization rate.

Environmental persistence: Loss of mechanical strength does not establish biodegradation or disappearance. The cited tests do not determine a transferable mineralization time in soil, water or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The Fluoropolymers Product Group handling guide explicitly identifies ETFE as a melt-processable fluoropolymer whose clean film trim can be returned to extrusion; startup and shutdown scrap can also be reprocessed. This is mechanical reclamation of production waste. The guide cautions that final properties may change and the recovered material will not suit every application. It does not establish broad collection of mixed or contaminated post-consumer ETFE articles.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: ETFE handling guidance distinguishes the supplied resin from fumes generated during heating. The Fluoropolymers Product Group guide covers PTFE, FEP, PFA, ETFE, ECTFE and PVDF and warns that overheated fumes can cause polymer fume fever; higher exposure can be more serious. It calls for effective extraction of fumes and dust, protection from molten material, and keeping tobacco away from resin-handling areas because contamination can create hazardous fumes when burned. Fillers and dispersion ingredients need separate assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: ETFE does not specify grade, copolymer composition or processing history. Foil behavior under a particular tensile test cannot be transferred directly to a molded part. Temperature, strain rate and specimen form must accompany mechanical results. Supplier data apply to their identified grades and test methods. A higher-temperature or faster-loading foil test is a different measurement condition; published test outcomes cannot be assigned to another thickness or fabrication method without checking.

sections.overview: Ethylene–chlorotrifluoroethylene (ECTFE) is a partially fluorinated copolymer of ethylene and chlorotrifluoroethylene. It is a melt-processable thermoplastic. ECTFE is used in chemical-resistant linings and other fabricated products. Grade composition and processing affect finished-part behavior. Its combination of chemical resistance and insulating behavior is useful in protective wire and cable constructions. Formulated parts and drawn fibers have different geometries and processing histories.
sections.history: ECTFE’s established industrial history centers on chemically resistant barriers and electrical protection. Zeus’s public material account documents Halar resin and its own extrusion of tubing and drawn fiber for chemical transfer, automotive wiring and aerospace wire harnesses. These sources do not settle an original invention date. A distinct recent advance was reported online in December 2025 by Mengli Xu, Qiankai Chen, Mao Chen and colleagues: photoredox-controlled copolymerization gave alternating ECTFE with chain ends that could be extended into blocks. That laboratory development broadened control of molecular architecture; it should be distinguished from the older commercial resin and its long-established protective uses.
sections.nomenclature: ECTFE is the abbreviation for the ethylene–chlorotrifluoroethylene copolymer. The name denotes this specific ethylene/CTFE copolymer composition; ETFE, PTFE, and other fluoropolymers are separate records, and a named commercial grade or finished article is not an alternate family name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–chlorotrifluoroethylene copolymer (ECTFE) is made from ethylene and chlorotrifluoroethylene (CTFE); material sequence distribution can depend on route, so it should not be assumed to be perfectly alternating. An Allied patent describes aqueous emulsion copolymerization using a water-soluble initiator and a water-soluble fluorosurfactant, producing an aqueous latex. A recent open research article demonstrates a different, controlled route: light-driven organocatalyzed reversible-deactivation radical copolymerization of ethylene and CTFE at 25 °C and below 5 atm, using a phenothiazine catalyst and a fluorinated dithiocarbamate chain-transfer agent. This mild photoredox method is an experimental alternative, not a general industrial process claim.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–chlorotrifluoroethylene copolymer (ECTFE) is a semicrystalline melt-processable fluoropolymer whose tensile and impact response vary with grade, molecular weight/flow class, crystallinity and thermal history, and finished geometry or process (film, extrusion, molding, coating, or fiber). Supplier guidance explicitly cautions that geometry and processing method can dramatically affect properties of extruded parts. Values from different Halar grades or shapes therefore cannot be treated as a single ECTFE constant.

A bounded official grade-family example is Solvay’s standard Halar ECTFE data: tensile stress at yield 30–32 MPa, stress at break 40–57 MPa, elongation at break 250–300%, tensile modulus 1,400–2,100 MPa, flexural strength 45–55 MPa, and flexural modulus 1,600–1,800 MPa. The tensile results are reported under ASTM D638 and flexural results under ASTM D790. These are typical values for the stated standard Halar materials, not design minima. Independently, Zeus lists a general ECTFE guide value of 54 MPa ultimate tensile strength, 250% elongation at break, 1,655 MPa tensile modulus (ASTM D638), and 1,690 MPa flexural modulus (ASTM D790), while cautioning that part geometry and processing affect the outcome.
sections.processing:
ECTFE is a melt-processable fluoropolymer available for pipe, sheet, film and profile extrusion, injection, compression, blow, rotational and transfer molding, powder coating, and secondary welding or machining. Solvay's Halar guide says routine melt processing should target the grade and article while avoiding stagnant hot resin: extended exposure above about 300 °C can produce discoloration and specks, and an interrupted run should be purged promptly with polypropylene or high-density polyethylene or reduced to 200 °C. Corrosion-resistant melt-contact surfaces are recommended. Shot size, residence time, mold temperature and cooling history influence fill, degradation, crystallinity, shrinkage, and surface quality.

The guide's illustrative Halar injection table uses rear-to-forward barrel settings of 230–275 °C, a 255–265 °C nozzle, a 100–110 °C mold, and 55–140 bar pressure, but explicitly treats them as starting examples. A separate Solvay patent provides a narrower blended-material example: a powder formulation containing an experimental ECTFE was twin-screw extruded at 100 rpm and about 8.8 kg/h to a 253 °C melt, water-cooled, dried and pelletized, then flat-die cast as a 70–75 µm PVDF/3 wt% ECTFE film. That cycle belongs to the patent blend, not neat ECTFE or commercial Halar grades.
sections.structureAndMorphology: ECTFE contains ethylene-derived and chlorine-containing fluorinated units along its carbon backbone. The material is semicrystalline, with ordered regions alongside less ordered polymer. In a microscopy study of a commercial resin, spherulites developed as the melt cooled, showing that processing creates structure on a scale larger than the individual chain. Cooling rate and fabrication history influence crystallization, so films and tubing need not have identical morphology.
sections.properties: ECTFE can provide chemical resistance and electrical insulating behavior. Its thermoplastic character permits melt processing into films and shaped components. Stiffness and other mechanical properties depend on the selected grade and part. Chemical performance also depends on the fluid and exposure conditions. Zeus lists low permeability, chemical resistance and dielectric strength among the characteristics of its ECTFE products. Its material guide reports 54 MPa ultimate tensile strength by ASTM D638 and cautions that geometry and processing affect extruded-part properties. The guide does not provide a complete specimen and conditioning description, so the value is an indicative supplier example rather than a family-wide specification. In a DSC study of Halar 1400LC resin, increasing the cooling rate from 10 to 40 °C/min shifted the crystallization peak from 226.97 to 221.27 °C. The authors calculated crystallinity of 54.55% and 47.23%, respectively, using their chosen reference enthalpy. This illustrates a processing-dependent response for that resin, not a fixed crystallinity for every ECTFE article.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. ECTFE is used to protect automotive and aerospace wire and cable and in tubing for chemical transfer. Zeus identifies chemical resistance and low permeability as attributes relevant to these products, and supplies ECTFE both as extruded tubing and as drawn fiber. The converter also describes drawn fiber for protective braiding, where abrasion resistance is useful. The performance of a particular tubing or braided construction depends on dimensions and processing as well as the base material.

Purchasing. Zeus documents ECTFE extruded tubing and drawn fiber. Specify the dimensions, tolerances and service conditions of the converted product rather than ordering by polymer abbreviation alone.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked material guide does not provide ECTFE annual resin sales or downstream purchased mass. It establishes product availability, not market share.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A Halar ECTFE processing guide warns that overheating and contamination can accelerate degradation. It does not identify the major individual molecular products. A separate solar-film patent reports a loss of ultraviolet transmission after accelerated exposure of an ECTFE sample; this optical change does not measure chemical mineralization.

Timescales: In the patent’s comparison, the ECTFE sample’s reported transmission fell from 86.7% to 69.9% after the described 1,000-hour UV exposure. By comparison, a Solvay guide reports little mechanical or optical change in its Halar ECTFE film after 9,000 hours of a different accelerated cycle, alternating UVB at 70 °C with dark condensation at 50 °C. Different film and test conditions matter; neither result predicts a universal service life or environmental degradation rate.

Environmental persistence: Overheating and transmission loss do not establish complete biodegradation. The sources do not give a transferable mineralization time in soil, water or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The guide describes adding less than 15% suitable regrind, with darkened or contaminated resin rejected. This is established, formulation-qualified production-scrap recovery rather than a general post-consumer route.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: ECTFE handling guidance distinguishes the supplied resin from fumes generated during heating. The Fluoropolymers Product Group guide covers PTFE, FEP, PFA, ETFE, ECTFE and PVDF and warns that overheated fumes can cause polymer fume fever; higher exposure can be more serious. It calls for effective extraction of fumes and dust, protection from molten material, and keeping tobacco away from resin-handling areas because contamination can create hazardous fumes when burned. Fillers and dispersion ingredients need separate assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: ECTFE names a copolymer family rather than one fixed molecular architecture. Crystallinity, grade and fabrication affect physical properties. Supplier guidance applies to its stated materials and test conditions. Compatibility with a particular chemical must be assessed for the actual exposure and part. A tubing component should be selected for its actual fluid, temperature and pressure, rather than assuming that a supplier’s generic material description guarantees compatibility for every service. In the DSC comparison, cooling more rapidly reduced the calculated crystalline fraction of the particular Halar resin; the calculation also depends on the reference enthalpy used. Crystallinity inferred from that experiment cannot by itself specify the permeability or mechanical performance of a differently processed tube.
