sections.overview: Poly(chlorotrifluoroethylene) (PCTFE) is a fluoropolymer made from chlorotrifluoroethylene. Its backbone contains chlorine as well as fluorine, distinguishing it from PTFE. PCTFE is melt processable and can be molded or extruded. It is used in applications where barrier performance and dimensional stability are useful. Supplier molding guidance identifies grades for distinct extrusion and compression processes; the part’s cooling history affects its structure and final properties.
sections.history: PCTFE entered postwar commerce through M. W. Kellogg’s Kel-F, becoming generally available in the early 1950s; 3M took over that business in 1957. Daikin independently records development of its DAIFLON PCTFE in 1953. These production milestones do not settle the earliest synthesis of the polymer. Later industrial uses included cryogenic valve seats and seals, chemical-processing components and aerospace hardware. The original Kel-F business ended in the 1990s, while resin supply continued through other manufacturers. Drake’s account documents its own later conversion of Arkema Voltalef resin into machinable shapes and precision components, showing how specialized fabrication extended the material’s engineering applications.
sections.nomenclature: PCTFE abbreviates poly(chlorotrifluoroethylene). The name refers to the chlorotrifluoroethylene homopolymer, not to fluoropolymers generally or to chlorotrifluoroethylene copolymers. In particular, ETFE and ECTFE contain different combinations of monomer units and are separate copolymer families. A grade name and article form provide additional information not specified by the PCTFE abbreviation.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(chlorotrifluoroethylene) (PCTFE) is the homopolymer of chlorotrifluoroethylene (CTFE), formed by radical polymerization of the vinyl monomer rather than by polycondensation. Reported routes include bulk, suspension, and aqueous emulsion polymerization. One aqueous redox example combines an alkyl hydroperoxide with an alkali-metal metabisulfite in water to initiate CTFE homopolymerization; historical work also demonstrates mechanically dispersed aqueous polymerization initiated by hydrogen peroxide under ultraviolet radiation. Peroxide, redox, radiation, diluent, and medium selection are route controls and do not change the homopolymer identity; CTFE copolymers with other monomers are outside this PCTFE homopolymer entry.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PCTFE is a semicrystalline fluoropolymer generally used as a rigid, low-moisture-uptake engineering plastic, with tensile, impact, and deformation-under-load response set by molecular mass, crystallinity and cooling/annealing history, residual porosity, moulding or extrusion orientation, temperature, and any filler or compound choice. Its very low water uptake means moisture conditioning is usually less consequential than temperature and morphology, but values still apply to the stated grade and article form. An AFT Fluorotec datasheet for AF708, molded from Daikin M400H PCTFE resin, reports ASTM D638 tensile strength at break of 40 MPa at 23 °C, 10 MPa at 100 °C, 4 MPa at 150 °C, and 150 MPa at −129 °C. These are supplier typical values for that molded resin and tensile method; specimen geometry, rate, and conditioning are not given, so they do not establish a universal temperature-strength curve for PCTFE.
sections.processing:
PCTFE is a melt-processable fluoroplastic converted by compression, injection and transfer molding; ram or screw extrusion into rod, tube, sheet and simple profiles; machining of molded stock; and powder coating or impregnation. Its high melt viscosity and crystallinity make molecular-weight grade, preform quality, melt residence, corrosion-resistant equipment, pressure, cooling rate, and wall thickness important. Rapid cooling can preserve a clearer, more amorphous thin article, while thick sections generally need slower, uniform cooling to avoid voids or cracks; cooling history also sets crystallinity, density, elongation, and dimensional behavior.

Daikin distinguishes granular compression-molding M-300H/M-400H grades from pelletized compression/extrusion grades and warns that heavy sections should be cooled slowly. A bounded independent experiment by Yang, Xu, Guo, and Shen vacuum-dried PCTFE granules and their fluorinated modifier at 60 °C for 8 h, melt-mixed them in an RM-200C torque rheometer at 240 °C and 30 rpm for 5 min, and hot-compressed sheets at 240 °C and 10 MPa. That sequence applies to the named PCTFE/modifier formulations and test sheets. It is not a general molding schedule, and it should not be transferred to high-molecular-weight thick-stock or extrusion grades without grade-specific validation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PCTFE is semicrystalline, with ordered regions dispersed among less ordered material. Its crystal fraction depends on molecular mass and cooling history, and processing can produce spherulitic structures. In NIST experiments, very rapid crystallization between about 120 and 170 °C made it difficult to quench a 2 mm specimen without substantial crystallization. Daikin notes that rapid cooling of thin sections can retain greater transparency, whereas thick sections cool less uniformly and require attention to avoid voids or cracks. These results describe different specimens and processing histories rather than a fixed crystallinity for every article.
sections.properties: PCTFE combines low moisture absorption and water-vapor permeability with electrical insulation and chemical resistance. Its barrier properties are useful for packaging and sealing, but exposure conditions and article construction matter. In one study of compression-molded sheets, the unmodified PCTFE had a dielectric constant near 2.26 across 3–18 GHz; adding a fluorinated oligomer changed it only slightly in that particular blend. The same work reported about 90% visible light transmission while haze varied with blend composition. Higher crystallinity generally reduces optical clarity, so measurements on a particular thin sheet cannot be assigned to every molded grade.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PCTFE is used in semiconductor and chemical equipment, electronics and cryogenic-fluid service. Daikin lists seals, gaskets and chemical tubing and gives the example of a PCTFE seat in a butterfly valve for pipes carrying cryogenic fluids. In that design low-temperature stability and low shrinkage help maintain the sealing function. The supplier distinguishes general-purpose M-300 material from its higher-molecular-weight M-400H grade for applications needing toughness or stress-crack resistance; neither description qualifies an arbitrary finished seal.

Purchasing. Daikin lists NEOFLON PCTFE M-Series grades with separate technical data sheets. Select the named resin grade and conversion form through the supplier, or specify a finished seal or tubing from a fabricator.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked sources do not report a separate annual purchase tonnage or end-use mass split. Supplier availability establishes a commercial route, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Additive-free PCTFE vacuum pyrolysis produced chlorotrifluoroethylene together with heavier chlorofluorocarbon fragments. The recovered volatile fractions reflected the high-temperature vacuum treatment rather than products necessarily released in ordinary use. In a separate laboratory reaction, researchers used nucleophiles in dimethyl sulfoxide to remove fluoride from PCTFE. Their proposed initial mechanism is nucleophilic substitution; the engineered reaction is not a natural-weathering pathway.

Timescales: In NIST’s vacuum experiment, a 0.2 mm PCTFE sheet heated over 45 minutes and held at 380 °C for 30 minutes retained 47.5% of its starting mass. In the nucleophilic study at 150 °C, methylthiolate recovered 92% of the available fluoride after 24 hours, while amide reached 94% after 72 hours. These are different test materials, treatments and endpoints, not comparable environmental-weathering rates.

Environmental persistence: The vacuum volatilization experiment and chemical defluorination experiment did not measure biodegradation or mineralization in soil or natural waters. Fluoride recovery is evidence that fluorine was removed under the laboratory reaction, not proof that the polymer carbon was completely mineralized. Neither experiment establishes a PCTFE lifetime in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Researchers investigated chemical defluorination of PCTFE with nucleophiles in dimethyl sulfoxide. At 150 °C the study recovered 92% of the fluorine as fluoride after 24 hours using methylthiolate; amide required 72 hours for 94% recovery. The study attributed the slower reaction of PCTFE relative to PVDF partly to difficulty dispersing the more hydrophobic polymer in the solvent. The reaction changes the polymer chemically and does not remold or recover the original PCTFE. The university describes this work as laboratory-stage and identifies waste-stream suitability, costs and product safety as remaining questions; a commercial collection and recycling system was not established.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PCTFE high-temperature processing and thermal removal require assessment of evolving fluorinated material rather than relying on the properties of the cool solid. The NBS vacuum-pyrolysis study identified chlorotrifluoroethylene and heavier fragments under severe heating. HSE’s general plastics guidance supports temperature/residence-time control and ventilation, while the specific PCTFE grade’s safety documentation is needed to characterize workplace emissions and any additives.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Molecular-weight grade, processing route and cooling influence crystallinity and article properties. Thickness and geometry affect how a part cools: the NIST report notes rapid crystallization in a temperature interval that a 2 mm specimen could not traverse quickly enough to prevent significant crystallization. In a separate blend study, a fluorinated oligomer increased haze even while transmission stayed near 90%, illustrating that clarity and transmission do not describe exactly the same property. Supplier tables, laboratory sheets and finished seals must therefore be compared with their processing and test conditions identified.

sections.overview: Poly(vinylidene fluoride), or PVDF, is a semicrystalline fluoropolymer made from vinylidene fluoride. Its carbon chain carries both hydrogen and fluorine substituents. PVDF is used in chemical-resistant components, membranes and electroactive material forms. The processing method and crystalline phase affect the finished product. Porous hollow-fiber membranes and solid electroactive films illustrate different forms of the polymer: preparation changes the morphology relevant to each use.
sections.history: Arkema traces its Kynar PVDF business to Pennsalt’s development of the resin in 1960 and completion of a Calvert City production plant in 1965. Kynar 500 architectural-coating resin was introduced in 1965; this grade’s launch should not be mistaken for the first synthesis of PVDF itself. The coating grade became a durable finish for exterior metalwork, sold through licensed paint companies and used on prominent buildings. Later Arkema expansion addressed water management and new-energy applications, continuing the business inherited through Pennsalt and Pennwalt.
sections.nomenclature: PVDF abbreviates poly(vinylidene fluoride). The name denotes the vinylidene-fluoride homopolymer and should not be used for vinyl fluoride polymers or PVDF copolymers without qualification. Labels such as α and β describe crystalline forms of PVDF, not different monomers or independently specified commercial grades. A porous membrane, a piezoelectric film and a molded article can share the homopolymer name while differing in structure and preparation.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) is made by free-radical polymerization of vinylidene fluoride (VDF), most commonly under pressure in aqueous emulsion or suspension. In an emulsion route, VDF, a fluorosurfactant-stabilized aqueous medium, a peroxydicarbonate initiator, and a chain-transfer alcohol can be fed together or incrementally; the feed pattern and chain-transfer level control conversion and molar mass. Suspension routes likewise use water, a dispersant, an organic peroxide, and optionally a chain-transfer agent, while liquid-full pressure control can improve dispersion of the gaseous monomer. These examples describe homopolymer manufacture. VDF copolymers, post-polymerization phase selection, electrical poling, and article fabrication are separate matters and are not treated as synthesis of PVDF itself.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) is a semicrystalline thermoplastic whose tensile response is strongly governed by crystalline fraction and alpha/beta/gamma phase content, molecular mass, thermal history, draw ratio and direction, temperature and rate, and—especially for porous forms—pore morphology and defects. Stretching can orient chains and pores and promote beta-phase formation; strength can increase while break elongation falls, so values from dense sheet, film, fiber, and porous membrane should not be combined. For a bounded porous-material example, a bicontinuous PVDF hollow-fiber membrane made by thermally induced liquid-liquid phase separation, stretched 50% at room temperature at 20 mm min−1 and then annealed at 145 °C, had tensile strength 7.47 MPa (36% above the unstretched 5.48 MPa control). That result is a directionally processed microporous membrane, not a neat injection-molded or cast PVDF value.
sections.processing:
Poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) is converted by pipe, tube, profile, wire-coating, filament, film, sheet, and plate extrusion; injection, compression, and transfer molding; welding and thermoforming; solution casting and coating; phase-separation membrane spinning; and, for suitable filament, fused-filament fabrication. Melt grades are fed cleanly to a low-hold-up line, plasticized without excessive shear or stagnation, shaped, and cooled at a rate selected for crystallinity and dimensional control. Virgin unfilled Solef pellets are described as non-hygroscopic and normally do not require drying, but closed packages should equilibrate before opening to prevent condensation and every compounded or filled grade should follow its own feed guidance. Melt temperature, residence, metal contamination, screw/die dead zones, shear, mold or chill-roll temperature, hold pressure, shrinkage, cooling, post-anneal, and any drawing or electrical poling govern degradation, crystal phase, orientation, voids, and final dimensions.

Solvay's guide provides grade-bound flat-film starting profiles: for Solef 1008 and 6008 it lists extruder zones of 190, 210, 220, and 230 °C, a 230 °C die, and a 95 °C chill roll; the same table gives different profiles for Solef 1010/6010 and copolymer 31508, illustrating why conditions cannot be generalized. It also warns that yellow or brown extrudate indicates excessive melt temperature, recommends immediate cooling after wire coating, and identifies hot-runner stagnation as an injection-molding degradation risk. In a separate membrane experiment, Tang and co-workers stretched 26 wt% PVDF TIPS hollow fibers at room temperature at 20, 40, or 80 mm/min over 20–100% stretch, held them under strain at 145 °C for 15 min, and found breakage above 100% stretch; their 50% stretch condition preserved a more uniform pore structure than larger draws. Those values are specific to the Solef grades and the study's microporous hollow fibers.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PVDF contains repeating vinylidene fluoride-derived units and can crystallize in several polymorphic forms. In the nonpolar α form, chain conformations largely cancel their dipoles, whereas the β form has a more aligned polar arrangement. Processing can change phase and orientation: in one study, stretching solution-cast PVDF films increased the characteristic β-phase signal in infrared measurements. A separate porous hollow-fiber membrane study found that stretching and annealing raised its measured crystallinity from 43.6% to 51.7% for a specimen stretched 50% at 40 mm/min. These examples concern distinct films and membranes; the same result should not be assumed for every PVDF article.
sections.properties: PVDF can provide chemical resistance and mechanical strength in suitable environments, while polar crystalline phases can produce electrical responses. In a polar β-rich film, mechanical strain changes polarization and can generate an electrical signal; processing and electrode geometry affect the measured response. Porous membranes perform a different function: in a hollow-fiber study, stretching by 50% at 40 mm/min and annealing at 145 °C increased the reported pure-water flux from 457 to 776 L/m²/h at 0.1 bar. Its tensile strength also rose from 5.48 to 6.56 MPa in the reported tests. These paired values concern the specific fibers and their preparation, not an inherent permeability or strength of dense PVDF.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PVDF is used in chemical equipment, filtration membranes, wire and cable, photovoltaic backsheets, architectural coatings and battery materials. Membrane performance depends on pore structure as well as polymer chemistry: in one laboratory study, a porous hollow fiber stretched 50% at 40 mm/min and annealed had tensile strength of 6.56 MPa versus 5.48 MPa for the untreated fiber, while its water flux also increased. These results apply to the studied fibers and processing conditions, not every commercial filter.

Purchasing. Arkema’s Kynar portfolio includes pellets, powders, latex emulsions, film, solution resins and formulated compounds. Specify homopolymer versus copolymer, purity and intended coating, membrane or melt-conversion route through the material database and technical sales.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked portfolio does not give standalone annual PVDF purchasing volume. Battery production or overall fluoropolymer demand cannot be assigned wholly to PVDF, and liquid-dispersion mass is not dry-polymer mass.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In vacuum pyrolysis experiments, PVDF eliminated hydrogen fluoride and produced wax-like fluorinated fragments and a dark carbonaceous residue. In a separate chemical-treatment study, alkaline processing released fluoride from PVDF isolated from a photovoltaic backsheet. Researchers have also used strong nucleophiles in dimethyl sulfoxide to recover fluoride from PVDF. These high-temperature or chemically driven treatments do not describe natural environmental weathering.

Timescales: The backsheet-derived PVDF concentrate reached 90.4% defluorination after 600 minutes in 4.0 M sodium hydroxide and 50 mM tetrabutylammonium bromide at 90 °C. In a separate test, nearly complete fluoride recovery from PVDF was reported within six hours at 90 °C using amide or methylthiolate nucleophiles in dimethyl sulfoxide. Different starting materials and reagents limit direct comparison; both are engineered treatment endpoints, not environmental lifetimes.

Environmental persistence: Measured mass loss or fluoride release in a controlled process does not demonstrate complete mineralization of PVDF in soil, water or landfill. The treatment studies did not establish the fate of PVDF articles under those environmental conditions. Their results cannot be converted into a natural-environment lifetime.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Industrial PVDF scrap can be re-extruded in specialist recycling streams; segregation and contamination govern suitability. In a separate laboratory study, researchers separated PVDF concentrate from a photovoltaic backsheet, treated it with alkali and precipitated calcium fluoride from the released fluoride. They recovered 88.3% of the fluorine originally present in the tested backsheet as calcium fluoride.

The latter route recovers a fluorine-containing feedstock, not the original polymer. It requires reactive chemicals and separation steps; the experiment does not establish a commercial recovery route for every PVDF product.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PVDF handling guidance distinguishes the supplied resin from fumes generated during heating. The Fluoropolymers Product Group guide covers PTFE, FEP, PFA, ETFE, ECTFE and PVDF and warns that overheated fumes can cause polymer fume fever; higher exposure can be more serious. It calls for effective extraction of fumes and dust, protection from molten material, and keeping tobacco away from resin-handling areas because contamination can create hazardous fumes when burned. Fillers and dispersion ingredients need separate assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PVDF grades differ in molecular weight and processing characteristics. Crystal phase, orientation and thermal history influence electrical and mechanical measurements; a β-rich film developed for a sensor is not equivalent to a porous hollow fiber. In the cited membrane study, stretching and 145 °C annealing changed both crystallinity and pore structure, so improved water flux cannot be attributed to chemistry alone. Chemical resistance depends on the specific fluid, temperature and exposure. Data for a laboratory membrane should not be assigned to a dense molded article or to another preparation without its test conditions.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical addition forms PVDF. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another.

sections.overview: Tetrafluoroethylene–hexafluoropropylene–vinylidene fluoride terpolymer is commonly called THV. It contains units derived from three fluorinated monomers and is available as a melt-processable thermoplastic. THV grades are used in films, tubing and other products. Their composition and properties vary by grade. The combination of three monomer units produces a range of possible chain compositions rather than one fixed repeat sequence. Specific grades must be identified when comparing flexibility, melt flow or thermal behavior.
sections.history: The commercial history of the TFE–HFP–VDF terpolymer is closely associated with THV and the collaboration between Hoechst and 3M. In its company history, 3M describes the formation of the Dyneon joint venture in 1996 and development of THV applications using Hoechst’s manufacturing capability and 3M’s market experience. Documented uses included automotive fuel-filler tube linings, greenhouse films and fiber-optic tubing. 3M bought Hoechst’s interest at the end of 1999. These are commercialization and application-development milestones; the account does not establish that the terpolymer was first synthesized when the joint venture was formed.
sections.nomenclature: THV is the common abbreviation for the TFE/HFP/VDF terpolymer. The name requires all three comonomer families in this record's scope; PVDF, TFE–HFP copolymers, and other fluoropolymer grades are related materials rather than aliases.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Tetrafluoroethylene–hexafluoropropylene–vinylidene fluoride terpolymer is made by free-radical copolymerization of the three fluoromonomers TFE, HFP, and VDF. Commercial thermoplastic members are commonly called THV. Aqueous emulsion polymerization is an established route: deoxygenated water, a fluorinated emulsifier or alternative dispersing system, buffer, and a water-soluble radical source are charged to a pressure reactor, an initial monomer mixture establishes pressure, and TFE/HFP/VDF feeds are metered during batch, semibatch, or continuous reaction. Persulfate or persulfate/redox systems are useful initiators; a chain-transfer agent can regulate molar mass and end groups. One cited example maintains composition and pressure by feeding all three gaseous monomers to an aqueous reactor and then coagulates, washes, and dries the dispersion. A distinct patent uses ammonium persulfate in an aqueous fluorosurfactant medium and documents a TFE/HFP/VDF feed as one fluoro-copolymerization example. Monomer-feed ratios and conversion must be controlled because the three monomers have different incorporation behavior. Composition and sequence distribution determine whether the isolated material is semicrystalline and melt-processable or amorphous and elastomeric; a route example for an amorphous composition is therefore not a family-wide THV grade specification. Initiator, surfactant, chain transfer, pressure, temperature, and feed profile control particle nucleation, molar mass, composition, and residual monomer. The latex is coagulated or spray-isolated, washed as required, stabilized, and dried.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
THV terpolymers combine thermoplastic processability with the ability to deform substantially. Their tensile response depends on the proportions of VDF, TFE and HFP, crystalline structure, processing history and test temperature. Freimuth and colleagues observed ductile uniaxial tensile behavior in a laboratory terpolymer containing 52 mol% VDF, 36 mol% TFE and 12 mol% HFP; its stress–strain response differed at 20 and 50 °C.

A historical distributor sheet for 3M THV 500GZ reports typical tensile strength at break of 28 MPa and elongation at break of 500% by ASTM D638, plus a 210 MPa flexural modulus by ASTM D790. The sheet does not give specimen preparation, dimensions, conditioning, temperature or test speed. Those values describe the named historical grade and the limited stated methods, not a family-wide design range.

The tubing manufacturer Zeus cautions that geometry and processing significantly affect extruded-part properties; its tabulated THV figures are general guidance rather than specifications. The three sources describe different material and test scopes and should not be merged into a single property range.
sections.processing:
TFE/HFP/VDF terpolymers can be melt processed into articles. A historical THV 500GZ distributor sheet describes pellets used for molding, film, tubing, profiles and wire coatings, and describes coprocessing with selected nonfluorinated plastics and elastomers. The appropriate forming conditions and adjoining layers depend on the selected material.

A Saint-Gobain patent gives a bounded tubing example: a TFE/HFP/VDF terpolymer was extruded at a 590–610 °F (about 310–321 °C) melt temperature and 230–255 ft/min line speed into 1.58 mm outside-diameter tube, quenched in a 60–80 °F (about 16–27 °C) tank, and then electron-beam crosslinked at 75 Mrad. The patent attributes differences in clarity to the extrusion and quench conditions. This is one unusually hot, fast, fine-tube experiment, not a universal processing window.

The 500GZ safety data sheet warns that extreme heat can cause thermal decomposition and that processing fumes require appropriate ventilation. A particular grade, equipment and article geometry require their own process qualification.
sections.structureAndMorphology: THV chains contain TFE-, HFP- and VDF-derived units in proportions that vary among grades. HFP incorporation can disrupt crystallization compared with more regular fluoropolymer chains. A study of one specified terpolymer observed crystalline lamellae within a predominantly less ordered structure. Drawing and temperature changed its observed morphology. Freimuth and colleagues studied one terpolymer containing 52 mol% VDF, 36 mol% TFE and 12 mol% HFP. Its melt-crystallized specimens showed lamellar ordering within a predominantly less ordered material; that composition is only one member of the class.
sections.properties: THV grades can combine flexibility, chemical resistance and melt processability. In a study of a specified VDF/TFE/HFP composition, specimens underwent substantial deformation in tensile tests. Commercial grade data show differences in mechanical and thermal response. Formulation and thermal history determine how a particular material behaves. For the Freimuth specimen containing 52 mol% VDF, 36% TFE and 12% HFP, DSC at 10 °C/min gave a glass transition of 3 °C and a broad melting peak near 120 °C. A specimen stretched at 20 °C showed stress whitening, which the authors associated with a cavitational contribution to deformation. These observations are specific to that composition and preparation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. The historical THV 500GZ grade was described for molded parts, extruded films, tubes, profiles and wire coatings. Its supplier identified flexibility, chemical resistance and a processing profile compatible with some polyolefins and hydrocarbon elastomers as features for such uses. A 3M data sheet named automotive fuel hoses as an example and listed good fuel-permeation resistance and bondability to other substrates for multilayer constructions. For that historical 500GZ formulation, the supplier reported a typical flexural modulus of 210 MPa by ASTM D790; this is a grade-specific guide rather than a performance guarantee for a finished hose. These are historical grade-specific descriptions, and present availability and suitability require separate verification.

Purchasing. A historical distributor data sheet identifies 500GZ as pellets. 3M reports that it completed its exit from PFAS manufacturing at the end of 2025; present stock and alternative suppliers require verification.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked accessible sources do not establish current annual production or purchases for this terpolymer. A historical listing does not establish current manufacture or availability.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The THV 500GZ supplier identifies hydrogen fluoride and perfluoroisobutylene among possible products under extreme overheating, with carbon oxides and other fumes. This product-specific hazard list is not an ambient fate inventory. In a separate study of a VDF/HFP/TFE fluororubber, researchers treated powdered terpolymer with hydrogen peroxide in high-temperature water and measured fluoride and carbon dioxide. That elastomer specimen is chemically related to, but not necessarily the same formulation as, the historical THV thermoplastic grade.

Timescales: In the fluororubber experiment, six hours at 350 °C with 4.0 M hydrogen peroxide produced reported yields of approximately 95% of initial fluorine as fluoride and 94% of initial carbon as carbon dioxide. The specimen and deliberately severe treatment conditions matter: this reactor endpoint is not an environmental lifetime for THV articles.

Environmental persistence: Although the related fluororubber was substantially converted under the specific reactor conditions, that result does not establish biodegradation in soil or natural water. Environmental mineralization time remains unmeasured for the historical THV grade and for finished articles under ambient exposure.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The 500GZ safety data sheet provides disposal guidance, but the checked material does not establish a demonstrated THV-specific reclamation process. Melt processability alone does not show that a mixed or contaminated finished article has an available recycling route.

Collection, sorting and thermal history would need to be assessed for a particular waste stream. A material-specific recovery yield or commercial recycling rate remains an evidence gap.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The 3M Dyneon THV 500GZ SDS revised 10 October 2025 identifies polymer fume fever from thermal-decomposition fumes and burns from hot material as handling concerns. These warnings apply to the named THV grade and its processing conditions. Prevent overheating, control processing emissions and use protection appropriate to molten resin; filled, modified or dispersion formulations need their own safety assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The THV name does not specify monomer ratio, molecular weight or sequence distribution. A morphology or tensile result from one composition is not a universal family value. Specimen shape, processing and test temperature affect measurements. Grade datasheets should be used with their stated conditions. The 52/36/12 mol% composition studied by Freimuth does not specify every commercial THV product. Its deformation conditions and measured morphology cannot be used as universal grade limits.

sections.overview: Poly(p-xylylene) polymers, commonly called parylenes, form a family of vapor-deposited coating materials. In a documented route, a cyclic precursor is vaporized and pyrolyzed to reactive species that polymerize on exposed surfaces. The resulting thin films can coat complex shapes conformally. Different substituted parylenes have different chemical structures and uses. Because polymerization occurs on the exposed surface, a thin coating can reach features that would be difficult to cover uniformly with a liquid. The coating and underlying device form an assembly whose interface is important to performance.
sections.history: Michael Szwarc discovered vapor-deposited poly(p-xylylene) during high-temperature studies of para-xylene at Manchester in 1947. His deposit prompted industrial investigation by ICI, DuPont, Kellogg and Polaroid. William Franklin Gorham at Union Carbide subsequently developed a more practical deposition route using the cyclic dimer; Donald Cram’s laboratory contributed a dimer synthesis in 1951. Union Carbide announced the commercial Parylene coating system on 17 February 1965. The principal historical product was therefore a deposited protective coating, with polymer chemistry and application method developed together. Nova Tran licensed the technology in 1971; the later Specialty Coating Systems business continued its commercialization.
sections.nomenclature: PPX and poly-para-xylylene identify the unsubstituted family boundary. Substituted parylene materials are related family members whose precursor substitution must be stated; a deposited film is an article form of a named PPX material, not a separate polymer synonym.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: The poly(p-xylylene) family is commonly made by vapour-phase polymerization of a [2.2]paracyclophane precursor. Heating cleaves the dimer to reactive p-xylylene diradicals, which are transported under reduced pressure and condense/polymerize on the receiving surface without a conventional solution initiator or catalyst. The precursor substitution pattern is a family-level control: unsubstituted [2.2]paracyclophane gives poly(p-xylylene), while substituted cyclophanes furnish correspondingly substituted parylene members. These references describe polymer formation rather than downstream coating-use conditions.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Poly(p-xylylene) materials are normally vapor-deposited films or conformal coatings, so mechanics depend on the substitution variant (for example PPX-N versus chloro-substituted PPX-C), deposition conditions and film thickness, substrate constraint, microstructure, test mode and loading rate, and thermal, humid, oxidative, or long-term aging exposure. A coating or thin-film indentation result is therefore not directly comparable with a free foil tensile test. In one open tensile study of five Parylene C foils, the measured Young's modulus was 2.81 ± 0.06 GPa, yield strength 42.5 ± 1.1 MPa, and yield strain 2.58 ± 0.17%. Those results are specific to the deposited Parylene C foils and the study's tensile protocol, not the entire PPX family. A separate open aging study of deposited Parylene C measured 3.56 GPa by nanoindentation initially and 3.93 GPa after approximately five years of non-accelerated aging; it explicitly notes that indentation values on thin films can differ from tensile measurements because of substrate influence.
sections.processing:
Poly(p-xylylene) family materials are unusual article-conversion polymers because the important route is conformal vapor deposition rather than melt extrusion or injection molding. In the commercial Parylene process, a solid dimer feed is vaporized and cracked upstream, and the reactive vapor reaches room-temperature articles in a low-pressure chamber, where a continuous poly(p-xylylene) coating grows on exposed surfaces and into small gaps. The precursor-to-polymer chemistry belongs in Synthesis; for Processing, the controlling operations are article cleaning and masking, fixture design, adhesion promotion where needed, chamber pressure and deposition rate, thickness monitoring, and post-deposition inspection. Surface contamination, shadowing, difficult cable or elastomer interfaces, and inadequate adhesion preparation can defeat an otherwise conformal coating.

Kohler and co-workers provide a bounded Parylene C encapsulation example for piezoelectric implant actuators. They used a Labcoater 300, treated the article with oxygen plasma at 300 W for 5 min, applied Silane A-174 adhesion promoter, and deposited at 2.0–4.0 Pa to obtain an 11.9 micrometre coating. Their separate free-film specimens omitted plasma and promoter and instead used a release layer on a silicon wafer, illustrating that surface preparation depends on whether adhesion or release is wanted. These settings and the reported coating thickness belong to that Parylene C experiment and its equipment; they are not a universal window for every poly(p-xylylene) derivative or article geometry.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Parylene films are deposited from vapor as linear polymers containing para-xylylene units. They are described as semicrystalline and can form thin conformal layers. Parylene N has an unsubstituted aromatic ring, while Parylene C has one chlorine substituent. Coating thickness and surface preparation affect the finished film and its interfaces. The deposited chains contain aromatic rings linked through methylene groups, with substitutions distinguishing variants. A Parylene C microdevice review notes that deposition and heat treatment affect the resulting film and its water barrier. Film structure and adhesion also depend on the substrate and deposition history.
sections.properties: Parylene coatings can act as electrical insulation and barriers. The Parylene C literature describes low moisture permeability and mechanical flexibility, and a specific study tested its use as an encapsulation layer for a piezoelectric actuator. Adhesion at interfaces is an important practical limitation, especially during prolonged wet use. These observations should be matched to the particular parylene and coating conditions. A microfabrication review reports that annealing a tested 9 µm Parylene C film reduced measured water-vapor permeability from 0.0547 to 0.0276 g mm/(m² day) at 20 °C and 30% relative humidity. The coating’s bulk barrier behavior is only one part of device durability: a weak parylene–metal or parylene–parylene interface can permit delamination during wet exposure.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Poly(p-xylylene) coatings protect components in electronics, automotive, aerospace and medical-device supply chains. Parylene variants differ in chemistry and must be selected for the application. In a coated electronic component, the deposited film insulates and protects the substrate; selection also requires attention to adhesion and coating continuity. Parylene C has been investigated for implantable microdevices: one study deposited an approximately 11.9 µm coating on piezoelectric actuators and evaluated dielectric breakdown after repeated actuation. The completed device and its interfaces require their own qualification, because a free film’s tensile behavior alone cannot establish device reliability.

Purchasing. Buy a coating service for finished components, or buy the appropriate dimer precursor for an in-house deposition system. SCS lists N, C and D dimers and offers Parylene HT through its coating services; the precursor is not a melt-processing polymer pellet.

Scale and evidence limits. The supplier page does not disclose annual dimer or deposited-polymer tonnage. Coated-part counts and dimer purchases cannot be equated without coating thickness, surface area and deposition yield.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A National Bureau of Standards study heated unsubstituted poly(p-xylylene) under vacuum and collected volatile fractions. The bulk of the volatilized material was a larger-fragment fraction with an average molecular mass of 661; the smaller fraction included xylene, toluene and benzene. Those results describe high-temperature molecular distillation of the tested polymer, rather than a product inventory for ordinary weathering. Halogenated parylene grades require separate evidence.

Timescales: The original small-sample experiment found 93.3% volatilization after 80 minutes at 430 °C in vacuum. At 415 °C, 80.4% volatilized over 230 minutes. These are thermal-distillation test endpoints for unhalogenated poly(p-xylylene), not ambient degradation times.

Environmental persistence: Vacuum volatilization is not an ambient mineralization endpoint; coating lifetime also depends on the specific parylene and substrate. In a separate 37 °C phosphate-buffered saline soak, impedance modeling of a Parylene-insulated platinum electrode showed a sharp decline in a resistance associated with the interface after one day. The authors identified water penetration or early delamination as possible explanations; the measurement does not establish polymer mineralization. The NIST work examined the unsubstituted polymer alone and does not establish products of chlorinated Parylene C or fluorinated grades.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: For parylene-coated electronics, practical reclamation often targets the valuable device: SCS describes microabrasion to remove local coating or expose an entire board for rework, with vacuum collection of coating and abrasive waste. Laser ablation offers precise local removal, while thermal and chemical methods have substrate, residue and solvent limitations. These are commercial repair/rework methods that can enable component reuse; they do not recover parylene monomer or establish a closed polymer-recycling loop. Removal can allow a component to be inspected or repaired, but abrasive particles and detached coating must be managed as waste. The method does not recover the original polymer as a reusable resin.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Parylene-coated devices can be reworked by microabrasion, which creates removed coating and abrasive particles; SCS describes vacuum collection at the operation. Thermal removal and laser ablation introduce different heat and residue considerations, and chemical methods require assessment of the actual solvent. These process exposures are distinct from contact with an intact coating; a coating’s barrier function is not a substitute for controls during its removal.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Parylene N, C, D and other variants differ chemically and should not be assigned identical properties. Film thickness, deposition conditions and the underlying surface affect performance. In a Parylene C actuator study, tensile results differed from prior reports, with coating conditions suggested as a possible explanation. A result from one film or device does not establish behavior for every parylene coating. For example, the electronics review highlights interface adhesion as a distinct concern for Parylene C. Results for an unsubstituted polymer heated in vacuum or for one coated device cannot be transferred to every substituted grade and environment.

sections.overview: Epoxy resins are a broad family of precursors containing reactive epoxy groups that can form crosslinked thermoset networks. They include glycidyl ethers, glycidyl amines and cycloaliphatic epoxies. A hardener and cure schedule turn the selected precursor into a solid network with properties suited to its application. Epoxy systems are widely used in coatings, adhesives and fiber-reinforced composites. A cured network is a different material state from the resin used to make it; the choice of hardener changes the network and its performance. In a DGEBA comparison, changing from an aromatic to an aliphatic amine produced a substantially lower glass transition in the tested materials.
sections.history: Modern epoxy-resin development involved several inventors and commercial routes. Pierre Castan’s patent, claiming Swiss priority in 1938 and issued in the United States in 1943, describes curing polyphenol–epichlorohydrin products with acid anhydrides. It proposed cast and molded articles, electrical components and varnishes. Independently, Sylvan Owen Greenlee at Devoe & Raynolds developed epoxy-derived drying compositions for coatings, documented in his 1948 patent. The Araldite brand dates its epoxy technology to 1946 and subsequently served industrial and household bonding. These early molding, coating and adhesive routes explain why the epoxy family developed as a platform of resins and curing systems rather than one fixed polymer.
sections.nomenclature: EP is the abbreviation used for the broad epoxy-resin family. The canonical record is a family boundary, not one molecular structure or one cured network: narrower novolac, cycloaliphatic, and other epoxy-resin subfamilies remain distinct records, and a hardener-cured formulation is not an alias for the resin precursor.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: The epoxy resin family comprises oligomeric or polymeric precursors bearing epoxide groups; a central commercial member is bisphenol-A diglycidyl ether (DGEBA/BADGE). Conventional DGEBA manufacture reacts bisphenol A with epichlorohydrin to form chlorohydrin ether intermediates, then uses sodium hydroxide to dehydrohalogenate them to glycidyl ends. The Canadian assessment identifies direct bisphenol A/epichlorohydrin preparation, DGEBA advancement or homopolymerization, and DGEBA/bisphenol A reaction as routes to resin mixtures with different oligomer distributions. A recent source-specific alternative uses a quaternary-ammonium catalyst to form BADGE in epichlorohydrin without the conventional sodium hydroxide cascade. These are precursor-synthesis routes, not general curing instructions for finished networks.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Epoxy resins become covalently cross-linked networks on cure, so their mechanical response is not a property of the uncured resin alone. Many conventional, fully cured, unmodified epoxy thermosets are stiff and glassy at room temperature, with useful tensile and compressive strength and dimensional stability but limited strain to failure, notch sensitivity, and comparatively low impact or fracture toughness. Their response becomes increasingly viscoelastic as temperature approaches the glass transition, and sustained or cyclic loading can produce creep, stress relaxation, fatigue damage, or interfacial debonding. Consequential variables include epoxy functionality and backbone rigidity, curing-agent chemistry and stoichiometry, conversion and cure or post-cure history, cross-link density, dangling chains and other network defects, nanoscale heterogeneity and free volume, service temperature relative to glass transition, strain rate, moisture uptake and hydrothermal aging, physical aging, porosity, specimen geometry and notches, and the amount, morphology, dispersion, and interface quality of rubber tougheners, thermoplastics, particles, fibers, or other fillers. Increasing cross-link density commonly raises glass-transition temperature and rubbery modulus, but changes in network architecture can trade ductility and fracture resistance against stiffness or heat resistance; incomplete cure and moisture plasticization can shift those balances. As one bounded conventional formulation example, Nabipour and co-workers mixed a commercial diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A prepolymer with 4,4'-diaminodiphenylmethane at a 1:1 N-H-to-epoxy-group molar ratio, degassed it for 24 h at 70 °C and 24 h at 90 °C, then cured it for 2 h at each of 120, 140, 160, and 180 °C. Tensile testing on an Instron 5966 to ASTM D3039-08 at 2.0 mm/min gave 51.8 MPa tensile strength, 4.8% elongation at break, and 2.5 GPa Young's modulus; DMA gave 1,620.7 MPa storage modulus at 30 °C and a 143 °C glass transition. The article does not report tensile specimen dimensions or pre-test conditioning, and ASTM D3039 is primarily a polymer-matrix composite tensile method, so this single neat DGEBA/DDM network is an illustrative formulation result rather than a range for the epoxy family. Finished laminates, adhesives, coatings, and castings additionally depend on reinforcement architecture, adherend or substrate preparation, bond-line thickness, residual cure stress, defects, and the service environment.
sections.processing:
Epoxy resins are converted as formulation-specific reactive systems rather than by one family-wide cycle. Liquid or heat-softened resin and hardener are accurately metered and mixed, then used for adhesive bonding, coating, casting or encapsulation, fiber wet-out and laminating, or filled molding before cure. Surface cleanliness, mix stoichiometry, filler addition, viscosity, air removal, wet-out, film or section thickness, and cure temperature all affect the article. Mixed mass and container geometry also matter because the exotherm can shorten working time and cause overheating; spreading a batch into a thin layer or using smaller batches improves heat removal. A post-cure may be used when the named system and service temperature require it.

A bounded research example mixed commercial DGEBA with 4,4′-diaminodiphenylmethane at a 1:1 N–H-to-epoxy-group molar ratio. The formulation was degassed for 24 h at 70 °C and another 24 h at 90 °C, then cured sequentially for 2 h each at 120, 140, 160, and 180 °C. That unusually long laboratory schedule belongs to the reported DGEBA/DDM formulation and specimen preparation; WEST SYSTEM mixing ratios, working times, and application guidance likewise apply only to its named resin/hardener products, not to the epoxy family as universal settings.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Epoxy precursors differ in molecular architecture, epoxy functionality and molecular weight. Reaction with a curing agent opens epoxy rings and connects molecules into a three-dimensional network. Network formation and the final structure depend on the chemistry and relative amounts of resin and curing agent. Real networks can also contain structural heterogeneity and incompletely reacted groups. Curing creates junctions between molecules as epoxy rings react; the molecular distance between junctions and the degree of reaction both affect the final network.
sections.properties: Cured epoxy networks can provide useful adhesion, stiffness and electrical insulation. Aromatic or cycloaliphatic structures and the density of network connections influence thermal and mechanical behavior. The liquid or solid precursor has different handling properties from the cured material. Toughness, heat resistance and other properties are formulated rather than inherent constants of the entire family. For example, one DGEBA study found initial glass transitions of 200 °C with the aromatic hardener DDS and 94 °C with octamethylenediamine. Those results compare specific cured specimens, not the temperature limit of every epoxy.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Epoxy systems are used as adhesives, moisture-barrier coatings and composite matrices. For example, the WEST SYSTEM marine guide describes bonding, glass-fabric laminating and barrier coating in boat construction and repair; a liquid resin/hardener system can wet cloth and adhere to prepared surfaces before it cures. Huntsman identifies its MY 721 glycidylamine resin for high-performance composite parts and filament winding, illustrating a different precursor and fabrication context from the marine repair kit. Aerospace composite matrices are separately formulated systems.

Purchasing. Buyers can obtain matched repair packs or separately specified industrial precursor and hardener components. WEST SYSTEM's 101 repair pack combines 250 g of 105 resin with 50 g of hardener, while Huntsman lists ARALDITE MY 721 as a resin component; a compatible curing system and process remain necessary.

Scale and evidence limits. Huntsman lists MY 721 drum sizes of 145–500 lb; these and the small repair pack illustrate supply formats, not production volume, market shares or a total amount purchased. The examples concern different epoxy chemistries and cannot be treated as interchangeable grades.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In a laboratory study, DGEBA specimens cured with different amines changed color and surface chemistry under UVA; the authors interpreted spectral changes as evidence of photooxidation and fragmentation. For the DDS-cured specimen, a new infrared carbonyl signal accompanied a decrease in water contact angle from about 62° to 49°, indicating a more wettable exposed surface. These measurements describe the surface of that specific network. Separately, hydrothermal liquefaction of a commercial bisphenol-A epoxy yielded bisphenol A in the oil and phenols in the water fraction. These reactor products are not an inventory of ambient weathering products.

Timescales: Samples approximately 30 × 30 × 2 mm, cured with DDS or a cycloaliphatic amine, were irradiated in air at 25 ± 5 °C for 500 hours. Reported mass losses were about 14% and 3.7%, respectively; the difference belongs to those formulations and test conditions. In a separate conversion experiment, milled commercial epoxy was treated in water, with or without potassium hydroxide, at 350 °C for 20 minutes. Neither endpoint is an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Color change, surface oxidation and loss of mass do not establish mineralization. The experiments do not establish how long cured epoxy persists in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A cured epoxy network does not simply melt back into the original precursor. Hydrothermal liquefaction can produce an oil and aqueous chemicals from the tested commercial bisphenol-A epoxy, but separating useful products and determining their compatibility with new formulations remain necessary.

A patent discloses a different laboratory procedure on an anhydride-cured DGEBA sample: dichloromethane and diethylenetriamine pretreatment followed by reflux and water precipitation. The inventors report recovery of an oligomer/small-molecule fraction and of predominantly diethylenetriamine solvent; this is a disclosed experimental route, not evidence of commercial collection or recovery of an unchanged cured resin.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Uncured epoxy systems can irritate skin and cause sensitization; hardeners have their own hazards. WEST SYSTEM warns that contact risks persist during partial cure and that sanding incompletely cured material creates hazardous dust. Avoid skin and eye contact and control dust and vapors. Large masses of mixed resin can self-heat rapidly during cure and ignite nearby combustible material.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The term epoxy alone does not identify the precursor, hardener, additives or cure schedule. Crosslink density, incomplete cure and network heterogeneity influence measured behavior. Highly crosslinked systems may be brittle, motivating toughening with modifiers. A property measured for one cured formulation cannot be assumed for another. In the same comparative study, the aromatic DDS-cured material lost more mass under the specified UVA exposure than the cycloaliphatic-amine-cured material, illustrating why heat resistance and light stability must be assessed separately.

sections.overview: Bisphenol A diglycidyl ether, often abbreviated DGEBA or BADGE, is a widely used epoxy resin precursor. The resin is made by reacting bisphenol A with epichlorohydrin and can contain molecules of different chain lengths. It is combined with a curing agent to make a thermoset network. DGEBA-based systems are used in adhesives, coatings and composites. A cured network is a different material state from the resin used to make it; the choice of hardener changes the network and its performance. In a DGEBA comparison, changing from an aromatic to an aliphatic amine produced a substantially lower glass transition in the tested materials.
sections.history: Bisphenol A–epichlorohydrin chemistry was present in Castan’s foundational epoxy patent, with Swiss priority in 1938 and United States publication in 1943. Its examples prepare the resin and cure it with phthalic or adipic anhydride, while the proposed uses include molded electrical articles and varnish. This chemistry became a central branch of the commercial epoxy industry. Araldite’s history dates its epoxy-technology launch to 1946 and records subsequent industrial and domestic adhesive markets. The invention and commercialization milestones concern resin systems and hardeners; they do not imply that all present liquid, solid or formulated DGEBA grades originated in the same year.
sections.nomenclature: DGEBA identifies bisphenol A diglycidyl ether and is narrower than the general term epoxy resin. A DGEBA/hardener network is not the uncured resin alone: hardener chemistry, stoichiometry, and cure state define the finished thermoset and should remain part of its material name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: DGEBA is a difunctional epoxy precursor made by reacting bisphenol A with epichlorohydrin under basic conditions; the finished article is a formulation-specific network after reaction with an amine, anhydride, catalyst, or other hardener. The DGEBA molecular-mass distribution and epoxy equivalent weight affect viscosity and network functionality, while hardener stoichiometry determines conversion and crosslink density. An open DGEBA/3,3′-DDS post-cure study distinguishes primary amine addition from etherification and dehydration reactions that can become important during extended high-temperature treatment. Those secondary reactions explain why a DGEBA network's final constitution depends on both resin/hardener chemistry and thermal history; they do not turn a post-cure schedule into a synthesis recipe for the uncured precursor.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cured DGEBA networks range from stiff and glassy to toughened or rubber-modified systems; modulus, yield/fracture response, and ductility vary with resin length, stoichiometry, crosslink density, toughener, cure conversion, and temperature. In an open molecular-modeling study of DGEBA/3,3′-DDS networks, etherification produced modest strength increases in stoichiometric models and larger increases in excess-epoxide models. Subsequent modeled dehydration generally reduced strength relative to the etherified state, except in the long-chain stoichiometric model, where stiffness and strength increased; the response is specific to those model chemistries and very high simulated strain rates. The existing open DGEBA blend study supplies a separate tensile comparison for neat cured resin and bio-oil-containing formulations. Together these sources support a formulation-bounded measured/mechanistic account, not a universal DGEBA strength or modulus.
sections.processing:
DGEBA resin is mixed with the selected hardener and any diluent, filler, or reinforcement, degassed while warm enough to lower viscosity, cast/impregnated or molded, and cured followed by optional post-cure. The open DGEBA/3,3′-DDS study treats post-curing as an extended exposure at or above the cure temperature intended to raise strength and glass transition while reducing residual stress and outgassing; it also identifies etherification and dehydration as possible high-temperature reactions. This is a processing constraint rather than a portable schedule: pot life, exotherm, section thickness, hardener stoichiometry, and allowable post-cure temperature must be established for each DGEBA formulation.

One experimental example used acetone-conditioned walnut-hull bio-oil/DGEBA (WH 600 1:4), TEPA hardener, and silicone molds: 50 °C for 8 h followed by 65 °C for 12 h. This schedule belongs to the specified blend and laboratory preparation; it is not general DGEBA cure guidance.
sections.structureAndMorphology: DGEBA contains aromatic bisphenol A units connected to reactive glycidyl ether groups. Commercial resin can contain oligomers as well as the shorter molecule, with chain length depending on preparation. Reaction with a multifunctional hardener joins these molecules into a crosslinked network. The network may be heterogeneous rather than an ideal uniform lattice. Curing creates junctions between molecules as epoxy rings react; the molecular distance between junctions and the degree of reaction both affect the final network.
sections.properties: The cured material can combine stiffness and adhesion with useful thermal and electrical properties. Both the aromatic precursor and the cured network structure influence its response to heat. Its toughness and glass transition also depend strongly on the curing agent and cure conditions. Uncured resin viscosity and cured mechanical properties describe different stages of the material. For example, one DGEBA study found initial glass transitions of 200 °C with the aromatic hardener DDS and 94 °C with octamethylenediamine. Those results compare specific cured specimens, not the temperature limit of every epoxy.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. DGEBA resins are ingredients for adhesives, coatings and fiber-reinforced composites rather than complete cured products by themselves. A formulator can combine resin with a suitable hardener so that the liquid or softened precursor wets the reinforcement or adherend before becoming a crosslinked solid. Resin must be paired with a curing agent appropriate to the process and desired properties. DGEBA is therefore a precursor choice rather than a complete qualification of an adhesive or composite. In one documented construction use, BADGE-based systems protect steel bridges and other metal structures. A study of Massachusetts coating sites describes a zinc-rich epoxy/polyamide primer, an epoxy intermediate coat and a polyurethane topcoat; the layers work together to protect the prepared steel against corrosion and weather. Their performance belongs to the complete coating system, not to uncured BADGE alone.

Purchasing. Huntsman's formulator guide lists liquid ARALDITE LY 556 and distilled TACTIX 123 examples. A buyer must select the specific resin, hardener and processing route together; their eventual performance belongs to the cured formulation.

Scale and evidence limits. The product listings demonstrate material availability and intended formulation routes, not actual annual purchases or a separate DGEBA consumption total. No reliable standalone tonnage was established in the checked sources.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In a laboratory study, DGEBA specimens cured with different amines changed color and surface chemistry under UVA; the authors interpreted spectral changes as evidence of photooxidation and fragmentation. For the DDS-cured specimen, a new infrared carbonyl signal accompanied a decrease in water contact angle from about 62° to 49°, indicating a more wettable exposed surface. These measurements describe the surface of that specific network. Separately, hydrothermal liquefaction of a commercial bisphenol-A epoxy yielded bisphenol A in the oil and phenols in the water fraction. These reactor products are not an inventory of ambient weathering products.

Timescales: Samples approximately 30 × 30 × 2 mm, cured with DDS or a cycloaliphatic amine, were irradiated in air at 25 ± 5 °C for 500 hours. Reported mass losses were about 14% and 3.7%, respectively; the difference belongs to those formulations and test conditions. In a separate conversion experiment, milled commercial epoxy was treated in water, with or without potassium hydroxide, at 350 °C for 20 minutes. Neither endpoint is an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Color change, surface oxidation and loss of mass do not establish mineralization. The experiments do not establish how long cured epoxy persists in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A cured epoxy network does not simply melt back into the original precursor. Hydrothermal liquefaction can produce an oil and aqueous chemicals from the tested commercial bisphenol-A epoxy, but separating useful products and determining their compatibility with new formulations remain necessary.

A patent discloses a different laboratory procedure on an anhydride-cured DGEBA sample: dichloromethane and diethylenetriamine pretreatment followed by reflux and water precipitation. The inventors report recovery of an oligomer/small-molecule fraction and of predominantly diethylenetriamine solvent; this is a disclosed experimental route, not evidence of commercial collection or recovery of an unchanged cured resin.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For bisphenol-A epoxy formulations, distinguish the reactive resin/hardener mixture from the fully cured article. WEST SYSTEM handling guidance identifies skin irritation and sensitization during mixing and partial cure, dust exposure during sanding, and strong heat release from large curing batches. Gloves appropriate to the formulation, eye protection, ventilation and controlled batch size address these fabrication hazards.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: DGEBA is not a complete formulation: hardener identity, proportions, additives and thermal history must be specified. Oligomer distribution changes precursor characteristics and potential network architecture. Incomplete cure or spatial variations can affect glass transition and mechanical measurements. Results for one DGEBA–hardener system should not be treated as universal DGEBA values. In the same comparative study, the aromatic DDS-cured material lost more mass under the specified UVA exposure than the cycloaliphatic-amine-cured material, illustrating why heat resistance and light stability must be assessed separately.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Primary amine + epoxide → secondary β-hydroxyamine. Secondary amine + another epoxide → tertiary amine junction + another hydroxyl. Repeated reactions connect multifunctional molecules into a network. Epoxide C–O cleavage and C–N bond formation retain the oxygen as an alcohol; no condensation water is required for this addition.

reagents.name: 4,4′-Diaminodiphenyl sulfone
reagents.detail: Two primary amines provide four potentially reactive N–H bonds. DDS is consumed as a hardener; it is not a radical initiator.

steps.body: Select resin epoxy equivalents and the amine-hydrogen balance. DGEBA oligomers and alternative hardeners change the resulting connectivity.

steps.title: Build the network
steps.body: Primary and then secondary amine additions generate hydroxyl-bearing links and branching; continued reaction leads to gelation.

steps.title: Distinguish subsequent chemistry
steps.body: A separate computational DGEBA/3,3′-DDS post-cure study models additional etherification and dehydration. Its simulations are not a laboratory preparation schedule for the displayed 4,4′-DDS example.

sections.overview: Bisphenol F diglycidyl ether, or DGEBF, is an aromatic glycidyl ether epoxy resin precursor. It is prepared from bisphenol F and epichlorohydrin and is cured with a suitable hardener to form a thermoset. The bisphenol F starting material can give positional isomers. DGEBF resins are used where the combination of resin handling and cured performance is useful. Unlike a fixed molecular species, commercial DGEBF can be a mixture of regioisomers and oligomers. Their proportions can matter after curing: in a comparison using the same amine, increasing ortho substitution lowered the network's glass transition and increased its methanol uptake.
sections.history: Bisphenol F epoxy developed as a distinct branch of glycidyl-ether resin technology. By 1968, John Pfann and Adam Kopacki’s Stauffer Chemical patent already listed bisphenol F glycidyl ethers among commercial epoxy resins, so that date is a documented lower bound on established use rather than an invention claim. Later formulation work sought advantages in demanding coatings: a 1993 flooring patent identifies Shell’s EPON DPL-862 bisphenol F resin and develops hardener and aggregate combinations for impact and chemical resistance. This history illustrates how supplier resin development and application-specific formulation advanced the material after its initial introduction.
sections.nomenclature: DGEBF denotes diglycidyl ether of bisphenol F and is distinct from the bisphenol A DGEBA subfamily. The uncured DGEBF resin and a named DGEBF/hardener network are different material states; hardener identity, stoichiometry, and cure conversion belong to the description of the finished thermoset.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: DGEBF is a bisphenol-F-derived difunctional epoxy precursor. In the cited thermoset studies it is combined with an aromatic amine such as DETDA or with an anhydride-based hardener system. DETDA opens the epoxide rings in two sequential additions to form hydroxyl-bearing tertiary-amine crosslinks. An open DGEBF/DETDA study validated this network chemistry experimentally and varied crosslink density from uncured through fully crosslinked states in its process model, while a separate anhydride study shows that reactive-diluent selection is formulation-specific. Resin grade, stoichiometry, catalyst/hardener, diluent, and conversion are therefore part of the material scope.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cured DGEBF networks are generally stiff and glassy, but modulus, yield strength, fracture response, and ductility vary with resin composition, hardener, crosslink density, diluent, temperature, and strain rate. In an open DGEBF/DETDA study, fully cured ASTM D638 Type I specimens prepared at a 100:26.4 resin/hardener mass ratio had an experimentally measured Young's modulus of 2.392 GPa and 0.2%-offset yield strength of 36.96 MPa at an estimated strain rate of 1.95 × 10−4 s−1. The paper's simulations separately show how stiffness and yield response evolve with crosslink density. These are bounded DGEBF/DETDA values, not universal DGEBF properties. The existing anhydride/diluent study provides a separate formulation comparison rather than a basis for merging disparate results into a family range.
sections.processing: DGEBF is mixed with its selected amine or anhydride, warmed to lower viscosity, degassed, cast or impregnated, and thermally cured; post-cure may be used to reach conversion and target Tg. In the open DGEBF/DETDA experiment, stoichiometric components were hand-mixed for 2 min, heated to 80 °C for 20 min to reduce viscosity, degassed for a further 20 min, and molded into ASTM D638 Type I tensile specimens. Gel-point and shrinkage measurements were run isothermally at 150 and 170 °C, and the reported experimental post-gelation volumetric shrinkage was 2.36 ± 0.08%. These are bounded laboratory conditions for one resin/hardener ratio; section thickness, exotherm, pot life, regioisomer composition, and post-cure require formulation-specific validation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: DGEBF contains bisphenol F-derived aromatic rings linked through a methylene bridge and glycidyl ether groups. Positional isomers differ in the locations of substitutions on the aromatic rings. Curing joins epoxy groups and hardener molecules into a network. The arrangement and concentration of network connections depend on both the precursor mixture and the hardener. The para–para, para–ortho and ortho–ortho precursors place the glycidyl ether substituents differently relative to the methylene bridge. In one study each purified isomer was cured with meta-xylylenediamine; increasing ortho content produced networks with lower measured crosslink density, consistent with differences in packing.
sections.properties: DGEBF resin is often discussed as a lower-viscosity alternative to comparable DGEBA resin before cure. Cured properties depend on the hardener and degree of network formation. Aromatic units and crosslinks contribute to the thermal and mechanical response of the solid material. The performance of an individual formulation must be measured under its intended conditions. In the meta-xylylenediamine-cured isomer comparison, the para–para network absorbed less methanol than the ortho–ortho network and reached a higher glass transition. Methanol uptake can swell and plasticize a coating, so resistance depends on both resin isomer composition and the exposure medium.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Bisphenol-F epoxy is used as a resin ingredient in chemical-resistant coatings, flooring, conductive adhesives, encapsulants and composite prepregs. Huntsman describes its undiluted EPALLOY 8220 as a low-viscosity resin, and lists both primary flooring and viscosity modification of other epoxy resins among its intended uses. The supplier also identifies the same resin as a viscosity modifier for other epoxies, so it may be used as one component of a blend. The final coating or adhesive properties depend on the hardener and the rest of the formulation.

Purchasing. EPALLOY 8220 is one liquid bisphenol-F resin example available through quotation or sample requests; price, lead time and minimum order require a quote. The supplied precursor is not itself a fully cured coating or an independently qualified replacement for another grade.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported DGEBF purchase or consumption tonnage was established in the checked open sources. Supplier-listed uses and regional availability show an intended commercial route, not quantities sold or market share.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A disclosed solvothermal experiment on methyl-tetrahydrophthalic-anhydride-cured DGEBF produced small molecules and oligomers. The inventors interpreted reduced ester signals in the recovered material as evidence of cleavage of ester links while much of the bisphenol-F backbone remained. The patent reports a precipitated resin fraction as well as a small insoluble residue; recovered material is not the same as complete conversion to individual monomers. That reaction uses an added solvent and amine; it does not describe ordinary outdoor weathering, and amine-cured formulations need separate evidence.

Timescales: The patent's 2 g cured specimen was presoaked for 48 hours with dichloromethane and diethylenetriamine, then refluxed for 50 minutes at 130 °C. It reports 97.14% degradation based on the small amount of dried insoluble residue; That figure is calculated from residual insoluble material, not from identification or mass balance of every product. It is not a mineralization measurement or a service lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The experiment does not measure complete biodegradation or establish a residence time in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill. Dissolution and conversion to smaller organic molecules do not alone establish environmental mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The patent describes a laboratory recovery experiment rather than established collection: after pretreatment and reflux, the filtrate was mixed with water to precipitate a DGEBF-derived fraction, and the remaining filtrate was distilled to recover diethylenetriamine. From the 2 g cured specimen the inventors report 1.0643 g of dried precipitated material, which they identify as small molecules or oligomers rather than the original cured network.

This example applies to the stated anhydride-cured preparation; solvent handling, product separation and suitability of the recovered fraction for new resin formulations require separate assessment. It does not establish municipal acceptance or commercial recycling for mixed DGEBF waste.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When working with uncured bisphenol-F epoxy systems, prevent skin contact with both resin and hardener. HSE identifies epoxy systems as occupational dermatitis hazards and recommends application tools and gloves suited to the chemicals involved. Handling controls apply to the complete formulation; curing changes the exposure scenario.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Bisphenol F resins can contain different isomer and oligomer distributions. Precursor viscosity is not a direct measure of the toughness or heat resistance of the cured network. Hardener, cure schedule and additives change the final material. Comparisons with DGEBA must therefore specify the actual resins and formulations. The study's para–ortho specimen and commercial isomer mixture gave intermediate behavior in several measurements, but the commercial material also contained more chain-extended molecules. The observed ordering therefore describes that particular amine cure and test, not every DGEBF hardener or chemical exposure.
