sections.overview: Epoxy novolac resins are multifunctional epoxy precursors derived from phenolic novolac structures. Several epoxy-bearing sites on a molecule enable formation of highly connected networks on cure. They are used in coatings, electronics and composite formulations requiring heat or chemical resistance. The precursor is not itself the final cured thermoset. Compared with a difunctional epoxy precursor, the many epoxy groups can allow more network junctions, although final connectivity also depends on the curing system.
sections.history: Epoxy novolacs combined established phenolic-resin chemistry with the expanding epoxy industry. Theodore Bradley and Herbert Newey at Shell Development filed a patent in 1952, issued in 1955, on epoxy resins made from alkylphenol novolacs. It documents an early route to resins with multiple reactive sites, rather than proving the first invention of every epoxy-novolac subtype. By 1968 Stauffer Chemical’s curing-agent patent listed epoxidized novolacs among commercial epoxy materials. Their history therefore includes both precursor synthesis and curing-system development, with coating and thermoset formulation work exploiting the additional functionality.
sections.nomenclature: Epoxy novolac (EPN) is used here for the novolac-derived epoxy-resin family. The name does not mean uncured phenol/formaldehyde novolac alone, a generic non-novolac epoxy resin, or one particular hardener-cured network; those scopes remain distinct even when related in a formulation.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Epoxy novolac resins are multifunctional glycidyl-ether precursors made by epoxidizing phenolic novolacs. A historical phenol example first prepares a novolac by acid-catalyzed phenol/formaldehyde condensation, then reacts it with epichlorohydrin and sodium hydroxide to form an epoxy resin. Phenolic oligomers often contain ortho and para methylene bridges, but their distribution depends on starting phenols and synthesis. A different patent example uses phenol, cresol and fluoral to form a fluorinated novolac, which is subsequently epoxidized; that preparation is not the selected historical phenol/formaldehyde example. Crosslinking of the resulting epoxy functionality is outside this section.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Epoxy novolac is a multifunctional epoxy-resin family, including phenol- and cresol-novolac epoxies, whose cured mechanical response depends on epoxide functionality/equivalent weight, curing-agent stoichiometry and schedule, network density, plasticizer or rubber toughener, and test temperature. The dense aromatic networks are often selected for high-temperature rigidity but can be brittle; open work on epoxy–novolac adhesive reports that reactive nitrile-rubber modification decreases Young’s modulus while raising failure strain and, at its optimum, tensile strength. Composite and filled molding-compound values must remain separate from neat cured-resin values.

A bounded unmodified epoxy–novolac adhesive example from Han and co-workers is the 0 wt% GNBR formulation: at room temperature its tensile strength was 68.1 MPa, Young’s modulus 2.27 GPa, and failure strain 2.88%; at 233 K the same formulation gave 78.7 MPa, 3.91 GPa, and 1.93%, respectively. The reported values are for that cured adhesive formulation, and the article’s table does not identify a tensile standard or specimen geometry. A separate cured epoxy cresol novolac example is Epon 164 with Epikure W: after 90 °C for 4 h plus 180 °C for 2 h, its storage modulus at 25 °C was 2.3 ± 0.3 GPa by DMA. That dynamic modulus is not interchangeable with tensile modulus and applies only to the named resin/amine cure.
sections.processing:
Epoxy novolac resins are converted as reactive thermosets by melting or dissolving the multifunctional prepolymer, mixing it with a hardener and catalyst, introducing filler or reinforcement where required, degassing, casting, coating, impregnation, or transfer into a mold, and then completing a formulation-specific cure and post-cure. High functionality and, for some commercial grades, a solid or high-viscosity feed can make wetting and homogeneous mixing harder than with lower-functionality liquid epoxies. Mix temperature, stoichiometry, catalyst level, degassing, part thickness, and staged heating must be coordinated to limit voids and cure exotherm.

Stanzione and co-workers provide a bounded commercial epoxy-cresol-novolac example: Epon 164 and Epikure W were mixed for 10 min at 2000 rpm in a centrifugal mixer, defoamed for 5 min at 2200 rpm, transferred to aluminum pans, vacuum-degassed for 15 min and held under oven vacuum for another 15 min, then cured for 4 h at 90 °C and post-cured for 2 h at 180 °C. A separate novolac/anhydride comparison cast its formulation in aluminum molds and used 3 h at 80 °C, 1 h at 120 °C, 3 h at 180 °C, and 10 min at 250 °C to control thermal gradients and runaway; its authors state that this laboratory schedule was longer than typical and not industrial. Both cycles are formulation-specific examples, not family windows.
sections.structureAndMorphology: A phenolic novolac backbone contains aromatic rings connected predominantly by methylene bridges. Glycidyl ether groups attached to the aromatic units provide sites for crosslinking with a hardener. The number and distribution of epoxy groups vary with the precursor molecular structure. Cure connects these species into a network whose architecture depends on formulation and reaction conditions. In a comparison using methyl nadic anhydride, the selected novolac precursor produced the highest estimated crosslink density among the three tested epoxy systems. This is a comparison of particular formulations rather than an intrinsic constant for the family.
sections.properties: The multiple reactive sites allow dense network formation and can support elevated thermal resistance. A comparative epoxy–anhydride study found that the selected novolac and other precursor structures produced different thermal and mechanical behavior. High connectivity can also make cured systems brittle. Viscosity and handling of the precursor are affected by its molecular structure and formulation. The same study found the selected novolac network had a DSC glass transition near 184 °C, between its bisphenol-A and cycloaliphatic comparators. The authors also found its uncured precursor less flowable than the cycloaliphatic precursor, making processing and cured heat response separate selection criteria.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Epoxy novolac precursors are ingredients for laminates, electrical materials, adhesives and composites where a formulated network may need chemical or heat resistance. Their multiple epoxy groups can provide many curing sites, but practical performance depends on the hardener and processing schedule. Huntsman describes epoxy phenol novolacs for high-glass-transition adhesives and composite routes such as prepreg and filament winding, while listing cresol novolacs for electrical and laminating products. A prepreg stores reinforcement impregnated with a formulated resin before final shaping and cure; an electrical laminate is a different construction with its own requirements. The precursor’s role is to help formulate the cured network; a catalog grade by itself does not describe the finished component.

Purchasing. The Huntsman formulator guide lists semi-solid ARALDITE EPN 1138 and separate solid cresol-novolac grades. A formulator selects the precursor, compatible hardener and processing route; the uncured resin is not the finished laminate or encapsulant.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for epoxy novolacs was established in the checked sources. The listed grades demonstrate availability and intended formulation routes, not market share.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A patent reports mass loss and carbonaceous residue for phenol-formaldehyde polyglycidyl-ether networks during thermogravimetry in air; flexibilizers changed the residue. Another study compared an anhydride-cured epoxy novolac with cycloaliphatic and bisphenol-A networks at high temperature. Neither experiment identifies a complete set of products formed during natural weathering.

Timescales: In the latter study, the specified novolac–methyl nadic anhydride formulation retained 93.7% of its initial mass after 100 hours at 250 °C, versus 85.5% for its cycloaliphatic comparator. A bisphenol-A-based comparison retained 92.6% under the same test. These are accelerated thermal mass-retention measurements on selected cured networks, not environmental lifetimes.

Environmental persistence: Mass loss and residue formation do not demonstrate complete biodegradation. The cited tests do not establish a mineralization time in soil, water or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A patent proposes grinding cured epoxy/fiber composite material and dispersing the particles in molten polypropylene with a functionalized polyolefin. This retains composite-derived material as a filler or reinforcement; it does not recover the original epoxy monomer or an intact cured article. Epoxy novolacs are included in the patent’s stated resin scope.

Its worked example chopped a carbon-fiber/epoxy composite and compounded the particles with polypropylene; adding a functionalized polypropylene improved tensile response relative to the tested unmodified blend. The example does not identify its epoxy as a novolac, however. It therefore illustrates the proposed approach rather than proving a dedicated novolac process or commercial collection.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When working with uncured epoxy-novolac systems, prevent skin contact with both resin and hardener. HSE identifies epoxy systems as occupational dermatitis hazards and recommends application tools and gloves suited to the chemicals involved. Handling controls apply to the complete formulation; curing changes the exposure scenario.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Epoxy novolac describes a family with variable molecular weights and functionality rather than one fixed molecule. Hardener choice, proportions, cure and additives control the final crosslink structure. Greater potential functionality does not by itself determine measured toughness or glass transition. Results from a particular epoxy–anhydride study should be kept with its specific resins and cure conditions. The comparative study’s most highly crosslinked network did not have the highest glass transition, illustrating that backbone mobility and other aspects of network structure also matter.

sections.overview: Glycidyl amine epoxy resins are reactive precursors with glycidyl groups attached to nitrogen-containing amine-derived structures. Examples include the tetrafunctional aromatic resin tetraglycidyl diaminodiphenylmethane (TGDDM). A selected hardener converts the precursor into a thermoset network. Such formulations are used in demanding applications including aerospace composites. Multiple epoxide groups on a single precursor allow several connections to develop during cure. The final network and its properties depend on the hardener and curing process, not just the precursor name.
sections.history: Glycidyl amine epoxies illustrate the conversion of known small-molecule chemistry into engineering resins. Norman Reinking’s Union Carbide patent, filed in 1956 and issued in 1960, explicitly states that aromatic glycidyl amines had previously been prepared for biological investigation, but that their resin potential had not been appreciated. His work improved synthesis of products with high epoxy content and described formulations combining workable uncured resins with high heat-distortion resistance after cure. Thus 1960 is an identifiable resin-development milestone, not the first preparation of all glycidyl amines. The historical advance was the practical use of multifunctional aromatic amines as epoxy precursors.
sections.nomenclature: Glycidyl amine describes an epoxy-resin subfamily defined by amine-derived glycidyl functionality, not every epoxy resin or a finished network. A particular tetrafunctional resin, hardener mixture, and cure schedule identify a narrower material state and should not be collapsed into the subfamily name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Glycidyl amine epoxy resins are multifunctional epoxides made by glycidylating an amine precursor; they are resin precursors, not the already-cured epoxy network. A widely documented route first adds epichlorohydrin to primary aromatic amine sites to form a chlorohydrin amine intermediate, then uses alkali to dehydrochlorinate and close glycidyl rings. The amine identity and epichlorohydrin excess determine the resulting N-glycidyl functionality and molecular distribution. A later example uses N-alkylated m-xylylenediamine and epichlorohydrin, followed by base-promoted ring closure, to prepare a different glycidyl-amine resin. Solvent, catalyst, base concentration, and purification are particular process choices, not family constants. Formulation with curing agent and the subsequent thermal cure create a network and are excluded from this resin-manufacture description.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Glycidyl-amine epoxies are multifunctional epoxy precursors that become highly cross-linked, glassy networks after cure; the resulting neat resins can be stiff and retain modulus at elevated temperature, but their cross-linked structure also makes unmodified matrices susceptible to brittle crack initiation and propagation. Mechanical response depends strongly on epoxy functionality, cure chemistry and stoichiometry, cure and post-cure schedule, conversion and network heterogeneity, test temperature relative to the network glass transition, and any reinforcing fibre or toughening phase. Thermoplastic and core-shell-rubber modifiers can trade some stiffness for crack-energy dissipation; their phase separation and dispersion are therefore consequential, rather than generic family properties.

As one bounded neat-network example, Van Velthem and co-workers cured tetrafunctional TGDDM (Araldite MY721) with DDS using 80 °C for 2 h, 100 °C for 1 h, 150 °C for 4 h, then 200 °C for 7 h. On 20 × 4 × 1 mm specimens, tensile-mode DMTA at 1 Hz gave a storage modulus of 2820 ± 120 MPa at 35 °C and 1960 ± 96 MPa at 160 °C (three specimens). These are viscoelastic storage moduli for that dry, fully specified network, not universal tensile moduli. In the same system, 5 wt% phenoxy plus 5 wt% core-shell-rubber masterbatch increased critical fracture energy by about 260% relative to the neat epoxy in ASTM D5045 single-edge-notched bending at 1 mm/min; the result is modifier- and morphology-specific. As an independent grade-specific reference, Huntsman lists 8.7 ksi tensile strength and 14.9 ksi flexural strength for ARALDITE MY 721, but does not give the cured formulation, specimen geometry, conditioning, or mechanical-test rate on the public product page, so those values are not comparable family constants.
sections.processing: Glycidyl amine epoxy resins are converted as reactive liquids or prepolymers: they are blended with a selected hardener and modifiers, degassed, impregnated or cast into a tool, and thermally cured to form the article's cross-linked matrix. In a TGDDM (Araldite MY721)/DDS study, phenoxy and core-shell-rubber additions were mixed into the resin at 115 °C, DDS was incorporated with continued stirring, and the mixtures were degassed under vacuum at 120 °C for 20 min. The reported cure cycle was 80 °C for 2 h, 100 °C for 1 h, 150 °C for 4 h, followed by a 200 °C post-cure for 7 h; the same formulation was used for carbon-fiber prepreg and autoclave laminates at 7 bar. Huntsman identifies MY721 as a tetrafunctional resin for filament-wound high-temperature composites with ARADUR 5200 and a long pot life at processing temperature. Hardener stoichiometry, viscosity, fiber architecture, pressure, and cure schedule are system-specific and must not be generalized to all glycidyl amine resins.
sections.structureAndMorphology: A glycidyl amine precursor incorporates reactive epoxide groups on an amine-derived molecular framework. TGDDM has four glycidyl groups, providing multiple potential connections between molecules. Reaction with a multifunctional hardener creates a three-dimensional network. The topology depends on the resin, hardener, stoichiometry and extent of cure. Four epoxide groups on TGDDM offer multiple reaction sites, but the number that form effective network connections depends on reaction conversion and stoichiometry. Fillers, fibers and tougheners introduce additional structure in a finished composite. In an infrared study of epoxy-rich triglycidyl aminophenol formulations, significant primary-amine reaction occurred at 130 °C with the 3,3′-diaminodiphenyl sulfone hardener, while consumption was slower with the 4,4′ isomer under the investigated cure schedule. The position of reactive groups changes molecular geometry and reaction sequence, so nominal functionality alone does not specify how rapidly the network forms.
sections.properties: Multifunctional aromatic glycidyl amine systems can be formulated for high glass transition and stiffness after cure. Network formation and cure conversion affect thermal and mechanical response. TGDDM cured with an aromatic diamine has been studied as a high-temperature composite matrix. Tougheners can modify the fracture behavior of a selected system. Huntsman describes its MY 721 with ARADUR 5200 as a filament-winding system intended to retain mechanical performance at elevated temperature. That claim describes the selected resin–hardener system and composite processing, not every glycidyl-amine formulation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Glycidyl-amine epoxies are used as matrices in aerospace and other high-temperature composites. Huntsman describes its tetrafunctional MY 721 with ARADUR 5200 hardener for filament winding, where liquid resin wets reinforcement before cure. Huntsman identifies resin wet-out and long working time at processing temperatures as useful features of this resin–hardener system. The complete composite, fiber arrangement and cure schedule determine the final performance; a liquid resin specification is not a completed laminate property.

Purchasing. Huntsman lists liquid MY 721 and offers quotation and sample inquiry. A buyer must specify the hardener and process in addition to the resin.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked product page establishes a grade and use, but no separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this epoxy family. It does not establish production quantities for the complete composite.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In a TGDDM epoxy cured with diaminodiphenyl sulfone, thermal analysis and spectroscopy indicated dehydration as an early process; at higher temperatures the residue developed carbonaceous structures and oxidation competed with carbonization. This is a particular glycidyl-amine formulation under thermal treatment, not an inventory of products from ambient weathering. A patent includes glycidyl-amine epoxy resins in the scope of networks made with specially designed degradable hardeners. Acid and solvent can break such a network into soluble resin-derived material and release reinforcement. The demonstrated carbon-fiber example uses a bisphenol-A epoxy system, so it does not establish equivalent results for ordinary glycidyl-amine networks.

Timescales: In that separate bisphenol-A example, concentrated hydrochloric acid and ethylene glycol at 125 °C were applied for four hours before fiber separation. Separately, the TGDDM/DDS study used thermogravimetric heating at 3 °C/min in air and nitrogen; its observed changes around and above 310 °C belong to that ramp and formulation. Neither the designed treatment nor the thermal scan establishes an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Separation of reinforcement or precipitation of resin-derived material does not demonstrate complete mineralization. The cited patent does not establish disappearance times in soil, water or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The patent proposes separating reinforcement and precipitating resin-derived material after acid–solvent treatment of deliberately cleavable epoxy composites. Its example separates carbon-fiber cloth from a specifically prepared bisphenol-A epoxy composite; glycidyl-amine resin is listed in its broader scope.

This is proof of a designed approach, not proof that an ordinary MY 721 composite can be disassembled under the same conditions. Fiber quality, resin chemistry and solvent recovery require separate validation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Huntsman’s ARALDITE MY 721 safety sheet identifies skin sensitization for the tetraglycidyl-methylenedianiline resin and advises avoiding skin contact and inhalation of vapor or mist. It also identifies aquatic toxicity, making spill containment important. These findings describe the uncured commercial glycidyl-amine component; the hardener and finished composite require separate assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Glycidyl amine is a class of precursors, so functionality and molecular structure need to be identified. High connectivity can make a cured system brittle, although toughness depends on the complete formulation. Resin viscosity, cure conditions and modifiers affect handling and performance. Data for one TGDDM–hardener formulation should not be assigned to every glycidyl amine resin. More potential reaction sites can increase network connectivity, but curing conditions and hardener choice also determine the actual network. A formulated composite result cannot be substituted for a neat-resin measurement.

sections.overview: Cycloaliphatic epoxy resins are a group of epoxide-containing precursors with cycloaliphatic structures. A common type is obtained by epoxidizing cycloalkene groups. The precursor is formulated with a suitable curing agent and converted into a thermoset network. These materials are used in applications including electrical and electronic encapsulation. Some commercial cycloaliphatic resins are also used as reactive diluents in other epoxy systems: they can reduce the viscosity of a formulation while participating in cure.
sections.history: Cycloaliphatic epoxies developed along a route distinct from bisphenol glycidyl ethers. Union Carbide’s 1972 patent traces relevant diepoxide monomers to Benjamin Phillips and colleagues’ patents of 1956 and 1959. The 1972 work addressed a practical limitation of liquid cycloaliphatic epoxides by making solid, curable intermediates. It targeted molding, coatings and laminates, emphasizing electrical applications after cure. These documents establish a sequence from postwar monomer chemistry to handling and formulation improvements. They support a history of several related monomers and resin systems, rather than one invention date for the entire cycloaliphatic epoxy category.
sections.nomenclature: CE is the abbreviation used here for cycloaliphatic epoxy resin. The name identifies an epoxy-resin subfamily by its cycloaliphatic precursor chemistry, not a particular hardener-cured network; glycidyl-ether epoxy families and their cured formulations are not aliases for this record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cycloaliphatic epoxy resin is a reactive resin class made by epoxidizing cycloalkene-containing precursor molecules; it should not be conflated with a glycidyl-ether epoxy merely because both cure to epoxy networks. A documented route uses a dicycloalkene ester precursor and peracetic-acid epoxidation to form a diepoxy cycloaliphatic ester. An alternative two-step patent first esterifies a cycloalkene carboxylic acid with an alcohol or polyol (or a cycloalkene alcohol with a carboxylic acid), then oxidizes the cycloalkene-terminated ester with hydrogen peroxide in the presence of base, stabilizer, and acetonitrile. The epoxide functionality is then available for formulation-specific network formation, for example by anhydride or cationic curing chemistry; the cure recipe and any article-shaping schedule are not universal properties of the resin family.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cycloaliphatic epoxy becomes a mechanical material only after the reactive resin is formulated and cured. Tensile, flexural, fracture, and viscoelastic response depend on the particular epoxide, anhydride or other hardener, catalyst, filler and toughener content, stoichiometry, and cure/post-cure; values for a cured electrical-casting compound are not properties of the uncured resin or of all cycloaliphatic epoxies.

A bounded manufacturer example used TTA21P cycloaliphatic epoxy with methylhexahydrophthalic anhydride (130 parts per 100 parts resin) and AO-4 accelerator (2 parts), cured 2 h at 100 °C, 2 h at 140 °C, and 1 h at 180 °C. The reported cured system had tensile strength 57 MPa, tensile modulus 3205 MPa, elongation at break 2.8%, impact strength 5.95 kJ/m², and KIC 0.45 MPa·m½. These figures apply only to that formulation and schedule.

In an independent comparison cured with methyl nadic anhydride and 1-methylimidazole, the cycloaliphatic ECy-MNA network had a 253 °C Tg and 13.2 MPa rubbery plateau storage modulus under the study's torsional thermomechanical protocol. Its contrast with the novolac and BADGE networks illustrates why hardener, catalyst, cure protocol, and the measurement temperature must accompany any mechanical value.
sections.processing:
Cycloaliphatic epoxy formulations are commonly handled as low-viscosity reactive liquids for casting, coating, impregnation, or composite lay-up and then converted by a formulation-specific thermal or cationic-radiation cure. Anhydride-cured systems can offer long flow windows for wetting and filling, but mix stoichiometry, catalyst level, part thickness, and heat removal govern gelation and exotherm. A comparative laboratory study poured a cycloaliphatic epoxy/methyl-nadic-anhydride/1-methylimidazole formulation into aluminum molds and used a staged oven cycle specifically designed to limit thermal gradients and runaway before completing the cure.

The reported laboratory cycle was 3 h at 80 °C, 1 h at 120 °C, 3 h at 180 °C, and 10 min at 250 °C; the authors explicitly describe it as longer than a typical process cycle and not an industrial profile. A distinct one-component UV-curable grade, EPV 3408CO, illustrates another route: the supplier reports a 0.5 mm layer cured for 30 s at 395 nm and 0.5 W/cm², with the stated exposure suitable for layers up to 4 mm in aluminum molds. That grade is stored at 2–8 °C in closed, light-protective containers. Neither schedule is a universal family cure window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Cycloaliphatic epoxy precursors can contain epoxide groups incorporated into alicyclic rings. Their molecular structures and epoxy functionality differ from common aromatic glycidyl ether precursors. Curing with an anhydride or another selected system links precursor molecules into a network. The resulting network structure depends on precursor geometry and cure chemistry. For example, the selected precursor in an epoxy–anhydride comparison contained epoxidized cyclohexane rings connected through an ester group. Its ring structure and hardener jointly influenced the resulting network.
sections.properties: Cycloaliphatic epoxy formulations can provide useful electrical and thermal properties. In one comparative study, cycloaliphatic, aromatic and novolac precursors produced different network properties when cured with the same anhydride system. Precursor viscosity and the cured glass transition are formulation-dependent. The performance of the uncured liquid and the solid network should be considered separately. In the comparative study, the selected cycloaliphatic–methyl nadic anhydride network had a DSC glass transition around 253 °C, higher than the tested novolac network. Yet it lost more mass during subsequent exposure at 250 °C, showing that glass transition and resistance to chemical degradation are different measures.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Cycloaliphatic epoxy resins are used in electrical casting and LED or optical-device encapsulants. Tetra describes clear TTA21 grades as reactive diluents: in its TTA21P and bisphenol-based resin mixture, increasing the TTA21P proportion lowered the mixture viscosity. A lower-viscosity mixture can aid handling during casting, but the curing agent and cure schedule also affect the final network. The supplier also describes an anhydride-cured TTA21P formulation, illustrating that the liquid precursor and its cured electrical material are different stages of the same system. Its data apply to that particular mixture and cure rather than every cycloaliphatic epoxy.

Purchasing. Tetra lists TTA21S, TTA21L and TTA21P as liquid grades, with stated minimum contents of 90%, 95% and 97%, respectively. Those are supplier specifications for named liquids, not properties of their cured networks. A buyer selects the resin and compatible curing system and, where appropriate, additional epoxy components rather than treating the liquid precursor as a finished encapsulant.

Scale and evidence limits. A November 2022 supplier article reports 9,500 tons/year annual capacity at its Shandong base in the context of TTA21 expansion. This is reported plant capacity, not actual production, purchases or the complete cycloaliphatic-epoxy market.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A degradable-hardener patent includes cycloaliphatic epoxies in specially designed networks that can form soluble fragments under acid treatment. The mechanism depends on the hardener and cannot be assigned to ordinary cured formulations. In another study, a conventional cycloaliphatic–anhydride network showed mass loss and surface damage after high-temperature testing, but the test did not provide an ambient degradation-product inventory.

Timescales: A study’s selected cycloaliphatic epoxy cured with methyl nadic anhydride retained 85.5% of its initial mass after 100 hours at 250 °C, compared with 93.7% for its novolac comparator. The bisphenol-A-based comparator retained 92.6% in the same comparison. This thermal mass-retention result is for those networks and conditions, not an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Acid treatment and thermal mass loss do not demonstrate biodegradation or mineralization in soil or water. Neither establishes the residence time of an encapsulant or composite in the environment.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A patent proposes acid/solvent disassembly of deliberately cleavable epoxy formulations, followed by separation of reinforcement and precipitation of resin-derived material. Cycloaliphatic epoxy appears in its permitted precursor scope, but the cleavable hardener is essential to the concept. This is a disclosed recovery approach, not proof that a conventional cured encapsulant or arbitrary composite can be recovered by the same treatment.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The 2019 US safety sheet for ARALDITE CY 179 identifies skin sensitization, suspected mutagenicity and repeated-exposure organ toxicity for the supplied cycloaliphatic diepoxide component. It recommends avoiding skin and eye contact and inhalation of vapor or mist, with suitable contact protection. These warnings concern the reactive resin formulation and are not a classification of all fully cured cycloaliphatic epoxy articles.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Cycloaliphatic epoxy refers to a group of structures, not one resin formulation. Hardener selection, ratios and cure schedule affect conversion and resulting properties. The cited comparative study used specified prepolymers, anhydride and accelerator. Its results cannot be generalized to every cycloaliphatic grade or curing system. The high glass transition in the comparative anhydride formulation did not imply the best mass retention under prolonged heating. Neither result establishes a safe service limit for every cycloaliphatic formulation.

sections.overview: Unsaturated polyester resins are polyester precursors containing carbon–carbon double bonds. They are generally prepared from unsaturated acids or anhydrides and diols, often with additional saturated acid components. The precursor is commonly combined with a reactive vinyl monomer and a radical initiator. Cure produces a crosslinked thermoset used in coatings and fiber-reinforced composites. The vinyl monomer participates in cure as well as reducing the viscosity of the uncured mixture, so its choice affects both handling and the final network. Glass-fiber reinforcement carries much of the load in a laminate while the resin binds and transfers stress between fibers.
sections.history: Carleton Ellis developed the modern unsaturated-polyester concept in the 1930s: unsaturated polyester could be cured with a peroxide, and reactive monomers such as styrene made the system easier to use. His patent work dates from 1936. Early glass-reinforced applications included aircraft ducting, followed by civilian boat hulls. Pultrusion and filament winding widened use to rods, electrical insulation, pipes and storage vessels. The important historical transition was from polyester chemistry to resin systems that could wet reinforcement and cure into shaped composites; later orthophthalic, isophthalic and modified grades represent diversification within that platform.
sections.nomenclature: UPR and UP are abbreviations for unsaturated polyester resin. The family covers unsaturated polyester precursors and their cured networks; saturated thermoplastic polyesters, vinyl ester resins, and one filled or cured formulation are related materials rather than aliases.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Unsaturated polyester resins (UPRs) are made in two chemically distinct stages. First, a difunctional alcohol such as propylene glycol, ethylene glycol, diethylene glycol, or neopentyl glycol is step-growth condensed with an unsaturated diacid or anhydride—classically maleic anhydride or fumaric acid and, in bio-based variants, itaconic acid—often together with a saturated aromatic or aliphatic diacid that adjusts rigidity and spacing of cure sites. Water is removed as ester bonds form, and the prepolymer is stopped at a target acid value. Nitrogen, a radical inhibitor such as hydroquinone, and controlled heating limit discoloration and premature reaction of the carbon–carbon double bonds; zinc acetate, organotin compounds, or acid catalysts are bounded catalyst examples. The unsaturated polyester is then dissolved in a copolymerizable reactive diluent. Styrene is conventional, while methyl methacrylate, dimethyl itaconate, and other multifunctional or bio-derived monomers are route variants. A peroxide, redox pair, or photoinitiator generates radicals that copolymerize the diluent with unsaturation in the polyester backbone, creating the thermoset network. One cited open study condenses itaconic and succinic acids with 1,2-propanediol using zinc acetate, toluene-assisted water removal, and hydroquinone, then crosslinks solutions in dimethyl itaconate/methyl methacrylate with methyl ethyl ketone peroxide. A distinct recycling route glycolyzes post-consumer PET with diethylene glycol using dibutyltin oxide, condenses the glycolysate with itaconic acid, and uses methacrylate or itaconate reactive diluent and a redox cure system. Diacid/diol balance, unsaturation spacing, acid value, inhibitor, reactive-diluent identity and fraction, initiator/promoter, and oxygen or moisture govern viscosity, gelation, network density, and residual monomer. Article-shaping cure schedules belong in Processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cured unsaturated polyester resin is a covalently crosslinked, usually glassy thermoset matrix. Neat castings characteristically sustain a relatively steep initial elastic response but fail at modest strain, so brittle cracking, notch sensitivity, and limited impact energy are recurring constraints. In reinforced parts, the measured response is no longer a resin-only property: fiber or fabric type, volume fraction, orientation, wet-out, interface quality, voids, laminate sequence, and loading direction can dominate stiffness, strength, fatigue, and fracture.

The network is highly formulation- and cure-dependent. Polyester backbone composition and spacing of unsaturation, reactive-diluent identity and loading, comonomer reactivity, and residual monomer govern crosslink density, segment mobility, microgel heterogeneity, and glass-transition behavior. Cure initiation, peak exotherm, conversion, post-cure, oxygen inhibition, shrinkage stress, and entrained pores can therefore alter both stiffness and failure. One open study of itaconate/MMA diluents found brittle tensile curves throughout its formulation set; changing diluent ratio shifted glassy storage modulus and tensile properties, while more volatile MMA was associated with cure-generated micro-/nanopores. Flexible backbone segments or diluents may raise failure strain or impact response but can reduce modulus or strength. Temperature approaching the formulation's glass transition, moisture or chemical exposure, fillers and tougheners, and test rate, geometry, and conditioning must also be reported.

A bounded example illustrates scale rather than a family specification. Rubeš and co-workers tested a 60 wt% solid UPET1 formulation made from glycolyzed post-consumer PET and itaconic acid with 40 wt% styrene (UPET1-STY40). After room-temperature cure overnight and sequential 1 h post-cures at 50, 70, and 90 °C, 2 mm dog-bone specimens tested at 5 mm min−1 gave ultimate tensile strength 82.4 ± 2.1 MPa, tensile modulus 2.71 ± 0.28 GPa, and elongation at failure 5.3 ± 0.4%. The same study showed large composition sensitivity in impact and bending: the corresponding UPET1-DMI40 formulation reached 140.4 ± 4.5 MPa ultimate flexural strength but only 4.9 ± 0.4% outer-face strain at failure, with 50 × 6 × 3 mm specimens in three-point bending over a 40 mm span at 1 mm min−1. These values apply only to those resin recipes, cure schedule, specimen forms, and test conditions; they are not general UPR design allowables.
sections.processing:
Unsaturated polyester resins are commonly supplied as low-viscosity reactive liquids that are shaped and cured in one operation. Important conversion routes include gel coating, casting, hand lay-up and spray-up, resin-transfer molding and vacuum-assisted infusion, filament winding, centrifugal casting, pultrusion, continuous lamination, and compression pressing of sheet- or bulk-molding compounds. Processing begins with controlled addition and dispersion of fillers, pigments, thixotropes, reinforcement, promoter and initiator appropriate to the supplied resin; mixing order, resin temperature, viscosity, pot life, and batch size govern whether the material can wet fibers and fill the tool before gelation. Molds require cleaning and release preparation, open laminates require complete wet-out and roller deaeration, and closed molds require balanced flow and venting. Cure exotherm, shrinkage, styrene or other reactive-diluent loss, entrained air, laminate thickness, and post-cure all require control. Preparation of the polyester prepolymer belongs in Synthesis; lay-up, molding, cure, and post-cure schedules belong here.

Aurer and Kasper describe the family-level conversion sequence and the major open- and closed-mold routes; their hand-lay-up procedure applies release agent and optional gelcoat, places and saturates cut glass mat, removes bubbles with serrated rollers, then cures at room temperature before demolding and finishing. A distinct experiment by Krishnan and co-workers gives a bounded schedule for Scott Bader Crystic 2-406PA, a preaccelerated UP resin containing 35–40 wt% styrene and 0.2 wt% cobalt octoate. They hand-stirred that resin with 2 wt% Catalyst M for about 5 min, cast it into 5 cm-diameter, 3 mm-deep molds, cured it at room temperature for 24 h, and post-cured it at 80 °C for 6 h. Their glass composite used eight individually impregnated 300 × 300 mm woven-E-glass layers, vacuum bagging, and the same resin-specific cure; these are experimental conditions, not universal UPR settings.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The polyester precursor contains ester linkages and sites of unsaturation along its chains. During radical cure, these sites react with a vinyl monomer such as styrene to connect the chains into a network. The network composition reflects both the polyester and the reactive monomer. Molecular structure and conversion affect the resulting network architecture. The unsaturated sites are spaced along polyester chains rather than comprising an all-vinyl backbone. The amount of unsaturation and copolymerization with the diluent affect how densely different chains are connected.
sections.properties: Cured unsaturated polyester systems can provide a rigid matrix for reinforced composites, but liquid handling and cured response are different measurements. For one DCPD-based product, Crystic 703PA, the supplier reports heat-deflection temperatures under 1.80 MPa of 59 °C and 64 °C for unfilled castings with two different post-cure schedules. The same sheet reports 49 MPa tensile strength for the first casting and 38 MPa for the second. These values show why cure and specimen preparation matter; they are not universal UPR limits, and the strength of a glass laminate includes the reinforcement and interface.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Unsaturated polyesters bind reinforcement in boat structures, building panels, sanitaryware and vehicle panels. Chemical-containment service requires a suitable resin grade. The liquid resin wets fibers before it hardens, making it useful as the matrix in laminates and molded composites. The matrix and fiber placement are selected together for the part. For Crystic 703PA, the supplier specifies a low-viscosity DCPD-modified resin for vacuum injection, where liquid must travel through reinforcement before the network gels. Its catalyst amount and workshop temperature determine the usable handling period for that grade.

Purchasing. Suppliers sell application-specific liquid laminating or closed-mold resins; Crystic 703PA is a DCPD-modified example. The supplier describes it as pre-accelerated and designed for vacuum injection of large parts, with low viscosity and controlled exotherm. Its published options include 25 kg, 225 kg and 1.1 tonne containers as well as tanker delivery; the resin and chosen reinforcement must be specified for the intended process.

Scale and evidence limits. The supplier lists container sizes from 25 kg to 1.1 tonnes and tanker delivery, spanning small-shop and bulk supply. This is supply format, not family consumption or use-share statistics.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: EURECOMP reported hydrolysis of several polyester-composite chemistries in heated, pressurized water. In its orthophthalic example phthalic acid was recovered, while the glycols underwent further conversion; the DCPD-modified resin produced additional organic compounds. These are products of controlled treatment, not a prediction of natural weathering.

Timescales: The project explored temperature and pressure in laboratory reactors, and reported longer processing for larger composite pieces and heavily calcium-carbonate-filled resins. The consortium also tested a 20 L prototype and reported that larger composite pieces took longer to separate because resin remained in their interiors. Higher temperatures shortened treatment but could damage the recovered glass fibers; those treatment times and tradeoffs are not environmental lifetimes.

Environmental persistence: In a separate exposure study, a pultruded glass-fiber/unsaturated-polyester profile immersed in deionized water at 23 °C for 360 days gained about 1.03% mass and lost about 24% tensile strength relative to the unexposed profile. The tests assess water uptake and composite performance, not conversion of resin carbon to carbon dioxide. The polyester chemistry and fiber construction were specific to the tested profiles, and the results do not establish a mineralization time in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
EURECOMP used water-based solvolysis to free reinforcement from polyester composites in laboratory and 20 L prototype reactors. The recovered fibers needed solvent washing, and a project trial substituted recycled fiber for 20% of the reinforcement in prototype electrical boxes; the specific starting-resin chemistry for that part was not identified.

The project found that higher temperatures shortened treatment but could damage glass fibers; its 270 °C example reported a 30% loss of fiber mechanical strength. Separating the individual organic products was difficult, and the project reported economics requiring improvement. The work demonstrates a prototype pathway, not an established closed-loop process for every unsaturated polyester formulation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For styrene-containing unsaturated polyester formulations, open molding can expose workers to irritating styrene vapor, which can also cause headache or drowsiness. HSE recommends reducing exposed resin area and capturing emissions with ventilation. These hazards concern the liquid formulation and its application process.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Unsaturated polyester covers many precursor compositions and is not one material with a fixed property set. Resin composition, initiator and thermal history determine cure behavior and final response. Rapid curing and shrinkage can create manufacturing difficulties in a part. Reported results should identify the resin, reactive diluent, specimen, cure and any reinforcement. For example, the degree of cure can differ with initiator package and temperature, changing the stiffness and transition temperature of otherwise similar starting mixtures. The amount and arrangement of reinforcing fiber introduce another large source of variation.

sections.overview: Orthophthalic unsaturated polyester resins are polyester precursors containing units derived from orthophthalic acid or phthalic anhydride. Unsaturated acid or anhydride units supply sites for subsequent crosslinking. The precursor is usually formulated with a reactive monomer and cured into a thermoset. These resins are used in reinforced parts and other molded products. Phthalic anhydride supplies the saturated aromatic portion, while a different unsaturated ingredient provides the sites for reaction with styrene. The category identifies one part of the recipe rather than a complete cured formulation.
sections.history: Orthophthalic unsaturated polyester belongs to the resin technology developed around Carleton Ellis’s 1930s work on unsaturated polyesters and reactive monomers. His 1941 patent includes phthalic-anhydride-containing formulations, documenting that this chemistry was already part of the early development period. The subsequent glass-reinforced polyester industry grew through aircraft ducting, boat hulls and other molded products. The parent-family history is better documented than a separate first-invention date for the orthophthalic grade category. Its historical significance lies in adapting an accessible aromatic acid component to practical reactive composite-resin formulations.
sections.nomenclature: Ortho-UPR abbreviates orthophthalic unsaturated polyester resin. “Orthophthalic” specifies a compositional subfamily and should not be used as a synonym for all unsaturated polyester resins.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Orthophthalic unsaturated polyester resin is an unsaturated-polyester subfamily distinguished by use of orthophthalic feedstock, conventionally phthalic anhydride or phthalic acid, as its saturated aromatic acid component. It is produced by polyesterification with one or more glycols and an unsaturated diacid or anhydride, commonly maleic anhydride, so the oligomer backbone retains carbon–carbon unsaturation. Published compositions specifically describe phthalic anhydride, propylene glycol, and maleic anhydride. The unsaturation may later participate in radical network formation with a vinyl reactive diluent such as styrene. The feedstock proportions, glycol package, inhibitor choice, and network formulation are grade- and source-specific, so the cited examples do not prescribe one universal orthophthalic resin or cure schedule.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Orthophthalic unsaturated polyester is a resin family whose measured mechanics belong to a specified formulation and cured article, not to the liquid resin alone. Styrene content, promoter/initiator package, cure and post-cure schedule, specimen quality/voids, and any fiber or mineral reinforcement can all change the response; laminate or filled-composite data should therefore not be substituted for neat casting data. Two publicly available technical sheets illustrate the need for this boundary by reporting different values and cure descriptions for different commercial ortho-UPR formulations.

As one bounded example, a Polynt Norsodyne® H 13212 TAE orthophthalic resin supplied through Resin Library is reported for cured, unreinforced resin after 16 h at 40 °C (and a separate 2 h at 120 °C step for HDT): ISO 527 tensile strength 57 MPa, tensile modulus 3,715 MPa, and break elongation 2.3%. These supplier values are not a family-wide range and omit specimen geometry, conditioning, cure initiator amount, and replicate statistics. An independent LRF sheet instead gives 40–60 MPa tensile strength, 2,500–3,500 MPa tensile modulus, and 1.5–2% elongation for a typical non-reinforced casting, tested to ISO 527/ASTM D638 but without a stated completed cure schedule.
sections.processing: Orthophthalic unsaturated polyester resin is supplied as a liquid reactive resin and converted by catalyst/accelerator mixing followed by casting or composite molding, gelation, and cure; section thickness, initiator level, reinforcement, and exotherm control make the cycle formulation-specific. The Polynt/Resin Library Norsodyne H 13212 TAE sheet reports cured unreinforced resin prepared with a 16 h at 40 °C curing cycle and gives the resulting ISO 527 tensile test context. A separate Laffan technical sheet gives a non-reinforced orthophthalic-resin casting example and its cure recommendation, with ISO 527/ASTM D638 test scope. These documents establish liquid-resin casting and bounded cure guidance for named products; they do not support treating either cycle as a universal orthophthalic-family window or as a laminate/RTM specification for every formulation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The polyester chain contains ester linkages and aromatic units derived from an orthophthalic feedstock. Other acid and glycol ingredients control the remaining chain structure and unsaturation. A reactive monomer such as styrene can react with the unsaturated sites during radical cure. This joins chains into a three-dimensional network. The positions of the substituents on the aromatic ring distinguish orthophthalic-derived units from their isophthalic counterparts. Other ingredients and the extent of cure still determine the network around those units.
sections.properties: An orthophthalic resin formulation must flow and wet reinforcement before it gels; after cure its network supplies a matrix for the composite. One Resin Library sheet reports that its unreinforced casting, cured for 16 hours at 40 °C, had tensile strength 57 MPa, modulus 3,715 MPa and 2.3% elongation at break by ISO 527. The liquid formulation is a pre-accelerated resin in styrene, rather than neat cured polymer as purchased. These results belong to the specified product and cure, while reinforcement, additives and processing change the finished part.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Orthophthalic UPR grades serve general-purpose, noncritical composite moldings; suitability for marine or chemical service must be established for the grade. The Resin Library example is a pre-accelerated, thixotropic orthophthalic resin in styrene, specified for hand lay-up and spray-up. Its sheet identifies it as general-purpose resin; it does not qualify every chemical exposure or finished laminate. The listed resin is thixotropic, allowing its flow to change under mixing and application, and contains styrene as part of the supplied liquid formulation. As a different product example, distributor Kevra recommends the orthophthalic Aropol M105 TB resin for reinforced boat manufacture and describes wetting of glass fibers during hand lay-up or spray-up. Its Polylite 32032-20 is instead a clear casting resin suggested for decorative castings and tabletops. Marine exposure or appearance requirements must be checked for the complete grade and part.

Purchasing. The checked Resin Library sheet describes a pre-accelerated, thixotropic liquid resin in styrene for hand lay-up or spraying. The 2020 sheet lists a gel time of 14–18 minutes at 23 °C with 1% MEKP50 for the named grade. This handling result depends on the specified initiator and temperature; package quantities for that product require a supplier quotation. Separately, Kevra lists Aropol M105 TB in 1, 3, 10 and 20 kg packs and identifies its suggested hand-lamination and spray-up methods.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size; the specified pack masses are examples of supply units rather than annual consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: EURECOMP reported that water hydrolysis of a simple orthophthalic resin released phthalic acid; glycols were converted in part to other molecules under the treatment conditions. Raising temperature favored additional side reactions in the study. This is an engineered process, not evidence of equivalent breakdown during environmental exposure. In a separate accelerated weathering experiment, the surface of a cured, unfilled orthophthalic resin developed numerous microcracks and rounded defects after repeated UV, water-spray and condensation cycles. Such surface damage does not identify all chemical products or imply complete decomposition.

Timescales: The project explored temperature and pressure in laboratory reactors, and reported longer processing for larger composite pieces and heavily calcium-carbonate-filled resins. Within the project’s studied range, raising temperature by 10 °C approximately halved the reported cycle time, with a tradeoff between shorter cycles and recovered fiber quality. The project reported that recovered glass fibers required acetone washing for reuse, and that hotter treatments could compromise fiber strength. Those engineered treatment times and recycling operations are not environmental lifetimes. The laboratory weathering study examined specimens after 100 hours of repeated exposure, including UV at 60 °C and condensation at 50 °C. The authors noted that continued curing may have occurred along with weathering, so changes in the tested resin cannot be attributed solely to one mechanism.

Environmental persistence: The solvolysis work recovered fibers and an organic liquid mixture under controlled conditions; it did not measure mineralization in a natural environment. The sources do not establish complete biodegradation or a transferable mineralization time in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
EURECOMP used water-based solvolysis to free reinforcement from polyester composites in laboratory and 20 L prototype reactors. The recovered fibers needed solvent washing, and a project trial substituted recycled fiber for 20% of the reinforcement in prototype electrical boxes; the specific starting-resin chemistry for that part was not identified.

The project found that higher temperatures shortened treatment but could damage glass fibers; its 270 °C example reported a 30% loss of fiber mechanical strength. Separating the individual organic products was difficult, and the project reported economics requiring improvement. The work demonstrates a prototype pathway, not an established closed-loop process for every formulation in this subfamily.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For styrene-containing orthophthalic polyester formulations, open molding can expose workers to irritating styrene vapor, which can also cause headache or drowsiness. HSE recommends reducing exposed resin area and capturing emissions with ventilation. These hazards concern the liquid formulation and its application process.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Orthophthalic identifies one component of the polyester, not a complete resin recipe. Unsaturation, glycol composition, styrene content and cure affect network properties. A technical sheet for a particular commercial orthophthalic resin gives data for its identified material and test conditions. Those values should not be treated as a family-wide specification. For example, changing the amount of styrene changes the proportion of reactive diluent incorporated into the network. A resin casting and a fiber-reinforced laminate of that resin must be evaluated separately.

sections.overview: Isophthalic unsaturated polyester resins contain isophthalic acid-derived units in an unsaturated polyester precursor. Unsaturated acids or anhydrides supply sites for network formation. A reactive vinyl monomer such as styrene can be used to formulate and cure the resin. Isophthalic formulations are used in reinforced products, including chemically resistant applications. Isophthalic acid supplies aromatic units in the polyester, but the cured network also contains the unsaturated acid, glycols and reactive diluent chosen for the formulation. Some commercial grades are selected for corrosion-resistant composite service.
sections.history: Isophthalic unsaturated polyester was an established development target by the 1950s. E. F. Carlston and G. B. Johnson’s California Research patent, filed in 1954 and issued in 1959, addressed the order of reaction: first forming an isophthalic-acid/glycol intermediate, then incorporating the unsaturated acid. The aim was to obtain useful curable polyester compositions without the difficulties encountered when all components were combined together. This provides a concrete process milestone in the diversification of unsaturated polyester resins. It does not establish a unique first-invention date for every isophthalic formulation or convert the patent examples into universal properties.
sections.nomenclature: Iso-UPR is narrower than the general unsaturated-polyester-resin family because it specifies the isophthalic component. The liquid resin and its styrene-crosslinked network are distinct material states; catalyst package, reactive diluent, reinforcement, and cure schedule must remain attached to a finished formulation.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Isophthalic unsaturated polyester resin is a condensation product rather than a single fixed formulation. Its backbone is made by polyesterification of isophthalic acid (or an isophthalate-containing aromatic diacid) with one or more glycols, together with an unsaturated diacid or anhydride such as maleic anhydride or fumaric acid. In the documented two-stage routes, the isophthalic-acid/glycol portion is first polycondensed while esterification water is removed; the unsaturated acid is then introduced and polycondensation continues to the desired resin state. The backbone alkene unsaturation can subsequently participate in radical network formation, commonly after dissolution in a reactive vinyl diluent such as styrene. The cited recipes are process examples, not a universal resin composition or cure prescription.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Isophthalic unsaturated polyester resins are cured cross-linked networks, so neat castings are typically stiff and strong but have limited tensile elongation and fracture tolerance. The mechanical balance depends on the isophthalic/maleate and glycol formulation, molecular weight and reactive-diluent content, initiator/accelerator and cure/post-cure history, conversion and shrinkage, void content, and temperature relative to the network transition. Glass or natural-fibre reinforcement changes the response into a composite property, with fibre volume, orientation, interfacial adhesion, laminate architecture, and specimen direction becoming decisive. Water uptake can plasticize and hydrolyze the matrix and weaken interfaces; nanofillers can improve or degrade properties according to dispersion and agglomeration.

For a grade-specific neat-casting example, the public AOC VIPEL F701 series data sheet identifies a high-molecular-weight, two-stage isophthalic unsaturated polyester and lists typical cast tensile strength 83.4 MPa, tensile modulus 3.8 GPa, tensile elongation 2.8%, flexural strength 127 MPa, flexural modulus 4.2 GPa, and Barcol hardness 43, using ASTM D638/ISO 527-1, ASTM D790/ISO 178, and ASTM D2583/EN 59 as listed. The page does not disclose cure schedule, specimen dimensions, conditioning, or test rate, and labels the values typical rather than specifications. As an independent composition-specific study, Merah and Mohamed tested MEKP/cobalt-cured SAUDPOL SP-351-BV13 isophthalic UP and its organoclay variants: ASTM D638-02a tensile specimens were machined as dumbbells and pulled at 1.0 mm/min, while 127 × 12.7 × 4 mm specimens underwent ASTM D790-02 flexure at 1.15 mm/min on a 60 mm span. After three months' room-temperature tap-water immersion, flexural-property reduction was reported as about 40% for neat UP but about 10% for the 3 wt% I.30E-clay formulation; that comparison is not a dry-neat-resin family value.
sections.processing:
Isophthalic unsaturated polyester resins are converted as liquid thermoset formulations by hand lay-up, spray-up, resin wet-out and filament winding, with the catalyst, promoter system, reinforcement, mold, and cure schedule selected for the article. AOC describes its VIPEL F701 isophthalic series as suitable for hand lay-up, spray-up, and filament winding and advises keeping shop conditions controlled, checking gel behavior in a small batch under actual conditions, and choosing catalyst level and post-cure for the formulation and service requirement. Mixing must distribute catalyst and fillers without entraining excessive air; laminate wet-out, exotherm, gel time, article thickness, ambient temperature, humidity, and the staged release/post-cure sequence all affect voids, shrinkage, and final cure.

For a bounded casting example, Merah and Mohamed prepared SAUDPOL SP-351-BV13 isophthalic-UP nanocomposites by pre-wetting 120 g resin batches with clay for 5 min, high-shear mixing at 3000 rpm for 1 h while using a water bath to limit heating, ultrasonication, and vacuum degassing for 30 min before adding MEKP and cobalt accelerator and pouring a 126 × 178 × 4 mm plate. They left the mold at ambient conditions for 24 h to limit shrinkage, then screened pre- and post-cure temperatures and times in a vacuum oven. That sequence is specific to the named resin, clay formulation, and specimen; it is not a universal cure schedule for isophthalic UPR articles.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Isophthalate units introduce aromatic rings into the polyester chain, while unsaturated units provide reactive carbon–carbon double bonds. The remaining chain architecture depends on the acid and glycol mixture used. In a styrene-containing system, radical curing joins the unsaturated polyester and monomer into a network. The cured network is distinct from the soluble precursor formulation. The placement of the two acid groups on the aromatic ring differs from the orthophthalic isomer. The resulting material is still a mixed polyester network, whose structure also depends on its other reactants and cure.
sections.properties: Cured isophthalic polyester formulations can be selected for particular chemical environments, but their properties depend on the complete recipe and cure. AOC reports 83.4 MPa tensile strength and 2.8% elongation for post-cured, unreinforced Vipel F701 base-resin castings containing 40% styrene, tested by ASTM D638 at 25 °C and 50% relative humidity. The supplier separately identifies the F701 series for selected acid and fuel exposures and directs users to its corrosion guide. Those cast values are not laminate properties or a guarantee for every isophthalic resin and fluid.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Isophthalic UPRs supply marine laminates and chemical-containment composites. AOC F701 is a corrosion-resistant example for selected acids and fuels. AOC describes its Vipel F701 isophthalic series for composites fabricated by hand lay-up, spray-up or filament winding, and reports resistance to specified acids and fuels. A fabricator must check the particular chemical environment and cured article rather than infer universal resistance from the family name.

Purchasing. F701 is supplied as a liquid grade series for laminating, spraying or filament winding; chemical exposure and fabrication method guide selection. The supplier’s technical sheet lists multiple versions with different viscosity, gel time and styrene content, so F701 alone does not specify one processing behavior. For example, its 2009 F701 series sheet lists 44% styrene for F701-ABK-15 and 50% for F701-FBG-20; both values describe supplied liquid, not cured-network composition. The sheet advises consulting its corrosion guide or technical staff for the particular chemical environment.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: EURECOMP reported successful hydrolysis of a tested isophthalic resin under conditions also used for an orthophthalic resin, while noting that the results were not fully comparable. The treatment separates reinforcement from the resin-derived organic mixture; it does not establish that the resin degrades at the same rate outdoors or in water.

Timescales: The project explored temperature and pressure in laboratory reactors, and reported longer processing for larger composite pieces and heavily calcium-carbonate-filled resins. Within the project’s studied range, raising temperature by 10 °C approximately halved the reported cycle time, with a tradeoff between shorter cycles and recovered fiber quality. Recovering the fibers also required a washing step, while resin-derived compounds remained in a liquid mixture. Those engineered treatment times and separation operations are not environmental lifetimes.

Environmental persistence: The solvolysis work recovered fibers and an organic liquid mixture under controlled conditions; it did not measure mineralization in a natural environment. The sources do not establish complete biodegradation or a transferable mineralization time in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
EURECOMP used water-based solvolysis to free reinforcement from polyester composites in laboratory and 20 L prototype reactors. The recovered fibers needed solvent washing, and a project trial substituted recycled fiber for 20% of the reinforcement in prototype electrical boxes; the specific starting-resin chemistry for that part was not identified.

The project found that higher temperatures shortened treatment but could damage glass fibers; its 270 °C example reported a 30% loss of fiber mechanical strength. Separating the individual organic products was difficult, and the project reported economics requiring improvement. The work demonstrates a prototype pathway, not an established closed-loop process for every formulation in this subfamily.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For styrene-containing isophthalic polyester formulations, open molding can expose workers to irritating styrene vapor, which can also cause headache or drowsiness. HSE recommends reducing exposed resin area and capturing emissions with ventilation. These hazards concern the liquid formulation and its application process.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Isophthalic polyester names a family and does not specify all of the components or cure. Chemical resistance varies with exposure environment, temperature and the particular formulation. Crosslinking, post-cure, filler and glass reinforcement change the observed properties. A result for a named laminate or formulation is not a universal value for the family. Chemical resistance depends on the liquid, temperature, exposure and the finished composite as well as the resin grade. Formulations and cure conditions cannot be inferred from the isophthalic label alone.
