sections.overview: Dicyclopentadiene-modified unsaturated polyester resins incorporate DCPD-derived structures into a polyester precursor. The precursor is generally formulated with a reactive monomer and cured to a thermoset. Such resins are used in products such as hulls, decks and bathroom components. They are distinct from polydicyclopentadiene made by ring-opening polymerization. DCPD incorporation changes the polyester precursor and its cure behavior, but DCPD content and other feedstocks vary. It is the polyester precursor, subsequently crosslinked with a reactive monomer, that forms the matrix in these formulations.
sections.history: Dicyclopentadiene modification was part of the later diversification of unsaturated polyester resins. A clear milestone is Omer Curtis’s United States Steel patent, filed in 1979 and issued in 1980, which develops DCPD-containing polyester formulations and demonstrates glass-reinforced laminates. It treats formulation, dilution with reactive vinyl monomers and curing as linked design problems. The examples include resins usable in laminating and molding, showing the application-driven character of the development. This patent documents an established route and its improvement; it should not be read as the first discovery of all DCPD-modified polyesters.
sections.nomenclature: DCPD-UPR is the abbreviation used for this modified unsaturated-polyester subfamily. The name denotes an unsaturated polyester containing dicyclopentadiene-derived chemistry, not neat poly(dicyclopentadiene), a generic unsaturated polyester without DCPD, or one universal cured network formulation.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Dicyclopentadiene-modified unsaturated polyester is a DCPD-containing unsaturated polyester precursor, not a poly(dicyclopentadiene) material. In the commonly described water process, maleic anhydride is hydrolyzed with water and reacted with DCPD to form a carboxy-functional DCPD–maleate adduct. The adduct is then esterified/polycondensed with the remaining acid or anhydride components and glycols to form the unsaturated polyester, which may be diluted in a reactive vinyl monomer such as styrene. The cited academic study identifies Diels–Alder and water-process variants and shows that DCPD feed purity and methyl-DCPD content are route variables. A Nippon Shokubai patent gives a complementary two-step maleic-anhydride/water/DCPD route followed by reaction with polyhydric alcohol and, optionally, polybasic acid. Radical crosslinking of the final reactive-diluent formulation forms the thermoset network, but its initiator, promoter, and cure schedule are formulation-specific and are not included as a universal synthesis recipe.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cured DCPD-modified unsaturated polyester resin is typically a rigid, cross-linked thermoset with low tensile elongation and brittle fracture rather than a tough poly(dicyclopentadiene) elastomer; the two material families should not be conflated. Its stiffness, strength, and deflection depend on the base polyester acids and glycols, DCPD incorporation route and purity, backbone unsaturation, styrene or other reactive-diluent content, initiator and promoter package, degree of cure and post-cure, specimen defects and shrinkage, temperature, and any fiber reinforcement or fillers. Increasing effective network density generally raises glassy storage and flexural modulus and hardness while reducing segmental mobility and deflection, but changes in DCPD or methyl-DCPD composition can also alter copolymerization efficiency and leave soluble or weakly linked material. Perrot and co-workers provide a bounded neat-resin comparison: DCPD-modified UPD90 and UPD85 specimens, prepared from 90% and 85% DCPD feeds and cured with the reported styrene/MEKP/cobalt system, were conditioned and tested at 23 °C and 50% RH by ISO 527-2. UPD90 gave Young's modulus 3.16 +/- 0.11 GPa, tensile strength 48.3 +/- 3.6 MPa, and strain at break 2.0 +/- 0.2%; UPD85 gave 3.16 +/- 0.05 GPa, 46.6 +/- 2.2 MPa, and 1.8 +/- 0.1%, respectively. The same formulations showed brittle fracture and lower tensile strength and elongation than the study's conventional UP2 reference. These values are not family-wide ranges and do not describe reinforced laminates. A separate study of DCPD-modified unsaturated epoxypolyester/styrene networks reinforces the formulation dependence: changing backbone double-bond content changed cross-link density, room-temperature storage and flexural moduli, hardness, and deflection. Because that work used epoxy-modified polyester chemistry and a specific staged cure/post-cure, its measurements are mechanistic context rather than representative values for ordinary commercial DCPD-UPR.
sections.processing:
Dicyclopentadiene-modified unsaturated polyester is normally converted as a reactive-liquid thermoset rather than melt-shaped after cure. Patent literature describes casting and lining, wetting reinforcement for fiber-reinforced plastic, and preparing sheet- or bulk-molding compound followed by compression molding. The resin is blended with its reactive diluent, filler or reinforcement, promoter, and initiator shortly before use; impregnation, air removal, mold filling, gel time, laminate thickness, and heat removal must be coordinated because the cure is exothermic and the working time is formulation-dependent.

A bounded patent example hot-molded a particular DCPD-polyester/styrene formulation at 100–177 °C and 0.69–10.3 MPa for roughly 30 s to 5 min, with time selected for formulation and part thickness; the same patent describes ambient casting or laminating packages based on benzoyl-peroxide/amine or methyl-ethyl-ketone-peroxide/cobalt initiation. Separately, Perrot and co-workers cast their named UPD85 and UPD90 research resins after adding styrene, cobalt accelerator, and MEKP and post-cured the specimens for 2 h at 100 °C. These are patent- and experiment-specific examples, not a universal DCPD-UPR molding or cure window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: DCPD can be incorporated during polyester manufacture by different reaction routes. One route uses an adduct of DCPD and maleic acid that subsequently reacts with other polyester ingredients. The resulting unsaturated precursor can be crosslinked with a vinyl monomer. The location and amount of DCPD-derived structures depend on the synthesis route and recipe. The water-process route introduces a DCPD–maleate adduct before polyesterification, whereas other routes place DCPD-derived structures differently. The resulting network reflects those choices and the subsequent radical cure with styrene or another diluent.
sections.properties: DCPD incorporation changes precursor and cured network behavior relative to the selected polyester formulation. The literature describes low shrinkage and rapid curing in thin sections for some DCPD-modified products. In one experimental series, changing the methyl-DCPD content affected the cured material’s mechanical behavior. These effects must be read alongside the precise composition and cure. In Perrot and colleagues’ specific cast resin series, tensile strength of UPD90 was 48.3 ± 3.6 MPa versus 63.0 ± 1.8 MPa for the conventional UP2 comparison; elongation fell from 3.9 ± 0.8% to 2.0 ± 0.2%. The comparison is for their recipes and 23 °C, 50% relative-humidity tensile tests, not a universal effect of adding DCPD. The Crystic 703PA technical sheet gives heat-deflection temperatures under 1.80 MPa of 59 °C and 64 °C for unfilled castings with two different post-cure schedules. These are properties of that supplied resin and its specified cures, not limits for every DCPD-modified laminate.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. DCPD-modified UPR supports composite manufacture for boats, building components and transport. Scott Bader describes Crystic 703PA as a pre-accelerated resin intended for large vacuum-injected parts; its liquid viscosity and exotherm characteristics are selected for that process. This is an example of tailoring liquid handling and cure to a process; the resin does not by itself define the reinforcement or finished part.

Purchasing. Scott Bader supplies Crystic 703PA in 25 kg, 225 kg or 1.1 tonne containers and by road tanker. Its technical sheet describes the material as pre-accelerated and calls for a catalyst before cure. The listed pot life with 1.5% Butanox M50 is 124 minutes at 20 °C and 84 minutes at 25 °C, illustrating why shop temperature and catalyst package matter for this grade.

Scale and evidence limits. The documented packaging spans tens of kilograms to tonnes, with larger bulk deliveries. It does not establish annual purchases, global production or this subfamily’s share of all polyester composites.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: EURECOMP reported that hydrolysis of a tested DCPD-modified polyester generated additional organic molecules from DCPD-derived chemistry compared with simpler polyester resins. The project did not identify a universal product inventory for all DCPD formulations or demonstrate an environmental mineralization rate.

Timescales: The project explored temperature and pressure in laboratory reactors, and reported longer processing for larger composite pieces and heavily calcium-carbonate-filled resins. Within the project’s studied range, raising temperature by 10 °C approximately halved the reported cycle time, with a tradeoff between shorter cycles and recovered fiber quality. Larger composite pieces required longer processing because the interior was less readily reached, and the recovered fibers required washing. Those engineered treatment times are not environmental lifetimes.

Environmental persistence: The solvolysis work recovered fibers and an organic liquid mixture under controlled conditions; it did not measure mineralization in a natural environment. The sources do not establish complete biodegradation or a transferable mineralization time in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
EURECOMP used water-based solvolysis to free reinforcement from polyester composites in laboratory and 20 L prototype reactors. The recovered fibers needed solvent washing, and a project trial substituted recycled fiber for 20% of the reinforcement in prototype electrical boxes; the specific starting-resin chemistry for that part was not identified.

The project found that higher temperatures shortened treatment but could damage glass fibers; its 270 °C example reported a 30% loss of fiber mechanical strength. Separating the individual organic products was difficult, and the project reported economics requiring improvement. The work demonstrates a prototype pathway, not an established closed-loop process for every formulation in this subfamily.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For styrene-containing DCPD-modified polyester formulations, open molding can expose workers to irritating styrene vapor, which can also cause headache or drowsiness. HSE recommends reducing exposed resin area and capturing emissions with ventilation. These hazards concern the liquid formulation and its application process.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: DCPD modification does not specify the amount or incorporation route, other polyester ingredients or reactive monomer. Reported trade-offs can include brittleness and lower glass transition or chemical resistance relative to some other polyester systems. A study of DCPD and methyl-DCPD blends found composition-dependent results for its particular recipes. Processing, cure and reinforcement also affect the finished material. The same study found that a different methyl-DCPD-rich formulation, UPMD65, had much lower tensile modulus and strength than UPD90. Feed composition and the rest of the recipe therefore matter when comparing this modification. In that supplier example the casting cured for 24 hours at 20 °C plus 16 hours at 40 °C, or for 24 hours at 20 °C plus 3 hours at 80 °C; the change in reported heat-deflection temperature illustrates why the cure schedule matters.

sections.overview: Vinyl ester resins are reactive oligomers commonly made by reacting epoxy resins with unsaturated acids such as methacrylic acid. The product retains polymerizable carbon–carbon double bonds. It is frequently formulated with styrene or another reactive monomer and cured by a radical reaction. Cured vinyl ester resins are used as matrices in reinforced structures and corrosion-resistant equipment. The epoxy-derived backbone and the polymerizable ester ends play different roles: the former contributes the molecular framework, while the latter join chains during cure. The liquid formulation is used to wet fibers before the crosslinked network develops.
sections.history: A major commercial milestone for epoxy vinyl esters was the 1965 development of Derakane for hot, wet, corrosive chlorine service. Ashland’s fiftieth-anniversary history identifies pulp bleaching and wastewater treatment as the original target markets, followed by chemical processing, air-pollution control and mineral processing. The family combined epoxy-derived precursors with a radical-curable resin system suited to reinforced plastics. Subsequent development also addressed formulation emissions: Giuseppe Palmese, John La Scala and James Sands’s 2008 patent describes multimodal vinyl esters intended to reduce volatile diluent requirements. The Derakane date applies to that product lineage, not necessarily the first synthesis of every vinyl ester.
sections.nomenclature: VE and VER abbreviate vinyl ester resin. The name describes an epoxy-derived, vinyl-functional resin family and its cured networks; vinyl acetate polymers, unsaturated polyester resin, and one specific epoxy or reactive-diluent formulation are separate scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Vinyl ester resins are thermosetting, unsaturated oligomers usually prepared by ring-opening addition of an epoxy resin with an ethylenically unsaturated monocarboxylic acid. A bisphenol-A diglycidyl ether epoxy is a common backbone precursor; novolac epoxies, urethane-modified epoxies, and other multifunctional epoxies give route variants. Acrylic or methacrylic acid opens the oxirane rings and installs terminal or pendant (meth)acrylate ester groups. Tertiary amines, quaternary ammonium or phosphonium salts, and phosphines are useful reaction catalysts, while hydroquinone-class inhibitors suppress premature radical polymerization. Acid value and disappearance of epoxy groups are practical reaction endpoints. The oligomer is commonly diluted with styrene or another copolymerizable monomer to lower viscosity. A cited patent example methacrylates a bisphenol-A epoxy with a triphenylantimony/triphenylphosphine catalyst system and then formulates the resulting vinyl ester with styrene. Network formation is a second reaction: peroxide/redox or photochemical initiation copolymerizes the resin's carbon–carbon double bonds with the reactive diluent, producing an infusible network. A distinct open study demonstrates a styrene-free photochemical variant formulated from Bis-GMA, Bis-EMA, and hexanediol dimethacrylate with a bis-acylphosphine-oxide photoinitiator; a urethane-acrylate resin is a co-network modifier in that bounded example. Epoxy functionality and backbone, acid/epoxy ratio, catalyst, inhibitor, reactive-diluent identity and fraction, initiator/promoter, oxygen inhibition, and double-bond conversion govern viscosity, gelation, network density, and residual monomer. Vinyl ester resin is not the same family as poly(vinyl acetate) or other thermoplastic polymers of vinyl-ester monomers. Article-shaping cure schedules belong in Processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cured vinyl ester resin is a crosslinked thermoset whose epoxy-derived backbone can provide useful strength and crack resistance, but the neat matrix is still commonly glassy and may fail with little plastic strain. It should not be assigned a single family modulus or strength: bisphenol-A, novolac, urethane-modified, and other backbones, molecular weight between reactive end groups, and the identity and fraction of styrene or another reactive diluent produce different network structures. Toughening can raise fracture energy and failure strain, sometimes at the expense of glass transition, stiffness, or strength.

Initiator/accelerator or photoinitiator package, cure temperature and conversion, post-cure, shrinkage and residual stress, oxygen inhibition, print or molding history, porosity, fillers, and phase morphology all influence the measured response. Temperature relative to the cured network's glass transition and loading rate are consequential. In laminates, fiber type, volume fraction, orientation, sizing, wet-out, interface quality, voids, and lay-up direction dominate many tensile, flexural, fatigue, and interlaminar results. Hydrothermal exposure may reversibly plasticize the matrix or promote further cure, while longer or hotter exposure can drive hydrolysis, swelling, interface weakening, cracks, and delamination; voids and existing damage accelerate water transport. Neat-resin, laminate, and interface-controlled measurements therefore must remain distinct.

One open, formulation-specific example makes the stiffness–toughness trade-off concrete. Idrees and co-workers formulated DA2, a methacrylated Bis-GMA vinyl ester comprising Bis-GMA, Bis-EMA, and 1,6-hexanediol dimethacrylate in a 3:3:2 mass ratio with 0.7 wt% photoinitiator. Vat-printed ASTM D638-14 Type IV dog bones were UV-post-cured for 2 h at 75 °C, polished, and tested in sets of at least five; DA2 gave tensile modulus 2.8 ± 0.2 GPa, tensile strength 54.1 ± 9.2 MPa, and strain at break 1.9 ± 0.5%. ASTM D5045-14 single-edge-notch-bend specimens from the same material gave KIC 0.45 ± 0.02 MPa·m^0.5 and GIC 0.058 kJ/m². Adding 60 wt% of the study's urethane-acrylate resin changed the printed blend to 2.9 ± 0.4 GPa modulus, 76.5 ± 2.7 MPa strength, 4.1 ± 1.0% strain at break, and GIC 0.18 kJ/m², illustrating that co-network composition can shift strength and fracture resistance non-monotonically. These figures belong only to those photoresin recipes, print/post-cure route, and test methods, not to conventional styrenated casting grades or reinforced vinyl-ester composites.
sections.processing:
Vinyl ester resins are generally handled as reactive liquid thermosets and can use many of the same article-conversion routes as unsaturated polyester resins: casting and coating, gel coating, hand or spray lay-up, resin-transfer molding and vacuum infusion, filament winding, pultrusion, and compression molding of prepared compounds. Vat photopolymerization is also possible for suitably formulated methacrylate-ended systems. Resin viscosity, reactive-diluent level, filler and reinforcement loading, mixing order, promoter–initiator compatibility, pot life or light exposure, mold filling, fiber wet-out, deaeration, exotherm, shrinkage, and post-cure determine article quality. Open processing also requires control of volatile reactive diluent, while thick sections and composite lay-ups require attention to heat removal and cure gradients. Formation of the vinyl-ester oligomer belongs in Synthesis; shaping, irradiation or thermal cure, and post-cure operations belong here.

Aurer and Kasper document the conventional liquid-resin routes and give a vinyl-ester vessel example in which a release film is placed on a mandrel, an approximately 500–1000 µm vinyl-ester surface layer and glass veil are applied and initially cured, and a chopped-glass/vinyl-ester corrosion barrier is then built to about 3 mm before the structural winding. Those values describe that corrosion-resistant construction, not all vinyl-ester articles. In a different conversion route, Idrees and co-workers formulated their DA2 photoresin from Bis-GMA, Bis-EMA, and HDDMA at 3:3:2 with 0.7 wt% PPO, blended it with 20–80 wt% of a commercial urethane-acrylate resin for 2 h at 2000 rpm, and vacuum-degassed it. On an Anycubic Photon Mono SE delivering 3.0 mW/cm², they printed 100 µm layers using 20 s for each of three bottom layers and 7 s for later layers, then wiped the parts and UV-post-cured them for 2 h at 75 °C. That window belongs to the DA2/Tenacious formulations and printer used in the study.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Epoxy-derived molecular segments are connected to unsaturated ester groups that participate in cure. Styrene can both reduce precursor viscosity and copolymerize with these unsaturated groups. Radical polymerization joins the species into a crosslinked thermoset. Studies of particular styrene-containing systems describe network regions with different local compositions and thermal responses. Bisphenol A epoxy and multifunctional epoxy novolac are distinct precursor choices. Their different numbers of reactive groups can change network connectivity, alongside styrene content and cure conversion.
sections.properties: Vinyl ester formulations can combine useful mechanical and chemical resistance with processable liquid viscosity. Cured response depends on precursor chemistry, reactive monomer and cure conversion. In one bisphenol-epoxy vinyl ester study, thin films lost more styrene and exhibited lower glass-transition features than thicker specimens under the reported air-exposed cure conditions. Reinforcement and exposure conditions also influence composite performance. The resin binds reinforcement in a laminate, but the fibers, their arrangement and the interface also carry and transfer load. A resistant matrix therefore does not by itself ensure that a complete composite will survive a particular chemical environment.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Vinyl ester resins are composite matrices for corrosion-resistant chemical equipment. BPA-based and novolac grades address different chemical and temperature conditions. For example, composite tubes and vessels benefit from a matrix that binds glass reinforcement and is selected for the chemical being contained. A resin-rich barrier layer can reduce direct exposure of reinforcement, while the laminate carries structural loads. The laminate construction and any barrier layer must also be specified for the fluid and temperature in service.

Purchasing. Liquid formulated resins are obtained from producers or composites distributors; Derakane 411-45 is a BPA-based example. Romar-Voss lists that resin in a 20 kg container and a Momentum 411-45 variant in a 205 kg drum. The product description reports 45% styrene for the named resin; this is part of the formulated liquid, not a mass fraction to assume for all vinyl esters.

Scale and evidence limits. That distributor lists 20 kg and 205 kg packs, representing tens to hundreds of kilograms per unit. No reliable separate family consumption total was established; packaging is not annual demand.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Vinyl ester composites can take up water and suffer plasticization, leaching, hydrolysis and damage at the fiber–matrix interface. Chemical uptake and changes in strength do not by themselves identify every molecular breakdown product.

Timescales: Rodera and colleagues conditioned glass-fiber laminates made with both a bisphenol A-based resin and an epoxy-novolac resin in 5% sulfuric acid at 95 °C and 15 bar and measured them after 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 2 years. The protective barrier-layer design influenced the observed performance. After two years, average panel mass had increased by 2.36% for the BPA-based laminates and 1.21% for the novolac-based laminates; the comparison measures whole-panel change, not resin-only mass loss. These results describe that test, not an environmental lifetime or a universal chemical-resistance rating.

Environmental persistence: In a separate study, glass-fiber composites made with 430LV vinyl ester were immersed in artificial seawater at 70 °C; their tensile strength decreased by 38.4% after 90 days compared with unimmersed specimens; specimens in deionized water lost 28.5% under the same temperature and duration. This is a material-performance endpoint for a specified composite under accelerated exposure, not a measurement of microbial conversion or complete mineralization. It does not establish a resin lifetime in soil, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A patent proposes granulating fiber-reinforced thermoset waste and incorporating the particles into a thermoplastic such as polyethylene to make composite lumber. Vinyl ester is included in its proposed thermoset scope; the reported post-automotive waste example does not establish the composition or recovery performance for each vinyl ester subtype.

This route retains resin fragments and fiber as constituents of a new material rather than regenerating the original resin monomers. Collection, composition and contamination control remain separate requirements.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: DERAKANE guidance treats vinyl ester fabrication as a complete-system handling issue: resin, solvents, accelerators and catalysts each require precautions. The manufacturer directs users to component safety sheets for handling and disposal. These instructions concern the reactive fabrication system; cured-laminate exposure requires assessment of its actual composition and subsequent operations.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Vinyl ester describes several resin chemistries, not a single uniform network. Cure can be exothermic and its progress depends on initiator, temperature and formulation. Heterogeneity, residual monomer and service environment may affect the measured properties. Composite results must be associated with the resin, processing, reinforcement and exposure used. The crosslinking potential of a multifunctional novolac precursor differs from a bisphenol A-based precursor; the distinction is one variable among reactive diluent, cure and service conditions. Results on one laminate or one chemical cannot establish resistance across the family.

sections.overview: Bisphenol A epoxy vinyl ester is a vinyl ester resin derived from a bisphenol A epoxy precursor. Reaction of epoxy groups with an unsaturated acid supplies reactive ester groups for radical cure. The resulting oligomer is often combined with styrene before forming a thermoset. Such systems are used in reinforced and chemically resistant products. The aromatic bisphenol A-derived epoxy provides the oligomer framework; its methacrylate ends supply sites for copolymerization with styrene. The mixed reactive liquid can wet glass fibers before cure fixes the matrix around them.
sections.history: Bisphenol A epoxy vinyl ester is one branch of the corrosion-resistant vinyl-ester industry whose Derakane lineage began in 1965. That product family first addressed chlorine-containing pulp-bleaching and wastewater environments. The family launch is not a separate invention date for all bisphenol A grades. A later research milestone is Palmese, La Scala and Sands’s 2008 patent, which uses bisphenol A epoxy-derived vinyl esters in multimodal formulations to reduce dependence on volatile reactive diluents. This records a shift from establishing reinforced corrosion-resistant plastics toward improving the formulation and processing of an established resin chemistry.
sections.nomenclature: BPA-VE is narrower than the general vinyl-ester-resin family and is not simply an uncured DGEBA epoxy. A styrene-containing resin grade, initiated mixture, cured neat resin, and fiber-reinforced composite are related but distinct material states; their formulation and reinforcement must be named with the vinyl ester.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: BPA epoxy vinyl ester is made by opening or esterifying a BPA-epoxy precursor with acrylic or methacrylic acid so that terminal vinyl groups are installed on the oligomer; a reactive diluent such as styrene commonly lowers viscosity and becomes part of the cure formulation. Peroxide initiators and accelerators generate radicals that copolymerize the vinyl groups into a crosslinked network. The acid/epoxy ratio, epoxy oligomer mass, inhibitor, diluent content, initiator/accelerator, and cure temperature control conversion and residual unsaturation. A commercial pultrusion study confirms that the cure chemistry is coupled to die temperature and residence time, while the patent route distinguishes resin manufacture from the later radical cure of the formulated vinyl ester.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cured BPA vinyl ester is a glassy thermoset whose strength, modulus, fracture response, and aging behavior depend on conversion, styrene or other diluent, voids, specimen orientation, and reinforcement. In an open industrial-pultrusion study, profiles cured with a 120 °C die showed higher mechanical performance than profiles cured at 140 °C; the authors relate the difference to cure conversion and internal stress, and the result belongs to the specified pultruded composite system. The existing water-aging study provides a separate neat-resin tensile context. Neither result is a universal vinyl-ester value, and pultruded fiber-direction properties should not be merged with neat cast resin data.
sections.processing: Vinyl ester is mixed with reactive diluent, peroxide initiator and accelerator, then cast, molded, infused, filament-wound, or pulled through a heated die before post-cure as required. An open pultrusion study varied die temperature and found the 120 °C condition gave the highest mechanical performance among its tested temperatures, whereas higher temperature increased conversion rate and internal stress sufficiently to reduce the measured performance at 140 °C. This is a bounded profile-line example, not a generic cure window. Control of resin pot life, exotherm, fiber wet-out, die residence, voids, inhibitor level, and post-cure is formulation- and section-specific.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The precursor retains the aromatic bisphenol A-derived framework of the starting epoxy resin. Its unsaturated ester groups can copolymerize with styrene under radical initiation. Curing connects molecules into a network containing resin-derived and reactive-monomer-derived segments. Network structure depends on precursor composition and the extent of cure. The precursor is typically difunctional, whereas an epoxy-novolac precursor can provide more reactive sites per molecule. The final network also includes styrene-derived segments, so the precursor alone does not fix its crosslink density.
sections.properties: A cured bisphenol-epoxy vinyl ester can serve as a matrix for fiber-reinforced structures. In a study of DION 1260 resin, a standard-cured film about 0.03 mm thick showed two first-scan glass-transition features at 55 °C and 81 °C, compared with a single transition at 109 °C for a roughly 3.9 mm plate. The researchers observed greater styrene loss and incomplete cure in the thin films; the specimens also differed in scale and preparation, so the comparison does not isolate thickness alone. Chemical and mechanical performance depend on formulation and exposure. A dense cured resin can resist selected chemical environments while glass reinforcement contributes stiffness and strength. The resin–fiber interface and any resin-rich barrier layer matter to the assembled laminate.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. BPA epoxy vinyl ester is used in fiber-reinforced tanks and chemical-process equipment, including pulp-and-paper applications. In a chemical vessel, a resin-rich surface layer helps protect the underlying glass reinforcement; the selected resin, glass architecture and cure all affect the assembled laminate. Filament winding and pultrusion use the liquid resin to wet and bind reinforcement, but the finished laminate also depends on fiber architecture and curing. The listed liquid resin is a component of that laminate rather than the finished vessel.

Purchasing. Romar-Voss lists liquid Derakane 411-45 in 20 kg containers and Derakane Momentum 411-45 in 205 kg drums. The distributor identifies 411-45 as a BPA epoxy vinyl ester with 45% styrene and describes filament winding and pultrusion as fabrication options. The named package contains formulated liquid resin, so its mass does not represent neat cured network.

Scale and evidence limits. These documented units are of order 10–100 kg and include the formulated resin’s styrene diluent. They are not measurements of annual purchases or the mass of cured polymer consumed.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Vinyl ester composites can take up water and suffer plasticization, leaching, hydrolysis and damage at the fiber–matrix interface. Chemical uptake and changes in strength do not by themselves identify every molecular breakdown product.

Timescales: Rodera and colleagues conditioned glass-fiber laminates made with a bisphenol A-based Derakane 455–400 matrix in 5% sulfuric acid at 95 °C and 15 bar and measured them after 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 2 years. The protective barrier-layer design influenced the observed performance, and the researchers found a gradual loss of composite ultimate strength across the two-year test. Average panel mass increased by 2.36% after two years, consistent with uptake in the complete laminate. These results describe that test, not an environmental lifetime or a universal chemical-resistance rating.

Environmental persistence: The acid-immersion study measured changes in the mechanical response of a reinforced laminate, not conversion of the resin to carbon dioxide. Hydrothermal or acid damage therefore does not establish complete biodegradation or a transferable mineralization time in soil, water or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A patent proposes granulating fiber-reinforced thermoset waste and incorporating the particles into a thermoplastic such as polyethylene to make composite lumber. Vinyl ester is included in its proposed thermoset scope; the reported post-automotive waste example does not establish the composition or recovery performance for each vinyl ester subtype.

This route retains resin fragments and fiber as constituents of a new material rather than regenerating the original resin monomers. Collection, composition and contamination control remain separate requirements.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: DERAKANE guidance treats bisphenol-A epoxy vinyl ester fabrication as a complete-system handling issue: resin, solvents, accelerators and catalysts each require precautions. The manufacturer directs users to component safety sheets for handling and disposal. These instructions concern the reactive fabrication system; cured-laminate exposure requires assessment of its actual composition and subsequent operations.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Bisphenol A epoxy vinyl ester does not specify reactive monomer content, initiator or cure history. Thermal and mechanical data depend on those choices and the specimen tested. Water or chemical exposure and reinforcement can alter the behavior of a composite. Results from a specified commercial resin and cure must not be generalized to all formulations. In one acid-ageing experiment, barrier-layer construction affected the measured behavior of a glass composite made with a specific BPA-based vinyl ester. The observation should not be transferred to another grade or laminate without its exposure and construction details.

sections.overview: Epoxy-novolac vinyl esters are reactive resins derived from multifunctional epoxy novolac precursors. Reaction with an unsaturated acid such as methacrylic acid supplies polymerizable groups. The resin can be combined with a vinyl monomer and cured by a radical reaction. It is used in formulations intended for chemically demanding and elevated-temperature service. The novolac-derived precursor can carry more reactive sites than a standard difunctional bisphenol A epoxy precursor. This provides greater potential for network connectivity during cure, depending on the complete formulation and conversion.
sections.history: Epoxy-novolac vinyl esters developed within the vinyl-ester industry as a separate, more highly functional resin branch. By 1997, F. V. Apicella Jr. and N. A. Dulzer’s patent explicitly used Dow’s commercial Derakane 470.36 novolac vinyl ester as a comparison material. Their work on curable compositions and protective applications demonstrates that this subtype had an established industrial identity by then. The comparison also shows why resin structure, cure package and application conditions must be tracked together. The source establishes a dated commercial-use milestone, but does not identify the first synthesis or launch of every epoxy-novolac vinyl ester.
sections.nomenclature: Novolac-VE is the abbreviation used here for epoxy-novolac vinyl ester. The name identifies a methacrylated, novolac-derived vinyl-ester subfamily; it excludes conventional bisphenol-A vinyl esters, uncured epoxy novolac without vinyl-ester conversion, and any one cured or reinforced composite formulation.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Epoxy-novolac vinyl ester is a functionalized resin precursor, not simply a cured epoxy network. Its formation couples the epoxide groups of an epoxy novolac with an ethylenically unsaturated carboxylic acid, commonly acrylic or methacrylic acid, so that terminal vinyl unsaturation is installed through acid–epoxide addition. The epoxy-novolac precursor itself is made by epoxidizing a phenol–formaldehyde novolac with epichlorohydrin. The European polymer-production reference lists tertiary amines, phosphines, or ammonium salts as catalyst classes for vinyl-ester formation. A patent separately describes commercial novolac vinyl esters as methacrylated epoxy novolacs. The radical curing of these vinyl groups is downstream network formation and is not presented as a synthesis schedule here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Epoxy-novolac vinyl ester is a crosslinked thermoset after radical cure. Tensile and flexural response depend on the specific novolac vinyl-ester grade, reactive-diluent content, initiator and accelerator package, casting or laminate form, and cure/post-cure; a supplier's clear-casting value is not a family-wide design value.

A bounded cured-resin example is Crystic VE673, an epoxy-novolac vinyl ester. Its technical data sheet reports for a cast resin cured 24 h at 20 °C followed by 3 h at 80 °C: tensile strength 75 MPa, tensile modulus 3.5 GPa, elongation to break 3%, flexural strength 120 MPa, and Barcol hardness 48. Those values apply to the named grade and schedule.

For comparison, ETERSET 2962 is a distinct novolac-based epoxy vinyl ester with 33–36% styrene. Its listed clear-casting ASTM D638 tensile strength is 70–80 MPa, tensile modulus 3.4–3.7 GPa, and tensile elongation 2.5–3.5%. The difference in grade and stated reactive-diluent content means these product values should remain separate rather than be merged into a universal range.
sections.processing:
Epoxy-novolac vinyl ester is supplied as a reactive, often styrene-diluted liquid for castings, corrosion-resistant coatings or linings, and fiber-reinforced laminates. The resin is combined with the grade-qualified promoter, initiator, and any filler shortly before use, applied or used to wet reinforcement, allowed to gel, and then cured or post-cured as required. Shop temperature, humidity, catalyst and promoter concentration, filler or pigment, laminate thickness, and heat removal all change gel time and peak exotherm. A room-temperature surface exposed to air may remain incompletely cured or tacky, so the selected grade's surfacing and post-cure guidance must be followed rather than extrapolated across the family.

For AOC Vipel F085, a named epoxy-novolac vinyl-ester series, the supplier tabulates distinct cumene-hydroperoxide/cobalt/dimethylaniline packages at 18, 25, and 35 °C and shows that modest formulation changes shift gel time and peak exotherm; it recommends checking a small batch under actual shop conditions and post-curing room-temperature laminates for 2 h at 70–100 °C for optimum performance. A separate Crystic VE673 cast-resin example used 24 h at 20 °C followed by 3 h at 80 °C. These are grade-specific fabrication examples, not universal vinyl-ester cure windows.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The epoxy novolac precursor provides a phenolic aromatic framework with multiple reactive sites. Conversion of epoxy groups with methacrylic acid introduces unsaturated ester groups. During cure, these groups and a reactive diluent such as styrene can form a crosslinked network. The number of reactive sites and cure conversion influence network connectivity. Multiple reactive groups along the aromatic precursor permit more connections between chains than a strictly difunctional precursor. Styrene content and degree of cure also influence the network actually formed.
sections.properties: Multifunctional novolac-derived resins can form highly connected networks. Their heat and chemical response depends on the particular precursor and formulation. A study of epoxy-novolac vinyl esters found that varying the acid value of its prepared resins changed cure and thermal decomposition behavior. Mechanical performance in a finished article additionally depends on reinforcement and processing. Reichhold describes greater crosslink density and improved heat and solvent resistance for its novolac vinyl ester chemistry relative to conventional bisphenol A epoxy-based grades. A service selection still requires the specific chemical, concentration, temperature and laminate construction. Scott Bader reports a heat-deflection temperature of 130–135 °C for a VE673 cast resin cured for 24 hours at 20 °C, then 5 hours at 80 °C and 3 hours at 120 °C. That supplier value describes the tested casting and post-cure, not a maximum service temperature for every laminate.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Epoxy-novolac vinyl esters form composite tanks, vessels, ducts, scrubbers and chimneys in chemical processing; selected grades also address hot flue gases. For these applications, chemical resistance depends on the resin and the exposed surface of the composite. Crystic VE673 is a specific epoxy-novolac vinyl ester liquid supplied for reinforced fabrication; a buyer must match the cured laminate to the intended exposure. Its supplier reports that specified laminates retained over 80% of flexural properties after 500 hours immersed in fuels at 45 °C; this is a product-specific test, not resistance to every chemical.

Purchasing. Crystic VE673 is a liquid resin for reinforced fabrication; specify the exact grade against chemical concentration and service temperature. Scott Bader lists it in 200 kg drums, 1,000 kg containers and tanker deliveries. The supplier calls this grade non-accelerated, so cure ingredients and processing requirements must also be specified for the application.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Vinyl ester composites can take up water and suffer plasticization, leaching, hydrolysis and damage at the fiber–matrix interface. Chemical uptake and changes in strength do not by themselves identify every molecular breakdown product.

Timescales: Rodera and colleagues conditioned glass-fiber laminates made with an epoxy-novolac Atlac E-Nova FW 1045 matrix in 5% sulfuric acid at 95 °C and 15 bar and measured them after 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 2 years. The protective barrier-layer design influenced the observed performance, and the researchers found a gradual loss of composite ultimate strength across the two-year test. Average panel mass increased by 1.21% after two years; the measurement concerns the whole laminate. These results describe that test, not an environmental lifetime or a universal chemical-resistance rating.

Environmental persistence: The acid-immersion study measured changes in the mechanical response of a reinforced laminate, not conversion of the resin to carbon dioxide. Hydrothermal or acid damage therefore does not establish complete biodegradation or a transferable mineralization time in soil, water or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A patent proposes granulating fiber-reinforced thermoset waste and incorporating the particles into a thermoplastic such as polyethylene to make composite lumber. Vinyl ester is included in its proposed thermoset scope; the reported post-automotive waste example does not establish the composition or recovery performance for each vinyl ester subtype.

This route retains resin fragments and fiber as constituents of a new material rather than regenerating the original resin monomers. Collection, composition and contamination control remain separate requirements.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: DERAKANE guidance treats epoxy-novolac vinyl ester fabrication as a complete-system handling issue: resin, solvents, accelerators and catalysts each require precautions. The manufacturer directs users to component safety sheets for handling and disposal. These instructions concern the reactive fabrication system; cured-laminate exposure requires assessment of its actual composition and subsequent operations.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Epoxy-novolac vinyl ester is a subfamily with different precursor functionality and composition. The cited thermal study used one epoxy novolac, styrene and benzoyl peroxide at specified proportions. Its results are not a general service-temperature rating for all novolac vinyl esters. Reactive diluent, cure, exposure and reinforcement must accompany comparisons. Higher nominal functionality does not establish an actual degree of cure or guarantee resistance to every solvent. For example, a supplier specifies its DION Impact 9400 series separately and gives it a limited shelf life, illustrating that reactive liquid storage and cured-part service are different questions.

sections.overview:
Phenol–formaldehyde (PF) resins are a family of condensation products made from phenol and formaldehyde. Two important precursor types are novolacs and resoles: novolacs are commonly made with excess phenol under acidic conditions and need an additional curing agent to form a network, while resoles are commonly made with excess formaldehyde under alkaline conditions and contain reactive groups that can crosslink on heating. The precursor and the cured material therefore have different processing behavior.

Curing produces an interconnected thermoset network, so the finished resin is not simply melted and reshaped like a thermoplastic. Phenolic materials are used in molding compounds, laminates, wood products and adhesives, often in combination with fillers or reinforcement. Heat and chemical resistance are useful characteristics, but the performance of an article depends on its formulation and cure; for example, voids generated during cure can affect mechanical behavior.
sections.history: Phenol–formaldehyde reactions were known before Leo Baekeland made them commercially useful. Baekeland and Nathaniel Thurlow initially sought a shellac substitute, then developed controlled heat-and-pressure curing in 1907. Baekeland publicly announced Bakelite in 1909 and formed a manufacturing company in 1910. Electrical insulators were an early market; radio components, automobile distributor caps, telephones, handles and household objects followed. The decisive contribution was control of an otherwise difficult condensation reaction and its conversion into reproducible molded products. Bakelite established the commercial thermoset industry, although the broader phenolic family subsequently encompassed many formulations and application-specific resins.
sections.nomenclature: PF abbreviates phenol–formaldehyde resin, and “phenolic” is a broader customary descriptor. Novolac and resole are important subfamilies with different precursor structures, so neither is simply a synonym for the whole PF family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Phenol–formaldehyde (PF) resins are condensation products of phenol or substituted phenols with formaldehyde. Feed ratio and catalyst regime define major precursor families: phenol-rich acid-catalyzed synthesis gives novolac-type prepolymers, whereas formaldehyde-rich alkaline synthesis gives resole-type precursors. Acid, base, water content, temperature, and reaction extent are architecture controls rather than universal settings. Documented patents describe both acid- or base-catalyzed phenol/formaldehyde condensation and an alkaline route with controlled catalyst composition. Novolacs require a later formaldehyde source or crosslinker for network formation, while resoles can self-condense on heating; those cure formulations and article schedules are not part of this family-level precursor synthesis account.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Phenol–formaldehyde (PF) mechanics belong to the cured network and material form, not to an uncured resole liquid or fusible novolac precursor. Novolac/hexamethylenetetramine and thermally cured resole networks are distinct cure systems; cure extent and voids, filler or fibre type and loading, laminate or moulded geometry, moisture/conditioning, and test direction can therefore dominate measured stiffness, strength, and impact response. A public datasheet for Bakelite® PF 14694, a mainly organically filled phenolic moulding compound, reports a tensile modulus of 7,800 MPa (ISO 527-1/-2), tensile strength of 55 MPa at 5 mm/min (ISO 527-1/-2), flexural strength of 90 MPa at 2 mm/min (ISO 178), and unnotched Charpy impact strength of 6 kJ/m² at 23 °C (ISO 179/1eU). Those are indicative values for that filled, cured molding grade; its source permits compression- or injection-moulded test specimens but does not assign the listed values to one route or report mechanical-test conditioning. In a separate resole-PF/areca-fibre study, fibre content was the dominant tested variable and fibre length and alkali treatment also changed tensile and flexural results, illustrating why adhesive joints, laminates, and reinforced mouldings must not be treated as neat-PF values.
sections.processing: Phenol–formaldehyde (PF) materials are converted either as reactive liquid resole adhesives/impregnants or as compounded novolac/hexamethylenetetramine and other phenolic molding compounds. Established article routes include wood and fiber lamination or hand lay-up, hot pressing, compression and transfer molding, and, for suitable filled grades, injection molding; cure, pressure, volatile removal, and post-cure must be selected for the resin family, filler, and article geometry. A bounded commercial example is Bakelite PF 14694 PF-X, a mainly organically filled phenolic molding compound whose supplier documents compression-molded and injection-molded test-specimen routes; those routes and the grade's flow behavior should not be treated as a universal PF window. In an independent resole-fiber laboratory example, resin was mixed with crosslinker and acidic catalyst for 30 min, poured over areca-fiber reinforcement in a mold, closed, and cured at room temperature for 48 h. Thus PF conversion may involve either melt-like molding of a compounded, already formulated molding grade or liquid adhesive impregnation followed by network cure. Phenol/formaldehyde condensation and the preparation of novolac or resole are upstream Synthesis; this section covers compounding, shaping, impregnation, pressing, and curing of the supplied resin.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Phenol–formaldehyde resins develop from phenolic rings joined at different reactive positions, commonly through methylene bridges. Novolac precursors are predominantly linear and require an added curing agent to form a network; resole precursors contain reactive hydroxymethyl groups that can participate in crosslinking on heating. Curing joins the precursor molecules into an interconnected structure rather than a single, uniform repeat sequence. The resulting material can contain voids when volatile by-products are trapped as the resin gels; the size and distribution of these voids depend on the formulation and curing conditions.
sections.properties: Cured phenolic resins are valued for thermal stability, resistance to many chemicals and electrical insulation; they can form a carbonaceous char during severe heating. Conventional cured phenolics can also be brittle, and fillers and reinforcement are used to tailor the balance of properties. In one novolac composite study summarized by Adem and coauthors, 5 wt% carbon nanotubes mixed by ball milling gave flexural strengths of about 100 MPa with untreated nanotubes and 120 MPa with functionalized nanotubes, compared with about 40 MPa for the neat resin control. Wet mixing gave a much lower strength in that study, illustrating the importance of dispersion as well as filler content. These results describe the tested composites and preparation, not all phenolic resins.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Phenol–formaldehyde resins bind friction materials, laminates and molding compounds for electrical, automotive and industrial parts. The cured resin binds the other ingredients in a friction material or the layers of a laminate; the reinforcement and manufacturing process strongly influence the finished article. A molding compound can contain fillers in addition to the phenolic precursor and cure system. The supplier’s liquid Fenokol 43 EXF is instead intended for bonding water-resistant plywood under heat and pressure, so its delivery and use differ from a granular molding compound.

Purchasing. PLENCO offers novolac and resole resin systems and formulated phenolic molding compounds through its resin-information and engineering inquiry channels. For a liquid-resole example, Chemko lists Fenokol 43 EXF for plywood bonding and bulk shipment in insulated road or rail tankers. The supplier specifies a 30-day durability at 20 °C for that product, so the form and storage conditions matter alongside the resin family.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Severe heating can break down a cured phenolic composite into a carbonaceous residue and volatile organic products. In one patent example, the starting material was a waste paper–phenolic printed board, so the measured fractions include the effects of that composite feed rather than pure PF resin alone.

Timescales: The example heated the separated board-derived material in air at 400 °C for one hour and reported roughly 45% solid residue and 50% collected thermal decomposition products. In the fungal study, the authors reported a color change in cultures as early as two days after introduction of resin fragments and examined chip surfaces after 28 days. These are signs observed in controlled culture, not a time to complete degradation. The 400 °C treatment is an engineered process rather than an ambient service life or environmental mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: In a laboratory culture study, cured, base-catalyzed phenol–formaldehyde resin fragments were exposed to the white-rot fungus Phanerochaete chrysosporium. The researchers detected phenol containing carbon isotopically labeled in the starting resin and observed pitted surfaces and holes after culture, while the resin control without fungus remained comparatively smooth. Together these observations support transformation under those culture conditions, without quantifying the fate of all polymer carbon. This study did not establish complete conversion of resin carbon to carbon dioxide or a natural-soil, freshwater or marine lifetime. Results for the experimental resin should not be generalized to every filled phenolic article.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A patent proposes recovering solid and phenolic decomposition fractions from cured phenolic waste. In its printed-board example, the residue was milled and used as the core material of a vacuum insulation panel; the feed was a paper–phenolic composite whose exact resin formulation was not identified. The patent also describes using decomposition products to form a porous gel.

These routes convert waste into different materials rather than remelting the original thermoset or recovering unchanged resin. They are process examples, not evidence of a universal collection system or a family-wide commercial recycling rate.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For uncured phenol–formaldehyde formulations, HSE identifies formaldehyde resins and releasers as occupational contact-sensitization concerns. Prevent skin contamination and assess the actual formulation; this does not classify every cured article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The family includes both novolac and resole precursors, various cure systems, and materials compounded with different fillers or reinforcements. Reported performance therefore depends on the material and cure history as well as the test and environment. In one study of a commercial resole, changing catalyst and cure schedule changed the observed void population and flexural response; those results describe the specimens studied rather than a family-wide value. In a separate areca-fiber/resole composite study, fiber loading and length also affected measured tensile and flexural strength. Results from these examples cannot be transferred directly to other resins, fillers, or article geometries.

sections.overview: Novolac phenolic resins are phenol–formaldehyde condensation products usually made with a deficiency of formaldehyde under acidic conditions. The resulting precursor is generally thermoplastic and requires a crosslinking agent to form a thermoset. Hexamethylenetetramine is a commonly used curing agent. Formulated novolac compounds are used in molded parts and other phenolic applications. The formaldehyde-deficient precursor can flow before cure, but the added hardener enables links to form between precursor molecules. A finished molded compound can also contain substantial reinforcement and filler.
sections.history: Novolac history reaches back to Baekeland and Thurlow’s search for a synthetic shellac before the successful Bakelite thermoset. Their initial Novolak product was commercially unsuccessful, but fusible phenolic precursors became an enduring branch of resin technology. A later milestone is Myron Annis’s 1980 patent on improving low-temperature processing stability of novolac-based phenolic compositions. Its focus on workable resin mixtures and subsequent cure illustrates the transition from an early coating substitute to engineered molding materials. The history of novolacs is therefore connected to, but not identical with, the 1907 invention of the fully cured Bakelite product.
sections.nomenclature: Novolac identifies a specific phenolic-resin architecture and is often qualified as novolac PF. It is not interchangeable with all phenol–formaldehyde resins, particularly resole-type materials.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Novolac phenolic resin is a thermoplastic phenol–formaldehyde prepolymer produced by acid-catalyzed condensation under phenol-rich, formaldehyde-deficient conditions. This precursor chemistry distinguishes novolacs from alkaline, formaldehyde-rich resole routes and from the later thermoset network. Documented preparations react phenol with formaldehyde under sulfuric, hydrochloric, oxalic, or sulfonic acid catalysis; acid choice and phenol/formaldehyde ratio influence the linkage distribution and molecular weight. A conventional novolac route removes water and volatile phenol after condensation, while high-ortho variants employ divalent-metal catalyst systems under mildly acidic conditions. Hexamethylenetetramine or other added crosslinker can later cure a novolac, but that network-forming formulation and any molding schedule are not part of the uncured-resin synthesis described here.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Novolac phenolic resin becomes a crosslinked phenolic material only after compounding and cure, so mechanical response depends on the particular novolac/crosslinker and cure or post-bake, as well as filler or fiber type/loading, molding route, specimen direction, and conditioning.  The readily open mechanical records in this pass are reinforced molding compounds, not unfilled cured novolac; their high stiffness and low tensile strain must not be assigned to the resin family alone.  A bounded example is Sumitomo Bakelite FM 4005: a granular fiberglass-reinforced phenolic novolac compound, measured on compression-molded ASTM specimens, with typical ASTM D638 tensile strength 75 MPa, ASTM D790 flexural strength 140 MPa and flexural modulus 15 GPa, ASTM D256A notched Izod 30 J/m, and ASTM D695 compressive strength 276 MPa.  Independently, Plenco 07552 is a transfer-molded, glass-fiber-reinforced two-stage phenolic novolac compound; laboratory-molded standard specimens gave typical ASTM D638 tensile strength 57 MPa and modulus 13.086 GPa, ASTM D790 flexural strength 102.4 MPa and modulus 12.790 GPa, and 0.6% tensile elongation.  Both supplier records label their values typical rather than design specifications.
sections.processing: Novolac phenolic resin is commonly converted as a thermoset molding compound: solid novolak is blended with a curing package such as hexamethylenetetramine and fillers or reinforcement, compounded at controlled roll temperatures, shaped by compression, transfer, or injection molding, and cured in the mold. Sumitomo's FM 4005 is a fiberglass-reinforced novolac compound offered for compression, transfer, and injection molding; its tabulated values are explicitly from compression-molded ASTM specimens. A bounded processing example in an open patent used 100 parts solid novolak with about 21 parts hexamethylenetetramine plus stearate/filler additions, ball-milled the mix, roll-milled it with approximately 70 °C front and 90 °C back rolls, and ground the compound. The same patent describes runnerless-injection stability near 125 °C in the hot manifold and rapid cavity cure near 170 °C, with its examples reporting roughly 60–76 s Brabender cure times at 170 °C. Those settings apply to the stated novolac formulations and equipment, not to all phenolic molding compounds.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The precursor contains phenolic aromatic units joined primarily by methylene bridges. Its limited residual hydroxymethyl content distinguishes it from a typical resole. Addition of a hardener and subsequent cure forms further links between molecules. The crosslinked material is an infusible network rather than the melt-processable precursor. The hardener creates new junctions that prevent the cured network from flowing like the precursor. The density and distribution of those junctions depend on the hardener and curing conditions.
sections.properties: Before cure, the precursor can be softened and shaped. Once crosslinked, phenolic formulations can provide rigidity and useful thermal performance. Fillers and reinforcement contribute substantially to the response of molded compounds. The properties of a commercial filled compound do not describe neat novolac resin. For example, Sumitomo Bakelite reports 140 MPa flexural strength by ASTM D790 for compression-molded FM 4005, a fiberglass-reinforced novolac compound. This typical supplier result describes that compound and test, not neat resin or the whole family.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Novolac phenolics are industrial binders and molding-resin ingredients for friction materials and laminates. The resin serves as a binder in friction and molded products, with reinforcement and fillers chosen for the required article. Sumitomo Bakelite’s FM 4005 is one granular fiberglass-reinforced novolac molding compound, rather than a neat-resin specification. Its supplier lists grades for compression, transfer and injection molding; the reinforcement and cure contribute to the properties of the finished molded part.

Purchasing. PLENCO markets novolac systems; procure a specified resin or filled molding compound with its cure package and application requirements. Sumitomo Bakelite identifies FM 4005 as a glass-reinforced novolac molding compound, so a molding-compound specification includes reinforcement as well as resin. A buyer comparing it with a neat precursor should confirm the supplier’s compound and processing information.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A patent includes cured novolac among its proposed phenolic feedstocks. Its example heated a waste paper–phenolic printed-board material and collected a solid residue and volatile thermal decomposition products; the example does not identify the resin subtype. The paper, cured resin and any remaining nonmetallic constituents all contribute to the recovered fractions. These products do not describe ambient weathering.

Timescales: The example heated the board-derived material in air at 400 °C for one hour and reported about 45% residue and 50% collected thermal products. The test applies to that mixed feed, not to every novolac grade or an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: A study of discarded novolac phenolic foam from healthcare transport detected phenol and formaldehyde in the tested material and its liquid extract. Its laboratory lettuce-germination assay found less germination as extract concentration increased, with no germination in its two highest tested extract concentrations; those findings concern a particular waste and extract, not every novolac formulation. The analysis does not establish whether the detected chemicals were newly formed by environmental degradation, nor a complete mineralization time in soil, water or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The patent proposes recovering both the solid residue and phenolic decomposition fraction from cured phenolic waste. Its printed-board example milled the residue and used it as the core of a vacuum insulation panel; the paper–resin feed was not identified as a specific novolac formulation.

This converts a composite waste into different materials rather than regenerating the original resin. It is disclosed process evidence, not proof of a general commercial recovery system or an established recycling rate.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For uncured novolac formulations, HSE identifies formaldehyde resins and releasers as occupational contact-sensitization concerns. Prevent skin contamination and assess the actual formulation; this does not classify every cured article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Novolac identifies a preparation class rather than a single molecular weight or finished compound. Hardener content, cure and additives affect the network and its performance. Formulation and molding conditions must accompany mechanical data. Results for a filled commercial grade should not be generalized to all novolacs. The FM 4005 example contains glass reinforcement; a change in fiber content, orientation or cure can change a molded part’s response. A flowable uncured precursor and a crosslinked article must also be evaluated separately.
