sections.overview: Thermosetting polyimides are imide-containing resins that form crosslinked networks during cure. One important approach uses oligomers capped with reactive phenylethynyl groups. Another is the polymerization of monomeric reactants (PMR) approach used in polyimide composite fabrication. These materials are studied as high-temperature matrices for fiber-reinforced components.
sections.history: Thermosetting polyimides became important in high-temperature aerospace composites. NASA’s account traces polymerization-of-monomeric-reactants, or PMR, addition-polyimide technology to Lewis Research Center in the 1970s. PMR-15 became a widely used first-generation material for demanding composite components. Later NASA work by Kathy Chuang and Raymond Vannucci developed DMBZ-15, replacing the diamine used in PMR-15 while seeking improved high-temperature performance. This is the history of an influential thermosetting-polyimide lineage, not all polyimide chemistry. It shows the movement from laboratory resin design into aircraft-engine applications and subsequent reformulation of an established aerospace matrix.
sections.nomenclature: Thermosetting polyimide is also abbreviated TSPI in materials literature. This record covers imide resins designed to crosslink on cure, including PMR and end-capped oligomer routes; thermoplastic polyimide and a cured composite containing the resin are related but distinct scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Thermosetting polyimides are usually prepared as finite-molar-mass imide or imide-precursor oligomers whose reactive end groups subsequently form an infusible network. Aromatic diamines and aromatic tetracarboxylic dianhydrides, or ester derivatives of those dianhydrides, build the imide-containing backbone; a calculated stoichiometric excess of a monofunctional reactive end cap limits oligomer length and supplies cure sites. In a cited phenylethynyl route, biphenyl tetracarboxylic dianhydride is converted to a diethyl ester in dry ethanol and reacted with an aromatic oxydianiline and a monoester derived from 4-phenylethynylphthalic anhydride. This produces phenylethynyl-endcapped poly(amic ester) solutions of controlled calculated molar mass. Heating removes solvent and converts the amic-ester precursor to imide rings; at higher conversion temperature the phenylethynyl termini undergo addition reactions that create the thermoset network without requiring a stoichiometric volatile coproduct from the crosslinking step. Low-molar-mass phenylethynyl-endcapped oligomers can act as reactive diluents and co-cure into that network. A historically important complementary route is PMR: the dimethyl ester of benzophenonetetracarboxylic acid and an aromatic diamine such as methylenedianiline are combined in methanol with a monoester of nadic acid as the end cap. Removal of solvent, imidization, and addition reaction of the norbornene-type termini yield a crosslinked polyimide. Diamine/dianhydride identity, end-cap chemistry and amount, target oligomer molar mass, solvent, imidization completeness, and cure-site conversion control flow before gelation and final network density. This entry excludes linear thermoplastic polyimides; article-shaping pressure and thermal schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Thermosetting polyimides form permanently crosslinked, usually aromatic networks whose room-temperature response is generally glassy: they can combine gigapascal-scale tensile stiffness and useful strength with only modest strain to failure. Their value is the ability to retain load-bearing stiffness at temperatures that soften many other organic matrices, but the same rigid backbones and network constraints can make neat resins notch- and flaw-sensitive. This is a broad chemistry class rather than one material specification; PMR, phenylethynyl-terminated, bismaleimide-like and other addition-cured imide systems should not be assigned one family-wide strength or modulus.

Consequential variables include backbone rigidity and symmetry, end-cap chemistry, formulated oligomer molecular mass, reactive-diluent or toughener content, crosslink density, cure and post-cure schedule, residual solvent or cure volatiles and the voids they create, oxidation and physical aging at temperature, moisture conditioning, reinforcement and fiber interface, specimen thickness and defects, and test temperature, rate and loading mode. A historical NASA PMR report independently illustrates why formulation and thermal history matter: it compared neat-resin tensile behavior at four formulated molecular-weight levels and before versus after post-cure, while treating fiber composites separately. Those composite results are not neat-resin properties.

One bounded neat-resin example comes from a phenylethynyl-endcapped thermosetting blend study. Its TMR-50/RDm-a-5 formulation combined the named TMR and reactive-diluent oligomers at 50/50 by mass, was B-staged, pressure molded through a 300–380 °C cycle, and held at 380 °C for 2 h. At 25 °C, 5 mm-wide specimens tested at 1 mm min⁻¹ to GB/T 1040-2006, with at least seven runs averaged, gave tensile strength 84.0 ± 4.36 MPa, tensile modulus 2.4 ± 0.10 GPa and elongation at break 4.1 ± 0.50%. Across that paper's formulation series, increasing calculated TMR oligomer molecular mass from 1500 to 5000 g mol⁻¹ raised tensile strength and elongation before the response largely plateaued. These values describe those cured formulations and protocol, not thermosetting polyimides generally.
sections.processing:
Thermosetting polyimide matrix resins are shaped while they remain soluble, fusible, or both, and are then imidized and/or addition-cured under a controlled pressure and temperature history. Solution impregnation and coating produce fiber prepreg; solvent removal and B-staging set a manageable volatile content before lay-up and autoclave or press consolidation. Neat molding powder can be compression molded, while appropriate low-viscosity formulations can impregnate reinforcement before cure. The critical window is bounded by solvent evolution, imidization by-products, oligomer melt viscosity, gelation, and crosslinking: pressure applied too early can trap volatiles, while pressure applied after the resin loses flow leaves porosity or poor fiber wet-out. Staged heating, vent paths, pressure timing, residence at cure temperature, cooling under pressure, and optional post-cure determine void content and residual stress. Oligomer and end-cap manufacture belongs in Synthesis; prepreg preparation, B-staging, consolidation, cure, post-cure, and cooling belong here.

Zhang and co-workers report one schedule for their TMR-50/RDm-a-5 phenylethynyl-terminated blend, not for all thermosetting polyimides. Neat powder in a stainless-steel die was held at 300 °C for 0.5 h under contact pressure, brought to 350 °C under 1.5 MPa, ramped from 350 to 380 °C at 5 °C/min while pressure was increased to 2 MPa, held at 380 °C for 2 h, and cooled to 100 °C before pressure release. For T700 prepreg made with the same matrix family, their solution-coated tape was dried for 24 h at 30 °C while retaining 10–15 wt% volatiles; autoclave holds at 120, 240, and 320 °C for 1 h each under contact pressure expelled volatiles, followed by a 3 °C/min ramp to 380 °C under 2 MPa and a 2 h hold. Pressure was maintained to 250 °C, and one variant was post-cured for 1 h at 420 °C. The historical NASA PMR report independently illustrates the same need to stage solvent removal and imidization before full-pressure molding; altered pressure/temperature sequences produced blisters or surface depressions.
sections.structureAndMorphology: A phenylethynyl approach starts with a poly(amic ester) oligomer containing reactive end groups. Heating converts the precursor toward imide structures and then promotes reactions of the end groups to form a network. Oligomer size and the amount of reactive diluent affect the starting mixture and ultimately the cured material. Reinforced composites additionally contain fibers and interfaces that distinguish them from neat resin.
sections.properties: Thermosetting polyimide matrices are investigated for retaining useful mechanical behavior at elevated temperatures. In one study, phenylethynyl-ended resin blends were cured as neat specimens and also processed into carbon-fiber composites. The researchers measured tensile and thermal properties of the cured resins and mechanical properties of the composites at room and elevated temperatures. The resulting values belong to those blend compositions and cure schedules. In one phenylethynyl resin study, a cured TMR–50/RDm–a blend had room-temperature tensile strength 84.0 MPa and elongation at break 4.1%. Its T700 carbon-fiber laminate had flexural strength 1552 MPa at 25 °C and 690 MPa at 370 °C before post-cure. These numbers describe the reported compositions, cure and tests.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Thermosetting polyimide systems serve aerospace engine and vehicle structures; PMR-15-derived composites also make wear liners and bushings for steel and aluminum mills. NASA describes the latter as carbon-fiber composites in which the polyimide binder and fibers contribute to a self-lubricating, wear-resistant surface. For one historical mill application operators reported service of a year or more for the composite liners, compared with 13–16 weeks for aluminum-bronze liners. That comparison describes the cited application, not a general service-life ratio for every polyimide part.

Purchasing. NASA documented commercial liquid and powder RP46 resin sales in 2001 and fabricated PMR-derived composite components in 1997. These historical forms require present-day supplier verification.

Scale and evidence limits. NASA’s 2001 RP46 report describes a Unitech reactor capable of small-production quantities up to two tons/month. This historical single-reactor capability is not actual sales, present capacity or family-wide consumption; no current separate total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Aminolysis followed by acid hydrolysis of the studied phenylethynyl-end-capped polyimide (PETI) breaks imide/amide bonds. Recovered products include the original diamines TFMB and 1,3-bis(4-aminophenoxy)benzene and hydroxyl-bearing aromatic oligomers retaining some imide structure. The cited PETI depolymerization uses deliberately applied chemical reagents and is a network-cleavage experiment. Its product recovery is not evidence of spontaneous ambient biodegradation.

Timescales: A separate PETI recovery study treated the resin with ethanolamine at 120 °C for one hour; the authors reported 96.9% degradation under the selected conditions. The resulting resin-derived material was used in an adhesive, so this endpoint describes chemical treatment and recovery, not complete mineralization or an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Aminolysis changes the imide-containing network into recoverable products under deliberately selected chemical conditions. The presence of those products does not establish their subsequent mineralization. Complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill remains unresolved.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Laboratory aminolysis-coupled hydrolysis recovers diamines and converts remaining PETI fragments into a flame-retardant component for polyester synthesis. This is demonstrated for the reported PETI chemistry, with incomplete diamine recovery, rather than a universal route for every thermoset polyimide. For the studied thermosetting PETI, the authors report up to 61% diamine yield under their optimized aminolysis-coupled hydrolysis conditions. The tested reaction also produces other fragments that retain imide structures, which the researchers used in a different polymer synthesis. This yield does not describe a recovered carbon-fiber composite or all thermoset polyimides. Material-specific identification and purification remain important to evaluating this research route.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The PMR-15 thermosetting-polyimide system illustrates precursor-specific health concerns: NASA identifies its methylenedianiline starting material as a liver toxin and describes special handling to limit exposure during fabrication and waste management. Development of alternative diamines was motivated partly by this issue. The finding applies to MDA-containing PMR formulations and should not be generalized to all thermosetting polyimides.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Polyimide precursor chemistry and network architecture vary with the monomers, reactive end cap and formulated oligomer size. Reactive diluent can improve melt processing but changes the composition of the cured material. Pressure, heating and post-cure also influence the final part; an older PMR study examined different formulated molecular weights and both molded and post-cured composites. Neat-resin measurements cannot be assumed to describe a fiber-reinforced laminate. In that same study, adding reactive diluent to the B-staged resin lowered the measured minimum melt viscosity, while the cured composition changed. Flow and cured properties therefore have to be assessed together for each formulation.

sections.overview: Natural rubber is a biologically produced material composed mainly of cis-1,4-polyisoprene. The rubber tree Hevea brasiliensis is the principal commercial source, with rubber collected from its latex. Other plants, including guayule and Russian dandelion, also produce natural rubber, although their rubber yield and composition can differ. Natural rubber is used in products ranging from tires to gloves. The liquid latex is a dispersion of rubber particles, whereas a tire or glove is a formulated, normally crosslinked article. Their behavior and end of life depend on the other ingredients and the way the material has been cured.
sections.history: Natural rubber has no single inventor. Indigenous Mesoamerican communities processed plant latex into useful rubber by about 1600 BCE; archaeological and experimental work by Dorothy Hosler, Sandra Burkett and Michael Tarkanian documents balls, figurines and tool bindings. Industrial development was a much later history. Charles Goodyear’s sulfur-vulcanization discovery in 1839 helped make rubber goods usable across seasonal temperatures. Pneumatic tires then greatly expanded demand: Dunlop’s bicycle work and Michelin’s removable and automobile tires were influential late-nineteenth-century developments. Plantation research, improved latex harvesting and later block-rubber production changed the supply industry. Michelin’s radial-tire development further reinforced the importance of natural rubber alongside synthetic elastomers.
sections.nomenclature: NR abbreviates natural rubber. The canonical name denotes plant-derived natural-rubber material and is not an alternate name for every polyisoprene elastomer or for synthetic isoprene rubber.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Natural rubber is principally cis-1,4-polyisoprene biosynthesized in latex-producing organisms, especially Hevea brasiliensis. Biosynthesis occurs at the surface of rubber particles in laticifer latex, where cis-prenyltransferase-associated machinery elongates isoprenoid chains; it is therefore distinct from synthetic isoprene rubber made by chemical polymerization. Harvested Hevea latex can be collected by tapping and the rubber fraction recovered by acid coagulation followed by concentration, or latex can be purified/concentrated by centrifugation, membrane separation, and washing. A recovery patent gives examples of solvent separation or coagulation followed by selective removal of non-rubber extractables. These recovery choices alter latex purity and physical form but are not sulfur-vulcanization instructions, which are excluded here.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Natural rubber develops its characteristic high extensibility, strength, fatigue resistance, and strain-induced crystallization only in a particular compounded and vulcanized form; raw latex, dried gum, and filled vulcanizates must not be conflated. Crosslink system and density, protein/non-rubber content, carbon black or silica reinforcement, temperature, strain rate, and aging all change tensile, tear, and hysteretic response. One open study reports for its D0 sulfur-vulcanized natural-rubber compound at room temperature: tensile strength 26.3 ± 0.7 MPa, elongation at break 584 ± 28%, 100% modulus 3.1 ± 0.2 MPa, Shore A 66, and tear strength 49 ± 5 kN/m. The test specimen, formulation, and cure details in that study govern these values; they are not raw-NR properties. A separate open study identifies naturally occurring network, protein and nonisoprene changes as variables affecting vulcanized-NR mechanics.
sections.processing: Natural rubber is converted either as stabilized latex or as dried raw rubber. Field latex is preserved and concentrated by routes such as centrifuging, creaming, or evaporation, then compounded or prevulcanized for dipped goods; dry rubber is masticated and compounded before operations such as calendering, extrusion, molding, and vulcanization. The open IntechOpen chapter covers field-latex handling, concentration, compounding/prevulcanization, and dipping, and emphasizes that latex stability must be maintained during mixing, pumping, and dipping. It reports a mechanical-stability-time test run at 14,000 rpm, with more than 650 s used as a standard criterion; short stability can cause coagulum and thickening during processing, while excessive stabilization can make deaeration and gelling on the former difficult. A separate processing review discusses mastication and compounding of natural rubber and the need to control raw-rubber conditioning, mastication temperature, and time. These constraints apply to the stated latex or rubber form and formulation, not to every natural-rubber article cycle.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Natural rubber chains are built predominantly from cis-1,4-linked isoprene units. In plants, the polymer is made on the surfaces of rubber particles, which are surrounded by a membrane and associated proteins. Latex contains both these rubber particles and non-rubber constituents. When a cured natural rubber specimen is stretched sufficiently, part of the polymer can crystallize; these crystallites melt when the load is released. Sulfur curing connects chains at multiple points, making the network difficult to dissolve or reshape as the original gum. Network density varies with the curing recipe.
sections.properties: Natural rubber is valued for elasticity, resilience, and resistance to abrasion and impact. Strain-induced crystallization can produce pronounced strain hardening at large deformations. In one study of sulfur-cured ribbed smoked sheet rubber, hardening occurred during planar extension as well as uniaxial stretching. The response therefore depends on the deformation imposed as well as the material itself. The crosslinked network helps a stretched article return toward its original shape, while its crystallization at high extension contributes to the increase in stiffness. A natural-latex balloon-waste recycling study also found substantial rebound in its revulcanized specimens, but pigment and remaining cure ingredients differed between samples.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Tires account for a majority of natural-rubber consumption according to ANRPC; other uses include gloves, balloons and components in aerospace, construction and healthcare. Elasticity and resilience are useful when a product must deform and recover, but a tire compound and a thin dipped latex article are different formulated products. In a laboratory study modeling balloon production, molds were dipped first in coagulant and then in concentrated natural latex to form thin gel films, which were washed and dried. This illustrates the use of latex as a liquid starting form, unlike a dry rubber bale for tire compounding.

Purchasing. Natural rubber is traded by grade, including technically specified rubber such as STR20 or SMR20, ribbed smoked sheet such as RSS3 or RSS4, and concentrated latex. A buyer selects the form and grade for the intended compounding or latex-processing route; a commercial source or specification for one form does not imply another is interchangeable.

Scale and evidence limits. CATAS’s June 2025 report, citing ANRPC, reports 2024 world production of 14.824 million tonnes and consumption of 15.364 million tonnes. These are reported global supply and use estimates, not buyer orders or a tonnage for any single product, and they may be revised.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Purified latex-clearing protein can oxidatively cleave cis-polyisoprene double bonds, producing oligomers with aldehyde and ketone ends. Ozone can also attack double bonds in the natural-rubber backbone; in stretched articles, surface damage can develop into cracks. These are different exposures, and neither finding alone describes the fate of every filled and vulcanized article.

Timescales: In one enzyme experiment, latex in pH-7 buffer was incubated with purified protein at 30 °C for 20 hours and oligomer products were identified. Separately, a 365-day simulated aerobic soil test at 25 ± 2 °C measured CO₂ evolution from 3 mm rubber pieces: the authors estimated about 57% biodegradation for neat NR versus about 28% for their highly crosslinked, high-curative formulation. These are different endpoints under controlled conditions, not a universal disposal time.

Environmental persistence: The soil experiment measured partial mineralization rather than merely disappearance or cracking, but its results depend on its soil, specimen size, curatives and exposure. It does not establish complete mineralization or a lifetime for a tire, glove or other article in natural environments.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Sulfur-cured natural rubber does not simply melt back into its original gum. Devulcanization seeks to break some of the sulfur-containing links so material can be processed and cured again, although backbone damage and retained additives can change the product.

In a laboratory study, prevulcanized natural-latex balloon manufacturing waste was sorted by color, mechanically devulcanized and revulcanized with a sulfur curing system. In abrasion testing, the revulcanized samples lost 161–196 mm³ of material versus 150 mm³ for the virgin-latex reference; more loss indicates lower abrasion resistance in that test. Residual pigments and cure ingredients may have influenced the result. The work demonstrates a route for the tested production waste, not collection or equivalent performance for mixed postconsumer rubber.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Proteins carried by natural rubber latex can cause allergic reactions ranging from skin symptoms to severe systemic reactions. Processing chemicals can separately cause contact rashes. NIOSH distinguishes these protein allergens from synthetic rubber latex, which does not supply the same natural proteins. Exposure depends on the product and contact route, so material selection must consider users with known latex allergy.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Natural rubber is not a single uniform formulation: plant species and latex constituents differ, and the polymer has a broad molecular-weight distribution. Vulcanization and added ingredients further distinguish finished rubber from raw latex. Results for a specified cured specimen and stretching geometry should not be taken as universal properties of every natural rubber product. The formulation also matters for biodegradation: in one controlled soil test, a highly crosslinked, high-curative specimen produced less CO₂ over one year than a lightly crosslinked specimen. Such a comparison does not predict the fate of every commercial article.

sections.overview: Synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene is an elastomer made by polymerizing isoprene so that cis-1,4 units predominate. Its backbone resembles the principal polymer in natural rubber, although its synthetic origin and composition differ. A documented route uses a neodymium-based coordination catalyst with aluminum-containing components. The resulting gum can be compounded and vulcanized for use as a rubber. Its cis configuration permits strain-induced crystallization in suitably cured formulations, which can contribute to the sharp rise in stress at large stretch. A finished tire or seal contains a compound of the polymer with cure chemicals and usually other additives.
sections.history: Synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene became practical when stereoselective catalysts of the 1950s allowed chemists to approach natural rubber’s chain configuration. Shell commercialized lithium-catalyzed isoprene rubber in 1960; Goodyear introduced its more highly cis-rich Natsyn material in 1962, followed by Goodrich-Gulf. Applications included tires, molded mechanical goods, footwear, rubber bands and nipples. Zeon began isoprene-rubber production in 1971 alongside its own isoprene-extraction technology, illustrating how monomer supply and polymer manufacture developed together. Later research continued to refine stereochemical control and processing; Goodyear’s 2004 neodymium-catalyst patent records one such manufacturing advance. Earlier rubberlike isoprene polymers should not automatically be identified as this highly cis-selective material.
sections.nomenclature: Synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene is also abbreviated cis-PI or IR in rubber contexts. The record is limited to the synthetic high-cis 1,4 polymer; natural rubber, trans-1,4-polyisoprene, and a particular sulfur-vulcanized compound are separate scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene is produced by stereoselective coordination polymerization of purified isoprene. The monomer and hydrocarbon medium must be kept dry and oxygen-free because the coordination catalysts are readily poisoned. A long-established solution route uses a Ziegler-type catalyst made from titanium tetrachloride and a trialkylaluminum compound; catalyst ratio, preparation history, temperature, solvent, and conversion control activity, molar mass, gel formation, and cis-1,4 content. A distinct high-cis route uses a neodymium catalyst assembled from a neodymium carboxylate, organoaluminum compound, and dialkylaluminum chloride, with isoprene present during catalyst aging. Polymerization is stopped by deactivating the catalyst, antioxidant is added, and the rubber is recovered by coagulation or steam/solvent removal and dried. Latex grades can instead be made by emulsifying a solution-polymerized high-cis rubber and removing the organic solvent. The uncured polymer is not the final load-bearing network. A documented sulfur system combines cis-polyisoprene with sulfur, zinc oxide, stearic acid, and an accelerator such as TBBS; sulfur bridges formed between chains convert it into a vulcanizate. Peroxide and other cure systems are route variants, but their network structures are not interchangeable. Article shaping and time–temperature cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Synthetic high-cis-1,4-polyisoprene is a soft elastomer whose useful engineering response normally comes from a cured network: it sustains large, nonlinear recoverable strains, but the measured stress response and set depend on loading history and test conditions. Its stereoregular chains can undergo strain-induced crystallization (SIC) at sufficiently large extension. The resulting oriented crystallites produce a stress upturn (strain hardening) and reinforce highly strained regions, including material near a crack tip; they disappear again as the sample is released. This response is therefore not represented by one small-strain modulus or strength value.

Principal controls include cis-1,4 stereoregularity, network crosslink density and distribution, sulfur/cure-package chemistry and cure state. Fillers can change tensile stress and hardness through loading, particle structure and surface area, rubber–filler interaction, coupling treatment, and dispersion or agglomeration; oils and other compounding ingredients also shift stiffness and extensibility. Mixing and curing history, ageing, specimen geometry and orientation, temperature, strain rate, cyclic preconditioning, and deformation mode must accompany comparisons. In particular, planar or biaxial extension orients chains differently from uniaxial extension and can move the apparent onset of SIC and strain hardening. Moisture is generally a secondary direct variable for the hydrocarbon network, but conditioning can matter when water-sensitive fillers or interfaces are present.

One bounded unfilled example was a laboratory sulfur-cured synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene compound containing, per 100 phr rubber, 5 phr ZnO, 2 phr stearic acid, 1 phr sulfur, 2 phr TBBS and 2 phr PEG. It was Banbury/two-roll mixed, press-cured as an approximately 2 mm sheet at 150 °C to its 9.5 min T90, conditioned overnight, and tested at 500 mm min−1. The authors used ASTM D412 procedures but explicitly substituted a smaller 25 × 4 mm dumbbell for the standard Die C specimen. Under that specific protocol the compound gave 1.2 MPa stress at 300% strain, 4.7 MPa at 600%, 19.0 MPa ultimate tensile strength, and Shore A hardness 35.7; these values should not be generalized to other grades, cure systems, or specimens. As a complementary mode-dependence example, a separately reported IR2200 sulfur vulcanizate (initial Young's modulus 1.42 MPa) tested at 25 °C in a custom thin-centre specimen at about 7 × 10−3 s−1 showed strain-hardening/SIC onset stretches of 4.7 in planar extension and 5.7 in uniaxial extension. Those onset stretches describe that formulation and protocol, rather than universal thresholds for synthetic polyisoprene.
sections.processing:
Synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene is commonly converted as a compounded elastomer: the gum is mixed with fillers, oils, antioxidants, activators, accelerators, and a vulcanizing package in an internal mixer or on rolls; curatives are often added in a later, cooler mill stage to preserve scorch safety; the stock is then sheeted, calendered, extruded, molded, or built into an article and vulcanized. Latex- and solution-dip molding are additional routes for thin films, gloves, and balloons, using controlled solution or latex viscosity, degassing, form preparation, withdrawal, repeated dip/dry cycles, residual-solvent removal or leaching, cure, cooling, rinsing, powdering, and stripping. Filler drying and dispersion, mixing sequence, rotor or roll shear, compound temperature, residence time, sheet gauge, green-stock tack, scorch time, and rheometer-derived optimum cure time are consequential. Polymerization and chemical modification of the polymer belong in Synthesis; compounding, article shaping, and the vulcanization equipment and schedule belong here.

Wang and co-workers provide a bounded dry-mixing and press-cure example for SKI-5 PM cis-1,4-polyisoprene (reported Mw 272,100). Fumed silica was dried at 150 °C for 2 h; IR, silica, TESPT, ZnO, stearic acid, and BHT were blended in a Banbury mixer, after which TBBS and sulfur were added on a two-roll mill and approximately 2.5 mm sheets were formed. The named formulation used, per 100 parts rubber, 30 parts silica, 3 TESPT, 5 ZnO, 2 stearic acid, 2 BHT, 1 TBBS, and 1.5 sulfur, and was press-cured at 145 °C and 15 MPa for its measured t90. Those settings apply to that laboratory composite. In a distinct dip-molding example, McGlothlin and Schmid dissolved 40 g NATSYN 2200 and 1.2 g dicumyl peroxide in 1,000 g tetrahydrofuran, allowed bubbles to dissipate, built a catheter balloon film through nine dip/dry repetitions, oven-dried the coated mandrel for 2 h, and cured it for 4 min in a 180 °C molten-salt bath before cooling and rinsing. That solvent/peroxide schedule is specific to the disclosed NATSYN 2200 balloon process, not a universal polyisoprene cure window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The isoprene units are predominantly joined in the cis-1,4 configuration, leaving unsaturation in the backbone. Catalyst composition and polymerization conditions influence the microstructure of the synthesized polymer. Vulcanization converts a compounded gum into a crosslinked material. Under sufficiently large extension, cured high-cis polyisoprene can develop strain-induced crystallites within the stretched network. Crosslinks limit permanent chain flow, while stretching can align parts of the network enough to crystallize. The amount and onset of that ordering depend on the sample and the deformation imposed.
sections.properties: The cured material can show strong nonlinear stiffening at high stretch as crystallization develops. In a study of sulfur-cured IR2200 sheets, the onset of hardening differed between planar and uniaxial extension. In another synthetic polyisoprene study, adding 25 parts N660 carbon black per 100 parts rubber increased the tensile stress at 600% extension from 4.7 MPa for the unfilled vulcanizate to 22.1 MPa for the filled compound. The study used smaller-than-standard dumbbell specimens, and the comparison applies to those cured formulations and conditions. These examples show why both deformation mode and compounding matter when comparing reported behavior. Planar and uniaxial loading impose different lateral deformation, so an onset of stiffening needs its test geometry as well as its cure recipe.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Synthetic isoprene rubber serves vehicle, bicycle and aircraft tires, conveyor/V-belts, seals and footwear. In these products, synthetic isoprene rubber is a compounding ingredient that is mixed, shaped and cured with an application-specific recipe. As a concrete tread-research example, one study compounded Nipol IR2200 with carbon black, oil, sulfur and other additives, then abraded the cured material to investigate wear particles. The rubber provides the continuous elastic matrix, while the filler and cure recipe also affect abrasion; the experiment is not a performance rating for a finished tire. The listed raw grades do not specify the performance of the finished tire, belt or seal.

Purchasing. Zeon lists Nipol IR 2200 and IR 2200L compounding grades through its rubber-materials inquiry channel. The supplier describes 2200L as the lower-Mooney-viscosity grade, with design values of 70 versus 82 for 2200. These are raw-rubber selection values rather than properties of a cured tire or seal.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon reported Japanese IR capacity of 40,000 t/year in May 2015. This historical company capacity is neither current capacity nor measured production, purchases or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A laboratory enzyme study found cleavage of purified synthetic cis-polyisoprene into carbonyl-bearing fragments. A later study of a different latex-clearing protein from Nocardia nova SH22a also detected carbonyl-containing products from both cis and trans polyisoprene, showing that enzyme identity matters.

Timescales: In the first study, purified synthetic rubber granules were incubated in pH-7 buffer for five days with enzyme added daily. In the separate Nocardia enzyme experiment, cryomilled synthetic cis-polyisoprene was incubated for 10 days with fresh enzyme added every 24 hours; extracted fragments were analyzed by mass spectrometry. In a separate 28-day respirometry test, one sample of unvulcanized synthetic isoprene rubber, ground to particles no larger than 125 micrometres, showed negligible oxygen consumption attributable to biodegradation in an activated-sludge inoculum. Natural rubber tested separately reached 35.4% of its theoretical oxygen demand, but the materials are not identical and the synthetic rubber result was based on one replicate. These laboratory exposures are not outdoor degradation rates.

Environmental persistence: Fragment formation does not establish complete mineralization or the fate of a filled, cured article. The cited tests cannot predict disappearance in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A patent proposes devulcanizing rubber waste and includes isoprene rubber within its stated scope; its demonstrated experiments used truck-tire crumb rather than an isolated synthetic cis-polyisoprene article. Reducing crosslinks may enable incorporation into another rubber compound, but excessive backbone damage can alter properties.

The enzyme studies instead demonstrate initial cleavage under laboratory conditions. They do not establish a commercial recovery process, complete mineralization or production of reusable isoprene monomer.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene is compounded, bag opening and ingredient weighing can release dust. HSE recommends dust-reduced or preweighed additives and local extraction. Ingredient-dependent skin allergy and dermatitis require contact control. This guidance concerns the uncured compound and its additives, rather than establishing a hazard classification for the base polymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: High-cis synthetic polyisoprene is a material class, and catalyst system and preparation can produce different polymer microstructures. The cited extension experiment used a particular IR2200 gum and sulfur recipe, so its onset stretches are not family-wide constants. The fly-ash study used a specific sulfur formulation and smaller-than-standard tensile dumbbells. Its reinforcement results depend on filler treatment and mixing as well as the rubber itself. Synthetic cis-polyisoprene and natural rubber share the predominant repeat-unit geometry but need not contain the same non-rubber constituents or have the same molecular-weight distribution. Filled and unfilled vulcanizates should be compared separately.

sections.overview: Trans-1,4-polyisoprene is a polyisoprene in which trans-1,4 links predominate along the backbone. It can be prepared by coordination polymerization of isoprene, including a documented supported titanium catalyst process. Its stereoregularity permits crystallization, giving it a useful combination of crystalline and rubbery behavior. Crosslinked trans-polyisoprene and its composites have been studied as thermally activated shape-memory materials. Its crystalline regions can fix a deformed shape while a crosslinked network helps the material recover on reheating. Dental gutta-percha points are formulated products containing this polymer, not pure trans-polyisoprene.
sections.history: Trans-1,4-polyisoprene has both a natural-material history and a later synthetic-polymer history. Gutta-percha was used in Southeast Asia for tool handles before its nineteenth-century introduction to European industry. William Montgomerie promoted medical uses in 1843; Werner Siemens’s cable-coating machinery helped make it central to submarine telegraph insulation. Golf balls and dental root fillings were other important uses of the natural material. Synthetic trans-polyisoprene was subsequently developed by producers including Polysar and Kuraray. Jack Lasky’s United States Rubber patent, issued in 1963, documents a stereoselective catalyst route. The nineteenth-century dates therefore concern natural gutta-percha and its processing, rather than invention of synthetic trans-polyisoprene.
sections.nomenclature: Trans-1,4-polyisoprene is commonly abbreviated TPI. This record is the synthetic high-trans 1,4 polyisoprene boundary; synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene, natural rubber, and a particular vulcanized compound are distinct scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Synthetic trans-1,4-polyisoprene is made by stereoselective coordination polymerization of purified isoprene, with the catalyst directing successive monomer additions predominantly into the trans-1,4 configuration. One industrial patent uses bulk precipitation polymerization with a supported titanium tetrachloride/magnesium chloride catalyst activated by a trialkylaluminum. In that route inhibitor and high-boiling impurities are removed from polymer-grade isoprene, the monomer is dried, low-temperature prepolymerization forms catalyst-centered particles, and a second polymerization stage grows them while hydrogen is used in a bounded range as a molecular-weight regulator. Unreacted monomer is recovered during vacuum devolatilization and drying, and antioxidant is added before product recovery. A distinct historical catalyst system combines finely divided vanadium trichloride, an aluminum trihydrocarbyl, and a tetrahydrocarbyl titanate in an inert hydrocarbon solvent; catalyst-component ratios, solvent, dilution, and temperature control activity and trans selectivity. Moisture, oxygen, inhibitors, and polar impurities deactivate these coordination catalysts, so monomer purification and inert handling are central controls. Uncrosslinked high-trans material can be semicrystalline. Where a rubber network is required, a cited formulation compounds trans-polyisoprene with sulfur, zinc oxide, stearic acid, and accelerator; sulfur amount controls the balance between covalent network formation and crystallization. That vulcanization route is a downstream chemical modification rather than part of the stereoselective chain-growth step, and not every trans-polyisoprene product is vulcanized. Article-shaping cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Trans-1,4-polyisoprene differs mechanically from the rubbery cis isomer because its regular trans chains can crystallize substantially near room temperature. Crystals can act as a stiff reinforcing and shape-fixing phase, so a high-trans material may behave as a hard, semicrystalline plastomer below its melting interval and soften markedly when those crystals melt. With an appropriate permanent network, recrystallization and melting can instead provide the reversible switching phase for thermally activated shape memory. It is therefore misleading to assign one elastomer-like strength or hardness to all trans-polyisoprene.

The response depends on trans content, molecular mass, crystal fraction and polymorph, cooling and annealing history, strain-induced orientation, chemical crosslink density and cure system, filler loading and dispersion, polymer–filler adhesion, plasticizer or blend components, oxidation and aging, temperature relative to melting, strain rate, cyclic history, specimen geometry and test mode. In one controlled sulfur series, Kuraray TP-301 (number-average molecular mass 7.0 × 10⁴ g mol⁻¹ and reported trans content above 98%) was compounded per 100 phr polymer with 5 phr ZnO, 2 phr stearic acid, 1 phr accelerator and 1–4 phr sulfur, mixed on a 60 °C two-roll mill, held 24 h, and compression cured at 150 °C and 15 MPa to t90. Raising sulfur from 1 to 4 phr reduced tensile strength from 23.5 to 10.8 MPa, tear strength from 60.3 to 17.3 kN m⁻¹, 100% modulus from 11.3 to 3.3 MPa, elongation at break from 360% to 237%, and Shore A hardness from 96.2 to 71.5. The authors linked the change to suppression of crystallinity as crosslinking increased. Results were means of three specimens, but the paper does not state the Chinese standard number, specimen geometry or test speed, so the values are bounded to that formulation series rather than treated as transferable specifications.

An independent study provides a second formulation-scale check. Its unfilled Qingdao Dipai TPI control contained, per 100 phr TPI, 2 phr stearic acid, 4 phr ZnO, 2 phr antioxidant, 1.2 phr NOBS accelerator and 1.5 phr sulfur; it was milled at 70 °C for 15 min, rested 24 h, and hot-pressed at 150 °C and 5 MPa for 10 min into 2 mm sheets. The reported room-temperature tensile strength was 17.7 MPa, elongation at break 380.5%, and Young's modulus 0.052 GPa. Because that article omits the tensile standard, specimen geometry and crosshead rate, these numbers are only a bounded control for its carbon-nanotube study. Its filled series further shows that nanoparticle dispersion and interfacial modification can change strength and stiffness without defining neat trans-polyisoprene behavior.
sections.processing:
Trans-1,4-polyisoprene can be mixed and shaped while warm, then used as a crystalline thermoplastic, a lightly crosslinked shape-memory material, or a more fully vulcanized elastomer depending on formulation. Reported article conversion uses two-roll or open-mill compounding followed by compression molding or vacuum hot pressing and sulfur cure. Fillers, zinc oxide, stearic acid, antioxidant, accelerator, and sulfur must be distributed without scorching; mill-roll temperature, mixing time and order, compound maturation, cure-meter endpoint, mold pressure, cure temperature, and sheet thickness all affect the result. Cooling and storage history are unusually important because crystallization near ambient conditions continues after molding and competes with crosslinking. For shape-memory articles, deformation above the crystalline transition, cooling under constraint, and reheating form an additional orientation and recovery operation. Polymerization and sulfur-network chemistry belong in Synthesis; mixing, molding, vulcanization schedule, cooling, crystallization conditioning, and shape programming belong here.

Fu and co-workers compounded Kuraray TP-301 (more than 98% trans structure) on an XK-160 two-roll mill at 60 °C with, per 100 phr TPI, 5 phr zinc oxide, 2 phr stearic acid, 1 phr accelerator, and 1–4 phr sulfur. After 24 h, the compounds were compression molded at 150 °C and 15 MPa for the rheometer-derived tc90; the reported tc90 values ranged from 470 to 550 s across that sulfur series. Zhang and co-workers provide an independent schedule: TPI and 0–3 phr polydopamine-modified nanotube were open-mill blended at 70 °C for 15 min with 2 phr stearic acid, 4 phr zinc oxide, 2 phr antioxidant 4010NA, 1.2 phr NOBS accelerator, and 1.5 phr sulfur, rested 24 h, and vacuum hot pressed at 150 °C and 5 MPa for 10 min into 2 mm sheets. Both windows belong to the stated recipes, and changing sulfur or filler changes crystallinity, cure response, and shape-memory behavior.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The trans configuration allows chains to organize into crystalline regions alongside less ordered material. A study of sulfur-cured trans-polyisoprene composites identified diffraction features associated with alpha and beta crystal forms. The same study found that crystallinity changed as the amount and surface treatment of carbon nanotube filler changed. Both the crystalline phase and the crosslinked network contribute to the composite’s response. Crystalline and amorphous regions coexist, so cooling and heating can change how much of the material is ordered. In a shape-memory compound, the permanent crosslinked network and the reversible crystalline phase have separate roles.
sections.properties: Crystallization and melting can be used to fix a temporary shape and release it on heating in appropriately formulated trans-polyisoprene networks. In one study, polydopamine-coated carbon nanotubes improved the tensile response and thermal stability of a sulfur-cured composite relative to its unfilled control. The researchers also measured crystallization and melting transitions by differential scanning calorimetry. These observations describe the tested compounds, not an unqualified property of every trans-polyisoprene. For a specific sulfur-cured composite study, 0.6 parts per hundred rubber of polydopamine-coated carbon nanotubes increased tensile strength from 17.7 MPa for the unfilled control to 19.8 MPa. This comparison is for the tested composites at room temperature and does not describe an unfilled commercial grade.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Trans-1,4-polyisoprene is the polymer basis of gutta-percha; formulated gutta-percha points remain a dental root-canal material. Golf balls and submarine-cable insulation are historical uses, not evidence of today’s main market. A dental point combines the trans-polyisoprene polymer with other components to produce a shaped root-canal filling material. Its size and formulation should be distinguished from laboratory pellets of the polymer. Its crystalline regions also make it a candidate for research on shape-memory devices: in a laboratory study, crosslinked trans-polyisoprene composites were stretched at 60 °C, cooled to −10 °C under load and reheated. The tested specimens recovered more than 96% of their programmed strain, illustrating thermal actuation for those compositions rather than a commercial device specification.

Purchasing. Material suppliers offer trans-polyisoprene pellets for laboratory work; Sigma-Aldrich lists a 50 g unit. Dental practices instead buy formulated points selected for size and taper; Dentsply Sirona lists a 60-point pack. Such points are not neat polymer pellets.

Scale and evidence limits. These examples establish tens-of-grams research packages and tens-of-points dental packages. No annual global trans-polyisoprene purchase tonnage is established; natural-rubber statistics primarily concern the cis material.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: One tested latex-clearing protein did not detectably cleave trans-polyisoprene under its conditions. A different enzyme from Nocardia nova SH22a did cleave synthetic trans-polyisoprene, producing carbonyl-containing fragments identified by spectroscopy and mass spectrometry. The contrasting results depend on the specific enzyme, not a universal rule that the trans isomer is inert.

Timescales: The first enzyme test reported no cleavage during its five-day pH-7 incubation. In a separate mineralization experiment with selected Nocardia isolates, 250–500 µm synthetic trans-polyisoprene particles in mineral-salts medium gave 3–54% conversion to CO₂ after 80 days, depending on the strain. A Gordonia strain able to use the cis isomer did not detectably mineralize the trans polymer in that experiment. These are selected-culture results for synthetic particles, not lifetimes in an unamended environment.

Environmental persistence: The CO₂ measurement provides evidence of partial mineralization under those laboratory conditions, whereas detection of fragments alone does not. Neither experiment establishes the fate of a formulated dental point in soil, water or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Initial enzymatic cleavage of purified trans-polyisoprene has been demonstrated in the laboratory, including by the Nocardia nova SH22a enzyme. Its carbonyl-containing products are fragments, not regenerated pure isoprene.

These experiments do not establish a collection system or industrial reclamation process for this polymer. Formulated dental points and filled or crosslinked composites contain other ingredients, so a purified-polymer result cannot be transferred to those wastes.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: In compounded trans-1,4-polyisoprene products, heating and conversion can generate rubber fume. HSE identifies dermatitis and skin-allergy risks from such process emissions and recommends ventilation that carries rising fume away from workers. This manufacturing guidance does not assign natural-latex protein allergy to every polyisoprene source or stereoisomer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The degree of crystallinity and mechanical response depend on formulation and thermal history. In the cited composite study, the effect of coated nanotubes on crystallinity changed with filler loading rather than increasing monotonically. Filler dispersion and surface treatment also affected the comparison with unmodified nanotubes. Reported shape-memory and tensile results are tied to the specified cure, specimen, temperature, and test protocol. For example, filler coating and dispersion affect reinforcement, while thermal history changes crystallinity. Neither an enzyme result on purified polymer nor a tensile result on a filled composite predicts performance of a finished dental point.

sections.overview: Polybutadiene rubber is an elastomer made by polymerizing 1,3-butadiene. Its chains can contain different proportions of cis-1,4, trans-1,4 and vinyl-1,2 units. Catalyst chemistry controls the relative abundance of these structures. Polybutadiene is often compounded or blended with other rubbers for tire applications. The unsaturated sites in these chains can participate in vulcanization, producing an elastic network once the material is compounded and cured. The final tire compound also includes reinforcing filler and often another rubber.
sections.history: Polybutadiene rubber’s industrial development includes successive generations of stereoselective catalyst technology. A documented Japanese production milestone is Zeon’s start of butadiene-rubber manufacture at Tokuyama in November 1965. Later, Thomas Knauf and Akhtar Osman’s Polysar patent, issued in 1995, sought a more active rare-earth catalyst system for producing high-cis polybutadiene. This illustrates continued refinement of a material already established commercially, rather than its original invention. Tire compounds have been a major outlet; Arlanxeo’s account also identifies plastic modification and golf balls as applications. The family encompasses different chain microstructures, so the launch of a particular high-cis grade is not a universal date for all polybutadiene.
sections.nomenclature: BR abbreviates polybutadiene rubber. The name denotes butadiene homopolymer rubber and is distinct from styrene–butadiene rubber or nitrile butadiene rubber copolymers.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polybutadiene rubber is made by chain-growth polymerization of 1,3-butadiene. Coordination catalysts are important because they control whether the chain is rich in cis-1,4, trans-1,4, or 1,2-vinyl units; polybutadiene is therefore a family of microstructures rather than one stereochemically uniform material. High-cis solution routes commonly use a rare-earth catalyst assembled from a neodymium carboxylate, an organoaluminum component, and a halogen-containing activator in a dry hydrocarbon solvent under inert atmosphere. One cited process uses neodymium carboxylate, alkylaluminum chloride, and dialkylaluminum hydride; another uses a monomeric neodymium carboxylate with halogen and organometallic cocatalysts. Catalyst ratios, aging order, solvent, temperature, and termination set activity, molar mass, and cis content. These examples do not imply that all polybutadiene is high-cis; lithium-anionic and other transition-metal systems can give different architectures.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polybutadiene rubber (BR) develops its useful elastic, rebound, abrasion, flex, and tensile response only after compounding and vulcanization; raw gum, a filled tire compound, and BR used as an impact-modifier phase are not mechanically equivalent materials. The cis/trans/vinyl microstructure, molecular mass and branching, crosslink type and density, carbon black or silica and coupling-agent package, oil/plasticizer, blend partner, cure temperature/time, strain amplitude/rate, temperature, and aging control stiffness, hysteresis, crack growth, and failure. High-cis BR may strain-crystallize and can give low heat build-up and high resilience, whereas higher trans or vinyl content changes modulus, hardness, transition behavior, and cure response. A deliberately bounded historical tire-tread example—not an intrinsic BR value—is an SBR/BR vulcanizate containing 25 parts Buton 500 polybutadiene and about 64–65 parts ISAF carbon black, with sulfur, zinc oxide, stearic acid, antioxidant, and accelerators: the UNIDO table reports 3,250–3,290 psi tensile strength (about 22.4–22.7 MPa), 660–685% elongation, 1,000–1,101 psi 300% modulus, and Shore A 62. Test temperature and procedure are not reported, and the SBR-rich reinforced blend cannot be assigned to neat or any single BR grade. Independent high-cis BR vulcanization work specifically attributes variation to stereopurity and cure recipe/temperature/time, while noting extension crystallization as a mechanism for strong high-cis vulcanizates.
sections.processing: Polybutadiene rubber is compounded with reinforcing fillers, oils or processing aids, and sulfur or peroxide curatives, then mixed, sheeted or extruded, shaped, and vulcanized. The high-cis polybutadiene vulcanization study discusses how cure ingredients, temperature, and time affect unfilled vulcanizates. A separate open study used high-cis Buna CB24 with 30 phr silanized silica and 1 phr dicumyl peroxide; the compound's cure properties were measured at 160 °C and its t95 was 32.31 min. These examples show the importance of filler dispersion and cure kinetics, but the peroxide formulation and 160 °C result are specific to that silica-filled compound; sulfur systems, cis content, branching, oil extension, and article geometry require separate rheometric and molding conditions.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Butadiene can add to a growing chain in several ways, producing cis-1,4, trans-1,4 and 1,2-vinyl structures. A documented neodymium catalyst route yields high-cis material. Carbon–carbon unsaturation remains available for vulcanization. The cured network and any filler or blending rubber contribute to the morphology of a finished compound. The three incorporation patterns describe different local arrangements in the same broad polymer family, not interchangeable test grades. Their proportions can affect chain packing and the properties of the resulting material.
sections.properties: Polybutadiene is used where resilient rubber behavior is desired, including tire compounds. An early comparison of unfilled cis-polybutadiene vulcanizates found that higher stereoregularity promoted crystallization on stretching, accompanied by a stronger rise in modulus at high elongation and higher tensile strength. These results concern the tested high-cis materials and vulcanization recipes; fillers and cure change a finished compound’s response. A separate tire-tread report compares filled compounds containing polybutadiene and styrene–butadiene rubber. Such measurements reflect both rubber composition and the entire cure and filler recipe. Supplier grades also differ before cure: Zeon lists design Mooney viscosity values of 44 for BR1220 and 50 for its low-cis BR1250H. These are raw-grade comparisons, not tensile properties of cured tire compounds.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polybutadiene rubber serves tire compounds, belts, seals, footwear and coated fabrics in transportation and industrial goods. ARLANXEO describes its high-cis neodymium-catalyzed BR grades as components of tire tread formulations, where compounds need abrasion and flex-cracking resistance. It describes blending selected grades with solution SBR to improve tread abrasion and rolling resistance; the outcome depends on the whole compound. Zeon identifies both BR1220 and low-cis 1250H for products including tire treads, conveyor belts and seals, illustrating that grades differ and are compounded before use.

Purchasing. Zeon lists distinct Nipol BR grades through supplier inquiry, including BR1220 and low-cis Nipol 1250H. Its grade table reports Mooney viscosity design values of 44 and 50 respectively, identifying a difference relevant to raw rubber handling. The chosen grade must still be compounded and cured to determine finished-article properties.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon reported Japanese BR capacity of 65,000 t/year in May 2015. This historical company capacity is neither current capacity nor measured production, purchases or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Air oxidation produces epoxide, peroxide and carbonyl-bearing structures. In the 100 °C film experiment, infrared signals associated with vinyl and 1,4 double bonds decreased while oxygen-containing signals appeared; nuclear magnetic resonance indicated epoxide structures in the tested 1,4 material. A primary study of low-molecular-weight 1,4- and 1,2-polybutadiene films identified epoxide-rich oxidized chains; subsequent hot-air analysis detected alcohols, aldehydes, ketones and acids, including 2-butenal, 2-butanone and acetic acid.

Timescales: The films were aged at 100 °C over hours; the 1,2 material became insoluble after 8 h. Volatile-product analysis covered 130–400 °C at a 10 °C/min ramp, a separate thermal protocol.

Environmental persistence: Insolubility and oxidation do not demonstrate mineralization. In a separate 28-day activated-sludge test at 20 ± 2 °C, a BR constituent showed negligible biodegradation as inferred from oxygen consumption, while the natural rubber comparator reached 35.4% of its theoretical oxygen demand. This controlled test does not give a lifetime in soil or water, and the constituent result cannot be treated as a measurement of every cured tire compound.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A patent proposes chemical devulcanization to break links in vulcanized rubber so reclaimed material can be reincorporated into a new compound. It includes polybutadiene among the possible rubbers, while the reported demonstrations use tire crumb, a mixed feedstock.

Breaking links can improve processability, but unwanted backbone scission changes molecular weight and properties. Performance depends on the original cure and processing conditions; the patent does not establish equivalent properties for every reclaimed polybutadiene product.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When polybutadiene rubber is compounded, bag opening and ingredient weighing can release dust. HSE recommends dust-reduced or preweighed additives and local extraction. Ingredient-dependent skin allergy and dermatitis require contact control. This guidance concerns the uncured compound and its additives, rather than establishing a hazard classification for the base polymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Different catalyst systems produce polybutadienes with different microstructures and molecular characteristics. High-cis experimental results are not representative of every polybutadiene grade. Fillers, blends, cure conditions and test temperature also affect measured behavior. The tire-tread data describe specific filled SBR/polybutadiene mixtures, not neat polybutadiene. In addition to microstructure, rubber grade and additives influence processing; a viscosity for raw polymer cannot be used as a mechanical property of its filled vulcanizate. Service performance requires the compound and test conditions.

sections.overview: Styrene–butadiene rubber (SBR) is a family of synthetic elastomers made by copolymerizing styrene and butadiene. Commercially important routes include aqueous emulsion polymerization and polymerization in organic solution. These routes provide different opportunities to control the resulting chains. SBR compounds are widely studied for tire treads, where traction, wear and energy dissipation must be balanced. Tire performance belongs to the entire cured compound: filler and cure choices influence the tradeoff as well as the polymer architecture.
sections.history: The styrene–butadiene rubber family grew from German Buna-S research and became a strategic mass-production material during the Second World War. When access to Southeast Asian natural rubber was cut off, the United States government coordinated a GR-S program involving Firestone, B. F. Goodrich, Goodyear, Standard Oil of New Jersey, United States Rubber and academic laboratories. Commercial wartime plants began operating in 1942. The collaborative effort turned a laboratory and pilot-scale technology into a large industrial supply of general-purpose rubber for tires and other essential equipment. Postwar production and research continued, and later emulsion and solution processes developed into distinct branches with different product and manufacturing histories.
sections.nomenclature: SBR abbreviates styrene–butadiene rubber. The canonical record is family-level: emulsion SBR, solution SBR, and functionalized SBR are narrower related materials rather than uniform aliases.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–butadiene rubber (SBR) is a family of random copolymer rubbers made from styrene and 1,3-butadiene. Emulsion SBR is produced by free-radical copolymerization in water with soap or another emulsifier. Hot recipes use thermal radical sources, whereas cold recipes use low-temperature redox initiation; mercaptans serve as chain-transfer agents to limit molar mass. Polymerization is stopped at a selected conversion, residual monomers are removed, and the latex is coagulated, washed, stabilized, and dried. One cited patent documents a conventional peroxide or peroxydisulfate emulsion recipe and mercaptan control. Solution SBR instead uses an organolithium initiator in a dry hydrocarbon solvent; polar modifiers or mixed-metal additives regulate random styrene placement and the butadiene 1,2/1,4 microstructure, while living ends permit coupling or functionalization. A distinct patent demonstrates amine-modified anionic initiation, end-group reaction, and solvent recovery. The uncured copolymer becomes an elastic network through vulcanization, most commonly sulfur crosslinking with zinc oxide, fatty acid, and accelerator; a third cited patent gives an SBR-specific sulfur-cure formulation. Polymerization and crosslink chemistry belong here, while compound shaping and article cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Styrene–butadiene rubbers are generally amorphous, non-strain-crystallizing elastomers. A vulcanized gum network can undergo large, nonlinear deformation, but unfilled SBR is comparatively weak; practical compounds obtain much of their tensile, tear, abrasion, and stiffness performance from carbon black, silica, or other reinforcement. Their response is viscoelastic and hysteretic rather than a single elastic constant: stress depends on strain amplitude, loading rate or frequency, temperature, and prior cycles, and filler networks add pronounced strain-dependent dynamic stiffness and energy dissipation.

Emulsion SBR (ESBR) and solution SBR (SSBR) are processing and molecular-design families, not grades with one inherent strength ranking. Emulsion free-radical routes commonly give broader molecular and sequence distributions, whereas solution carbanionic routes can more closely control molar mass, dispersity, styrene distribution, butadiene 1,2-vinyl versus cis/trans-1,4 microstructure, branching, and chain-end functionality. Increasing bound styrene or 1,2-vinyl content generally raises the glass-transition region, tending to increase hardness and stiffness at a fixed temperature near that transition while reducing low-temperature flexibility; the actual balance also depends on sequence distribution and molar mass. Functional SSBR chain ends can strengthen interaction with polar silica, but any comparison must retain the filler and cure formulation.

Consequential compound variables include filler loading, particle surface area and aggregate structure, silica or carbon-black surface chemistry, macrodispersion, mixing history, bound-rubber interphase, and silane or polymer-end coupling. Crosslink chemistry, density and spatial distribution, accelerator/sulfur ratio, and cure state change modulus, set, strength, and extensibility; fillers can also alter cure kinetics. Process oil, plasticizer, tackifying resin, and oil extension change compound viscosity, glass-transition/damping behavior, and effective network and filler volume fractions, while antioxidants and antiozonants affect retention of properties. Higher loading rates or lower temperatures normally give a stiffer response and can suppress extensibility, whereas higher temperatures or longer times promote softening, creep, and stress relaxation. Thermal-oxidative or ozone ageing can cause both additional crosslinking and chain scission, often changing hardness and reducing ultimate elongation; fatigue, abrasion, crack geometry, specimen direction, and conditioning therefore matter. Moisture is usually a weaker direct variable for the hydrocarbon matrix, but it can affect silica surfaces, coupling, interfaces, and wet-friction or abrasion tests.

One bounded specification example is SIBUR SBR-1502, a cold-emulsion copolymer described as 23.5% styrene and 76.5% butadiene, with bound styrene specified at 23.5 ± 1.0 wt%. For grades B and C compounded using the ASTM D3185 Method A standard recipe, cured at 145 °C for 35 min, and tested by ASTM D412, the technical sheet sets minimum requirements of 13.0 MPa tensile stress at 300% elongation, 22.5 MPa tensile strength, and 420% elongation at break. These are quality-control limits for that named grade in the referenced standard compound—not measured properties of raw SBR, a typical family range, or finished-product design values; the sheet does not independently restate specimen geometry, conditioning, or test speed.
sections.processing:
Styrene–butadiene rubber (SBR) articles are made by compounding the gum with process oil, reinforcing filler, activators, antioxidants, and a cure package, shaping the uncured compound, and vulcanizing it. General rubber operations directly applicable to SBR compounds include internal or Banbury mixing, two-roll milling, extrusion, calendering, cloth coating, fabrication, compression or transfer molding, continuous vulcanization, press cure, and autoclave cure. Mixing order, fill factor, rotor and roll shear, filler moisture and agglomeration, silane distribution, dump temperature, cooling before curatives, sheet gauge, scorch safety, residence time, mold pressure, and a formulation-specific rheometer cure time are important. Curative chemistry and network formation belong in Synthesis; mixing, article shaping, and the cure equipment and schedule belong here.

The UK Health and Safety Executive's rubber-process flow maps rubber, oil, carbon black, bulk filler, and rubber chemicals through internal mixing and/or two-roll milling to extrusion, coating, calendering, fabrication, molding presses, continuous vulcanization, or autoclaving. A distinct bounded experiment by Staropoli and co-workers used an 80 phr SBR/20 phr polybutadiene compound: the rubbers were blended in an 85 cm³ internal mixer at 80 °C and 40 rpm, oil, activators, antioxidant, silane, and 80 phr silica were mixed for 10 min, and the compound received six roll-mill passes at 50 °C with a 5 mm gap before one hour of cooling. Sulfur and accelerators were then mixed at 60 °C and 40 rpm for 2 min, followed by six more mill passes and hot-press cure at 170 °C and 150 bar for 10 min. Those settings belong to that filled SBR/PBD formulation and laboratory equipment, not to every SBR compound.
sections.structureAndMorphology: SBR chains contain units derived from both styrene and butadiene; their proportions and the arrangement of butadiene units vary with the polymerization recipe. The butadiene-derived portion retains unsaturation that can participate in vulcanization. In one solution process, the ratio of alkoxide modifier to organolithium initiator controls the diene microstructure. The eventual morphology also includes the crosslinked rubber network and any reinforcing filler. For example, an E-SBR comparison changed its accelerator recipe to obtain similar crosslink density in conventional and controlled-polymerization samples, allowing the researchers to compare their dynamic behavior more closely.
sections.properties: SBR is commonly formulated with fillers and curatives, so the rubber gum alone does not determine the final response. In one silica-filled solution-SBR series, increased sulfur at fixed silica content increased hardness and modulus while reducing elongation at break. In a separate carbon-black-filled emulsion-SBR comparison, the researchers observed different abrasion and dynamic response for conventional and narrower-dispersity polymers. Neither experiment establishes a single property value for the whole family. In that carbon-black-filled E-SBR comparison, the controlled-polymerization sample with matched crosslink density had a 29% lower measured loss tangent at 60 °C than the conventional sample. That laboratory indicator is not a direct measurement of vehicle rolling resistance or fuel consumption.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. SBR compounds are used in tires, footwear, sports flooring and other rubber goods. Tire treads require a balance of grip, abrasion and energy dissipation, and producers formulate different polymers, fillers and curing systems to target that balance. In a laboratory comparison of carbon-black-filled emulsion SBR compounds, a narrower-distribution material with a modified cure showed 9% better abrasion resistance and 29% lower loss tangent at 60 °C than the conventional comparator, at similar measured crosslink density. These are properties of the tested compounds, not direct measurements of vehicle fuel consumption or road-tread lifetime.

Purchasing. Zeon lists non-oil-extended and oil-extended emulsion grades, while ENEOS lists separate solution-polymerized grades for carbon-black or silica-containing compounds. A buyer chooses a raw-rubber grade and then specifies the formulation and processing needed for the article.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon’s undated corporate page, checked September 2026, lists 70,000 tons/year capacity for its Singapore solution-SBR plant. This is one supplier’s stated capacity, not measured output, purchases or global SBR demand; the page gives no statistical reference year.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A patent describes chloramine-assisted disruption of sulfur-crosslinked SBR and recovery of degraded organic material. Its illustrated feed was ground end-of-life truck tread and whole-tire rubber, rather than a precisely identified single commercial SBR grade; the products are not a list of substances formed by ambient weathering. In a separate thermal-aging study of three carbon-black-filled industrial SBR compounds, oxidation and additional crosslinking coincided with rising hardness and reduced elongation at break; the researchers also observed evaporation of low-molecular-weight material.

Timescales: In the disclosed experiment, about 50 g of tire-derived powder was exposed to monochloramine solution at 50 °C with repeated solution changes over 30 days, followed by extraction. This is a controlled chemical-treatment period, not a biodegradation time or expected life of an SBR article. In the thermal study, elongation at break fell by about half in less than 90 days at 70 °C and in less than two days at 120 °C for the three tested compounds. These are accelerated, formulation-specific mechanical endpoints; they do not predict environmental mineralization.

Environmental persistence: Breakdown of crosslinks or extraction of a film does not establish mineralization. The cited experiment does not establish a residence time for SBR-containing products in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Grinding tire rubber enables its incorporation into some rubber-containing products, but does not regenerate the original uncured polymer. The patent describes treating tire-derived powder with monochloramine, concentrating the solution and extracting a degraded SBR-containing film with acetone. This is a disclosed chemical-recovery experiment: it does not establish commercial collection, recovery of pure monomers, or restored properties of a finished revulcanized article.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Mixing styrene–butadiene rubber family compounds can generate dust and expose skin to sensitizing additives. HSE recommends enclosed or extracted mixing, maintained seals and dust-suppressed ingredient forms. The formulation’s safety sheets determine chemical hazards; the polymer name alone does not identify the risk of a finished rubber article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Emulsion SBR and solution SBR identify production routes rather than single interchangeable grades. Bound styrene, diene microstructure, molecular-weight distribution and functionalization can differ among products. Filler type and loading, coupling chemistry and cure system add further differences in the finished compound. Comparisons should identify the grade, formulation and test rather than transferring one result to all SBR. The E-SBR loss-tangent comparison uses specific filled compounds and cure adjustments; it cannot establish that a particular solution-SBR tire tread will show the same change.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical emulsion copolymerization forms SBR chains. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another. For the diene component, addition leaves residual unsaturation whose position depends on the addition microstructure.

steps.title: Propagate the radical chain
steps.body: Successive monomer additions convert alkene π bonds into backbone σ bonds while regenerating the radical growth site. The cited initiator, feed composition and reaction medium determine the particular preparation; transfer, grafting and termination control architecture alongside propagation.

steps.title: Form and recover the product
steps.body: Stop at the selected conversion, remove residual monomers, and coagulate, wash, stabilize, and dry the latex polymer.
