sections.overview: Emulsion styrene–butadiene rubber (E-SBR) is a copolymer of styrene and butadiene produced by free-radical polymerization in an aqueous latex. A representative process uses emulsifier, initiator and a molecular-weight modifier before recovery of the rubber. E-SBR is one of the main SBR routes used in tire compounds. The recovered polymer is generally mixed with additives and vulcanized to obtain a finished rubber. Aqueous latex production and recovery identify the synthesis route; the final tire or footwear compound also contains fillers and a curing system.
sections.history: Emulsion SBR began with I. G. Farben’s Buna-S work in the 1930s. The United States wartime program began commercial production in 1942, initially using the hot-polymerization process. Development of cold-polymerized SBR in 1947 improved the practical rubber platform; government plants were subsequently sold or closed as the industry moved into private ownership. Tires remained an important driver of research. Howard Colvin and Michael Senyek’s 1999 Goodyear patent application sought emulsion-SBR tread formulations combining traction, rolling-resistance and wear objectives. These later formulation developments built on the original emulsion platform and should not be mistaken for its invention.
sections.nomenclature: E-SBR is the abbreviation used for emulsion styrene–butadiene rubber. The record is limited to styrene–butadiene copolymers made by the emulsion route; solution-polymerized SBR, block copolymers, and a particular filled or vulcanized compound are not alternate names for this record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Emulsion styrene–butadiene rubber (ESBR) is the aqueous-latex route to a copolymer of styrene and 1,3-butadiene, rather than solution SBR. The aqueous polymerization medium contains water, soap/emulsifier, the two monomers, and a free-radical source; the resulting latex can be coagulated, washed, and dried to recover rubber. A Goodyear patent records a historical GR-S recipe with butadiene, styrene, soap, potassium peroxydisulfate, water, and a mercaptan modifier, followed by brine/acid coagulation. In a separate Bridgestone example, water, electrolyte, soap, reductant, styrene, butadiene, and a peroxide-containing feed were used for redox emulsion polymerization. These feed compositions and reaction controls are source-specific examples, not a universal ESBR specification.
sections.mechanicalProperties: E-SBR is a non-strain-crystallizing diene elastomer whose useful strength and wear resistance normally arise from vulcanization and reinforcing fillers rather than from the raw gum alone. Cured compounds show large, nonlinear, time- and temperature-dependent deformation, with hysteresis, stress softening after the first loading cycles, creep or stress relaxation under sustained load, and a strong change in stiffness and damping as the glass-transition region is approached. Mechanical performance depends on bound-styrene content and butadiene microstructure, molecular mass and dispersity, oil extension, filler type, loading, aggregate structure and dispersion, polymer-filler interaction, sulfur and accelerator system, total cross-link density and sulfide structure, mixing history, cure state, test rate and temperature, and thermal, oxidative, or fatigue aging. Carbon black generally increases small- and large-strain stiffness, tensile and tear strength, and abrasion resistance, but also changes heat build-up and hysteresis; its surface area, aggregate morphology, surface chemistry, and the bound-rubber interphase are consequential. Hwang and co-workers provide one bounded E-SBR compound example. Their laboratory emulsion polymer contained 23.5 wt% styrene, 20.7% vinyl within the butadiene units, weight-average molecular mass about 540,000, and dispersity 4.1. An E60 compound contained, per 100 phr E-SBR, 60 phr N330 carbon black, 3 phr ZnO, 1 phr stearic acid, 1.8 phr sulfur, and 1 phr TBBS and was press-cured at its t90 at 160 °C. ASTM D412 dumbbells (100 x 25 x 2 mm) gave stresses of 26 kgf/cm2 at 100% strain (about 2.55 MPa) and 138 kgf/cm2 at 300% strain (about 13.5 MPa), elongation at break of 470%, and DIN 53516 abrasion loss of 58 mg. The paper does not report tensile crosshead speed or specimen conditioning, and this synthesized, carbon-black-filled cure is not a family-wide E-SBR range. In finished products, geometry, reinforcement, residual strain, notches, multiaxial loading, and temperature history further govern fatigue, tear, and service life.
sections.processing:
E-SBR is converted through rubber compounding, shaping, and vulcanization. The polymer is mixed with reinforcing filler or mineral filler, oil or other process aid, zinc oxide and stearic acid, antidegradants, and a formulation-specific accelerator/sulfur cure package; ingredients whose early addition could shorten scorch safety are commonly staged. The compound can then be calendered, extruded, or molded, assembled with reinforcement where needed, and cured under pressure or by a continuous heating route. Mixing energy and temperature control are important because filler dispersion and polymer–filler interaction affect performance, while excessive thermal history can promote premature crosslinking or, for functionalized variants, gelation.

Kumho's public SBR grade table gives one supplier-bounded reference compound—100 phr SBR, 50 phr HAF carbon black, 3 phr ZnO, 1 phr stearic acid, 1 phr TBBS, and 1.75 phr sulfur—press-vulcanized for 35 min at 145 °C; it is a test formulation, not a production recipe for every E-SBR grade. In a separate GMA-functional E-SBR/silica study, a wet-masterbatch route was used to improve silica dispersion and avoid the high compounding temperature that caused gelation in the functional polymer; final compounds were press-cured at 160 °C for their measured t90. That constraint applies to the reported GMA-E-SBR formulation, not ordinary E-SBR as a whole.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The copolymer contains styrene-derived and butadiene-derived units, with residual diene unsaturation available for curing. Conventional radical E-SBR can have a broad molecular-weight distribution and chain branching. A study using reversible addition–fragmentation chain transfer produced a narrower-distribution E-SBR than the conventional comparator at similar weight-average molecular weight. Once cured and filled, its structure also includes crosslinks and dispersed reinforcing particles. In that study, changing accelerator content brought the controlled-polymerization and conventional rubber compounds to similar measured crosslink densities, making the comparison more specific than a comparison of untreated gums.
sections.properties: E-SBR compounds are evaluated for properties such as abrasion resistance, tensile behavior and dynamic energy loss. Hwang and coauthors compared carbon-black-filled conventional and RAFT E-SBR compounds using controlled cure systems. Their matched-crosslink comparison showed lower measured dynamic loss at 60 °C and better abrasion resistance for the RAFT sample. Those measurements are indicators for the studied compounds, not a direct measurement of vehicle fuel consumption. The matched-density controlled-polymerization compound had a 29% lower loss tangent at 60 °C and 9% better measured abrasion resistance than its conventional counterpart. Those relative numbers apply to the reported carbon-black compounds and cure conditions.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Emulsion SBR is compounded for tire carcasses and treads, footwear, sports flooring and mechanical rubber goods. For a tire-tread compound, abrasion and energy dissipation are among the relevant measures: one laboratory study compared conventional and narrower-distribution E-SBR in carbon-black-filled cured compounds. Its measured loss tangent does not directly measure vehicle fuel consumption. For a controlled comparison, a carbon-black-filled RAFT E-SBR compound with a cure adjusted to give similar crosslink density to a conventional E-SBR compound showed a 29% lower loss tangent at 60 °C and 9% greater abrasion resistance. Those are laboratory compound measurements; they do not establish the fuel consumption or road wear of a finished tire.

Purchasing. Zeon lists Nipol 1502 as a non-oil-extended grade and 1723/1739 as oil-extended grades. These are raw-rubber components, available through supplier inquiry, and the final product additionally requires an application-specific filler and cure recipe.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon reported Japanese E-SBR capacity of 80,000 t/year in May 2015. This historical company capacity is not a current capacity measurement, actual output, purchasing quantity or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Heating sulfur-cured E-SBR compounds can produce additional network links as well as other aging changes. Researchers attributed increased crosslink density in their filled KER 1500 compounds after hot-air aging partly to further reaction of residual curatives. A separate patent describes chloramine-assisted disruption of sulfur-crosslinked tire-derived rubber and recovery of degraded organic material. Its illustrated feed was ground end-of-life truck tread and whole-tire rubber, rather than a precisely identified single commercial E-SBR grade; those treatment products are not a list of substances formed by ordinary weathering.

Timescales: In the hot-air study, filled KER 1500 compounds were aged for seven days at 100 °C. Carbon-black-filled vulcanizates containing the MBT accelerator increased in hardness by 8–11 Shore A points, whereas the silica-filled reference increased by 20 points. The authors observed different crosslink-density changes with filler and cure system, showing that the recipe matters to the response. In the separate patent, about 50 g of tire-derived powder was exposed to monochloramine solution at 50 °C with repeated solution changes over 30 days, followed by extraction. These are controlled aging and chemical-treatment periods, not environmental lifetimes.

Environmental persistence: Hardening and further crosslinking affect the service properties of a rubber without measuring disappearance of its carbon. Conversely, breakdown of crosslinks or extraction of a film does not establish mineralization. Neither study establishes a residence time for E-SBR products in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Grinding tire rubber enables its incorporation into some rubber-containing products, but does not regenerate the original uncured polymer. The patent describes treating tire-derived powder with monochloramine, concentrating the solution and extracting a degraded SBR-containing film with acetone. This is a disclosed chemical-recovery experiment: it does not establish commercial collection, recovery of pure monomers, or restored properties of a finished revulcanized article.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When emulsion styrene–butadiene rubber is compounded, bag opening and ingredient weighing can release dust. HSE recommends dust-reduced or preweighed additives and local extraction. Ingredient-dependent skin allergy and dermatitis require contact control. This guidance concerns the uncured compound and its additives, rather than establishing a hazard classification for the base polymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The latex recipe, polymerization control and polymer composition affect the recovered E-SBR. In the cited comparison, the researchers adjusted the cure system to make crosslink density and structure more comparable; other formulations need not show the same difference. Carbon black loading and dispersion, crosslink structure and test conditions also influence measured performance. The results do not establish that every RAFT E-SBR outperforms every conventional grade. In particular, changing the accelerator was necessary to obtain the closely matched crosslink structures; the reported dynamic and abrasion advantages cannot be attributed to every formulation produced by the same polymerization route.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical emulsion copolymerization forms ESBR latex. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another. For the diene component, addition leaves residual unsaturation whose position depends on the addition microstructure.

steps.title: Propagate the radical chain
steps.body: Successive monomer additions convert alkene π bonds into backbone σ bonds while regenerating the radical growth site. The cited initiator, feed composition and reaction medium determine the particular preparation; transfer, grafting and termination control architecture alongside propagation.

steps.title: Form and recover the product

sections.overview: Solution styrene–butadiene rubber (S-SBR) is a styrene–butadiene elastomer made by polymerization in an organic solvent. A documented route uses an organolithium initiator with an alkoxide modifier to influence copolymer structure. Solution polymerization can provide control over diene microstructure and chain-end functionalization. The resulting polymer is commonly compounded with fillers and curatives for rubber applications such as tires. Solution grades can be tailored for particular filler systems; ENEOS, for example, lists different grades for carbon-black and silica/carbon formulations.
sections.history: Solution SBR developed as a distinct way to control styrene–butadiene rubber architecture through organometallic polymerization. Ralph Farrar’s Phillips Petroleum patent, filed in 1977 and issued in 1979, documents coupling-agent addition during organolithium polymerization, including styrene–butadiene examples. It targeted processable rubbers for tires, hose, belting and related goods and treated solution polymerization as an established technology. Zeon began solution-SBR production at Tokuyama in 1986 and later opened production in Singapore in 2014. These milestones show continued process development and geographic expansion; they do not establish the first synthesis of the entire solution-SBR class.
sections.nomenclature: S-SBR abbreviates solution styrene–butadiene rubber. It is a process-defined SBR subfamily and is distinct from emulsion SBR; it does not name every styrene–butadiene rubber material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Solution styrene–butadiene rubber (S-SBR) is made by copolymerizing styrene and 1,3-butadiene in a dry hydrocarbon solvent, usually by anionic polymerization with an organolithium initiator such as n- or sec-butyllithium. Water, oxygen, and other protic impurities terminate the living chains and are therefore excluded. Because styrene and butadiene have different propagation behavior, a polar randomizer or an alkali-metal alkoxide can promote statistical styrene placement and also alter the fraction of 1,2- versus 1,4-butadiene units. One cited patent combines organolithium with an alkali-metal alkoxide in an alkane solvent to prepare random rubber at controlled styrene content. A distinct patent uses n-butyllithium, tetrahydrofuran or potassium tert-amyloxide as randomizer, and silicon tetrachloride or tetraethyl orthosilicate as a coupling agent. Monomer feed profile, randomizer level, temperature, initiator concentration, and hydrogen-free chain transfer or termination determine composition, vinyl content, molar mass, and sequence distribution. Living ends may be coupled into branched architectures or reacted with functional end-group modifiers before antioxidant addition, solvent removal, and drying. Sulfur crosslinking with an accelerator and activator package subsequently creates the elastomer network; article cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Solution styrene–butadiene rubber is an amorphous random diene copolymer whose useful mechanical response normally refers to a compounded and vulcanized network, not the uncured polymer gum. Above its formulation-dependent glass transition, a cured S-SBR compound can undergo large, substantially recoverable tensile deformation with pronounced rate-, temperature-, and strain-amplitude-dependent hysteresis. Unfilled S-SBR does not provide the strain-crystallization reinforcement of natural rubber, so tensile strength, tear, abrasion, fatigue, hardness, and modulus are commonly governed by sulfur crosslinks and by carbon-black or silica reinforcement. Tire-tread formulations deliberately balance wet traction, rolling-loss hysteresis, heat buildup, wear, and crack resistance rather than maximizing one static endpoint.

Styrene fraction and sequence, 1,2-vinyl versus cis/trans 1,4-butadiene microstructure, molar mass and distribution, branching and chain-end or backbone functionalization set glass transition, chain mobility, and filler affinity. Oil extension and plasticizer, S-SBR/BR or other rubber blending, silica or carbon-black loading, surface area and dispersion, silane type and dosage, mixing temperature and silanization, sulfur/accelerator chemistry, crosslink density and sulfur rank, cure time and temperature, antidegradants, moisture on silica, oxidative aging, test temperature, loading rate and strain history all change the observed response. Reinforcing filler can raise modulus and wear resistance, while too much filler networking or crosslinking can reduce extension and strength; polymer–silica coupling and functionalization can reduce filler–filler hysteresis while improving load transfer.

A bounded tread-compound example used oil-extended Trinseo SLR4630 S-SBR (25 wt% styrene, 63% vinyl within the butadiene fraction, and 37.5 phr oil), 60 phr Ultrasil 7000GR silica, 4.8 phr TESPT silane, and 0.9 phr sulfur with the reported activator/accelerator package. The silica–silane mix was held for 3 minutes at 145 °C, the sheet was press-vulcanized at 160 °C for 1.2 times its measured t90, and ASTM D412 tension was run at 500 mm/min. That formulation gave Shore A 57, stress at 100% and 300% elongation of 1.7 and 7.3 MPa, tensile strength 14.6 MPa, and elongation at break 460%. Raising sulfur alone to 1.5 phr in the same 60-phr-silica system raised Shore A to 61 and M300 to 10.1 MPa but reduced tensile strength to 13.5 MPa and break elongation to 370%. These are compound-specific results, not properties of neat S-SBR, other microstructures, carbon-black compounds, blends, or commercial tire treads.
sections.processing: Solution-SBR (SSBR) is converted as a compounded elastomer: plasticize the rubber, incorporate filler and coupling/activating chemicals under controlled shear and temperature, sheet the intermediate, add sulfur and accelerators in a cooler finishing stage, and then press-mold or otherwise shape and vulcanize the compound. In an open silica-filled S-SBR tire-tread study, the rubber was premixed for 30 s at 15 rpm; silica, silane, zinc oxide, and stearic acid were added during the first stage, silanization was held for 3 min at 145 °C, and the batch was dumped at 145 °C. After sheeting, sulfur and accelerators were added in stage 2 and the compound was dumped below 100 °C; 60/80 phr silica and 0.9–1.5 phr sulfur formulations had 160 °C rheometer t90 values of 14.7–18.2 min, and hydraulic-press vulcanizates used 160 °C for 1.2×t90. An independent silica-filled SSBR/BR study used a 70 rpm initial rotor speed and 160 °C cure testing for 30 min, with tensile specimens cured for 30 min. These are filler-, sulfur-package-, and machine-specific examples; keeping curatives out of the hot silanization stage limits scorch risk, and SSBR manufacture in solution is outside this Processing section.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The polymer contains styrene-derived units and butadiene-derived units, whose distribution and 1,2 versus 1,4 addition content depend on synthesis conditions. In the cited organolithium process, the modifier-to-initiator ratio is used to adjust microstructure and glass transition. Functionalized chain ends offer another way to alter polymer interaction with filler. After sulfur curing of a silica-filled compound, the material contains both rubber crosslinks and silica–rubber interactions. Filler interaction is not the same as sulfur crosslinking: both influence the response of the cured compound, and each depends on the mixing and formulation.
sections.properties: Both molecular design and compound formulation influence the properties of S-SBR vulcanizates. In an oil-extended SLR4630 series with silica and a sulfide–silane coupling agent, raising sulfur at fixed silica loading increased hardness and tensile modulus. Elongation at break and tensile strength decreased in that same comparison. The study also related the trends to changes in chemical crosslink density and filler–rubber interactions. Thus, increasing sulfur in this specific series raised the compound’s stiffness while reducing the stretch it could sustain before failure; changing cure conditions is a way to alter that balance rather than a universal performance improvement.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Solution SBR grades are used in tire compounds designed around grip and rolling-resistance targets. ENEOS lists HPR341 for silica or carbon formulations with low glass-transition temperature and good rolling resistance, while HPR355H is presented as balancing rolling resistance with strength. Their polymer structure and the chosen filler and cure system jointly determine the compound response. A supplier description or laboratory vulcanizate is not a direct measurement of a complete tire. A study of silica-filled solution-SBR compounds illustrates how cure formulation affects the energy-loss measure: at the same silica loading, raising sulfur from 0.9 to 1.5 parts per hundred rubber lowered the 60 °C loss tangent from 0.112 to 0.101 in the tested 60-phr silica series. This is a dynamic test of specific compounds, not a direct measurement of vehicle fuel consumption.

Purchasing. ENEOS lists SL grades intended for carbon-black compounds and HPR grades intended for silica or carbon-black formulations. Its tabulated grades differ in vinyl and bound-styrene content, and technical and supply inquiries go through the producer.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon’s undated corporate page, checked September 2026, lists 70,000 tons/year capacity for its Singapore S-SBR plant. The number is one supplier’s stated capacity, not measured output, purchases or global demand; the page supplies no statistical reference year.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In a laboratory study, formulated solution-SBR compounds lost tensile strength and elongation after thermal-oxidative aging. Researchers compared a reference formulation with formulations containing chemically modified graphene oxide; the measured response reflects the complete compounds, not just the base polymer. The study does not identify a complete inventory of small molecules released by aging. Separately, a patent describes chloramine-assisted disruption of tire-rubber crosslinks; its mixed tire feed is not an identified single S-SBR grade or an inventory of ambient weathering products.

Timescales: After 96 hours of thermal-oxygen aging at 90 °C, tensile strength of the tested reference compound fell from 16.6 ± 0.3 to 6.3 ± 0.3 MPa, while elongation at break fell from 301 ± 19% to 194 ± 26%. A formulation with four parts modified graphene oxide per hundred parts rubber had a higher post-aging tensile strength, but started with a higher unaged strength as well. These comparisons are specific to the tested recipes and tensile method, not a universal service life. The separate patent treated tire-derived powder with monochloramine at 50 °C with repeated solution changes over 30 days.

Environmental persistence: Reduced strength, crosslink cleavage or extraction of a film does not establish conversion of the polymer to carbon dioxide or biomass. Neither accelerated aging nor the tire treatment establishes a residence or mineralization time for an S-SBR article in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Grinding tire rubber enables its incorporation into some rubber-containing products, but does not regenerate the original uncured polymer. The patent describes treating tire-derived powder with monochloramine, concentrating the solution and extracting a degraded SBR-containing film with acetone. This is a disclosed chemical-recovery experiment: it does not establish commercial collection, recovery of pure monomers, or restored properties of a finished revulcanized article. The mixed-tire example is family-level context; it does not establish the outcome for a particular solution-SBR formulation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When solution styrene–butadiene rubber is compounded, bag opening and ingredient weighing can release dust. HSE recommends dust-reduced or preweighed additives and local extraction. Ingredient-dependent skin allergy and dermatitis require contact control. This guidance concerns the uncured compound and its additives, rather than establishing a hazard classification for the base polymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Solution SBR grades can differ in bound styrene, vinyl content, molecular structure and functional groups. Silica loading, silane, sulfur and accelerator amounts then alter the cured compound. The cited sulfur study used a named oil-extended polymer and defined recipes and tests. Its measured trends should be interpreted in that context rather than as universal S-SBR values. The supplier lists distinct vinyl and bound-styrene percentages even within its S-SBR portfolio, so neither one formula nor the measured response of SLR4630 describes every grade.

sections.overview: Carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber (XSBR) is a styrene–butadiene copolymer that also contains carboxyl functionality. One documented latex route introduces an acid comonomer during aqueous emulsion polymerization. The functional groups distinguish XSBR from an unmodified styrene–butadiene copolymer. XSBR latex and compounds have been studied for uses including textile and carpet backing. The acid-containing units offer a handle for formulation with fillers or other phases in waterborne products. Once dried, the response of the film reflects both the polymer and the other ingredients.
sections.history: Carboxylated SBR belongs to the development of functional latex binders, where small amounts of acid functionality broadened the usefulness of styrene–butadiene copolymers. Paul Steinwand’s Union Oil patent, filed in 1989 and issued in 1991, describes carboxylated copolymer binders intended to improve wet strength in nonwoven fabrics. The application context included wipes, disposable medical products, carpet backings and durable textile goods. The patent’s subsequent assignment history runs through Rohm and Haas and Mallard Creek Polymers. This is a documented formulation and ownership lineage within an already developed latex field, rather than evidence that carboxylated SBR was first invented in 1991.
sections.nomenclature: XSBR denotes carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber. The name describes a functionalized styrene–butadiene copolymer family rather than one fixed styrene, butadiene, or carboxyl-group composition; it does not make ordinary SBR an alias for this record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber is made by aqueous free-radical emulsion copolymerization of styrene and butadiene with an ethylenically unsaturated carboxylic-acid comonomer. The acid component can be selected from acrylic, methacrylic, itaconic, maleic, or fumaric acid; its identity, proportion, and any crosslinking comonomer define the particular latex rather than a single universal composition. One patent example starts an itaconic-acid, surfactant, and seed-latex aqueous charge with persulfate, then feeds styrene and butadiene; tertiary-dodecyl mercaptan is included during the feed as a chain-transfer control. A separate staged patent route uses batch and continuous emulsion-polymerization charges of styrene, butadiene, acrylic and itaconic acids, anionic emulsifier, and persulfate/redox initiation; it specifically uses the chain-transfer agent and the late acid-monomer addition to control gel content. These are route-specific latex examples, not a general formulation for every carboxylated SBR.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Mechanical response in the accessible evidence is formulation- and material-state-dependent: an unvulcanized latex film, a filled film, and a sulfur-cured tire compound are not interchangeable XSBR states. Visakh and co-workers used an XSBR latex containing 59% styrene (47% dry-rubber content) as an unvulcanized control and as the matrix for cast films with 4.1–9.0 wt% crab-chitin whiskers. In nanoindentation creep at 23 °C (Berkovich tip, 0.05 mN maximum load, 200 s hold; 20 tests per sample), their fitted Burgers-model constants for the unannealed neat XSBR control were K1 = 48.664 N/m and K2 = 80.901 N/m. Those surface-creep fit parameters are not a bulk Young’s modulus; the authors also found that annealing neat XSBR at 100 °C for 90 min did not show the increased indentation resistance observed for the higher-chitin films. In a separate sulfur-cured tire-compound example, 50 phr of a named carboxylated SBR was combined with 50 phr E-SBR, 127 phr N330 carbon black, 95 phr paraffinic oil, zinc oxide, sulfur, and accelerator. The reported compound had tensile strength 8.7 MPa, elongation at break 673%, 300% ring modulus 3.32 MPa, and Shore A hardness 61 at 23 °C; stress–strain data were obtained on a Zwick 1445 tester. This is a filled, oil-extended, sulfur-cured blend—not a neat-XSBR property—and the document does not give tensile specimen geometry, test speed, or statistical basis. These bounded examples should therefore not be combined into family-wide ranges.
sections.processing: Carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber (XSBR) can be compounded and vulcanized as solid rubber, or used as a waterborne latex for sprayed and dried coatings. Formulation, filler loading, and final cure are article-specific. In a laboratory ENR/XSBR experiment, latex blending preceded coagulation; recovered rubber was mixed with ZnO, stearic acid, CBS, and sulfur, sheeted on a cold two-roll mill, and compression molded at 130 °C for its measured t90. Those conditions apply to that ENR-30/XSBR blend, not all XSBR compounds. A separate carpet-backing patent demonstrates wax-modified XSBR latex sprayed onto wet, skinned foam then dried at 130 °C for 12 min; its 10% solids coating and 60 g/m² dry application rate are example-specific, and heavier coatings can crack on bending and lengthen drying.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The polymer contains styrene- and butadiene-derived units together with carboxyl-containing units. The cited preparation introduces itaconic acid into an emulsion polymerization of styrene and butadiene. Latex can be formed into films or combined with other components such as particulate filler. The resulting material structure depends on latex composition, drying and any subsequent treatment or cure. In the cited itaconic-acid route the polymer is made as a dispersion in water rather than a homogeneous dry film. Drying brings the dispersed material together, and subsequent treatment can change its response.
sections.properties: XSBR films can exhibit time-dependent deformation under load. In one study, researchers measured nanoindentation creep and dynamic response of XSBR with and without small additions of chitin. Chitin also provided some barrier effect against toluene absorption in that specific system. The response depended on both filler and whether the samples had been annealed. In that study, annealing increased resistance to nanoindentation for two higher-chitin samples, but not for the unfilled XSBR or lowest-chitin sample. This is a local indentation observation on the tested films, not a general prediction for every XSBR compound.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Carboxylated SBR is supplied within industrial latex portfolios serving paper coatings, carpet backing, foam and fiber-to-rubber adhesives. In a carpet backing the latex is compounded with filler, applied to the textile and dried to bind the layers. A patent demonstrates a specially designed acid-comonomer formulation intended to maintain wet strength while allowing fiber separation under controlled treatment; this is not a property of every commercial latex.

Purchasing. ENEOS identifies SBL0696, 0533 and several other grades specifically as carboxy-modified aqueous emulsions. Buyers select solids content and grade through supplier inquiry.

Scale and evidence limits. Listed carboxy-modified latex examples contain approximately 48–54% total solids. This characterizes purchased dispersion, not annual tonnage; no separate XSBR consumption total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A specially formulated XSBR carpet adhesive can detach from nylon under shear in an alkaline surfactant solution while the adhesive remains insoluble. This separates an adhesive-containing fraction rather than demonstrating molecular depolymerization. In a separate study of XSBR/chitin films, thermogravimetry under nitrogen showed the main polymer weight-loss peak remained approximately unchanged with the tested filler additions; it does not identify all degradation products.

Timescales: In the carpet patent, 1 cm² pieces were blended in a 1% surfactant solution at pH 9.5–10 for 2–10 minutes, typically two. This engineered separation endpoint is not an environmental mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: The XSBR/chitin thermal scan used nitrogen and a temperature ramp from 30 to 900 °C; it measures mass loss under heating rather than microbial conversion. Neither this test nor the controlled carpet separation establishes complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A patent proposes shredding carpet, wet granulation and hydrocyclone separation to reclaim face fibers from specially formulated XSBR backing. In its laboratory comparison, the six-percent methacrylic-acid formulation separated completely from nylon fibers under the specified shear and alkaline surfactant conditions; the conventional XSB comparator did not. The adhesive itself remained insoluble.

This is an example of fiber recovery from a designed composite, not regeneration of XSBR monomers or evidence that all carboxylated latex carpets behave identically.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Mixing carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber compounds can generate dust and expose skin to sensitizing additives. HSE recommends enclosed or extracted mixing, maintained seals and dust-suppressed ingredient forms. The formulation’s safety sheets determine chemical hazards; the polymer name alone does not identify the risk of a finished rubber article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Carboxyl content, monomer ratio and latex preparation vary between XSBR materials. The chitin experiment used a particular unvulcanized matrix and studied filler contents up to 9 weight percent. Its nanoindentation results are local measurements and should not be equated directly with a bulk tensile modulus. Drying, heat treatment, filler and test conditions must accompany comparisons across formulations. The filler and heat-treatment dependence means the direction of change cannot be assigned to carboxylation alone. For a carpet adhesive, adhesion also depends on the fiber and backing construction.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical terpolymerization introduces carboxyl sites into SBR latex. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another. For the diene component, addition leaves residual unsaturation whose position depends on the addition microstructure.

sections.overview: Nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) is an elastomeric copolymer of acrylonitrile and butadiene. It is commonly produced by emulsion copolymerization. The acrylonitrile content is an important grade variable, particularly for contact with oils and fuels. NBR is used in products such as seals, gaskets and fuel hoses. The polar nitrile-containing units help distinguish NBR from nonpolar diene rubbers in oil-contact applications. The polymer is compounded with a cure system and other ingredients before it becomes a functional seal or hose.
sections.history: Nitrile rubber emerged from the interwar search for useful synthetic elastomers. Erich Konrad and Eduard Tschunkur’s I. G. Farben patent, with 1930 German priority and a United States grant in 1934, describes rubberlike copolymers made from butadiene and polymerizable nitriles. It provides a firm early milestone for the family. Zeon began Japan’s first domestic nitrile-rubber production in 1959 and subsequently expanded its rubber and feedstock technology. Industrial development produced a range of specialty grades: Arlanxeo’s Krynac products, for example, serve adhesives, sealants and plastics modification. Later hydrogenated and carboxylated derivatives developed their own application histories rather than simply inheriting the original polymer’s invention date.
sections.nomenclature: NBR abbreviates nitrile butadiene rubber. The name identifies the acrylonitrile–butadiene rubber family and should not be treated as a synonym for butadiene rubber without nitrile comonomer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) is the synthetic copolymer of acrylonitrile and 1,3-butadiene. Commercially relevant routes use aqueous free-radical emulsion polymerization with emulsifier, initiator, and often a molecular-weight regulator, followed by coagulation and recovery of the latex polymer. Acrylonitrile feed and staged butadiene addition influence bound acrylonitrile content and the copolymer’s composition; they are not universal values for all NBR grades. One continuous patent describes incremental butadiene feeds during free-radical emulsion polymerization, while another identifies the binary aqueous-emulsion route and a carboxylated-NBR terpolymer variant. Hydrogenation of NBR produces HNBR, a different material, and finished-article vulcanization is excluded from this synthesis account.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) is a cured acrylonitrile--butadiene elastomer, so tensile, modulus, tear, and compression response are compound rather than raw-polymer constants.  Acrylonitrile content and polymer Mooney viscosity, carbon-black or mineral reinforcement, plasticizer, sulfur/peroxide cure system, cure time and temperature, specimen geometry, temperature, strain rate, and ageing environment can all change a reported result.  Two 34%-acrylonitrile supplier compounds demonstrate the required limits.  Astlett NBR B6240 (34% bound acrylonitrile, ML1+4 42 at 100 °C) is tested in ASTM D3187 compound with 40 phr HAF black, 3 phr zinc oxide, 0.7 phr TBBS, and 1.5 phr sulfur; after 35 min at 145 °C, it reports ASTM D412 tensile strength 285 kgf/cm², elongation 600%, and 300% modulus 120 kgf/cm².  Separately, Kumho KNB 35L has 34 ± 2% bound acrylonitrile and a stated ASTM D3187/D412 test compound cured at 150 °C for 40 min in a press with carbon-black IRB #7; it lists tensile strength at least 220 kgf/cm², elongation at least 420%, and 300% modulus 150 ± 30 kgf/cm².  These are deliberately non-interchangeable compound-and-cure examples, not an NBR family range.
sections.processing: Nitrile butadiene rubber is normally converted as a compounded elastomer: the gum is mixed with reinforcing filler, zinc oxide, stearic acid, sulfur, and an accelerator, then shaped by extrusion, calendering, or molding and vulcanized. The Astlett B6240 sheet identifies that grade as suitable for extrusion and calendering and gives an ASTM D3187 compound of 100 parts B6240 NBR, 40 parts HAF carbon black, 3 parts zinc oxide, 1 part stearic acid, 0.7 part TBBS, and 1.5 parts sulfur; its stated cure example is 35 min at 145 °C. A separate Kumho KNB 35L sheet gives a different bound-acrylonitrile grade and an IRB #7 carbon-black compound press-cured at 150 °C for 40 min. The formulations and cure cycles are named-grade test recipes, so they should not be generalized across NBR grades, acrylonitrile levels, filler systems, or article thicknesses.
sections.structureAndMorphology: NBR chains contain both nitrile-bearing acrylonitrile units and butadiene-derived units. The copolymer retains diene unsaturation, which permits sulfur vulcanization in a compounded rubber. A documented continuous emulsion route controls bound acrylonitrile by regulating the butadiene feed. The cured material also contains crosslinks and often reinforcing filler, so it differs from the raw polymer. The proportion of nitrile-bearing units is set during copolymerization, whereas the density and type of network links depend on the later cure. Fillers and other ingredients add another level of structure to a finished compound.
sections.properties: NBR is selected for resistance to many nonpolar oils and fuels. In one pump-stator comparison, vulcanized compounds with 18%, 26% and 41% acrylonitrile were immersed in a specific crude oil for 168 hours at 120 °C. Their measured volume changes were 29.13%, 7.14% and approximately zero, respectively: the higher-acrylonitrile compounds resisted swelling more in this test. Carbon-black content was adjusted to achieve similar hardness, so this is a comparison of compounds rather than an isolated measurement of acrylonitrile content alone. A commercial B6240 grade contains 34% bound acrylonitrile; its supplier reports 600% elongation for a specified carbon-black-filled sulfur-cured test compound. That tensile result describes the formulation and cure, not the unfilled raw polymer.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. NBR serves oil-contact hoses, seals, membranes, belts and roll covers in vehicles and industrial machinery; selected grades also serve adhesives and footwear. For example, Astlett recommends B6240 for O-rings and molded oilfield or automotive parts. Another study tested NBR compounds for screw-pump stators, where crude-oil swelling changes the fit between the rubber stator and metal rotor. After 168 hours at 120 °C, the 18%-acrylonitrile compound increased in volume by 29.13% while a 41% compound changed little; carbon-black loading also differed to match hardness. Selection therefore depends on the particular compound, fluid and service conditions rather than the raw polymer name alone.

Purchasing. Suppliers offer grade-specific raw rubber. Zeon lists bale, liquid and powder forms; these are distinct products for compounding rather than interchangeable forms of one specification.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon reported Japanese NBR capacity of 60,000 t/year in May 2015. This historical company capacity is neither current capacity nor measured production, purchases or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: NBR O-ring pyrolysis produces butadiene and acrylonitrile, with additional nitriles such as benzonitrile and aromatic fragments. Separately, an 80 °C ageing study finds increased crosslinking; its ketone/aldehyde mechanism is supported by molecular simulations rather than direct product collection.

Timescales: The O-ring analysis flash-pyrolyzed 100–200 µg portions at 700 °C in helium. The ageing experiment used 10 mm cylinders compressed 30%, sampled over 19–228 h at 80 °C. Neither is a natural mineralization test.

Environmental persistence: These heat-driven endpoints do not establish disappearance in soil, freshwater or seawater. The ageing formulation was proprietary, further limiting transfer to other NBR grades. Oxidation and further network formation can change sealing behavior long before the entire article disappears.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A study of NBR production scrap used calendering to mechanically devulcanize the cured material and then compression-molded compounds with recycled contents of 20%, 80% and 100%. The 20% compound had mechanical properties comparable to the virgin reference in that study. At 100% recycled content, stress and strain at break were approximately 25% and 50% lower, respectively, illustrating a material-dependent tradeoff as replacement increased.

The work used separated industrial scrap from a specific rubber compound and did not add fresh crosslinking agent in the tested reprocessing route. It does not establish the same properties for mixed NBR waste, different cure packages or every seal specification.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Mixing nitrile butadiene rubber compounds can generate dust and expose skin to sensitizing additives. HSE recommends enclosed or extracted mixing, maintained seals and dust-suppressed ingredient forms. The formulation’s safety sheets determine chemical hazards; the polymer name alone does not identify the risk of a finished rubber article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Acrylonitrile content, polymerization conditions and molecular characteristics distinguish NBR grades. Fluid compatibility depends on the actual fluid and exposure conditions as well as compound composition. The B6240 supplier data use a named grade, a specified recipe and a 145 °C cure. Its reported values are not a single range applicable to all nitrile rubbers. A fluid exposure can cause swelling or extraction of ingredients, and the result depends on the particular liquid and compound. The raw polymer grade does not specify the filler, cure or construction of a seal.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical emulsion copolymerization produces nitrile rubber. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another. For the diene component, addition leaves residual unsaturation whose position depends on the addition microstructure.

sections.overview: Hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber (HNBR) is obtained by selectively hydrogenating nitrile–butadiene rubber. This reaction reduces carbon–carbon double bonds in the butadiene-derived portions while retaining nitrile groups. Different degrees of hydrogenation and acrylonitrile content produce distinct grades. HNBR compounds are used in demanding sealing and oil-contact applications. The reduced unsaturation helps improve aging resistance compared with its NBR starting material, but the nitrile units remain important to oil-contact behavior. The commercial polymer is compounded and cured for the specific seal, hose or belt.
sections.history: Hydrogenated nitrile rubber developed as a heat- and oil-resistant extension of nitrile-rubber technology. A clear commercialization milestone is Zeon’s introduction of Zetpol in 1984. Its account identifies automotive timing belts as an important application, alongside other demanding mechanical rubber goods. The advance lay in producing a durable specialty elastomer from an existing nitrile-polymer platform; the much earlier invention of NBR is therefore not the invention date of HNBR. Zeon’s continued emphasis on controlled specialty-elastomer manufacture and automotive performance shows how hydrogenation created a commercially distinct branch of the nitrile family.
sections.nomenclature: HNBR is not a synonym for unmodified nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR): it specifically denotes hydrogenated NBR. Residual unsaturation, acrylonitrile content, and a subsequent vulcanized network are separate grade or formulation descriptors that should accompany any particular HNBR material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber (HNBR) is a chemically modified nitrile-butadiene rubber, made by selectively hydrogenating the residual carbon–carbon unsaturation in NBR rather than by a new acrylonitrile/butadiene copolymerization. NBR itself is the acrylonitrile–butadiene copolymer precursor. Documented solution-hydrogenation routes contact dissolved NBR with hydrogen and noble-metal catalysts, including rhodium, ruthenium, or palladium systems; catalyst and ligand choice, solvent, hydrogen pressure, and conversion determine the degree and selectivity of hydrogenation. A heterogeneous palladium/rhodium catalyst patent and an open-access report on metathesis/hydrogenation provide complementary examples. Hydrogenation of nitrile groups is a different, more extensive modification and should not be assumed for conventional HNBR. Vulcanization of the finished rubber is a separate formulation step and is not included here.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber (HNBR) is used as a cured elastomer; its tensile and recovery response is governed by acrylonitrile content, residual unsaturation and crosslink density/cure, reinforcement and plasticizer package, temperature, and ageing history.  An open study of sulfur-vulcanized HNBRs containing 34 or 36 wt% acrylonitrile and varied crosslink density reports an amorphous room-temperature state without strain-induced crystallization; stretching instead orients amorphous segments, with the orientation influencing tensile strength, strain hardening, toughness, and recovery.  A bounded compound example is M-Seals HNBR-F/101, a black nominal 75-Shore-A material: the supplier's standard-test-specimen record gives 71 Shore A hardness, 22.70 MPa tensile strength and 346% ultimate elongation by ASTM D412/C, plus 21% compression set after 22 h at 150 °C by ASTM D395/B.  The data sheet expressly cautions that standard specimen results are not directly comparable with finished parts.
sections.processing:
Hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber (HNBR) is converted as a compounded elastomer: the polymer is masticated and mixed with carbon black or other fillers, plasticizer/process aids, antioxidants, metal oxide, coagent, and a sulfur, sulfur-donor, or peroxide cure package. Internal mixers and two-roll mills are used; staged addition of curatives and strong cooling are important because HNBR compounds build heat and premature scorch would reduce processing safety. Shaped compounds can be extruded, injection-, transfer-, or compression-molded, then vulcanized and, where specified, post-cured. Cure choice and temperature are formulation- and peroxide-specific; oxygen exposure can cause surface reversion in pressureless peroxide cures.

A supplier guide describes a common two-pass internal-mixer sequence: masterbatch discharge near 140 °C, then addition of cure chemicals and second discharge near 100–110 °C, followed by cooled milling. In an independent HNBR-4307 hose-compound study, rubber was thin-pass plasticized on a two-roll mill, ingredients were added in stages, the compound was press-vulcanized at 170 °C for its measured T90, and samples were secondarily cured at 165 °C for 4 h. Those conditions apply to that carbon-black/plasticizer/DCP/TAIC formulation and recycled-powder variants, not to every HNBR grade. Selective hydrogenation of NBR is upstream Synthesis; compounding, shaping, and crosslinking the article belong here.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The starting NBR copolymer contains nitrile-bearing units and unsaturated butadiene-derived units. Catalytic hydrogenation converts much of the residual carbon–carbon unsaturation into saturated bonds. The amount left depends on the selected hydrogenation process and grade. Compounded HNBR can subsequently be crosslinked and filled to form an elastomeric network. Hydrogenation changes the diene-derived portions without removing the nitrile groups. Residual unsaturation and the crosslinking system distinguish one cured compound from another.
sections.properties: HNBR is used where oil exposure and aging resistance are important. In a study of peroxide-cured HNBR composites, higher-acrylonitrile samples showed a smaller mass change after exposure to hot transformer oil. Filler and plasticizer levels also affected modulus, elongation and swelling behavior in those formulations. The same study observed different compression-set responses in hot air, cold air and hot oil. In Han and colleagues’ filled formulations, adding plasticizer increased elongation at break while reducing stress at a given extension; adding more carbon black had the opposite tendency for extension and stiffness. These are comparisons within the reported peroxide-cured compounds.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. HNBR serves automotive timing belts, seals, hoses and axle boots, oilfield packers and drilling seals, and industrial paper-machine rolls. In a seal or hose, the selected compound must maintain sealing and mechanical performance in its actual fluid and temperature. The supplied raw HNBR is not a finished seal, and different grades can have different nitrile and hydrogenation levels.

Purchasing. Zeon supplies Zetpol grades distinguished by acrylonitrile content, hydrogenation and viscosity, plus named latex variants. For example, the supplier lists 36% acrylonitrile and 96% hydrogenation for 2010, while 2000 has the same listed acrylonitrile but more than 99.5% hydrogenation. A buyer selects the grade and asks for application guidance; the raw polymer still requires an appropriate compound and cure.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon reported Japanese HNBR capacity of 4,500 t/year in May 2015. This historical company capacity is neither current capacity nor measured production, purchases or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Thermo-oxidative ageing of peroxide-cured HNBR involves both chain scission and additional crosslinking; the balance changes with ageing. Broken load-bearing chains and network changes explain loss of elastic recovery. The experiment does not identify a complete small-molecule product inventory.

Timescales: A commercial peroxide-cured HNBR containing 36 wt% acrylonitrile was studied as O-ring segments and 2 mm sheets in circulating air at 125 °C for 2 hours to 31 days. Compression relaxation and compression set measured network damage, not mass disappearance or mineralization.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill. In a separate HNBR-composite series, 72 hours at 125 °C and at 150 °C produced different tensile responses; the higher temperature reduced elongation and tensile strength in the tested samples. Exposure conditions and formulation govern the result.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Used HNBR vulcanizate can be mechanically reduced to powder and incorporated into fresh HNBR compounds. A laboratory study froze and roll-ground the scrap, then modified its surface with 5 wt% trans-polyoctenamer before compounding it into HNBR-4307 hose-lining formulations. The modified powder performed better than unmodified powder at the same loading, although increasing powder content generally reduced tensile and tear properties and increased compression set. This route retains crosslinked particles in a new peroxide-cured rubber matrix; it does not recover HNBR monomer or establish unrestricted replacement of virgin rubber. The study evaluated a particular powder treatment and test compound; contamination and the properties required of the next article limit how much reclaim can be used.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Freshly molded HNBR rubber articles can remain an exposure source while cooling. HSE recommends extraction at cooling racks, avoiding skin contamination, and gloves suitable for chemical and heat exposure. These are process controls for formulated rubber articles; the cure package and other ingredients determine additional chemical hazards.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: HNBR is a family of grades rather than one fixed composition: acrylonitrile content and residual unsaturation both vary. The cited transformer-oil study compared specific fully saturated polymers and peroxide-cured formulations. Its results depend on oil type, exposure temperature and time as well as filler and plasticizer content. A positive result in one fluid or temperature cannot establish compatibility with every service environment. The same experiment showed that filler and plasticizer both matter alongside acrylonitrile content. A ranking in hot transformer oil is not automatically a ranking in a different fluid or at another temperature.

sections.overview: Carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber (XNBR) is an acrylonitrile–butadiene rubber containing carboxyl functionality. It may be prepared with a carboxylic-acid comonomer or by modifying an existing nitrile rubber. The functional groups create additional possibilities for crosslinking and interaction with fillers. XNBR latex is used in the study of thin protective glove materials. These groups allow interactions with metal oxides as well as sulfur curing, so an ionic network and a sulfur-cured network are different formulations. This distinction also affects how a compound may be reprocessed.
sections.history: Carboxylated nitrile rubber developed as a functional extension of the nitrile-latex platform. By 1999, Pascale Francine Jeanne Muller’s Goodyear patent application described it as widely used for gloves, nonwoven fabrics, masking tapes, seals and coating or binding applications. The proposed advance was emulsifier-free latex manufacture, aimed at reducing residual emulsifier in products and wash water. This is a useful dated stage in a longer development history: it demonstrates that XNBR was already established and that research had moved toward product cleanliness and manufacturing improvements. The document does not establish a first invention or launch date for all carboxylated nitrile rubbers.
sections.nomenclature: XNBR identifies carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber and is not interchangeable with unmodified nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR). Acid-comonomer level, latex grade, crosslinker, and any filler define narrower materials; a dipped or vulcanized XNBR article is a formulation-specific network rather than the base copolymer alone.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber (XNBR) is an acrylonitrile–butadiene rubber modified by incorporation of an unsaturated carboxylic-acid comonomer, such as methacrylic or acrylic acid, through free-radical aqueous emulsion terpolymerization. In one publicly described emulsifier-free latex route, 1,3-butadiene, acrylonitrile, and methacrylic acid are initiated with potassium persulfate plus an acid-active co-initiator in an aqueous reactor, giving a seed latex before a delayed feed of butadiene, acrylonitrile, and additional initiator. That patent reports 25–80 °C for the polymerization and, for its preferred embodiment, an initial charge of 20–40 wt% acrylonitrile, 5–9 wt% methacrylic acid, and 51–75 wt% butadiene; these are route-specific composition and operating ranges, not a definition of all XNBR grades. It also notes that differing monomer reactivities can make bound-unit composition depart from the charge. Chain-transfer agent, conversion/solids target, neutralization, and stabilizer choice are therefore manufacturing controls. The separate phase-transfer study provides a second, independently published context for carboxylated-nitrile-rubber preparation rather than evidence for one universal recipe.
sections.mechanicalProperties: XNBR mechanical response is governed by the carboxyl groups’ ability to form ionic as well as covalent networks, so cure system, crosslink density, filler, latex grade, and film history must remain attached to any reported value. In an XNBR-latex glove-material study conditioned at 21 ± 3 °C and 50 ± 5% relative humidity, unfilled films crosslinked with 1.5 phr sulfur had tear resistance of 2.7 ± 0.4 N, whereas films crosslinked with 2.0, 4.0, and 8.0 phr magnesium oxide gave 6.3 ± 1.1, 7.5 ± 0.6, and 9.8 ± 2.1 N, respectively, in the reported EN 388 testing. The same formulations had puncture resistance from 42 to 63 N and 2000 abrasion cycles, emphasizing that a change in ionic/covalent cure balance shifts endpoints differently. Those are thin, conditioned glove-film results, not a tensile or tear range for every XNBR compound. A separate open XNBR study compared ZnO ionic, sulfur covalent, and hybrid networks using ASTM D412 tensile specimens; it found that ionic crosslinks dominate room-temperature stiffness at low covalent-crosslink density while extra covalent crosslinking increases modulus at elevated temperature. Its AFM-derived values describe phase-scale modulus, not a bulk-grade specification. Together, the sources support the qualitative cure–mechanics relationship and bounded examples, while leaving grade-to-grade tensile comparability unresolved.
sections.processing: XNBR is commonly converted from an aqueous latex after compounding into dipped or coagulated films, coatings, binders, and related rubber articles; it is then dried and crosslinked. In one bounded flat-film glove-material procedure, a mold was dipped in either 35 wt% calcium nitrate or 20 wt% calcium chloride in methanol, dried at 30–50 °C, dipped into a sulfur- or magnesium-oxide-formulated XNBR latex, dried at 55–60 °C, and crosslinked at 100–115 °C for 180 min. Those laboratory conditions show why coagulant/dip history, cure system, and formulation cannot be treated as interchangeable family settings. For a different laboratory XNBR formulation, an open study measured cure behavior at 160 °C for 30 min by ASTM D5289 rheometry before preparing tensile specimens; that is a formulation-specific cure-screening condition, not a general production schedule. Upstream latex manufacture imposes separate controls—aqueous-phase solids, initiator/feed sequence, pH adjustment, and stabilization in the documented emulsifier-free route. Article processing should therefore specify the named latex/compound and conversion route; the sources do not establish one universal oven cycle, coagulant recipe, or cure window for XNBR.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The material combines nitrile-bearing and butadiene-derived units with carboxyl groups. Depending on the formulation, metal oxide can form ionic interactions involving the carboxyl groups, while sulfur-based curing produces covalent sulfur linkages. The cited glove study compared films crosslinked with magnesium oxide and with sulfur. It also examined films containing modified bentonite as a dispersed filler. In an ionically crosslinked formulation, zinc ions associate with carboxylate groups to form reversible ionic junctions. Such a network is different from a conventional permanent sulfur-crosslinked compound.
sections.properties: XNBR latex films have been studied for mechanical resistance and resistance to mineral-oil permeation. In one study, sulfur- and magnesium-oxide-crosslinked films showed long breakthrough times for the tested mineral oil. Adding modified bentonite increased tear resistance in the tested formulations, although puncture resistance decreased. These observations depend on the specific film composition and test. In the cited glove-film study, modified bentonite improved tear resistance but reduced puncture resistance in the tested recipes. The trade-off illustrates why a protective film must be qualified for the specific hazard and composition.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. XNBR serves abrasion-resistant linings and belts and modifies epoxy adhesives for aircraft structures, printed circuit boards and electronics. XNBR latex is also investigated for protective gloves, where a thin cured film must balance tear, puncture and fluid-barrier performance. The experimental film results do not certify a commercial glove for any particular fluid.

Purchasing. ARLANXEO offers Krynac X grades; Zeon separately lists Nipol NX775 as carboxylated rubber in bale form. Formulation and grade selection precede a supply inquiry.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A patent proposes preferential cleavage of sulfur crosslinks at reclaimed rubber crumb surfaces while retaining a cured core and much of the backbone. It lists sulfur-cured carboxylated nitrile rubber among possible materials but its reported examples use other rubbers; an XNBR-specific outcome is not established. This proposed route does not describe every ionic or peroxide-cured XNBR formulation, and ambient products remain unresolved.

Timescales: In a separate study, a specifically ionically crosslinked XNBR sheet was cut and re-pressed at 160 °C and 200 bar for one hour per cycle, up to three cycles. This controlled network-reprocessing procedure differs from the patent’s proposed surface devulcanization. Neither provides a transferable environmental mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill. Mechanical reprocessing of a specially designed ionic XNBR network is a separate phenomenon from oxidative or biological degradation.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Utrera-Barrios and colleagues designed a single ionically crosslinked XNBR formulation using 100 parts rubber and 10 parts zinc oxide. They cut cured sheets, hot-pressed them at 160 °C and 200 bar for one hour, and repeated the cycle up to three times. Their molecular analysis found that estimated crosslink density increased from 3.69 to 6.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol/cm³ after the third cycle.

The approach reprocesses this particular ionic formulation into sheets; it is not a general recipe for sulfur-cured glove waste or all XNBR compounds. Existing patents also propose surface devulcanization or use of ground XNBR in PVC, neither of which regenerates pure monomers.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Mixing carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber compounds can generate dust and expose skin to sensitizing additives. HSE recommends enclosed or extracted mixing, maintained seals and dust-suppressed ingredient forms. The formulation’s safety sheets determine chemical hazards; the polymer name alone does not identify the risk of a finished rubber article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Acrylonitrile and carboxyl content, preparation route and formulation vary across XNBR. The cited glove experiments used one specified latex and particular crosslinking agents and filler loadings. The improvement in tear resistance did not mean every measured property improved. Oil permeation and mechanical results should be interpreted for the stated film and exposure conditions. An XNBR/ZnO formulation designed for ionic reprocessing cannot be assumed to represent a sulfur- or peroxide-cured product. Latex-film behavior also cannot be transferred directly to a thick molded seal.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical terpolymerization places acid functionality in nitrile-rubber chains. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another. For the diene component, addition leaves residual unsaturation whose position depends on the addition microstructure.

steps.title: Propagate the radical chain
steps.body: Successive monomer additions convert alkene π bonds into backbone σ bonds while regenerating the radical growth site. The cited initiator, feed composition and reaction medium determine the particular preparation; transfer, grafting and termination control architecture alongside propagation.

steps.body: Form seed latex, then feed additional butadiene, acrylonitrile, and initiator as specified.

sections.overview: Butyl rubber (IIR) is an elastomer made by copolymerizing isobutylene with a small amount of isoprene. Its chains are therefore largely polyisobutylene-like, with comparatively few sites of unsaturation. The material is used where retention of air is valuable, including tire inner tubes. Halogenated butyl rubbers are related materials made by subsequently modifying IIR. The small isoprene fraction supplies reactive sites while most of the chain retains the low-permeability butyl structure. A cured inner tube also contains fillers and other ingredients.
sections.history: William Sparks and Robert Thomas developed butyl rubber at Standard Oil of New Jersey in 1937 while investigating isobutylene-based materials. The Second World War created an urgent demand for synthetic rubber and drove the transition toward large-scale supply. Butyl’s air-retention behavior made it particularly useful in tire inner tubes, while subsequent uses included protective coatings, tapes and other industrial rubber goods. ExxonMobil’s company history preserves this Standard Oil research lineage. Later chlorination and bromination produced separate halobutyl branches for improved curing and tire construction; those modifications are later developments, rather than part of the original 1937 formulation.
sections.nomenclature: IIR and isobutylene–isoprene rubber identify the same copolymer boundary in this record. Halobutyl rubbers are chemically modified derivatives made after IIR production and are not synonyms for unmodified butyl rubber; a filled and vulcanized compound is likewise a separate formulation state.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Butyl rubber (IIR) is a low-unsaturation random copolymer of isobutylene with approximately 0.5–2.5 mol% isoprene, produced by carbocationic polymerization at low temperature. The isoprene fraction supplies isolated unsaturation for sulfur, resin, or other cure chemistry, while the polyisobutylene-rich sequence gives the family its dense, low-permeability backbone. Open industrial and manufacturing accounts describe catalyst/initiator choice, chlorinated-solvent or slurry/solution phase, temperature, monomer ratio, and molecular-mass control before the rubber is isolated and compounded. Postpolymerization halogenation or other functionalization produces a modified IIR rather than redefining the unmodified family.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Unvulcanized IIR is soft and tacky; vulcanization and compounding create the useful elastomeric tensile, damping, fatigue, and compression response. In an open phyllosilicate/IIR study, Butyl 206 containing about 2.3 mol% unsaturation was compounded on a two-roll mill and vulcanized at 160 °C under 150–180 bar for 30 min. At a tensile-test speed of 500 mm min−1, the unfilled vulcanizate gave 2.5 ± 0.0 MPa tensile strength and 590 ± 57% elongation at break, while the filled formulations spanned 5.3–13.4 MPa and 1260–1289%, depending on the silica/phyllosilicate package. These are filler-specific compound examples, not neat-IIR constants. Molecular mass, isoprene level, filler dispersion, cure system, crosslink density, temperature, and strain history must accompany comparisons.
sections.processing: IIR is plasticized and compounded with zinc oxide, stearic acid, accelerators, sulfur, carbon black or mineral fillers, then sheeted/extruded, molded, and vulcanized. The open IIR composite study mixed the rubber and ingredients on a two-roll mill at 30–35 °C for 5–8 min, then compression-vulcanized filled plaques at 160 °C, 150–180 bar, and 30 min; cure kinetics were measured by MDR at 160 °C under ASTM D5289-17. This bounded example illustrates the need to manage filler incorporation, scorch/cure time, pressure, and heat transfer; actual innerliner, tube, sealant, or TPV processing depends on grade and formulation. Dynamic vulcanization or postpolymerization functionalization should not be folded into the base IIR process description.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Most units in a conventional butyl rubber chain derive from isobutylene, while a smaller fraction comes from isoprene. The remaining isoprene-derived double bonds provide sites for vulcanization. This makes the unsaturation level an important difference from polyisobutylene homopolymer. Curing joins chains into a network whose details depend on the compound. The isoprene double bonds are much less frequent than in fully diene-based rubbers; the cure recipe must account for that lower concentration of reactive sites.
sections.properties: Butyl rubber is valued for its low permeability to air. Its predominantly polyisobutylene backbone also contributes to the material’s oxidative stability and fatigue resistance, according to the cited patent background. The limited unsaturation is sufficient for vulcanization in inner-tube compounds. Actual dynamic and mechanical performance depends on the cured formulation. Its low gas permeability is useful in an inner tube because it slows air loss. This function belongs to a finished compound and construction rather than an unqualified permeability value for every butyl formulation. In one patent comparison, 1 mm vulcanized butyl and bromobutyl compound specimens from example 15 transmitted nitrogen at 21.048 and 29.989 cm³ per square metre per day, respectively, at 23 °C under the stated pressure difference of 0.1 MPa. The formulations differ, so the comparison is an illustration of tested compounds rather than a universal penalty for halogenation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Regular butyl rubber is used in inner tubes, curing bladders, protective clothing and adhesive tapes; designated food grades also serve chewing gum. Its low gas permeability helps inner tubes retain air and makes it useful in bladders. ARLANXEO also identifies high hysteresis, or energy dissipation during deformation, among its butyl vulcanizate properties. The final performance of a tube or bladder depends on its compound, curing and construction.

Purchasing. ARLANXEO lists X_Butyl RB100, RB301 and RB402 in bales and separately designates RB101-3 as a food grade. A buyer specifies the grade and then selects the cure and additives appropriate to the intended article.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for regular butyl rubber was established in the checked sources. Grade listings establish availability and use categories, not sales or market share.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Unhalogenated butyl rubber is included in a patent’s proposed thermochemical devulcanization scope; the intended process breaks network links, while backbone damage can also occur. Separately, gamma-irradiation experiments on a raw Butyl 268 thin film observed oxidation-related carbonyl signals. This radiation treatment is not an inventory of environmental weathering products.

Timescales: In the laboratory film study, the measured oxidation-induction time at 180 °C changed from 62 minutes without irradiation to 31 minutes after a 100 kGy gamma dose. That endpoint describes the onset of an instrument-observed oxidation signal for this raw grade and test, not a service lifetime or environmental degradation rate.

Environmental persistence: Crosslink cleavage and oxidative changes do not establish complete biodegradation or mineralization. The cited sources do not determine how long a finished unhalogenated butyl product persists in soil, water or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A 1991 UNIDO-hosted technical report describes grinding discarded butyl tire-curing bladders and treating the rubber with high-energy electrons to produce reclaim. The authors report an experimental 1.5-tonne lot and tests in which up to 20 parts reclaim per hundred parts of rubber were incorporated into the specified bladder formulation. They also observed pores or blisters in some reclaim vulcanizates, illustrating the importance of processing and cure conditions.

This is historical pilot-scale evidence for the tested bladder waste and formulations, not confirmation of a currently operating recycling route or equivalent performance for every butyl product. Electron irradiation and thermal or mechanical devulcanization are different treatments.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When butyl rubber compounds are processed on two-roll mills, HSE recommends extraction for dust and hot-process fume. Capture should cover the mill’s emission sources and remain effective during operation. Skin-contact controls and suitable cleaning methods address dermatitis risks from the compound and its additives; these are manufacturing exposure controls.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: IIR grades differ in molecular weight and isoprene-derived unsaturation. The small number of reactive sites makes ordinary IIR less readily covulcanized with highly unsaturated diene rubbers than halogenated butyl grades. Fillers, curatives and cure history also influence the final product. A property measured for an inner-tube formulation should not be assigned to all IIR grades. For example, brominated and chlorinated grades alter the reactivity of the isoprene-derived units; they are related derivatives, not identical replacements in every cure recipe.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Carbocationic copolymerization builds an isobutylene-rich chain with isolated unsaturation. An electrophilic initiating species adds to isobutylene and creates a tertiary carbocation growth site. Addition of further monomer regenerates the cationic end. Nucleophilic capture or elimination can stop that chain; elimination and transfer affect end groups and molecular mass.
