sections.overview: Bromobutyl rubber (BIIR) is a brominated derivative of isobutylene–isoprene butyl rubber. Bromination modifies the small isoprene-derived unsaturated fraction of the parent polymer. The resulting material retains the largely isobutylene-derived backbone associated with low gas permeability. Its additional cure reactivity makes it useful in tire inner-liner compounds. The combination is useful for a liner that must retain gas and join to other cured tire layers. Bromobutyl remains a formulation ingredient, not a complete inner liner by itself.
sections.history: Bromobutyl belongs to the halogenated-butyl technologies developed during the 1950s to overcome ordinary butyl rubber’s slow curing. This is later chemistry than the parent butyl material’s 1930s origins. Eric George Kent and John Walker’s Polysar patent, with priority in 1972 and issued in 1976, documents continued work on peroxide-containing cure systems for bromobutyl. Tire air-retention applications became a principal outlet for halobutyl materials. A later industrial account by JSR researcher Takuo Sone identifies Japan Butyl, the JSR–ExxonMobil venture, as a producer of both brominated and chlorinated grades. These milestones trace development and manufacture without assigning a single first-commercialization date to every bromobutyl grade.
sections.nomenclature: BIIR identifies brominated butyl rubber, not unmodified butyl rubber (IIR) or the separately halogenated chlorobutyl material. Bromine content and starting-IIR microstructure remain grade-defining variables, while a vulcanized BIIR compound is a formulation-specific network rather than the base modified polymer alone.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Bromobutyl rubber (BIIR) is made by brominating residual isoprene-derived unsaturation in IIR after low-temperature cationic copolymerization of isobutylene and a small isoprene fraction. In an open industrial account, unreacted monomers are first removed, the IIR is redissolved in a hydrocarbon solvent such as heptane or hexane, and liquid bromine is contacted with the polymer solution at about 40–60 °C before solvent recovery and finishing. A separate current technical sheet independently describes commercial BIIR as a butyl-rubber derivative reacted with bromine in a continuous process. These sources distinguish upstream halogenation from later compounding and vulcanization; bromine content and starting-IIR composition remain grade qualifiers rather than a unique repeat-unit definition.
sections.mechanicalProperties: BIIR retains the low gas permeability and elastomeric flexibility associated with IIR while bromination increases cure reactivity and compatibility with other unsaturated rubbers. In ISO 37 tests on 2 mm S2 specimens at 500 mm min−1, an open study of carbon-black-filled 50/50 natural-rubber/BIIR vulcanizates found that adding 3 phr of a bismaleimide co-curative to the conventional accelerated-sulfur formulation increased tensile strength by 60% and the modulus at 100% elongation by about 97% relative to the study's CV-only blend. The result is a filled/blended vulcanizate, not intrinsic BIIR. The existing industrial account separately reports faster cure and improved co-vulcanization after halogenation. Compound hardness, filler, sulfur/accelerator ratio, co-rubber, and cure state must accompany any numeric BIIR claim.
sections.processing: BIIR is compounded on an internal mixer or two-roll mill with fillers, activators, sulfur or peroxide curatives, and blend partners, then shaped and vulcanized. In the open BIIR/NR study, the rubbers were masticated in an internal mixer at 50 °C and 50 rpm, combined with zinc oxide, stearic acid, 25 phr carbon black, sulfur/CBS, and selected bismaleimide and dicumyl-peroxide additions, homogenized on a two-roll mill, and compression-molded at 170 °C using rheometer-derived cure times. Varying bismaleimide and DCP changed cure, tensile, and compression-set response; the work does not provide a universal tire-innerliner schedule. Mixing sequence, stock temperature, scorch safety, filler dispersion, vulcanization time, and section thickness should be established for the selected bromine grade and compound.
sections.structureAndMorphology: BIIR contains predominantly isobutylene-derived units and a smaller population of modified isoprene-derived units. Bromination forms reactive allylic bromide structures, with different isomers possible depending on reaction conditions. The halogenated sites participate in cure chemistry. Mixing with curatives and fillers followed by vulcanization creates the finished network. The reactive sites are a minority of the predominantly isobutylene-derived chain. Their distribution and the chosen cure system influence the crosslinks in the finished material.
sections.properties: The parent butyl structure provides a useful barrier to air, while brominated sites increase cure reactivity and help the material co-cure with more unsaturated rubbers. This combination helps a tire inner liner retain gas while joining adjacent rubber layers. For one commercial fast-cure polymer grade, ExxonMobil gives a target functional bromine content of 1.08 mol% and a Mooney viscosity target of 32 under its modified ASTM D1646 test at 125 °C. These are grade-specific polymer targets, not mechanical specifications for a finished liner; filler and cure formulation also affect the final compound.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Bromobutyl is used in tire inner liners and other rubber compounds, including pharmaceutical closures and sealants. Its low gas permeability and reactive sites make the polymer useful in a liner that must retain air while bonding to other rubber layers. A finished closure requires a separately qualified formulation.

Purchasing. ARLANXEO lists X_Butyl BB2030, BB2040 and BBX2 raw rubbers in bales. Buyers select the grade before compounding and curing, and the supplier listing does not by itself qualify every finished application.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported bromobutyl purchase or consumption tonnage was established in the checked open sources. Grade availability and listed uses do not establish market share.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Bromobutyl rubber is included in a patent’s proposed thermochemical devulcanization scope; the intended process breaks network links, while backbone damage can also occur. Separately, gamma-irradiation experiments on a raw Bromobutyl 2222 thin film observed oxidation-related carbonyl signals. This radiation treatment is not an inventory of environmental weathering products.

Timescales: In the laboratory film study, the measured oxidation-induction time at 180 °C changed from 25 minutes without irradiation to 15 minutes after a 100 kGy gamma dose. That endpoint describes the onset of an instrument-observed oxidation signal for this raw grade and test, not a service lifetime or environmental degradation rate.

Environmental persistence: Crosslink cleavage and oxidative changes do not establish complete biodegradation or mineralization. The cited sources do not determine how long a finished bromobutyl product persists in soil, water or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The patent proposes treating rubber vulcanizates to reduce crosslinking and then reincorporating material into rubber compounds. It lists bromobutyl among possible feedstocks, but its demonstrated examples used truck-tire crumb, a mixed material; that does not establish recovery performance for this exact polymer grade or cure system.

Breaking crosslinks can improve processability, but nonselective backbone scission can lower molecular weight and alter properties. A proposed reclaiming process does not by itself establish collection or equivalent performance in a new product.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When bromobutyl rubber compounds are processed on two-roll mills, HSE recommends extraction for dust and hot-process fume. Capture should cover the mill’s emission sources and remain effective during operation. Skin-contact controls and suitable cleaning methods address dermatitis risks from the compound and its additives; these are manufacturing exposure controls.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Bromine content, parent polymer and the distribution of reactive structures can vary between grades. The balance of allylic isomers depends on bromination conditions and subsequent handling. Filler, cure package and mixing further affect the properties of the finished product. Data on one commercial compound or one experimental recipe do not establish universal BIIR performance. The effect of bromination is not captured by a single family-wide bromine content, and a liner or pharmaceutical closure requires its own compound qualification.

sections.overview: Chlorobutyl rubber (CIIR) is butyl rubber modified by chlorination of its isoprene-derived sites. It retains a predominantly isobutylene-derived backbone while introducing reactive chlorine-containing groups. This halogenation changes cure behavior relative to unmodified butyl rubber. Chlorobutyl-based compounds are used for applications such as tire inner liners and protective linings. The chlorinated sites aid curing with other rubbers while much of the backbone retains the air-barrier character of the parent butyl rubber. A finished liner or seal is a compound rather than raw CIIR alone.
sections.history: Chlorobutyl emerged from the 1950s modification of butyl rubber to improve curing and compatibility in rubber assemblies. Francis Baldwin and Robert Thomas’s Standard Oil research lineage is documented in a patent issued in 1960. It describes controlled chlorination and applications in tubeless-tire inner linings, bonding layers and tire-curing bags. Those examples show why the modification mattered commercially: air retention had to be combined with workable cure and adhesion behavior. Later producers included Japan Butyl, the JSR–ExxonMobil venture. The 1960 patent is a dated technical milestone in chlorobutyl development, rather than a claim that all halobutyl materials were invented at that moment.
sections.nomenclature: CIIR is the customary abbreviation for chlorobutyl rubber. It is distinct from unhalogenated butyl rubber (IIR) and from bromobutyl rubber; those related elastomers are not synonyms for this chlorine-functionalized material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Chlorobutyl rubber is a chemically modified butyl rubber. Its parent elastomer is an isobutylene–isoprene copolymer made by low-temperature copolymerization; an NPTEL course example describes methyl chloride as the polymerization medium and 1–3% isoprene in the feed description. Chlorination is then a separate post-polymerization reaction: the parent rubber is dissolved in an inert hydrocarbon, commonly hexane, and contacted with chlorine. The cited industrial patent makes clear that hydrogen chloride accompanies chlorine incorporation, so chlorine charge and removal or neutralization are route controls. Vulcanization belongs to subsequent rubber compounding and is not part of the synthesis claim here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Chlorobutyl rubber (CIIR) is an elastomeric butyl-rubber derivative whose tensile, compression-set, stiffness, and damping response are compound properties rather than family constants. Open experimental work describes CIIR as a comparatively high-damping rubber, but its dynamic response varies with temperature and excitation frequency; reinforcing filler, oil or resin additions, crosslink system, and blending with other rubbers further change the result. In particular, a CIIR reference compound had a loss-factor peak at subzero temperature and substantially lower damping above 0 °C, while CIIR/NBR/CPE blends changed both tensile response and temperature-dependent damping.

A bounded tensile example is the reference CIIR compound reported by Roshan-Tabari and co-workers: 100 phr CIIR, 30 phr carbon black, 20 phr paraffinic oil, 3.5 phr coumarone resin, 2 phr sulfur, 5 phr zinc oxide, 1 phr stearic acid, and 3 phr accelerators. Before ageing, it had tensile strength at break of 7.0 ± 0.9 MPa and elongation at break of 762 ± 91% by ISO 37; after 168 h at 70 °C, the corresponding values were 8.1 ± 0.7 MPa and 720 ± 51%. The paper does not report the ISO 37 specimen geometry or tensile-test temperature. These values describe that filled and cured reference compound, not unfilled CIIR or a universal chlorobutyl-rubber range.

A commercial lining sheet further illustrates formulation specificity: Polycorp 1055 is explicitly a blended chlorobutyl lining with a soft natural-rubber tie gum. Its press-cured ASTM D3182 sample-sheet data specify a minimum ASTM D412 tensile strength of 900 psi and minimum elongation of 400%, with face hardness 55 ± 5 Shore A. Those minimum values do not define the CIIR family or a neat chlorobutyl grade.
sections.processing: Chlorobutyl is converted as a compounded, vulcanizable elastomer into hose, tire-inner-liner or sidewall, belt, sheet, roofing, and wire-insulation articles. Fillers, plasticizers/softeners, tackifiers, stabilizers, pigments, and cure ingredients should be mixed to homogeneity before shaping. In a filled chlorobutyl hose example, an 1100 cm³ Banbury mixed compound and cure ingredients for 4–6 min; approximately 2.3 mm sheet was applied to a steel mandrel and steam-autoclave cured at about 150 °C for 40 or 60 min. This is a formulation/article example, not a universal schedule. A separate carbon-black/ZnO/stearic-acid compound was vulcanized at 160 °C for 30 min, illustrating compound-dependent cure conditions.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The parent rubber is an isobutylene–isoprene copolymer with comparatively low unsaturation. A documented production route treats butyl rubber in hydrocarbon solution with chlorine. Chlorination creates allylic chloride structures associated with the modified isoprene units. The cured product is a network that may also contain reinforcing fillers or other rubber polymers. The allylic chlorine-containing sites are located in the isoprene-derived minority of the chain, so variations in parent composition and halogenation can change the available cure chemistry.
sections.properties: The predominantly butyl backbone contributes low gas permeability, while the chlorinated sites increase cure reactivity. Halogenation can improve compatibility during covulcanization with more highly unsaturated rubbers. For a historical blended chlorobutyl lining with a natural-rubber tie gum, the supplier lists face hardness of 55 ± 5 Shore A and at least 400% elongation at break. The elongation was measured by ASTM D412 on a press-cured sample sheet, so it describes the finished blend and test preparation rather than the unfilled parent polymer. The combination of a low-permeability butyl backbone and more reactive halogenated sites is useful when an air barrier must bond to another rubber layer. The cited chlorobutyl/natural-rubber lining sheet describes a blend rather than a pure polymer property.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Chlorobutyl rubber is compounded for tire inner liners, pharmaceutical closures, sealants and protective linings. Low gas permeability supports a liner’s air-barrier function. ARLANXEO identifies faster cure and better compatibility with unsaturated rubbers as advantages of its halogenated butyl grades, useful when a liner must be joined to other tire components during vulcanization. As a separate lining example, the historical Polycorp 1055 product is a blended chlorobutyl compound with a natural-rubber tie layer for chemical service; its resistance is specified for that product and chemical exposure.

Purchasing. ARLANXEO lists X_Butyl CB1240 as chlorobutyl rubber supplied in bales. A fabricator selects the grade and qualifies the compound for a specific closure, tire or lining rather than assuming a raw-rubber listing specifies the final article.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported chlorobutyl purchase or consumption tonnage was established in the checked sources. Supplier availability and applications do not establish sales or market share.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Chlorobutyl rubber is included in a patent’s proposed thermochemical devulcanization scope; the intended process breaks network links, while backbone damage can also occur. Separately, gamma-irradiation experiments on a raw Chlorobutyl HT 1066 thin film observed oxidation-related carbonyl signals. This radiation treatment is not an inventory of environmental weathering products.

Timescales: In the laboratory film study, the measured oxidation-induction time at 180 °C changed from 36 minutes without irradiation to 20 minutes after a 100 kGy gamma dose. That endpoint describes the onset of an instrument-observed oxidation signal for this raw grade and test, not a service lifetime or environmental degradation rate.

Environmental persistence: Crosslink cleavage and oxidative changes do not establish complete biodegradation or mineralization. The cited sources do not determine how long a finished chlorobutyl product persists in soil, water or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A laboratory study incorporated 30 parts gamma-irradiated butyl rubber per 100 parts total rubber into a chlorobutyl compound, with the remaining 70 parts virgin chlorobutyl. The reclaim had been irradiated at 25 kGy before mixing; the resulting compound had higher minimum rheometer torque and a shorter scorch time than the virgin-chlorobutyl comparator. This demonstrates use of reclaimed butyl in a CIIR-containing compound, not recovery of CIIR from a used chlorobutyl article.

A separate patent includes chlorobutyl among possible feedstocks for devulcanization, but its demonstrated feed was mixed truck-tire crumb. Neither example establishes a chlorobutyl-specific collection system or equivalent properties for all new products.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When chlorobutyl rubber compounds are processed on two-roll mills, HSE recommends extraction for dust and hot-process fume. Capture should cover the mill’s emission sources and remain effective during operation. Skin-contact controls and suitable cleaning methods address dermatitis risks from the compound and its additives; these are manufacturing exposure controls.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Chlorine content and the underlying butyl grade affect the material before compounding. Cure system, fillers and any added rubber modify its behavior further. The cited lining sheet is for a blended product, not a pure chlorobutyl reference. Its tensile and hardness values cannot be transferred to all CIIR formulations or service environments. Compatibility and measured durability depend on cure chemistry, fillers and the second rubber in a blend; the same name does not fix these choices.

sections.overview: Polychloroprene rubber is an elastomer made by polymerizing chloroprene. Its chlorine-bearing units and residual unsaturation distinguish it from polybutadiene. A documented route uses free-radical emulsion polymerization. The polymer can be compounded and cured into articles such as seals, coatings and flexible components. Polychloroprene can also crystallize as it is stretched: in an unfilled cured specimen this ordering accompanied a rise in resistance to further extension. Other formulations can be blended with a second rubber, and the choice of metal oxide in the cure changes the response of the resulting blend.
sections.history: Polychloroprene’s development is closely associated with DuPont’s Wallace Carothers laboratory. In April 1930 Arnold Collins isolated chloroprene and observed its polymerization; Elmer Bolton encouraged the company to develop the material commercially. The resulting Neoprene became an important early synthetic rubber, with an industrial introduction in 1931. Its history subsequently extended beyond that original DuPont lineage into multiple producers and specialty grades. Industrial applications included footwear, adhesives and technical rubber goods. The discovery therefore involved a team and subsequent process development, rather than Carothers alone.
sections.nomenclature: CR abbreviates polychloroprene rubber, and chloroprene rubber is an equivalent common name. “Neoprene” is a commercial name and should not be used as the canonical family name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polychloroprene is produced by free-radical polymerization of chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene), most commonly in alkaline aqueous emulsion. Water, emulsifier, radical initiator, and a chain-transfer or sulfur-based modifier are used to manage latex stability, conversion, molar mass, branching, and crystallization behavior. A historical example uses an azo initiator and an alkane thiol in aqueous dispersion. A separate sulfur-free route uses a persulfate/dithionite initiator and a combination of xanthogen disulfide and bis(acylaminophenyl) polysulfide transfer agents, then stops polymerization, removes residual monomer, and isolates the polymer. These are formulation-specific examples; not all polychloroprene uses the same transfer package. Copolymerized chloroprene grades should retain their comonomer limitation, and vulcanization is network formation after polymer manufacture rather than the chloroprene-polymerization step.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Polychloroprene is normally used as a formulated and crosslinked elastomer, so the mechanics of an uncured gum, a dense vulcanizate, an adhesive film, and an open- or closed-cell foam should not be combined. A dense cured compound can undergo large, nonlinear, substantially recoverable deformation with hysteresis and rate-dependent stiffness. Chain regularity and crystallization can add green strength or time- and temperature-dependent stiffening, while the crosslink network controls low-strain modulus, set, strength, tear, and fatigue. Grade modification and molar mass, crystallization rate, metal-oxide and accelerator cure chemistry, cure time and temperature, crosslink density, carbon-black or mineral reinforcement, plasticizer and antioxidant loading, foam density and cell structure, fabric reinforcement and orientation, specimen thickness and notch, temperature, strain rate, cyclic history, oil or water exposure, and ozone or thermal aging are all consequential. Oxidative aging can continue crosslinking and raise stiffness while reducing extensibility before chain scission or cracking dominates.

A bounded compound example is Denka DCR-30, a mercaptan-modified, very-slow-crystallizing polychloroprene grade. Denka's one-sheet test formulation contains 100 parts DCR-30, 1 part antioxidant, 4 parts calcined magnesia, 5 parts zinc oxide, and 0.35 part 2-mercaptoimidazoline, cured at 141 °C for 25 minutes. For that formulation the supplier lists 500% modulus of 1.0–4.0 MPa, tensile strength of at least 14.0 MPa, and elongation at break of at least 750%. These are descriptive formulation-control values, not neat-polymer constants or universal design allowables; specimen geometry, tensile rate, conditioning, and scatter are absent from the sheet. Independently, compression and dynamic-mechanical tests on a commercial black, 5 mm polychloroprene sheet showed increasing stress with rising strain rate or falling temperature, a largely rubbery response down to about −40 °C, and a sharp transition toward glassy behavior below that range. That study's filled commercial sheet and compression geometry are separate from the DCR-30 tensile formulation and should not be numerically merged.
sections.processing: Polychloroprene (CR, neoprene) is processed as a compounded elastomer by mastication, internal or two-roll mixing, calendering, extrusion, compression/transfer/injection molding, and subsequent vulcanization. Cure packages commonly use metal oxides and accelerators; scorch safety, compound viscosity, mold venting, section thickness, and heat removal control the balance between flow and premature cure. Denka's DCR-30 grade sheet gives a bounded test formulation containing 100 parts DCR-30 with 4 parts calcined magnesia and a 141 °C × 25 min cure; the values are for that mercaptan-modified, very-slow-crystallizing grade and formulation. A separate polychloroprene vulcanization patent describes conventional kneaders, rolls, internal mixers, and mixing extruders, a 16 min example mixing sequence, and vulcanization preferably at 140–210 °C under optional pressure, while emphasizing that the exact temperature/time pair depends on formulation, mold, and thickness. Chloroprene emulsion polymerization belongs in Synthesis; this section covers compounding, shaping, vulcanization, and post-cure conditioning.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polychloroprene chains contain chlorine-bearing repeat units with unsaturation remaining in the backbone. The relative amounts of structural isomers depend on the polymer. In one study an unfilled sulfur-cured polychloroprene developed crystalline regions under extension. These crystallites formed and changed during mechanical cycling. Chain ordering is not fixed solely by the chemical name: a predominantly trans-1,4 chain can also contain smaller amounts of other addition structures. Crosslinking ties chains together, while fillers and a second rubber change the morphology of a compounded article. In one chloroprene–butadiene blend study, specimens cured with different metal oxides showed different swelling and tensile responses; these measurements describe the blends and cure recipes studied, not neat polychloroprene.
sections.properties: Polychloroprene compounds are used for flexible articles exposed to weathering and fluids. A study of one commercial rubber sheet found that compression stress increased with strain rate and changed markedly as temperature decreased. An unfilled cured sample also exhibited strain hardening associated with strain-induced crystallization. Both results are tied to the tested materials and conditions. In a study of chloroprene rubber taken from a commercial air spring, oven aging at 343–373 K hardened the material and reduced its fatigue resistance in subsequent crack-propagation tests. This observation connects thermal exposure to fatigue performance for that particular compounded material rather than providing a universal lifespan.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polychloroprene serves hoses, belts and molded rubber parts, and contact adhesives in footwear and construction. Adhesive grades illustrate how crystallization changes a use: ARLANXEO’s faster-crystallizing Baypren 300 grades build high initial bond strength quickly, allowing bonded shoe parts to be handled early in production. Its more slowly crystallizing 200 grades give longer open time and a softer, more flexible bond line, which the supplier associates with flooring and roofing. Compound formulation also matters for rubber goods used in sustained cold exposure.

Purchasing. ARLANXEO offers Baypren grades for rubber-goods compounding and separate adhesive grades through its sales channel. The adhesive portfolio includes faster-crystallizing 300 and medium-fast 200 series, with different viscosities within each series. A buyer specifies the grade for the intended formulation, initial bond strength and open-time needs.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Polychloroprene is explicitly listed in a thermochemical devulcanization patent. The intended breakdown is crosslink cleavage yielding reusable rubber chains; excessive heating can also damage the backbone. A complete ambient degradation-product inventory remains a gap. A separate study aged chloroprene rubber for air-spring applications at 343–373 K (70–100 °C) and measured fatigue crack propagation. The experiments track a mechanical degradation endpoint; they do not identify a complete inventory of chemical breakdown products.

Timescales: As a verification exposure, researchers aged material cut from a commercial train air-spring bag for 20 days at 333 K (60 °C), then measured fatigue crack growth. This accelerated mechanical test is bounded by its sample and loading conditions. It does not establish a transferable environmental mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: Sandia compared elongation of an Okonite chloroprene cable jacket at 150 °C in air and nitrogen; the jacket lost elongation much faster in air. This demonstrates atmosphere-dependent mechanical ageing in one formulation. It does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent proposes controlled devulcanization and reincorporation into rubber compounds. Listed applicability alone does not prove performance for every cure system; peroxide- and sulfur-cured materials need separate qualification. In the patent’s example, the feed is truck-tire scrap, and the rubber is treated in an internal mixer at 170 °C for 10 minutes before recompounding. This example does not demonstrate the same result for a polychloroprene article.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When polychloroprene rubber compounds are processed on two-roll mills, HSE recommends extraction for dust and hot-process fume. Capture should cover the mill’s emission sources and remain effective during operation. Skin-contact controls and suitable cleaning methods address dermatitis risks from the compound and its additives; these are manufacturing exposure controls.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Polymer microstructure, cure and filler vary between polychloroprene compounds. The cited crystallization study used a specific unfilled, sulfur-cured W-type gum and defined temperatures. The compression study used a commercial sheet whose behavior depended on rate and temperature. These observations do not establish a universal service range or resistance to every fluid. The air-spring study tested specimens at several accelerated temperatures and developed a model under specified assumptions. Actual fatigue behavior depends on the part, its formulation and its service loading.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical polymerization produces polychloroprene. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another. For the diene component, addition leaves residual unsaturation whose position depends on the addition microstructure.

sections.overview: Ethylene–propylene rubber (EPM) is a binary copolymer of ethylene and propylene. Unlike EPDM, it contains no intentionally incorporated diene cure sites. Its saturated backbone contributes to resistance to oxidative and weathering environments. The polymer is compounded and crosslinked to obtain finished elastomeric articles. The distinction in cure sites matters in manufacturing: peroxide curing can connect the saturated chains, while a studied peroxide–sulfur hybrid formulation introduced a different combination of crosslinks. A finished seal or cable compound also contains fillers and other ingredients, which influence its response alongside the polymer.
sections.history: Ethylene–propylene rubber arose from the 1950s expansion of coordination-catalyst chemistry. Giulio Natta, Giorgio Mazzanti and Giorgio Boschi’s Montecatini patent lineage claims Italian priority in December 1955 for amorphous elastomeric ethylene–propylene copolymers. The Natta archive records a Ferrara plant milestone in 1958. These saturated copolymers provided an alternative rubber platform with subsequent uses in electrical insulation and industrial rubber products. Later addition of a diene produced the related EPDM branch, with different curing possibilities. The research dates, plant milestone and later applications describe distinct stages; they should not be collapsed into a single invention date for all ethylene–propylene elastomers.
sections.nomenclature: EPM is the abbreviation used for ethylene–propylene rubber; EPR is also used in the cited literature for the binary copolymer. The record excludes EPDM, which adds a diene, as well as a particular vulcanized compound or an ethylene/propylene copolymer with a different modifier scope.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–propylene rubber (EPR, also called EPM) is the binary coordination copolymer of ethylene and propylene; it is distinct from EPDM because no diene feedstock is used. Conventional solution routes use a vanadium compound with an alkylaluminum cocatalyst, whereas metallocene catalyst systems offer an alternative documented route. One patent describes passing the two monomer gases into dry n-hexane containing vanadium oxychloride and an alkylaluminum catalyst, followed by catalyst removal and solvent flashing. A later patent describes metallocene catalysts for EPR production and contrasts them with vanadium-based production. Catalyst selection, monomer ratio, solvent, and process conditions are route-dependent; sulfur or peroxide vulcanization of a finished rubber article is not part of binary EPR synthesis.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–propylene rubber (EPM) is a saturated elastomer whose useful mechanical response is established after compounding and crosslinking, rather than being a single resin constant. Ethylene content and Mooney viscosity vary across commercial ethylene–propylene grades; in filled vulcanizates, filler/oil loading, cure chemistry, crosslink density and crosslink type, and specimen history govern strength, modulus, extensibility, compression set, and dynamic response. A peroxide network favors thermally robust carbon–carbon links, whereas the cited hybrid sulfur–peroxide study found that a mixed network can change the stiffness–extensibility balance; those findings are formulation-specific.

A bounded research example is Dutral CO 38 EPM (72 wt% ethylene; Mooney 60 MU) compounded with 70 phr N550 carbon black and 10 phr paraffinic oil. Its EPM6 formulation also contained 3 phr ZnO, 1 phr stearic acid, 1 phr sulfur, and 5 phr peroxide. Dumbbells punched from 2 mm compression-molded sheets gave a mean tensile strength of 15.7 MPa when tested at ambient temperature by ASTM D412 at 500 mm/min. This is a result for that cured, filled compound and test protocol—not a general EPM specification.
sections.processing:
EPM/EPR is normally compounded with fillers, oils, and a selected cure package before extrusion or molding; processing behavior varies with ethylene content, Mooney viscosity, oil extension, and filler loading. ENEOS lists EPM/EPDM grades with distinct processability choices: some have excellent extrusion characteristics, some high-speed vulcanization or unplasticized compounds, and others retain extrusion performance at high filler loading. These product-line descriptors support grade selection but do not define one family-wide extrusion or cure schedule.

A bounded high-ethylene EPM/EPDM cable-coating example used an ASTM D2230 tube extrusion test with a 50-mm device, 70 °C screw temperature, 90 °C head temperature, and 20 rpm; the reported samples were subsequently vulcanized at 160 °C for 20 min. The patent treats EPM and EPDM together, so the extrusion and cure settings are an equipment-, compound-, and specimen-specific example rather than a universal EPM recipe.
sections.structureAndMorphology: EPM consists of ethylene- and propylene-derived units in a saturated backbone. Its composition and molecular weight can be controlled during copolymerization, giving different grades. Without the pendant diene unsaturation of EPDM, conventional accelerated sulfur cure is ineffective. Peroxide curing creates crosslinks through radical reactions; the cited study also examines a peroxide–sulfur hybrid route. The hybrid route produces a network with both carbon–carbon and sulfur-containing links; it is an engineered formulation and does not mean that EPM contains diene groups. In a study using carbon-black-filled Dutral CO 38, a peroxide/TAIC formulation reached 719% elongation at break, while a peroxide–sulfur/TAIC formulation reached 1058%, measured on molded specimens at ambient temperature. Those values compare two specific recipes rather than establish limits for the EPM family.
sections.properties: EPM is valued for resistance to heat and oxidative environments. In a study using the Dutral CO 38 grade, researchers compared peroxide-based and peroxide–sulfur curing systems. The resulting compounds differed in tensile and dynamic response as the crosslinking system changed. These findings illustrate the role of network chemistry in addition to polymer composition. In the cited EPM study, room-temperature tensile tests of 2 mm molded sheets gave elongation at break of 719% for a co-agent-assisted peroxide formulation and 1058% for one hybrid peroxide–sulfur formulation. Cure chemistry changes the network as well as the tensile response; these are specific compounds tested at 500 mm/min.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. EPM serves automotive rubber goods, cables, appliances, masterbatch binders and polymer modification. Ethylene–propylene rubber has a saturated main chain, which ENEOS connects with heat, ozone and weather resistance; those properties are relevant where an exposed rubber component must remain serviceable. Products are delivered for downstream compounding, so fillers, cure chemistry and geometry also influence the performance of a finished cable or automotive part. ENEOS discusses EPM and EPDM together, so an application listed for the broad EP range does not by itself prove use of a specific EPM grade.

Purchasing. Versalis supplies Dutral CO054 as polyethylene-wrapped bales for downstream compounding. Its technical sheet specifies a typical 25 kg bale, with 30 bales in a 750 kg box. The listed weight is raw supply material, not the weight or performance of a finished rubber article.

Scale and evidence limits. The November 2022 sheet specifies a typical 25 kg bale and a 750 kg box containing 30 bales: tens-of-kilograms units consolidated toward a tonne. These are package sizes, not annual EPM demand.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Ethylene-propylene rubber is explicitly listed in a thermochemical devulcanization patent. The intended breakdown is crosslink cleavage yielding reusable rubber chains; excessive heating can also damage the backbone. A complete ambient degradation-product inventory remains a gap.

Timescales: In a laboratory study, silica-filled, peroxide-cured EPM samples with and without added antioxidants were exposed to air at 100 °C for 14 days. A separate 14-day UV protocol alternated eight hours of irradiation at 60 °C with four hours without UV at 50 °C. The resulting infrared and color changes characterize those accelerated treatments, not an environmental mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: The EPM study compared carbonyl formation by infrared spectroscopy and found that stabilization depended on the antioxidant and exposure protocol. Carbonyl formation indicates an oxidation-related change, but does not quantify the fraction of carbon mineralized. Complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill remains unresolved.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent proposes controlled devulcanization and reincorporation into rubber compounds. Listed applicability alone does not prove performance for every cure system; peroxide- and sulfur-cured materials need separate qualification. The cited patent’s experimental feed is truck-tire scrap; its internal-mixer treatment at 170 °C for 10 minutes does not independently validate EPM recovery. Its EPM mention defines a proposed scope of the method.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Press curing of ethylene–propylene rubber compounds can release rubber fume, especially when a mold opens. HSE recommends source extraction around presses and control of skin contact with process residues. Assessment should use the complete compound formulation because curatives, fillers and processing aids contribute to exposure alongside the elastomer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: EPM grades differ in ethylene content, molecular characteristics and compounding ingredients. The hybrid-cure study used a specific commercial grade and specified formulations; its results are not generic EPM values. Filler, peroxide, sulfur and other cure ingredients alter the resulting network. Product information that combines EPM and EPDM should be read with the grade identity in view. The experimental hybrid formulation and the peroxide/co-agent formulation also differ in ingredients, so the comparison describes the whole formulations rather than the isolated effect of sulfur alone.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Coordination copolymerization forms the binary EPR chain. Olefin first coordinates to an active metal site and then inserts into the metal–carbon bond of the growing chain. The longer metal-bound chain can coordinate and insert another monomer; catalyst environment and feed selection govern the resulting sequence and stereochemistry.

steps.title: Prepare the reaction
steps.body: Introduce the two gases to dry n-hexane containing the vanadium/aluminum catalyst.

steps.title: Coordinate and insert monomer
steps.body: Follow repeated olefin coordination and insertion at the activated catalyst. Each insertion adds carbon atoms to the chain and regenerates a metal-bound growth site. Apply the catalyst and comonomer choices of this route when interpreting branching or stereoregularity.

steps.title: Form and recover the product
steps.body: Copolymerize, remove catalyst residues, and flash solvent to recover the rubber.

synthesisRoutes.limitations: This outline does not specify a universal recipe, reagent loading, operating schedule, or conversion endpoint. sections.overview: Ethylene–propylene–diene rubber (EPDM) is an elastomer made from ethylene, propylene and a nonconjugated diene. The diene introduces a limited number of reactive sites for later vulcanization. This combination distinguishes EPDM from the binary ethylene–propylene copolymer EPM. EPDM compounds are used in applications including roofing membranes and seals. The largely saturated backbone contributes to its resistance to ozone and weathering, while the diene supplies sites used in sulfur curing. Resistance is a formulation-dependent behavior, not immunity to aging.
sections.history: EPDM developed from ethylene–propylene rubber by incorporating a diene to provide additional curing chemistry. The Society of Polymer Science, Japan’s chronology records DuPont and Montecatini production in 1963, followed by other manufacturers. DSM’s Keltan production at Geleen began in 1967; the later Arlanxeo site chronology documents additional lines in 1973 and 2003 and adoption of its ACE catalyst on the third line in 2013. Major application areas have included automotive seals and hoses, building membranes and electrical products. This sequence shows the progression from a new terpolymer platform to large-scale manufacture and later catalyst improvements, with supplier milestones distinguished from the earliest ethylene–propylene research.
sections.nomenclature: EPDM is the abbreviation for ethylene–propylene–diene rubber. The diene comonomer is the defining boundary: binary EPM/EPR is excluded, and a cured EPDM compound, reclaimed rubber, or reinforced membrane is a formulation/article state rather than a separate synonym for the terpolymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–propylene–diene rubber (EPDM) is produced by coordination terpolymerization of ethylene, propylene, and a diene, commonly a nonconjugated diene such as ethylidene norbornene (ENB), dicyclopentadiene, or vinylidene norbornene. An open review describes the family as catalytic coordination terpolymerization and surveys Group IV catalyst systems; a separate patent identifies solution or slurry Ziegler–Natta manufacture using vanadium compounds such as VOCl3, V(acac)3, or VCl4 with aluminum cocatalysts. A specific historical solution example charges a diene feedstock before ethylene and propylene in a vanadium/organaluminum-catalyzed solution. Diene selection, catalyst chemistry, and monomer conversion govern the product architecture. The retained unsaturation may subsequently support formulation-specific vulcanization, but cure-agent packages and curing schedules do not define EPDM synthesis and are excluded here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–propylene–diene rubber (EPDM) is a vulcanizable terpolymer, so its tensile, tear, hardness, elastic recovery, and aging response are properties of a particular cured compound and construction. Relevant variables include ethylene/propylene balance, diene type and content, cure system and crosslink network, carbon-black/filler and oil loading, reclaimed-rubber fraction, and thermal or weathering exposure. An open study of a Keltan 8550 ECO sealing compound found that replacing virgin polymer with devulcanized EPDM changed network structure: increasing reclaimed content raised Shore A hardness but reduced tensile strength and elongation; reducing the accompanying carbon black and softener partially changed that response. This trend should not be read as a general EPDM value.

A bounded product example is FlexWhite EPDM roofing membrane. The 60 mil membrane, listed at 1.549 mm actual thickness, reported 9.2 MPa tensile strength and 420% ultimate elongation by ASTM D412, Die C; the corresponding 90 mil product reported 11.0 MPa and 495%. These are specific reinforced membrane constructions, not properties of unfilled EPDM resin or every EPDM compound.
sections.processing:
EPDM articles are made from compounded rubber by internal or two-roll mixing, extrusion or calendering, and heat/pressure vulcanization; the cure schedule must be matched to the diene, curative package, section thickness, and target article. A public GenFlex reinforced-membrane process flow lists mixer → extrusion → calendering (with optional scrim) → curing with heat/steam and pressure → trimming and packaging. This is a membrane manufacturing route, not a universal requirement for every EPDM product.

A laboratory EPDM formulation study illustrates bounded feed and cure handling. EPDM, zinc oxide, stearic acid, carbon black, and naphthenic oil were charged sequentially to an internal mixer at 90 °C and 60 rpm; sulfur and accelerator were added in a second stage at 50 °C. After more than 16 h storage, the compound was press-vulcanized at 170 °C under 15–20 MPa. Those temperatures, pressure, dwell history, and formulation apply to the tested vulcanizates; other extrusion profiles, peroxide cures, and thick sections require separate rheometry and heat-transfer validation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: EPDM has a largely saturated ethylene–propylene backbone with unsaturation introduced by the diene component. Diene identity and content vary among grades and influence curing. Sulfur vulcanization can link the chains through different sulfur-containing crosslinks. Fillers, oils and other additives are incorporated into many finished EPDM compounds. The diene permits sulfur linkages to connect chains into a network without making the backbone highly unsaturated. Peroxide-cured EPDM instead forms carbon–carbon links; the resulting network and its recovery behavior are not automatically equivalent to those of a sulfur cure.
sections.properties: EPDM is valued for resistance to outdoor weathering and thermal oxidation in suitable formulations. One aging study used a carbon-black-filled and oil-extended EPDM vulcanizate with a defined sulfur cure. The authors measured changes in structure and properties during hot-air exposure and compared compounds with and without antioxidants. Such measurements show how a particular formulated network responds to aging. At 120 °C in air, both of the study’s sulfur-cured formulations became harder and showed decreasing elongation at break as exposure continued. The formulation containing antioxidants retained more of its elongation than the otherwise comparable antioxidant-free sample; this comparison does not establish the service life of a roof or seal.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. EPDM compounds are used for automotive body seals and radiator hoses, roofing and geomembranes, electrical cable, and appliance components. Their flexibility and resistance to weathering are useful for seals exposed outdoors, while the supplier also identifies electrical properties as relevant to wire and cable. Each use calls for a suitably compounded and cured material rather than an interchangeable raw polymer. A commercial roofing example is GenFlex FlexWhite, a single-ply EPDM membrane with a reflective white surface; its environmental declaration lists nominal 60- and 90-mil products. The 60-mil specimen has a reported 420% ultimate elongation in the stated ASTM D412 test, a finished membrane result that depends on its full formulation.

Purchasing. ARLANXEO offers Keltan EPDM grades through its product and technical-sales channels. A compounder selects a grade and specifies the cure, fillers, oil and additives to meet the needs of the finished part; a raw-rubber listing does not itself specify a finished roofing membrane or hose.

Scale and evidence limits. The supplier examples establish product availability and intended uses, not quantities sold or independent market share. No reliable separately reported global EPDM purchase or consumption tonnage was established in the checked sources.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Heat and oxygen can change a cured EPDM network through competing oxidation, chain scission and additional crosslinking. In a study of carbon-black-filled, oil-extended EPDM 3760P with a sulfur cure, infrared changes accompanied thermal aging; the authors interpreted the changes as oxidation. The experiment does not identify a complete inventory of products released outdoors.

Timescales: The researchers aged specimens in circulating air at 120 ± 2 °C for intervals up to 336 hours. Hardness and crosslink density increased while elongation at break decreased; the antioxidant-containing formulation retained elongation better than the antioxidant-free one. These are measurements on particular compounds under accelerated conditions, not an environmental residence time.

Environmental persistence: A change in physical properties or spectral chemistry does not establish biodegradation or mineralization. The cited tests do not establish how long a particular EPDM article persists in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Sulfur-cured EPDM is a crosslinked network and cannot simply be remelted like a thermoplastic. In a laboratory study, sulfur-cured EPDM containing carbon black and dolomite was treated on a two-roll mill to reduce its crosslink density, then mixed with virgin compound and revulcanized. Tensile strength fell by about 15% and 20% at 25% and 50% recycled content, respectively, compared with the study’s virgin compound; substantially larger deterioration was observed at higher recycled content.

Devulcanization aims to break crosslinks, but chain scission and oxidation can also occur. The result depends on the feedstock and treatment: this experiment does not establish recovery performance for peroxide-cured EPDM or the availability of a collection route for every finished product.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Press curing of ethylene–propylene–diene rubber compounds can release rubber fume, especially when a mold opens. HSE recommends source extraction around presses and control of skin contact with process residues. Assessment should use the complete compound formulation because curatives, fillers and processing aids contribute to exposure alongside the elastomer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Ethylene and diene content, filler, oil, antioxidant and cure system all vary among EPDM products. The cited aging experiment used one rubber grade and a specified filled formulation at 120 °C. Its aging behavior depends on exposure duration and additive package. A reinforced roofing membrane is a constructed product, so its test results should not be treated as intrinsic values for every EPDM. A grade is not the same as a finished rubber compound: changing antioxidant levels can alter aging, while replacing a sulfur cure with a peroxide cure also changes the network chemistry.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Coordination terpolymerization retains diene-derived sites for later cure. Olefin first coordinates to an active metal site and then inserts into the metal–carbon bond of the growing chain. The longer metal-bound chain can coordinate and insert another monomer; catalyst environment and feed selection govern the resulting sequence and stereochemistry. The selected nonconjugated diene provides residual unsaturation for a later vulcanization step.

sections.overview: Acrylic rubber (ACM) is an elastomer based on copolymers of acrylate esters. Ethyl and butyl acrylate are among the monomers used in this family. A small amount of a cure-site monomer is often included to enable vulcanization. Finished compounds are used where resistance to heat and oils is needed. The ester side groups also affect how the rubber responds to oils and low temperatures. A patent describing these materials notes that longer alkyl groups generally improve cold flexibility at the expense of oil resistance, while more polar acrylates can reduce oil swelling but raise the glass transition. These are formulation trends, and a finished gasket or hose contains a selected cure package and other ingredients.
sections.history: Acrylic rubber was already the subject of dedicated United States government research during the 1940s. W. C. Mast and C. H. Fisher’s December 1948 report describes the Eastern Regional Research Laboratory’s Lactoprene elastomers, pilot-scale work and B. F. Goodrich’s commercial production. This establishes activity and manufacture by 1948 without claiming a unique first synthesis. Heat- and oil-resistant automotive seals, gaskets and hoses became important uses. Manabu Sugiyama’s 2016 Zeon account describes later demand from hotter engine compartments and identifies Zeon and Unimatec as major producers at that time. Across this history, incorporation of cure sites and development of reliable curing systems were recurring routes to useful acrylic elastomers.
sections.nomenclature: ACM is used here for acrylic rubber as a family name, rather than for one specified acrylate-ester copolymer or cured compound. Cure-site chemistry and the resulting crosslinked network remain part of the particular grade or formulation, not alternate names for the family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Acrylic rubber (ACM) is a family of acrylate-ester copolymer elastomers, generally made by emulsion free-radical copolymerization. Acrylate-ester selection establishes the base elastomer, while a small cure-site comonomer is incorporated so that the chosen cure system can subsequently form the finished network. The industrial emulsion route and cure-site/cure-agent pairing therefore describe family chemistry, not one invariant ACM recipe. The resulting gum is later compounded with a grade-matched cure system to form the finished network.
sections.mechanicalProperties: ACM is used when an elastomeric response is needed alongside oil and heat resistance, but tensile behavior depends on acrylate composition, cure-site chemistry, crosslink density, fillers, and any blend phase. The sliding-graft study likewise shows that vulcanization and formulated additions alter ACM-composite damping and mechanical response. As a bounded neighboring formulation example, an NBR/ACM 90:10 dual-vulcanized seal compound reported tensile strength 21.15 MPa, elongation at break 276%, and 100% modulus 6.35 MPa; these are values for that NBR-rich, filled covulcanizate, not ACM-family constants.
sections.processing: ACM is normally compounded and shaped while uncured, then vulcanized with a cure package selected for its cure-site comonomer. Two-roll-mill mixing, molding, and thermal cure are therefore meaningful conversion steps, but the settings belong to the named compound. In the NBR/ACM 90:10 study, ingredients were mixed on a two-roll mill and vulcanized in a flat press at 165 °C before an oven stage at 160 °C; that procedure cannot be transferred unchanged to another ACM grade, cure chemistry, or part geometry. Supplier or compound-specific guidance remains necessary for mixing, mold filling, and cure time.
sections.structureAndMorphology: ACM chains contain acrylate-derived units with ester side groups. Different alkyl or alkoxyalkyl acrylates change the side-group composition of the polymer. Cure-site monomers can introduce functional groups such as carboxyl, epoxy or chlorine-containing groups. The selected cure chemistry links the compounded polymer into a network. For example, ethyl acrylate and butyl acrylate change the ester side group, while a smaller proportion of glycidyl methacrylate or another cure-site monomer can provide reactive functionality. The polymer composition and the subsequent cure therefore perform different roles: the former helps determine chain mobility and fluid interactions, while the latter connects chains into the finished network.
sections.properties: ACM vulcanizates are valued for resistance to heat and oil, but low-temperature flexibility and oil swell can trade off. A patent discussing ACM and related acrylate rubbers notes that increased acrylate polarity can reduce oil swelling while raising glass-transition temperature. In an ADEKA formulation comparison after 70 hours at 150 °C, the compound with RS-107 plasticizer lost 14% of its elongation at break and increased eight hardness points; the RS-735 compound lost 3% and increased two points. These are specific filled and cured compounds, not a universal grade specification or a prediction for other oils and exposures.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. ACM serves automotive and industrial oil seals and hoses, where a rubber must maintain sealing or flexibility while exposed to oil and heat. Zeon lists heat-resistant AR71 for molded oil seals, cold-resistant AR72LS for molded seals, and AR22 for hoses. In another supplier comparison, HyTemp AR71 is identified for high-temperature service and has a Gehman T100 value of −18 °C, while AR72LF is described as balancing low-temperature and oil resistance with a T100 of −28 °C. The latter indicates flexibility at a lower test temperature for the stated grades; it is not an operating guarantee for an independently compounded seal.

Purchasing. Purchase a raw-rubber grade through supplier inquiry and specify its cure-site chemistry and intended compounding route. The final cure package and fillers determine the properties of the seal or hose.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon reported Japanese ACM capacity of 8,500 t/year in May 2015. This historical company capacity is neither current capacity nor measured production, purchases or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A hydrothermal-devulcanization patent lists acrylic rubber among possible feedstocks and describes breaking sulfur crosslinks while seeking to preserve the polymer backbone. The patent does not establish an ACM-specific outcome, and that mechanism cannot be assumed for grades cured by other chemistry. It does not identify ambient acrylic-rubber breakdown products.

Timescales: The patent proposes water treatment at elevated temperature and pressure, but does not give an ACM-specific degradation time or recovery yield. No transferable environmental mineralization duration is established.

Environmental persistence: In a supplier’s acrylic-rubber compound containing RS-107 plasticizer, 70 hours at 150 °C reduced elongation at break by 14% and increased hardness by eight points. This is a formulation-specific hot-ageing test, not a direct measurement of chemical breakdown or biodegradation. The proposed devulcanization route and this test do not establish complete mineralization in soil or water.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent proposes grinding and treating vulcanized rubber in hot pressurized water, then blending the devulcanized material with uncured rubber for recompounding. Acrylic rubber is included in its scope, but an ACM-specific example and yield are not established. Its sulfur-crosslink rationale must not be generalized to every ACM cure system or taken as evidence of commercial implementation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Press curing of acrylic rubber compounds can release rubber fume, especially when a mold opens. HSE recommends source extraction around presses and control of skin contact with process residues. Assessment should use the complete compound formulation because curatives, fillers and processing aids contribute to exposure alongside the elastomer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: ACM is a family of copolymers, so cure-site chemistry and the choice of acrylate esters differ between grades. The cited patent’s low-temperature claims concern its described polymers and vulcanizates. Filler, plasticizer, cure and test medium affect the properties of a finished rubber. Resistance to one oil or exposure condition does not establish resistance to all fluids.

sections.overview: Ethylene–acrylic elastomer (AEM) is a rubber family based on ethylene and alkyl-acrylate units. Some grades also incorporate a cure-site monomer. A documented synthesis uses free-radical copolymerization of these monomers in solution. The polymers are compounded and crosslinked for applications needing heat- and oil-resistant rubber. Ethylene content and acrylate chemistry affect both fluid resistance and mobility at low temperature. The acrylate ester side groups increase the range of possible polar interactions compared with a hydrocarbon-only chain; adjusting the comonomers can shift the balance between oil swelling and glass transition. The rubber in a hose or seal is a formulated and cured compound, not the uncrosslinked base polymer.
sections.history: Ethylene–acrylic elastomers became commercial materials when DuPont introduced Vamac in 1975. Their development sought to combine resistance to oils and oxidation with useful low-temperature flexibility. Anestis Logothetis’s DuPont patent, with a 1971 application lineage and issued in 1975, documents ethylene/alkyl-acrylate copolymers incorporating cure-site monomers. Automotive sealing became an important application, including cylinder-head-cover gaskets. Later grades and formulations developed both terpolymer and dipolymer branches with different cure systems. The early patent records a particular polymerization approach; it is evidence of the development effort, not proof that every commercial AEM grade uses that exact route.
sections.nomenclature: AEM is the abbreviation used for ethylene–acrylic elastomer. The record covers ethylene/alkyl-acrylate elastomer copolymers, including specified cure-site variants; it excludes the thermoplastic ethylene–acrylic acid copolymer (EAA), ethylene–methacrylic acid copolymer (EMAA), and a particular cured compound as synonyms.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–acrylic elastomer (AEM) is an ethylene–alkyl-acrylate copolymer family, not the acid copolymer EAA. A manufacturer reference identifies a common AEM composition as ethylene, methyl acrylate, and a small amount of a carboxylic-acid-containing cure-site monomer. A historical DuPont patent supplies one bounded polymerization example: ethylene, a C1–C8 alkyl acrylate, and a cure-site monomer react in an inert solvent with boron trifluoride and a free-radical initiator. The cure-site is relevant only for formulations intended to be subsequently crosslinked; it should not be treated as mandatory for every ethylene–acrylate copolymer, and cure schedules are outside this synthesis record.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–acrylic elastomer (AEM) is an ethylene/acrylate rubber, commonly with a small cure-site comonomer, whose mechanical behavior is determined after vulcanization. Ethylene-to-acrylate balance controls low-temperature behavior, while cure-site chemistry, crosslink density, filler, plasticizer, hardness, and heat or fluid ageing control tensile, tear, damping, and compression-set results. An openly available AEM technical chapter notes that most commercial AEM materials include a third cure-site monomer enabling diamine crosslinking, so base-polymer composition alone does not define finished-part mechanics.

A bounded AEM technical-sheet example describes an ethylene/methyl-acrylate AEM family with 8–40% methyl acrylate and reports, for its stated test material, 100% tensile stress 6.00 MPa, tensile strength 16.0–16.4 MPa, elongation at break 260–280%, Shore A hardness 63–64, and compression set 16% after 70 h at 150 °C. Tensile values are labeled ASTM D412, hardness ASTM D2240, and compression set ASTM D395. These are supplier test-sheet values for that material, not a universal AEM range. A separate compound supplier reports 60- and 70-Shore-A AEM compounds at 13.8 MPa tensile strength with 450% and 400% elongation, respectively, further showing the formulation and hardness dependence.
sections.processing:
Ethylene–acrylic elastomer is converted as a compounded and vulcanized rubber. The selected AEM grade is mixed with filler, plasticizer or process aid, antioxidant, and its compatible cure package in an internal mixer or on an open mill, sheeted or pelletized, then extruded, calendered, compression-, transfer-, or injection-molded and cured. Cure chemistry is grade-dependent: acid-cure-site terpolymers commonly use diamine systems and may require post-cure, whereas ethylene/methyl-acrylate dipolymers can use peroxide/coagent systems. Ingredient compatibility, stock temperature, dispersion, scorch safety, venting, oxygen inhibition, article thickness, and post-cure requirements must therefore be qualified together.

DuPont's bounded Vamac DP examples were mixed in a small laboratory internal mixer, sheeted on a roll mill, and press-cured for 10 min at 177 °C. The same guide describes extrusion-head temperatures around 70 °C for its dipolymer compounds, pressure of at least 0.41–0.55 MPa during autoclave cure to avoid sponging, nitrogen purging because oxygen inhibits peroxide cure, and 160–190 °C molds. These values apply to the cited Vamac dipolymer compounds and equipment; diamine-cured AEM terpolymers use different packages and usually different cure/post-cure schedules.
sections.structureAndMorphology: AEM chains combine ethylene-derived units with acrylate units bearing ester side groups. Terpolymer grades may contain a small amount of a functional cure-site monomer. A documented cure route uses an amine to react with carboxyl-containing cure sites. Dipolymers and terpolymers need not have identical network chemistry or curing requirements. As an example, a patent reports one commercial terpolymer as 62.7 wt% methyl acrylate, 33.4 wt% ethylene and 3.9 wt% monoethyl fumarate. That composition is an identified grade, not the recipe for all AEM. The minor functional monomer permits a cure route distinct from the ethylene and methyl acrylate units forming most of that polymer.
sections.properties: AEM formulations balance flexibility, heat resistance and oil resistance. A patent discussing AEM and ACM notes that more polar acrylate units can reduce oil swell while raising the glass transition, which can work against low-temperature flexibility. In its particular vulcanizate comparison, example M1 had a DSC glass transition of −33 °C and 42% volume increase after 70 hours in IRM 903 oil at 150 °C; comparator VM1 had −29 °C and 49% under that test. These are distinct, formulated samples, not a universal composition–property rule or a rating for every AEM grade.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. AEM serves automotive fluid-contact seals and gaskets, extruded hoses and wire/cable compounds. DuPont identifies heat and resistance to engine and transmission fluids as relevant to demanding automotive service. Its high-viscosity Vamac Ultra DX formulation is intended to improve uncured compound strength during extrusion, helping a formed tube resist collapse and facilitating application of reinforcement. This processing benefit is specific to that grade and compound, while the finished part’s resistance depends on its formulation and service conditions.

Purchasing. The documented Vamac Ultra DX product is a raw-rubber bale grade intended for compounding and peroxide cure. The historical DuPont bulletin establishes product form; current supplier and availability require confirmation.

Scale and evidence limits. The bulletin gives nominal bale dimensions but no order mass or annual purchasing/consumption figure. No independent AEM-specific tonnage was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The manufacturer lists alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, esters and organic acids among the possible thermal decomposition products of VAMAC Ultra EV. Named examples include acetaldehyde, formaldehyde, acrolein, acrylic acid and maleic anhydride; carbon oxides and phosphorus-containing products are also listed. These are formulation-specific thermal products, not a measured inventory from ordinary weathering. In a separate patent, cured, carbon-black-filled ethylene–methyl acrylate terpolymer compounds changed tensile behavior after hot-air aging; the cure formulation affected the result.

Timescales: The SDS states that thermal decomposition accelerates above 282 °C and depends on both temperature and time at temperature. In the patent’s four formulated and post-cured compounds, six weeks in air at 150 °C led to reported tensile-strength changes of −6.6%, −14.4%, −17.3% and −19.6%, respectively, compared with their initial values. They used the same commercial polymer and carbon-black loading but different cure-agent or accelerator formulations. These are property changes for those specimens and recipes, not complete decomposition or a family-wide service life.

Environmental persistence: The supplied grade is water-insoluble and stable under normal handling. The safety sheet supplies no persistence or degradability data, and the patent measured tensile performance rather than conversion to carbon dioxide or biomass. Neither establishes a soil, water or landfill lifetime.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: For VAMAC Ultra EV as supplied, Celanese lists recycling, energy-recovery incineration and landfill as disposal options, emphasizing the material’s fuel value when recycling is unavailable. These are grade-specific waste-management options, with treatment subject to local requirements. The safety sheet does not establish a devulcanization process or recovery of AEM from a cured automotive part.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Celanese’s VAMAC Ultra EV safety sheet distinguishes the supplied AEM bales from hot processing conditions: heated material can emit irritating fumes, while contact with hot material can burn skin. It recommends local exhaust during hot processing, eye protection and gloves. These handling findings describe the specified commercial grade and its formulation, rather than every ethylene–acrylic elastomer compound.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Ethylene content, acrylate type and cure-site functionality vary among AEM grades. The chosen curative and post-cure can further change a finished vulcanizate. A supplier’s hardness, tensile or compression-set values describe the specific material and test stated in its sheet. They do not establish universal properties or fluid compatibility for the entire family.
