sections.overview: Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber, designated CO, is made by polymerizing epichlorohydrin. It belongs to the epichlorohydrin elastomer family but differs from copolymers containing ethylene oxide. Its polymer contains chloromethyl-bearing units and is compounded before use. The resulting vulcanizates have been used for oil- and fuel-contact applications. The chloromethyl-substituted polyether differs from the ethylene-oxide copolymer in its chain composition. In a historical EPA comparison of compounded vulcanizates, the homopolymer showed lower rebound and higher brittleness temperature than the copolymer, but less volume increase in the specified hot oil. That combination illustrates why fluid resistance and low-temperature recovery must be assessed together for a particular seal compound.
sections.history: The useful rubber form of polyepichlorohydrin must be distinguished from earlier crystalline polymer. Pruitt and Baggett at Dow prepared semicrystalline material in 1954; Edwin Vandenberg at Hercules developed amorphous polyepichlorohydrin in 1957. In his oral history, Vandenberg describes discovering the importance of water-modified organoaluminum catalysts and the subsequent licensing arrangement with B. F. Goodrich. Hercules and Goodrich commercialized epichlorohydrin elastomers under Herclor and Hydrin names. The oil-resistant rubber platform supported hoses, seals and air ducts, while later research explored membranes and electrolytes. Those later applications include copolymers and modified materials, and should not all be assigned to the unmodified homopolymer.
sections.nomenclature: CO is the abbreviation for the epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber record; poly(chloromethyloxirane) is an alternate chemical name. The homopolymer boundary excludes ECO, the epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide copolymer, and does not equate a cured compound with the uncured polymer record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber (CO, polyepichlorohydrin) is the ring-opening polymerization product of epichlorohydrin; the resulting repeat units retain chloromethyl side groups. A historical assessment identifies high-molecular-weight CO as a distinct elastomer made from the single epichlorohydrin feedstock. In one modern, source-specific activated-monomer route, epichlorohydrin is added in a controlled manner to a boron trifluoride diethyl etherate/water initiating system in toluene; the report describes operation at 20–40 °C and polymer isolation after conversion. These are polymer-formation examples, not a recommendation of a universal catalyst system or an article cure schedule.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber (CO) is a cured elastomer, so its tensile, elongation, hardness, rebound, and compression-set response belong to a specified vulcanizate rather than to the uncured gum alone. The chlorine-rich CO homopolymer is described as having good oil resistance and low-temperature flexibility but poorer rebound than the ethylene-oxide copolymer. Cure chemistry and crosslink density, carbon-black reinforcement, plasticizer, hardness target, and ageing environment all materially change the measured response; the public EPA report specifically notes carbon black as a tensile-strength improver and plasticizer as a low-temperature-flexibility aid.

A bounded published vulcanizate comparison in that EPA report gives the ECH homopolymer 15.9 MPa tensile strength, 230% ultimate elongation, 82 Shore A hardness, −18 °C low-temperature brittleness, and Lupke rebound 26% at 23 °C and 75% at 100 °C. The report does not identify the complete formulation or the tensile test standard, so these are comparative vulcanizate values, not neat-gum properties or a family range. A separate rubber-compound supplier illustrates the formulation issue: its 50-Shore-A CO/ECO compound 571AG lists 9.7 MPa tensile strength and 400% elongation; because it does not distinguish CO from ECO or disclose a full cure package, it is contextual compound evidence only.
sections.processing:
Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber is converted by conventional elastomer compounding, shaping, and vulcanization. Fillers, plasticizers, process aids, antidegradants, metal oxides, and the selected cure package are incorporated on a mill or internal mixer before extrusion, calendering, or molding. Because many CO cure systems release or generate acidic species, the Vanderbilt handbook emphasizes acid acceptors and pH control; magnesium oxide, calcium carbonate, or calcium oxide may be used in formulation-specific roles to bind hydrogen chloride and support the cure. Mixing sequence and temperature must preserve scorch safety and dispersion, and the chosen press, injection, steam, hot-air, infrared, or microwave cure must be qualified for the compound and article thickness.

A bounded Osaka Soda patent example mixed a stated epichlorohydrin-rubber formulation for 15 min on rolls held at 80 °C, sheeted it, and pressure-molded it at 160 °C and 7.8 MPa for 20 min. The patent also gives a much broader 100–200 °C and 0.5–60 min cure envelope across its examples and cure systems. Neither the roll/mold schedule nor that broad patent envelope is a universal CO production window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polymerization of epichlorohydrin yields a polyether chain carrying chloromethyl side groups. The homopolymer contains no ethylene-oxide comonomer and is distinct from the related ECO copolymer. Catalyst and polymerization conditions affect the polymer produced, while compounding and curing convert the raw gum into a network. The finished article can also contain fillers, plasticizers and stabilizers, so its morphology and response are not determined by the homopolymer alone. In the historical assessment, the homopolymer is described as predominantly head-to-tail epichlorohydrin units. Chloromethyl groups along the side chains supply functionality for curing, while the polyether main chain remains the structural backbone. Formulation and degree of cure control the network that actually bears load in the finished article.
sections.properties: An EPA assessment compares specified vulcanizates of epichlorohydrin homopolymer and ethylene-oxide copolymer. The homopolymer had 26% Lupke rebound at 23 °C versus 67% for the copolymer, and a brittleness temperature of −18 °C versus −40 °C. After 70 hours in No. 3 oil at 150 °C, its volume change was 4% versus 8%. Thus the reported homopolymer was less resilient and less flexible at low temperature, but swelled less in that oil; these are formulation-specific comparisons, not family-wide limits.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber serves automotive fuel and oil hoses, diaphragms and gaskets, where a flexible component must contact fluids. Zeon identifies Hydrin H75 specifically as a homopolymer and lists these applications for its epichlorohydrin rubber portfolio. An older fuel-hose patent describes a test compound based on Herclor H, an epichlorohydrin homopolymer. After 14 days in sour gasoline at 40 °C, a cured sheet without the added blending elastomer retained about 19% of its initial tensile strength, while the example blended with a polythiodiethanol elastomer retained about 58%. This shows why resistance must be tested for the actual blend and fuel; the specimens were test sheets, not production hoses. Manufacturers compound and cure the supplied rubber before making parts; the resistance and mechanical response of a finished hose or seal therefore depend on the compound and exposure, not only the polymer name.

Purchasing. Zeon explicitly identifies Hydrin H75 as the homopolymer and supplies it in bales for compounding; it is distinct from ECO copolymers and GECO terpolymers. Its product table lists a Mooney viscosity design value of 75 for H75 and identifies a non-staining antioxidant. The bale is a raw-compounding material rather than a ready-made seal.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber is explicitly included in a heat-stabilization patent describing hydrogen chloride release during curing or severe heating. A complete inventory of environmental breakdown products remains unresolved.

Timescales: A patent describes accelerated ageing of blends containing epichlorohydrin homopolymer and nitrile rubber at 150 °C, including a three-day measurement. The patent also reports that after 20 days at 150 °C a crosslinked homopolymer control softened, while its homopolymer/nitrile-rubber blend remained hard. This contrast concerns those particular formulations and does not establish the environmental lifetime of the homopolymer. Cure and additives also influence ageing response.

Environmental persistence: The cited chlorine-containing elastomers resist weathering and ozone. This resistance is not a measured mineralization lifetime; stabilizers and cure chemistry influence the finished compound.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Laboratory chlorine reclamation has been demonstrated using commercial polyepichlorohydrin (PECH; reported Mw about 700,000). Liu and colleagues reacted this polymer with 7,8-benzoquinoline using Cu/Pd catalysts and sodium nitrate in DMSO under 3 bar oxygen at 140 °C for 15 h, producing 10-chlorobenzoquinoline. This chemical-reclamation route transfers chlorine into a new product; it does not recover intact rubber or epichlorohydrin monomer. The study used purchased pure polymer, so its result does not establish recovery of compounded, vulcanized CO service parts or commercial operation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber articles, trimming and finishing are distinct exposure-generating operations. HSE recommends local extraction for finishing emissions, appropriate protection against skin contamination and cleaning without dispersing dust. These controls address fabricated rubber compounds; any additional chemical hazards must be assessed from the grade’s curatives, fillers and processing conditions.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: CO homopolymer and epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide copolymers are not interchangeable material identities. Cure system, filler and plasticizer affect the properties of the finished vulcanizate. The EPA comparison uses specified formulations and fluid-exposure conditions. A sealing supplier’s values are likewise tied to its named compound and cannot describe every CO grade.

sections.overview: Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber (ECO) is an elastomeric copolyether made from epichlorohydrin and ethylene oxide. It is distinct from CO, the epichlorohydrin homopolymer. A documented route uses a catalyst system to copolymerize the two cyclic ethers. ECO is compounded and cured for products such as seals and hoses. Adding ethylene oxide alters the chain relative to the epichlorohydrin homopolymer. In a historical comparison of cured compounds, the copolymer had greater room-temperature rebound and a lower brittleness temperature, but more swelling in the specified hot oil. Those measurements show a practical tradeoff for the compared recipes, not a guarantee for every ECO grade.
sections.history: Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber emerged from Edwin Vandenberg’s Hercules research into high-molecular-weight polyethers. Adding ethylene oxide developed the amorphous epichlorohydrin platform into a distinct copolymer rubber. Vandenberg’s 1976 technical account identifies both Hercules and B. F. Goodrich as substantial producers, under the Herclor and Hydrin names, and explains the appeal of combining oil resistance with useful rubber and environmental behavior. The Hydrin business subsequently became associated with Zeon. Automotive fuel-system parts were an important outlet, and later grades also served conductive printer and copier components. These are milestones for the copolymer branch, rather than an independent discovery date inferred from the first epichlorohydrin homopolymer.
sections.nomenclature: ECO is the abbreviation used for the epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide copolymer rubber. This copolymer record excludes CO homopolymer and other epichlorohydrin copolymers with different comonomer scopes; a vulcanized ECO compound is a formulation state, not a separate synonym for the base copolymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber (ECO) is a copolyether elastomer made by ring-opening copolymerization of epichlorohydrin and ethylene oxide. The historical assessment distinguishes ECO from CO and describes trialkylaluminum/water catalyst systems, with acetylacetone as a catalyst-promoting additive, for epichlorohydrin elastomer manufacture; it also notes that ethylene oxide reacts more rapidly than epichlorohydrin in a cited copolymer operation. An independent patent example instead polymerizes the two epoxides in ether/toluene using an organomagnesium/resorcinol catalyst system, then precipitates and purifies the copolymer. These route examples establish feedstocks and polymer-formation chemistry only; downstream vulcanization is not included here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber (ECO) is a vulcanized copolyether elastomer whose physical response varies with epichlorohydrin/ethylene-oxide composition, polymer molecular weight, cure chemistry and density, reinforcement and plasticizer loading, hardness target, and ageing medium. Relative to the epichlorohydrin homopolymer, the ethylene-oxide-containing copolymer is described in a public comparison as having better low-temperature flexibility and rebound but lower oil resistance. Zeon likewise presents tensile, elongation, and compression set as values of a ‘typical Hydrin compound’ and a broad compound range, rather than ECO constants.

A bounded vulcanizate example in the EPA comparison reports ECH–ethylene oxide copolymer tensile strength 15.0 MPa, ultimate elongation 320%, Shore A hardness 74, low-temperature brittleness −40 °C, and Lupke rebound 67% at 23 °C and 63% at 100 °C. The source does not give full formulation or tensile-method details, so these are comparative cured-compound values only. Zeon’s current ECO page lists, for a typical Hydrin compound, tensile at break 14 MPa, elongation at break 450%, and compression set 15% after 22 h at 100 °C; the listed across-compound ranges are 8–18 MPa, 150–600%, and 10–25%, respectively. These supplier figures are illustrative formulation ranges, not specifications for every ECO grade.
sections.processing:
Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber is processed by compounding the gum with reinforcing or mineral filler, plasticizer and process aid, antidegradant, metal oxides or other acid acceptors, and a cure system, followed by extrusion, calendering, injection molding, or compression molding and vulcanization. The Vanderbilt handbook notes that ECO is compounded broadly like other elastomers but that cure-package acidity and compound pH deserve particular control: acid acceptors such as magnesium oxide, calcium carbonate, or calcium oxide can bind hydrogen chloride and influence cure behavior. Mixing order and stock temperature should therefore be set to obtain dispersion without consuming scorch safety, and cure time must be adjusted for the formulation and article thickness.

A patent example covering an epichlorohydrin/ethylene-oxide copolymer mixed the specified compound for 15 min on 80 °C rolls, formed a sheet, and pressure-molded it at 160 °C and 7.8 MPa for 20 min. The same patent lists press and injection molding plus steam, hot-air, infrared, and microwave heating as possible cure routes and gives a broad 100–200 °C, 0.5–60 min range across its formulations. Those conditions are examples from that cure chemistry, not universal ECO settings.
sections.structureAndMorphology: ECO chains contain chloromethyl-bearing epichlorohydrin units and ethylene-oxide-derived units along a polyether backbone. Their relative amounts and arrangement depend on synthesis, so the copolymer is distinct from CO homopolymer and epichlorohydrin terpolymers. Introducing ethylene oxide changes the balance of chlorinated and nonchlorinated units. Compounding and vulcanization create the finished network, with fillers and curatives contributing further structural differences. The EPA assessment notes that an approximately 1:1 copolymer can contain sequences of ethylene-oxide units rather than a perfectly alternating pattern. The chain sequence and ratio are set during polymerization; cure and compounding subsequently create the elastic network. An ECO formulation consequently cannot be inferred from the homopolymer structure alone.
sections.properties: ECO is used where fluid resistance and low-temperature flexibility must be balanced. In an EPA assessment’s comparison of specified vulcanizates, the ethylene-oxide copolymer had 67% Lupke rebound at 23 °C and brittleness temperature −40 °C, versus 26% and −18 °C for the homopolymer. Its volume change after 70 hours in No. 3 oil at 150 °C was 8%, compared with 4% for the homopolymer. This example shows greater resilience and lower brittleness temperature with greater oil swelling in those particular compounds, not in every ECO formulation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber is used in automotive fuel and oil hoses, diaphragms and gaskets, where flexible parts encounter fluids. Zeon describes a multilayer fuel hose with a bisphenol-cured fluororubber (FKM) inner layer, a Hydrin C2000 copolymer tie layer with reinforcing braid, and a separate epichlorohydrin terpolymer cover. The tie layer helps the hose layers adhere; the FKM and terpolymer are distinct materials with different functions. The finished hose's fluid resistance and flexibility depend on the compound, cure, layers and service conditions.

Purchasing. Zeon lists Hydrin C2000 and C2000L specifically as epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide copolymer bales. Its Japanese grade table gives design Mooney viscosities of 96 and 70, respectively; the U.S. table gives ranges of 90–102 and 65–75, measured as ML(1+4) at 100 °C. These are raw-rubber grade distinctions that help a compounder select processing behavior, not specifications for the cured part. Other Hydrin grades include the epichlorohydrin homopolymer and terpolymers, so the grade and composition must be checked.

Scale and evidence limits. The supplier identifies industrial grade forms and applications but does not provide a separate annual ECO copolymer production or purchase total. A hose includes other materials and formulation ingredients, so its mass cannot be assigned entirely to the copolymer. The multilayer construction is a supplier example rather than a market-share estimate.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A pyrolysis study of a named 50/50 epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide copolymer detected hydrogen chloride and mass-spectral signals consistent with low-molecular-weight hydrocarbons and chlorinated hydrocarbons. The researchers proposed free-radical chain cleavage and subsequent reactions as a route to these volatile products. A separate heat-stabilization patent describes hydrogen chloride release from chlorine-containing elastomers during curing or severe heating. Products generated by analytical pyrolysis are not an inventory of compounds released during ordinary service or environmental weathering.

Timescales: A patent reports a carbon-black-filled, cured copolymer containing 68 wt% epichlorohydrin: tensile strength fell from 2,500 to 960 psi after five days in circulating air at 300 °F (about 149 °C). That result describes the specified compound and oven test. In the pyrolysis study, samples were subjected to repeated two-second heating intervals at 350, 387 or 400 °C to follow volatile-product evolution; these much hotter analytical exposures are not service-life tests. In another study, ethylenethiourea-cured copolymer irradiated in air at room temperature over 0–20 Mrad showed decreases in modulus, hardness and calculated network-chain density; the authors interpreted its solubility data as consistent with main-chain scission. The radiation dose describes a different stress and is not an outdoor exposure duration.

Environmental persistence: Zeon describes ozone resistance for its epichlorohydrin elastomer portfolio, but resistance to a particular exposure does not measure complete mineralization. Loss of tensile strength, changes in network density and production of volatile fragments are distinct endpoints. The cited tests do not establish the lifetime or carbon mineralization of a specified ECO article in soil, freshwater or seawater; formulation, additives and exposure conditions matter.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Laboratory chlorine reclamation has been demonstrated using commercial poly(epichlorohydrin-co-ethylene oxide) containing 64–69 wt% epichlorohydrin. Liu and colleagues reacted this polymer with 7,8-benzoquinoline using Cu/Pd catalysts and sodium nitrate in DMSO under 3 bar oxygen at 140 °C for 15 h, producing 10-chlorobenzoquinoline. This chemical-reclamation route transfers chlorine into a new product; it does not recover intact rubber or epichlorohydrin monomer. The study used purchased pure polymer, so its result does not establish recovery of compounded, vulcanized ECO service parts or commercial operation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber articles, trimming and finishing are distinct exposure-generating operations. HSE recommends local extraction for finishing emissions, appropriate protection against skin contamination and cleaning without dispersing dust. These controls address fabricated rubber compounds; any additional chemical hazards must be assessed from the grade’s curatives, fillers and processing conditions.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Comonomer ratio, catalyst, grade and cure system influence ECO properties. The EPA comparison is for defined vulcanizate recipes and exposure conditions, not every CO or ECO grade. Supplier data similarly describe particular compounded materials and tests. Fluid resistance and low-temperature response should be evaluated for the intended formulation and exposure.

sections.overview: Chlorinated polyethylene elastomer (CPE) is made by replacing some hydrogen atoms in polyethylene with chlorine. The starting polyethylene and the degree of chlorination affect the material obtained. Elastomeric grades can be compounded and crosslinked into rubber articles. Uses described in the cited sources include wire and cable and hoses. Chlorine substitution changes how the original polyethylene chains pack and can reduce the crystalline regions that make polyethylene rigid. Elastomeric CPE is then formulated for flexibility, for example as a cable jacket or hose; fillers and the cure package still determine the finished compound. Other CPE grades serve as modifiers for plastics, so the name alone does not specify a rubber article.
sections.history: Chlorinated polyethylene developed as manufacturers learned to turn polyethylene into products ranging from flexible plastics to rubbers by controlling chlorination. Peter Canterino’s Phillips Petroleum patent, filed in 1955 and issued in 1963, records an early route and discusses tubing, electrical insulation and protective coatings. A later industrial milestone was Dow’s 1971 introduction of Tyrin made by aqueous-suspension chlorination. This helped develop an economical production platform with different residual-crystallinity grades. Wire and cable coverings and hose became major elastomer applications, while more crystalline or blended CPE served plastics modification. The histories overlap, but an impact-modifier grade should not automatically be treated as equivalent to crosslinked CPE rubber.
sections.nomenclature: CPE is the general abbreviation for chlorinated polyethylene, while CM is also used for the chlorinated-polyethylene elastomer class. This record is scoped to elastomeric CPE and should not make every chlorinated polyethylene grade an automatic synonym.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Chlorinated polyethylene elastomer is obtained by chemical post-chlorination of a polyethylene feedstock, not by an ethylene/chlorine copolymerization. A documented solution route keeps polyethylene dissolved in chlorinated solvent while chlorine is introduced, then recovers chlorinated polyethylene; the cited example limits its stated product range to its selected linear, high-density polyethylene feedstocks and chlorine contents. A separate aqueous-suspension manufacturing example charges HDPE and auxiliaries to water, heats the suspension, and feeds chlorine; its reported sequence includes acid removal, centrifugation, and drying after reaction. These are alternative documented manufacture routes, not a universal recipe or a family-wide elastomer specification.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Chlorinated polyethylene elastomer (CPE, CM) is a chlorine-substituted polyethylene whose tensile and elastic response depends on chlorine content and distribution, molecular-weight/entanglement characteristics, filler and plasticizer package, crosslinking agent and cure, and article form. A public patent describing wire-and-cable CPE distinguishes uncrosslinked CPE from filled/crosslinked compounds and specifies that its reported ASTM D412 outcomes depend on chlorine content and the chlorination/cure process. As a narrowly bounded material example, the CPE 135A supplier sheet specifies 35 ± 1% chlorine, Shore hardness no greater than 60, tensile strength at least 8 MPa, and elongation at break 700%; it does not state the test standard, specimen preparation, cure, or temperature, so those numbers are useful only as grade-sheet targets, not a CPE property range. The patent's separately bounded chlorinated material, made by slurry chlorination at 120–140 °C for 2–5 h, reports for 33–38 wt% chlorine an ASTM D412 tensile strength of 12.5–15 MPa and tensile elongation of 900–1200%; its process-specific results likewise do not establish values for other CPE compounds.
sections.processing: CPE elastomer compounds can be calendered, injection molded, or extruded into cable jackets, hose, tubing, and foam. Molecular-mass distribution and residual crystallinity affect the processability/performance balance; CPE can also be blended or plasticized before conversion. For one CPE/hard-resin composite, heated-shear mixing in an extruder, roll mill, Banbury mixer, or kneader was specified at 130–210 °C, with 210 °C identified as the upper thermal-deterioration limit; these are composite-specific conditions. Its examples used Banbury mixing (120 °C jacket, 80 rpm, 3 min; compound reached 160 °C), roll-sheeting/pelletizing, and 180 °C press molding for 5 min, followed where required by coextrusion or insert molding.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Chlorination introduces chlorine-containing sites along the polyethylene-derived chains. Chlorine content and the structure of the parent polyethylene influence residual crystallinity and flexibility. An elastomeric grade is one outcome of this family of modified polyethylenes, which also includes other material types. Compounding and curing can join chains into a network. The parent polyethylene is part of the design as well as the chlorine level. In a patent series using different precursor polyethylenes, an example containing 38.4 wt% chlorine had a reported uncured CPE tensile strength of 12.6 MPa and elongation of 1010% under ASTM D412 at 500 mm/min. Those are measurements on the specified material and test, not values for an arbitrary cured cable compound.
sections.properties: CPE compounds can be designed for flexible wire, cable or hose uses, but their response depends on the starting polyethylene, chlorination and formulation. In a patent example, chlorinated polyethylene with 38.4 wt% chlorine gave a tensile strength of 12.6 MPa and elongation of 1,010% in an ASTM D412 test at 500 mm/min. A separately compounded material using that series had different tensile values, illustrating the effect of additives and crosslinking. These patent measurements are sample-specific, not a family-wide allowable or finished-hose rating.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Chlorinated polyethylene elastomers serve wire and cable jackets, hoses and tubing in construction, industrial and vehicle service. These articles use a compounded elastomer formulation, while other CPE products function mainly as plastics modifiers. The required flexibility, fluid resistance and manufacturing process guide selection. A supplier datasheet lists Keliren CM3680F for wire and cable, cable jackets and hoses, with extrusion and injection molding among its conversion methods. This is a grade description, and final performance depends on the compounded material and cure.

Purchasing. The supplier-authored article identifies powder as the raw-material form and lists application-specific Keliren CM grades. Buyers specify the elastomer grade and conversion requirements before compounding or curing.

Scale and evidence limits. The February/March 2022 article identifies wire/cable and hose as the two largest CPE applications in North America, without tonnage or percentages. No reliable separate consumption total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Chlorinated polyethylene rubber is explicitly included in a heat-stabilization patent describing hydrogen chloride release during curing or severe heating. A complete inventory of environmental breakdown products remains unresolved.

Timescales: Filled, peroxide-cured CPE specimens based on Tyrin CM 0836 were aged for 168 hours in dry air at 150 °C. Elongation retention was 49–62%, depending on stabilizer loading. In the 12-phr barium sulfate formulation, elongation retention was 62% after dry-air aging but 47% after the same duration in Dextron IIE transmission fluid, with 12.9% volume increase in the fluid. These results compare different exposures of one compounded material; they show service-related property changes rather than mineralization.

Environmental persistence: The cited chlorine-containing elastomers resist weathering and ozone. This resistance is not a measured mineralization lifetime; stabilizers and cure chemistry influence the finished compound.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Dow lists licensed recycling or reclamation among preferred destinations for unused, uncontaminated TYRIN CM 3551E CPE; permitted thermal treatment or landfill are alternatives. This guidance concerns uncured material as supplied and does not demonstrate recycling of a crosslinked CPE part. Waste handling must also account for combustible powder and hydrogen-chloride evolution during thermal degradation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For TYRIN CM 3551E CPE powder, Dow identifies combustible-dust and static-ignition hazards during conveying and handling. Dust can mechanically irritate eyes, hot material can burn skin, and thermal degradation can release irritating hydrogen chloride. Prevent dust accumulation, control ignition sources, and use ventilation and task-appropriate eye and thermal protection. The sheet describes the supplied formulated powder.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: CPE is not defined by one chlorine content or one polyethylene starting material. Chlorination can reduce the crystallinity of the parent material, but resin and elastomeric grades differ in their actual composition and structure. The patent’s measured chlorinated polymer and filled, crosslinked compound are separate specimens and cannot be treated as the same material. Processing, cure and test conditions should accompany any reported mechanical comparison.

sections.overview: Chlorosulfonated polyethylene rubber (CSM or CSPE) is a polyethylene-derived elastomer bearing chlorine and sulfonyl functionality. A documented route reacts chlorinated polyethylene with chlorine and sulfur dioxide. The functionalized polymer can be compounded and cured into rubber. Its composition and network differ from those of chlorinated polyethylene without sulfonyl functionality. The additional sulfonyl functionality provides sites for cure, while chlorine content is one variable distinguishing grades. A study compared CSM with 29%, 35% and 43% bound chlorine, each cured with iron oxide, and found different mechanical responses. These are experimental compounds; a finished lining or cable formulation can also contain fillers and other additives.
sections.history: Chlorosulfonated polyethylene developed through chemical modification of polyethylene into a curable specialty rubber. Heinz Noeske and Otto Roelen’s patent, issued in 1959, already describes conventional solution chlorosulfonation and proposes a solid-phase route for newer polyethylene feedstocks. It therefore records process development within an existing field. Tosoh began CSM production in November 1983 and later broadened the platform with its extos materials. Applications included industrial and automotive hoses, cable coverings, inflatable boats, linings and construction joints. The later supplier milestones concern production and application development, rather than the first synthesis of this established polymer family.
sections.nomenclature: CSM abbreviates chlorosulfonated polyethylene. The name distinguishes this material from chlorinated polyethylene, because chlorosulfonation introduces an additional functional group; commercial names are not treated as canonical family names.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Chlorosulfonated polyethylene rubber is post-modified polyethylene bearing chlorine and sulfonyl-chloride substituents. One cited route contacts finely divided polyethylene with chlorine and sulfur dioxide gases without a solvent. Another prepares a particulate chlorinated polyethylene first and then contacts it with a chlorine/sulfur dioxide gas mixture; the starting grade, prechlorination and operating conditions are specific to that example. Later curing is a separate step.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Chlorosulfonated polyethylene rubber (CSM) develops its useful elastomeric mechanics after compounding and curing. Tensile strength, elongation, stiffness, tear response, hardness, and compression behavior depend on chlorine/sulfonyl-chloride content, cure chemistry and crosslink density, filler type and loading, and the test specimen; a cured-compound result is not an intrinsic property of all CSM grades.

A bounded unfilled-vulcanizate example used CSM43 (43% bound chlorine) crosslinked with iron(II,III) oxide at 160 °C for 15 min. Tensile testing to PN-ISO 37:2017 reported tensile strength at break of 6.97 ± 0.56 MPa and elongation at break of 38 ± 12%. In the same study, CSM29 and CSM35 vulcanizates gave lower tensile strengths (1.61 ± 0.10 and 1.25 ± 0.10 MPa) with different elongation, illustrating the sensitivity to CSM composition and cure network.

For comparison, a supplier’s named acid-resistant CSM compounds 399ES and 399BL (60 and 70 Shore A) list tensile strengths of 12.4 and 13.8 MPa with elongations of 400% and 300%, respectively. Those values are compound-specific and demonstrate why commercial CSM performance must remain attached to the formulation, cure, hardness, and method rather than combined into a family range.
sections.processing: CSM rubber is compounded with fillers, plasticizer/extender, stabilizers, and a cure package, then shaped and vulcanized; dynamically vulcanized CSM/polyolefin blends can be sheeted, compression molded, extruded, or injection molded. One CSM-containing thermoplastic-elastomer patent describes completing cure on a heated two-roll mill or static oven. Its single-Banbury procedure used a 70% load, about 5 min melt blending, then 3 min at 176.7–204.4 °C after addition of cure ingredients; that dynamic-vulcanization procedure is blend-specific. A separate filled/plasticized CSM formulation mixed internally at 65–75 °C for 8–12 min, on an open mill at 75–85 °C for 3–4 min, added accelerators at 88–93 °C for 1–3 min, and ventilated-cooled to 15–35 °C; these values apply only to that formulation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The polyethylene-derived chains contain chlorine and sulfonyl-chloride-derived groups. In the cited route, chlorosulfonation is performed on particulate chlorinated polyethylene. The functional groups enable curing reactions, and additives become part of the formulated material. One study compared several CSM grades cured using iron oxide, both unfilled and with mineral or carbon fillers. Filler choice can change the structure and mechanical response of the cured material. In the same study of CSM43, adding arsil silica raised reported tensile strength from 6.97 to 12.40 MPa and elongation at break to 187% relative to the unfilled specimen. The paper lists the unfilled elongation as 38% and 46% in separate tables without explaining the difference. These comparisons use the study’s particular iron-oxide cure and mixing conditions; they are not universal predictions for every CSM compound.
sections.properties: Mechanical response depends strongly on CSM grade and formulation. In one study using iron oxide as a crosslinker, unfilled CSM43 had tensile strength of 6.97 MPa, while the tested arsil-filled CSM43 reached 12.40 MPa and 187% elongation, under the authors’ respective cure conditions. The paper reports unfilled elongation as 38% in one table and 46% in another without explaining the discrepancy. This illustrates that reinforcement can change both strength and deformation, but the unconventional cure system and specific formulations prevent extrapolation to all CSM vulcanizates.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Chlorosulfonated polyethylene compounds are used for cable sheaths, acid hoses, linings, seals, diaphragms and roller coverings. KRAIBURG identifies resistance to ozone and weather, oxidizing agents, and many hot acids and alkalis among the reasons for selecting its CSM compounds. Acid hoses and linings use this resistance in contact with process media, while a cable sheath can face outdoor weathering. Resistance depends on the specific compound, chemical, temperature and exposure; a general material listing does not qualify every service.

Purchasing. KRAIBURG offers CSM rubber compounds for component manufacture; buyers specify the compound and part for the intended service. The checked Minnesota Rubber guide describes material properties but no longer displays the previously listed compound designations.

Scale and evidence limits. KRAIBURG describes applications ranging from cable sheaths to acid hoses and roller coatings. Its documentation does not give the quantities of CSM in those uses or a CSM-specific production, purchase or consumption total.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Chlorosulfonated polyethylene rubber is explicitly included in a heat-stabilization patent describing hydrogen chloride release during curing or severe heating. A complete inventory of environmental breakdown products remains unresolved.

Timescales: In a Sandia comparison of a Samuel Moore Dekoron chlorosulfonated-polyethylene cable jacket at 138 °C, elongation fell more rapidly in air than in argon. The accelerated test lasted on the order of weeks and shows the influence of oxygen on mechanical ageing of this particular jacket. It does not establish a natural-environment mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: The cited chlorine-containing elastomers resist weathering and ozone. This resistance is not a measured mineralization lifetime; stabilizers and cure chemistry influence the finished compound.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A hydrothermal-devulcanization patent lists CSM among rubber feedstocks and proposes grinding, hot pressurized-water treatment and blending the treated rubber with fresh material. The stated mechanism targets sulfur crosslinks, so its relevance depends on the actual CSM cure system. The patent listing does not establish a CSM-specific trial, recovery yield or commercial deployment.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Press curing of chlorosulfonated polyethylene rubber compounds can release rubber fume, especially when a mold opens. HSE recommends source extraction around presses and control of skin contact with process residues. Assessment should use the complete compound formulation because curatives, fillers and processing aids contribute to exposure alongside the elastomer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Chlorine and sulfonyl content can vary with polymer and reaction conditions. The iron-oxide study evaluated particular grades and an unconventional curing system, so its values do not define all commercial CSM vulcanizates. Filler selection, dispersion and curing schedule further change the response. Fluid or weather resistance must be assessed for the compound and exposure rather than inferred solely from the family name.

sections.overview: FKM is a family of fluorinated elastomer copolymers. Common architectures include vinylidene fluoride–hexafluoropropylene copolymers and related terpolymers containing tetrafluoroethylene. Different monomer combinations and cure systems produce materials for different operating conditions. FKM compounds are widely used for seals requiring resistance to heat and fluids. Chemical and heat resistance make FKM useful in seals, but different grades balance this against flexibility at low temperature. Cure systems also differ: a gum polymer may be compounded with a separate curative, while other grades are supplied as precompounds. Selecting the material therefore requires the intended fluid, temperature and cure method.
sections.history: A major FKM milestone was DuPont’s development of Viton in 1957 from vinylidene fluoride and hexafluoropropylene. Its early aerospace sealing role expanded into automotive valve-stem and transmission seals, chemical equipment and other demanding gasket applications. The material subsequently diversified into grades with different fluorine contents and comonomers, balancing fluid resistance and low-temperature behavior. Daikin’s chronology records its own DAIEL fluoroelastomer launch in 1970, illustrating the growth beyond the original DuPont product lineage. The 1957 date belongs to Viton’s development; it should not be treated as the invention date of every fluorinated rubber or every later FKM composition.
sections.nomenclature: FKM is a family designation, not a single fluoropolymer composition or cured rubber compound. The VDF/HFP dipolymer and peroxide-curable FKM compositions with additional cure-site monomers are distinct members of the family, so monomer architecture and cure system must remain identified for a specific material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: FKM is a vinylidene-fluoride-containing fluoroelastomer family, not a single fixed copolymer. Documented backbones include vinylidene fluoride (VDF) with hexafluoropropene (HFP), and may add tetrafluoroethylene, ethylene, or perfluorovinyl ethers. A Unimatec patent illustrates aqueous-emulsion manufacture of VDF/HFP and related fluoroelastomer architectures, with a perfluorocarboxylate emulsifier and optional cure-site-forming monomer or bromine/iodine source. Cure-site monomers or halogenated chain ends are composition features selected when later network formation is needed; they should not be confused with the free-radical copolymerization that creates the base FKM. An independent FKM source also distinguishes peroxide-curable terpolymers from VDF/HFP dipolymers lacking those reactive sites.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
FKM is a family of fluorocarbon elastomers whose useful mechanical response follows compounding and cure. Tensile strength, elongation, hardness, compression set, and temperature response depend on fluoroelastomer type, cure system and state, fillers, plasticizers, specimen geometry, and thermal or fluid exposure; compound data cannot be used as an intrinsic FKM family range.

A bounded sheet-compound example is J-Flex A-type FDA-compliant FKM, a 66% fluorine dipolymer. The data sheet reports 64 ± 5 Shore A, tensile strength 14 MPa and elongation at break 250% by ASTM D412, plus 18% compression set by ASTM D395 Method B after 22 h at 200 °C. These values are specific to that cured sheet compound and condition.

An open FKM-compound study printed peroxide-cured FKM tensile bars to ASTM D412-C and used DMA/DSC to establish the processing and cure window. It illustrates that curing route and manufactured form affect the measured elastomer response.
sections.processing: FKM is converted as a compounded, uncured elastomer: polymer gum is mixed with fillers and a cure package, then shaped by compression, transfer, or injection molding and vulcanized. Extrusion can also be used for preforms or specialized additive manufacturing, but the compound must remain below its cure onset until shaping is complete. In an open FKM/FFKM demonstration, Tecnoflon 959 FKM with peroxide and silica was mixed in an internal mixer, single-screw extruded to 1.75 mm filament, and printed on a modified FDM printer. DSC placed the FKM compound's cure onset near 95 °C and completion near 187 °C; the reported printing trial used 130 °C, dry-ice precooling near the drive gears, a short constrained filament path, and a large nozzle to limit premature cure, buckling, and under-extrusion. For a conventional Viton A-201C compound containing MgO, calcium hydroxide, and N-990 carbon black, Chemours reports slabs cured 10 min at 177 °C and post-cured 24 h at 232 °C. These settings are formulation- and equipment-specific rather than FKM-family constants.
sections.structureAndMorphology: FKM chains contain fluorinated monomer units, with composition varying across the family. A vinylidene fluoride–hexafluoropropylene dipolymer differs from a terpolymer that also contains tetrafluoroethylene. Cure-site monomers or reactive chain ends may be introduced for a particular cure system. The finished rubber contains crosslinks and frequently fillers in addition to the base polymer. One documented peroxide-curable group contains reactive cure-site monomers in addition to VDF and HFP; peroxide and a multifunctional coagent can then form crosslinks. Other FKM grades use bisphenol or diamine cure chemistry, so a cure package suitable for one grade cannot automatically be transferred to another. Fillers and cure conditions further determine the final network.
sections.properties: FKM compounds are used for resistance to heat, fuels, oils and many chemicals, but their fluid resistance and low-temperature flexibility can pull in opposite directions. Chemours reports that increasing fluorine content among its standard A, B and F types improves resistance to some fluids while reducing low-temperature flexibility. In typical 30-phr carbon-black-filled, 75-durometer vulcanizates, A and F showed 90% and 5% volume increase respectively after 168 hours in methanol at 23 °C, and TR-10 retraction temperatures of −17 °C and −6 °C. These formulation-specific values illustrate a tradeoff, not a universal FKM rule or a service specification.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. FKM is used for automotive fuel-system seals and hoses, chemical-processing gaskets and aerospace seals. Chemours identifies its low-temperature GLT types for fuel, chemical and petroleum-industry seals, while GFLT types are intended for fuel-system parts needing both low-temperature flexibility and resistance to oxygenated fuels. The application and fluid exposure determine which compound is suitable.

Purchasing. Chemours distinguishes gum polymers from curative-containing precompounds and matches grades to molding, extrusion or coatings. Buyers specify the polymer grade or finished compound, cure system and fluid compatibility rather than selecting by the family name alone.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage was established. The catalog documents product availability and intended uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: FKM formulations can age through more than one mechanism. In hot-air tests of a bisphenol-cured VDF/HFP O-ring, the authors interpreted infrared changes as initial loss of hydrogen fluoride, forming double bonds that can undergo further crosslinking or oxidation. They associated subsequent carbonyl formation with chain scission; the balance of these reactions depends on temperature and material. A separate hydrothermal experiment proposed hydroxide attack on VDF units, followed by fluoride release and chain cleavage. Its detected fluoride, dissolved organic carbon and carbon-rich solids were products of that deliberately alkaline treatment, not a list of products established for ordinary outdoor weathering.

Timescales: One study aged type-1 FKM Vi655 O-rings, initially compressed by approximately 25%, in circulating air at 200, 225 and 250 °C. At 250 °C the tested O-rings had changed from blue to grey after two days and were brown with greater deformation after eight days; pigment and polymer changes could both contribute to colour. Using a 75% equilibrium compression-set criterion linked to the authors’ leakage tests and time–temperature superposition, they estimated 73, 17 and 4 days to that criterion at 200, 225 and 250 °C, respectively. These are model-based estimates for that seal, geometry and test procedure, not times to complete chemical decomposition. In a separate forced-air study of two ternary FKM hose compounds, one compound took 577–805 hours at 160 °C and 87–97 hours at 200 °C to reach a 10% hardness-change criterion; the comparison shows that the observed endpoint depends on both temperature and the measure selected.

Environmental persistence: Neither the hot-air sealing tests nor alkaline treatment measured biodegradation in soil, fresh water or seawater, so they do not establish an ambient environmental lifetime for FKM. In the chemical-treatment study, both uncrosslinked VDF/HFP 78/22 copolymer and a peroxide-cured, carbon-black-filled version gave approximately 100% fluoride yield after 18 hours at 200 °C in 0.20 M KOH under argon. At that endpoint, the uncrosslinked sample also left measurable dissolved organic carbon and a carbon-rich solid. Fluoride recovery therefore measures conversion of fluorine to inorganic fluoride, not disappearance or complete mineralization of all carbon-containing material.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Hamaura and coauthors investigated laboratory-scale fluorine recovery from a VDF/HFP 78/22 copolymer and a peroxide-cured, carbon-black-filled version. Treating approximately 30 mg samples in 0.50 M aqueous KOH at 250 °C for six hours converted the measured fluorine to dissolved fluoride; subsequent addition of calcium hydroxide produced calcium fluoride. The reported calcium-fluoride yields were 100% for the uncrosslinked material and 93% for the cured compound. The product is an inorganic fluorine feedstock, not recovered intact rubber or its original monomers.

The results are for two specified samples and controlled hydrothermal conditions. The study does not establish collection infrastructure, commercial treatment of mixed FKM waste, or complete conversion of all carbon-containing residues. Crosslink chemistry, fillers and contamination in other compounds would require separate evaluation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Chemours’ Viton A-201C is a vinylidene-fluoride/hexafluoropropylene elastomer supplied with cure chemicals. The manufacturer advises preventing skin contact and washing after handling, while assessing other compounding ingredients separately. This is useful grade-specific guidance: the hazards of an uncured FKM compound depend on its cure package and additives as well as its fluorinated base polymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: FKM grades differ in monomer composition and cure chemistry. Resistance to a fluid depends on the compound, temperature and exposure time. Cure chemistry and fillers also change the response of a finished compound. Selection therefore requires compound-specific data for the intended conditions.

sections.overview: Perfluoroelastomers, commonly designated FFKM, are highly fluorinated elastomers designed to form rubber networks on curing. Typical base polymers combine tetrafluoroethylene with a perfluoroalkyl vinyl ether and a cure-site monomer. They differ in chemistry from partially fluorinated FKM materials. FFKM compounds are used for seals in demanding chemical and high-temperature environments. The perfluorinated backbone and ether components provide chemical and temperature resistance relevant to aggressive sealing environments. Their suitability still depends on the specific compound and process. For instance, AGC describes an unfilled peroxide-curable PM-3500 material for semiconductor etching and a nitrile-curable PM-5000/5500 series for high-temperature plasma service; these are different product and cure choices.
sections.history: Perfluoroelastomers became commercial sealing materials in the 1970s. The American Vacuum Society dates DuPont’s Kalrez perfluorocarbon elastomers to approximately 1975, consistent with DuPont’s fiftieth-anniversary announcement in 2025. O-rings and gaskets for aggressive chemical and thermal environments were central applications; electronics, oil and gas and chemical processing became major markets. Anestis Logothetis’s 1995 DuPont patent addressed the cost and speed of molding by developing combined cure chemistry for nitrile-containing perfluoroelastomers. The product line continued to grow, with a new Newark, Delaware manufacturing facility opened in 2023 to serve semiconductor and industrial demand. These are milestones in the Kalrez lineage and continuing FFKM development, not one invention date for all perfluoroelastomer formulations.
sections.nomenclature: FFKM is the conventional shorthand for perfluoroelastomer. It is a family designation whose detailed copolymer composition and cure chemistry vary; it should not be used as a synonym for every fluoroelastomer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Perfluoroelastomer is a family of curable perfluorinated copolymers, not a single composition. A common architecture copolymerizes tetrafluoroethylene with one or more perfluoro(alkyl vinyl ethers), often perfluoro(methyl vinyl ether), and incorporates a small amount of a functional cure-site monomer. Documented cure-site families include nitrile-functional perfluorovinyl ethers and bromine- or iodine-bearing fluorinated comonomers or chain-end functionality. The base copolymer can be made by aqueous emulsion free-radical polymerization; molecular weight can be adjusted with a chain-transfer agent. The elastomeric network is then formed through the selected cure-site chemistry. This identifies network precursor architecture and polymerization routes without treating a particular curing formulation or schedule as universal.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Perfluoroelastomers are highly fluorinated, crosslinked amorphous elastomers whose useful mechanical response is recoverable deformation rather than high stiffness. In seals they show time-, temperature-, and rate-dependent hysteresis, creep, and stress relaxation, so compression set and retained sealing force are often more consequential than a single tensile strength. They stiffen as temperature approaches the glass-transition region and relax more rapidly at high temperature. Tetrafluoroethylene/perfluoro alkyl vinyl ether/cure-site composition, molecular weight, cure chemistry and crosslink density, post-cure, filler loading and dispersion, and residual volatiles all affect modulus, strength, elongation, hardness, and set. Component geometry, imposed compression, exposure time and temperature, chemical swelling or aging, rapid gas decompression, and surface defects further control service response.

A bounded supplier example is AGC AFLAS FFKM PM-5500, a nitrile-curable tetrafluoroethylene/perfluoro alkyl vinyl ether compound. AGC compared a formulation containing 0.8 parts BOAP curative and 5 parts N990 carbon black per 100 parts polymer with a filler-free formulation containing the same curative; both were press-cured for 20 minutes at 180 °C and post-cured in nitrogen through a schedule ending at 305 °C. For JIS B2401 P-26 O-rings compressed 18% at 300 °C, the reported compression set after 168 hours was 16% for the carbon-black formulation and 21% for the filler-free formulation, increasing after 336 hours to 22% and 28%, respectively. These are in-house typical results for the named recipes, cure schedule, ring geometry, compression, temperature, and duration—not family-wide constants. An industry-coauthored open review supports the family description but does not provide a comparably contextualized independent mechanical endpoint.
sections.processing: Perfluoroelastomers are converted as compounded, uncured elastomers: the gum is mixed with fillers and a cure system, shaped by compression, transfer, or injection molding, and then vulcanized and commonly post-cured. The cure-site chemistry and filler package vary substantially across FFKM compounds, so a family-level schedule is not portable. AGC's AFLAS FFKM PM-5500 information gives a bounded formulation comparison—5 phr N990 versus a filler-free recipe—along with press/post-cure guidance and compression-set testing on a JIS B2401 P-26 O-ring. The independent fluoropolymer review describes fully fluorinated TFE/perfluoroalkyl-vinyl-ether/cure-site elastomers, compounding, and their use as sealing articles, providing family context but not a universal cure recipe. The AGC temperatures, times, formulation, geometry, and test values therefore remain specific to PM-5500 and the named O-ring method.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The base copolymer combines perfluorinated tetrafluoroethylene-derived and vinyl-ether-derived units. A small amount of a cure-site monomer enables formation of a crosslinked network. The selection of cure site and curative changes that network. Commercial seal compounds also include formulation ingredients beyond the base polymer. The cure-site comonomer is present to provide a route to joining chains even though the principal monomers are highly fluorinated. The network type depends on the chosen cure chemistry: AGC lists peroxide-curable and nitrile-curable FFKM product series. Reinforcement and other formulation ingredients also affect the final sealing compound.
sections.properties: FFKM compounds are selected for resistance to chemicals and elevated temperatures, but the cure system and filler also determine seal performance. For example, AGC describes PM-3500 as a peroxide-curable polymer that can reach hardness 70 without filler, a useful feature when filler-derived particles could contaminate a semiconductor process. Its PM-5000/5500 products instead use nitrile curing and target high-temperature and oxygen- or NF3-plasma service. These supplier descriptions concern named polymer series and do not guarantee performance in every chemical or finished seal.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. FFKM seals serve semiconductor etching and other plasma processes, where seal erosion and particles can contaminate a wafer. AGC describes unfilled PM-3500 for plasma etching and nitrile-curable PM-5000/5500 for oxygen and NF3 plasmas. AGC describes PM-3500 as peroxide-curable and the PM-5000/5500 series as nitrile-curable, so selecting a polymer also entails selecting a compatible cure formulation. The choice depends on process chemistry, temperature and the actual seal location; the supplier descriptions do not replace qualification of a finished seal.

Purchasing. AGC supplies the PM series as polymer compounding materials and offers product and sample inquiries. The buyer must distinguish a polymer from a finished, qualified seal and specify its cure system and service conditions.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage was established. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The safety sheet for cured Gumlast perfluoroelastomer parts lists hydrogen fluoride, carbonyl fluoride, carbon monoxide and low-molecular-weight fluorocarbons among gases produced in a fire. These severe thermal-decomposition products are not evidence of ambient leaching. In a separate hot-air O-ring study, the authors interpreted infrared changes and falling hardness of a peroxide-cured FFKM as consistent with chain scission; they also proposed reactions involving ether-side groups and cure sites. These interpretations describe the tested compound, not a complete inventory of degradation products for every FFKM.

Timescales: A manufacturer’s standard FFR75PC peroxide-cured FFKM compound lost 39% of its tensile strength after 70 hours of heat ageing at 250 °C; the same sheet reports a 64% loss at 275 °C. In the separate O-ring study, time–temperature superposition gave estimates of 16, 9 and 2 days to 75% equilibrium compression set at 250, 275 and 300 °C. That threshold was chosen using leakage tests; it describes loss of sealing performance for the studied geometry and procedure, not complete chemical decomposition or a universal service life.

Environmental persistence: The Gumlast sheet describes its cured product as stable and insoluble in water under ordinary handling conditions. The seal tests and fire-product listing do not measure biodegradation or mineralization in soil, fresh water or seawater. A transferable ambient FFKM lifetime therefore remains an evidence gap.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The manufacturer provides disposal guidance for its cured parts but no validated monomer-recovery or material-recycling process. An open study recovered fluorine as calcium fluoride from two VDF/HFP fluoroelastomers after alkaline hydrothermal treatment. Those tested samples were partially fluorinated FKM, not the fully fluorinated FFKM family; the experiment does not establish recovery efficiency for FFKM.

FFKM-specific feedstock recovery, collection and commercial treatment therefore remain evidence gaps in this entry. An example for a different fluoroelastomer should not be presented as proof of a process for every cured seal.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: FloDynamix’s Gumlast perfluoroelastomer-parts sheet warns that overheating or burning can generate hazardous fumes, including hydrogen fluoride, and can cause polymer-fume-fever symptoms. Keep fluorinated material away from tobacco and smoking contamination, and control dust and fire-decomposition exposure. These severe-heat hazards are distinct from normal handling of the specified cured sealing parts.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Perfluoroelastomers are not a single composition or universal service rating. The perfluoroalkyl vinyl ether, cure-site chemistry, filler and cure schedule can differ. Chemical exposure, temperature and duration influence retention of sealing properties. Product-specific compatibility and test data are necessary for a particular application.

sections.overview: Tetrafluoroethylene–propylene elastomer is a fluorinated copolymer commonly designated FEPM. It combines tetrafluoroethylene and propylene units and may include a cure-site comonomer. One documented synthesis uses free-radical aqueous emulsion polymerization. The resulting polymer is compounded and cured for seals and other rubber articles. Its fluorinated copolymer backbone is used in demanding fluid and heat environments, but individual fluids can behave very differently. For its AFLAS line the supplier identifies uses including engine-oil seals and gives a less favorable rating for gasoline; compatibility depends on the actual fluid and formulation. The final sealing article is a filled, crosslinked compound.
sections.history: Tetrafluoroethylene–propylene rubber developed as a distinct alternative to vinylidene-fluoride-based fluoroelastomers. AGC dates development of its AFLAS material to 1971; Takashi Okazoe’s industrial history identifies commercialization by Asahi Glass in 1975. This distinction separates laboratory development from market introduction. The company developed applications in seals and cable coverings for chemical plants, oilfield equipment and transport. Later uses included railway and electric-vehicle cables, semiconductor facilities and space equipment, where combinations of heat, chemical and electrical demands mattered. AGC’s subsequent account emphasizes continued formulation development and work with users. These documented milestones apply to the TFE–propylene product lineage, while later AFLAS terpolymers require their own compositional scope.
sections.nomenclature: FEPM and TFE–propylene rubber are names used for this copolymer elastomer. The record covers the TFE/propylene backbone and its cure-site variants; FKM/VDF-rich fluoroelastomers, nonfluorinated EPM, and a particular cured compound are excluded.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Tetrafluoroethylene–propylene elastomer (FEPM or TFE/P rubber) is formed by free-radical copolymerization of tetrafluoroethylene and propylene, often with a small cure-site comonomer or halogen-bearing chain-end control. Aqueous semibatch emulsion polymerization is established: deoxygenated water, fluorinated surfactant, buffer, and a persulfate or redox initiator are charged to a pressure reactor, which is pressurized with TFE/propylene feed and replenished as polymerization consumes monomer. The strong cross-propagation tendency produces a substantially alternating fluorocarbon/hydrocarbon backbone, while feed ratio, temperature, pressure, initiator, and chain transfer govern composition and molar mass. One cited patent example adds a fluorinated cure-site monomer during ammonium-persulfate-initiated emulsion polymerization, then coagulates, washes, and dries the latex. A distinct patent prepares TFE/propylene chains in the presence of radical initiator and bromine salt or brominated cure-site species so that the isolated rubber has bromine-bearing terminal or pendant sites. Useful networks are then formed with an organic peroxide, which generates radicals at the cure sites, commonly with a multifunctional coagent such as triallyl isocyanurate to increase crosslink efficiency. Filler and activator packages may be included, but they are formulation choices. Dipolymer, VDF-containing terpolymer, and cure-site-modified FEPM grades must remain distinguished because polymerization and cure chemistry differ. Article shaping and press/post-cure schedules belong in Processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Tetrafluoroethylene–propylene elastomer (FEPM) is normally used as a cross-linked rubber compound, so its useful response is a combination of tensile strength and extensibility, tear resistance, hardness, resilience, and resistance to permanent compressive set rather than the properties of the uncured copolymer alone. The alternating TFE/propylene backbone supports retention of rubber properties under heat, steam, bases, and many oils, but low-temperature elasticity is a limitation: an AGC technical brochure lists glass-transition temperatures near −3 °C for its TFE/P dipolymer grades and notes that formulation-dependent brittleness and usable low-temperature limits are not interchangeable. Core TFE/P dipolymers should also be distinguished from supplier grades that add vinylidene fluoride or a cure-site monomer, because those terpolymers can change low-temperature behavior, molding, and compression set.

The principal mechanical variables are TFE/propylene ratio and sequence distribution, molecular weight and raw-polymer viscosity, cure-site chemistry, peroxide and coagent identity, cross-link density, carbon-black type and loading, other fillers and process aids, mixing dispersion, press-cure and post-cure histories, and molded-part geometry. Temperature, strain rate, compression duration, cyclic loading, and thermal aging affect the rubber network. Fluid exposure can change volume, hardness, strength, elongation, and sealing force even when the backbone is chemically resistant, so hot water, steam, acid, base, lubricant, fuel, and amine environments must be reported with concentration, temperature, and time. Moisture by itself is not a single family-wide predictor; hot-water and steam exposure can instead act through compound swelling, additives, cure chemistry, and interfaces.

A formulation series in the AGC brochure isolates one major formulation effect. AFLAS 150P was compounded at 100 parts polymer with 5 phr triallyl isocyanurate, 1 phr peroxide, 1 phr sodium stearate, and 10–50 phr N990 carbon black, then press-cured at 170 °C for 20 minutes and post-cured at 200 °C for 4 hours. Across that series, tensile strength stayed at 16–17 MPa while 100% modulus rose from 2.3 to 9.5 MPa, Shore A hardness rose from 63 to 80, and elongation at break fell from 360% to 210%; compression set after 22 hours at 200 °C changed from 20% to 17% and remained about 28–29% after 70 hours. These values describe those exact supplier formulations and cure schedule, not neat FEPM or a family range. As an independent compound example, SKF's black Ecoflas TFE/P test material is reported as Shore A 85 ± 5, 14 MPa tensile strength, 11 MPa 100% modulus, 150% elongation at break, 15 N/mm tear strength, and 20% compression set after 24 hours at 175 °C, with DIN or ISO methods named for each endpoint. The datasheet does not disclose its full recipe, specimen conditioning, or uncertainty for most values, so it should be used as a grade-level reference only.
sections.processing:
Tetrafluoroethylene–propylene elastomer (FEPM) is converted as a curable rubber compound. Directly supported routes include two-roll, kneader, Banbury or extruder compounding; compression and transfer molding; extrusion of wire insulation, tube, and tape; and molding with heat by extrusion or injection. A typical workflow mixes the gum with filler, processing aid, coagent, acid acceptor where required, and a peroxide package, preforms or extrudes the uncured stock, then press-cures or continuously cures and often post-cures the article. Polymer manufacture and the identity of the cure chemistry belong in Synthesis; mixing, preforming, article shaping, vulcanization equipment, and cure schedules belong here.

Mix cleanliness, gum viscosity, ingredient premixing and dispersion, roll or rotor shear, active cooling, peroxide addition sequence, dump temperature, storage and coagent bleed, remilling, mold release, scorch margin, compound temperature in extrusion, cure-line length, winding speed, part thickness, and staged post-cure heating are important controls. AGC notes that its AFLAS grades cure relatively slowly and may resist mold release; insufficient cure can worsen release. Its guide calls for cooling during milling, keeping rolls below 80 °C, and adding peroxide after the hotter internal-mixer stage or in a cooled second pass. For the named AFLAS 150E extrusion grade, the guide says to keep compound temperature below 100 °C to prevent premature cure and identifies steam autoclaves, fluidized salt baths, oil baths, or electron-beam devices as downstream cure equipment. Its 170–180 °C and 10–20 min compression-molding recommendation is expressly for small parts such as O-rings made from its grades, not all FEPM.

Ukihashi, Yamabe, and Kojima provide a separate bounded conversion example for their Example 11 TFE–propylene copolymer. Example 12 blended 100 parts polymer with 5 parts 2,2'-bis(t-butylperoxy)-p-diisopropylbenzene, 3 parts triallyl isocyanurate, 10 parts magnesium oxide, and 25 parts MT carbon black on a 4-inch roll mill; the compound was press-vulcanized at 150 °C for 40 min and then oven-vulcanized at 200 °C for 20 h. Those settings belong to that patent formulation and are not a universal FEPM cure schedule.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The base polymer contains tetrafluoroethylene-derived and propylene-derived units. A cure-site monomer or reactive halogen functionality can be introduced to support peroxide crosslinking. The cured compound is a network and can contain substantial reinforcing filler. Its structure therefore depends on the base polymer, cure chemistry and compound recipe. Filler loading changes the compound as well as the polymer network. For example, AGC’s peroxide-cured AFLAS 150P series increased carbon black from 10 to 50 parts per hundred rubber: the reported 100% modulus rose from 2.3 to 9.5 MPa while elongation at break fell from 360% to 210%. These values are for the specified filler series and cure schedule, not inherent properties of all FEPM.
sections.properties: FEPM compounds are used where resistance to heat and selected oils, chemicals or steam is required, but resistance depends on the fluid and formulation. AGC reports that its standard AFLAS 100S JIS No. 3 dumbbell retained 92% of its tensile strength after 1,000 hours in SJ engine oil at 175 °C; the tested specimen also increased 7% in volume. Such oil swelling and retention are measured responses of one compound in one exposure, not family-wide guarantees.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. FEPM serves seals in oil and gas or chemical equipment, wire and cable insulation, and automotive multilayer hoses. AGC identifies 400E and 600X for engine-area hose constructions and offers 100/150 series for compounding. The particular medium and operating temperature guide the compound choice; the same grade need not suit every fuel or oil.

Purchasing. AGC identifies AFLAS 100 and 150 series for compounding in open mills or internal mixers before molding, extrusion or calendering into parts. Buyers can request a named grade or sample and specify the conversion route and cure formulation. The polymer feedstock and finished hose or seal are separate purchasing stages.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage was established. The supplier examples document product availability, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A safety sheet for a formulated TFE–propylene rubber sheet lists carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and hydrogen fluoride as hazardous products of decomposition. This concerns severe heating or combustion, not a measurement of degradation in the natural environment. Separately, a supplier oil-aging comparison shows that exposure can change a seal compound’s volume and mechanical response without demonstrating chemical mineralization.

Timescales: A standard AFLAS 100S test specimen retained 92% of its tensile strength and gained 7% in volume after 1,000 hours in SJ engine oil at 175 °C. That accelerated, fluid-specific exposure is not a lifetime prediction for another formulation or environment.

Environmental persistence: The safety sheet describes the specific formulated material as a stable solid with negligible solubility. Its handling description and the separate 1,000-hour oil exposure do not measure biodegradation or carbon mineralization. A transferable soil, freshwater, marine or landfill lifetime remains unresolved.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The manufacturer identifies controlled incineration as its disposal route; this is destruction, not recovery of polymer or monomers. A directly supported FEPM recycling process remains unresolved.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Trelleborg’s Style AFLAS sheet safety document warns that its formulated elastomer can cause an allergic skin reaction. Dust can irritate eyes and airways, while combustion can produce hydrogen fluoride and carbon oxides. Control machining dust and skin contact and use suitable protection for fire residues. These statements concern the specified finished sheet formulation, rather than every TFE–propylene elastomer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: TFE–propylene copolymers vary in composition and cure-site design. Filler type, loading and the cure package further distinguish finished elastomers. The cited supplier brochure and seal datasheet describe named products with specified test conditions. Compatibility with a fluid or temperature must be checked for the chosen compound and exposure.
