synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical copolymerization builds the TFE/propylene elastomer backbone. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another.

steps.title: Prepare the reaction
steps.body: Prepare deoxygenated water, surfactant, buffer, initiator, and initial monomer charge.

steps.title: Propagate the radical chain
steps.body: Successive monomer additions convert alkene π bonds into backbone σ bonds while regenerating the radical growth site. The cited initiator, feed composition and reaction medium determine the particular preparation; transfer, grafting and termination control architecture alongside propagation.

steps.title: Form and recover the product
steps.body: Replenish monomers during reaction, then coagulate, wash, and dry the latex polymer.

synthesisRoutes.limitations: This outline does not specify a universal recipe, reagent loading, operating schedule, or conversion endpoint. Those details must retain the material and process limits of the cited source. Figure notes distinguish exact molecules from representative motifs and variable architectures.

sections.overview: Silicone rubbers are elastomers based on polysiloxane chains cured into flexible networks. The silicon–oxygen backbone distinguishes them from many carbon-backbone rubbers. Silicone formulations may be supplied as liquid or high-consistency materials and cured by different chemistries. They are used in molded parts, tubing and other flexible components. A cured silicone is a network: crosslinks restrict permanent flow, while the flexible polymer strands can deform and recover. Reinforcing fillers such as fumed silica can improve tensile and tear resistance, but also change stiffness and the way the material responds to repeated deformation. These effects depend on the actual formulation and processing.
sections.history: Silicone rubber developed from the industrial siloxane chemistry enabled by the 1940 direct-process work of Eugene Rochow and Richard Müller. Wacker’s documented milestones include heat-vulcanizing rubber in 1953, room-temperature-vulcanizing rubber in 1955, building sealants in 1960 and addition-curing rubber in 1970. These are supplier milestones within a wider industry. Subsequent uses diversified into industrial rollers, electric-wire coverings and molded or extruded technical components, as illustrated by Shin-Etsu’s product families. In 1993, Toshio Takago and colleagues at Shin-Etsu patented a modified silicone platform aimed at improving strength while retaining transparency, documenting continuing development beyond the early filled rubber systems.
sections.nomenclature: Q is a class abbreviation used for silicone rubbers, and silicone elastomer is a broad equivalent descriptor. Specific classes such as VMQ and FVMQ are narrower silicone-rubber chemistries rather than aliases for the entire family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Silicone rubbers are elastomeric networks made from linear or lightly branched organopolysiloxanes, most often polydimethylsiloxane-based gums or fluids bearing vinyl, silanol, or other reactive groups. Three major network chemistries are documented. Organic peroxides generate radicals that crosslink suitable silicone gums. Condensation-curing systems react silanol-terminated polysiloxanes with tri- or tetrafunctional hydrolyzable silanes, often using tin carboxylate or amine catalysts and releasing water, alcohol, oxime, acetate, or another leaving product depending on the crosslinker. Addition-curing systems hydrosilylate vinyl-functional polysiloxanes with Si–H-functional crosslinkers using a platinum-group catalyst and release no condensation byproduct. One cited patent describes both peroxide and moisture/condensation formulations, including hydroxyl polymers, multifunctional silanes, and metal-carboxylate catalysts. A distinct patent provides an addition-cure RTV example based on vinyl-bearing organopolysiloxane, organohydrogenpolysiloxane, and a platinum catalyst. Polymer functionality, crosslinker functionality and ratio, catalyst or inhibitor, and filler surface chemistry control network formation. Precursor polysiloxane manufacture is covered by the family record; article-specific mixing, molding, and cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Silicone rubbers are soft, highly extensible crosslinked polysiloxane networks whose tensile response is viscoelastic and usually nonlinear beyond small strain. The siloxane backbone remains mobile far below room temperature, while covalent junctions provide elastic recovery; unfilled or lightly filled formulations commonly have elastic moduli no more than a few MPa and ultimate strains well above 300%. Soft grades generally trade lower modulus and ultimate stress for greater extension. Rate, load duration, and temperature affect stress–strain response, hysteresis, creep, stress relaxation, compression set, and tear propagation, so tensile, tear, hardness, and compression values are not interchangeable family constants.

Molecular weight between crosslinks, crosslinker functionality and stoichiometry, cure chemistry, catalyst level, cure conversion, and post-cure set the network density and defect population. Short strands or over-crosslinking can embrittle the network; incomplete cure, entrained air, residual solvent, poor mixing, and specimen flaws depress ultimate strength. Reinforcing fumed silica and some silicone resins can greatly improve tensile and tear resistance but usually raise modulus and hardness; oils, plasticizers, pigments, flame retardants, conductive fillers, and other additives shift the balance again. Condensation-, peroxide-, and addition-cured RTV, HCR, and LSR products, as well as methyl-, vinyl-, phenyl-, and fluoro-containing families, therefore require grade-specific treatment. Moisture during condensation cure, swelling liquids, thermal aging, test rate, notch geometry, specimen thickness, and processing orientation or voids are also consequential.

As one bounded commercial example, Wacker lists platinum-cured, 1:1 A/B ELASTOSIL LR 3003/50 for molded seals and similar parts at Shore A 50, tensile strength 10.3 N mm⁻² and elongation at break 490% by ISO 37 type 1, tear resistance 26 N mm⁻¹ by ASTM D624 die B, and compression set 13% after 22 h at 175 °C by DIN ISO 815-1. The same product series changes substantially with nominal hardness, and the guide presents typical grade data rather than a universal silicone-rubber range. These values should remain attached to LR 3003/50 and the listed methods and conditioning.
sections.processing: Silicone rubber processing spans solid high-consistency/heat-vulcanizing rubber (HCR/HTV), liquid silicone rubber (LSR), and room-temperature-vulcanizing RTV-2 compounds. HCR/HTV is compounded as a solid feed and can be extruded or coextruded, calendered, or compression-, transfer-, or injection-molded; Wacker describes the extruder screw as homogenizing, compacting, and degassing the stock before die vulcanization, with post-cure selected by grade, part volume, and stabilizer requirements. LSR is metered as two components through a static mixer into a heated mold, while RTV-2 is mixed, degassed, poured or brushed into a mold, and allowed to cure. A Lidor technical brochure describes equal A/B metering, a static mixer, chilled nozzle/cylinder hardware near 20 °C to delay premature vulcanization, and grade-dependent molding cure in seconds at 140–230 °C. For a bounded RTV-2 moldmaking example, SiSiB MR21030 specifies 10:1 A:B by mass, low-speed mixing to minimize air, approximately 90 min working time at 23 °C, vacuum degassing at 30–50 mbar for 5–10 min, and room-temperature cure; it warns that sulfur-containing materials, tin-catalyzed silicones, tin-stabilized PVC, amine-cured epoxies, and some solvents can inhibit platinum cure. Feed temperature, screw/static-mixer cleanliness, mold venting, part thickness, cooling before demolding, residence time, and any post-cure must remain grade-, formulation-, and tooling-specific; silicone network chemistry remains in Synthesis.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polysiloxane chains have alternating silicon and oxygen atoms with organic groups attached to silicon. Curing joins chains into a network; for example, hydrosilylation reacts vinyl-functional polymer with hydride-functional crosslinker. The network also contains defects such as dangling chains or unreacted material. Reinforcing silica or other additives can be dispersed in the network to modify its behavior. Network formation depends on the relative amounts of functional polymer and crosslinker, not only on the identity of the siloxane backbone. An imbalance can leave dangling chains and other defects, while filler particles form interfaces with the network and alter mechanical response. Thus two addition-cured silicone formulations can differ even when both use the same basic vinyl–hydride reaction.
sections.properties: Silicone elastomers can remain flexible across a wide range of temperatures. Longer network strands generally reduce stiffness, while increasing crosslink density tends to raise modulus and can limit extensibility; cure conversion and defects affect the response as well. Reinforcing silica can improve tensile and tear strength but also increase stiffness, so formulation balances stretchability against resistance to damage. For example, Shin-Etsu reports that its C-8-cured KE-555-U and KE-575-U compounds have hardnesses of 53 and 70 Shore A and elongations at break of 650% and 550%, respectively, after the specified press and post-cure. Those supplier results compare complete formulations, not an isolated crosslink-density or filler effect; filler dispersion and the specific network determine the finished response.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Silicone rubbers serve appliance gaskets, electrical wire insulation, office-equipment parts and leisure products. Shin-Etsu identifies KE-552-U and KE-582-U for microwave-oven window gaskets, where heat resistance and low compression set are useful. For its C-23N-cured KE-552-U test pieces, the supplier reports 18% compression set after 22 hours at 150 °C: the result measures residual deformation under that test and does not guarantee the seal performance of an assembled oven. The supplier also associates electrical insulation and temperature resistance with appliance wires and transparency and strength with swimming goggles.

Purchasing. The supplier catalog maps application-specific compounds and curing agents to manufacturing and provides a sales contact. Specify grade, cure system and applicable end-use requirements; an industrial grade alone does not establish medical suitability.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage was established. The catalog examples show applications and product availability, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Catalytic cleavage of silicone waste can release cyclic siloxanes and leave a nonvolatile residue. In one patent example, the feed combined cut cured silicone tubing with waste PDMS gum, polyethylene and a clay catalyst; it was heated and degassed in an extruder. Products condensed in the subsequent stage were mainly cyclic siloxanes, with some other siloxanes.

Timescales: A 50 g portion of the first-stage residue was heated under vacuum up to 260 °C for six hours, yielding 12.9 g of collected liquid. This is controlled treatment of a mixed feed, not a recovery yield for tubing alone. In a separate study of a silicone rubber used in manufacturing equipment, samples were held under 200% strain in polyalkylene-glycol heat-transfer fluid at 180 °C for six weeks. Tensile strength fell by 86% and elongation at break by 90% relative to the unaged sample; temperature, fluid and strain interacted, so the result cannot be attributed to heat alone or generalized to every seal.

Environmental persistence: The same study found little change in its infrared spectra despite severe mechanical deterioration. Neither loss of mechanical performance nor the patent's chemical treatment measures conversion of silicone rubber to environmental mineralization products in soil or water.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent demonstrates extrusion and catalytic depolymerization of a mixed stream containing cured tubing and uncured PDMS gum, followed by heating the solid residue and condensing volatile siloxanes. The authors calculate 66.85% total conversion across both stages for that mixture; conversion and collected product are distinct, and the calculation cannot be assigned to the tubing alone. The disclosed example does not establish commercial operation or recovery rates for every silicone formulation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: WACKER’s silicone-rubber processing guidance identifies flammable low-molecular siloxanes, and sometimes peroxide by-products, in post-cure emissions. A circulating-air oven needs fresh-air supply and effective exhaust to prevent vapor accumulation. Post-cure conditions and contamination control depend on the formulation; the safety of a cured article is not established solely by calling it silicone.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Silicone rubber is a family of formulations rather than a single polymer or curing recipe. Liquid and high-consistency materials differ in viscosity and processing. Cure ratio, filler dispersion and incomplete mixing can lead to different network structures and mechanical response. Fluid compatibility and durability should be evaluated for the particular formulation and exposure.

sections.overview: Methyl-vinyl silicone rubber (VMQ) is a silicone elastomer containing methyl and vinyl groups on a siloxane backbone. Vinyl functionality provides sites for forming a cured network. The material can be supplied in forms suitable for molding or extrusion. Its final properties reflect the chosen polymer, filler and cure system. In a typical addition-cure system, vinyl-functional siloxane reacts with a hydride-functional crosslinker to form an elastic network. Silica reinforcement can raise tensile and tear resistance but changes the compound’s stiffness and response to repeated loading. The selected VMQ grade, filler and cure process therefore matter for the final part.
sections.history: Methyl-vinyl silicone rubber has a specific early patent milestone: James Marsden at General Electric filed in June 1945 and received a patent in 1948 for methyl silicone elastomers containing small amounts of silicon-bound vinyl groups. The work sought better hardness and recovery after compression. By 1956 Union Carbide was presenting a new vinyl-containing silicone rubber, and a subsequent patent records General Electric methyl-vinyl gums among commercially available materials in 1957. Norbert Dickmann’s 1957 Dow Corning patent developed a related blending approach to reduce compression set without the toxic additives used in some earlier formulations, with food and pharmaceutical uses explicitly motivating the work. These developments made curing and molded-part performance central to this silicone branch.
sections.nomenclature: VMQ is the conventional designation for methyl-vinyl silicone rubber. It distinguishes this vinyl-containing silicone rubber from fluorosilicone rubber (FVMQ) and other silicone-elastomer classes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Methyl-vinyl silicone rubber is an organopolysiloxane gum containing mainly dimethylsiloxane units and vinylmethylsiloxane units; it is a polymer precursor distinct from the subsequently crosslinked silicone article. A documented industrial route ring-opens/equilibrates dimethyl cyclic siloxanes or octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane with a vinyl cyclic siloxane and an end-blocker in the presence of catalyst. Vinyl-ring feed, end-blocker, catalyst, water content, and devolatilization conditions control vinyl content, chain ends, and molecular-weight distribution. One high-vinyl route uses tetramethyltetravinylcyclotetrasiloxane and tetramethyldivinyldisiloxane with tetramethylammonium hydroxide; another uses a tubular polymerizer starting from dimethyl cyclic siloxane. These are source-specific routes. Peroxide or addition curing turns the gum into a network and is deliberately excluded from this synthesis account.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Methyl-vinyl silicone rubber (MVQ) is normally compounded and cured before its mechanical response is measured. Its Si–O backbone supports a wide useful temperature range, but unreinforced silicone has modest tensile, tear, and abrasion strength; reinforcement, cure chemistry, crosslink density, hardness, and temperature are decisive. A specific SKF Ecosil 85 Shore A MVQ sealing compound is reported with DIN 53504 tensile strength of at least 6.5 MPa, elongation at break of at least 130%, and 100% modulus of at least 4.5 MPa; its DIN ISO 34-1 tear strength is 9 N/mm and DIN ISO 815 compression set is at most 20% after 24 h at 175 °C. The sheet limits these values to standardized test specimens and distinguishes nominal batch requirements from general guidance, so they are compound-specific rather than silicone-gum constants. Independent silicone technical data show that commercial grades vary substantially in tensile strength and are selected by hardness, elongation, and service requirements.
sections.processing: Methyl-vinyl silicone rubber (VMQ/MVQ) is converted in formulation-dependent HTV, LSR, or RTV forms by extrusion, calendering/coating, compression molding, transfer molding, and injection molding. The compound normally contains reinforcing silica and a peroxide or platinum cure system; filler level, hardness, cure chemistry, and article thickness determine the usable window. Mesgo's technical page lists extrusion with hot-air, microwave, salt-bath, or steam reticulation, plus calendering/coating and compression or injection molding. A separate VMQ processing guide states that compression or transfer molding is typically carried out at 150–180 °C for a few minutes, followed when needed by post-curing to complete crosslinking and reduce volatiles; the exact schedule varies with mold and wall thickness. These are process-family and guide-level constraints, not a universal recipe for every methyl-vinyl silicone grade.
sections.structureAndMorphology: VMQ chains consist of alternating silicon and oxygen atoms with methyl and vinyl substituents. Vinyl groups participate in crosslinking, for example through peroxide chemistry or addition reactions with a hydride-functional siloxane. Silica can reinforce the cured network. The amount and distribution of these components affect the resulting structure. In addition curing the number and location of reactive vinyl and hydride groups help determine how chains are connected. Mixing ratio, unreacted groups and dangling chains can make the actual network differ from an ideal uniform one. Reinforcing silica adds particle–polymer interfaces and can change the stress response, so the neat polymer chain does not define the complete compound.
sections.properties: VMQ compounds are valued for flexibility over a wide temperature range, but exposure to many fuels, oils and aromatic solvents can cause swelling and damage. In one foam study, a methyl silicone reference reached 4.98 times its initial volume after 24 hours in xylene at room temperature, versus 1.08 times for the foam containing 50 mol% trifluoropropyl groups. The latter is a fluorosilicone, and this comparison is specific to the experimental foams, not dense commercial seals. Fillers, network design and cure affect the response of each finished VMQ compound.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. VMQ is used for molded seals, hoses and profiles in machinery and other equipment. Its flexibility and weather resistance are useful for seals that must remain elastic across changing temperatures, while contact with fuels or oils calls for separate compatibility testing because of swelling. Specially qualified compounds also serve food, skin-contact medical and drinking-water components. The fabricator distinguishes high-temperature-vulcanizing solid silicone, used in compression, transfer or injection molding, from liquid silicone rubber used in two-component injection molding. These forms have different equipment and production requirements.

Purchasing. GUME offers application-specific molded components; buyers specify part geometry, compound and any required qualification. A silicone family designation alone does not establish suitability for food or medical use.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage was established. The documented parts illustrate applications, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A silicone-depolymerization patent includes methylvinylsiloxane in its scope and describes catalyst-assisted cleavage to volatile cyclic siloxanes. Its worked example uses a mixture of cured silicone tubing and waste PDMS gum, not a separately characterized VMQ feed, so it does not establish VMQ-specific products or yields. In service, loss of sealing function can instead be followed by the ability of a compressed gasket to recover its thickness; that physical endpoint does not by itself identify a chemical degradation product.

Timescales: One study of a VMQ radiator-gasket formulation reported compression sets of 9.2% after 22 hours and 33.6% after 1,000 hours at 150 °C, using ASTM D395 method B. A greater compression set means less recovery after removal of the imposed deformation. The figures apply to the tested formulation and test, not all silicone seals or an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The same study’s accelerated tests and a separate 175 °C hot-air study measure changes in physical behavior rather than conversion of polymer to small inorganic products. The controlled heating and vacuum used in the recycling patent likewise cannot be converted to a natural-weathering lifetime. None establishes complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A patent describes feeding cut waste silicone medical tubing together with waste PDMS gum, polyethylene and a clay catalyst into an extruder. It collects vapors at vacuum ports and heats the remaining solid in a second stage; the reported liquid products are mainly cyclic siloxanes. These molecules are recovered feedstocks rather than the original cured article.

Although methylvinylsiloxane is within the patent’s proposed feedstock scope, the tubing and gum mixture is not a separately characterized VMQ feed. The example does not establish a VMQ-specific recovery yield, a collection system or commercial deployment.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: WACKER’s methyl-vinyl silicone-rubber processing guidance identifies flammable low-molecular siloxanes, and sometimes peroxide by-products, in post-cure emissions. A circulating-air oven needs fresh-air supply and effective exhaust to prevent vapor accumulation. Post-cure conditions and contamination control depend on the formulation; the safety of a cured article is not established solely by calling it silicone.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: VMQ grades differ in polymer architecture, vinyl functionality, filler and curatives. Manufacturer guidance notes that resistance to fuels and many oils can be limiting. Processing and post-cure also affect the finished component. A temperature range or property listed for one compound should not be transferred to all VMQ materials.

sections.overview: Fluorosilicone rubber (FVMQ) is a silicone elastomer with fluorinated organic groups attached to its siloxane backbone. A common substituent is trifluoropropyl, and vinyl groups can provide cure functionality. The material is designed to combine silicone-like flexibility with improved resistance to some hydrocarbon fluids. Specific fluorosilicone compounds and foams are made for different applications. The fluorinated side groups alter interactions with liquids without replacing the siloxane backbone. A laboratory comparison of foams showed lower swelling in xylene as the proportion of trifluoropropyl groups increased, illustrating a potential composition–fluid relationship. That result is for the tested foamed materials and does not directly establish behavior of a dense commercial seal.
sections.history: Fluorosilicone rubber reached the market through Dow Corning’s Silastic LS-53 in 1957. A 1961 review by G. V. Odabashyan, V. A. Ponomarenko and A. D. Petrov describes its resistance to fuels, oils and hydraulic fluids and its use for aircraft gaskets. This application was an important reason to combine a siloxane backbone with fluorinated organic substituents. Development continued after that launch: John Razzano and Verne Simpson at General Electric patented a copolymerization method in 1976 that broadened the attainable fluorosilicone composition range. Their work aimed to tune resistance to hydrocarbon swelling more efficiently than blending separate silicone polymers. The commercial date therefore identifies an early product, while later copolymers represent further formulation and synthesis advances.
sections.nomenclature: FVMQ is narrower than generic silicone rubber: the name identifies fluorosilicone compositions containing fluorinated organosiloxane units. The exact balance of trifluoropropyl-, dimethyl-, and methylvinyl-siloxane units, and any post-cure network, defines a specific material rather than an alternative name for the subfamily.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Fluorosilicone rubber is based on polyorganosiloxane chains bearing fluoroalkyl substituents, commonly 3,3,3-trifluoropropylmethylsiloxane units, and may also contain dimethylsiloxane and low levels of vinylsiloxane units. It is distinct from a fluorocarbon elastomer and from a filler/cure package. Documented raw-polymer routes use ring-opening/equilibration polymerization of fluoroalkyl cyclic trisiloxanes alone or with other cyclic siloxane comonomers. One route uses a fluoroalkyl cyclic trimer and a second trisiloxane in an aprotic solvent with an organolithium catalyst; another describes sequential living polymerization of cyclic siloxanes with alkyllithium or lithium silanolate to make a trifluoropropyl/dimethyl/vinylsiloxane block copolymer. The exact fluoroalkyl fraction, end groups, and vinyl content are route-specific. Silica reinforcement and peroxide or addition cure form formulated rubber articles and are deliberately not treated as universal polymer synthesis steps.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Fluorosilicone rubber (FVMQ) is a cured elastomer, so tensile, tear, hardness, and damping values reflect the gum composition, fluorinated substituent level, reinforcing or non-reinforcing filler, cure chemistry, and cure schedule. An open composition study reports that changing filler and fluorinated-polysiloxane formulations shifts ASTM D412 modulus, tensile strength, and elongation, and that dynamic loss factor also varies with temperature and frequency. Its press-cured examples therefore demonstrate formulation sensitivity rather than a material constant.

A bounded sheet example is Viking Extrusions' VFL60SH 60 Shore A fluorosilicone sheeting, which reports 900 psi tensile strength and 200% elongation by ASTM D412, and 40 ppi tear by ASTM D624 Die B. The supplier explicitly presents these figures as guide values rather than a specification. In separately disclosed press-cured formulation examples (170 °C for 10 min), one cited sample reported 9.1 MPa tensile strength, 540% elongation, 0.95 MPa M100, and 36.4 kN/m tear (ASTM D412 and D624 Mold B); it must remain associated with that patented formulation and cure.
sections.processing: Fluorosilicone rubber is processed as a filled gum or liquid formulation, followed by heat curing or vulcanization. High-consistency compounds can be mixed on a two-roll mill or other mixer, shaped by compression, transfer, or injection molding, and post-cured; addition-cure systems must be protected from premature room-temperature reaction and are often packaged as separate components. A patent example mixed fluorinated polysiloxane, fumed silica, surface-treatment agent, fluorinated hydrosiloxane crosslinker, platinum catalyst, and retardant on a 6-inch two-roll mill, press molded a 2 mm sheet at 165 °C for 10 min under 100 kg/cm², and post-cured at 200 °C for 4 h. The same disclosure gives a broad preferred cure range of 50–300 °C for 1–30 min followed by 100–250 °C post-cure for 0–8 h. An independent fluorosilicone-composition patent reports press curing at 170 °C for 10 min for formulation-specific articles. Filler, viscosity, catalyst, cure system, mold design, and shrinkage make these operating conditions formulation-specific.
sections.structureAndMorphology: FVMQ retains the alternating silicon–oxygen backbone of a silicone polymer. Fluorinated side groups distinguish it from an otherwise similar methyl silicone. In one study, vinyl-terminated copolymers with varying trifluoropropyl content were foamed and crosslinked. The resulting network and porosity are features of that particular material preparation. In the foam study, the researchers used vinyl-terminated fluorosilicone copolymers and a hydride-containing siloxane. The mixture crosslinked while gas generation formed bubbles, producing a cellular elastomer rather than a dense rubber. Both the side-group composition and the pores can affect the observed solvent uptake and mechanical behavior.
sections.properties: Fluorosilicone is used where flexibility and resistance to some fuels or oils are both desired. In one study, silicone foams containing 12.5 and 50 mol% trifluoropropyl groups reached 4.41 and 1.08 times their initial volume, respectively, after 24 hours in xylene at room temperature. The lower swelling at higher fluorinated-group content is a result for these particular foams; network, formulation and fluid choice affect other products, including dense commercial seals.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Fluorosilicone is used in fuel- and oil-contact diaphragms, check valves, connectors and gaskets. Shin-Etsu lists FE-251-U and FE-271-U for diaphragms and O-rings where heat, oil and flex-fatigue resistance are sought. In its reported press-cured and post-cured test specimens, those grades have Shore A hardnesses of 54 and 73, respectively, illustrating why grade selection matters when a sealing component needs a particular compliance. The selected compound, fluid, temperature and part geometry still determine suitability in service.

Purchasing. Viking offers fluorosilicone sheet in rolls, cut lengths and custom gaskets by quotation, with listed sheet width of 914 mm and multiple thicknesses. A part buyer must also specify dimensions and the operating fluid.

Scale and evidence limits. Width and thickness describe sheet supply, not resin order mass or market tonnage. No separate FVMQ consumption total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A patent includes fluoroalkyl silicones in its proposed feedstock scope for catalytic cleavage to volatile siloxanes. Its example uses cured tubing mixed with waste PDMS gum, without identifying the tubing as fluorosilicone. It therefore does not establish FVMQ-specific products or fluorine fate.

Timescales: A separate study tested peroxide-cured FVMQ and FVMQ/VMQ blends after 70, 250, 500 and 1,000 hours of heat ageing at 175 °C. The researchers measured tensile response and compression set; a higher VMQ fraction showed better compression-set performance in longer exposures within that formulation series. These service-related tests do not establish a natural-environment mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: The proposed process does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill. The heat-ageing study measures property retention under controlled exposure rather than disappearance or conversion of the rubber to mineral products.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Catalytic extrusion, condensation of volatile siloxanes and further heating of residual solids are demonstrated for a mixed silicone feed. Although the patent includes fluorosilicones in its scope, it does not supply a fluorosilicone-specific product balance or recovery yield; suitability and fluorine fate remain unresolved.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Freshly molded fluorosilicone rubber articles can remain an exposure source while cooling. HSE recommends extraction at cooling racks, avoiding skin contamination, and gloves suitable for chemical and heat exposure. These are process controls for formulated rubber articles; the cure package and other ingredients determine additional chemical hazards.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Fluorinated side-group content, molecular structure and cure chemistry vary between formulations. Fluid resistance depends on the specific liquid, exposure and polymer composition. The cited solvent comparison used foamed samples with defined fluorine contents and preparation. Fillers, network structure and part geometry can alter the response of other fluorosilicone products.

sections.overview: Polysulfide rubber is a family of sulfur-containing materials made from organic polysulfide polymers. A documented route reacts sodium polysulfide with organic dihalides or polyhalides to make polymer precursors. Liquid precursors can be produced with terminal thiol groups. Oxidative curing then joins these precursors into rubbery networks used in applications such as sealants and coatings. The liquid precursor lets a sealant be placed in a joint before it becomes an elastic solid. Once cured, the network can accommodate joint movement while keeping the joint sealed, provided the particular formulation adheres to the substrate and stays within its specified movement capability. The curing agent and other ingredients are part of the finished sealant.
sections.history: Commercial polysulfide rubber grew from Joseph Patrick and Nathan Mnookin’s interwar experiments. A 1958 account places their accidental rubber formation in 1926, during antifreeze research, followed by financing and formation of the Thiokol business. Solvent resistance distinguished the material, but early sales were limited. Liquid polysulfide developed in 1943 offered a more useful route to room-temperature-cured aircraft fuel-tank sealants. A further historical turn came at Caltech’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory: Charles Bartley filed his polysulfide-binder composite-propellant patent in 1946, issued in 1961. Thiokol then expanded into solid propulsion under Joseph Crosby. This history distinguishes the early solid rubber from later liquid, curable polysulfides that supported sealing and binder applications.
sections.nomenclature: Polysulfide rubber and polysulfide elastomer identify the sulfur-containing elastomer family, not one liquid precursor or cured sealant compound. Chain branching, end-group functionality, oxidant, filler, and coating formulation define particular networked materials and must remain explicit.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polysulfide rubbers are made by condensation of organic dihalides with alkali-metal polysulfides, creating chains whose backbone contains recurring organic groups separated by sulfur sequences. A common feed is bis(2-chloroethyl) formal; ethylene dichloride, propylene dichloride, or other dihalides can change the organic segment, and a small multifunctional halide introduces branching. One cited patent describes aqueous-dispersion condensation of bis(2-chloroethyl) formal and related dihalides with sodium polysulfide, followed by reductive cleavage of a high-molar-mass intermediate with sodium hydrosulfide and sodium sulfite to yield thiol-terminated liquid polymer. A distinct historical patent identifies the same dihalide/polysulfide chemistry and branched liquid precursors. The terminal thiols are then oxidatively coupled into an elastomeric network with curing agents such as lead dioxide, manganese dioxide, zinc peroxide, or organic peroxides; filler and accelerator packages are formulation-specific. Sulfur rank, dihalide mixture, branching-agent level, reductive cleavage, and end-group content control precursor architecture. Article-shaping cure schedules and application equipment remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polysulfide-rubber (PSR) materials span liquid polysulfide oligomers and cured or compounded elastomer networks, so their response is governed by molecular structure, cure chemistry and crosslink density, plasticizer or resin modification, filler loading and interfacial coupling, cure history, temperature, aging, and test rate. A study of PSR with a liquid-polysulfide-oligomer-modified MoS2 crosslinker identifies the inherently limited mechanical response of neat PSR and the importance of crosslinker and filler dispersion. In a separate marine-deck-coating experiment, the polysulfide-rubber-modified formulation designated L1 gave static tensile strength 12.4 MPa, compared with 5.5 MPa for the unmodified coating (L0). This is a formulation-specific, cured coating comparison; it is not a tensile specification for unfilled polysulfide rubber or for sealants cured by other chemistries.
sections.processing:
Liquid polysulfide rubber sealants and molding compounds are article-converted by accurately metering a base and curing component, low-speed mixing to a uniform color, optional vacuum degassing, and prompt pouring, gun application, or tooling into a prepared joint or mold before the pot life expires. Substrates and molds must be clean and compatible with the specified primer or release practice; joint geometry, backing material, adhesion faces, and bead depth control movement accommodation. Mixing speed and time, scraping the vessel walls and bottom, entrained air, batch size, material and ambient temperature, humidity, and elapsed time after mixing govern viscosity, flow, bubble retention, working life, surface tooling, and cure. The applied material should be protected from disturbance and incompatible contamination while it develops a crosslinked network, and demolding or service loading should wait for the formulation's stated cure. Manufacture of the liquid polysulfide prepolymer belongs in Synthesis; metering, mixing, application, and the cure schedule that creates the finished seal or molding belong in Processing.

The numerical schedules are formulation-specific. Sika Polysulphide PG specifies a 95:5 A:B mass ratio, about 5 min mixing with a drill or electric mixer at no more than 500 rpm, about 2 h pot life at 25 °C, application from 5–50 °C, and about one week cure; its joint guidance is 6–50 mm width with width:depth near 2:1. Smooth-On's distinct FMC-201 polysulfide compound calls for thorough separate stirring, combining the two parts for 3 min, optional vacuum degassing to reduce bubbles, and prompt pouring while viscosity is low. Neither schedule is a universal polysulfide-rubber cure window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Liquid polysulfide precursors contain organic segments connected by sulfur linkages and can carry thiol groups at their ends. Polyfunctional starting materials or branching agents can introduce branches. Oxidation of terminal thiols links chains into a crosslinked network. The final structure depends on precursor functionality, curing agent and formulation. In a conventional process, the liquid is made from a higher-molecular-weight polysulfide by reduction to thiol-terminated chains. A curing reaction then connects the chain ends into a larger network; branching or multifunctional precursors allow connections at more than two points. Network architecture therefore depends on the precursor and curing formulation rather than on sulfur content alone.
sections.properties: Cured polysulfide sealants must deform with the joint while remaining attached to its sides. Sika reports approximately 20 Shore A hardness by ASTM C661 and ±25% movement capability by ASTM C719 for its particular Polysulphide PG product. Joint design must account for the movement capability, and these numbers are not intrinsic properties of every polysulfide rubber. Precursor molecular weight, branching, curing agent and fillers change a finished network.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polysulfide sealants serve horizontal expansion joints in floors, bridge decks, reservoirs, roads and airport runways. Sika describes its self-leveling Polysulphide PG for joints that need a flexible seal as adjacent structures move. Its approximately ±25% movement capability by ASTM C719 helps a designer relate anticipated joint movement to an appropriate joint width; this rating belongs to the named sealant, not all polysulfide rubbers. Correct dimensions, backing and substrate preparation are also necessary for the assembly.

Purchasing. The July 2018 data sheet lists two-component A+B packs of 4 L and 18 L and a mixing ratio of 95:5 by weight. It specifies about two hours of pot life at 25 °C and approximately one week to cure, so users must plan mixing and application around the job and conditions. These values apply to that particular formulation and data sheet.

Scale and evidence limits. The listed 4 L and 18 L volumes refer to paired, formulated sealant components. They indicate order-size options, not annual demand or the quantity of neat polysulfide polymer used.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A patent cautions that conventional cured polysulfide rubber can suffer irreversible polymer-chain damage when heated enough to flow. Its specially formulated hot-applied material is intended to flow under heat and recover rubber-like behavior on cooling, but excessive temperature may still cause decomposition or reversion to a permanent liquid. The patent does not identify the molecular products.

Timescales: Sandia studied a two-component cured polysulfide sealant by ageing fresh specimens at 95–140 °C, including a 125 °C series sampled over 64 days. Hot-air ageing increased crosslinking and hardness while reducing elasticity; immersion in hot water instead showed evidence of chain scission and softening. The comparison concerns a specific sealant and exposure, not an environmental mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: Property changes and network scission in the sealant experiments do not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill. The Sandia study was designed around seal performance, and it did not measure a natural-environment mineralization time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent describes selected thiol-terminated polysulfide formulations cured with zinc oxide and specified sulfur-containing accelerators. A cured ribbon can be extruded under heat and pressure and then regain rubber-like properties on cooling; excessive heating risks permanent degradation. This is reprocessability of a deliberately designed material, not evidence of a general post-consumer recycling industry.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For the two-part FMC-201 polysulfide molding compound, the supplier warns that components can severely irritate eyes and skin and advises against heating the uncured components. Avoid direct contact and use appropriate eye and hand protection during mixing. These are formulation-specific handling instructions; the hazards of a cured polysulfide seal or mold depend on its remaining additives and service conditions.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Liquid polysulfide precursors vary in molecular weight, branching and terminal functionality. Curing agents and fillers determine how the finished network develops. The cited MoS2 and marine-coating experiments use distinct formulations and specimen preparations. Their values should not be applied to every polysulfide sealant or elastomer. In the marine-coating study, the authors report higher tensile strength for the L1 formulation than L0, but their fitted equation does not reproduce those reported values and the discussion gives inconsistent maximum-strength claims. The direction is an observation for those coatings; the numerical trend should be treated cautiously.

sections.overview: Polyisobutylene (PIB) is the homopolymer of isobutylene, commonly made by cationic polymerization. It is a saturated hydrocarbon polymer distinct from isobutylene–isoprene butyl rubber. Different molecular weights and terminal groups provide materials suited to different uses. PIB is used in products including adhesives and formulated additives. Molecular weight has a practical consequence for adhesives: short PIB chains flow readily and help wet a surface, while longer chains can entangle and resist separation. A model tack study used mixtures of low- and high-molecular-weight PIB to examine both contact and debonding. Its findings illustrate formulation choices rather than specifying the behavior of every PIB product.
sections.history: BASF traces its polyisobutylene development to Michael Otto’s 1931 work and a patent filed that year. Its 2026 history distinguishes this laboratory milestone from the industrial Oppanol plant that began production in 1938. The polymer’s subsequent uses ranged from cable insulation, roofing and pipeline coatings to insulating-glass sealants, adhesive bandages and chewing-gum formulations. Later research increasingly controlled molecular weight and reactive chain ends, enabling specialized additives and functional materials. A recent product milestone was BASF’s 2026 introduction of Oppanol N PLUS as a binder for emerging battery designs. These examples illustrate the breadth of the homopolymer platform; they do not make polyisobutylene identical to isoprene-containing butyl rubber.
sections.nomenclature: Polyisobutylene and polyisobutene identify the isobutylene homopolymer in this record. PIB is distinct from butyl rubber, which includes an isoprene comonomer; end-functional PIB grades and PIB-containing block copolymers are narrower materials rather than synonyms for the base polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyisobutylene is made principally by cationic addition polymerization of isobutylene. An electrophilic initiating species generated by a Lewis-acid/coinitiator system adds to the electron-rich olefin, and the resulting tertiary carbocation propagates; low reaction temperature suppresses chain transfer and rearrangement when high molar mass is sought. Lewis acids such as aluminum, boron, titanium, or iron halides can be paired with water, alcohol, hydrogen halide, ether, or an organic initiator, with solvent polarity, temperature, monomer concentration, and transfer or termination chemistry controlling molar mass and whether chain ends are exo-olefinic or halide terminated. The cited review compares catalytic systems for controlled and highly reactive PIB, including water/TiCl4/alcohol initiation. A distinct patent example scopes low-temperature slurry copolymerization in a polar diluent with a Lewis acid and initiator; it is included as an industrially relevant isobutylene-polymerization variant and not as evidence that every PIB contains a comonomer.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyisobutylene (PIB) covers low-molar-mass viscous materials through high-molar-mass elastomeric grades, and its mechanical response is controlled by molecular weight/distribution, chain architecture and end groups, temperature and rate, and—when used in a network or block material—crosslink density, hard-block fraction, and processing history. Accordingly, values for a PIB-based block copolymer or polyurethane are not values for neat linear PIB. As a bounded example, a poly(styrene-block-isobutylene-block-styrene) (SIBS) material with number-average molecular weight 33,000 g mol−1 was tested as ISO 37:2017 type-1A dumbbells at 10 mm min−1 and had tensile strength 3.51 MPa. This describes that specific SIBS block copolymer, not a general PIB tensile specification.
sections.processing:
Polyisobutylene (PIB) is commonly article-converted as the elastomeric base or viscosity modifier in solvent-borne and hot-melt pressure-sensitive adhesives, sealants, barrier coatings, and highly filled compounds. Documented application methods include spraying, dipping, spreading, troweling, and coating a carrier film. Production operations therefore center on dissolving or melt-mixing selected molecular-weight grades with lower-molecular-weight PIB, tackifiers, oils, waxes, fillers, and antioxidants, followed by thin-layer application, solvent removal or cooling, slitting, winding, pelletizing, or slab forming. Molecular mass and solids content strongly control viscosity and equipment choice: low-viscosity solutions can use high-shear mixers, while high-viscosity mastics require churns, planetary mixers, kneaders, mills, or Banbury-type equipment. Thin coats and adequate intercoat drying are important because PIB's low permeability can trap solvent and create porosity. Hot processing should minimize air exposure and unnecessary heat history because the oxidation risk rises as low-molecular-weight material is handled near its melt-processing temperature.

Petrie's SpecialChem guide gives formulation-specific rather than universal ranges: it describes about 5–10% solids for spraying, 10–30% for dipping, 25–50% for spreading, and 50–70% for trowel or spatula application, and assigns 50,000–200,000 cP products to jacketed turbine mixers, 200,000–1,000,000 cP products to churns or double-arm planetary mixers, and products above 1,000,000 cP to kneaders, mills, or Banbury mixers. It also reports a typical PIB hot-melt viscosity of 30,000–60,000 cP at 177 °C depending on grade, not a family specification. A distinct industrial example from BUSS uses an 11 L/D continuous kneader: PIB and rubber fractions are melted or masticated by dissipative shear in the first zone, fillers and resins enter the second, and waxes, plasticizers, antioxidants, and optional rework are distributed downstream before hot-cut granulation, rotoforming, or slab molding. That equipment-specific sequence illustrates how short residence, staged feeding, temperature control, and distributive mixing are used for a viscous PIB gumbase formulation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The PIB chain is built from isobutylene-derived units with a saturated carbon backbone. Cationic synthesis can be controlled to yield polymers with different molecular weights and terminal groups. The cited synthesis review discusses routes to exo-olefinic and chloride-terminated chains. PIB blocks in a copolymer are part of a different material architecture from PIB homopolymer. PIB homopolymers in the cited tack study were amorphous and not chemically crosslinked. Long chains can instead become physically entangled; as the adhesive is pulled away, these interactions help sustain stretched fibrils. That reversible physical constraint differs from the covalent links of a cured butyl-rubber network.
sections.properties: PIB behavior changes strongly with molecular weight. In a probe-tack study, model mixtures contained 80% low-molecular-weight PIB and 20% of a higher-molecular-weight PIB. At 25 °C, significant fibril formation during debonding appeared when the high-molecular-weight component reached about 850 kg/mol, whereas the 88 kg/mol component showed little fibrillation. The result illustrates how long-chain entanglement changes adhesive deformation; it belongs to the tested mixtures and contact conditions, not all PIB formulations. A styrene–isobutylene block copolymer has a different physical structure and must be evaluated separately.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PIB is used in sealants, adhesives and electrical insulation, and as a modifier in rubber, wax and asphalt. ENEOS lists these applications for its high-consistency TETRAX product. In model PIB adhesive blends, a soft low-molecular-weight fraction assists surface contact while a longer-chain fraction supports fibrillation during debonding. In one 80/20 blend series tested at 25 °C, strong fibrillation was observed only when the higher-molecular-weight component was at least about 850 kg/mol. That threshold belongs to the tested model blends; a commercial formulation also depends on its other components.

Purchasing. ENEOS supplies TETRAX by grade in 20 kg cartons. Buyers specify the molecular-weight grade and required formulation rather than treating the polymer name as a finished adhesive specification.

Scale and evidence limits. The carton is a purchasing unit, not annual demand. No reliable separate PIB consumption total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Vacuum pyrolysis of PIB produces volatile fragments and lower-molecular-weight residue. The NBS study interprets the rapid molecular-weight reduction as largely random chain initiation with substantial chain transfer; earlier analyses cited there reported different monomer fractions in the volatiles, so monomer yield cannot be assumed universal.

Timescales: For purified 4–5 mg samples at 298.5 °C under high vacuum, roughly 68–84% volatilized after 23–25 hours depending on fraction. Volatilization is not the same as environmental mineralization or complete monomer recovery.

Environmental persistence: The heated vacuum experiment measured volatile loss and changes in the remaining polymer, not microbial conversion. Its high-temperature result cannot be converted into a soil, seawater or landfill lifetime; no transferable natural-environment mineralization time is established.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Thermal/catalytic fragmentation followed by reaction with elemental sulfur in an extruder is proposed in a patent explicitly listing PIB. Its worked examples do not establish PIB-specific product yield or commercial recycling maturity.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Heated polyisobutylene processing calls for control of fume and adherence to formulation-specific temperature and dwell-time guidance. HSE recommends ventilation and assessment of additives and degradation products. This process guidance does not assign a universal toxicity classification to the polymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PIB grades span different molecular weights and terminal functionalities. Neat PIB, a PIB-containing blend and a styrenic block copolymer do not have interchangeable mechanical properties. Synthesis and formulation choices determine the relevant behavior. A measurement should identify molecular characteristics, article form and test conditions.

sections.overview: Ethylene–octene elastomers are polyolefin copolymers of ethylene and 1-octene. The octene-derived branches affect crystallization and make soft elastomeric grades possible. These materials can be melt processed and may also be used in blends. Polymerization catalyst, comonomer content and molecular structure distinguish individual grades. The octene branches interrupt the packing of long ethylene sequences, so composition affects how much ordered material can form. The remaining crystals can hold the material together during deformation but soften on heating, allowing an uncrosslinked grade to be melt processed. Blending and chemical crosslinking modify that behavior.
sections.history: Ethylene–octene elastomers became prominent within the 1990s commercialization of precisely controlled ethylene–alpha-olefin copolymers. A contemporary legal record documents Dow’s ENGAGE product line by February 1994, including two cable grades, followed by another wire-and-cable product that June. That is a dated milestone for the broader ENGAGE platform, not proof of the first synthesis of every ethylene–octene composition. Dow’s subsequent product guides distinguish ethylene–octene from ethylene–butene grades and describe their use in flexible and impact-modified thermoplastic olefins. Automotive bumpers, instrument panels and exterior trim became important outlets. Later development expanded melt-flow and melt-strength options to support injection molding, thermoforming and blow molding of application-specific compounds.
sections.nomenclature: POE is the abbreviation used for ethylene–octene elastomer, also described as an ethylene–octene copolymer. The record covers binary ethylene/1-octene elastomer grades; it excludes EPDM (which contains a diene), EPM/EPR (ethylene–propylene), and a dynamically crosslinked blend as synonyms for the neat copolymer family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–octene elastomers are coordination copolymers made from ethylene and 1-octene, rather than blends of polyethylene and an octene-containing additive. Molecular catalysts, including metallocene, post-metallocene, and vanadium systems, provide routes whose catalyst/activator pair and monomer feeds influence octene incorporation and molecular-weight distribution. In a documented metallocene solution experiment, ethylene and 1-octene were polymerized in decane with MAO/borate activation and triethylaluminum scavenger; a separate open review reports vanadium/alkylaluminum catalyst systems tested for ethylene/1-octene copolymerization. These are route-specific examples, not a universal elastomer composition or manufacturing prescription. The resulting material is a thermoplastic copolymer; later compounding or crosslinking, when used, is outside this synthesis account.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Ethylene-octene elastomers are semicrystalline thermoplastic elastomers in which octene-derived short-chain branches interrupt polyethylene crystallization. The amorphous, branched segments provide rubber-like extensibility, while small polyethylene-rich crystals act as reversible physical junctions that provide strength and recovery. Their tensile response is therefore nonlinear and viscoelastic, often combining low initial stiffness, very large elongation, strain hardening, hysteresis, and some permanent set; stiffness and recovery can fall rapidly as service temperature approaches the grade's crystal-melting interval. Octene content and comonomer distribution, density and crystallinity, random versus blocky sequence architecture, molecular mass and long-chain branching, entanglement density, crystal size and morphology, cooling and annealing history, orientation, strain rate, test temperature, cyclic history, and oxidative or thermal aging are consequential. Greater crystallinity generally raises hardness, modulus, yield stress, and heat resistance but reduces softness; stretching can reorganize or fragment physical crystals. Fillers, blends, foaming, and interfacial adhesion further change strength, tear, impact response, and set. Peroxide, silane, or radiation cross-linking adds permanent junctions and can improve high-temperature strength, compression set, and dimensional recovery, although excessive cross-linking or phase separation can reduce elongation and melt reprocessability. As one bounded commercial-grade example, Dow's ENGAGE 8150 technical information identifies a density-0.868 g/cm3 ethylene-octene copolymer. Compression-molded specimens tested to ASTM D638 at 508 mm/min had a reported 100% modulus of 2.6 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 9.5 MPa, and ultimate elongation of 810%; the same sheet reports Shore A 70 and Shore D 20 hardness to ASTM D2240 and Type C tear strength of 37.3 kN/m to ASTM D624. These are typical, non-specification values for that grade, not ranges for all ethylene-octene elastomers. The sheet does not state tensile specimen dimensions, conditioning, or test temperature, and its grade-specific results should not be transferred to foams, filled compounds, blends, cross-linked articles, or differently crystallized moldings without new testing.
sections.processing:
Ethylene–octene elastomers are melt-processable thermoplastic elastomers used in compounding/blending with polyolefins and in hose, tube, profile, and injection-molding operations. Dow's ENGAGE processing guide recommends conventional thermoplastic equipment, cooling the feed throat below 50 °C to limit pellet bridging, and fast injection to promote shear thinning; its temperatures are reference starting points that can vary by about ±5 °C and may be increased by at most 20 °C. The advice is grade- and machine-dependent, and should not be treated as a universal POE recipe.

A bounded dynamic-compounding example used ENGAGE 8480 (20 wt% octene) in POE/EPDM blends. EPDM and dicumyl peroxide were first mixed on a two-roll mill at 25 °C for 3 min; the preblend was then combined with POE in a torque rheometer at 110 °C, 40 rpm, for about 6 min, and the temperature was raised to 165 °C for cure during compounding. This two-step sequence was selected to preferentially crosslink the EPDM phase and belongs to the reported blend formulation; neat ethylene–octene resin need not be dynamically crosslinked.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Ethylene sequences can form crystalline regions, while octene incorporation disrupts regular packing. The resulting materials contain crystalline and amorphous portions rather than a uniform crosslinked network. In thermoplastic elastomers, crystalline regions can act as physical junctions. Chemical crosslinking or blending with EPDM creates a different morphology from the neat copolymer. The crystals are physical junctions rather than covalent bonds, so their response depends on temperature and the sample’s thermal history. In a study of ENGAGE 8480 with EPDM, the researchers compared the blend before and after peroxide-induced dynamic crosslinking. Its measured crystallization and mechanical behavior reflected the complete blend and treatment, not only the ethylene–octene copolymer.
sections.properties: Octene incorporation disrupts regular chain packing, changing crystallinity and the balance of softness and strength. In one study, ENG 8100 had the highest elongation at break among the tested ethylene–octene grades and lower strength at break, which the authors attributed to its higher comonomer content and lower crystallinity. Those observations are specific to the compared grades and specimens; cure, blending and processing can change the response.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Ethylene–octene elastomers are used for impact modification in polypropylene and polyethylene, thermoplastic-olefin compounds and wire/cable materials. Dow describes ENGAGE 8150 REN for low-temperature impact performance in PP/PE blends and lists hose, profile and injection-molding fabrication routes. The elastomer is a component of the finished blend, whose properties depend on all ingredients.

Purchasing. Dow offers ENGAGE 8150 REN through buying and sample channels and identifies it as ISCC PLUS certified for bio-circular-based plastics. The buyer should verify the applicable certification and documentation with the supplier, as well as the grade needed for the intended blend. The certification claim does not by itself specify the bio-based fraction in an individual finished part.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage was established. The supplier listing documents product and intended uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A twin-screw extrusion study observed small melt-flow decreases for ENG 8480 and ENG 8003, which the authors interpreted as possible crosslinking, while ENG 8100 showed a small increase interpreted as greater degradation. Melt flow alone does not identify the reaction products or independently prove the proposed mechanisms.

Timescales: The extrusion study used a twin-screw machine with a 60–225 °C temperature profile and 350 rpm screw speed. The subsequent comparison of melt flow describes those processing exposures, not weathering over time. It does not establish a transferable environmental mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: The reported extrusion behavior does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill. A change in melt flow is an indirect indicator of processing-induced molecular changes and does not quantify carbon mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: In a laboratory blend study, replacing 5 percentage points of ground tire rubber in a 50/50 LLDPE/tire-rubber mixture with ENG 8480 or ENG 8003 ethylene–octene improved ultimate tensile properties. Dynamic mechanical results suggested a compatibilizing effect, although the authors called for morphological analysis to confirm the interface. This demonstrates reuse of tire rubber in a formulated composite, not recovery of the ethylene–octene copolymer from waste.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Heated ethylene–octene elastomer processing calls for control of fume and adherence to formulation-specific temperature and dwell-time guidance. HSE recommends ventilation and assessment of additives and degradation products. This process guidance does not assign a universal toxicity classification to the polymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Comonomer content, molecular architecture and crystallinity vary between ethylene–octene grades. A grade datasheet depends on its specimen preparation and test methods. Dynamic crosslinking and EPDM addition change both structure and mechanical behavior. Comparisons should identify the grade, whether it is blended or crosslinked, and the conditions of measurement.

sections.overview: Styrene–butadiene–styrene (SBS) is a block copolymer combining polystyrene end blocks with a polybutadiene middle block. The unlike blocks separate into small domains while remaining joined along the same molecule. This structure gives SBS thermoplastic-elastomer behavior: the material can be elastic at ordinary temperatures and softened for processing. SBS materials include linear and branched architectures. The hard styrene domains act as physical junctions at service temperatures, while the flexible diene midblocks permit stretching. On heating, these associations soften and the material can flow for shaping.
sections.history:
SBS became an industrial thermoplastic elastomer through Shell’s styrenic block-copolymer program in the early 1960s. Kraton’s retrospective identifies a 1964 footwear introduction and the opening of the dedicated Belpre, Ohio plant in 1971. These dated commercial milestones are more secure than assigning one invention date to every SBS architecture.

Shoe compounds were an early market. Adhesives followed, while roofing modification expanded in Europe during the 1970s and in the United States during the early 1980s; road-bitumen modification grew subsequently. Shell and its successor Kraton thus helped establish SBS across footwear, bonding and infrastructure. Later production by Asian suppliers broadened the industrial base, with Asahi Kasei recording its own Tufprene production from 1970.
sections.nomenclature: SBS abbreviates styrene–butadiene–styrene block copolymer. The name specifies a block copolymer and should not be confused with random styrene–butadiene rubber.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–butadiene–styrene (SBS) is a triblock copolymer made from styrene and 1,3-butadiene, most commonly by living anionic polymerization under rigorously dry, oxygen-free conditions. In a sequential route, an organolithium initiator such as sec- or n-butyllithium first forms a living polystyryl block in a hydrocarbon solvent; butadiene is then added to form the rubbery midblock, followed by a second styrene charge to complete the linear S–B–S chain. One cited example uses cyclohexane, n-butyllithium, and tetrahydrofuran to prepare SBS, reporting an initial styrene charge followed by addition of butadiene and additional styrene. An alternative cited route makes living S–B diblocks and reacts their carbanionic ends with a multifunctional coupling agent; a difunctional coupling event gives a nominal linear SBS architecture, while higher-functionality coupling gives branched or radial material. Initiator concentration and block-feed amounts set molar mass and block fractions, while polar modifiers and temperature influence butadiene 1,2/1,4 microstructure. Polymerization is terminated and the antioxidant-stabilized polymer is recovered from solvent. At service temperature, incompatible polystyrene end blocks associate into hard domains that physically connect the polybutadiene chains; this reversible physical network is intrinsic to the thermoplastic elastomer and is not a covalent cure network.
sections.mechanicalProperties: SBS is a physically crosslinked thermoplastic elastomer: glassy polystyrene-rich domains act as reversible junctions in a rubbery polybutadiene midblock. Tensile and recovery behavior therefore change with styrene fraction and block lengths, butadiene microstructure, molecular mass and linear/radial topology, uncoupled styrene–butadiene diblock content, microphase morphology and orientation, oil/resin/filler formulation, oxidation or UV exposure, molding/casting history, temperature, and loading rate. An open tensile/DMA study of solution-cast SBS/SB blends found the viscoelastic and large-strain response sensitive to diblock content; at equal diblock content the storage-modulus plateau fell more sharply for linear than radial SBS. As one deliberately grade-bounded endpoint, Solprene 4318 is a linear pellet/powder SBS with 32 wt% total styrene (at least 31 wt% block styrene): its listed tensile strength is 3.7 MPa, 300% modulus 1.2 MPa, and elongation above 1000%. The published grade listing does not supply a tensile standard, specimen geometry, conditioning, or temperature, so these values are not a design basis or an SBS-family range.
sections.processing:
Styrene–butadiene–styrene (SBS) is a thermoplastic elastomer that can be compounded and shaped by conventional thermoplastic operations including extrusion, injection molding, blown-film or blow molding where the formulation has adequate melt strength, and solution or hot-melt coating and casting. Heating releases the physical polystyrene-domain junctions so the material can flow and cooling restores the elastomeric network; ordinary shaping therefore does not require vulcanization. Grade architecture, styrene and diblock content, oil and resin loading, filler dispersion, solvent removal, melt temperature, shear rate, residence time, gate or die geometry, cooling time, and regrind history control flow, anisotropy, surface defects, and recovery. Unsaturated SBS is more vulnerable than hydrogenated SBCs to excessive heat and oxidation.

Avient's supplier bulletin says its SBS/SIS-based formulations normally do not require drying and gives a general processing band of 290–350 °F (about 143–177 °C); it warns that processing above 400 °F (about 204 °C) can produce gels and discoloration. It also links low-shear/high-melt-strength behavior to extrusion, blown film, and blow molding, high-shear thinning to thin-wall injection, excessive shear to separation and gate splay, and soft grades to longer cooling before ejection. These are GLS formulation observations, not settings for neat SBS of every architecture. In a distinct actual casting study, Adhikari prepared named linear and radial SBS/SB blends in toluene, evaporated solvent over about 10 days to make roughly 1 mm films, dried them for several further days, and vacuum-annealed them at 120 °C for 48 h. That long solvent-removal and annealing schedule belongs to those laboratory blends.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The polystyrene and polybutadiene blocks are chemically connected but tend to form separate microdomains. Polystyrene-rich regions can act as physical junctions in an elastomeric network. Depending on architecture and composition, the phase arrangement need not be the same for every grade. A study of solution-cast SBS and styrene–butadiene diblock blends reported lamellar morphologies. These junctions are physical domains rather than the sulfur crosslinks of a conventional vulcanizate. The block ratios and architecture influence which domain arrangement forms.
sections.properties: SBS combines elastomeric deformation with thermoplastic processing. Its physical junctions differ from the permanent chemical crosslinks of a conventional vulcanized rubber. In a study of solution-cast films, adding up to 20 wt% styrene–butadiene diblock to a linear SBS sample caused a small decrease in tensile strength but a substantial increase in strain at break; adding more than 30 wt% caused a rapid fall in tensile stress. Comparable radial blends were less sensitive to the added diblock. These results belong to the particular film compositions and architecture. Heating can release physical associations and permit flow, while cooling allows domains to form again; reprocessing remains sensitive to oxidation and formulation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. SBS is used as a modifier in bitumen for roads, roofing and pipe coatings and in adhesive and sealant formulations. Its rubber-like response can increase the elastic recovery of a suitable bitumen binder, helping the binder recover after deformation. For example, Viva Energy describes its SBS-modified A20E binder for heavily trafficked roads and airports, where it aims to improve resistance to permanent deformation and fatigue cracking. This performance claim concerns that complete binder and asphalt mix; it should not be transferred to every SBS loading or base bitumen.

Purchasing. Kraton’s D1101 A European sheet describes a linear SBS with 31% bound styrene, supplied in porous-pellet or powder forms with different dusting agents. Those supply forms are raw polymer grades, not finished roofing compound or adhesive.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported SBS purchase or consumption tonnage was established in the checked sources. Supplier-listed grade and end uses demonstrate availability, not market share.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A comparative thermal study examined styrenic block copolymers using infrared spectroscopy, chemiluminescence and calorimetry. The two SBS samples lost less than 1% mass in three cycles to 300 °C, while their infrared spectra indicated ketone-containing oxidation products. The authors attributed volatile loss above 250 °C to products including water, carbon dioxide and organic compounds; these deliberately heated specimens are not an inventory of environmental weathering products.

Timescales: The mass comparison used three heating/cooling cycles from 30 to 300 °C. A separate five-cycle test heated from 30 to 180 °C and held at 180 °C for 10 minutes per cycle. In another experiment, SBS-based composites with 5–20% Chlorella biomass were incubated under composting-test conditions at 58 °C for 180 days. After 100 days, the biomass-containing composites produced more CO₂ than the SBS/oil control in that test; the preparation also contained paraffin oil.

Environmental persistence: The composting experiment measures CO₂ from the whole composite and microbial background; it does not establish what fraction came from SBS rather than algal biomass or oil. Thermal oxidation and mass loss do not establish mineralization either. Neither study determines a residence time for a finished article in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
SBS-containing asphalt can be recycled as a mixture without isolating the block copolymer. In one laboratory study, reclaimed SBS-modified pavement from Beijing was blended into new hot-mix asphalt at 30%, 50% and 70% reclaimed pavement, with a rejuvenating agent added. The researchers found that the agent improved moisture and low-temperature cracking measures, but high-reclaimed-content mixtures did not readily recover the performance of the reference mixture.

That experiment evaluates the complete recycled pavement and binder, not recovery of pure SBS or proof that its original molecular structure is restored. Composition, ageing history and the requirements of the new pavement affect the outcome.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Heated SBS processing calls for control of fume and adherence to formulation-specific temperature and dwell-time guidance. HSE recommends ventilation and assessment of additives and degradation products. This process guidance does not assign a universal toxicity classification to the polymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The relative block amounts, molecular architecture and uncoupled diblock content matter when comparing SBS materials. The cited mechanical study used particular solution-cast, annealed films and studied both linear and radial forms. Its trends should not be treated as fixed property values for every commercial formulation. Additives and final processing can further change finished-product behavior. Even two SBS specimens with different styrene fractions behaved differently in one thermal-oxidation study; neither result describes all SBS grades or additives.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Living anionic sequential polymerization forms a single S–B–S triblock. Organolithium addition creates a nucleophilic, resonance-stabilized carbon chain end. Further monomer additions regenerate the active anionic end; preserving that end permits additional growth before an intentional quench or coupling reaction.

steps.title: Prepare the reaction
steps.body: Initiate styrene to form a living polystyryl block, then add butadiene.

steps.title: Extend the active anionic chain
steps.body: Keep the living chain end available for the selected monomer feed or subsequent block-forming charge. Sequential feed and randomizing modifiers have different roles: the former can establish block order, whereas the latter alters incorporation and diene microstructure in the cited route.

steps.title: Form and recover the product
steps.body: Add a further styrene charge to extend S–B chains into S–B–S blocks.
