sections.overview: Poly(p-phenylene/3,4′-oxydiphenylene terephthalamide) is an aromatic copolyamide made using p-phenylenediamine, 3,4′-diaminodiphenyl ether and terephthaloyl chloride. The ether-containing diamine distinguishes it from PPTA homopolymer. The copolymer is processed from solution into oriented high-performance fibers; Technora is a commercial example. Ropes, hose reinforcements and protective fabrics use different fiber forms and must be evaluated for their particular loads and exposures.
sections.history: Teijin developed the copolyaramid associated with Technora in 1974 and dates its market introduction to 1986. This is a separate history from the earlier PPTA fiber route. Its copolymer design supported applications involving repeated loading and abrasion, including automotive transmission belts, hoses, industrial ropes and composite reinforcement. Teijin also describes later use in offshore flexible pipes and umbilical hoses, protective fabrics and Mars-landing equipment. These developments trace the commercial Technora embodiment of this copolymer; the trade name does not denote all para-aramids.
sections.nomenclature: ODA-PPTA identifies a copolyaramid containing oxydiphenylene-derived units as well as para-phenylene units. It is not identical to PPTA homopolymer or to the entire aramid family. Technora is the commercial fiber product studied in the cited alkaline-aging work, while T240 specifies a particular finished fiber in that study. The polymer composition, yarn finish and final article should remain distinct in comparisons.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(p-phenylene/3,4′-oxydiphenylene terephthalamide) is a copolyaramid whose diamine feed contains p-phenylenediamine and 3,4′-diaminodiphenyl ether, with terephthaloyl chloride providing the terephthalamide linkages. Its name therefore describes a composition boundary: both the para-phenylene and 3,4′-oxydiphenylene diamine-derived units are part of the chain, rather than a PPTA homopolymer merely blended with an ether additive. Disclosed solution-polycondensation examples dissolve the two diamines in dimethylacetamide or N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone, then add terephthaloyl chloride at low temperature; salt-containing solvent systems are also used in route-specific examples. Subsequent spinning and drawing details are outside this synthesis scope.
sections.mechanicalProperties: This copolyaramid is principally used as a highly oriented continuous fiber, so its tensile and fatigue response reflects copolymer composition, dope and spinning history, post-draw orientation and crystallite morphology, yarn finish and construction, and conditioning or exposure environment. Moisture, alkaline pH, temperature, and exposure time are particularly important limitations for fiber measurements; a dry single-filament result is not a fabric, rope, or composite value. In an open thesis, as-received Technora T240 fibers identified as this copolyaramid gave tensile strength 3.7 ± 0.4 GPa, failure strain 4.2 ± 0.5%, and tangent modulus 86 ± 7 GPa measured between 0.3% and 0.6% strain at ambient temperature. These values are specific to the T240 fiber and that strain window. The same work found modulus remained broadly similar after long alkaline exposures while strength changes depended on pH and temperature. A public patent for copolyparaphenylene/3,4′-oxydiphenylene terephthalamide fiber also specifies a preferred 4.00–4.50% tensile elongation, reinforcing that process-defined fiber specifications—not a bulk-polymer constant—govern use.
sections.processing:
Poly(p-phenylene/3,4′-oxydiphenylene terephthalamide), often described as ODA/PPTA copolyaramid, is converted from solution rather than by conventional melt injection or extrusion. Commercial aromatic-polyamide processing reviews identify wet spinning, dry spinning, and dry-jet wet spinning for ODA/PPTA, producing continuous multifilament yarn, staple fiber, and pulp that can be converted further into paper and composites. In a typical air-gap route the polymer dope is filtered and extruded through a spinneret, partially coagulated, drawn while still plasticized, washed to remove solvent, dried, hot-drawn, and wound. Dope concentration, coagulation rate, plastic-state draw, hot-draw temperature and ratio, filament breakage, and solvent removal are coupled process variables.

Teijin's JP 2013-170334 A supplies a bounded example for the 1:1 p-phenylene/3,4′-oxydiphenylene copolyaramid. Example 1 used a 6 mass% polymer solution in N-methylpyrrolidone, extruded it across an air gap into a 50 °C aqueous bath containing 30 mass% NMP, drew the plasticized coagulated yarn 1.2 times, washed it in water, dried it, then hot-drew it 11 times at 520 °C and wound it. Examples 2–4 varied the plastic draw through 1.3, 1.4, and 1.5. The patent bounds that plastic-state step at 1.2–1.5: below 1.2 it reports inadequate initial draw, while above 1.5 it reports single-filament breakage and poor line passage. Those limits and the 520 °C hot draw are specific to the patent's dope, copolymer composition, and equipment.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The copolymer contains aromatic amide units derived from two different diamines, including an ether-linked diphenylene unit. A model cited in a Technora aging paper describes both more flexible ether-containing segments and more rigid PPTA-like segments, with chains highly oriented along the fiber. This is a structural model for the studied commercial fiber rather than proof of one sequence distribution for every copolyaramid grade. Solution spinning, drawing and surface finish also affect the morphology of the final yarn.
sections.properties: This copolyaramid is used as a high-performance fiber material, but the response depends on the material form and exposure. In one study, Technora T240 fibers aged in pH 11 water at 80 °C for one and a half years retained a mean normalized tensile strength of 96% of the as-received reference, with reported variability of ±10 percentage points. The same study observed chemical and finish changes despite the small measured strength change, illustrating why one endpoint cannot describe all effects of aging. This result is for a specified yarn and laboratory exposure, not a general lifetime under all chemicals.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. The commercial copolyaramid Technora reinforces offshore mooring ropes, industrial belts, hoses and technical fabrics; staple grades also serve protective clothing. Its high tensile strength and modulus provide load-bearing capacity and limit elongation, useful in ropes and other tensioned components. Teijin describes stretch-broken yarn as having a larger surface area that improves bonding with rubber, and identifies turbocharger hoses and timing belts as applications of that form. A fiber property alone does not establish the service life of a complete rope or hose.

Purchasing. Teijin offers filament yarn, stretch-broken yarn, staple and short-cut forms. The supplier lists staple at 51 mm and short-cut products from 1 to 30 mm; those are catalog examples rather than universal fiber lengths. Buyers should specify the copolyaramid grade, form and finish instead of ordering by the generic label para-aramid.

Scale and evidence limits. Staple and short-cut dimensions describe available products rather than quantities sold or consumed. Resin, rubber and other components in finished articles cannot be counted as copolyaramid fiber tonnage. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was established from the checked sources.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Warm alkaline water can change the chemistry of Technora copolyaramid yarn, and its finish can also affect measurements. In a study of T240 fibers, infrared and thermal analyses indicated slight surface change under the tested conditions and bulk changes in the alkaline exposures; microscopy also showed rearrangement of the finish. The study discusses amide hydrolysis but does not provide a complete inventory of released molecules or environmental metabolites.

Timescales: Technora T240 yarn was aged for one and a half years in deionized water and in pH 9 and pH 11 solutions at 20 or 80 °C. At pH 11 and 80 °C, its mean tensile strength was 96 ± 10% of the as-received reference; the authors reported no significant strength change across their tested conditions. These are specific accelerated fiber-aging tests and do not measure complete polymer destruction.

Environmental persistence: The chemical and tensile measurements describe a selected yarn in controlled aqueous solutions, not biological conversion of its carbon to carbon dioxide or biomass. They do not establish how long this copolyaramid persists in soil, freshwater or seawater. A lifetime claim would require a defined environmental exposure and a measured endpoint.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
For Technora yarn waste, the supplier's safety guidance calls for segregation and handling according to a licensed collector's instructions. It notes that wet treatment may remove yarn additives and that the resulting wastewater requires treatment. These are documented waste-handling considerations rather than a demonstration of polymer recovery.

A yarn may carry a finish and be incorporated into a rubber belt, hose or other composite, so separating its polymer from the article is an additional practical issue. The checked guidance does not establish a process that returns this copolyaramid to monomers or produces equivalent new fiber, nor does it establish local collection for every finished product.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The March 2026 Technora yarn sheet identifies eye and respiratory irritation from dust and possible skin irritation. It recommends extraction and filtered cleanup; heating can volatilize or decompose applied finishes. High-speed yarn presents a cutting hazard. Its industrial-use guidance does not establish suitability for food or body-fluid contact.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: This entry describes a copolyaramid rather than PPTA homopolymer. Diamine proportions, spinning and yarn finish distinguish its fibers. The alkaline-aging researchers found that the finish complicated interpretation of density and surface measurements, while strength values varied among specimens. Comparisons should identify the grade, the conditioning medium, temperature and test endpoint rather than assume all Technora products behave alike.

sections.overview: Polybenzimidazoles (PBIs) are a family of aromatic heterocyclic polymers containing benzimidazole units in their chains. Heat resistance supports uses in protective fibers and engineering stock shapes. Researchers also make PBI separation membranes and acid-doped proton-conducting membranes for fuel cells, where the acid changes the membrane's properties. A fiber, a machined shape and an acid-loaded membrane therefore cannot be treated as the same material form.
sections.history: NASA traces aromatic PBI to Carl Marvel’s research on high-temperature polymers in the late 1950s and further development with Herward Vogel in 1961. NASA and the U.S. Air Force supported textile development from 1963; NASA subsequently contracted Celanese to develop protective fabrics. Spaceflight uses during the 1970s and 1980s included clothing, webbing and tethers. PBI entered U.S. firefighting applications in 1978, and a dedicated commercial fiber plant opened in Rock Hill in 1983. Celanese sold the business to PBI Performance Products in 2005. Protective textiles remained important while the Celazole line extended PBI into high-temperature polymer components.
sections.nomenclature: PBI abbreviates polybenzimidazole and refers to a family of polymers containing benzimidazole units, not one fixed chain structure or product. The arrangements of aromatic groups linking those units distinguish different PBI chemistries; m-PBI and 2,5-PBI are examples discussed in the literature. An acid-doped membrane is a PBI-based formulation rather than the undoped polymer alone. Commercial fiber, stock-shape and membrane grades should be identified separately when interpreting properties.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polybenzimidazoles (PBIs) are aromatic heterocyclic polymers formed by step-growth condensation and cyclization of an aromatic tetraamine with an aromatic or heterocyclic dicarboxylic acid, ester, or related difunctional precursor. The most established PBI uses 3,3′,4,4′-tetraaminobiphenyl with isophthalic acid or diphenyl isophthalate to form poly[2,2′-(m-phenylene)-5,5′-bibenzimidazole]. Melt polymerization releases water or phenol while forming benzimidazole rings; near-equimolar functionality, atmosphere, catalyst, agitation, and any solid-state finishing govern conversion and molecular mass. A foundational patent documents tetraamine/diphenyl-dicarboxylate polymerization, while a later single-stage route directly reacts tetraaminobiphenyl with isophthalic acid under nitrogen, with catalyst-free and phosphorus-catalyst variants. These routes form PBI resin; solution preparation, fiber spinning, and membrane casting are downstream processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polybenzimidazole (PBI) families contain rigid benzimidazole-rich backbones whose intermolecular hydrogen bonding can give high stiffness, strength, compressive resistance, and mechanical retention at high temperature. Response depends strongly on whether the material is a drawn fiber, a powder-molded or machined stock shape, a thin membrane, an acid-doped membrane, or an aliphatic/modified PBI; molecular mass, orientation, void content, moisture/acid uptake, temperature, and reinforcement are consequential. A stock-shape number is therefore not a fiber or proton-conducting membrane number. For black CELAZOLE PBI stock shapes, the 23 °C supplier sheet reports dry-material tensile stress at break of 140 MPa and strain at break of 3% (ISO 527 type 1B, 5 mm/min), tensile modulus 5.8 GPa (1 mm/min), 375 MPa compressive stress at 1% strain, and 3.5 kJ/m² notched Charpy impact. The sheet identifies rods/plates/tubes but not molding route or exact composition, so these are indicative dry stock-shape values. Independent aliphatic PBI research shows how backbone flexibilization shifts the balance: C7-, C10-, and C14-PBI tensile strengths were 95.5 ± 6.2, 129.3 ± 7.1, and 83.9 ± 5.3 MPa with 19.8–39.1% elongation, explicitly not values for conventional wholly aromatic PBI.
sections.processing: Polybenzimidazole (PBI) is converted either from dry resin into stock shapes or from concentrated solutions into fibers and membranes. A PBI hollow-fiber study used a degassed 15–20% PBI/DMAc dope, extruded it through a spinneret at 35–55 °C and 1–2 cc/min into an alcohol coagulation bath at 5–15 °C, then washed and dried the fibers; the air gap was varied from 0.5 to 4 in. A separate Celazole U-60 moisture-management guide gives a post-fabrication drying cycle that ramps to 130 °C, then to 200 °C (or 150 °C under vacuum), with a 4–72 h hold depending on part size, moisture, and service conditions. The spinning and drying examples are route- and grade-specific; high solution viscosity, solvent removal, moisture uptake, and part thickness must be controlled rather than assigned a single PBI-family cycle.
sections.structureAndMorphology: A PBI backbone contains aromatic benzimidazole rings with nitrogen atoms, but the units connecting those rings depend on the particular chemistry. Interactions between chains contribute to the properties of cast membranes. Adding phosphoric acid changes the membrane material: the acid is taken up by the polymer and provides proton-conducting pathways, while the amount incorporated and the membrane's structure depend on preparation. These acid-loaded membranes are distinct from undoped PBI fiber and machined stock.
sections.properties: PBI materials are valued for thermal stability, but thermal limits depend on chemistry and test conditions. In a study using thermogravimetry in nitrogen at 10 °C per minute, a laboratory 2,5-PBI reference reached 10% mass loss at 689 °C; this measured endpoint is not a continuous-use temperature for commercial fiber or stock. Acid doping changes a PBI membrane's electrical response. In one study, a membrane immersed in 14 M phosphoric acid reached 0.05 S/cm proton conductivity at 140 °C; the result also changed over measurement cycles. Acid loading, temperature and membrane preparation matter, and the result does not describe an undoped fiber.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PBI fiber is supplied for heat- and flame-protective fabrics, particularly firefighter clothing. Its heat resistance helps protective fabric maintain a barrier against break-open when exposed to flame; a finished protective ensemble depends on its fabric blend, layers and construction. PBI is also being investigated as a separation membrane, a distinct use from the textile fiber. In one laboratory hollow-fiber desalination study, a surface treatment increased salt rejection from 93.8% to 99.0% while water flux fell from 1.73 to 1.47 L/m² per hour, at 300 psi with the tested feed; those values describe the experimental membranes, not all PBI products.

Purchasing. PBI Performance Products provides the specialist fiber and fabric channel; its published staple-fiber scope includes natural gold and solvent-dyed black. A separate historical Celazole data sheet lists PBI stock shapes as rods, plates and tubes for machining. Buyers should specify fiber, stock or membrane and any blend constituents for the intended use.

Scale and evidence limits. The listed fiber forms and stock dimensions describe product offerings, not annual consumption. The membrane result is a laboratory demonstration and does not establish the market size of PBI filtration products. No reliable separately reported annual purchased or consumed PBI tonnage was established from the checked sources.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PBI stability depends on backbone chemistry and exposure. In a laboratory study of 2,5-PBI and its aramid-containing derivatives, thermogravimetry measured changes in sample mass during heating in nitrogen. It did not identify a complete set of thermal breakdown molecules or environmental degradation products. A high thermal mass-loss temperature should not be interpreted as evidence of biological mineralization.

Timescales: The researchers heated approximately 5 mg samples in nitrogen at 10 °C per minute and reported a 10% mass-loss temperature of 689 °C for their 2,5-PBI reference. A related laboratory copolymer containing 15 mol% para-polyamide reached the same endpoint at 743 °C. These temperatures describe a programmed heating experiment on particular materials, not a duration of outdoor service or environmental disappearance.

Environmental persistence: Neither thermal measurement follows conversion of PBI carbon to carbon dioxide or biomass in soil or water. The evidence here does not establish a condition-qualified environmental mineralization time for PBI fibers, stock shapes or membranes. Material chemistry and form would need to be identified in a suitable environmental study.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Reversible Diels–Alder links enabled laboratory recycling of a specially modified PBI membrane. This proof of concept depends on deliberately introduced reversible bonds and does not demonstrate recycling of conventional commercial PBI fibers.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The PBI polymer powder safety sheet recommends ventilation and avoidance of generated dust. Strong thermal stability does not eliminate fire or overheating hazards: decomposition can release carbon oxides, nitrogen oxides and other irritating or toxic fumes. These are handling considerations for the named polymer powder, not evidence of implant compatibility.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PBI chemistry, molecular mass and material form distinguish fibers, membranes and stock shapes. A stock-shape supplier's values apply to its product and test conditions, while an acid-doped membrane contains additional material that influences proton transport. In a laboratory comparison, a 2,5-PBI film and PBI–polyamide copolymer films reached different 10% mass-loss temperatures under the same nitrogen heating program. Such results illustrate composition dependence but do not establish service temperatures for commercial articles.

sections.overview: Poly(p-phenylene benzobisoxazole), or PBO, is an aromatic heterocyclic polymer with a rigid, rodlike backbone. It is made into high-strength fibers such as Toyobo's ZYLON for ropes, tire cords and other demanding reinforcement applications. Those fibers combine strength and heat resistance, but exposure to moisture, light and repeated flexing can reduce their performance. A product must therefore be assessed over its intended service exposure rather than by its initial fiber strength alone.
sections.history: PBO emerged from the search for rigid, thermally stable polymers for high-strength fibers. A documented development milestone is Wilfred Sweeny and Stephanie Kwolek’s DuPont patent, filed in 1985 and published in 1986, improving an existing polyphosphoric-acid synthesis by using terephthalate esters. Thus this patent represents a process advance rather than the first discovery of PBO. Toyobo records the start of full-scale Zylon PBO-fiber production in 1998. The commercial fiber extended rigid-chain polymer research into reinforcing materials; Toyobo identifies automotive friction materials and industrial manufacturing equipment among its application targets.
sections.nomenclature: PBO abbreviates poly(p-phenylene benzobisoxazole); the more explicit name poly(p-phenylene-2,6-benzobisoxazole) identifies the phenylene and benzobisoxazole connections in the chain. It is distinct from PBZT, a related sulfur-containing benzobisthiazole polymer. ZYLON is a commercial PBO fiber rather than a synonym for every PBO article. Its AS and HM designations identify as-spun and high-modulus fiber grades, respectively, and a grade or fabric specification is needed when comparing their performance.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(p-phenylene benzobisoxazole) (PBO) is a para-ordered, rigid-rod benzobisazole made by high-temperature step-growth condensation and ring closure, not by fiber spinning. The standard monomer pair is 4,6-diaminoresorcinol dihydrochloride and terephthalic acid (or a reactive terephthalate diester) in polyphosphoric acid (PPA). PPA functions as a strongly dehydrating reaction medium and solvent for the growing polymer; polymerization couples the amine/phenolic monomer with the terephthalate-derived unit and cyclodehydrates to the fused oxazole rings. Near-stoichiometric monomer balance, acid concentration, exclusion of moisture/oxygen, feedstock particle size or ester reactivity, and stabilizer choice are route controls relevant to molecular mass. The acid dope may later be used for spinning, but spinning, drawing, and heat treatment are post-synthesis operations and are excluded here.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PBO is a rigid-rod, lyotropic-liquid-crystal fiber polymer whose exceptional axial stiffness and strength arise only after highly oriented fiber formation. Fiber grade, molecular mass, spinning and draw history, filament count and yarn construction, gauge length and loading rate, temperature, moisture, ultraviolet exposure, hydrolysis, abrasion, and composite impregnation can all change the observed response; transverse and compressive response should not be inferred from axial tensile data. A FibrXL sheet for commercial Zylon yarns reports 5.8 GPa tenacity/strength for AS and HM yarn types, with 180 GPa initial modulus and 3.5% elongation at break for AS types and 270 GPa and 2.5%, respectively, for HM types. The sheet does not give test method, gauge length, rate, conditioning, or temperature, so these are supplier values for specified oriented yarn families rather than intrinsic PBO constants. Independent NIST testing of yarns removed from penetrated PBO body armor found a 30% tensile-strength decrease relative to new, unworn vests of the same model; hydrolytic degradation signatures correlated with the strength loss, underscoring the environmental durability limitation of an article rather than a virgin-fiber benchmark.
sections.processing:
Poly(p-phenylene benzobisoxazole) (PBO) is not ordinarily shaped by melt processing. The important primary conversion route is dry-jet wet spinning of an optically anisotropic PBO/polyphosphoric-acid dope: the dope is filtered and deaerated, metered through a spinneret, elongated across an air gap, rapidly coagulated in a nonsolvent bath, thoroughly washed to remove acid, dried, and wound. Spinneret shear and air-gap draw establish much of the axial orientation, while coagulation rate, washing, tension, and any subsequent heat treatment influence the retained structure. The National Research Council review emphasizes that suitable dope concentration and temperature and the as-spun orientation history are integral to processing these otherwise intractable rigid-rod polymers.

A Lockheed Martin patent provides one bounded continuous-spinning and acid-removal example. Its demonstrated PBO dope was filtered through a 74 µm stainless-steel mesh and degassed at 100 °C, then extruded through a single 20 mil (0.5 mm) spinneret opening at 90 °C and 1000–1100 psi with draw ratios of 40–50. The wet filament crossed an air gap and sequential distilled-water, 5% aqueous ammonium-hydroxide, and distilled-water baths before winding; the spools were then immersed in distilled water for a few days and air-dried, and some fibers were treated under dry nitrogen at 300 °C for 30 s. The patent's practical constraint is that residual phosphoric acid should be neutralized while the freshly coagulated fiber remains wet and permeable; it reports that delayed post-fabrication treatments were ineffective. This is the patent's monofilament example, not a universal PBO spinning schedule.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PBO chains consist of para-phenylene segments connected to fused benzobisoxazole units. This aromatic, rigid-rod backbone is oriented along the axis during fiber formation, making fiber direction important to the properties of a yarn or composite. Commercial products include as-spun and high-modulus fibers rather than a single morphology. The interaction between fiber and a surrounding resin also depends on the exposed surface: a research study modified PBO surfaces before applying a protective coating, illustrating that the surface of the finished fiber is not fixed solely by the repeat unit.
sections.properties: PBO fiber combines thermal resistance with high tensile stiffness, but the reported characteristics depend on the specific fiber grade and test. A distributor lists moisture regain at 65% relative humidity as 2.0% for ZYLON AS and 0.6% for ZYLON HM, illustrating a difference between commercial fiber forms. The same product table lists a 650 °C decomposition temperature in air; that value is not a continuous-use temperature or a prediction of strength retention in humid service. The manufacturer also reports loss of fiber strength after exposure to light, so a high decomposition temperature alone does not establish outdoor durability. In a NIST chamber study of body-armor material, the mean tensile strength of extracted PBO yarn fell from 4.8 to 3.64 GPa after 84 days at 50 °C and 60% relative humidity. This is an exposure-specific fiber result, not a strength prediction for every PBO grade.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Toyobo identifies ZYLON PBO fiber for racing-car tire tethers, tire cords, timing belts, friction components and welding-spark covers. The supplier relates these applications to the fiber's strength, stiffness and heat resistance: cords and tethers carry tensile loads, while spark covers must also tolerate heat. The different yarn, fabric and chopped-fiber forms are chosen for different manufacturing routes. Finished-article suitability depends on construction and exposure, including protection against light and moisture.

Purchasing. The supplier lists as-spun (AS) and high-modulus (HM) filaments, chopped fibers and fabrics through specialist channels. Teijin Frontier's product listing gives examples of 165–1,670 dtex AS filament and 273–3,270 dtex HM filament; these are catalog options rather than universal order sizes. Buyers should specify grade, linear density, finish and final form with the supplier.

Scale and evidence limits. The listed fiber and fabric dimensions describe particular product offerings, not mass sold or annual demand. The product page does not provide a PBO production or consumption total, and no reliable separately reported annual purchase volume was established from the checked sources. Data for downstream rope, fabric or reinforced composites must not be counted as neat PBO fiber tonnage.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In PBO fiber, heat and moisture can promote changes associated with benzoxazole-ring hydrolysis and loss of strength. Infrared analysis in a NIST study was consistent with ring opening to amide groups and subsequent hydrolysis to carboxylic-acid and aminophenol groups. The measurements concern aged fibers and the proposed chemical pathway, rather than a complete inventory of molecules released to the environment. Separate mechanical folding can also damage fibers without establishing polymer mineralization.

Timescales: In the chamber study of body-armor panels, the mean tensile strength of extracted PBO yarn fell from 4.8 to 3.64 GPa after 84 days at 50 °C and 60% relative humidity. Following another 73 days at 60 °C and 37% relative humidity, it fell to 3.08 GPa; subsequent very dry storage did not produce further measured loss. In a comparison, yarns sealed in argon-purged tubes lost less than 4% tensile strength over 210 days, highlighting the role of exposure conditions. These strength endpoints in specified tests do not define an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The chamber and sealed-tube experiments assess changes to fiber chemistry and strength, not the conversion of polymer carbon to carbon dioxide or biomass. They do not establish a soil, freshwater or marine mineralization rate. A relevant persistence study would need to identify the PBO article, exposure and measured endpoint; its environmental residence time remains unresolved here.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The supplier's safety sheet directs waste PBO fiber to applicable waste-management arrangements and warns that loose long fibers can entangle wildlife. Its warning about toxic combustion products is relevant if incineration is used; it does not by itself establish an appropriate disposal method for every jurisdiction. The sheet does not document recovery of PBO polymer or conversion back into usable fiber.

Recycling also depends on the form entering the waste stream. A woven PBO fabric, a reinforced resin composite and loose production fiber present different separation problems, and any finish or matrix remains part of the discarded article. No demonstrated, generally available PBO-to-fiber recycling process was established from the checked evidence.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Toyobo's 2016 safety sheet identifies a cutting hazard from high-strength ZYLON fibers and recommends care with fibrils and moving yarn. It warns that fire or severe overheating can release toxic fumes including hydrogen cyanide; this describes an emergency or severe-heating hazard, not measured emissions in normal handling. The same sheet lists medical-product use as a restriction for that supplier's product. NIST investigations of PBO-containing armor documented loss of fiber strength with humidity and folding, showing why qualification and maintenance of the complete protective article matter; a fiber data sheet alone does not guarantee continuing ballistic protection.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PBO is used in different fiber forms and constructions, and the behavior of a rope, fabric or composite depends on more than the polymer's initial tensile properties. In a NIST study of yarns from armor panels, elevated temperature and humidity reduced strength while infrared spectra showed chemical change. A separate NIST project found that repeated folding could also weaken PBO fibers; its laboratory protocol represents a particular wear simulation, not the service life of every article. Fiber type, finishing, protection from light and moisture, and the actual loading history should therefore accompany comparisons.

sections.overview: Poly(p-phenylene benzobisthiazole), often abbreviated PBZT or PBT, is a rigid aromatic heterocyclic polymer. Its sulfur-containing benzobisthiazole units distinguish it from the oxygen-containing PBO analogue. PBZT has been investigated in highly oriented fibers, films and carbon-fiber precursors. Its strong-acid solutions can form ordered phases that are used to prepare fibers, but documented laboratory or patent examples do not establish a current commodity market.
sections.history: Poly(p-phenylene benzobisthiazole), often abbreviated PBT in the rigid-rod literature, was already under study as a high-strength, high-modulus and thermally stable material before the mid-1980s. DuPont’s Wilfred Sweeny and Stephanie Kwolek filed a process patent in 1985 that explicitly built on earlier PBT synthesis, including work reported in 1981. Their improvement addressed slow dissolution of terephthalic acid in polyphosphoric acid by substituting selected terephthalate esters. This establishes a documented stage in the development of the polymer for demanding structural materials; it does not establish a first commercial launch or imply the commercial history of the unrelated polyester also called PBT.
sections.nomenclature: PBZT abbreviates poly(p-phenylene benzobisthiazole), a sulfur-containing rigid-chain polymer. Some older sources abbreviate it PBT; that abbreviation can also mean poly(butylene terephthalate), a chemically different polyester. PBZT is distinct from the oxygen-containing polybenzobisoxazole PBO. A carbon fiber produced from PBZT is a converted product rather than the unchanged starting polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(p-phenylene benzobisthiazole) (PBT) is the sulfur analogue of PBO: a para-ordered rigid-rod polymer made through step-growth polycondensation and cyclodehydration to fused benzobisthiazole rings. Its established monomers are 2,5-diamino-1,4-benzenedithiol dihydrochloride and terephthalic acid, or a more reactive terephthalate derivative, in polyphosphoric acid. In this dehydrating acidic medium, monomer stoichiometry, terephthalate reactivity, acid concentration, agitation, and water management affect conversion and inherent viscosity. Diethyl and related terephthalate esters have been used to avoid the slow dissolution of terephthalic acid in PPA, while terephthaloyl chloride provides a separate reactive prepolymer route. These are polymer-forming chemistries; lyotropic-dope spinning and conversion of PBT fiber to other materials are outside this synthesis scope.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PBZT is a rigid-rod, lyotropic-liquid-crystal fiber polymer. Its high axial stiffness and tensile strength belong to highly oriented spun and heat-treated fibers, not to an unoriented polymer mass. Molecular mass, liquid-crystalline dope quality, dry-jet wet-spinning and draw conditions, heat treatment under tension, fibril/void morphology, yarn construction, gauge length and rate, and composite impregnation determine the reported response. Axial compression is much weaker because of fibrillar kinking and weak lateral chain interaction; moisture and temperature exposure can further matter for a particular article. A reference table for PBZT fiber reports 325 GPa tensile modulus, 4.1 GPa tensile strength, and 0.26–0.41 GPa compressive strength. It does not identify a supplier grade, heat treatment, specimen geometry, method, rate, or conditioning, so these values are only an indicative high-orientation fiber comparison. A Georgia Tech study used PBZT of molecular mass about 25,000, dry-jet wet spun from a nematic dope, then heat-treated under tension at about 650 °C. In its introduction, the authors cite an earlier comparison in which PBZT fiber had tensile behavior comparable to good carbon fiber but compressive strength only about one-tenth of tensile strength; that comparison is not identified as a new measurement in their conversion study.
sections.processing:
Poly(p-phenylene benzobisthiazole) (PBZT) is an intractable rigid-rod polymer whose principal article-conversion route is solution spinning rather than melt extrusion. Optically anisotropic PBZT/polyphosphoric-acid dopes can be dry-jet wet spun: filtration and deaeration precede spinneret extrusion, elongational flow in the air gap aligns the chains, and a nonsolvent coagulation bath removes acid and fixes the filament. Washing, drying, take-up draw, and optional heat treatment under controlled tension must be coordinated because final orientation and morphology retain the dope rheology and spin-line history. The same dope route has also been used for highly oriented PBZT films, although the National Research Council review notes that wet extrusion of lyotropic polymers is less straightforward for film formation than for uniaxial fibers.

In a bounded fiber-forming example embedded in a University of Dayton conductive-fiber patent, a 13.7 wt% PBZT/polyphosphoric-acid solution was homogenized in a Haake Rheomixer at 130 °C for 4 h, filtered and deaerated at 80 °C through a 74 µm stainless-steel mesh, and extruded at 80–100 °C through a 0.010 in spinneret by dry-jet wet spinning. The single filament was taken up at about 60 times the extrusion rate and coagulated in 10 wt% aqueous phosphoric acid. Those settings describe the PBZT precursor fiber used in that patent's later metallization experiment; the subsequent metal treatment is specialized and is not a general PBZT conversion step.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The PBZT chain contains aromatic phenylene segments and fused benzobisthiazole units, forming a stiff backbone. In one study, fibers spun from a nematic solution contained fibrils with molecular chains oriented approximately along the fiber axis. A separate solution-crystallization study reported flat fibrillar crystals after quenching and rod-like aggregates after isothermal treatment. These are sample- and preparation-specific observations; neither an isolated solution crystal nor a carbonized fiber is a complete description of every PBZT article.
sections.properties: PBZT is described as a thermally stable polymer in a patent reporting its preparation, and particular strong-acid solutions exhibit liquid-crystalline behavior. This ordered solution can be shaped into filaments before the polymer is recovered in a nonsolvent. Its properties are directional as well as processing-dependent: a study of oriented fibers reported fibrillar structures aligned along the fiber direction. The patent and laboratory fiber study do not establish a universal service temperature or property specification for every PBZT sample.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PBZT fibers and sheets are documented in high-performance materials research. A 2001 patent describes making a conductive fiber by infiltrating a spun PBZT filament with a silver precursor and chemically reducing it to silver; the metal addition supplies conductivity while the PBZT provides the fiber substrate. The patent proposes signal or power transfer, electromagnetic shielding, antennas and microelectronics as uses of metal-containing polymer fibers and sheets. These are development proposals and do not establish commercial PBZT articles in those markets.

Purchasing. That patent names SRI International as a historical PBZT source. The checked evidence does not establish a currently orderable commodity grade, catalog pack size or continuing supplier.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable current PBZT purchase, consumption or production tonnage was found. Historical patent availability does not establish present commercial scale or broad industrial adoption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PBZT fibers can be converted to carbon-rich fibers by controlled heating under nitrogen. In a research study, elemental analysis of selected products showed carbon enrichment and reduced nitrogen and sulfur content as treatment temperature increased. This describes the material remaining after thermal conversion, not a full inventory of released gases or environmental products. The carbonized fiber is chemically different from intact PBZT.

Timescales: The researchers used sequential heat treatment up to about 850 °C and then higher-temperature carbonization under nitrogen and tension; a laboratory report describes treatment up to roughly 1,550 °C. These are severe process conditions for making a different material, not an ambient aging experiment. The source does not establish a condition-qualified time to mineralization.

Environmental persistence: Carbonization in a furnace does not measure conversion of PBZT in soil, freshwater or seawater. Nor do changes in the fiber's elemental composition establish biodegradation. No environmental mineralization rate or residence time was established from this evidence.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Researchers converted selected PBZT precursor fibers into carbon fibers by controlled heating. They used nitrogen and tension during precarbonization and a higher-temperature stage; the resulting carbon-rich fibers retained oriented fibrillar features but also showed surface defects and voids. This is conversion to a different material, not recovery of intact PBZT or its monomers.

The study used a defined research precursor fiber and tested its converted structure and properties. It does not demonstrate post-consumer PBZT collection or establish that coatings, mixed composites or other fiber grades can enter the same route without separation and qualification.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PBZT solution spinning uses polyphosphoric-acid dopes, so acid containment and removal during coagulation and washing are central processing concerns. The acid supplier identifies severe skin and eye damage hazards for polyphosphoric acid. Those hazards belong to the processing medium and acid-contaminated material; they are not a toxicological classification of washed PBZT fiber.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Molecular mass, solution conditions and processing history affect PBZT organization and resulting fiber behavior. The cited crystallization study observed different laboratory morphologies after quenching and isothermal treatment. In the carbon-fiber study, the precursor was a particular oriented yarn that had been dried and heat-treated under tension; its structure and subsequent conversion cannot be generalized to all possible PBZT preparations. A reported acid solution, precursor fiber and heat-converted carbon fiber must be distinguished.

sections.overview: Polyoxadiazoles are a family of polymers containing oxadiazole rings in their chains. Their surrounding chemical units and molecular architecture vary with the monomers and synthesis route, so the family includes chemically distinct materials. Researchers have made aromatic fibers for heat-resistant applications and separate fluorescent polymers for films and imaging. Results for a particular fiber or laboratory formulation should not be assigned to the whole family.
sections.history: Polyoxadiazole fiber research was established by the 1960s. Milliken’s public historical account points to A. H. Frazer and F. T. Wallenberger’s 1964 fiber study and V. V. Korschak and collaborators’ 1966 synthesis work. A later application milestone was Milliken’s introduction in 2015 of industrial protective fabric containing polyoxadiazole together with cotton and polyester. Its 2019 petition for a generic fiber designation explains the role of the fiber in clothing for workplaces with flame or electrical-arc exposure. Milliken was the fabric developer and user, not the manufacturer of the polymer fiber. This chronology concerns the aromatic fiber branch of the broader polyoxadiazole family.
sections.nomenclature: POD is an abbreviation for polyoxadiazole, a family designation rather than one unique ring placement or polymer architecture. Aromatic para-poly(1,3,4-oxadiazole) is a narrower fiber-forming example. Phosphorus-containing derivatives and hyperbranched polymers introduce further differences in composition or chain architecture. A commercial fiber name or a laboratory material code identifies a particular product or preparation rather than every POD.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Conventional aromatic poly(1,3,4-oxadiazole)s are formed by condensation followed by cyclodehydration. A direct route reacts hydrazine sulfate with aromatic or heteroaromatic dicarboxylic acids in a strongly dehydrating medium such as polyphosphoric acid, generating the heterocyclic backbone in one polycyclocondensation step; precipitation into basic aqueous medium neutralizes and isolates the polymer. An indirect route first makes a soluble polyhydrazide from a diacid chloride and a dihydrazide in a polar solvent, then thermally or chemically cyclodehydrates it to oxadiazole rings. The cited patent demonstrates the direct heated-PPA route under inert gas and basic precipitation. An independent laboratory study both documents those established routes and demonstrates a structurally distinct catalyst-free Ugi-type multicomponent route from dialdehydes, dicarboxylic acids, secondary amines, and (N-isocyanimino)triphenylphosphorane. Monomer functionality controls linear versus hyperbranched architecture; the Ugi route is a functional-polyoxadiazole example, not a claim that it replaces high-temperature aromatic-POD manufacture.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Aromatic polyoxadiazoles are used predominantly as fibers, so response is strongly controlled by backbone/comonomer design, molar mass, crystallinity and porosity, and the spinning and orientation history rather than by one bulk-resin value. In an open wet-spun p-POD/triaryl-phosphine-oxide-modified POD study, single-fiber tensile strength was 198–368 MPa and elongation at break was 18.5–25.6%; increasing the phosphorus-containing comonomer reduced molar mass and crystallization and produced a more porous interior, with lower strength and elongation. Those values apply only to the study’s as-spun fibers; gauge and conditioning details were not reported in the cited mechanical-results passage. An independent Milliken petition for the fiber designation reports a different commercial polyoxadiazole-fiber example of 3.2 cN/dtex breaking strength and 15–30% breaking elongation under its named internal method. The two examples have different chemistry, fiber form, and test methods and must not be combined into a family range.
sections.processing:
Aromatic polyoxadiazoles are commonly converted from solution because many high-performance grades are not practical conventional melt-processing materials. Directly documented article routes include wet spinning of fibers and solvent casting or evaporation of thin films, including humidity-templated breath-figure films. A wet-spinning line degasses the polymer dope, meters and filters it, extrudes it through a spinneret into a coagulation bath, washes the filaments, draws them, and takes them up. Polymer intrinsic viscosity and concentration, dope temperature and homogeneity, filtration, spinneret shear, air gap if used, solvent/nonsolvent exchange, coagulation-bath conditions, wash completeness, draw ratio, drying, and winding tension govern spinnability, pores, cross-section, orientation, and strength. Film casting additionally depends on solubility, solvent volatility, concentration, substrate wetting, ambient humidity, evaporation time, and final desiccation. Polymer-forming cyclodehydration belongs in Synthesis; preparing a spinnable or coatable dope and carrying it through deposition, coagulation, washing, drawing, drying, and take-up belongs in Processing.

Liu and co-workers converted their p-POD and phosphorus-containing pho-POD polymerization solutions by wet spinning through a sequence of degassing, metering, filtering, extrusion, coagulation, washing, drawing, and take-up. They found that solvent outward diffusion and nonsolvent counter-diffusion during coagulation controlled the porous internal morphology, and that reduced chain mobility in pho-POD-15 left a more porous, open structure than p-POD under the same stated coagulation conditions. A distinct bounded film example comes from Xie and co-workers' soluble fluorescent POD P6. They cast a 1.0 mg/mL chloroform solution onto silicon in a sealed water-vapor environment, preconditioned the vessel for 30 min, heated its bottom at about 70 °C for 2 min, immediately sealed the syringe opening, and left the assembly at room temperature for 30 min; that method gave ordered approximately 10.2 ± 1.5 micrometer pores. Toluene, THF, dichloromethane, and concentrations of 0.5, 2.0, or 5.0 mg/mL gave different or inferior morphologies, so this schedule must remain attached to P6 and the static breath-figure apparatus.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Oxadiazole heterocycles occur in polymer chains whose connecting units and substituents depend on the synthesis. A multicomponent-polymerization study made linear and hyperbranched examples using different monomers; the linear examples formed microporous films under its selected conditions. In a separate fiber study, wet-spun aromatic POD had a compact cross section, whereas a phosphorus-containing sample made under the reported coagulation conditions showed a more porous interior. These are different formulations and processing experiments, not a universal morphology.
sections.properties: Thermal and flame-test results depend on the specific polyoxadiazole composition and article. In one study of wet-spun aromatic fibers, incorporating phosphine-oxide-containing units raised the measured limiting oxygen index from 28% for the reference fiber to 35% for the highest-content sample in the reported series. The same study found an increase in char yield under its nitrogen heating test, while the temperature of the maximum mass-loss rate fell. These are experimental fiber comparisons, not a fire-performance specification for every POD material. Separately, fluorescent polyoxadiazoles for microscopy rely on deliberately introduced functional units.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. A legacy supplier catalog describes Arselon polyoxadiazole for hot-gas filter bags in metallurgy, cement and asphalt, as well as protective textiles, seals and rubber or resin reinforcement. Heat-resistant filament and sewing thread are relevant to filter-bag construction, where both the fabric and its seams encounter hot gas. The same catalog lists short-cut fiber for composite reinforcement, illustrating why textile yarn and dispersed short fibers are sold in different forms. The listed temperature values are reference information, not specifications for a complete filter or guarantee of service life.

Purchasing. Swicofil’s legacy specialist catalog describes filament yarn, staple, fabrics and sewing threads. The producer/merchant must confirm current availability and grade; the catalog does not provide an order minimum.

Scale and evidence limits. The catalog describes industrial production but gives no annual tonnage. No reliable separate purchased or consumed volume was found; its industrial-volume wording is not a quantified market statistic.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: For the aromatic para-poly(1,3,4-oxadiazole) fibers tested in a laboratory pyrolysis study, detected products included carbon dioxide, benzonitrile, terephthalonitrile and 4-aminobenzonitrile. A phosphorus-containing variant also produced a phosphorus-containing volatile, while a substantial residue remained in the thermal experiment. These analytical products arise during severe heating and are not an inventory of environmental metabolites.

Timescales: The study used programmed heating and examined pyrolysis products at 500, 550 and 600 °C. In its nitrogen thermogravimetric comparison, the reported temperature of maximum mass-loss rate was 532 °C for the reference fiber and 508 °C for the phosphorus-containing sample with the highest listed additive-unit content. The experiments report thermal endpoints for selected fibers, not time to breakdown in the environment.

Environmental persistence: Heat resistance and carbon-rich residue formation do not measure biodegradation or establish a soil, freshwater or marine mineralization time. The pyrolysis study neither exposed the fibers to those environments nor measured conversion to biological products. The persistence of a particular discarded POD article remains an evidence gap here.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Thermal-conversion experiments on aromatic POD fibers identified carbon-rich residues and volatile aromatic nitriles. The phosphorus-containing comparison produced more residual char under the reported nitrogen heating conditions, illustrating that composition changes the residue. The findings are analytical evidence about heating, not a demonstrated method of recovering intact POD polymer.

Any proposed thermal treatment would need to account for its volatile products and the downstream use of the residue. The cited study does not establish a collection-and-recycling system or recovered polymer-quality product for discarded POD articles.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Biological response varies with polyoxadiazole structure and formulation. In one study of fluorescent, non-conjugated PODs, encapsulating P6 in DSPE-PEG nanoparticles reduced its cytotoxicity toward 4T1 cells compared with the unencapsulated polymer. These cell-imaging results concern the specially synthesized polymers and do not establish the safety of heat-resistant POD fibers or implanted devices.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Polyoxadiazole denotes a broad family rather than a single fiber grade or polymer structure. Ring surroundings, branching and processing can change the result: the phosphorus-containing fibers studied in one report showed a more porous cross section and a different thermal response from its unmodified comparison fiber. The fluorescent microporous films and biological-imaging experiments involved separate laboratory-made polymers. Their properties cannot automatically be transferred to commercial heat-resistant fibers or resins.

sections.overview: Modacrylics are acrylonitrile-based copolymers made into synthetic fibers with substantial amounts of other monomers. The comonomer recipe and additives can be selected for flame behavior as well as fiber formation. Commercial grades are used in protective clothing, fire-barrier textiles and other applications, often blended with companion fibers. Their performance depends on the particular grade and finished textile construction.
sections.history: Modacrylic fibers are a group of acrylonitrile copolymers with several commercial histories. A well-documented example is Kaneka’s Kanekalon/Kanecaron, manufactured at Takasago and marketed from 1957. Hairlike texture, colorability and flame resistance supported wigs, hairpieces, artificial fur, curtains, bedding and stuffed toys. In its 2014 annual report, Kaneka described an additional Malaysian manufacturing facility intended to supply hair-extension markets in Africa. This illustrates how development moved from introducing a new synthetic textile fiber to tailoring large-scale production to specific consumer uses. The 1957 date belongs to Kaneka’s product line, not a universal invention date for all modacrylic compositions.
sections.nomenclature: Modacrylic is a family designation for a class of acrylonitrile-based fibers, not one fixed copolymer recipe. It should not be treated as an unqualified synonym for acrylic fiber, whose generic composition boundary differs. Acrylonitrile–vinylidene-chloride is one commercial fiber chemistry; other comonomer combinations are possible. Product names such as Protex identify particular commercial grades rather than the whole family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Modacrylic fiber polymers are acrylonitrile-containing copolymers in the modacrylic composition range, commonly incorporating vinyl chloride or vinylidene chloride and optional ionic or vinyl-ester comonomers. The polymer family is defined by the copolymer composition and is distinct from the wet- or dry-spinning operation that turns a solution into fiber. Documented examples use acrylonitrile, vinylidene chloride, vinyl acetate, and an ionic comonomer, while another route uses acrylonitrile with vinyl chloride or vinylidene chloride and a sulfo-containing vinyl monomer. Emulsion and solution polymerization are both reported; feed composition, monomer-addition timing, initiator/redox system, and conversion control the copolymer architecture. The cited monomer ratios are particular flame-resistant or color-control examples, not a universal modacrylic formulation.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Modacrylic is supplied chiefly as drawn staple or filament fibre, so tenacity and elongation apply to a defined fibre grade, linear density, orientation, and conditioning rather than an isotropic bulk polymer. Acrylonitrile/comonomer composition, draw and heat-setting history, denier, crimp, moisture, and blend construction control textile response; flame-retardant comonomers and finishing can alter strength and elongation. Protex® regular FR modacrylic grades are reported at less than 3.3 dtex with tenacity 2.6–2.8 cN/dtex and elongation 27–29%; these reference values are grade- and fibre-size-specific, with no test rate or conditioning stated. Independently, a modacrylic/polyacrylate/lyocell yarn study reports its specified 1.0 and 1.7 dtex modacrylic staple fibres at 3.13 and 3.17 cN/dtex, respectively, with about 36% breaking elongation; those fibre data do not establish intrinsic bulk-modacrylic properties or a general textile-fabric value.
sections.processing: Modacrylics are generally converted to fiber by solution spinning because the acrylonitrile-based copolymer family is not normally melt-spun. Wet spinning extrudes a polymer dope through a spinneret into a water/solvent coagulation bath, followed by washing, drawing, drying, and sometimes heat setting; dry spinning instead removes solvent in a heated gas stream. An open study of poly(acrylonitrile-co-vinyl chloride) used a 20 wt% DMSO dope, a 100-hole spinneret with 0.07 mm holes, and coagulation baths containing 20, 35, or 50 wt% DMSO at 60 °C; coagulation and draw ratio changed voids, orientation, and fiber performance. A separate high-retraction modacrylic patent gives a bounded sequence for its particular copolymer composition: draw 2× in an 80 °C bath, dry in air at 110–120 °C with 25–30% free contraction, then draw 2× in air at 70–80 °C. It warns that air-drawing above 100 °C can deteriorate characteristics and below 50 °C can cause filament breakage. These dope, bath, draw, and thermal settings are formulation- and line-specific, not family-wide spinning specifications.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Modacrylic chains contain acrylonitrile together with other comonomer units. One patent describes a composition incorporating vinylidene chloride, vinyl acetate and an ionic comonomer; that recipe is one example rather than the family definition. The relative amounts and distribution of units change the chemistry of the chain, while spinning and drawing affect the resulting fiber. A finished fabric can also contain several fiber types, making its construction distinct from a single copolymer filament.
sections.properties: Modacrylic fibers can be designed for flame resistance, with the selected comonomers and additives influencing the result. Kaneka lists limiting oxygen indices of 26 for SB and 31 for Protex-SYS, with 32 for several Protex grades, as reference values for the listed fibers. Limiting oxygen index is a laboratory measure of the oxygen concentration needed to sustain burning in a defined gas mixture; it is not a complete fire test. Fiber blend, fabric construction and exposure also affect the behavior of a finished article.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Modacrylic grades serve protective clothing, mattress fire barriers, upholstery, curtains and nonwoven filters. Kaneka lists its Protex-C grade for flame-resistant clothing and mattress barriers, and describes its flame resistance as allowing blending with aramid and cellulosic fibers. Protex-S is intended for blends with polyester and is listed for filter nonwovens and automotive applications. In a laboratory study of potential protective underwear, a 65% modacrylic/35% cotton blend knitted in triple-tuck and 2:1 tuck-rib structures had afterflame and afterglow times below two seconds in an ISO 15025 limited-flame-spread test. The authors also found that the cotton blend wetted and absorbed water slowly, a comfort tradeoff for the tested fabrics. This test does not certify a finished garment or establish performance of other fabrics. The fiber grade and blend proportions matter: a flame-resistant fiber alone does not establish the performance of a finished fabric or mattress assembly.

Purchasing. Kaneka Protex offers staple grades selected by linear density, cut length, color and blend compatibility, plus uncrimped tow for short-cut battery use. For example, the catalog lists Protex-C in 1.7 dtex fibers cut to 38 or 51 mm. These are product dimensions, not evidence of a minimum order size or the composition of every modacrylic grade.

Scale and evidence limits. A fiber's length and linear density characterize an offered product rather than annual production or consumption. Textile blends contain additional fibers and their total fabric mass is not modacrylic polymer tonnage. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was established from the checked sources.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Chlorine-containing modacrylic fibers can release hydrogen chloride during burning and leave a carbonaceous residue. For a specified acrylonitrile–vinylidene-chloride fiber, a supplier safety sheet also lists carbon monoxide and hydrogen cyanide among possible combustion products. These fire products depend on composition and exposure; they are not an inventory of substances released during normal use or slow environmental aging.

Timescales: The checked fire-behavior and safety information concerns thermal exposure and its products. It does not report an environmental degradation duration or a mineralization endpoint for the listed fiber. A burn response therefore cannot be used as a disappearance time for discarded textiles.

Environmental persistence: Self-extinguishing behavior is a fire property, not a measurement of biological mineralization. Neither the cited fire discussion nor the safety sheet establishes a soil, freshwater or marine lifetime for shed modacrylic fibers. Composition, finish, fiber form and the conditions and endpoint measured would matter in a relevant environmental test.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The Cellusuede modacrylic-fiber sheet recommends reclaiming spilled material for processing when possible. Its disposal discussion concerns the named acrylonitrile–vinylidene-chloride fiber and requires compliance with applicable waste rules. This supports recovery of suitable clean production material, rather than demonstrating closed-loop recycling of blended, dyed or contaminated textiles.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For Cellusuede’s acrylonitrile–vinylidene-chloride modacrylic fiber, the safety sheet treats eye, skin and inhalation exposure as fiber-dust concerns. The specified copolymer composition matters: guidance for this product should not be generalized to every modacrylic blend or finish. Handling should limit dust and follow the actual fiber formulation’s fire precautions.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Modacrylic is a fiber family, not a single comonomer recipe. An acrylonitrile/vinylidene-chloride/vinyl-acetate formulation is one example; different grades can include different additives or finishes. Kaneka's catalog shows distinct oxygen-index reference values and fiber cut lengths across its products, illustrating why a grade must be named. Neither a fiber-level flammability number nor a supplier claim guarantees the performance of every textile blend.

sections.overview: Vinyon is a generic manufactured-fiber family based on polymers rich in vinyl chloride units. The U.S. fiber definition specifies at least 85% vinyl chloride units by weight in the fiber-forming polymer. Historical examples include vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate copolymers and afterchlorinated materials. A 1970 National Bureau of Standards guide describes vinyon as a heat-sensitive bonding fiber used to join other fibers in nonwoven fabrics and felts. Its composition and article form are narrower than bulk PVC resin.
sections.history: Vinyon’s development belongs to the early industrial use of vinyl-chloride-rich resins as textile fibers. A concrete postwar milestone is Theophilus A. Feild Jr.’s Union Carbide and Carbon patent, filed in 1946 and published in 1951, for coloring vinyl-resin yarns without losing their useful physical properties. It builds on existing vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate fiber technology and addresses the difficulty of applying ordinary textile dyeing methods to these water-resistant fibers. By 1970, the U.S. National Bureau of Standards described vinyon principally as a bonding fiber for nonwoven fabrics, as well as in embossed carpets, pressed felts and waterproof clothing. These sources document established fiber technology and its uses rather than prove a unique first-invention date.
sections.nomenclature: Vinyon is a fiber generic name, not one fixed polymer composition or one trade grade. Its U.S. definition concerns the vinyl-chloride-unit fraction of the fiber-forming substance; a finished textile may contain other fiber types. Historical fiber products include copolymer and afterchlorinated lineages. Ordinary PVC resin, other vinyl fibers and a bonded fabric are related but distinct scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Vinyon is a regulated fiber-family name rather than one unique resin recipe. Under the cited U.S. generic-name definition, the fiber-forming long-chain polymer contains at least 85 wt% vinyl chloride units. The principal chain-forming step is therefore free-radical polymerization of vinyl chloride, either as the homopolymer or with a limited amount of a compatible comonomer. Historically important fiber resins include vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate copolymers; vinyl acetate disrupts the PVC sequence and can lower softening temperature or improve solution handling, but enough vinyl chloride must remain to meet the vinyon compositional boundary. A cited historical patent uses aqueous suspension polymerization with partially hydrolyzed poly(vinyl acetate) as protective colloid and diisopropyl peroxydicarbonate as initiator. Vinyl chloride is polymerized first, then a small vinyl acetate charge is introduced and polymerization continues at a higher temperature before residual monomer is vented and the copolymer is centrifuged, washed, and dried. Afterchlorination is an optional historical modification, not a requirement for every vinyon: the same patent suspends the vinyl chloride copolymer in an inert medium, introduces chlorine under oxygen-excluding conditions, follows hydrogen chloride evolution, removes residual chlorine and medium, and isolates the more highly chlorinated polymer. A second historical patent confirms textile use of both conjointly polymerized vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate resin and its afterchlorinated variant. Monomer ratio and addition sequence, initiator, polymerization temperature, degree of polymerization, residual monomer removal, and optional chlorine content control resin solubility, softening behavior, and suitability for a fiber route. Solution preparation, spinning, drawing, and textile finishing belong in Processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Vinyon is a historical fiber-family label rather than a single invariant formulation; the original commercial fibers were predominantly vinyl chloride copolymers, especially vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate compositions, while later similarly named variants used different comonomers and should not have their measurements pooled. At family level, vinyon is described as a soft, flexible, low-strength and highly extensible thermoplastic fiber. Its low moisture affinity helps preserve broadly similar wet and dry behavior, but its low strain-release and softening temperatures make shrinkage and loss of orientation under heat central mechanical limitations. These traits made it more useful as a heat-activated binder in nonwovens, felts, and carpets than as a load-bearing spun yarn; in those bonded structures, web architecture, vinyon fraction, contact area, and bonding temperature, time, and pressure govern strength, tear resistance, drape, and dimensional stability.

Composition and molecular weight, comonomer content, after-chlorination, plasticizer and stabilizer package, solvent-spinning history, filament fineness, draw ratio and draw temperature, molecular orientation, heat setting, residual strain, and subsequent thermal or solvent exposure all affect the measured response. Temperature is especially consequential: a National Bureau of Standards guide reports shrinkage above 150 °F (about 66 °C), tackiness at 185–215 °F (about 85–102 °C), and melting near 260 °F (about 127 °C), values intended as historical fiber guidance rather than universal transition temperatures. As one bounded numerical example, U.S. Patent 2,577,846 reports a 100-denier, initially unoriented yarn made from an after-chlorinated vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate copolymer containing about 60% chlorine. The starting yarn had wet tenacity below 1.0 g/denier and elongation above 100%; after dye application and 510% drawing through a 181 °C radiant heater, the 16-denier yarn had wet tenacity 2.59 g/denier and elongation 16.2%. This is a process-specific patent example—not a family range—and the document does not report a modern tensile standard, conditioning protocol, specimen count, or uncertainty. Those omissions, and the broad chemistry hidden by the vinyon name, should remain explicit when comparing grades or products.
sections.processing:
Vinyon compositions are converted primarily as fibers, but the spinning route depends on whether the material is a vinyl-chloride homopolymer, a vinyl chloride copolymer, or an after-chlorinated composition. Historical practice includes wet or dry solution spinning followed by solvent removal, while suitably stabilized formulations can be melt compounded and melt spun. Important operations are resin/additive mixing, filtration or gel homogenization, metering through a spinneret, take-up, drawing and orientation, heat relaxation or setting, dyeing where required, and winding or cutting. Vinyl-chloride polymers have a narrow heat-processing margin: heterogeneous fusion can leave particles that break filaments, while excessive melt temperature, pressure, shear, or residence time promotes yellowing and decomposition. Solvent-spun routes additionally require controlled coagulation or evaporation and solvent recovery. Finished fibers may also be used as heat-activated binder fibers, so subsequent web temperature must be high enough to tack or bond yet controlled against excessive shrinkage or melting. Polymerization and after-chlorination belong in Synthesis; compound preparation, spinning, drawing, dyeing, heat setting, and binder activation belong here.

Kaneka's patent provides a bounded melt-spinning example for its PVC/CPVC/EVA/stabilizer/lubricant compositions, not a universal vinyon window. Four kilograms of vinyl-chloride resin mixture and additives were mixed in a 20 L Henschel mixer until the compound reached 115 °C, then jacket-cooled with continued mixing to 75 °C. The resulting powder was spun on a 40 mm, 24:1 single-screw extruder through 120 spinneret holes of 0.063 mm²; cylinder zones were 155–170 °C, the adapter 175 °C, and turn-head and nozzle 180 °C, followed by drawing and relaxation atmospheres at 110 °C. The patent warns that spinning above 195 °C caused marked yellowing and ties drawing temperature and ratio to strength, feel, and filament breakage. A separate historical example in Feild's patent treated a 100-denier after-chlorinated vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate yarn at 25 °C in a dye bath and drew it to 510% of its original length through a 181 °C radiant heater; that combined dye-fixing/drawing operation is specific to the stated yarn and apparatus.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Vinyon identifies a fiber composition range rather than a single molecular architecture. Vinyl chloride-derived units make up the major part of the fiber-forming polymer; historical products can also contain comonomers or be further chlorinated. The polymer is formed and drawn into fibers, and a finished nonwoven may contain vinyon alongside other types of fibers. Its chain chemistry, processing and textile arrangement therefore cannot be inferred completely from the generic name.
sections.properties: A historical National Bureau of Standards guide describes vinyon as a heat-sensitive fiber useful for bonding other fibers. The guide notes that heating can cause shrinkage and tackiness. It also describes chemical resistance and low strength for the materials discussed. These are historical product observations, rather than a current specification for every vinyon fiber. In its 1970 guide, NBS reported that the vinyon products it described shrank above 150 °F (about 66 °C) and became tacky at 185–215 °F (85–102 °C). This combination helps explain its historical use as a bonding fiber, but is not a current specification for all vinyl-chloride-rich fibers.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. The 1970 National Bureau of Standards account identifies vinyon principally as a binder for nonwoven fabrics, pressed felts and embossed carpets, with additional coated-textile uses. Heat and pressure made the documented binder fibers soften and adhere to companion fibers. This enabled the fabric to hold together, while its strength and hand reflected the entire blend. These are historical applications, not proof that the same products remain available today.

Purchasing. The cited historical account identifies past vinyon fiber products but is not a current sales catalog. A buyer needs a specialist supplier to confirm vinyl-chloride-unit content, grade and bonding behavior for the proposed process. Current orderable grades and package sizes were not established by these sources.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable current annual vinyon production or consumption statistic was established. Bulk PVC resin output includes applications other than this narrower textile-fiber family and cannot be assigned to it. Historical descriptions of uses likewise do not establish current sales quantities.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Vinyl-chloride-rich fiber formulations can suffer thermal decomposition during melt spinning. A patent on related vinyl-chloride fibers describes using stabilizers to limit processing damage and discoloration in its specific compositions. For PVC generally, the UK Health and Safety Executive identifies hydrogen chloride in fumes produced above the recommended upper processing temperature; this is contextual evidence, not a measured product inventory for every vinyon grade. The cited sources do not identify the products of slow environmental degradation of the fiber.

Timescales: In a patent's vinyl-chloride-rich fiber tests, a drawn sample was heated at 100 °C for 25 minutes to measure shrinkage. The result characterizes dimensional response under a controlled treatment rather than polymer mineralization. Processing stability also depends on temperature and formulation, and these tests do not establish a soil or outdoor lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The melt-spinning and shrinkage experiments did not measure biodegradation or conversion of discarded fiber carbon to carbon dioxide or biomass. Their processing endpoints cannot be used to calculate persistence in soil, freshwater or seawater. A condition-qualified environmental lifetime remains an evidence gap for this fiber family.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: PVC-family recycling provides context for vinyl-chloride-rich vinyon: segregated material can undergo mechanical size reduction and reprocessing, while dissolution and chlorine/additive separation are investigated recovery routes. The cited review addresses PVC waste generally; it does not validate a dedicated process for every vinyon copolymer fiber, textile blend or finish.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Vinyon is a vinyl-chloride-rich fiber family, so PVC processing-fume guidance is relevant when its formulations overheat. The UK Health and Safety Executive identifies hydrogen chloride among substances detected when PVC is heated above its recommended processing temperature, and recommends controlling melt temperature, residence time and extraction. The actual fume composition depends on the formulation and additives. A finished textile cannot be evaluated solely from the hazards of its starting monomer, and the PVC example is not a measured fume profile for every vinyon fiber.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Vinyon includes different resin lineages within its generic composition definition. Comonomer content, afterchlorination and fiber processing distinguish products. The National Bureau of Standards description dates from 1970 and does not establish every modern product’s behavior. Binder-fabric performance also depends on the other fibers and bonding conditions. The NBS bonding temperatures describe historical fiber products, while the patent includes different stabilizer and lubricant combinations to control melt-spinning behavior.
