sections.overview: Elastane, also called spandex, is a family of segmented elastic fibers used to give textiles stretch and recovery. The U.S. generic-fiber definition specifies a fiber-forming polymer containing at least 85% segmented polyurethane. Flexible and harder segments can be made from different feedstocks and proportions, producing fibers with different responses. Elastane is commonly combined with other fibers, so a garment's behavior depends on its blend and fabric construction as well as the elastic component.
sections.history: Elastane grew from the effort to replace heavy rubber threads in foundation garments with fine synthetic elastic fibers. Joseph Shivers developed the DuPont material that became Lycra during the 1950s; the National Inventors Hall of Fame identifies his work on segmented synthetic elastomers as the central breakthrough. The material spread from underwear into sportswear, fashion and other stretch textiles, with additional applications in healthcare, furnishings and automotive products. DuPont’s 2004 sale of its Invista synthetic-fibers business to Koch Industries transferred the Lycra business as part of a larger industrial reorganization. Lycra is one commercial lineage within the broader elastane or spandex family.
sections.nomenclature: Elastane and spandex are names used for this family of elastic fibers, not one fixed polyurethane composition. The record covers segmented polyurethane and polyurethane-urea fiber materials; not every polyurethane is an elastane fiber. LYCRA is a commercial fiber brand rather than the generic name for all members. A fabric containing elastane is a blend, and a fiber content or finished garment should not be reported as pure polymer without qualification.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Elastane (spandex) is a family of segmented polyurethane and polyurethane-urea elastomers. A common polyether polyurethane-urea route first caps a macrodiol, such as poly(tetramethylene ether) glycol, with excess diisocyanate (often MDI) to make an isocyanate-terminated prepolymer; diamine chain extension then forms the polyurethane-urea hard segments. Polyester, polyether, and polycarbonate glycols are all documented macrodiol families, so no single soft-segment composition defines all elastane. In one patent example, the prepolymer and ethylenediamine/diethylamine chain-extension mixture are handled in dimethylacetamide; another documented route uses ethylenediamine and 1,2-diaminopropane as a specified chain-extender mixture. These feedstock, NCO/OH ratio, chain-extension, and chain-termination choices set segmented-polymer architecture. Dry, wet, reaction, and melt spinning are fiber-forming operations applied after or during polymer formation; they are conversion routes, not evidence that a single spinning method defines the elastane family.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Elastane fibers are segmented polyurethane or polyurethane-urea elastomers designed for very large, substantially recoverable extension. Their soft segments supply low-temperature chain mobility and entropic elasticity, while hydrogen-bonded hard-segment domains act as reinforcing physical cross-links; deformation and rearrangement of those domains produce stress softening, hysteresis, delayed recovery, and fatigue sensitivity. Mechanical response varies with soft-segment chemistry and molecular mass, hard-segment fraction and sequence, hydrogen-bond cohesion and phase separation, chain-extension chemistry, spinning and draw-induced orientation, filament bundle structure, test temperature and rate, imposed prestrain, hold and recovery time, and cyclic history. Yoshihara and Ishihara found that room-temperature instantaneous and delayed unrecovered strain in model segmented polyurethane-urea fibers passed through a minimum near a PTMG soft-segment molecular mass of about 2000. At low temperature, higher-molecular-mass PTMG could undergo strain-induced crystallization that persisted after unloading and impaired recovery; copolymerizing dissimilar soft segments suppressed this fixed crystallization and broadened the useful recovery range. A separate bounded measurement on the commercially available spandex fiber used by Zhang and co-workers gives a numerical example: in room-temperature uniaxial tests at 5 mm/s, the multifilament fiber had an initial modulus of 1.38 MPa, maximum stretch ratio 7.0 (about six times its initial length added before fracture), and work of fracture 71.1 MJ/m3. The same material showed substantial cyclic hysteresis attributed to hard-segment plastic deformation. The paper does not identify a commercial grade, linear density, conditioning humidity, or a detailed cross-sectional-area protocol for the porous multifilament bundle, so these results are illustrative for that tested fiber only and are not a specification or family range. Fabric-level stretch, tear, and recovery additionally depend on elastane fraction, yarn covering, knit or weave geometry, and interaction with companion fibers and must not be inferred directly from single-fiber values.
sections.processing:
Elastane is converted primarily as continuous filament by solution dry spinning or wet spinning; reaction spinning and melt spinning are also documented for suitable chemistries. In dry spinning, a filtered polymer solution is metered through a spinneret into a heated, usually inert-gas shaft, the solvent is removed, elementary filaments are combined, a finish is applied to control sticking and friction, and the yarn is wound. Wet spinning instead extrudes solution into a nonsolvent coagulation bath, then washes, draws where required, dries or heat-sets, finishes, and winds the filament. Solution viscosity, spinneret pressure, solvent removal or bath mass transfer, filament coalescence, draw, and residual solvent therefore belong to the qualified spinning process rather than to the family as fixed settings.

A bounded Bayer wet-spinning example used a 30 wt% polyurethane-urea solution whose viscosity was 18 Pa·s at 50 °C after a specified 140 °C pretreatment. It was extruded through 397 holes of 0.08 mm diameter into an 85 °C bath containing 20% dimethylacetamide in water, followed by the patent's washing, drying, setting, finishing, and winding sequence. Those settings apply to that polymer solution and spinning line; they do not define a universal elastane wet-spinning window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Elastane polymers combine flexible soft segments with harder urethane- or urea-containing segments. Association of hard segments provides physical junctions, while the soft segments extend when the fiber is stretched and can retract after the load is released. Depending on formulation, a soft segment can also crystallize during deformation, changing recovery. Segment chemistry, molecular mass, spinning and the fiber's thermal history therefore influence its organization and response.
sections.properties: Elastic fibers can extend and recover after the load is released. In a study of segmented polyurethane-urea fibers, recovery depended on soft-segment chemistry, molecular weight and temperature. Some high-molecular-weight soft segments crystallized under stress at low temperature and showed greater unrecovered strain. These results apply to the studied formulations and test protocol.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Elastane supplies stretch and recovery in underwear, jeans, hosiery, swimwear and activewear, generally as a constituent of a textile blend. Its elastic component contributes extension while companion fibers provide other fabric characteristics. In a textile-separation study, the researchers examined a sports shirt labeled 85% polyester and 15% elastane and underwear labeled 88% polyamide and 12% elastane. These examples illustrate two uses of mixed fibers, not a fixed composition for either garment type.

Purchasing. Mills purchase specified spandex or elastane fibers, whereas clothing producers may buy fabrics containing them. LYCRA is one commercial fiber portfolio, and a LYCRA-containing fabric is not pure elastane. The intended blend, fiber count and fabric construction matter to selection.

Scale and evidence limits. Textile Exchange reports just under 1.5 million tonnes of global elastane fiber production in 2024, of the order of 10⁶ tonnes per year. This is fiber output, not the total mass of garments containing elastane or purchases by one apparel segment. A textile blend's total mass includes companion fibers and should not be counted as elastane alone.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Solvent treatment can chemically alter an elastane fiber. In a laboratory study, NMR of fibers treated with tetrahydrofurfuryl alcohol showed methylenedianiline-containing species alongside remaining carbamate structures; the authors interpreted this as partial cleavage of the tested polyurethane. In their comparison, spectra after dimethylformamide treatment indicated more of the original carbamate structure remained. These are results for specific fibers and deliberate solvent treatments, not an inventory of environmental degradation products.

Timescales: To compare pure fibers, the researchers stirred material in solvent for four hours at 100 °C and measured dissolved polymer by a thermogravimetry-corrected method. They also investigated solvent-treated blended textiles. The four-hour treatment is a laboratory separation condition, not a soil or water mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: Dissolving or chemically changing an elastane fiber does not demonstrate conversion of its carbon to carbon dioxide or biomass. The textile-separation study did not establish how long discarded fibers persist in soil, freshwater or seawater. Fiber chemistry, additives, environmental conditions and the endpoint measured would matter for a meaningful persistence study.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Selective dissolution is being studied to separate elastane from the major fiber in mixed textiles. In a laboratory study, researchers treated an 85/15 polyester/elastane sports shirt and 88/12 polyamide/elastane underwear using dimethylformamide and tetrahydrofurfuryl alcohol, leaving a solid fraction enriched in the companion fiber. Thermal analysis was used to check separation because retained solvent and extracted additives can distort a simple mass balance.

The elastane-containing solvent stream is a separate recovery problem. NMR indicated partial chemical change after tetrahydrofurfuryl alcohol treatment, while dyes and other additives could complicate purification. In the authors' modeled process, the residue containing elastane and additives was assumed to be incinerated, with recovery of elastane itself identified for future research. These experiments and model do not demonstrate routine collection or virgin-equivalent elastane recycling.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Elastane separation and recycling can involve DMF or DMAc and therefore requires solvent-specific exposure and emission controls. A study of selective dissolution compares these established solvents with alternatives using health, safety and environmental criteria. These are process-solvent concerns, distinct from the biological response to a washed, finished elastane-containing textile.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Elastane is a family designation rather than one fixed formulation. Soft-segment chemistry, chain extender and processing change the response of the fiber, while the fraction and construction of a fabric affect how that response is used. In a study of selected polyurethane-urea fibers, some higher-molecular-weight soft segments crystallized under stress at low temperature and showed greater unrecovered strain. That result is specific to the polymers and test protocol; it is not a fixed recovery rate for all elastane textiles.

sections.overview: Novoloid fibers are crosslinked phenolic fibers made from novolac-type resins. In a documented commercial route, the precursor is melt-spun into fibers and then chemically cured into an infusible network. The cured fiber chars rather than melting when exposed to flame, a feature used in fire-blocking textiles. Novoloid fibers can also be converted into carbon or activated-carbon products, which are different materials from the original cured fiber.
sections.history: Novoloid fiber’s commercial history is closely tied to Kynol. The Museum of Fine Arts conservation reference attributes its development in 1968 to Carborundum, followed by licensing to Nippon Kynol and American Kynol. The manufacturer’s history places this work in U.S. space-technology development and dates full-scale industrial production to 1982. Flame-resistant clothing and spacecraft were early application areas. Later product development included carbon fibers and activated carbon fibers derived from the phenolic precursor, extending use into filtration and adsorption. These dates concern the Kynol novoloid-fiber lineage; phenol-formaldehyde resins themselves have a substantially earlier history.
sections.nomenclature: Novoloid is a family name for crosslinked phenolic fiber materials and is not synonymous with an uncured novolac resin. Kynol is one supplier's commercial novoloid fiber product, with yarns, felts and further converted activated-carbon products made from it. A description of the precursor resin, cured fiber or converted carbon should identify which material is meant. Product form and cure history remain relevant when comparing properties.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Novoloid denotes a family of infusible, cross-linked phenolic fibers whose precursor is a novolac, rather than a separate linear fiber polymer. The cited routes prepare the thermoplastic novolac by acid-catalyzed condensation of a phenolic feedstock, commonly phenol, with formaldehyde under phenol-rich conditions. Network formation then converts the novolac precursor to novoloid: documented cross-linking agents include hexamethylenetetramine, paraformaldehyde, trioxane, or tetraoxymethylene, with an acid catalyst or acidic environment used to promote formation of the phenolic methylene-bridge network. Phenol–formaldehyde is the common example, while substituted phenols can also be precursors. These sources establish precursor and cross-link chemistry only; fiber-forming equipment and individual cure schedules are not generalized here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Novoloid fibers are cured, amorphous, cross-linked novolak networks rather than meltable linear-fiber grades. Their tensile response therefore depends on fiber diameter/linear density, curing profile and the resulting cross-link gradient, and—when used as reinforcement—fiber length, loading, dispersion, and fiber–matrix bonding. A published friction-material study describes the fibers as modest in strength but comparatively extensible, and reports that their reinforcing effect in phenolic composites is strongly formulation- and interface-dependent; those composite observations are not intrinsic-fiber properties.

A bounded virgin-fiber reference is Kynol's 15–33 µm (2.2–11 dtex) novoloid-fiber range: the supplier lists tensile strength of 12–16 cN/tex, elongation of 10–50%, and modulus of 260–350 cN/tex. These are typical supplier values that explicitly vary with diameter; specimen conditioning, gauge length, test rate, and statistical basis are not supplied, so they should not be treated as universal novoloid-fiber specifications.
sections.processing: Novoloid fiber is made by converting a novolac precursor into a fiber before infusibilization: the precursor is melt-spun through a conventional spinnerette and then treated with formaldehyde or a formaldehyde-generating system to produce an amorphous, three-dimensional crosslinked network. Once cured, the fiber is infusible and insoluble, so downstream conversion is cutting, blending, or forming it into fiber-filled friction and sealing materials rather than remelting it. Hayes' open article directly describes melt spinning followed by formaldehyde curing and discusses novoloid fiber in friction and sealing formulations. A separate Toray patent describes melt-spun curable phenol-formaldehyde fibers, acid-catalyzed curing chemistry, crosslinking agents, and subsequent heat treatment. Exact spinning, curing, and heat-treatment conditions depend on precursor molecular mass, fiber diameter, catalyst, and crosslinker; the cited sources do not establish a universal cycle.
sections.structureAndMorphology: A phenolic novolac precursor can be melt-spun before curing. Kynol describes acid-catalyzed crosslinking that converts its spun fibers into an amorphous, insoluble three-dimensional network. The supplier also describes the individual fibers as generally elliptical in cross section; that fiber geometry is distinct from the chemical connectivity of the network. Cure conditions and diffusion of curing agents can influence the final structure, and a felt or yarn adds another level of arrangement.
sections.properties: The cured network makes the documented Kynol fiber infusible and insoluble rather than melt-processable. The supplier reports limiting oxygen-index values generally between 30 and 34, with the result depending on the textile structure and test method; this measure is the oxygen concentration needed to sustain burning under the test conditions. Kynol also describes charring during flame exposure, with the remaining surface layer acting as a barrier. That behavior does not imply unlimited thermal stability: the supplier distinguishes brief flame resistance from gradual loss of strength at elevated service temperatures.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Novoloid fiber serves fire-blocking layers, protective textiles and friction materials. Kynol attributes its thermal-barrier role partly to charring without melting: the remaining char can limit heat and oxygen reaching the material beneath. The supplier also lists brake linings and gaskets, where the rest of the composite formulation contributes to the finished part. Novoloid fibers can be converted to activated-carbon materials for uses such as air filtration and solvent recovery; those converted products have a different chemistry and function.

Purchasing. Gun Ei supplies Kynol fibers, while partner factories convert yarn, felt and activated-carbon products. Its bulletin lists standard fiber lengths of 51, 70 and 100 mm, with crimped and uncrimped variants as well as short-cut material. These are product dimensions, not an order-size or availability guarantee; the supplier offers small samples by inquiry.

Scale and evidence limits. Fiber dimensions and a sample-inquiry route document forms in which material can be offered, not the quantity purchased annually. A finished felt or activated-carbon product is not equal to the mass of uncured novolac resin. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed novoloid tonnage was established from the checked sources.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The supplier identifies char, water vapor and carbon dioxide as principal flame-exposure products of its cured phenolic novoloid fibers, with carbon monoxide possible under oxygen limitation. Under fire exposure the char can preserve the shape of a residue even as the fiber chemistry changes. These combustion products describe flame conditions, not the products of slow ambient aging.

Timescales: Kynol reports that a particular 290 g/m² woven fabric withstood an oxyacetylene flame described as 2,500 °C for at least 12 seconds without breakthrough. That is a supplier-reported barrier endpoint for a fabric, not proof that its polymer is unchanged or a lifetime for all novoloid articles. The same bulletin notes gradual loss of weight and strength at high temperatures over time.

Environmental persistence: A flame-barrier test and char formation do not measure biological conversion of the polymer carbon to carbon dioxide or biomass. They do not establish a soil, freshwater or marine mineralization time. Persistence of a particular discarded novoloid article remains unquantified by these sources.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The supplier identifies novoloid fibers and textiles as precursors for activated-carbon materials used in applications including filtration and solvent recovery. Conversion to activated carbon changes the material and should not be described as recovery of the original phenolic polymer. The bulletin does not establish a route that returns the fiber to novolac or its monomers.

Using a supplied precursor to manufacture a carbon product is also different from collecting and processing discarded consumer textiles. The checked source does not establish a post-consumer collection system or closed-loop recycling service for every novoloid article.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Kynol novoloid chars rather than melting, but flame resistance does not mean smoke is harmless. The supplier reports carbon monoxide when oxygen is limited, alongside char, water and carbon dioxide. These are fire-exposure considerations for the supplier’s phenolic fiber, and should remain separate from the behavior of coatings, blends and additives.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The precursor resin, fiber diameter, formation and extent of cure affect novoloid material. Kynol lists fiber diameters from 15 to 33 µm and notes that its reported properties vary with diameter; it also supplies several lengths and textile forms. The cited curing patent identifies diffusion of curing agents into the fiber as a process limitation. A result for a felt, friction composite or activated-carbon product should therefore not be treated as a universal value for the original fiber.

sections.overview: Regenerated cellulose is cellulose reshaped from a dissolved or chemically converted feedstock into a new material. Viscose, modal, lyocell and cupro are commercially distinct regenerated-cellulose fiber routes. Dissolution, spinning and drawing reorganize the chains and produce fibers suited to textiles and nonwovens. Cellulose acetate is a cellulose ester and is a distinct material, not regenerated cellulose itself. The parent cellulose backbone remains, but its organization and the shape of the final fiber depend on the route used to make it. Regenerated fibers interact with water, making wet strength and dimensional behavior important in textile use. The fiber class encompasses several manufacturing routes and is not a single grade.
sections.history: Regenerated cellulose developed through multiple ways of dissolving and re-forming plant cellulose. Charles Frederick Cross, Edward John Bevan and Clayton Beadle’s 1892 viscose patent became a foundation for the rayon and cellophane industries. Subsequent fiber development improved wet performance and changed solvent systems. Lenzing dates its first high-wet-modulus fiber to 1965 and large-scale lyocell production at Heiligenkreuz to 1997; it acquired the Tencel business in 2004. Textile fibers remained central, while regenerated films provided a separate use of the same underlying cellulose chemistry. These dates distinguish a particular viscose process from later regenerated-cellulose technologies rather than assigning the whole class one invention date.
sections.nomenclature: Regenerated cellulose is a process-defined cellulose subfamily. Rayon and viscose cellulose are common names for particular regenerated-cellulose fiber routes and should not be treated as names for every regenerated-cellulose material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Regenerated cellulose starts with purified native cellulose, commonly dissolving-grade wood pulp or cotton linters; the cellulose backbone is dissolved or temporarily derivatized and then precipitated back as cellulose rather than polymerized from a small-molecule monomer. In the viscose route, pulp is steeped in sodium hydroxide to form alkali cellulose, pressed, shredded, and aged to adjust degree of polymerization. Reaction with carbon disulfide gives soluble cellulose xanthate, which is dissolved in dilute sodium hydroxide, filtered, and deaerated. Contact with an acidic salt bath coagulates the solution and decomposes the xanthate, regenerating cellulose that is washed to remove sulfur compounds, acid, and salts. One cited patent documents this full viscose sequence. A distinct lyocell patent directly dissolves pulp in aqueous N-methylmorpholine N-oxide by controlled water removal, filters the dope, regenerates cellulose in an aqueous bath, washes out the amine oxide, and recovers solvent. Pulp purity and degree of polymerization, solution filtration, solvent/water balance, and coagulation chemistry control the regenerated material. Fiber drawing and article-specific spinning settings remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Regenerated cellulose covers viscose/rayon, modal and high-wet-modulus viscose, lyocell, cupro, and laboratory solvent-spun cellulose-II products, so fiber, film, sponge, membrane, yarn, fabric, and composite results must remain separate. In a drawn filament the hydrogen-bonded cellulose-II network gives a strongly anisotropic response: axial stiffness and tenacity rise as long chains, crystallites, and amorphous tie material become aligned, while transverse cohesion, bending, fibrillation, knot or loop strength, and fatigue can be limiting. Lyocell commonly retains more dry and wet strength and has higher modulus but lower extension than ordinary viscose because its direct-solution dry-jet wet-spinning route can preserve greater degree of polymerization, crystallinity, and axial orientation. Water penetrates amorphous regions, swells and plasticizes the hydrogen-bonded structure, generally lowering modulus and strength and increasing deformation; the loss is especially consequential for ordinary viscose, whereas modal/high-wet-modulus and lyocell variants are designed for better wet retention.

Mechanical response depends on pulp degree of polymerization and purity, hemicellulose content and prior chain degradation, solvent and regeneration chemistry, dope concentration and entanglement, spinneret and air-gap geometry, extrusion and take-up speed or draw ratio, coagulation-bath composition and mass transfer, washing and drying tension, crystallinity and crystal orientation, skin–core and void morphology, filament diameter and defects, fibrillation, crosslinking and finishes, moisture history, temperature, aging, gauge length, strain rate, and whether a single filament, yarn, nonwoven, woven fabric, film, or composite is tested. A bounded laboratory example used bamboo pulp of viscosity-average molecular mass 1.2 × 10^5 g/mol (reported DP 760) at 5 wt% in tetrabutylammonium acetate/DMSO, wet-spun through a 0.355 mm needle into ethanol at 20 °C. The resulting cellulose-II fiber table reports dry tenacity 3.85 cN/dtex, wet tenacity 3.21 cN/dtex, and 11.9% elongation at break. Dried filaments were tested over a 20 mm gauge length with 30 replicates, but the paper does not report tensile rate, scatter, final filament diameter, or the wet-conditioning/test protocol. The endpoint therefore applies only to that bamboo-pulp solvent/spinning experiment and is not a specification for commercial viscose, modal, lyocell, films, or regenerated cellulose generally.
sections.processing:
Regenerated cellulose is converted from a cellulose solution or dope into fibers, films, membranes, powders, or related articles by regeneration rather than melt processing. In conventional wet spinning, a filtered and deaerated dope is metered through a spinneret into an aqueous or acidic coagulation bath; solvent exchange and precipitation form a gel filament, which is withdrawn, washed (often first with hot water and then with distilled water), and dried. Dry-jet wet spinning adds a controlled air gap before coagulation, while dry spinning and related solution-spinning variants use solvent removal or a different nonsolvent path. Take-up speed, air-gap or bath conditions, spinneret geometry, dope viscosity and concentration, and draw ratio control filament diameter, orientation, skin–core structure, voids, and fibrillation. Drawing may occur during take-up or in subsequent wet/dry zones; it increases axial orientation but must be matched to the gel strength and coagulation state. Commercial route names such as viscose, lyocell, and cupro therefore denote different solution/coagulation and post-treatment windows rather than one universal spinning schedule.

Casting is used for regenerated-cellulose films and membranes: a solution layer is spread on a plate or support, immersed in or contacted with a coagulation bath, washed to remove solvent and soluble reagents, and dried under controlled tension, humidity, temperature, or relaxation conditions. Coagulant identity and miscibility, bath temperature, layer thickness, and mass-transfer rate affect regeneration kinetics, shrinkage, porosity, crystallinity, and the final film surface; drying can compact or collapse the wet gel and alter morphology, so film and fiber settings are not interchangeable.

A bounded film example from Nguyen et al. dissolved 20 wt% cellulose in 50 wt% aqueous tetrabutylphosphonium hydroxide at 23 °C for 30 min, cast the clear solution as an approximately 500 µm layer on glass, and rapidly immersed it in propylene carbonate. Coagulation occurred within seconds in that formulation; the regenerated film was washed with distilled water and dried at 80 °C. These conditions are an experiment-specific example for that solvent, cellulose concentration, layer thickness, and coagulant, not a family-wide operating window. The general spinning and post-treatment sequence likewise varies with pulp degree of polymerization, solvent system, dope rheology, spinneret, bath composition, draw history, washing endpoint, and drying tension.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Regeneration retains the linked-glucose cellulose backbone but reorganizes how chains pack. Spinning and drawing can orient polymer along the fiber axis, while conditions influence ordered and less ordered regions and cross-sectional shape. Lyocell's aligned fibrillar structure can split into fine surface fibrils during wet abrasion. Other routes and processing conditions produce different fiber structures. The alignment that contributes to lyocell strength also makes surface fibrillation possible: fine fibrils can separate from the fiber when wet material is abraded. Finishing treatments can alter that behavior, so it is not fixed solely by the cellulose repeat unit.
sections.properties: The hydroxyl-rich cellulose chain interacts with water, allowing regenerated-cellulose fibers to absorb moisture. The cited review describes higher wet tensile strength for lyocell than conventional viscose, although product and test conditions matter. Lyocell's aligned fibrils can also separate at the surface under wet mechanical abrasion. Fiber strength, elongation and wet behavior depend on processing and conditioning, not simply cellulose chemistry. The cited review also describes lower elongation for lyocell than conventional viscose and notes that its moisture regain is slightly lower. These are comparative trends for the reviewed fibers, not specifications for all textile grades; finishes and fabric construction can change finished-article performance.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Regenerated-cellulose fibers supply apparel, home and technical textiles, nonwovens and hygiene products. Their moisture interaction and fiber form help make them useful in fabrics, while processing and finishing affect strength, surface feel and handling. Viscose, modal and lyocell are distinct fiber products with different production routes. Lyocell’s wet strength and moisture interaction are relevant to textile selection, while its tendency to fibrillate during wet abrasion makes finishing and use conditions important. Applications and handling therefore depend on the particular fiber and fabric rather than cellulose identity alone.

Purchasing. Textile and nonwoven manufacturers obtain specified fiber grades from producers such as Lenzing; subsequent buyers purchase yarns, fabrics or finished products. Dissolving pulp is a precursor to fiber manufacture rather than a regenerated-fiber product.

Scale and evidence limits. Lenzing reported worldwide fiber sales of 962,000 tonnes in 2024 across its cellulosic fiber portfolio. This is a company sales figure, not global demand or the output of a single viscose grade.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Cellulases can cleave accessible cellulose chains into smaller carbohydrates that microorganisms may use. Fiber disintegration, dissolution and conversion of carbon to carbon dioxide are distinct endpoints. Finishes and other fibers in a blend can alter the behavior of the complete article.

Timescales: In a California coastal study, mean disappearance times for tested viscose, modal and lyocell textiles ranged from about 22 to 30 days across sea-surface and seafloor experiments. In a separate closed bioreactor at 30 °C, chopped viscose, modal and lyocell samples reached approximately 82%, 81% and 76% biodegradation, respectively, based on carbon dioxide production after 28 days. The field observation and the controlled carbon-dioxide test measure different endpoints; neither is a universal rate for all regenerated-cellulose textiles.

Environmental persistence: The study concerns selected fabrics and conditions rather than every regenerated-cellulose article. The tested lyocell/polyester and lyocell/polypropylene blends did not disintegrate during the observation periods, even though some translucent areas appeared. A thicker, coated or blended textile can therefore have a different fate from a pure fiber specimen, and measurements in one coastal environment do not set its lifetime elsewhere.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Mechanical textile recycling can open and shred cellulosic fabrics for reuse, though shortened fibers may require blending with stronger carrier fibers for spinning. Lenzing describes using cotton or regenerated-cellulose textile waste with virgin pulp in its REFIBRA process; its ECOVERO example contains at least 20% recycled material. This concerns accepted feedstocks and a specified process rather than every mixed garment.

In an experimental Ioncell route, researchers dissolved selected white, black and blue viscose and white modal in an ionic liquid, spun new lyocell-type fibers, and made yarn and knitted demonstrators. Sorting and handling of dyes or mixed textiles remain separate challenges.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Regenerated cellulose articles can generate cellulose dust during cutting or abrasion. NIOSH identifies eye, skin and respiratory irritation and treats cellulose as a combustible solid. Its powder-handling guidance concerns airborne particles; it does not imply the same exposure from an intact fiber, film or paper article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Viscose, modal, lyocell and cupro do not have one common set of fiber properties. Feedstock, chain length, regeneration route, drawing, cross section and finishing affect the product. Wet strength and fibrillation are especially relevant when comparing textile handling or laundering. Results for a pure regenerated fiber cannot be assumed for a blended or coated fabric. Fibrillation may affect a fabric surface during use, while wet tensile strength concerns its response under load; these are separate measurements. A fiber listing should therefore be read together with its route, conditioning and intended finished product.

sections.overview: Cellulose acetate is a family of cellulose esters made by replacing some of cellulose's hydroxyl groups with acetyl groups. The average degree of substitution describes how many of the three available hydroxyl sites per glucose unit are substituted; commercial diacetate and triacetate differ in this average. Acetylation changes the hydrogen bonding and solvent behavior of the cellulose backbone, making particular grades suitable for fibers, films and molded compounds. Molecular weight, substitution and added ingredients determine which processing route and performance are suitable. Substitution and formulation also influence how readily water and enzymes can access the chains. A fiber, free film and plasticized molded article have different surface areas and compositions, so their mechanical and degradation results need that context.
sections.history: Cellulose acetate was developed by Paul Schützenberger in 1865, decades before it became an important commercial plastic and fiber. The Museum of Fine Arts account identifies Eastman Kodak’s introduction of acetate safety film in 1908 and Dreyfus production by 1910 as early industrial milestones. British production of acetate textile fibers followed in 1919 under the Celanese name. Film, lacquers and transparent sheeting were joined by textile, eyewear, tool-handle and cigarette-filter applications. Its history therefore spans chemical discovery, film-base manufacture and fiber commercialization, with different dates for each rather than one date applicable to every acetate grade.
sections.nomenclature: CA is a common abbreviation for cellulose acetate. This record covers cellulose acetate generally; cellulose triacetate is a more highly acetylated cellulose-acetate material and is maintained as a distinct record rather than a synonym.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cellulose acetate is a cellulose-ester subfamily whose degree of acetyl substitution distinguishes materials such as highly acetylated triacetate and lower-substituted secondary acetates. It is made from cellulose feedstock, including dissolving pulp, cotton linters, or purified plant cellulose, by acetylating hydroxyl groups. A conventional acetic-acid process first produces highly acetylated material with excess acetic anhydride in acetic acid and an acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid; controlled partial hydrolysis can then lower the substitution level. A laboratory example first isolated cellulose from Agave sisalana, then treated it with acetic acid, sulfuric acid, and acetic anhydride before water precipitation and drying. That plant source and laboratory sequence are a bounded example, not evidence that all cellulose acetate is made from Agave or under identical conditions.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cellulose acetate mechanics depend on molecular-chain length and distribution, degree and distribution of substitution, feedstock, and article form; values for cast films, fibers, plasticized compounds, and membrane structures are therefore not interchangeable. In an early film study, cellulose-acetate fractions with degree of polymerization (DP) 30 could not form coherent films; properties increased rapidly with chain length above that point, while further improvement was slight above DP 150. That study also found ultimate elongation and folding endurance more sensitive than tensile strength to chain length and its distribution. A later cast-film study illustrates a bounded tensile endpoint: cellulose acetate made by homogeneous acetylation of tunicate-cellulose material (TCM; DS 2.66) was cast from 1 wt% dichloromethane solution onto polyethylene, air-dried for one week (mean thickness 29 µm), and pulled at 5 mm/min. It gave a Young’s modulus of 6.6 GPa and tensile strength of 58.9 MPa. Within that experiment, films obtained by heterogeneous acetylation or from powdered-tunicate and cotton celluloses were lower in modulus and strength, consistent with the authors’ reported molecular-mass and reaction-route differences. The article does not report specimen geometry, test temperature/humidity, or replicate statistics, so these values describe that cast-film preparation rather than a cellulose-acetate family range.
sections.processing: Cellulose acetate (CA) can be solvent-cast or solution-blown into films and melt-compounded, extruded, and injection molded when the formulation provides adequate flow. Because CA is moisture-sensitive and its melt-processing window can be constrained by thermal sensitivity, drying, plasticizer level, shear, and residence history must be set for the particular grade/formulation. Erdmann and co-workers dried CA before twin-screw compounding and again before injection molding; their 15–40 wt% plasticizer formulations used lower injection-unit temperatures for more highly plasticized materials, illustrating that plasticizer content changes the usable settings. Eastman’s cellulosic-plastics drying guidance gives moisture limits only as supplier operating guidance; it notes that permissible moisture depends on the individual extrusion operation. These moisture observations and experimental settings are not universal CA-family specifications.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The linked glucose backbone remains after acetylation, while acetate ester groups occupy some hydroxyl sites and others remain available for hydrogen bonding. Degree of substitution is an average over the chain, not a guarantee that every glucose unit has the same pattern of substituents. For example, cellulose diacetate used in fiber applications commonly has a degree of substitution around 2.5, whereas triacetate is more highly substituted. Solution casting and drawing, plasticizers and drying produce different film or fiber structures even for chemically similar material. A fiber tow bundles many fine filaments, while a solvent-cast film has a different geometry and surface available to water. Differences in the starting degree of substitution and finished additives further complicate direct comparisons.
sections.properties: Acetate content and plasticization affect how a cellulose acetate softens and can be processed. In a differential scanning calorimetry study of one acetate grade, the midpoint glass transition of the raw powder was 196.6 °C; a blend containing 15 wt% glycerol triacetate had a midpoint of 122.8 °C and one with 15 wt% triethyl citrate had a midpoint of 142.4 °C. These are measurements for the named mixtures and a specified heating run, not a glass-transition range for the entire family. The plasticizer lowers the transition temperature, helping make processing and the finished material less rigid; the two additives did not act identically. Moisture and the selected plasticizer also affect a finished article, so a glass-transition measurement on dry powder is not enough to describe the behavior of a filter or molded part in use.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Cellulose acetate is used as fiber tow in cigarette filters and in films and molded articles. In a conventional filter tow, a small quantity of glycerol triacetate is applied to bond the fibers into a firm plug; this is a formulated fiber product rather than neat acetate resin. Daicel describes cellulose acetate compounds for molded daily goods, furniture parts, packaging sheets, profiles and additive manufacturing. Film, fiber and molded applications require different handling and finishing, including selection of solvent or plasticizer where appropriate. These examples cover different processing forms and do not imply that each grade is suited to every use.

Purchasing. Producers supply application-specific fibers and compounds. Daicel identifies distinct CAFBLO molding/extrusion and 3D-printing grades and offers samples and technical-sales contact. Buyers must specify the intended product form and grade, because an acetate fiber tow, optical-film feedstock and compounded molding resin are not interchangeable purchases.

Scale and evidence limits. The catalog documents product availability and intended applications but does not establish an annual purchase volume or market share. No reliable separate consumption tonnage was established from the checked sources.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Acetyl groups can impede cellulase access to the cellulose backbone. Microbial breakdown can involve esterases that remove acetyl groups and cellulases that cleave the backbone; a separate initial abiotic hydrolysis step was not required in the reported diacetate tests. Substitution and the microorganisms present both matter.

Timescales: In a pilot compost test, a cellulose acetate film containing 39.8 wt% acetyl showed no visible disintegration after 12 weeks; the compost reached 70.7 °C early in the test. In a separate freshwater laboratory test at 21 °C, cryomilled cellulose diacetate fibers of degree of substitution 2.5 reached 72.3% ± 11.6% absolute biodegradation after 118 days, estimated from oxygen consumption. The fibers lacked the triacetin used in typical finished cigarette filters; these two results concern different forms, media and endpoints. In another study, tow and cast film with degree of substitution 2.45 each lost less than 3% of their dry mass after 16 weeks in static river water, seawater or laboratory-made seawater. Those observations concern the prepared samples and conditions and do not contradict the separate oxygen-consumption test on much smaller fibers.

Environmental persistence: The controlled respirometry result demonstrates biodegradation of the tested small fibers, while visible disintegration in compost is a different observation. Neither study sets a universal lifetime for intact filters, other acetate grades, soil or seawater. Formulation, surface area, microbial adaptation and local conditions can change the outcome.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
In a laboratory recovery study, used cigarette filters were separated from paper, washed in water and ethanol, and dried. The recovered cellulose acetate was dissolved in acetone and cast into a transparent film; the authors reported that the film was brittle and would need a suitable plasticizer for toughness. This recovers and reuses polymer rather than demonstrating mineralization.

The experiment used a specified collected feedstock and cleaning process. Contaminants in used filters and the resulting solvent or wash streams require attention, and the demonstration does not establish a broad collection system or a commercial closed-loop route.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For cellulose acetate photographic film, the archival term “safety film” distinguishes it from nitrate film, while acidic deterioration remains possible. NARA recommends identifying vinegar syndrome and using controlled cold storage to slow it. The guidance concerns film preservation rather than a general toxicological assessment of every cellulose-ester formulation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: A cellulose acetate designation does not specify a unique degree or pattern of substitution, molecular weight or additive package. In one acetate formulation, equal 15 wt% additions of glycerol triacetate and triethyl citrate produced different glass-transition midpoints, illustrating why the plasticizer type must accompany its amount. Fiber versus film geometry, moisture and processing history also influence the performance of a finished article. Results for a named formulation or degradation test should not be generalized to every acetate grade or product. A study of tow and cast film with degree of substitution 2.45 compared both physical forms in several water environments. Its mass-loss endpoint is not directly equivalent to the oxygen-consumption endpoint used for the separately tested cryomilled fibers.

sections.overview: Cellulose triacetate (CTA) is a highly acetylated cellulose ester, commonly described by an average degree of substitution of about 2.7–3 acetyl groups per glucose unit. It retains the cellulose backbone but most of its hydroxyl sites have been esterified. CTA has been used as a photographic film base and is supplied for optical films used with display polarizers. Researchers also formulate it with other materials to make separation membranes, whose properties cannot be attributed to neat CTA alone. The degree of acetylation affects both interactions with water and access to the cellulose-derived backbone. A photograph, an optical polarizer film and a research coating are multilayer or formulated products rather than identical sheets of neat CTA.
sections.history: Cellulose triacetate’s photographic history followed earlier, less highly acetylated cellulose films. The Canadian Conservation Institute dates production to 1948, when it offered a more stable base than earlier acetates. By about 1950, many film manufacturers were making triacetate roll film. Motion-picture use persisted partly because acetate can break when a projector jams and can be spliced readily. This is the history of commercial film-base development, not a claim that the triacetate chemical structure was first synthesized in 1948.
sections.nomenclature: CTA abbreviates cellulose triacetate, and “triacetate” is a common shortened name. It is not interchangeable with the broader cellulose acetate record, because the degree of acetylation defines an important material boundary.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cellulose triacetate (CTA) is the highly acetylated cellulose ester obtained by converting essentially all three hydroxyl groups per anhydroglucose unit; it is a modified natural polymer, not a polymerization of acetate monomer. Purified cellulose can be obtained from wood pulp, cotton linters, or other cellulose-rich biomass before acetylation. A date-palm-cellulose study describes heterogeneous reaction with acetic anhydride and acid catalysts and reports CTA at degree of substitution 2.9; it also distinguishes subsequent partial hydrolysis used to make lower-substitution cellulose acetates. As a different route example, mild-acid-pretreated sugarcane bagasse was dissolved in an EmimOAc/DMSO medium and acetylated homogeneously with isopropenyl acetate, then reprecipitated to separate a cellulose-triacetate-rich fraction from lignin acetate. That one-pot biomass conversion is a source-specific alternative to direct acetylation of isolated cellulose.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cellulose triacetate mechanical response is sensitive to article form and sorbed liquid: fiber viscoelasticity, a dense membrane, and a filled film should not be treated as equivalent materials. Okiyama and co-workers report that the dry triacetate fiber they studied had a glass-transition temperature of 193 °C, but during drying of a wet fiber a mechanical-loss-tangent peak occurred at room temperature; polar and nonpolar organic solvents also induced a room-temperature glass transition. Their comparison with regenerated cellulose fibers found a lower loss-tangent maximum for the triacetate fiber, which they interpreted qualitatively as a smaller water-affected moving unit. A focused membrane example gives a bounded strength endpoint: Nakanishi and co-workers prepared dense membranes under 35 °C and 70% relative humidity and reported, for their commercial cellulose-triacetate control membrane, Young’s modulus of 0.74 GPa and maximum stress of 46.3 MPa. The same study found its sugarcane-bagasse-derived triacetate membranes too fragile to handle for modulus measurement, whereas its lower-acetylated diacetate materials formed mechanically measurable membranes. The commercial-control values are therefore condition- and membrane-specific; the report does not give specimen geometry, loading rate, or replicate statistics, and they are not a cellulose-triacetate family range.
sections.processing: CTA is commonly converted as film or membrane by solution casting: prepare a homogeneous dope, cast from a die or blade onto a support, evaporate solvent until self-supporting, peel, then dry, cool, and wind as needed. A CTA-film patent describes this route and, for its tear- and fold-endurance process, uses a principal methylene-chloride solvent with 13–25 wt% poor solvent and a support below 10 °C; those conditions are process-specific. A distinct CTA/CDA mixed-matrix membrane experiment vacuum-dried powder at 120 °C overnight, dissolved an 80/20 (wt.%) CTA/CDA blend in NMP with stirring at 40 °C overnight, sonicated the filler suspension before mixing, blade-cast on glass, evaporated at 100 °C overnight, peeled, and vacuum-dried at 120 °C for at least 24 h. That is a formulation-specific membrane route, not a general CTA window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Cellulose's linked glucose backbone remains, but acetyl ester groups occupy most hydroxyl sites. Degree of substitution is an average across the available sites, not proof that each individual glucose unit is fully substituted. One experimental triacetate prepared from date-palm-derived cellulose had a reported degree of substitution of about 2.9 and showed semicrystalline character by X-ray diffraction. Solvent, casting, blending and additives affect the structure of a finished film or membrane. In a research coating on a PHB film, alkaline treatment partially removed surface acetyl groups and increased wettability. The CTA coating and PHB substrate are distinct components, so their combined response cannot be assigned to the coating alone.
sections.properties: CTA can form films and membranes, but transport properties depend on the membrane's formulation and preparation. In one laboratory study, a cellulose triacetate/cellulose diacetate blend had a pure-gas CO₂ permeability of 7.56 Barrer at 35 °C and 5 bar; adding 15 wt% amine-functionalized ZIF-8 particles increased it to 11.33 Barrer and increased CO₂/CH₄ selectivity from 27.0 to 33.3. The results describe the tested blend membranes, not neat CTA or all particle loadings. For optical films, clarity and other optical characteristics must likewise be evaluated for the selected film and application. In a separate coated-PHB film experiment, the reported water contact angle fell from about 86° to 43° after alkaline treatment of the CTA coating. This describes a treated surface in a specific multilayer film, not a universal value for CTA resin.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Cellulose triacetate films have served as photographic and motion-picture film bases and are used as components of optical films for display polarizers. Daicel describes designing optical retardation into TAC films to compensate for light leakage at oblique viewing angles; different display designs require different film properties. An industrial optical film is therefore a designed component rather than simply an unspecified acetate sheet. As a separate research application, scientists have combined CTA with cellulose diacetate and amine-functionalized particles to make laboratory membranes for CO₂/CH₄ separation.

Purchasing. Industrial film manufacturers source optical TAC resin and convert it into films or polarizer components; Daicel identifies resin supplied to Fujifilm for film manufacture. Buyers of finished optical film and buyers of resin therefore occupy different steps in the supply chain and should specify the intended form and performance. The membrane study uses a blend and filler, not a catalog specification for a commercial gas-separation product.

Scale and evidence limits. The June 2026 supplier announcement documents a resin-to-film supply relationship but does not disclose resin sales, consumption tonnage or an optical-film market share. The membrane example is a laboratory demonstration, not evidence of installed commercial capacity.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Acetate film can undergo hydrolysis that removes acetyl groups and releases acetic acid. In stored cellulose triacetate motion-picture film this is associated with the vinegar smell known as vinegar syndrome; affected film may shrink or distort and the image layer may crack. This archival aging mechanism is different from a claim of environmental mineralization.

Timescales: The rate and onset of damage depend on the film and its storage conditions, including temperature and moisture. The consulted preservation and industrial hydrolysis sources do not establish a single condition-qualified lifetime for all CTA films. Cooling and appropriate humidity control are used to slow damage to archival material. In a separate 25 °C seawater/sediment laboratory test, a CTA-coated PHB film showed no measurable mass loss over 30 days, whereas a film whose coating was first treated with alkali lost 56% of its initial mass. These measurements concern a multilayer film and cannot determine how much CTA alone degraded. In a separate respirometry experiment, milled cellulose acetate with supplier-reported degree of substitution 3.0 mineralized at an initial rate of about 0.1% per day in soil compost held at 60 °C. This is a measured initial CO₂ rate for one highly substituted sample, not a measured lifetime; the authors’ longer-term estimates extrapolated from initial rates.

Environmental persistence: The production of acetic acid or physical failure of an archival film does not show that its polymer backbone has mineralized. The coated-film test measures total sample mass, not complete conversion of either component to CO₂. Available sources do not establish a transferable mineralization time for CTA films in soil, freshwater or seawater.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A patent application proposes hydrolyzing cellulose acetate ester waste in an acid-containing reactor, separating solid material and collecting a water-soluble stream that may contain acetic acid and sugars. It lists cellulose triacetate among possible feedstocks, while its tabulated examples identify other cellulose acetate waste forms rather than a separately specified triacetate specimen.

The proposed process is chemical conversion and recovery of soluble products rather than recovery of intact CTA polymer. The patent's broad feedstock description does not establish operating commercial collection, a triacetate-specific yield or a closed-loop CTA recycling system.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For cellulose triacetate photographic film, the archival term “safety film” distinguishes it from nitrate film, while acidic deterioration remains possible. NARA recommends identifying vinegar syndrome and using controlled cold storage to slow it. The guidance concerns film preservation rather than a general toxicological assessment of every cellulose-ester formulation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Triacetate is a more highly substituted member of the cellulose acetate family, not interchangeable with a partially acetylated material of unspecified substitution. Feedstock, residual hydroxyl content, molecular weight and film preparation can vary. A membrane's permeation behavior depends on any blended diacetate and filler as well as on temperature, gas composition and pressure; results from a composite membrane should not be used as neat-polymer constants. Degradation of a stored photographic film also depends on its complete construction and storage conditions. In the coated-PHB experiment the measured mass change belongs to the whole film, not separately to the triacetate coating. Prior chemical treatment and the test medium both affected the outcome.

sections.overview:
Cellulose is a natural polysaccharide made of linear chains of glucose units joined by β-(1→4) linkages. It is a major load-bearing component of plant cell walls, where its chains associate into microfibrils embedded among other wall polymers. The organization of these microfibrils helps determine the strength and directional behavior of the wall.

Cellulose is a raw material for paper, textiles, construction materials, and chemical derivatives. Cellulose from wood pulp or plant fibers can also be dissolved and regenerated into textile fibers. The source, arrangement and crystallinity of cellulose, its associated constituents, and processing affect material behavior, so natural tissues, pulp fibers, and regenerated products need to be considered in their own context.
sections.history: Cellulose is a natural material, so its history begins with human use and scientific identification rather than invention. Anselme Payen isolated and characterized the plant substance in work reported in 1838; the name cellulose entered the literature in 1839. Paper, textiles and construction materials made it an industrial raw material long before modern structural analysis. Nishikawa and Ono obtained cellulose-fiber X-ray diffraction patterns in 1913. Later milestones included VanderHart and Atalla’s 1984 recognition of two native cellulose allomorphs and diffraction studies resolving their structures. This scientific progression supported a broader understanding of the material used for fibers, paper and chemical derivatives.
sections.nomenclature: Cellulose names the polymer itself. “Cellulosic” is a broader material descriptor and can include derivatives or composite materials, so it is not a synonym for the canonical cellulose record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cellulose is a natural polymer family produced by plants, algae, selected bacteria, and some other organisms. In biological synthesis, membrane-associated cellulose synthase uses UDP-glucose to form beta-(1→4)-glucan chains, which are assembled into microfibrils; this biosynthetic route is distinct from industrial isolation. Technical cellulose fiber is commonly isolated from lignocellulosic feedstocks by pulping that removes much of the lignin rather than by creating the glucan chain anew. The kraft example uses wood chips and aqueous sodium hydroxide/sodium sulfide cooking liquor in a batch or continuous digester, followed by washing and chemical recovery. Feedstock species, biological origin, and pulp-isolation route therefore need to remain explicit when describing a particular cellulose material.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cellulose mechanics are hierarchical and strongly anisotropic rather than describable by one family-wide modulus or strength. Linear glucan chains assemble into partly crystalline microfibrils that carry load principally along their axes. Crystallinity, cellulose allomorph, microfibril size and orientation, and interactions with neighboring cellulose and matrix polymers therefore govern stiffness, strength, and extensibility. Native plant walls, purified pulp fibers, regenerated fibers, films, and nano- or microfibrillar materials are mechanically different forms. In plant material, the more hydrated and disordered primary wall is comparatively flexible, whereas the more oriented cellulose arrangement and lignified matrix of secondary walls produce greater rigidity. Source species, noncellulosic constituents, moisture, defects introduced during pulping, drawing or other processing, and test direction must consequently remain attached to reported results.

A single-fiber study by Zizek, Czibula, and Hirn illustrates loading-rate sensitivity under bounded conditions. The authors tested chemi-thermomechanical softwood pulp, bleached chemical softwood pulp, unbleached softwood kraft pulp, and regenerated viscose fibers after water swelling, drying for 1 h at 95 °C, and conditioning for five days at 25 °C and 50% relative humidity. Fibers mounted across a 0.8 mm gap were cycled in longitudinal tension at ten strain rates from 0.113 to 800% s⁻¹ while maximum displacement was limited to 15 µm. Across the tested materials, longitudinal modulus increased approximately log-linearly with rate; per tenfold rate increase, the reported increase was 5–7% for the bleached chemical-pulp fibers and 11–18% for the viscose fibers, depending on the loading protocol. The pulp results showed substantial fiber-to-fiber scatter, and the authors judged some CTMP and unbleached-kraft comparisons statistically uncertain. These rate effects apply to the particular conditioned single-fiber forms and protocol, not to bulk cellulose, films, crystals, or a universal cellulose modulus.
sections.processing: Native cellulose is normally shaped after dissolution or as fibers/pulp rather than by ordinary melt molding. Regenerated-fiber routes include viscose wet spinning, Lyocell air-gap spinning, and ionic-liquid wet or dry-jet-wet spinning; all-cellulose composites and solution-cast materials are further options. Solvent, pulp molecular mass, dope concentration/rheology, coagulation, draw, and orientation materially affect spinnability and final structure. Hermanutz and co-workers describe viscose and Lyocell as established fiber routes and note the need to stabilize an NMMO spinning dope against side reactions. In the Ioncell experiment by Ma and co-workers, dissolving pulps with intrinsic viscosity 360–820 mL/g and cellulose dope concentration 11–15 wt% produced fibers; these narrow feed-window values are for the stated Ioncell system, not a generic cellulose-processing range.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Linear β-(1→4)-linked glucan chains associate into microfibrils containing ordered and less ordered regions. In plant cell walls these fibrils form a hierarchical network with matrix components such as hemicelluloses and pectins; their size and orientation vary with the biological source and wall. Native cellulose I includes Iα- and Iβ-rich crystalline forms, whose relative abundance depends on the source. Dissolution and regeneration, or alkali treatment, can produce cellulose II with a different arrangement of chains.
sections.properties: Cellulose interacts with water and can absorb moisture and swell, although it is insoluble in water and most common solvents. Water uptake depends on the structure and accessibility of a particular cellulosic material; high-surface-area nanocellulose materials can swell more than fiber-based materials. Moisture can also lower the wet strength of a cellulose article. Fibril arrangement, orientation and crystallinity influence behavior, so the properties of an individual fiber or film are not determined by chemical constitution alone. Moisture sensitivity is relevant to a paper sheet: water changes interactions within its bonded fiber network, so dry and wet strength should be measured separately. Properties of a reconstituted film or high-surface-area material cannot be inferred directly from an intact plant wall. In one study, untreated eucalyptus-sulfate paper of 80 g/m² had a dry tensile index of about 17.6 N·m/g and a substantially lower wet tensile index after at least five minutes in water. The article reports inconsistent reference wet values, so the numerical wet result is not resolved here. This is a comparison of one paper’s fiber network, not an intrinsic tensile strength of a cellulose molecule or a guarantee for wet-strength-treated paper.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Cellulose-rich pulp is a feedstock for paper and paperboard and for regenerated textile fibers. In paper, the network of bonded fibers provides the sheet structure; in regenerated fibers, cellulose is dissolved and formed into new filaments. Purified microcrystalline cellulose serves as a tablet binder or filler, and specialty cellulose particles can act as removable pore formers in technical ceramics. These products have different purity and processing requirements. For example, a pharmaceutical powder is selected for controlled particle characteristics, whereas a pulp is selected for fiber-based sheet production.

Purchasing. Buyers specify pulp, pharmaceutical microcrystalline-cellulose powder or a technical fiber or particle grade for the intended process. JRS lists VIVAPUR excipient grades with different particle sizes and bulk densities and offers samples through its supplier channel. A pulp specification is not interchangeable with a pharmaceutical excipient specification.

Scale and evidence limits. FAO reports global wood-pulp production of 193 million tonnes and trade of 71 million tonnes in 2023. These figures describe wood pulp, which includes other constituents and many grades; they are not purchases of chemically pure cellulose or pharmaceutical cellulose.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Cellulases hydrolyze accessible cellulose chains to smaller carbohydrates, including reducing sugars. The state of the material matters: one enzyme experiment compared regenerated cellulose hydrogel and microcrystalline cellulose with a slightly acetylated water-soluble derivative, which hydrolyzed faster than either. These are distinct substrates rather than interchangeable forms of native cellulose.

Timescales: The enzyme study used 50 °C and a cellulase loading of 30 filter-paper units per gram of substrate. Such a controlled hydrolysis experiment does not provide a soil or marine lifetime. In a separate coastal study, mean disappearance times for selected cotton and regenerated-cellulose textiles ranged from about 22 to 42 days across surface and seafloor exposures. In separate 30 °C bioreactors, tested lyocell, modal, viscose and organic cotton samples reached approximately 76–82% biodegradation based on CO₂ evolution after 28 days. The field disappearance and laboratory gas measurements are distinct endpoints.

Environmental persistence: Hydrolysis, visible disintegration and mineralization are different endpoints. Lignin, coatings, fiber geometry and mixtures can impede access or leave other material behind, so an enzyme result on a particular substrate cannot be generalized to every cellulose-rich article.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Paper recycling commonly repulps cellulose-rich sheets in water, screens and cleans the fibers, and forms new paper. Sappi describes flotation deinking, washing and bleaching for coated fine papers and blending recovered fiber with virgin fiber and mill broke. This recovers fibers rather than purified glucose; fiber damage and contaminants influence the resulting paper.

Selected cellulosic textiles also enter dissolution-and-regeneration routes. Lenzing describes using pre- and post-consumer cotton or regenerated-cellulose textile waste with virgin pulp to make new fibers. Mechanical shredding is another route, although shortened fibers can require carrier fibers before spinning. These examples apply to specified waste streams and do not establish equivalent recyclability for every coated or composite cellulose article.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Cellulose powder presents an occupational dust exposure. NIOSH identifies eye, skin and respiratory irritation and treats cellulose as a combustible solid. Its powder-handling guidance concerns airborne particles; it does not imply the same exposure from an intact fiber, film or paper article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The same polymer can appear in plant tissues, isolated pulp, bacterial cellulose, and regenerated fibers with different accompanying materials and structures. For example, pulping and purification can alter chain length, while dissolution, regeneration and drawing influence the organization of a manufactured fiber. Compare results only with the source, processing history, specimen and moisture condition in view. Reported crystallinity values also depend on the measurement and analysis method; estimates obtained by different techniques need not be directly interchangeable. The fiber network and other constituents can also influence degradation, even though their chemistry is not the cellulose repeat unit. Particle or fiber size and water access should accompany a comparison of enzyme experiments.
