sections.overview: Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) is a mixed cellulose ether carrying both methyl and hydroxypropyl substituents. Suitable grades dissolve in water, thicken formulations and form films or hydrated matrices for food and pharmaceutical use. In a matrix, water uptake changes the polymer layer surrounding an ingredient and can influence release. Substitution, molecular weight and the rest of the formulation distinguish products within this family.
sections.history: Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose developed through the tailoring of mixed cellulose ethers to different solvents and applications. A 1974 Dow patent by George Greminger Jr., Carl Strange, Karl Krumel and James Hudson Jr. describes earlier commercial HPMC as a thickener for water-based paints and coatings. Their advance increased hydroxypropyl substitution to obtain grades soluble in anhydrous alcohol, addressing pharmaceutical-coating applications where water or chlorinated solvent mixtures were undesirable. Tablet coatings and water-soluble films therefore accompanied the established coatings-thickener role. The patent documents a particular grade-development milestone, not a first invention date for all HPMC.
sections.nomenclature: HPMC identifies the mixed methyl/hydroxypropyl cellulose derivative, distinct from unmodified cellulose, methylcellulose and hydroxypropyl cellulose alone. Methyl degree of substitution and hydroxypropyl molar substitution describe different features of an HPMC grade. Commercial names such as METHOCEL cover a portfolio that includes both MC and HPMC products. Viscosity, composition and intended specification must therefore accompany a product name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) is a mixed cellulose ether made by first forming alkali cellulose and then methylating and hydroxypropylating cellulose hydroxyl groups with methyl chloride and propylene oxide. It is distinct from methylcellulose or hydroxypropyl cellulose because both substituent classes are intentionally installed. The feed ratio and addition sequence of methyl chloride and propylene oxide, the alkali-cellulose composition, reaction medium, and temperature determine methoxyl degree of substitution and hydroxypropoxyl molar substitution. A historical patent describes concurrent methyl-chloride/propylene-oxide etherification of alkali cellulose; a later process documents controlled feed ratios with dimethyl ether as an inert medium. These are grade-specific examples. Recovery, drying, and final use as a thickener or film former are outside this synthesis-only account.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
HPMC is commonly used as a water-soluble film-former or coating, and the mechanics of a dried HPMC film depend on substitution and molecular-weight grade, residual moisture, casting and drying history, thickness, and the identity and loading of plasticizers, pigments, oils, or reinforcing particles. Strong intermolecular interactions make unplasticized films relatively stiff and low-elongation; small-molecule plasticizers increase segmental mobility and elongation while reducing tensile strength and modulus. The material's hydrophilicity means humidity and water exposure remain consequential to any measured film response.

In a bounded solvent-cast-film study, Owusu-Ware and co-workers tested HPMC containing 0, 6, 8, 11, or 17 wt% PEG 400. Films were pulled between texture-analyzer grips at 0.2 mm/s (0.1 N trigger force) to break or a 300 mm travel limit. The unplasticized formulation gave tensile strength 31 ± 2 MPa, elongation 4 ± 1%, and elastic modulus 1271 ± 105 MPa; at 17 wt% PEG the corresponding values were 21 ± 2 MPa, 23 ± 1%, and 565 ± 54 MPa. Film dimensions, conditioning humidity, and HPMC substitution grade are not specified in the summarized report, so these results demonstrate a particular cast-film/plasticizer trend rather than a family range. An independent open review likewise identifies casting formulation and additive type, loading, moisture sensitivity, and filler dispersion as central controls on HPMC-film strength, modulus, and flexibility.
sections.processing:
Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) is most often converted as a water- or mixed-solvent solution into films, coatings, capsules, and other cast articles. The usual sequence is controlled dissolution and hydration, addition and dispersion of plasticizer, oil, active ingredient, or reinforcement, casting or coating, and drying under controlled humidity. HPMC grade viscosity, methoxyl/hydroxypropoxyl substitution, solids content, plasticizer level, and drying history determine solution rheology, gelation, film coalescence, flexibility, and residual moisture. These sources support solution casting and additive-sensitive film processing; they do not establish a general HPMC melt-processing window.

Owusu-Ware and co-workers provide a bounded example in which HPMC/PEG 400 formulations were prepared as solvent-cast films and mechanically tested; PEG level was a formulation variable rather than a family-wide prescription. A separate open review surveys HPMC film/coating preparation and shows that plasticizers, oils, cellulose reinforcement, and humidity alter drying behavior and tensile flexibility. Accordingly, plasticizer choice, drying atmosphere, and film thickness should be optimized for the named formulation. Methylation/hydroxypropylation of alkali cellulose belongs in Synthesis, not this article-conversion account.
sections.structureAndMorphology: HPMC retains the β-1,4-linked glucose backbone of cellulose while carrying methyl and hydroxypropyl ether groups. The hydroxypropyl substituents retain hydroxyl groups that can react further, so side chains may contain more than one hydroxypropyl unit. Methyl degree of substitution counts occupied original sites on average, whereas hydroxypropyl molar substitution counts added hydroxypropyl units. The relative amounts and distribution of both substituent types distinguish grades and influence hydration.
sections.properties: HPMC forms aqueous solutions and films useful for thickening and release matrices. In a study of selected 1 wt% solutions, higher-molecular-weight HPMC samples produced greater viscosity and shear thinning. For the highest-molecular-weight sample, adding 2 wt% sodium chloride reduced viscosity to 0.78 of its salt-free value at the study's low shear rate of 0.1 s⁻¹; lower-molecular-weight samples showed a smaller effect. This comparison applies to the tested grades and solution conditions rather than every salt or formulation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. HPMC helps provide structure in gluten-free bakery formulations and can form pharmaceutical controlled-release matrices. Ashland describes its food-grade HPMC as improving the height, softness and crumb structure of gluten-free baked products. In a drug matrix, hydration and the resulting polymer layer can influence release, while the active ingredient and dosage form also matter. Food and pharmaceutical uses call for appropriate specifications.

Purchasing. Ingredient suppliers offer food grades such as Benecel and the METHOCEL pharmaceutical portfolio documented in 2024. METHOCEL includes both HPMC and methylcellulose products, so the material and viscosity grade should be specified rather than inferred from the brand. Buyers also select the quality specification appropriate to the intended use.

Scale and evidence limits. Supplier portfolios identify applications and grades but do not provide a separate annual HPMC purchase or consumption total. A baked product or finished tablet includes other ingredients, and its total mass is not HPMC mass. No reliable separate annual HPMC tonnage was established in the checked sources.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Cavitation can mechanically shorten HPMC chains in solution. When hydrogen peroxide is also present, oxidation produces carbonyl-containing material; formic acid and other small products were tentatively assigned by spectroscopy. Without added peroxide, the study observed little oxidation in its spectra, consistent with mechanical effects predominating. These deliberate-treatment results do not establish the products of ordinary environmental exposure.

Timescales: In a laboratory test of dilute K4M HPMC, hydrodynamic cavitation with peroxide at 60 °C reduced weight-average molecular mass from about 335 to 4 kg/mol in 30 minutes. Peroxide alone at 60 °C reduced it from 335 to 184 kg/mol over the same period. The endpoint is chain shortening in a specified treatment, not complete mineralization.

Environmental persistence: The controlled dilute-solution experiment did not measure HPMC conversion to carbon dioxide or biomass in soil or water. Dissolution and lower molecular mass are distinct from complete biological conversion. The study therefore does not establish a soil, freshwater or seawater half-life for a discarded HPMC article.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Cavitation and oxidation are laboratory methods for producing shorter-chain HPMC in solution. In the tested K4M sample, the combination of hydrodynamic cavitation and peroxide produced a much greater molecular-mass decrease than peroxide alone at 60 °C over 30 minutes. This changes the polymer's chain-length distribution rather than demonstrating recovery of equivalent high-molecular-weight HPMC.

The cited study does not establish commercial postconsumer collection or recycling of HPMC-containing articles. Food, pharmaceutical and coating formulations also contain other components that would have to be considered when assessing a practical recovery route.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: EFSA’s 2018 EU assessment of hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (E464) found no safety concern at reported food uses and levels and no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake. This conclusion concerns specified food additives, not all industrial or medical applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The proportions and distribution of methyl and hydroxypropyl groups, molecular weight and concentration vary across HPMC products. The observed sodium-chloride response in the rheology study differed among molecular-weight grades and with shear rate. Film properties also depend on casting and moisture, while drug release depends on the dosage form and active ingredient as well as the polymer. A result for one solution or matrix is not a family-wide specification.

sections.overview: Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) is a cellulose ether made by attaching carboxymethyl groups to the cellulose backbone. It is commonly used as the sodium salt, whose charged groups help suitable grades dissolve in water. The dissolved polymer increases viscosity, making it useful as a thickener and stabilizer in products such as foods, pharmaceuticals and personal-care formulations. CMC can also be cast from solution into films and coatings, although its affinity for water limits the moisture resistance of neat films.
sections.history: Carboxymethyl cellulose’s early history includes a German preparation patent issued in 1918. Hercules began commercial U.S. production in 1943, according to BeMiller’s historical review. Initially developed as a replacement for natural gums, it expanded into applications that used its ability to alter solution behavior. This chronology distinguishes the early patent from later industrial scale-up and explains why CMC belongs to the history of formulated products as much as to the history of plastics.
sections.nomenclature: Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) identifies a cellulose ether family rather than one fixed substitution pattern or salt form. Sodium carboxymethyl cellulose, also called sodium CMC or Na-CMC, is the sodium salt of that polymer. In food-additive terminology, the sodium salt is also called cellulose gum and designated E 466 in the EU. Cross-linked sodium CMC and enzymatically hydrolysed CMC have separate EU additive designations, E 468 and E 469 respectively. These food-additive names do not by themselves specify the substitution pattern, molecular weight or grade of every CMC product.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Carboxymethyl cellulose is a chemically modified cellulose subfamily: carboxymethyl ether groups replace some of the hydroxyl hydrogens on a cellulose backbone. Plant-derived cellulose is a common feedstock, with alternative cellulosic residues also reported. A conventional heterogeneous route first alkalizes cellulose with sodium hydroxide, then etherifies the activated material using monochloroacetic acid or sodium monochloroacetate. Degree of substitution is route- and feedstock-dependent; the available studies identify alkali concentration, carboxymethylating-agent concentration, solvent system, temperature, and time as important controls. In one laboratory example, microcrystalline cellulose was alkalized in mixed alcohol solvent before sodium monochloroacetate addition, followed by neutralization, washing, and drying. That example demonstrates a particular preparation and should not be read as a family-wide manufacturing recipe.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) can form free-standing films and can act as a structural or reinforcing component in films and paper-like composites. Its tensile response is not a family constant: the review literature reports that moisture lowers the mechanical properties of CMC-containing films, while the degree of substitution, added fillers or cross-linking, and plasticizer content alter the strength–stiffness–ductility balance. In the surveyed film literature, well-dispersed fillers commonly increased tensile strength and elastic modulus while reducing strain at break; increasing glycerol typically increased ductility while reducing tensile strength and modulus.

One bounded neat-film example comes from a sodium CMC (USP-grade) control film. Zhang and co-workers cast 25 g of their CMC film-forming solution in a 5.5 cm PTFE mold and dried it at 40 °C for 48 h; the reported film thickness was 0.126 ± 0.015 mm. In tensile strips 4.0 × 1.0 cm tested at a crosshead speed of 0.2 cm/min, the film had tensile strength 13.57 ± 0.47 MPa, elongation at break 44.41 ± 0.61%, and Young’s modulus 30.84 ± 0.96 MPa. The article does not report a test standard or conditioning protocol. These values describe that cast, dried sodium-CMC film, not all CMC grades, film preparations, or hydrated formulations.
sections.processing: Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) is commonly converted from aqueous solution by casting, coating, spraying, or electrospinning; thermo-mechanical extrusion and compression molding are reported chiefly for suitably plasticized CMC or blends. For cast films, CMC is dissolved in water with plasticizer and any functional additive, spread into a mold, then dried; its hydrophilicity means that moisture response and water resistance remain formulation-dependent, often motivating blends, ionic/covalent crosslinking, or fillers. In Basu and co-workers’ CMC/PEG wound-film experiment, material was formed by solution casting; this is a laboratory route for that CMC/PEG system rather than a general CMC melt-processing window. The packaging review likewise emphasizes that degree of substitution, molecular mass, additive selection, and processing conditions limit direct comparison among CMC films.
sections.structureAndMorphology: CMC retains the β-1,4-linked glucose backbone of cellulose, with carboxymethyl groups attached through ether bonds at some of the hydroxyl sites. The degree of substitution (DS) is the average number of substituted sites per glucose unit, from zero to a theoretical maximum of three; it does not specify their distribution along a chain. In the sodium form, the carboxylate groups carry negative charges balanced by sodium counterions. Substitution changes how chains interact with water and one another: lower-substituted materials can retain associated regions, while a studied sodium CMC sample with measured DS 1.17 ± 0.10 was molecularly dispersed in water. That observation describes the sample and conditions studied, not a sharp solubility boundary for every grade.
sections.properties: Dissolved sodium CMC thickens water, and increasing polymer concentration raised the low-shear viscosity for each of the grades compared in one study. More concentrated solutions can be shear thinning: their apparent viscosity falls as the rate of shearing increases. For example, at 20 °C and ambient pressure, a 10 wt% solution of the studied C7XS grade was approximately Newtonian below 1,000 s⁻¹, whereas a 15 wt% solution showed shear thinning; both included 0.1 wt% preservative. CMC films absorb moisture and generally allow water vapor to pass through them. Adding a lipid such as oleic acid has reduced water-vapor permeability in reported CMC films, although barrier and mechanical properties must be evaluated together for the chosen formulation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Sodium CMC is used as a thickener and stabilizer in foods such as salad dressings, syrups and dairy products: its water-soluble chains raise viscosity and help keep ingredients dispersed. CMC also contributes to textile sizing and soil suspension in liquid detergents, while pharmaceutical formulations use selected grades as excipients. Researchers cast CMC-rich films and coatings for food packaging; their attraction to water can weaken the moisture barrier, so blends, fillers and crosslinking are being studied to improve performance. In lithium-ion electrode research, water-soluble sodium CMC binds graphite particles to each other and to the current collector; water-based slurry preparation avoids the organic solvent used for some conventional binders. A separate laboratory study combined CMC with polyethyleneimine in a crosslinked hydrogel to adsorb dissolved dyes.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich lists product 419311 as a sodium CMC powder with approximate weight-average molecular weight 250,000 and degree of substitution 0.7, in 100 g and 1 kg packages. These are catalog sizes for a specified research product, not a universal CMC grade or a stated minimum industrial order. Formulators need to distinguish the salt form, viscosity or molecular-weight grade and substitution when selecting material; food-contact and pharmaceutical uses require material appropriate to that use.

Scale and evidence limits. CMC is used across several industries, but the cited catalog sizes measure package quantity rather than annual demand. The packaging review describes numerous laboratory solution-cast films and notes that water removal and long drying times present scale-up challenges. Neither those experiments nor the graphite-electrode and hydrogel studies establish the installed capacity, market share or commercial adoption of the particular formulations. No reliable separate annual CMC purchase or consumption tonnage is established by these sources.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Cellulases can cleave accessible β-1,4 bonds in the cellulose-derived backbone, producing shorter soluble fragments and reducing sugars. Carboxymethyl substitution and its distribution can restrict enzyme access, and higher substitution generally reduced enzymatic hydrolysis in a comparison of modified cellulose films. In an aluminum-crosslinked CMC film test, a cellulase mixture produced measurable reducing sugars, but that assay did not demonstrate conversion of all of the film carbon to carbon dioxide.

Timescales: In that same study, 48 hours at 40 °C in pH 5 buffer with a cellulase mixture gave approximately 17% hydrolysis for the tested aluminum-crosslinked CMC film, measured using released reducing sugars. In a separate aerated pilot-compost test, the film was no longer visible after two weeks, with compost temperature peaking at 70.7 °C. The latter endpoint is visual disintegration and may include dissolution of the water-soluble material; it is not a measurement of complete mineralization.

Environmental persistence: A study of a CMC sample with degree of substitution 0.7 measured net carbon dioxide evolution in aerated garden-soil compost at 60 °C and activated-sludge wastewater at 30 °C. Its initial mineralization was slower than unmodified cellulose in the corresponding tests, and the CMC response was slower in the wastewater system than in the hotter compost. The authors’ model attributed much of the initial mineralization to less-substituted portions; this interpretation and extrapolated lifetimes depend on the model and test conditions. Neither pilot compost disintegration nor these controlled assays defines a universal lifetime for CMC in natural soil, freshwater or marine environments.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The aluminum-crosslinked CMC film disappeared in a specific aerated pilot-compost experiment, but visible disintegration alone does not prove mineralization or establish acceptance of a finished product by a composting facility. Formulation, coating additives and local collection rules must be considered separately for an actual article.

Reuse can also be possible for particular CMC-containing products. In a laboratory experiment, a crosslinked CMC/polyethyleneimine hydrogel used to capture methylene blue or acid orange dye was washed after each adsorption–desorption cycle; the dyes were removed from the gel with acid or base, respectively. After ten cycles, the hydrogel retained more than 93% of its initial dye-removal efficiency for each dye under the reported test conditions. This is reuse of a tested composite adsorbent, not recovery of purified CMC polymer or evidence of a commercial recycling route.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: In its 2018 assessment, EFSA found no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake for the evaluated cellulose food additives and no safety concern at their reported uses and levels, apart from uses in specified infant and young-child foods for special medical purposes. A 2022 EFSA follow-up found that the available data still did not permit an adequate safety assessment for those special food categories. EU Regulation 2025/666 schedules withdrawal of E 466 authorizations for those categories and certain nutrient preparations from 27 April 2027, with transitional provisions for foods lawfully placed on the market before that date. In the United States, 21 CFR 182.1745 recognizes sodium CMC meeting the section’s composition and viscosity specifications as generally recognized as safe when used according to good manufacturing practice. These food-use assessments concern defined materials, populations and routes of exposure rather than every CMC grade or use. For powder handling, the safety data sheet for a Redox sodium-CMC formulation warns that airborne dust can be combustible and recommends avoiding dust generation and ignition sources.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The same average degree of substitution can conceal differences in where substituents occur, while molecular weight and counterion form also distinguish grades. Their effects depend on the medium: in a study using 2.2 wt% sodium CMC in an 80 wt% propylene glycol–water mixture, samples with DS 0.62 and 0.79 formed weak physical gels, while a sample with DS 1.04 behaved as a viscoelastic fluid. The authors attributed the difference to changes in associations between chains and the solvent; it is not a universal rule for all CMC solutions. Film performance is likewise formulation and humidity dependent. In the reviewed CMC film studies, increasing glycerol generally made films more extensible while reducing tensile strength and stiffness, illustrating a tradeoff rather than a single family-wide value.

sections.overview: Starch is the principal storage polysaccharide in many plants and is deposited in granules containing mainly amylose and amylopectin. The proportions and granule characteristics depend on the crop and its growing conditions. Heating starch with water causes granules to swell and lose their native order, providing the thickening and gel-forming behavior used in foods. Starch is also processed into adhesives, paper additives and formulated packaging materials; those products can differ substantially from native granules. Amylose and amylopectin differ in branching and do not respond identically to every enzyme or heating history. Their relative amounts help determine texture and film formation, while processing and other ingredients determine the behavior of a formulated product.
sections.history: Starch is a natural plant material with a long history as food and adhesive. FAO’s historical account connects wheat-starch preparation with ancient Egyptian papyrus manufacture and identifies Kirchhoff’s 1811 conversion of starch to sugar by acid hydrolysis as an important chemical milestone. Later industries used starch in paper and textile sizing, coatings, adhesives and glucose manufacture as well as food. Wartime loss of tapioca supplies helped drive American Maize Products and National Starch Products to commercialize waxy maize starch in 1942. High-amylose maize followed commercially in 1958, extending the range available for formulated foods. These dates concern extraction, conversion and crop development rather than invention of starch.
sections.nomenclature: Starch is a family-level material name, not one uniform polymer. “Starch polymer” is descriptive, while amylose and amylopectin are constituent molecular fractions rather than interchangeable synonyms for the whole material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Starch is a plant-produced polysaccharide stored as semicrystalline granules composed chiefly of amylose and branched amylopectin. Commercial material is isolated from biological feedstocks rather than synthesized from glucose in a reactor. Major sources include cereal endosperm, especially maize, and roots or tubers such as cassava, potato, and wheat-derived fractions. In corn wet milling, cleaned kernels are steeped to soften the protein matrix, coarsely milled, and separated from germ. Further milling releases granules; screening and countercurrent washing remove fiber, while centrifuges or hydrocyclones separate starch from gluten and repeatedly wash the starch-rich stream before dewatering and drying. One cited patent documents the integrated corn sequence of germ separation, fiber washing, starch–gluten separation, and starch washing. A distinct cassava patent washes and peels fresh roots, disrupts tuber cells, washes and separates liberated granules from fiber, and removes soluble matter and residual fiber from the slurry. Botanical source, granule integrity, steeping chemistry, milling severity, and washing efficiency affect the isolated fraction. Chemical derivatization, gelatinization, and thermoplastic-starch formulation are separate modification or processing routes.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Native starch is a semicrystalline particulate material composed principally of linear amylose and highly branched amylopectin, so a single bulk tensile property is not meaningful for the family. Mechanical response depends first on material form. Intact granules behave as a powder; hydrated dispersions and gelatinized pastes are viscoelastic soft matter; dried, gelatinized films form hydrogen-bonded glassy networks that can be stiff but brittle when dry; and foams, fiber-filled articles, coatings, and blends introduce their own cellular or interfacial failure modes. Melt-plasticized thermoplastic starch is treated separately in this encyclopedia and should not inherit a cast-film value.

In a dried starch film, intermolecular hydrogen bonding and chain entanglement provide cohesion, while water and polyol plasticizers lower the effective glass transition and increase segmental mobility. Increasing water or compatible plasticizer therefore commonly lowers modulus and tensile strength while increasing elongation, but the balance is unstable: loss of water at low relative humidity can embrittle a film, whereas sorption at high humidity can soften it and sharply reduce load bearing. Amylose-to-amylopectin ratio and molar-mass distribution, botanical source and minor lipid/protein/phosphate components, native granule and crystal structure, degree of gelatinization and molecular degradation, drying temperature and rate, film thickness, plasticizer identity/loading/compatibility or migration, storage time and retrogradation, chemical modification or crosslinking, blend and filler content/dispersion/orientation, porosity, specimen conditioning, test temperature, strain rate, and notch or defect population are all consequential. Greater effective amylose network formation often raises film strength and stiffness and reduces extensibility, but that trend is conditional on preparation, moisture, and recrystallization and is not a family-wide numerical rule.

One bounded cast-film comparison used commercial hydroxypropyl cornstarch reported as degree of substitution 0.4%, moisture 13 wt%, and molar mass 130,000. Ten grams of dry starch was gelatinized with water at 98 °C for 1 hour, cast, and dried at 35 °C for 10–12 hours. After conditioning at 40% relative humidity, ASTM D882 tension at 25 °C and 5 mm/min (seven specimens) gave the water-only St-W film, about 156 ± 4 µm thick, a modulus of 1152 ± 119 MPa, tensile strength of 57.3 ± 2.9 MPa, and elongation of 3.6 ± 0.7%. In the otherwise analogous St-WG-4 casting formulation containing 3 parts glycerol per 10 parts starch (30 parts glycerol per 100 parts dry starch), the approximately 181 ± 9 µm film gave 933 ± 86 MPa, 49.4 ± 5.6 MPa, and 8.6 ± 0.6%, respectively. These values demonstrate the plasticizer tradeoff within one modified-corn-starch film system; they are not properties of native starch granules, unmodified starch from other plants, gels, foams, thermoplastic starch, or commercial starch composites.
sections.processing:
Starch is converted into articles after water and/or a plasticizer disrupts the native granular structure and produces a continuous thermoplastic-starch phase. Important routes include aqueous solvent casting and tape casting, hot extrusion followed by film blowing or thermocompression, and formulation-dependent injection molding, compression molding, foaming, and melt, wet, or electrospinning. Feed-water level, botanical source and amylose/amylopectin balance, plasticizer type and loading, mixing order, gelatinization, screw shear, die pressure, drying rate, and conditioning humidity all matter. Insufficient heat or shear can leave ungelatinized granules or uneven plasticizer distribution, whereas excessive moisture loss, later water uptake, plasticizer migration, and retrogradation can change dimensions and embrittle or soften the article after conversion. Starch extraction and chemical modification belong in Synthesis; gelatinization, melt mixing, shaping, drying, and conditioning belong here.

Muñoz-Gimena and co-workers' open review identifies casting, extrusion/thermocompression, and blow molding as the three main starch-film routes and describes injection molding, compression molding, foaming, and spinning as additional options. Its literature-typical casting sequence mixes starch and plasticizer in water, heats the suspension at 80–95 °C for 10–15 min, casts it on a plate, and oven-dries at 40–75 °C for about 24 h; those aggregated values are review guidance, not a universal starch schedule. In a distinct bounded experiment, Niu and co-workers dispersed potato starch in 100 mL distilled water and stirred for 30 min at 80 °C until gelatinized, added glycerol and gelatin sequentially, ultrasonically degassed for another 30 min, cast the solution on a plate, and dried it at 40 °C for 36 h. That schedule belongs to their potato-starch/glycerol/gelatin films.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Native starch granules contain relatively linear amylose and much more highly branched amylopectin. Ordered amylopectin chain segments contribute to semicrystalline regions, interspersed with less ordered material. In sufficient water, heating disrupts that order and swells the granules; on cooling, the chains can reassociate in a process called retrogradation. Amylose commonly associates earlier, while amylopectin reorganization can continue more slowly during storage. Heating and cooling therefore change the organization as well as viscosity: swelling disrupts the native granule, and subsequent reassociation can expel water from the gel. The relative speed of amylose and amylopectin rearrangement helps explain why texture can change during storage.
sections.properties: The swelling and dispersal of heated starch granules increase viscosity and can yield a gel when the mixture cools. Amylose reassociation contributes to early gel firmness, while the more slowly rearranging amylopectin contributes to later changes. In starch-based films, continued retrogradation can increase stiffness but also make a film more brittle; water and plasticizers increase chain mobility and change that response. These behaviors depend on the particular starch source, water content and processing history. In an extruded film made from 70% amylose corn starch, the control had a tensile strength of 9.51 MPa and elongation at break of 31%; a 10% sodium-hydroxide-treated film measured 7.96 MPa and 60%, respectively. These results include processing and formulation effects and do not describe a pure amylose film.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Starch is used in food manufacture as an ingredient that can thicken and gel when heated with water, and in nonfood applications including corrugating adhesives and papermaking. Its ability to form films also motivates starch-based packaging, but packaging may contain plasticizers or other polymers alongside starch. For a packaging film, the matrix must balance flexibility and strength, while water sensitivity and changes during storage affect performance. Native starch, chemically modified starch and starch-derived sweeteners are different commercial categories.

Purchasing. Industrial processors supply crop- and function-specific native and modified starch ingredients to food and industrial manufacturers. The buyer must specify botanical source and functional grade, and distinguish starch polymer from downstream sweeteners when comparing products or volumes.

Scale and evidence limits. Starch Europe reports 9.8 million tonnes of EU starch and derivative production in 2024. Its overview gives 7.2 million tonnes EU consumption, split 54% food, 2% feed and 44% nonfood; 48% of the consumption is starch sweeteners. These industry aggregates include derivatives and are not pure native starch production or a count of starch packaging.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Enzymes can cleave starch glucan chains into smaller carbohydrates, but their specificity matters. In one study a bacterial neopullulanase converted the amylose fraction of heated potato starch mainly to maltose while leaving much of the amylopectin fraction; other amylases in the comparison hydrolyzed both components. In the longer potato-starch test, the amylopectin fraction also declined in molecular size without disappearing, illustrating why fraction size and fraction amount are different endpoints.

Timescales: In that experiment a 1% solubilized potato-starch mixture was treated with the enzyme in pH 6 buffer at 50 °C. The chromatographic amylose fraction was no longer observed after 120 minutes, while the amylopectin fraction remained. This describes a controlled enzyme reaction and analytical endpoint, not the lifetime of a starch article. Separately, a simulated-compost experiment measured carbon dioxide released from powdered cassava starch and from a glycerol-plasticized starch material. At 58 ± 2 °C the researchers reported approximately complete mineralization of the powdered starch by 60 days, versus about 45% for the thermoplastic material. The samples differed in particle size and composition, both of which can affect access to the starch.

Environmental persistence: Enzyme cleavage into sugars differs from measurement of complete mineralization to carbon dioxide. The compost respirometry experiment offers a carbon-conversion measurement for those particular samples, unlike simple mass loss or enzyme cleavage. It does not establish how quickly an intact starch-containing film, blend or other product mineralizes in soil, freshwater or seawater; temperature, oxygen availability and formulation matter.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Enzyme-assisted saccharification converts starch to smaller carbohydrates rather than regenerating the original polymer. The selective neopullulanase experiment produced mainly maltose from the amylose fraction of solubilized potato starch; it did not show equivalent conversion of the amylopectin fraction.

That reaction is a controlled laboratory demonstration, not a recovery process established for contaminated post-consumer starch packaging. Products containing other polymers, fillers or additives require separate assessment of the feedstock and output.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Starch powder involves dust exposure. NIOSH identifies irritation of the eyes, skin and respiratory tract and an explosion hazard when starch dust disperses in air. This guidance addresses starch powder, rather than establishing the toxicology of every isolated fraction or finished blend.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Botanical source affects granule size, amylose proportion and amylopectin branching, so one crop cannot stand for every starch. The temperature and water available during heating control gelatinization; subsequent cooling and storage influence retrogradation and texture. Packaging films and other starch products can contain plasticizers, other polymers or fillers. A property or degradation result from one formulation therefore is not automatically a property of native starch or all starch blends. A high-amylose corn starch still contains amylopectin, and a comparison of alkali-treated films also reflects the treatment and resulting structure. Relative humidity during measurement and storage matters because water changes chain mobility.

sections.overview: Amylose is the predominantly linear glucan fraction of starch, built mainly from glucose units linked by alpha-(1→4) bonds. Some amylose molecules contain branches, and their molecular lengths vary. Amylose can associate into helices and networks, contributing to the initial firmness of cooled starch gels. Isolated amylose is used as a research substrate, while high-amylose starch remains a mixture rather than pure amylose. The predominance of linear segments helps neighboring chains associate into the network that forms after starch is gelatinized and cooled. Amylose is consequently relevant to food texture and film development, although results on whole starch reflect other components too.
sections.history: Amylose was identified through research on natural starch, rather than invented as a synthetic polymer. Thomas J. Schoch’s separation work in the 1940s established the distinction between its comparatively linear chains and branched amylopectin. In 1958, Bear Hybrids Corn Company, American Maize Products and National Starch and Chemical commercialized a high-amylose maize hybrid. Such crop development made amylose-rich ingredients accessible to industry. Research by Hizukuri and colleagues in 1981 subsequently demonstrated limited branching in amylose, refining the earlier structural picture.
sections.nomenclature: Amylose denotes the linear starch polysaccharide, not starch as a whole; amylopectin is the distinct branched component. High-amylose starch is a compositionally enriched starch material rather than a synonym for isolated amylose, so its film and extrusion evidence remains formulation-specific.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Amylose is the mostly linear alpha-(1→4)-glucan fraction of plant starch. It is sourced from botanical starch; high-amylose maize is an enriched starch source, not identical to purified amylose. Isolation history, residual amylopectin, molecular mass, and subsequent chemical treatment all delimit a particular material. Heating starch in water mobilizes chains after granule disruption and cooling enables reassociation, but these article-preparation steps are distinct from biosynthesis or extraction of amylose.
sections.mechanicalProperties: The mostly linear architecture can promote chain alignment and hydrogen-bonded reassociation in starch films, often yielding a stronger but potentially more brittle matrix than amylopectin-rich systems. The 70% high-amylose corn-starch extrusion study reported 10.03 MPa tensile strength and 40% elongation at break for its 2% NaOH-treated film; those values are for an alkali-treated, composition-variable starch film, not pure amylose. In a separate glycerol-plasticized, 6 wt% montmorillonite film series spanning waxy starch through nominally 100% amylose, regular corn starch gave the highest tensile strength, elongation decreased as amylose increased, and neither endpoint changed significantly above 50% amylose. That second result is composite- and process-specific and does not define an intrinsic amylose property.
sections.processing: Amylose-containing starch articles can be produced by gelatinization/casting or by thermomechanical extrusion with controlled water and plasticizer. In a laboratory starch–clay study, dry starch, 15 wt% glycerol, 0–21 wt% clay, and 19 wt% water were processed at 200 rpm in an 18 mm twin-screw extruder with an 85–90–95–100–110–120 °C barrel profile; ground extrudate was then dispersed in water, heated at 95 °C for 10 min, cooled, cast, and dried. The authors cautioned that the 120 °C maximum might be insufficient for extensive gelatinization of the high-amylose samples. These conditions produced nanocomposite granulate followed by cast films and are not a melt-processing window for isolated amylose.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Amylose chains are much less branched than amylopectin and can form helical conformations or associate with one another and suitable guest molecules. When a starch granule is heated in sufficient water, the granule swells and some amylose can move into the surrounding phase. Upon cooling, amylose chains can reassociate into ordered regions and a gel network. The source, chain-length distribution and treatment affect the organization that develops. Association is affected by the amount of water and by substances able to fit within the helix. These organized regions form after the native granule is disrupted; they should not be assumed to be identical to the ordered domains present in an unheated granule.
sections.properties: Amylose chains contribute strongly to early gel formation after gelatinized starch cools. Their reassociation produces a more ordered network and can increase the firmness of a starch gel, while slower amylopectin reorganization affects longer-term changes. High-amylose starch is studied for films because chain association can assist film formation, but such films also contain other starch fractions and often plasticizer. Humidity and processing must be specified when interpreting their performance. In one study of extruded 70%-amylose corn-starch films, 10% sodium hydroxide treatment produced 7.96 MPa tensile strength and 60% elongation at break versus 9.51 MPa and 31% in the untreated control. These are measurements of a mixed starch film under the stated processing and test conditions, not properties of isolated amylose.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Isolated amylose is used as a laboratory substrate to study amylase activity and starch chemistry. Its predominantly linear chains allow researchers to compare enzyme action on amylose with action on branched amylopectin. High-amylose crop starch is also explored for films, where chain association helps form a continuous network. In one extrusion study, alkali treatment changed the balance of tensile strength and elongation of a 70%-amylose corn-starch film. That film remains a mixed starch material rather than an isolated amylose product.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich offers potato amylose powder described as essentially free of amylopectin, with 250 mg, 1 g, 5 g and 25 g catalog packs. The botanical source and stated purity are part of the reagent specification; this purchase is distinct from buying bulk high-amylose starch.

Scale and evidence limits. Catalog pack sizes describe research purchasing units, not production or annual consumption. The checked sources do not establish a separate annual isolated-amylose market volume, and total starch-industry tonnage cannot be assigned to this fraction.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A bacterial neopullulanase can cleave amylose into mainly maltose and a small amount of glucose. In an experiment comparing amylose and amylopectin, that enzyme acted much more strongly on the amylose fraction; the result is specific to this enzyme and substrates. The comparison used chromatographic separation to follow the two fractions, so the analytical result concerns the measured substrate distribution rather than complete fate of the products.

Timescales: A mixture of synthetic amylose and potato amylopectin was incubated with the enzyme in pH 6 buffer at 50 °C. The chromatographic amylose peak disappeared during 120 minutes of treatment, while the amylopectin peak remained. Disappearance of a chromatographic fraction is an analytical reaction endpoint, not a universal environmental residence time.

Environmental persistence: Release of maltose or smaller chains does not itself measure complete mineralization. The enzyme assay does not determine the lifetime of an amylose-containing material in soil, fresh water or seawater.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The enzyme experiment demonstrates conversion of amylose in solution to low-molecular-mass sugars, mainly maltose; it does not regenerate the original amylose chains. In the study the sugar-rich fraction was separated analytically from the remaining amylopectin. Applying such selectivity to actual waste would require separate evidence for feedstock preparation, contamination, process recovery and the usable product.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Amylose is a constituent of starch; general starch-powder handling involves dust exposure. NIOSH identifies irritation of the eyes, skin and respiratory tract and an explosion hazard when starch dust disperses in air. This guidance addresses starch powder, rather than establishing the toxicology of every isolated fraction or finished blend.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Amylose is not a single molecule of fixed length or necessarily perfectly unbranched. Botanical source, isolation, treatment and molecular-weight distribution affect how it associates and reacts with enzymes. Evidence from a high-amylose crop starch includes residual amylopectin and cannot be treated as a measurement of every purified amylose sample. A cooled gel or film also changes with water content and storage. The film comparison changes processing chemistry as well as chain organization, so its strength and elongation cannot be attributed to amylose alone. Gels made at different water content or stored for different times can form different networks.

sections.overview: Amylopectin is the highly branched glucose polymer that generally makes up much of a native starch granule. Waxy starches are particularly rich in amylopectin, although a waxy starch product is not the same thing as purified amylopectin. Its branches help form the ordered domains within granules and affect how starch swells and reorganizes after heating. Isolated amylopectin is used in laboratory studies of starch structure and enzyme action. The branch architecture matters to gelatinization and subsequent texture because short chains can associate in a native granule and reorganize again after heating. Its contribution to a real paste or film must be considered alongside amylose, water and other ingredients.
sections.history: Amylopectin’s history combines starch fractionation with development of waxy crop starches. Schoch’s work in the 1940s established its branched character. Waxy maize starch entered use during that decade to provide thickening with reduced gel formation. Later structural advances included the amylopectin cluster models proposed independently by Z. Nikuni in 1969 and Dexter French in 1971, followed by refinements from Robin and colleagues and Hizukuri. These were discoveries about a naturally produced polymer; commercialization concerned amylopectin-rich starch ingredients rather than a newly invented molecule.
sections.nomenclature: Amylopectin names the branched starch polysaccharide, not starch as a whole; ordinary starch also contains amylose. Waxy starch is amylopectin-rich rather than automatically purified amylopectin, so composition-specific starch-film or thermoplastic-starch results should retain that distinction.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Amylopectin is the highly branched glucan fraction of botanical starch, not a commodity polymer made by a separate monomer process. Its practical feedstock is plant starch, while botanical source, branch-chain distribution, and the amylose/amylopectin ratio remain material-defining. Waxy corn starch is amylopectin-rich rather than automatically purified amylopectin. To form articles, starch is commonly gelatinized in water or thermomechanically processed with controlled water/plasticizer; those operations disrupt granules and are conversion steps, not synthesis of the polysaccharide.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Amylopectin-rich starch matrices are generally more flexible and less dominated by the dense reassociation associated with high-amylose formulations, but moisture, plasticizer, botanical source, crystallinity, filler, and retrogradation can dominate the observed response. In one bounded composition study, films made from glycerol-plasticized starch and 6 wt% montmorillonite compared waxy corn starch (approximately 0% amylose), regular corn starch, high-amylose starches, and nominally 100% amylose. Regular corn starch gave the highest tensile strength, elongation decreased as amylose content increased, and neither tensile strength nor elongation changed significantly above 50% amylose. These are results for starch–clay nanocomposite films; waxy starch was an amylopectin-rich endpoint, not isolated amylopectin, and the series does not yield an intrinsic amylopectin property.
sections.processing: Amylopectin-containing starch is converted either by aqueous gelatinization followed by casting/drying or by thermomechanical extrusion with controlled water and/or plasticizer. In a laboratory starch–clay study that included waxy corn starch, dry starch, 15 wt% glycerol, 0–21 wt% clay, and 19 wt% water were processed at 200 rpm in an 18 mm twin-screw extruder with an 85–90–95–100–110–120 °C barrel profile. Ground extrudate was then dispersed at 4 wt% in water, held at 95 °C for 10 min, cooled to 65 °C, cast, and dried at 23 °C and 50% relative humidity for 24 h. These are study-specific nanocomposite-granulate and casting conditions; waxy corn starch was one composition and not purified amylopectin.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Amylopectin consists chiefly of alpha-(1→4)-linked glucose chains with alpha-(1→6) branch points. Neighboring branch segments can organize into ordered regions in the native starch granule. Heating in sufficient water disrupts the granular structure; on cooling, amylopectin chains can reassociate more slowly than amylose. Branch-length distributions and the resulting organization vary with botanical source. The α-(1→6) links create junctions connecting α-(1→4) chain segments. Their lengths and arrangement influence how segments pack in a granule and how readily they reassociate after gelatinization.
sections.properties: Amylopectin-rich starch granules swell during gelatinization and contribute to the viscosity of the resulting paste. Its branched chains can reorganize over storage, contributing to gradual changes in gel texture after the earlier amylose-dominated stage. Film and gel behavior depends on the surrounding starch components, water and added plasticizers as well as on amylopectin. A measurement on waxy or whole starch should not be presented as a constant for isolated amylopectin. In a cooled starch gel, the slower rearrangement can contribute to firming and water separation during storage. Those changes arise in a mixture and depend on processing and composition; they are not a fixed response of all purified amylopectin. In one experiment with a commercial wheat starch containing 25% amylose, gelatinized samples were stored for seven days at 4 °C and reheated in a calorimeter. The endotherm attributed to melting reassociated amylopectin was about 4.26 J/g in 60% fructose solution versus 0.78 J/g in 60% sucrose solution. That is a comparison of particular starch–sugar mixtures, not a property of purified amylopectin or a direct measurement of eating texture.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Isolated amylopectin is used in laboratory studies of starch architecture and enzyme specificity. Comparing it with amylose helps researchers distinguish the response of branched and predominantly linear substrates. Amylopectin-rich waxy starch is used in food and starch formulations, where swelling contributes to paste viscosity and later chain rearrangement can alter stored texture. The whole ingredient is a different material from an isolated reagent, so a formulated food cannot be specified by the isolated polymer alone.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich lists potato-starch amylopectin powder as product A8515 in a 25 g catalog pack. The crop source, stated product composition and intended experiment should be checked when selecting a reagent, especially when comparison with another starch fraction matters.

Scale and evidence limits. A 25 g catalog unit documents research-scale supply rather than annual consumption or a market share. No separate isolated-amylopectin production or purchasing total was established, and broad starch tonnage includes other constituents and derivatives.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Enzymatic response depends on the enzyme. In a comparison of potato amylopectin with amylose, bacterial neopullulanase acted much less extensively on amylopectin, whereas the other tested amylases hydrolyzed both substrates. Branching changes access and the kinds of links that an enzyme encounters, so the enzyme’s specificity matters when interpreting the comparison. The difference is relevant to the chosen enzyme and test, not proof that amylopectin is intrinsically nondegradable.

Timescales: In a pH 6 mixture incubated at 50 °C, the amylopectin chromatographic peak remained after 120 minutes of the neopullulanase treatment while the amylose peak disappeared. In a separate longer potato-starch assay, amylopectin molecular mass declined from above 10⁸ to about 10⁷ Da but was not reduced further under that treatment. These are controlled reaction and molecular-size endpoints rather than environmental lifetimes.

Environmental persistence: Retention of an amylopectin peak or loss of molecular mass is not a measurement of mineralization. The cited enzyme experiments do not establish how quickly amylopectin-containing articles degrade in soil, freshwater or seawater.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Enzymatic hydrolysis converts starch glucans into smaller carbohydrates rather than recovering unchanged polymer. The cited neopullulanase experiment preferentially converted amylose; it cannot be used as evidence of equal sugar recovery from amylopectin. Other enzymes did hydrolyze the tested amylopectin, but a recovery route for a specific used product would need its own feedstock, yield and contamination evidence.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Amylopectin is a constituent of starch; general starch-powder handling involves dust exposure. NIOSH identifies irritation of the eyes, skin and respiratory tract and an explosion hazard when starch dust disperses in air. This guidance addresses starch powder, rather than establishing the toxicology of every isolated fraction or finished blend.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Amylopectin is a distribution of branched chains, not a single fixed molecular size or branch length. Botanical source and treatment influence granule and gel behavior, and waxy starch can still contain ingredients other than amylopectin. Enzymes differ substantially in how they attack the branched molecule; weak response to one enzyme cannot be generalized to all hydrolysis. Film data from whole starch or blends likewise cannot automatically be assigned to isolated amylopectin. The comparison with amylose in the cited reaction uses a particular bacterial enzyme, a synthetic amylose and potato amylopectin. Another enzyme, botanical source or physical form could yield a different result.

sections.overview: Thermoplastic starch (TPS) is starch converted into a processable material by heat and shear with water or other plasticizers. Processing disrupts native granules and allows the starch-rich material to flow and be formed. The material's sensitivity to moisture and tendency to reorganize during storage are central to its performance. Commercial starch-containing compounds often contain additional polymers rather than TPS alone. Plasticizers enable mobility at processing temperatures, but absorbed or lost water can later change the stiffness of a finished article. Blending and fillers add further interfaces, so a commercial compound needs its full formulation and processing context.
sections.history: Thermoplastic starch developed through efforts to turn starch into material processable with plastics equipment. A Novamont patent published in 1992 by Catia Bastioli, Vittorio Bellotti and Alessandro Montino documents one route: plasticized starch combined with synthetic thermoplastic polymers. This was part of a broader development field, not the invention date of every thermoplastic-starch grade. Novamont, established in 1990 from the Montedison research tradition, records a Mater-Bi biodegradable bag in 1992 and later packaging, foam and food-service applications. Mater-Bi illustrates the commercial history of starch-containing blends; its formulations should not be equated with pure plasticized starch.
sections.nomenclature: TPS is the abbreviation for thermoplastic starch. The record covers plasticized, thermomechanically destructured starch containing amylose and amylopectin; native granular starch, chemically modified starches, and a particular starch blend or film are not alternate names for the base material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Thermoplastic starch (TPS) is produced by destructuring native starch granules in the presence of plasticizer rather than by polymerizing new glucose chains. The biological feedstock may be maize, potato, cassava, wheat, or another purified starch; amylose/amylopectin ratio and granule structure remain consequential. Water and low-molar-mass hydrogen-bonding plasticizers such as glycerol, sorbitol, urea, or compatible mixtures penetrate the granules. Heat and intensive shear then disrupt native crystallites and the inter- and intramolecular hydrogen-bond network, producing a continuous thermoplastic phase in which amylose and amylopectin chains can flow. The cited open review describes plasticizer selection, water content, melt mixing, extrusion, and optional blending or compatibilization across TPS formulations. A distinct laboratory study prepares water-plasticized potato TPS by equilibrating starch with water, thermomechanically destructuring it in an extruder, and recovering a homogeneous amorphous material before later sheet formation. Feedstock moisture, plasticizer identity and ratio, temperature, shear and residence time must be balanced: insufficient treatment leaves residual granules, while excessive heat or mechanical energy causes chain scission. Drying or conditioning after conversion sets the retained water content, and storage can permit retrogradation. Chemical esterification, etherification, oxidation, grafting, or limited crosslinking can be used as modification variants, but they are not required for TPS identity. Article geometry and shaping conditions belong in Processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Thermoplastic starch (TPS) is produced when native starch granules are destructured and plasticized under heat and shear so that the material can be shaped by melt-processing equipment. Its solid response is not a fixed property of botanical starch: it ranges from glassy and brittle below its moisture- and formulation-dependent glass transition to yielding/ductile or soft-rubbery above that transition. TPS is viscoelastic and strongly rate dependent; creep, stress relaxation, hysteresis, and fracture can change with service time and water exchange. Neat TPS usually lacks the moisture stability and toughness of commodity polyolefins, while commercial “starch plastics” may be TPS/polyester or TPS/polyolefin blends whose mechanics are controlled by phase morphology and compatibilization rather than starch alone.

Water is both a processing aid and a powerful solid-state plasticizer. Increasing equilibrated moisture or compatible polyol content generally lowers glass transition, modulus, and strength while increasing deformability, but low plasticizer levels can show antiplasticization and excess or migrating plasticizer can phase-separate. Botanical source, amylose/amylopectin ratio and molar-mass distribution, residual granules and degree of destructuring, extrusion temperature/shear/specific mechanical energy and molecular scission, water and glycerol/sorbitol/urea/ionic-liquid content, moisture gradients, conditioning relative humidity and duration, storage-driven retrogradation and physical aging, chemical modification or crosslinking, filler and fiber dispersion/orientation, blend ratio and interfacial adhesion, processing orientation, porosity and weld lines, specimen thickness, loading rate, temperature, and strain history all affect the result. Reported tensile values must therefore carry both conditioning and test environment; temperature and relative humidity can move the same formulation across its glass transition.

A bounded demonstration used Roquette potato starch with a 23/77 amylose/amylopectin mass ratio and water as the only stated plasticizer. Feed was adjusted to 35 wt% water on a dry-starch basis, equilibrated, single-screw extruded at a 110 °C die temperature and 25 rpm (about 170 kJ/kg specific mechanical energy), rehydrated, and compression molded at 120 °C and 180 bar into 1 mm sheets. At 80 °C, dumbbells cut from those sheets (20 mm by 5 mm, initial strain rate 10−2 s−1, at least three tests) changed from a glassy-side response at 30% RH—12 wt% water, Young's modulus 80 ± 10 MPa, break stress 4 ± 1 MPa, and break strain 15 ± 4%—to a rubbery response at 90% RH—20 wt% water, modulus 0.4 ± 0.1 MPa, break stress 0.3 ± 0.2 MPa, and break strain 240 ± 80%. This is one amorphous, water-plasticized potato-TPS sheet tested hot under controlled humidity; it is not a room-temperature family range or a value for glycerol-plasticized, retrograded, reinforced, blended, foamed, injection-molded, or commercial TPS grades.
sections.processing:
Thermoplastic starch is converted by combining feed conditioning with heat and shear, then shaping the destructured, plasticized material before moisture redistributes. Twin- or single-screw extrusion is widely used for plasticization, compounding, pellet production, sheet or cast-film extrusion, and film blowing; injection molding, compression molding, and thermoforming are also suitable for formulation-dependent articles. Water and polyols govern both flow and the later glass transition, so starch source, amylose/amylopectin balance, initial moisture, plasticizer loading, mixing order, screw shear, specific mechanical energy, residence time, and die temperature must be controlled together. Too little treatment leaves granules or an inhomogeneous melt, whereas excessive heat or shear can reduce molar mass. Drying and humidity conditioning after shaping are part of the process because moisture gradients, plasticizer migration, physical aging, and retrogradation can change dimensions and embrittle or soften the article. Chemical derivatization of starch belongs in Synthesis; destructuring, compounding, shaping, cooling, and conditioning belong here.

Leroy and co-workers provide a bounded example for their water-plasticized Roquette potato starch, not a universal TPS window. They adjusted the feed to 35 wt% water on a dry-starch basis, equilibrated it for two days at 5 °C, and used a single-screw extruder at 25 rpm with a 110 °C die temperature and about 170 kJ/kg specific mechanical energy. Extruded rods were conditioned for at least one week at 20 °C and 58% relative humidity, then rehydrated overnight at 20 °C and 89% relative humidity before compression molding into 1 mm sheets at 120 °C and 180 bar. The sheets were subsequently conditioned for at least three days at the selected humidity. This sequence illustrates why feed equilibration and post-forming humidity history must accompany any reported TPS temperature or pressure.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Native starch granules contain amylose and branched amylopectin arranged in ordered and less ordered regions. Plasticization and processing disrupt this structure, although residual granule fragments can remain. During storage the chains can reassociate and form ordered regions in a process called retrogradation. Fillers and other polymers create additional phases and interfaces in a formulated TPS material. The size of remaining granule fragments and the extent of later recrystallization depend on water, shear, temperature and storage. In a starch/clay composite, the clay creates an additional phase whose interaction with the matrix can affect both water uptake and mechanical behavior.
sections.properties: Water acts as a plasticizer and increases starch-chain mobility. In one water-plasticized potato-starch study, samples stored at 20 °C had glass-transition temperatures of 95 °C at 58% relative humidity and 45 °C at 89% relative humidity. In tensile tests at 80 °C, low humidity produced brittle behavior while higher humidity gave a more rubbery, stretchable response. These results concern the specified material and conditioning, not a universal TPS temperature range. Higher humidity lowers the transition in this example, allowing more molecular motion at the same temperature. Consequently a value measured after one conditioning history is not directly transferable to a dry or more humid sample.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Starch-containing compounds are used for packaging including loose-fill protection, films, bags, coated substrates, trays and molded articles. Plasticization permits starch-rich formulations to be processed, while blend composition helps determine their strength, moisture sensitivity and suitability for a product. Performance belongs to the finished formulation and cannot be inferred from starch alone. A processor must balance flow during forming with moisture sensitivity and changes in flexibility during storage. For a packaging-film example, researchers tested extruded MATER-BI EF51V film reported to contain over 85% starch. At 25 °C its tensile modulus was approximately 100 MPa along the machine direction and 38 MPa across it, so orientation is relevant when choosing film dimensions and loading direction. These results apply to the tested 100 µm film, not every grade or thickness.

Purchasing. Novamont's MATER-BI is a commercial family of process-specific starch-containing compounds. A buyer selects a grade for the intended forming process and application; the product can contain other polymers and should not be assumed to be neat TPS.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual neat-TPS purchase or consumption figure was established. Output for commercial starch blends and all starch-derived ingredients covers broader categories and cannot be assigned entirely to TPS.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Enzymes can cleave starch chains into smaller carbohydrates, and water can also swell a TPS article and leach soluble plasticizer. Loss of material mass does not by itself show which components were removed or converted to carbon dioxide. Other polymers in commercial blends may follow different pathways.

Timescales: In one soil-burial study of starch and clay formulations, a modified-starch composite containing modified clay lost approximately 50% of its mass after five days. Specimens were cut from compression-molded sheets and buried in a controlled soil box; the authors noted that early mass loss could include leaching of glycerol plasticizer. The 1 mm-thick specimens were dried and weighed after removal from soil, so the endpoint was specimen mass loss. This is not a mineralization time or a result for all TPS formulations.

Environmental persistence: Moisture, microorganisms, composition and article size affect degradation. A soil-box weight-loss curve does not establish persistence in seawater or complete conversion of every component of a finished product.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Researchers ground and reinjection-molded commercial Mater-Bi EI51N0 and an almond-shell-filled formulation to examine production-scrap reprocessing. For the unfilled commercial compound, notched impact strength declined from about 6.0 to 4.5 kJ/m² between the first and later injection cycles. The filled specimens were tested without notches and are not directly comparable on that basis.

This experiment demonstrates controlled reprocessing of the specified formulations, not a general postconsumer recycling route. Repeated heat and shear, moisture and the presence of fillers can affect the properties of the recovered material.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Raw starch feeding and mixing in thermoplastic-starch manufacture involves dust exposure. NIOSH identifies irritation of the eyes, skin and respiratory tract and an explosion hazard when starch dust disperses in air. This guidance addresses starch powder, rather than establishing the toxicology of every isolated fraction or finished blend.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: TPS is a family of formulations rather than a single polymer grade. Starch source and amylose content, amount and type of plasticizer, processing, humidity and storage history all influence the final material. Retrogradation and plasticizer loss can increase stiffness and reduce elongation during ageing. Commercial blends and composites must be considered as complete formulations, including their other polymers and fillers. A soil-burial result for a glycerol-plasticized starch/clay sheet includes other mobile components and cannot identify the fate of starch alone. Thickness and preparation influence exposure to water as well as the measured mechanical response.
