sections.overview: Silk fibroin is the structural protein component of silk fibers. It can be isolated after removal of the surrounding sericin and regenerated into films, fibers, gels and other forms. Processing reorganizes the protein and affects the mechanical response. Native silk textile and isolated fibroin solution are distinct materials and markets. Its peptide chains can form ordered β-sheet-rich regions that help reinforce the material, while intervening less ordered regions contribute to its response. Regeneration and treatment change that organization, making a cast film mechanically different from the original fiber. Its use in textiles is established, while many purified-fibroin scaffold formulations remain research materials.
sections.history: Silk fibroin is a natural protein with a textile history extending into antiquity. The Metropolitan Museum preserves Chinese woven silk dated to the Warring States period, 475–221 BCE. Silk later supplied Byzantine court and ecclesiastical clothing, with state and private workshops developing elaborate woven fabrics. Modern research sought to recover fibroin for uses beyond textiles. A documented process advance came from Jen-Chang Yang and colleagues at Taipei Medical University: their patent, filed in 2010 and granted in 2012, used precipitation under shear to recover fibroin without conventional dialysis. It addressed a production bottleneck for regenerated material. The patent describes application directions including cell-culture supports, wound-dressing membranes and tissue-engineering materials. These developments concern processing a natural protein and proposed biomedical uses, not an invention of silk itself.
sections.nomenclature: Fibroin protein is a descriptive synonym for silk fibroin. The canonical name identifies the structural protein rather than whole silk fiber, which also contains other components such as sericin.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Silk fibroin is a natural structural protein obtained chiefly from the core filaments of domesticated Bombyx mori silkworm cocoons. Raw cocoon silk contains fibroin coated and cemented by sericin, so preparation begins with degumming rather than monomer polymerization. An alkaline, soap, hot-water, or enzymatic treatment removes sericin; the fibroin fibers are then thoroughly rinsed and dried. For regenerated fibroin solutions or powders, the hydrogen-bonded protein is dissolved in a concentrated salt or chaotropic medium, purified to remove salt and particulates, and recovered by dialysis, membrane filtration, antisolvent precipitation, or drying. One cited patent degums cocoons with pressurized hot water, dissolves the recovered fibroin in calcium chloride/ethanol/water, and uses a dialysis-free organosoluble recovery route. A distinct patent uses sodium-carbonate degumming, water washing, and choline-hydroxide ionic-liquid dissolution followed by antisolvent precipitation, centrifugation, washing, filtration, and drying. Degumming severity and dissolution conditions must balance sericin removal against fibroin-chain degradation. Regenerated films, fibers, gels, or scaffolds are later shaping choices and remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Native silkworm fibroin is a strong, tough, anisotropic protein fiber in which oriented β-sheet crystallites act as load-bearing junctions and less ordered chain regions supply extensibility and energy dissipation. Its tensile response depends on the intact hierarchical fiber structure rather than composition alone. Regenerated fibroin films, fibers, mats, foams, and hydrogels have lost or rebuilt different parts of that hierarchy and can range from stiff and brittle to soft and highly extensible; numerical results therefore must remain attached to species, material form, secondary structure, and processing history.

Principal variables include silkworm species and strain, reeling and fiber diameter measurement, residual sericin, degumming chemistry and severity, protein-chain molecular weight, dissolution and regeneration solvent, β-sheet content and crystallinity, porosity, defects, and molecular or fibril orientation from drawing, rolling, spinning, or pressing. Water is both a temporary plasticizer and a structural-processing agent: absorbed moisture can soften amorphous regions, whereas water treatment followed by drying can promote β-sheet reorganization and stiffening. Humidity, temperature and annealing, crosslinking, blends or plasticizers, test direction, gauge geometry, loading rate, and conditioning consequently alter modulus, strength, elongation, and toughness.

Two bounded examples illustrate this sensitivity. Feng and co-workers tested Grade 6A Bombyx mori 20/22-denier reeled single fibers after degumming for 60 min at 85 ± 2 °C in 3.0 g L⁻¹ papain at pH 6, drying at 60 °C, and conditioning for 24 h at 20 ± 2 °C and 65 ± 5% RH. For 20 specimens at 20 mm gauge length and 10 mm min⁻¹, they reported breaking stress (tenacity) 2.7 ± 0.2 cN dtex⁻¹, breaking strain 16.5 ± 2.2%, and specific Young's modulus 0.7 ± 0.1 cN dtex⁻¹; the harsher Na₂CO₃-degummed comparison was 1.5 ± 0.2 cN dtex⁻¹, 8.7 ± 2.2%, and 0.4 ± 0.1 cN dtex⁻¹, respectively. In a separate regenerated-film study, a formic-acid/CaCl₂-cast Mori fibroin film had reported elastic modulus 787.9 MPa and maximum elongation 19.0%; after 24 h water soaking and 72 h vacuum drying, the corresponding film reached 1.645 GPa modulus but only 1.97% elongation under the study's ambient ASTM D3039-type tensile protocol at 2 mm min⁻¹. Neither fiber nor film values define silk fibroin generally.
sections.processing:
Once an aqueous or solvent-based silk-fibroin dope is available, the directly documented article routes in this pass are solution casting of films and electrospinning of fibrous mats or tubes. A uniform dope is metered onto a casting surface or through an electrospinning needle, shaped, dried, and then annealed or otherwise post-treated to change water stability, orientation, and beta-sheet content. Concentration, fibroin molecular mass, blend ratio, pH and solvent, dope viscosity and entrained bubbles, applied flow and shear, humidity, electric field and collector geometry, casting thickness, drying rate, and annealing conditions can alter jet stability, film or mat morphology, shrinkage, and handling. Extraction and degumming of silk, fibroin dissolution chemistry, and any network-forming chemistry remain in Synthesis; metering, casting or electrospinning, drying, annealing, and final article handling belong in Processing.

In one casting study, aqueous, HFIP, and formic-acid silk-fibroin solutions were each adjusted to 5% (w/v); 2.5 mL was poured into a 35 mm Petri dish and dried overnight at 37 °C. The films were then exposed to water vapor, methanol vapor, or steam in the study's covered treatment arrangement at 37 °C for 24 h and air-dried. This schedule applies to those solvent systems, concentration, dish geometry, and annealing treatments rather than all silk-fibroin films.

An independent electrospinning study blended aqueous silk with PEO at 2 mL silk solution to 1–4 g PEO to raise dope viscosity, then used 0.7–2.0 mL/h flow, potentials up to 20 kV, and an 18 cm needle-to-collector gap. Its mats or tubular grafts were water-vapor annealed under vacuum overnight at 4, 24, 37, or 55 °C. Those settings are bounded to the reported fibroin/PEO blends, electrospinning apparatus, collector, and post-treatment; they are not a general spinning window, and they do not establish melt processability for silk fibroin.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Fibroin chains contain regions able to organize into β-sheet-rich structures alongside less ordered regions. These ordered domains act as physical junctions in silk and many regenerated materials. Dissolution, casting and subsequent treatment can change their arrangement and the balance of conformations. Molecular weight and processing also influence larger-scale morphology. Processing can also change the shape and connectivity of these regions: in one enzyme study, films made by slow drying, water annealing or stretching showed different nanostructures and degradation behavior. The same nominal protein therefore need not have the same morphology in each form.
sections.properties: Native fibers and regenerated fibroin films can have very different responses to load. In one comparison, a silk–sorbitol film had an elastic modulus of 27.99 ± 4.93 MPa, while a silk–glycerol film had 6.98 ± 0.8 MPa. Those values describe the tested composite formulations, showing that the added ingredient can change stiffness; they are not properties of all fibroin. Hydration and β-sheet organization also affect the response. In another film comparison, water treatment followed by drying increased the reported modulus from about 788 to 1,645 MPa while reducing elongation at break from 19% to about 2%. The researchers associated that change with structural reorganization; treatment and drying conditions must accompany such values.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Silk fibers are used in textiles; isolated or regenerated fibroin is studied for tissue-engineering scaffolds and cell-culture materials. Fibroin can be formed into hydrated or solid structures, but their function depends on processing and the complete formulation. For example, a scaffold can be designed to support cells while its protein structure and enzymatic susceptibility affect how it changes during use. Research suitability of a formulation is not proof of approval for a particular implant. A silk fabric and a purified solution are different purchasing products.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich lists Bombyx mori fibroin solution at 50 mg/mL in a 20 mL pack, corresponding nominally to 1 g fibroin. This is a research supply example and does not establish a medical-device specification.

Scale and evidence limits. Textile Exchange reports 91,415 tonnes of global raw silk production in 2024. That broader raw-silk figure is not a measure of isolated fibroin sales; the documented research solution is supplied at gram scale.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Proteases can cleave fibroin peptide chains and release soluble peptide-rich material. In regenerated films, susceptible connecting regions may be removed while more ordered fragments remain. The organization of these regions matters in addition to the total β-sheet fraction. The study observed particles and short filaments in enzyme-treated solutions, consistent with release of structured material as connecting regions are attacked; such fragments are not a complete inventory of final products.

Timescales: A controlled study followed film mass loss over hours to days in protease XIV and buffered solution at 37 °C and pH 7.4. Its methods and discussion report differing enzyme concentrations, so a transferable numerical rate is not assigned here. In that comparison, a stretched film with the highest β-sheet content lost mass faster than water-annealed and slowly dried films. The authors related this to differences in their nanoscale organization, showing why β-sheet fraction alone did not predict the observed trend.

Environmental persistence: Loss of film integrity does not establish disappearance of released crystalline fragments or a lifetime in soil or water. Native fibers, regenerated films and crosslinked products can differ substantially.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Researchers degummed defective cocoons and silk-production waste, dissolved the fibroin and cast regenerated films. Autoclave and chemical degumming were compared; dissolution conditions required adjustment for defective cocoons. The process uses a defined production-waste feedstock rather than proving recovery from any silk-containing article.

Dyes, coatings, blends and contamination would require separate assessment in a broader recycling stream.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Silk fibroin responses depend on material format and processing. The review distinguishes fibroin from residual sericin and other processing-associated constituents, whose contributions to inflammation are not uniform across studies. Degumming and a favorable cell test do not by themselves establish the safety of a specific implanted silk device.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Silk source, degumming and regeneration affect chain length and structure. Film, gel and native fiber results must be compared with specimen form, moisture and processing in view. Additives can change both stiffness and extensibility, so composite values do not specify pure fibroin. β-sheet content alone does not predict every degradation outcome. The water-treated film comparison also shows that greater stiffness can accompany less extension before failure. Conversely, additive-containing film measurements reflect both the fibroin and the added component, and cannot establish the behavior of an untreated native fiber.

sections.overview: Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are a family of aliphatic polyesters accumulated by many microorganisms as intracellular storage materials. They include homopolymers such as poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) and copolymers containing additional hydroxyalkanoate units. Side-chain length and comonomer composition change how the recovered polymer crystallizes and performs. PHA grades are used and studied as thermoplastics, including packaging compounds, but the family name does not specify a single grade or environmental lifetime. Their ester-linked chains can be recovered from cells and fabricated into a variety of solid forms. A copolymer may be selected to change flexibility or melting behavior, but changing composition also changes the basis for comparison. An observed biological breakdown of one specimen cannot establish the fate of the entire family.
sections.history: PHA research grew from observations of bacterial storage granules. Maurice Lemoigne’s studies in the 1920s identified the polyester now called poly(3-hydroxybutyrate); subsequent work established a much broader family of microbial polyesters. Macrae and Wilkinson clarified the storage role in 1958, and W. R. Grace attempted commercial production from 1959. Later work varied microbial strains and monomer composition to expand material behavior. Packaging, agricultural products and biomedical materials became major development directions. This family history begins with discovery of natural polymers; individual PHA homopolymers and copolymers have separate commercialization histories.
sections.nomenclature: PHA abbreviates polyhydroxyalkanoate. The name is family-level; PHB and PHBV are particular members or copolymer compositions, not synonyms for all PHAs.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are intracellular polyesters biosynthesized by bacteria and other microorganisms from assimilable carbon sources rather than conventionally polymerized after isolating a monomer. Sugars, lipids, organic acids, and carbon-rich waste streams can feed the cells; organism, PHA-synthase pathway, substrate composition, and cultivation regime determine whether the accumulated material is a homopolymer or a copolymer containing hydroxyalkanoate units of different chain lengths. Recovery therefore follows cultivation: cells are separated, concentrated or dried, disrupted or digested, and the polymer is extracted and purified by solvent recovery, washing, and/or precipitation. One cited study fermented industrial-waste substrates with a Bacillus isolate, harvested biomass, and extracted intracellular PHA. A distinct patent route first acidogenically ferments a water-based waste feed into fatty acids, feeds that stream to PHA-producing bacteria, separates a PHA-rich cell paste, and extracts the polymer with a polar organic solvent. These are bounded production examples; strain, feed, and downstream recovery method remain route-specific.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are a compositionally broad family: short-chain-length P(3HB)-rich materials are commonly semicrystalline and stiff/brittle, whereas 4HB, 3HV, 3HHx, and medium-chain-length units can lower crystallinity and modulus while increasing extensibility and toughness. Molecular mass, monomer ratio and sequence, crystallinity/aging, thermal and moisture history, plasticizer/nucleant/fiber package, and processing into film, injection molding, fiber, or porous scaffold are therefore controlling variables. An open composition review reports P(3HB) values of 1.1–3.5 GPa modulus, 0.4–5% elongation, and 19–40 MPa tensile strength, versus a 3HB:3HV 80–90:10–20 mol% copolymer at 0.8–1.2 GPa, 50–100%, and 20–32 MPa. These literature summaries do not retain a common grade, method, or conditioning and are composition envelopes, not a PHA-wide specification. A second open review independently attributes the broad PHA response to monomer composition and highlights crystallinity as a key determinant of PHB mechanics.
sections.processing:
Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are compositionally diverse thermoplastic polyesters that can be shaped by solution casting and particulate leaching; compression or melt molding; extrusion, blown film, and injection molding; melt, dry, wet, and electrospinning; phase separation and freeze drying; gas foaming; and additive manufacture. Processability cannot be reduced to one family temperature window: PHB has a narrow margin between melting and damaging thermal exposure, whereas comonomers such as hydroxyvalerate, hydroxyhexanoate, or 4-hydroxybutyrate can lower melting temperature and crystallinity. Dry feed, short and controlled melt residence, low unnecessary shear, oxygen and moisture control, and appropriate plasticizers, nucleating agents, fillers, or blends can reduce chain scission and improve melt strength. Mold or chill-roll temperature and cooling rate control crystallization, skin-core orientation, shrinkage, brittleness, and cycle time; solution routes additionally require complete dissolution or dispersion, solvent control, and removal of residual solvent or porogen.

Puppi, Pecorini, and Chiellini review these melt- and solution-based article routes and explicitly warn that PHB's narrow melt-processing interval and slow or composition-dependent crystallization require formulation and process control. Vanheusden and co-workers provide a bounded melt example for Aonilex X151A PHBHHx containing 10.5 mol% 3-hydroxyhexanoate. They dried pellets for at least three days at 65 °C, twin-screw extruded them, immediately transferred the melt to a heated piston-injection cylinder, and optimized their test bars at a 145 °C processing temperature, 80 °C mold, 50 rpm screws, and 60 s mold cooling. Their study found that higher mold temperature allowed more chain relaxation and reduced oriented skin formation, while elevated temperature plus shear narrowed the practical interval through thermo-mechanical and thermo-oxidative degradation. Those values apply to that grade, specimen, and laboratory line, not to PHB, PHBV, P4HB, or every PHBHHx composition.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PHA chains contain ester-linked hydroxyalkanoate units that can differ in side-chain length and sequence. Regular PHB chains readily form crystalline regions, whereas incorporating other units can interrupt that packing and change the balance of crystalline and amorphous material. The outcome also depends on molecular weight, cooling and subsequent aging. Microbial storage granules, recovered powder and a melt-processed article are different physical states of the material. Crystallization after processing can continue during storage and affect mechanical properties over time. Copolymer units can change packing, but the effect depends on their identity and proportion rather than on the PHA name alone.
sections.properties: The PHA family spans relatively stiff, crystalline polyesters and more flexible copolymers. For example, replacing some PHB units with 3-hydroxyvalerate can disrupt PHB-type lamellae and lower melting temperature in particular copolymers, improving their processing flexibility. PHB itself has a relatively narrow interval between melting and thermal degradation. Composition, thermal history and additives therefore matter when selecting a grade or comparing measurements. In a comparison of PHB and PHBV films, tensile properties changed far more quickly in water-saturated soil than at 40% relative humidity. That environmental response is also specimen-specific: changing polymer composition and water availability changes what is being compared.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PHA grades are sold for packaging and food-service products, including straws, cutlery, coffee capsules, bags and films. Kaneka identifies its Green Planet material as a specific PHBH copolymer, while PHB is also used as a research material for tissue engineering and controlled-release studies. Packaging requirements differ between flexible films and rigid molded items, so composition and processing must be matched to the product. The different polymers and applications require different formulations and evidence; a laboratory use does not establish medical-product approval.

Purchasing. Specify PHA chemistry and grade when buying from producers, compounders or research catalogs. Kaneka Green Planet is one PHBH product family, whereas Sigma-Aldrich lists natural-origin PHB as a separate research material in 10 g and 100 g packs. A resin grade, a blend and a finished article are different purchases.

Scale and evidence limits. Kaneka's February 2022 announcement reported 5,000 tonnes/year of existing PHBH capacity and another 15,000 tonnes/year planned at Takasago, Japan. These are dated capacity figures for one copolymer, not worldwide PHA purchases, verified subsequent output or proof that the announced expansion was completed.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PHA ester bonds can be cleaved biologically or chemically, but products depend on the polymer and conditions. For PHB, laboratory hydrolysis gives 3-hydroxybutyric acid; dehydration can instead produce crotonic acid under other reaction conditions. PHBV and longer-side-chain PHAs have different repeat-unit compositions and require their own product evidence.

Timescales: In a soil study at 25 °C, prepared PHB and PHBV films rapidly lost tensile performance in water-saturated soil, while samples kept at 40% relative humidity showed much smaller changes over six weeks. Under saturated conditions the PHB tensile strength fell from 8.43 to 3.98 MPa after three days, while the 8 wt% hydroxyvalerate PHBV film fell from 18.75 to 9.21 MPa. That comparison concerns the named films, soil and measured properties, not a universal degradation rate for all PHA products.

Environmental persistence: Mechanical failure, film disappearance and CO₂ evolution are distinct endpoints. The soil study did not measure complete mineralization, and chemical-recycling reactor conditions do not establish a family-wide lifetime in soil, freshwater or seawater.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
One laboratory chemical-recycling route hydrolyzes PHB with taurine in water to obtain 3-hydroxybutyric acid, a potential chemical building block. The authors report 98% selectivity to that product under their optimized PHB conditions, with crotonic acid as a competing product. That result is specific to the tested PHB reaction and is not an intact-polymer recycling process.

The study also examines selected PHB-based copolymers and blends, but does not establish that every PHA composition or contaminated mixed product can be treated at the same yield. Commercial collection and operation at scale require separate evidence.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PHA intended for biomedical use requires control of impurities from microbial production, especially bacterial endotoxin released during recovery. The PHA review emphasizes purification and material-dependent host responses. Reported compatibility of selected films or scaffolds is evidence for those preparations, not authorization of every polymer grade or device.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PHA is a chemical family rather than a specification of comonomer content, molecular weight or formulation. Crystallinity and thermal processing window depend on those choices and on cooling and storage; PHB homopolymer results do not automatically describe a PHBV or PHBH copolymer. A biodegradation result also depends on specimen geometry and the conditions and microorganisms present. Commercial blends can include other polymers and additives whose fate must be assessed separately. A wet-soil comparison of PHB and one PHBV formulation does not establish a corresponding rate for PHBH, nor does loss of strength quantify mineralization. A resin, filled compound and finished item may differ in thickness and composition.

sections.overview: Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate), or PHB, is a polyhydroxyalkanoate made from 3-hydroxybutyrate units. Many microorganisms accumulate it as an intracellular storage polyester, which can be recovered and processed into thermoplastic articles. PHB chains readily crystallize, contributing to stiffness and brittleness as well as a narrow melt-processing window. PHB-based compounds are supplied for packaging and molded products, while purified polymer is also used in materials research. As a semicrystalline material, the balance of ordered and less ordered regions helps determine its response to load. Further crystallization after cooling can change that response during storage. Commercial compounds use additives to adjust behavior, so the family of PHB-based products is broader than a neat polymer specimen.
sections.history: PHB was identified through Maurice Lemoigne’s bacterial research during the 1920s. In 1958, Macrae and Wilkinson helped establish its role as a microbial carbon and energy reserve; W. R. Grace explored industrial production from 1959. By 1982, published work was comparing its material behavior with polypropylene and investigating biodegradability and biocompatibility. These developments encouraged interest in packaging and biomedical materials, while brittleness and processing limitations helped motivate copolymer development. PHB is therefore a discovered microbial polymer subsequently developed as a plastic; the later Biopol PHBV copolymer should not be treated as chemically identical to PHB.
sections.nomenclature: PHB and P3HB are abbreviations used for poly(3-hydroxybutyrate). The record covers the 3HB homopolymer; PHBV and PHBHHx copolyesters, blends, and recovered formulations are distinct scopes rather than aliases.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) is a microbial polyhydroxyalkanoate made by intracellular biosynthesis, not normally by direct condensation of purchased 3-hydroxybutyrate. In the canonical pathway, acetyl-CoA is converted through acetoacetyl-CoA and 3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA before PHA synthase polymerizes the hydroxybutyrate-CoA monomer. Bacterial culture requires a carbon feedstock and cultivation conditions that support PHA accumulation; source and nutrient regime affect productivity. A patent example cultures Bacillus mycoides on sucrose, molasses, or pineapple waste and isolates PHB, while another production method uses bacterial cultures with agricultural food-waste feedstocks. Extraction, cell disruption, solvent washing, and purification are recovery choices whose applicability depends on the organism and process, rather than universal PHB chemistry.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PHB is a highly stereoregular semicrystalline polyester that is commonly stiff and brittle in ordinary molded or cast forms: its crystallinity, lamellar/spherulitic morphology, and secondary crystallization during storage suppress ductility and can embrittle the article. Molecular mass and dispersity, microbial source and recovery, thermal history and degradation during melt processing, annealing, drawing/orientation, temperature, plasticizers, and blend or filler design all alter the response. A reported highly drawn P3HB example (draw ratio 12; crystallinity 78%) had tensile strength 161 MPa, elongation at break 45%, and Young’s modulus 2.8 GPa. Those are not neat isotropic-PHB values: they are specifically cold-drawn material, and the review table does not provide specimen geometry, test temperature, rate, or conditioning.
sections.processing:
PHB can be converted by extrusion and compounding, injection and compression molding, film blowing, melt or solution spinning with drawing, solvent casting and particulate leaching, electrospinning, thermoforming of suitable sheet, and filament-based additive manufacturing. Its processing margin is constrained by a melting region close to the onset of rapid thermal degradation, low melt strength, crystallization during cooling, and continuing secondary crystallization after shaping. Pellets should be dried for the selected grade; melt temperature, shear, residence time, oxygen exposure, stabilizers or plasticizers, die pressure, mold temperature, cooling, and post-molding conditioning must be managed together. Repeated melt histories can lower molar mass and change flow and crystallinity, so regrind cannot be treated as equivalent to virgin feed without qualification.

Main and co-workers provide a bounded example for Biomer P263 injection grade. Feed with an incoming moisture content of 0.18% was dried at 60 °C for 2 h, compounded through a 17.8 mm co-rotating twin-screw extruder with L/D 48 at 5 kg/h, a 160 °C die, and 500 rpm, then air-cooled as strands and granulated. Their virgin material was injection molded with a 185 °C nozzle at 10 cm3/s, while reprocessed material used a 165 °C nozzle and 15 cm3/s; the mold was 38 °C with 30 s cooling. The measured loss of molar mass and higher melt flow after repeated cycles make these a degradation study on P263, not a general PHB processing window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Regular PHB chains pack into semicrystalline regions within less ordered material. Crystallization occurs during cooling and can continue more slowly after processing, changing the structure as the article ages. A review describes one sample whose crystallinity rose from 20.5% after one day to 28.2% after seven days; that example depends on the sample and storage history. Blending, drawing and added nucleating agents can alter the morphology further. The initial processing conditions affect the number and organization of crystals, and subsequent secondary crystallization can continue at room temperature. This evolution helps explain why properties measured immediately after fabrication need not match those measured later.
sections.properties: PHB is relatively stiff and can be brittle, with properties influenced by crystalline structure and secondary aging. Its melting temperature lies close enough to the onset of thermal degradation that long or excessive heating during melt processing can reduce molecular weight. A supplier adds nucleating agents and plasticizers to its PHB-based pellets to improve processing and mechanical behavior. Those formulated pellets are not identical to neat PHB, and a property measured for one preparation cannot describe them all. In a separate aging study summarized by the review, PHB samples held at 15 °C in a dry environment for 168 days became stiffer and less extensible. The trend is specific to those specimens and storage conditions, illustrating why age should accompany a mechanical comparison.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PHB-based compounds are offered for packaging and molded articles. Biomer describes its granules as water-resistant and suitable for articles that encounter water or oily materials; additives are included to improve their processability. The conversion route and the resulting wall thickness affect the performance of a finished package or molded article. Natural-origin PHB is separately used in tissue-engineering and controlled-release research, which does not establish approval of a finished medical device.

Purchasing. Biomer describes PHB powder and formulated pellets containing processing aids; Sigma-Aldrich lists natural-origin PHB research material in 10 g and 100 g packs. A compounded pellet and a purified research polymer have different specifications, so buyers must identify the material and intended conversion method.

Scale and evidence limits. Catalog quantities establish research purchasing units, not annual market demand. The checked sources do not provide a reliable separate PHB consumption total; capacity for the broader PHA family includes other copolymers.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PHB ester bonds can undergo hydrolysis to 3-hydroxybutyric acid; under different hot chemical conditions dehydration can produce crotonic acid. In biological environments smaller products may be metabolized by microorganisms, but the pathway and observed rate depend on exposure. Chemical hydrolysis in a heated reactor is distinct from environmental aging.

Timescales: In a study of prepared PHB films at 25 °C, water-saturated soil caused tensile strength to fall from 8.43 to 3.98 MPa within three days; films in soil at 40% relative humidity showed much smaller changes over six weeks. In a separate laboratory soil experiment, 30–50 µm solvent-cast films were buried at 30 °C in two soils kept moist: after 63 days, the recovered film mass loss was reported as 65.2% in ash-containing alkaline landfill soil and 100% in neutral campus soil. The soils differ in microbial populations and composition as well as pH, so the comparison cannot isolate one cause.

Environmental persistence: Film weakening or loss of recoverable mass does not establish that all polymer carbon has become CO₂. The controlled soil comparisons and laboratory hydrolysis reaction do not establish one PHB lifetime for every article or environment.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
In a laboratory experiment, PHB was hydrolyzed in water with taurine at 180 °C and pH 5.5. After a 12-hour reaction, the authors reported 98% selectivity to 3-hydroxybutyric acid, while limiting the competing crotonic-acid product; they also studied separation of the products. This is chemical recovery of a building block, not recovery of intact PHB.

The result is tied to the tested material and conditions. It does not establish a commercial PHB recycling service or the performance of a contaminated mixed waste stream.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PHB intended for biomedical use requires control of impurities from microbial production, especially bacterial endotoxin released during recovery. The PHA review emphasizes purification and material-dependent host responses. Reported compatibility of selected films or scaffolds is evidence for those preparations, not authorization of every polymer grade or device.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Microbial production and recovery affect molecular mass and residual materials, while cooling and storage affect crystallization. The reported rise in crystallinity after seven days describes one PHB sample and cannot be assigned to all grades. Melt reprocessing, plasticizers and blends can change the mechanical and thermal response of a finished article. Degradation also depends on specimen geometry and its environment. The 168-day dry-storage comparison measures aging in a particular preparation, whereas the wet-soil study measures exposure under different conditions. The two observations should not be treated as interchangeable estimates of service life.

sections.overview: Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate), or PHBV, is a PHA copolyester containing 3-hydroxybutyrate and 3-hydroxyvalerate units in the same polymer chains. Microbial synthesis can vary the hydroxyvalerate content, changing how the material crystallizes and responds to heat. PHBV resins are supplied for molded articles, thermoforming and films, and research materials are used in tissue-engineering studies. A stated copolymer fraction and formulation are needed to interpret a particular result. The hydroxyvalerate fraction is one part of its specification; different chain distributions and processing histories can yield different crystalline structures. The copolymer can also be supplied in compounded form, so an article need not have the properties of a purified resin.
sections.history: PHBV developed as a way to modify the behavior of bacterial PHB through a second monomer. Imperial Chemical Industries’ Paul A. Holmes, Stephen H. Collins and Leonard F. Wright documented fermentation-based 3-hydroxybutyrate copolymers in a patent family with a 1981 priority date, including hydroxyvalerate-containing materials. Its U.S. patent was published in 1984. Later commercial PHBV was known as Biopol; Procter & Gamble’s 2000 patent describes that existing ICI material and earlier efforts to make films for diaper backsheets. These records trace the shift from a microbial storage polyester toward processable disposable-product materials, without assigning all PHBV formulations one invention date.
sections.nomenclature: PHBV is the abbreviation for poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate). The copolymer boundary requires both 3HB and 3HV units; PHB homopolymer, PHBHHx, blends, and a particular extracted or molded formulation are separate scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) is a biosynthesized PHA copolyester with both 3HB and 3HV units. In one common biological route, an organism such as Cupriavidus/Ralstonia is supplied glucose or another carbon source together with propionate or another odd-carbon precursor; intracellular metabolic conversion to propionyl-CoA provides the 3HV precursor. The timing and rate of propionate feed control 3HV incorporation and may trade off with biomass or polymer productivity. Alternative engineered hosts can make PHBV through a propionate-independent pathway from unrelated carbon sources. These microbial and feed controls determine copolymer composition; solvent extraction or other cell-recovery methods are downstream recovery choices, while blending or shaping the recovered polymer is not synthesis.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PHBV is a semicrystalline thermoplastic polyester whose 3-hydroxyvalerate (3HV) fraction disrupts PHB crystal packing: higher 3HV generally lowers crystallinity and shifts the response away from the stiff, brittle PHB homopolymer toward greater flexibility. Molecular mass and dispersity, crystallization/annealing and physical aging, moisture and temperature, plasticizer or fibre/filler additions, and draw or moulding history can therefore change modulus, strength, ductility, and fracture. A data-bearing study of a commercial PHBV containing 8% HV reported tensile strength of 25.9 ± 2.2 MPa and Young’s modulus of 0.75 ± 0.09 GPa; the same study’s higher-HV pilot-plant materials gave lower strengths and moduli. These results are limited to the reported purified material and its composition; the table used does not specify the tensile specimen geometry, test rate, temperature, or conditioning, so they are not a general PHBV design range.
sections.processing:
PHBV is converted by extrusion and compounding, injection and compression molding, cast and blown film, extrusion coating, melt or solution spinning, electrospinning, solvent casting, and additive manufacturing. Increasing 3-hydroxyvalerate content generally changes melting and crystallization behavior, so drying, melt temperature, screw shear, residence time, die or mold cooling, orientation, and post-forming crystallization must be selected for the exact composition and grade. Its thermal margin can be narrow: an extra melt history or a small temperature increase can cause chain scission even when a lower-3HV material remains processable.

Alfano and co-workers provide a bounded comparison of PHBV materials containing 3, 18, or 28 mol% 3HV. They vacuum-dried mixtures for 24 h, compounded them in an 11 mm, L/D 40 twin-screw extruder at 150 rpm with profiles of 130-160-180-180-180 °C for PHBV3 or 130-130-160-160-160 °C for PHBV18/28, cooled and pelletized the strands, redried the pellets, and thermopressed 100 micrometre films. The press sequence used a 5 min plate contact, a 50-to-100 bar ramp over 1 min, 150 bar for 1 min, and 10 min cooling. PHBV28 properties deteriorated when its pressing temperature rose from 160 to 170 °C. Those observations apply to the named compositions, blends, and laboratory equipment, not to every PHBV grade.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PHBV chains contain both hydroxybutyrate and hydroxyvalerate repeat units. The extra comonomer can disrupt PHB-type crystalline lamellae, changing the relative amount and structure of crystalline and amorphous material. Molecular weight, comonomer fraction and distribution, cooling and later storage all influence the observed morphology. A particular PHBV grade is therefore not structurally identical to PHB homopolymer. Altered lamellar packing can change the temperature at which crystalline material melts. Cooling and storage can then further rearrange the semicrystalline structure, affecting both stiffness and the processing response.
sections.properties: Introducing 3-hydroxyvalerate can reduce PHB-like crystallinity and melting temperature, and selected copolymers can be more flexible than PHB. The size of the effect depends on the comonomer content rather than following a single fixed PHBV value. For example, Tianan's 2014 Y1000P datasheet lists a DSC melting point of 170–176 °C for that named commercial resin, not a melting range for all PHBV. Processing, crystallization and additives influence the result. In a soil exposure of one PHBV film with 8 wt% hydroxyvalerate, tensile strength decreased from 18.75 to 9.21 MPa after three days in saturated soil. This illustrates how the measured response also depends on the state of an aged specimen, rather than establishing a fresh-resin property.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PHBV resins are supplied for packaging, molded and thermoformed articles and blown films. Tianan's ENMAT Y1000P processing guide identifies those conversion routes for its named resin; the choice of grade and process helps determine the final article. Blown film, thermoforming and molding impose different requirements on melt handling and the shape of the finished product. A research-grade PHBV is also listed for tissue-engineering and analytical calibration studies, which does not establish approval of a specific medical product.

Purchasing. The 2014 Tianan guide describes pelletized Y1000P supplied in foil-lined bags. Sigma-Aldrich lists a separate natural-origin research copolymer with 12 mol% hydroxyvalerate; a current pack size was not visible in the checked listing. Buyers should distinguish comonomer content, resin form and additives.

Scale and evidence limits. The historical datasheet documents a product form and intended uses but gives neither a bag mass nor annual sales. No reliable separate PHBV production or purchase tonnage was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Cleavage of PHBV ester bonds can release products derived from its hydroxybutyrate and hydroxyvalerate units. In hot chemical recycling, dehydration can also form crotonic acid. In biological exposures, surface erosion and colonization are observations of material change rather than a complete inventory of dissolved products.

Timescales: In a soil study at 25 °C, films of PHBV containing 8 wt% hydroxyvalerate lost tensile strength from 18.75 to 9.21 MPa in three days in water-saturated soil; samples held at 40% relative humidity showed much smaller changes over six weeks. A separate seven-month seawater study observed biofilms on PHBV. Neither endpoint is a direct measurement of complete polymer mineralization.

Environmental persistence: Moisture, microbial communities and specimen geometry affect behavior. Film weakening, surface erosion and biofilm formation cannot be used alone to calculate a universal environmental lifetime or the fraction converted to CO₂.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A laboratory study applied taurine-catalyzed hydrolysis to a PHBV sample and recovered hydroxy-acid products. This converts polyester chains into smaller chemicals, rather than mechanically returning the same polymer to use. The product distribution depends on the specific copolymer and reaction conditions, and the PHB homopolymer's reported selectivity should not be transferred to all PHBV.

The demonstration does not establish commercial mixed-waste collection or an industrial closed-loop process.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PHBV intended for biomedical use requires control of impurities from microbial production, especially bacterial endotoxin released during recovery. The PHA review emphasizes purification and material-dependent host responses. Reported compatibility of selected films or scaffolds is evidence for those preparations, not authorization of every polymer grade or device.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The name PHBV does not specify one hydroxyvalerate fraction, molecular-weight distribution or formulation. A resin datasheet, a purified laboratory copolymer and a filled or blended product therefore need not behave alike. Thermal history and cooling affect crystallinity, while specimen size and exposure conditions affect degradation. Measured values must remain attached to the specified grade, comonomer content and test. The reported soil film had 8 wt% hydroxyvalerate; the separate research listing is described in mol%, so the two compositions are not directly interchangeable. Conditioning and specimen age are essential when comparing properties.

sections.overview: Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyhexanoate), or PHBHHx, is a microbial PHA copolyester containing 3-hydroxybutyrate and 3-hydroxyhexanoate units in the same chain. The hydroxyhexanoate fraction can vary with the organism and production conditions. Its longer side chain disrupts PHB-type packing, allowing selected copolymers to be more flexible than PHB homopolymer. Commercial PHBH grades are used in packaging and food-service articles, with properties tied to grade and formulation. A longer pendant group reduces regular PHB-like packing, allowing some compositions to stretch more readily. The amount of that unit and the molecular weight both matter in a measured comparison. Commercial PHBH and laboratory copolymers are related materials but are not necessarily identical grades.
sections.history: Kaneka began developing this hydroxybutyrate/hydroxyhexanoate copolymer in the early 1990s. Its researchers identified a producing microorganism in soil at the company’s Takasago site, then combined strain development and polymer engineering to improve production. This documents Kaneka’s development route rather than a universal first discovery date. The resulting Green Planet PHBH line expanded into straws, shopping bags, cutlery and food packaging. Collaborations with Japan Airlines and Seven-Eleven illustrate adoption, while a Shiseido cosmetics-container project began in 2019. The history is one of fermentation scale-up followed by application development; the trade name denotes Kaneka’s materials within the copolymer class.
sections.nomenclature: P(3HB-co-3HHx) and PHBHHx are abbreviations used for this copolyester. The copolymer boundary requires both 3HB and 3HHx units; PHB homopolymer, PHBV, and a blend or modified article are not aliases for this record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyhexanoate) (PHBHHx) is a bacterial PHA copolyester containing 3-hydroxybutyrate and 3-hydroxyhexanoate units. Its composition is controlled biologically by microorganism/catalytic enzyme choice and carbon feedstocks, not by physically mixing PHB and a separate polymer. Documented routes include engineered Cupriavidus necator production from CO2 and Aeromonas production from vegetable oil, fatty acids, or other C6-derived feedstocks under nutrient limitation. The 3HHx content is a route-dependent outcome, and reported feedstock ratios or gene sets must not be generalized to every PHBHHx material. Following fermentation, intracellular polymer must be recovered and purified by a process appropriate to the organism; article molding is outside this synthesis entry.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyhexanoate) is a semicrystalline thermoplastic polyester whose 3-hydroxyhexanoate units disrupt close packing of the 3-hydroxybutyrate-rich chains. Relative to poly(3-hydroxybutyrate), increasing the 3HHx fraction generally lowers crystallinity, tensile modulus, and tensile strength while increasing extensibility; it can therefore shift from a comparatively stiff response toward a flexible, ductile one. Mechanical behavior also depends on molecular weight, crystallization and physical-aging history, melt temperature and residence time, mold or chill temperature, cooling time, orientation, test rate and temperature, and the presence and dispersion of plasticizers, blend partners, fillers, or pores. Moisture and hydrolytic or thermal degradation can further reduce molecular weight and load-bearing performance.

A bounded melt-processed example used Kaneka Aonilex X151A containing 10.5 mol% 3HHx. Pellets were dried for at least three days at 65 °C, twin-screw extruded at 145 °C and 50 rpm, injection molded into ISO 527-2 type 5A specimens in an 80 °C mold, cooled for 60 seconds, and conditioned at 23 °C and 50% relative humidity for at least three days. At 23 °C and 50% relative humidity with a 20 mm/min crosshead speed, the five-specimen validation run reported 21.4–22.0 MPa tensile yield strength, 320–342% nominal elongation at break, and 883–1007 MPa Young's modulus. The elongation was calculated from the 50 mm grip distance rather than the 20 mm gauge length. These values are limited to this 10.5 mol% grade, process window, specimen, conditioning, and test definition; the same study showed that mold temperature, processing temperature, and test speed materially changed the measured response.
sections.processing:
PHBHHx is shaped by extrusion and compounding, injection and compression molding, film and fiber routes where the grade has sufficient melt strength, solution casting and phase inversion, electrospinning, and filament-based additive manufacturing. Incorporating 3-hydroxyhexanoate generally changes flexibility and crystallization relative to PHB, but the usable window remains composition- and grade-specific. Feed drying, melt and mold temperatures, screw speed and shear, pressure, residence time, cooling and demolding time, crystallization, and post-molding conditioning must be balanced against thermal and mechanical degradation. Slow crystallization or premature demolding can distort an article, while excessive melt temperature and residence can lower molar mass and produce defects.

Vanheusden and co-workers mapped a bounded design space for Aonilex X151A containing 10.5 mol% 3-hydroxyhexanoate. They dried pellets at 65 °C for at least three days, extruded them through an 11 mm, L/D 40 twin screw at a feed setting of 4 rpm, and evaluated melt profiles centered at 145, 152.5, and 160 °C, mold temperatures of 40, 60, and 80 °C, screw speeds of 50, 100, and 150 rpm, and cooling times of 60, 180, and 300 s. Injection used 200 bar for 15 s followed by 150 bar for 10 s. Their preferred validation combination used the lower 140-145 °C profile, an 80 °C mold, 50 rpm screw speed, and 60 s cooling; combinations above 160 °C or with low mold temperature produced deterioration or defective specimens. This window applies only to that grade, machine, and study geometry.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The chain contains both short hydroxybutyrate and longer-side-chain hydroxyhexanoate units connected by ester bonds. The longer side chain disrupts packing in the PHB crystal lattice, reducing the ability of selected compositions to crystallize in the same way as PHB. The amount and distribution of hydroxyhexanoate influence the resulting crystalline and amorphous regions. Cooling and subsequent storage also affect the morphology of a finished article. As the packing of the short-side-chain segments changes, the relative amounts of ordered material and more mobile regions can change. The final structure depends on cooling and aging as well as the repeat-unit fraction.
sections.properties: Increasing the hydroxyhexanoate fraction can make selected copolymers softer and more extensible while lowering crystallinity and melting temperature relative to a PHB-rich material. The relationship is composition and preparation dependent: the reviewed literature includes samples with different molecular weights and processing histories as well as different comonomer fractions. Flexibility, heat resistance and other properties should therefore be checked for the selected grade rather than assumed from the PHBHHx name. Additives and blending can further change the response. The cited review lists a 0.1 mm film with 10 mol% hydroxyhexanoate at 400% elongation at break and another with 15 mol% at 760%; their reported molecular weights also differ. This comparison illustrates the range of reported responses but does not isolate comonomer fraction as the sole cause.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Kaneka's PHBH polymer is used in straws, cutlery, coffee capsules, bags and films for food-service and packaging applications. The copolymer's adjustable flexibility helps explain its use in articles with different form requirements, though a commercial finished product has its own grade and formulation. A bag or film and a molded item also impose different forming and mechanical requirements. Kaneka and JALUX also reported a reusable side-dish container for international in-flight meals in 2024.

Purchasing. Kaneka Green Planet provides an industrial PHBH supplier channel for converters. Buyers should specify the intended grade, processing method and any other blend ingredients rather than assuming every Green Planet article is neat copolymer.

Scale and evidence limits. In February 2022 Kaneka reported 5,000 tonnes/year existing capacity and announced an additional 15,000 tonnes/year planned at Takasago, Japan. The combined 20,000-tonne/year figure was a dated capacity target, not measured annual production or proof that the expansion was completed.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Microorganisms can colonize and erode PHBH films; breakdown of ester-containing chains can produce smaller compounds that microbes may use. One harbor-water study found different bacterial communities on intact versus visibly broken PHBH films, suggesting that the community changed as degradation progressed. The authors sampled biofilms from the different film states to compare the associated communities. It did not establish a complete soluble-product inventory.

Timescales: In nutrient-amended Takasago harbor seawater incubated at 23 °C with shaking, approximately 100 µm PHBH films formed biofilms after one month in samples collected in March and April; one April sample was partly degraded. In a separate June water sample, tested PHBH films were mostly or partly degraded after two weeks. These are visual biofilm and film-breakdown observations for the stated incubations, not mineralization times.

Environmental persistence: Seasonal source-water differences, nutrient addition, film thickness and shaking limit transfer of this laboratory result to open-ocean conditions or thicker articles. Disintegration or microbial colonization alone does not show complete conversion of the polymer to CO₂.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Kaneka reported that a Green Planet side-dish container was designed for reuse in international in-flight meals from June 2024. Reusing an intact container is different from recovering the polymer as a raw material.

In a separate 2024 announcement, Kaneka described a planned on-site composting demonstration for PHBH straws used at Japanese model schools. The announcement describes a proposed biological-treatment route and does not report the completed outcome or a general composting time. Neither example demonstrates monomer recovery from mixed waste.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PHBH intended for biomedical use requires control of impurities from microbial production, especially bacterial endotoxin released during recovery. The PHA review emphasizes purification and material-dependent host responses. Reported compatibility of selected films or scaffolds is evidence for those preparations, not authorization of every polymer grade or device.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PHBHHx describes a family of copolymers, not one fixed hydroxyhexanoate content or molecular weight. The production organism and feed conditions influence composition, while cooling, crystallinity and additives affect the finished article. Reports of greater flexibility at higher hydroxyhexanoate content are not universal numerical specifications. Degradation evidence must also retain specimen geometry, formulation and the conditions and microorganisms of the test. Even two films in the same literature table differ in molecular weight as well as comonomer content, making a simple composition-only causal interpretation unsafe. Mechanical comparisons need the film thickness, fabrication and test conditions.

sections.overview: Polylactide (PLA) is a family of aliphatic polyesters built from lactate-derived repeat units. A common route makes the polymer from lactide, the cyclic dimer of lactic acid. Its L- and D-configured units and their arrangement influence whether a given chain can pack into crystals, so PLA is not one fixed material. Different grades serve packaging, fibers, 3D-printing filament and biomedical research.
sections.history: Polylactide’s development predates its modern packaging market. George Lowrance Dorough’s DuPont patent, filed in 1931 and issued in 1935, documents lactide resins for coating compositions and cellulose-derivative formulations. Allan K. Schneider’s DuPont work, filed in 1951 and patented in 1955, advanced stronger polymers from purified high-melting lactide. The later growth of large-scale fermentation and polymer manufacture changed the economics: NatureWorks dates its Blair, Nebraska plant to 2002. Its Ingeo materials expanded into packaging, food-service ware, fibers, durable goods and 3D-printing filament. These milestones distinguish early resin chemistry from subsequent industrial scale and application development.
sections.nomenclature: PLA and poly(lactic acid) identify the polylactide family, not one stereochemical form, molecular weight, or compounded grade. A plasticized, blended, or reactively modified PLA is a formulation based on the family and should retain those additions in its material description.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polylactides are most commonly made by ring-opening polymerization of lactide, the cyclic dimer derived from lactic acid. Lactic acid is first oligomerized by water removal and the oligomer is depolymerized to lactide; purification and selection of L-lactide, D-lactide, or meso-lactide establish the stereochemical feed. Bulk or solution ring-opening polymerization then uses a catalyst or organocatalyst, usually with an alcohol initiator or chain-transfer agent. Tin(II) 2-ethylhexanoate is a widely used manufacturing catalyst, while zinc-, aluminum-, and organic bases provide alternatives. The cited patent describes the lactic-acid-to-lactide sequence and metal-catalyzed ring opening. A distinct patent demonstrates controlled lactide polymerization with an organic guanidine/alcohol pair. Lactide stereochemistry, monomer-to-initiator ratio, catalyst, and racemization control determine molar mass, end groups, and whether the product is PLLA, PDLA, stereoblock material, or a stereochemically mixed PLA; direct condensation of lactic acid is a lower-molar-mass route variant.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PLA can be relatively stiff and strong but brittle in a glassy state; stereochemistry, molar mass, crystallinity, thermal and ageing history, orientation, strain rate, and blend, plasticizer, or filler formulation can each change the stiffness–ductility balance. An open review identifies this brittleness as the principal mechanical limitation and discusses plasticization, blending, and reactive compounding as routes to tougher formulations. As one tightly bounded example, Ingeo 3051D PLA pellets were hot-pressed into 100 μm films at 190 °C (5 min melt, then 0.5 MPa for 3 min) and water-cooled; room-temperature dog-bone tensile tests at 0.003–0.01 s⁻¹ gave a Young’s modulus of 4.4 GPa and showed yield followed by post-yield softening. That value is for this hot-pressed commercial film and its rate window, not a PLA-family range or a substitute for molded, printed, oriented, or compounded grades.
sections.processing:
Polylactides (PLA) can be converted by injection molding; profile, sheet, cast-film, and blown-film extrusion; injection-stretch and other blow molding; thermoforming; foaming; fiber and nonwoven spinning; melt compounding; compression molding; solvent casting and electrospinning; and fused-filament fabrication. Grade selection is inseparable from route selection because molecular mass, melt-flow rate, D-lactide content, branching, crystallization rate, and additives determine melt strength, drawability, cycle time, and achievable heat resistance. Pellets should be protected from atmospheric moisture and normally dried before melt conversion: water, heat, oxygen, and shear can reduce molecular mass and viscosity. Melt temperature and residence should therefore be kept only as high and long as the grade and operation require, with planned low-temperature purging or shutdown during interruptions. Screw design and speed, mixing sequence, die pressure, draw or blow-up ratio, mold or chill-roll temperature, cooling, annealing, and uniaxial or biaxial orientation govern crystallinity, shrinkage, warpage, gauge, interlayer bonding, and anisotropy.

NatureWorks' Best Practices guide is supplier guidance for Ingeo resins, not every PLA: it recommends drying before extrusion or injection molding, cool dry storage below 50 °C, minimizing pellet exposure, and recognizing that even an interruption shorter than two hours at a controlled temperature below 240 °C can reduce molecular mass and viscosity. Naser, Deiab, and Darras independently document the broader PLA route set and distinguish amorphous from semicrystalline grades. For a bounded injection example, Liparoti, Speranza, and Pantani molded NatureWorks PLA 3251D and 4032D at a 200 °C melt temperature, 2.8 cm3/s average flow rate, and 8 s hold; their trials used 30 or 63 MPa holding pressure and rapidly modulated the instrumented cavity surface from a 30 °C passive condition to selected 50, 100, or 150 °C levels for 1, 8, or 13 s. Those values belong to the two named grades, microfeature mold, and replication experiment rather than defining a family-wide PLA window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PLA chains contain ester-linked lactate units with L or D stereochemistry. More regular sequences can crystallize, while stereochemical irregularity can disrupt packing; cooling rate and annealing influence how much order develops in an article. Films, fibers and molded parts can therefore have different crystalline and oriented structures even when derived from similar resin. Blends and additives introduce further phases and interfaces.
sections.properties: Many PLA grades are stiff but relatively brittle. In one tensile comparison, a melt-blended material containing 90 wt% PLA and 10 wt% PBAT reached a strain at break of 136.2 ± 53.4%, compared with 7.0 ± 1.0% for the neat PLA; its modulus fell from 2.04 to 1.64 GPa. The reported specimens and preparation determine this result, and another PLA/PBAT study observed little ductility increase while PLA remained the main phase. Glass transition, crystallinity, testing rate and article processing also affect the mechanical response.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PLA grades are used in food-service articles, packaging, coffee capsules, fibers, tea bags, appliances and 3D-printing filament. Producers select different grades for extrusion, film, fibers or injection molding because the required processing and article performance differ. For example, NatureWorks describes its Ingeo 2003D as a transparent extrusion and thermoforming grade, used as supplied or in a formulated blend. Its grade comparison lists a heat-distortion temperature of about 55 °C under the stated test conditions, so thermal service requirements still matter. A fabricated filament or package may also contain additives that are not described by the PLA name alone.

Purchasing. NatureWorks provides regional purchasing routes for its Ingeo resin grades, with separate series for extrusion, molding, films, fibers and 3D printing. Converters buy resin for processing, whereas a printer user may buy a converted filament; the grade and product form should accompany the purchase.

Scale and evidence limits. NatureWorks reported a 150,000-tonne/year nameplate capacity at its Blair, Nebraska plant in 2013, reiterated in 2021. That is a dated capacity for one plant, not worldwide PLA consumption, current realized production or the output of a particular stereochemical grade.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Water can cleave PLA ester bonds to shorter lactyl chains and lactic acid. The rate depends on temperature, water access, crystallinity, article dimensions and composition. A heated laboratory reaction on PLLA demonstrates this chemistry for one PLA family member; it does not establish that the whole family breaks down at the same rate.

Timescales: In a California seawater study, PLA textile samples showed no visible degradation during 231 days in field exposure and remained similar after extension to 428 days in flow-through aquariums. The observation concerns that textile and those conditions, not an exact time to disappearance or mineralization. By contrast, a standard laboratory compost test of PLA powder at 58 ± 2 °C found approximately 88% biodegradation by CO₂ evolution after 90 days. Powder in a controlled mature compost is not the same article or environment as a textile in seawater.

Environmental persistence: Industrial compostability and marine behavior are separate questions. Visible integrity, chain cleavage and CO₂ evolution are different endpoints; the seawater study does not establish complete mineralization or an environmental lifetime for all PLA products.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Mechanical reprocessing can be limited by heat- or moisture-driven chain degradation, while industrial composting and chemical hydrolysis pursue different outcomes. In a laboratory microwave-assisted process, researchers treated flakes from a postconsumer PLLA cup with water and a zinc catalyst; at 150 °C for two hours with 15 water equivalents, they reported a 98% lactic-acid yield by NMR. This recovers a small-molecule feedstock from one PLLA article, rather than mechanically recovering intact PLA chains.

The laboratory reaction does not establish commercial mixed-waste collection or identical conversion of all PLA formulations. Composting acceptance and conditions likewise depend on the specific article and facility.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For implanted PLA, hydrolysis and accumulation of acidic degradation products can affect local tissue responses. Stereochemistry, crystallinity, geometry and degradation rate influence the exposure. The biomaterials literature therefore treats compatibility as a property of a particular device and degradation environment, rather than an unconditional property of the polymer name.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PLA alone does not specify stereochemical composition, molecular weight, crystallinity, additives or article geometry. The degree of toughening in a blend depends on dispersed-phase morphology and preparation as well as composition: two experimental PLA/PBAT series did not show the same ductility response at low PBAT contents. Cooling and storage change crystallization, while a clear film and a fiber can have different processing histories. Degradation results likewise need the formulation and exposure conditions.

sections.overview: Poly(L-lactide), or PLLA, is a stereoregular member of the polylactide family made predominantly from L-configured lactate units. It can be prepared by ring-opening polymerization of L-lactide. Its regular chain can crystallize, though the final morphology depends on processing and thermal history. PLLA is supplied for particular medical-material uses and is studied in fibers and tissue-engineering scaffolds. Its ester backbone can be hydrolyzed, but loss of chain length, mechanical function and material mass can occur on different timescales. Those distinctions matter when a medical part must provide support before it loses integrity. The stereochemical name alone does not specify a particular device or a rate of resorption.
sections.history: Poly(L-lactide)’s medical development is documented in Allan K. Schneider’s Ethicon patent on polylactide sutures. Issued in 1972, it traces related applications back to 1962 and describes drawing and annealing L-lactide-polymer filaments to obtain absorbable surgical materials. The program addressed the handling, strength and dimensional stability needed for tissue joining. It also covered lactide/glycolide copolymers, which must be distinguished from PLLA homopolymer. This provides a dated application-development milestone for the stereoregular polymer; it is not a claim that PLLA was first synthesized in 1962 or that all modern PLA packaging grades are pure PLLA.
sections.nomenclature: PLLA and poly(L-lactic acid) identify the L-lactide-derived member of the broader polylactide family. The name is narrower than unqualified PLA and should not be used for D-lactide, meso-lactide, racemic, or stereoblock materials; a blend or crosslinked scaffold is a separately qualified formulation.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(L-lactide) (PLLA) is the stereodefined polylactide made principally by ring-opening polymerization of enantiopure L-lactide, the cyclic dimer associated with L-lactic acid. Industrial and laboratory routes use catalyst/initiator systems such as tin octanoate, whereas alternative metal complexes can control the opening and stereochemical sequence. Monomer stereochemical purity is central to the PLLA boundary: L-lactide gives the L-rich chain, while meso-lactide or racemic D/L-lactide feeds introduce stereochemical defects or different PLA microstructures rather than simply providing equivalent PLLA feedstock. An open study of L-lactide/meso-lactide mixtures contrasts conventional tin-octanoate melt ROP with a zirconium catalyst that directs stereogradient structures. A separate review documents how the S,S, R,R, meso, and racemic lactide feeds, together with catalyst stereoselectivity, give isotactic, atactic, heterotactic, or syndiotactic poly(lactide) microstructures. These are polymer-formation controls, not molding or annealing instructions.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PLLA is a semicrystalline aliphatic polyester whose tensile and impact response is governed by stereochemical purity, molar mass, crystallinity and crystal form, thermal/aging history, orientation, temperature and rate, and any blend, plasticizer, or filler. These variables can trade stiffness and strength against ductility; porous biomedical scaffolds are additionally controlled by pore structure and porosity. In an open RSC study, NatureWorks 4032D PLLA was vacuum dried, melt-mixed at 190 °C, then injection molded at 200 °C melt and 60 °C mold temperatures. For the neat PLLA control, tested at room temperature under ASTM D638 at 5 mm/min and averaged over at least five specimens, the reported tensile strength was 64.9 ± 2.7 MPa, elongation at break 8.0 ± 0.9%, tensile modulus 2001.6 ± 71.0 MPa, and notched Izod impact strength 16.9 ± 1.4 J/m. This is an injection-molded, high-molar-mass control after that study's thermal history, not a family-wide PLLA range. A separate open review reports that scaffold response varies especially strongly with molecular weight, crystallinity, aging, microstructure, and porosity, so scaffold values must not be compared directly with the molded control.
sections.processing:
PLLA can be melt-extruded, injection or compression molded, thermoformed, melt-spun and drawn, solvent-cast, electrospun, phase-separated into porous scaffolds, and additively manufactured by filament extrusion or melt electrowriting. Hydrolytic sensitivity makes pellet drying important before melt conversion. Melt temperature, shear and residence time must limit molar-mass loss, while mold/bed temperature and cooling determine crystallization, warpage, shrinkage, heat resistance, and interlayer bonding. Solution routes additionally require control of concentration, solvent removal, porosity, and residual solvent; fiber and printed routes depend on draw or raster orientation.

Krug, Zarges, and Heim give a bounded injection-molding comparison of three named PLLA materials. They vacuum-dried Luminy L130 for 4 h at 100 °C and NP HT 202/203 for 4 h at 60 °C. Luminy L130 used a 205/205/215/215 °C barrel-to-nozzle profile, a 40 °C mold, 40 s cooling, and 50.8 s total cycle; the two NP grades used 175/180/185/185 °C and a 25 °C mold, with grade-specific cooling and cycle times. These are specimen-preparation settings for those grades and that Arburg machine; stereochemistry, nucleation, additives, moisture, geometry, and desired crystallinity can require different conditions.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PLLA chains contain predominantly L-configured lactate units linked by ester bonds. Their regularity permits crystalline regions, but rapid cooling can leave more disordered material and annealing or drawing can change crystal content and orientation. A porous scaffold adds pore geometry and interfaces on top of this molecular structure. Molecular weight, processing and residual additives therefore matter alongside stereochemistry. In one hydrolysis comparison, laboratory PLLA began with higher crystallinity than a commercial PLA sample containing 4.5% D-lactide units. Their molecular-weight distributions also differed, so the comparison does not isolate crystallinity alone.
sections.properties: PLLA can provide a stiff, strong framework but unmodified material may be brittle. Crystal content and chain orientation influence its mechanical and thermal response; a review describes a glass transition around 60 °C and melting around 170–180 °C for PLLA, with variation from molecular and material factors. These review values are context, not a universal specification for every grade. Hydrolysis reduces molecular weight and can change a device's strength before all of the polymer disappears. In that comparison, the number-average molecular weight of the laboratory PLLA fell to 61% of its initial value after 28 days in phosphate buffer at 37 °C. This is chain-length change in a specified laboratory specimen, not a measured loss of mechanical strength or a device lifetime.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Medical-material PLLA grades are used or investigated for orthopedic screws, nails and anchors, vascular-device development and dermal fillers. Their ability to provide initial structural support and undergo gradual hydrolysis makes degradation behavior a design consideration, alongside strength and device geometry. A specified medical-device material is different from generic printing PLA, and suitability requires evidence for the finished product. Component shape, initial strength and the pace of hydrolysis all matter to whether a selected material is appropriate for an intended use.

Purchasing. Evonik identifies RESOMER L 210 S as a PLLA homopolymer supplied as granules or chips and offers samples by request. Buyers specify polymer identity, molecular-size or viscosity grade, and the quality and device requirements relevant to their application.

Scale and evidence limits. The grade listing documents a supply form but does not report annual PLLA purchases or medical-device demand. Capacity figures for broad commodity PLA do not quantify the market for this particular medical material.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Water cleaves PLLA ester linkages, producing shorter lactyl chains and ultimately lactic acid. The resulting reduction in molecular weight can precede the loss of visible integrity, which matters for a load-bearing scaffold or device. Exposure temperature, water access, crystallinity and geometry affect the course of the reaction.

Timescales: A laboratory study treated postconsumer PLLA cup flakes with water and a zinc catalyst under microwave heating. At 150 °C for two hours with 15 water equivalents per lactyl unit, it reported a 98% lactic-acid yield calculated by NMR. These heated reactor conditions are not an implant-resorption or ambient environmental timescale. In a different study, laboratory PLLA retained 61% of its initial number-average molecular weight after 28 days in phosphate buffer at 37 °C. A commercial PLA comparison had 24% remaining, but also differed in D-unit content, molecular-weight distribution and crystallinity. The measurement follows chain length, not complete disappearance of the material.

Environmental persistence: Chemical conversion in a reactor is different from mineralization in soil, freshwater or seawater. The cited experiment does not establish a transferable environmental lifetime for PLLA articles.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The microwave-assisted laboratory process chemically hydrolyzed a postconsumer PLLA cup into lactic acid using water and a zinc complex. The researchers analyzed conversion and product yield by NMR; the product is a small-molecule feedstock, not the intact starting polymer.

The test used a specified cup-derived feedstock and controlled reaction, and it does not establish a commercial collection system or performance for all additives, mixed waste or medical devices.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For implanted PLLA, hydrolysis and accumulation of acidic degradation products can affect local tissue responses. Stereochemistry, crystallinity, geometry and degradation rate influence the exposure. The biomaterials literature therefore treats compatibility as a property of a particular device and degradation environment, rather than an unconditional property of the polymer name.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Stereochemistry alone does not specify PLLA molecular weight, residual monomer, crystallinity or end groups. Processing and aging change the structure, and a porous scaffold, oriented fiber and molded medical component have different geometries. Sterilization and exposure may further alter an individual article. A laboratory recycling reaction or an implant test cannot be generalized to all PLLA products or environments. The laboratory PLLA and commercial PLA comparison differed in both stereochemical content and molecular-weight distribution, in addition to crystallinity. A result for those samples cannot be assigned solely to one factor or extended to every PLLA grade.
