sections.overview: Poly(glycolic acid), or PGA, is an aliphatic polyester made from glycolate-derived repeat units. It can be produced by ring-opening polymerization of glycolide, a cyclic dimer. Its regular chains pack into crystalline regions, and ester bonds can be cleaved by water. PGA is used in absorbable medical materials and supplied for industrial articles including downhole tools; a biomedical grade and an industrial compound are different products. The same ester chemistry that enables gradual hydrolysis also makes moisture control important during storage and processing. In an intended temporary component, the initial mechanical function and the later loss of integrity must be considered together. Fiber, solid downhole component and medical material are distinct forms with different specifications.
sections.history: A pivotal application of polyglycolic acid was the synthetic absorbable suture. Edward Emil Schmitt and Rocco Albert Polistina filed American Cyanamid’s surgical-suture patent in 1963; it was granted in 1967. The work addressed the need for reproducible fibers that could hold tissue and subsequently be absorbed, a different milestone from the polymer’s first chemical preparation. Later material development broadened beyond surgical thread. Kureha’s Kuredux technical literature documents commercial PGA resins for films, molded parts and bottle applications, including grades with controlled hydrolysis. The polymer’s history thus spans medically useful degradation and the development of processable barrier materials.
sections.nomenclature: PGA abbreviates poly(glycolic acid), also called polyglycolide. The name denotes the glycolic-acid homopolyester and is distinct from copolymers such as PLGA.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(glycolic acid) (PGA, also polyglycolide) is the aliphatic polyester derived from glycolic acid or, for common high-molar-mass routes, glycolide, its cyclic dimer. Direct melt polycondensation of glycolic acid removes water but is usually limited in molar mass by water removal and the glycolide/polymer equilibrium. High-molar-mass PGA is instead commonly made by ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of purified glycolide; monomer free-acid/water content, catalyst loading, initiator, and thermal history are consequential route controls. One free-access study reports sequential melt–solid glycolide ROP using tin(II) chloride dihydrate and 1-dodecanol; catalyst and initiator concentrations were associated with polymerization rate, end groups, and molar mass. That is a process-specific example, not an assertion that all PGA uses that tin catalyst or an alcohol initiator. PGA is a homopolymer; lactide-containing materials are PLGA/PLA-related copolymers rather than alternate names for PGA.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PGA is a stiff, semicrystalline aliphatic polyester whose practical tensile response is sensitive to molar mass and chain architecture, crystallinity and orientation, thermal and molding history, and hydrolytic moisture exposure. Drawing can substantially increase oriented-specimen strength, while chain extension or branching, blends, and nucleating or toughening additives trade stiffness against ductility; water uptake and hydrolysis make wet or aged results unsuitable as dry-material constants. In one open injection-molding study, neat PGA had a tensile modulus of 6412.10 MPa and elongation at break of 9.8%; adding 0.9 phr of a multifunctional epoxy chain extender produced a modified PGA with 8372.40 MPa modulus and 57.2% elongation. Those values are specific to the study's injection-molded neat and chain-extended formulations and should not be presented as general PGA values. An independent open molecular-dynamics tensile study examined PGA model systems with 1.7%, 2.9%, and 5% water by mass, providing a separate, model-scale indication that water content is a mechanical variable rather than a transferable bulk-test endpoint.
sections.processing:
Poly(glycolic acid) (PGA) can be melt extruded or coextruded into mono- and multilayer film or sheet, injection molded, thermoformed, laminated, and biaxially stretched or stretch-blow molded; drawn monofilament and multifilament are also established article forms. Because PGA is hydrolysis-sensitive, moisture control continues from bag opening through the hopper, and insufficient drying lowers melt viscosity and can compound thermal degradation. Short melt residence, prompt purging after an interruption, moderate screw compression, and controlled cooling/orientation are important because melt degradation, crystallization, and draw history strongly affect the finished article.

Kureha's November 2011 Kuredux technical guide gives grade-family starting guidance, not a universal PGA window: re-dry opened resin at 120 °C for 12 h with −40 °C-dew-point dry air (not more than 24 h), and reject as a starting point resin left about 4 h at 23 °C/60% RH. It lists extrusion zones of 220–240 °C feed, 230–260 °C compression, 250–270 °C metering, and 240–270 °C adapter/die, with a warning not to exceed 280 °C. For its ASTM-family-mold test piece it reports a 230–270 °C cylinder, 90–120 °C mold, 50–100 MPa injection pressure, and 2–3 m/min injection speed. Independently, Gao and co-workers dried one supplied PGA at 60 °C for 8 h, mixed it with 0–0.9 phr Joncryl ADR-4370s at 235 °C and 50 rpm for 10 min, and injection molded that formulation; prolonged 235 °C mixing reduced neat-PGA torque, directly illustrating residence-time degradation. Both schedules remain tied to their named grade or experiment.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PGA's repeating ester chain lacks the methyl side group found on lactate units in PLA. Its relatively regular structure allows chains to pack into crystalline regions alongside less ordered material. Molecular weight, cooling, orientation and processing affect the structure of a particular article. The balance of ordered and disordered regions influences water access and the subsequent degradation response. In a separate research example, recycled PGA was electrospun into fine fibers and twisted into yarns; adding graphene oxide or carbon nanotubes produced composite yarns with their own morphology. Their fiber diameter and filler interfaces add structural variables beyond the crystallinity of neat PGA.
sections.properties: PGA is a stiff polyester with useful gas-barrier performance in suitable forms, but its ester linkages are susceptible to hydrolysis. Water exposure can reduce molecular weight and ultimately affect strength; crystallinity and article thickness influence how water reaches the chains. A manufacturer describes high strength and abrasion resistance for its Kuredux industrial material, properties that help motivate downhole components. Those product-specific characteristics are not a mechanical specification for every PGA grade. In that laboratory yarn study, the composite containing 3 wt% graphene oxide had a reported tensile strength of 21.36 MPa and elastic modulus of 259.51 MPa. Those values describe the electrospun, twisted composite, not a strength specification for neat PGA resin or a machined plug.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PGA is used in absorbable medical materials and in industrial components where hydrolysis is useful. Kureha describes its Kuredux resin for downhole tools, including machined balls and plugs used in shale oil and gas extraction; its mechanical strength supports the initial function, while degradation is relevant to the temporary tool. A separate laboratory study used recycled PGA to make electrospun yarns with graphene oxide or carbon nanotubes, exploring possible temporary textile and downhole uses. This composite is a research example rather than a commercial product claim. The supplier distinguishes industrial Kuredux from separately qualified biomedical PGA.

Purchasing. Kureha offers Kuredux resin and describes downstream forms including extruded bars and machined balls; purchasers contact a representative for the application-specific material. A medical user needs a separately specified biomedical grade and finished-device requirements, not an assumed equivalence with the industrial product.

Scale and evidence limits. A September 2011 supplier announcement stated that the Belle, West Virginia plant had begun commercial production and was expected to produce 4,000 tonnes/year. This is a dated expected plant output, not verified realized output or present global PGA demand.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Water cleaves PGA ester bonds, producing shorter glycolate chains and glycolic-acid-containing products. In a distinct heated depolymerization process, PGA can instead generate glycolide, a cyclic dimer that can be recovered by distillation. The product and mechanism depend on the process conditions.

Timescales: One biomedical study prepared hydrolyzed PGA by holding it in buffered solution for three to four days at 4 °C before examining its interaction with human serum. That pretreatment is an experimental condition, not a measured complete degradation time. In a different study, electrospun yarn made from recycled PGA lost about 30% of its mass after 24 hours in distilled water at 60 °C; nanocarbon-containing composite yarns showed less mass loss. This comparison describes small, engineered yarns in heated water, not all PGA materials or natural waters. A separately described high-temperature glycolide recovery route is likewise not an ambient environmental test.

Environmental persistence: Hydrolysis, material failure and eventual microbial mineralization are different endpoints. The cited buffer and reactor studies do not establish a transferable mineralization time for PGA articles in soil, freshwater or seawater.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A patent application proposes heating PGA with a polyethylene glycol ether to depolymerize it and distilling the resulting glycolide with solvent, followed by recovery from the distillate. The patent describes the method for glycolic-acid oligomers and also identifies high-molecular-weight PGA product waste and molding scrap as possible feedstocks. The resulting glycolide is a chemical building block rather than the intact starting polymer.

A patent and its examples do not establish that a municipal PGA recycling stream operates or that every contaminated product can be processed in this way.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PGA biomaterials require evaluation of the complete implant and its degradation products. The reviewed polyester studies link degradation rate and local acidic products to inflammation and cell response; scaffold architecture and release rate change the exposure. Biodegradability alone is not evidence of compatibility for every site, dose or formulation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PGA's molecular weight, crystallinity, residual moisture and article geometry affect processing and performance. Exposure to water during storage or use can change chain length and strength, and temperature and pH further influence hydrolysis. Medical materials, downhole compounds and copolymers with lactide are not interchangeable. Data for a specified product and test should not be generalized to all PGA articles. The electrospun yarn experiment also shows how the form and added filler affect both mechanical properties and water exposure. An industrial downhole component is not interchangeable with a fine research yarn or a medical suture.

sections.overview: Poly(lactide-co-glycolide), or PLGA, is a copolyester containing both lactate- and glycolate-derived units. It is used in controlled-release formulations and studied for particles, implants and scaffolds. The lactide-to-glycolide ratio affects water uptake and hydrolysis, while molecular weight and end groups also influence behavior. A drug-loaded particle or device is a formulated article, not simply a PLGA resin. Water uptake and cleavage of ester bonds can change the matrix that holds a drug. Release is a property of the complete formulation as well as the polymer: particle size, drug distribution and preparation all matter. A copolymer ratio does not identify one release rate or environmental fate.
sections.history: Lactide/glycolide copolymers were part of the development of synthetic absorbable surgical materials during the 1960s. Allan K. Schneider’s Ethicon patent, issued in 1972 with related applications dating to 1962, describes lactide-rich copolymers containing glycolide for sutures and other tissue-supporting devices. Extrusion, drawing and annealing were integral to turning the polymer into a useful fiber. This documents one early application lineage within PLGA, whose composition can vary widely. It should not be interpreted as a first synthesis date for every lactide/glycolide ratio or as evidence that all PLGA grades behave like the specific suture compositions.
sections.nomenclature: PLGA abbreviates poly(lactide-co-glycolide). The name describes a composition-variable copolymer family, not a single fixed lactide:glycolide ratio, and it is distinct from PLA and PGA homopolymers.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) is a copolyester made by ring-opening copolymerization of lactide and glycolide, not a physical blend of preformed PLA and PGA. The lactide stereoisomer, lactide:glycolide feed and incorporation ratio, catalyst/initiator choice, monomer-to-catalyst ratio, temperature, and conversion all affect the resulting chain composition and molar mass. A high-glycolide study polymerized d,l-lactide and glycolide with tin(II) 2-ethylhexanoate and 1-dodecanol, then varied initiator/catalyst concentration, temperature, and time; its 25:75 L:G material is a composition-specific example. A separate open study emphasizes that high-molar-mass PLGA is obtained by cyclic-dimer ROP rather than direct lactic-acid/glycolic-acid polycondensation, and explicitly evaluates lactide-content variation. Thus PLLA, PGA, and PLGA are related but distinct scopes, and neither a bulk polymerization recipe nor a particle formulation should be generalized to all PLGA compositions.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PLGA is a composition-variable copolyester rather than a single mechanical material. Lactide:glycolide ratio, sequence distribution, molar mass and end groups, crystallinity, thermal and solvent-casting history, orientation, porosity, hydration, and hydrolytic aging all change tensile response. An open review specifically reports that raising glycolide content relative to a more lactide-rich PLGA tends to increase brittleness and lower tensile strength, so named ratios should not be collapsed into one PLGA range. In a separate open thin-film study, solvent-cast PLGA containing 30% glycolide reached a tensile strength of up to 58 MPa; the paper contrasts this result with separately cast PLLA and PDLA films. That endpoint is limited to the reported cast-film composition and study preparation; the available result does not establish a universal PLGA value or a value for a hydrated implant, porous scaffold, or degradatively aged specimen.
sections.processing:
Poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) is article-converted by melt injection molding and fiber forming, as well as by solvent casting, particulate-leached casting, emulsion/solvent evaporation, electrospinning, and formulation-specific thermal gelation or photocuring for porous carriers and hydrogels. Solvent routes require complete dissolution and dispersion, controlled casting or droplet/fiber formation, solvent evaporation, and, where applicable, leaching and final drying. Copolymer ratio, molecular mass, end groups, drug/filler content, residual solvent, and thermal history all change viscosity, glass transition, degradation, and solidification, so conditions must be attached to a grade and article geometry.

A bounded injection-molding study used Purasorb PLG 8531, an 85:15 lactide:glycolide grade, in an Arburg 270S/250-70 machine. Four conditions combined melt temperatures of 240 or 210 °C with volumetric flow rates of 25 or 10 cm³/s; the fixed settings included a 25 °C mold, 25 MPa holding pressure, 2 s injection, 90 s cooling, and 100 rpm screw speed. The lower-temperature conditions produced broader birefringence and greater residual stress, while flow rate changed shear, molecular orientation, and failure strain. Those values describe the cited small notched and unnotched test specimens, not all PLGA ratios or medical devices; they also show why rapid cooling, gate/geometry, shear, and post-molding stress cannot be separated from nominal melt temperature.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PLGA chains contain lactate and glycolate ester units in proportions set by synthesis. Their ratio, stereochemistry and sequence distribution influence how chains pack; many drug-delivery grades are amorphous, while particular compositions can crystallize. Particle size, pores and interfaces add larger-scale structure to a formulation. Different water-access paths through these structures affect degradation and release. Water can enter through pores and interfaces, while acidic fragments generated inside a particle or device may remain locally concentrated. This makes a thick device, a porous particle and a thin film different physical systems even when their nominal composition is similar.
sections.properties: Water can cleave PLGA's ester linkages, reducing molecular weight and producing lactate- and glycolate-derived oligomers and acids. Changes in molecular weight and particle structure can influence both mechanical integrity and drug release. Glycolate-rich compositions are often more water-accessible than lactate-rich ones, but crystallinity, molecular weight and end groups complicate any simple ranking. A formulation's release behavior also depends on its incorporated drug, geometry and preparation. In one soil comparison at 25 °C, particles with 12/88 and 6/94 lactate/glycolate ratios reached 37 ± 2% and 53 ± 9% conversion to CO₂ after 53 days, respectively. Their crystallinity also differed, and water-hydrolysis results followed a different ordering at longer times. This illustrates why composition and physical structure must be considered together, not as a single universal ranking.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PLGA excipients are used in controlled-release parenteral drug formulations and investigated in other delivery systems. Hydrolysis and water transport can change the polymer matrix over time, allowing a formulation designer to adjust release behavior by selecting copolymer composition, end groups and molecular size. Water entering a formulation can change the polymer matrix and create paths for the incorporated drug to leave; the actual release profile also depends on loading and particle design. The complete drug product and its clinical performance must be considered separately from the polymer grade.

Purchasing. Evonik identifies RESOMER RG 502 as a solvent-purified 50:50 D,L-lactide/glycolide copolymer with ester end groups, supplied as a white to off-white solid; samples and technical supply are available by inquiry. Developers should specify the actual grade and the requirements of their formulation.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked grade listing establishes an available excipient but does not provide a standard lot mass or separate annual PLGA consumption. No reliable material-specific purchase total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Water hydrolyzes PLGA ester bonds into shorter oligomers and ultimately lactate- and glycolate-derived acids. In a controlled study, hydrolysis products included lactate dimers and trimers. The presence of short oligomers can therefore precede measurable mineralization. Release of smaller molecules and subsequent biological mineralization are distinct steps.

Timescales: In soil respirometry at 25 °C, particles of PLGA12/88 and PLGA6/94 reached 37 ± 2% and 53 ± 9% conversion to CO₂, respectively, after 53 days. The ratios denote lactate/glycolate composition, and the result applies to those prepared particles and that soil. In a separate water-hydrolysis comparison, crystallinity helped explain why the ordering of the two rates changed over longer periods.

Environmental persistence: The soil study demonstrates partial carbon conversion under defined conditions; it does not give the lifetime of all copolymers, implants or marine debris. Composition, crystallinity, microorganisms and article geometry can change the result.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
The appropriate waste pathway for a PLGA-containing healthcare product depends on the complete formulation and its use. WHO guidance distinguishes pharmaceutical, infectious and other hazardous healthcare wastes from ordinary non-hazardous waste; residual drug or contamination may therefore determine handling.

This is healthcare waste management, not evidence that PLGA chains are recycled. The polymer's ability to hydrolyze does not by itself establish a collection, composting or material-recovery route for used drug-delivery articles.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PLGA biomaterials require evaluation of the complete implant and its degradation products. The reviewed polyester studies link degradation rate and local acidic products to inflammation and cell response; scaffold architecture and release rate change the exposure. Biodegradability alone is not evidence of compatibility for every site, dose or formulation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: A monomer ratio alone does not specify PLGA sequence, stereochemistry, molecular weight, end groups or crystallinity. Acidic products may accumulate locally and influence hydrolysis, while particle size, porosity, sterilization and storage affect the response. In one soil study, 12/88 and 6/94 lactate/glycolate particles behaved differently, but the two materials also differed in crystallinity. Neither that comparison nor a release study defines a universal degradation profile for all devices. The reported CO₂ production describes particles in one soil test, whereas drug release depends on a formulated payload and its geometry. Neither value by itself measures the performance of a particular approved medicine.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Ring-opening copolymerization incorporates lactyl and glycolyl units in one chain. An oxygen nucleophile attacks a cyclic-ester carbonyl and opens the ring, forming an ester bond while regenerating an oxygen-bearing chain end. In the selected metal-catalyzed route, carbonyl activation and the alcohol/alkoxide growth site support repeated insertion without releasing a condensate at each propagation step.

sections.overview: Polycaprolactone (PCL) is an aliphatic polyester commonly made by ring-opening polymerization of ε-caprolactone. Its flexible methylene-rich chains form crystalline and less ordered regions, and thermoplastic grades can be shaped from the melt. Commercial materials are used in adhesives and blends, and porous PCL scaffolds are studied for tissue engineering. Cleavage of its ester bonds depends on the chemistry and exposure conditions. Its low melting temperature makes melt shaping practical, while a finished adhesive, blend or scaffold contains its own additional components or structural features. In a scaffold, pore geometry changes both space available for cells and mechanical support. Degradation must be evaluated for the particular form and environment.
sections.history: Polycaprolactone’s industrial development included new ways to polymerize cyclic esters. Eugene F. Cox and Fritz Hostettler’s Union Carbide patent, filed in 1959 and issued in 1962, demonstrated caprolactone polymerization using metal-amide catalysts. This was a synthesis advance within an existing lactone-polymer field. Later commercial materials served both as thermoplastic polymers and as polyols for other resins. Perstorp’s 2008 Capa expansion announcement describes uses in coatings, cast elastomers, hot-melt adhesives, footwear supports and orthopedic braces. Perstorp sold the Capa business, including its Warrington manufacturing site, to Ingevity in 2019, continuing the commercial development of the product family.
sections.nomenclature: PCL abbreviates polycaprolactone. The canonical name denotes the epsilon-caprolactone homopolyester and is distinct from other degradable polyesters such as PLA and PGA.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polycaprolactone (PCL) is the aliphatic polyester most commonly produced by ring-opening polymerization of ε-caprolactone. An alcohol, water, amine, metal alkoxide, or other active-hydrogen compound can initiate a chain, and the initiator functionality determines whether the product is linear, branched, or a multifunctional caprolactone polyol. Tin(II) octoate is a common catalyst, while aluminum complexes, enzymes, and organocatalysts provide alternatives. A continuous-process patent describes ε-caprolactone ROP with active-hydrogen or organometallic initiators and optional catalyst. An open study uses an aluminum phenoxide complex with several alcohol initiators and directly links initiator identity to end groups and molar-mass evolution. Monomer-to-initiator ratio, catalyst, water content, and conversion are architecture controls. Caprolactone copolymers or PCL blocks are distinct from the homopolymer unless their composition is stated.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polycaprolactone (PCL) is a semicrystalline, low-melting aliphatic polyester that typically yields and draws to high strain in dense bulk form, but its apparent stiffness and strength vary sharply with molecular mass, crystallinity and cooling history, branching or crosslinking, temperature, hydrolytic aging, blend or reinforcement chemistry, and processing into a dense part, filament, or porous scaffold. At body-relevant temperatures it is closer to its melting transition than at room temperature, so thermal history and service temperature are especially consequential. A bounded bulk example is Perstorp Capa 6800 (Mw 80,000 g/mol): 2 mm compression-molded plaques (170 °C, 4.9 MPa, 1 min, then room-temperature cooling) tested at room temperature to ISO 527-2 at 50 mm/min had 149 ± 25 MPa Young modulus, 13.1 ± 0.2 MPa yield stress, 30.0 ± 1.2 MPa break stress, and 611 ± 25% elongation at break (five repeats). These are not values for electrospun PCL or a scaffold. Independent laser-sintered PCL work shows that build orientation and especially designed porosity reduce tensile modulus and strength markedly compared with near-dense PCL, so scaffold architecture must remain attached to its endpoint.
sections.processing: Polycaprolactone (PCL) is a low-melting semicrystalline thermoplastic converted by melt extrusion, injection/compression molding, fiber spinning, and powder-bed processes such as selective laser sintering; solution electrospinning is also used for scaffold fiber formation. Molecular mass, branching or peroxide modification, powder size, build orientation, and the desired porosity change the usable window. A bounded Capa 6800 example was formed as a compression-molded plaque for tensile specimens, whereas an independent scaffold study used selective laser sintering to fabricate dense and orthogonally porous PCL architectures. The latter route requires control of powder spreading, laser energy, layer fusion, and cooling because insufficient fusion leaves connected porosity while excessive thermal exposure can distort the scaffold. Those are process examples for named PCL feedstocks, not a universal temperature or laser window. Ring-opening polymerization and peroxide functionalization belong in Synthesis; this section covers shaping of supplied PCL resin or powder and post-build conditioning.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PCL chains contain ester groups separated by flexible methylene segments. The material is semicrystalline, with ordered crystallites and less ordered regions whose proportions depend on molecular weight and cooling. Processing can also produce larger-scale features: laser-sintered scaffolds, for example, contain designed channels and pores. Chemical branching or crosslinking changes chain connectivity and can alter the response to load. Designed channels lower the amount of load-bearing solid and introduce direction-dependent paths through the structure. The manufacturing process can also leave unintended pores, so the fabricated scaffold may differ from its nominal design.
sections.properties: PCL is a low-melting thermoplastic that can be shaped and blended with other polymers. In a laser-sintering study, porous PCL specimens with measured porosities of 44.8–76.5% had mean compressive moduli of 14.9–113.4 MPa; solid specimens had substantially higher values. This illustrates how scaffold architecture changes the response in addition to polymer chemistry. A different study found that peroxide modification changed the mechanical response of compression-molded Capa 6800. In the same laser-sintering study, solid PCL specimens had mean compressive moduli of about 299–317 MPa, above those of its porous designs. These are specific specimen and build conditions; the comparison shows why scaffold geometry matters when selecting a support.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Ingevity describes Capa thermoplastics for hot-melt adhesives in footwear, leather goods, furniture, construction, automotive products and textiles. A low melting point allows selected thermoplastics to be shaped by heating; actual bond performance depends on the complete adhesive formulation. PCL is also used to modify bioplastic films and studied as a porous support for tissue engineering. Laser-sintering research demonstrates interconnected channels in a PCL scaffold, with the tradeoff that introducing pores reduces compressive stiffness compared with a solid specimen.

Purchasing. The supplier lists high-molecular-weight linear grades including Capa 6250, 6400, 6500 and 6800 and provides product and regional contact channels. These thermoplastics should be distinguished from low-molecular-weight caprolactone polyols used as reactive polyurethane feedstocks.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchase or consumption tonnage for thermoplastic PCL was established. Caprolactone monomer or a supplier's broader portfolio includes other products and cannot be treated as PCL thermoplastic volume.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PCL ester bonds can be cleaved chemically or by enzymes. In an intentionally catalyzed methanolysis, PCL produced methyl 6-hydroxyhexanoate; that alcoholysis product is not a measurement of environmental metabolites.

Timescales: In a laboratory seawater experiment, approximately 100 μm Capa 6500 PCL film formed a small surface biofilm after one month in nutrient-amended harbor water collected in March. Film incubated with water collected in June was mostly or partially degraded within two weeks at the same 23 °C incubation temperature. The observations concern separate water samples and surface or visible breakdown, not complete mineralization. Different microbial populations in the sampled water and nutrient addition may contribute to the differing observations.

Environmental persistence: Microbial populations, temperature history, film dimensions and exposure conditions affect the outcome. The seawater observations do not establish a transferable lifetime for all PCL products or environments.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
In a laboratory study, a bisguanidine catalyst converted PCL to methyl 6-hydroxyhexanoate by methanolysis at 100 °C in 60 minutes, with 97% product yield determined by proton NMR. This product can be used as a PCL building block. The reactor conditions and alcohol are intentionally supplied and do not represent ambient breakdown.

Chemical conversion of a research sample does not establish an operating commercial collection and recycling loop for postconsumer PCL articles.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PCL biomaterials require evaluation of the complete implant and its degradation products. The reviewed polyester studies link degradation rate and local acidic products to inflammation and cell response; scaffold architecture and release rate change the exposure. Biodegradability alone is not evidence of compatibility for every site, dose or formulation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Molecular weight, crystallinity, thermal history and article geometry influence PCL performance. Porosity and direction of loading can make a scaffold much less stiff in compression than a solid specimen made by the same method. Results from modified or crosslinked PCL do not automatically describe unmodified grades. Exposure conditions and thickness also influence degradation. A scaffold modulus is a structural measurement that reflects porosity as well as polymer properties. The scaffold result does not predict the bond strength of an adhesive or the properties of a different melt-processed grade.

sections.overview: Poly(butylene succinate), or PBS, is an aliphatic polyester made from succinic acid or its derivatives and 1,4-butanediol. Esterification or transesterification forms shorter chains, and subsequent polycondensation builds molecular weight. PBS can crystallize and be processed into films, molded articles, coatings and blends. Its ester bonds can undergo cleavage, but breakdown depends on the material and exposure conditions. Semicrystalline packing and polymer molecular weight help determine how a particular grade flows, stretches and carries load. Commercial resins can be formulated for different conversion routes, while copolyesters and blends add further components. The presence of ester bonds does not by itself specify an environmental lifetime.
sections.history: PBS became an important target of biodegradable-polyester development in Japan. Showa Highpolymer’s patent work, with priority claims from 1992 and a U.S. grant in 1994, developed succinate-based polyester fibers through molecular-weight control and melt processing. A later Hitachi Plant Technologies patent, published in 2012, addressed continuous PBS manufacturing through staged polycondensation reactors. The BioPBS line licensed from Mitsubishi Chemical subsequently incorporated bio-derived succinic acid into commercial production in Thailand. Its documented applications include coated paper, packaging, fibers and molded food-service items. These milestones concern industrial processing and renewable feedstocks, not a claim that PBS first existed in the 1990s.
sections.nomenclature: PBS is the abbreviation used for poly(butylene succinate). This record is the succinate polyester; PBSA, PBAT, physical blends, and a particular chain-extended or processed formulation are chemically or materially distinct scopes rather than aliases.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(butylene succinate) is an aliphatic polyester made by step-growth polycondensation of succinic acid, or a succinate derivative, with 1,4-butanediol. The direct-acid route first esterifies the diacid and diol to hydroxyl-terminated oligomers while removing esterification water. Polycondensation then raises molecular weight under reduced pressure in the presence of a catalyst, with removal of volatile 1,4-butanediol helping drive the equilibrium. Dimethyl or diethyl succinate and succinic anhydride are documented alternative acid-side feeds. The cited procedures are route examples; catalyst selection, staged vacuum operation, and any optional chain extension are process-specific and are not universal requirements for PBS.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PBS is semicrystalline, so molar mass, crystallinity, thermal history, chain extension or branching, draw/orientation, and degradation or moisture/temperature exposure control measured mechanics. An open PBS review notes that higher molecular weight can increase tensile strength, while comonomers that lower crystallinity tend to reduce stiffness/strength and increase extensibility. A separate stretching study links changing crystalline morphology and orientation to the PBS tensile/cyclic response.

A bounded film result from one PBS/PBAT study is its neat PBS control: elastic modulus 725.6 ± 15.6 MPa, stress at break 29.6 ± 1.5 MPa, and strain at break 7.1 ± 0.3%. The paper identifies the tested PBS as a specific material (reported Mw 62 kg/mol); these film values are not a general PBS grade range and should not be applied to chain-extended, oriented, blended, or filled PBS.
sections.processing:
PBS can be extruded and compounded, injection or compression molded, blown and cast into film, thermoformed, blow molded, spun into fiber, foamed, and processed by filament-based additive manufacturing. Molar mass and branching select the route: lower-flow molding/extrusion grades and higher-melt-strength film grades are not interchangeable. Drying, melt temperature, shear, residence time, die or mold cooling, crystallization, draw/blow ratio, and repeated heat history influence hydrolysis, degradation, film stability, shrinkage, and final morphology. Nucleants and branching agents may alter both crystallization and melt strength.

Zaverl and co-workers provide a bounded blend example using Biocosafe 1903 PBS and Biocosafe 2003 PBAT. They dried materials overnight at 80 °C, hand-mixed a 60/40 PBS/PBAT skin blend, compounded it in a co-rotating twin-screw extruder at 112 rpm with a 130-150 °C barrel-to-die profile, cooled the strands in water, pelletized them, and molded the skin phase with nominal 185-190 °C zones while studying co-injection temperature, speed, pressure, and mold effects. This is a specific two-polymer co-injection formulation, not a neat-PBS window. The open PBS review likewise makes clear that molecular weight, branching, crystallization, and thermal stability determine whether a grade is suited to injection, extrusion, casting, or film blowing.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The PBS chain alternates butylene and succinate units joined by ester bonds. It is semicrystalline: ordered domains coexist with less ordered polymer, and their proportions depend on crystallization during processing. Molecular weight and orientation also influence how chains pack and how a film responds to stretching. PBSA copolymers and physical blends introduce additional components and should be distinguished from neat PBS. Cooling and drawing change the amount and orientation of ordered material, so two articles formed from the same starting polymer need not have identical structures. A chain-extended resin or composite has additional variables beyond the neat polymer.
sections.properties: PBS combines processability with useful strength and flexibility in selected articles. In one study, a neat PBS film of reported molecular weight 62 kg/mol had an elastic modulus of 725.6 ± 15.6 MPa and strain at break of 7.1 ± 0.3%; these figures describe that film, not all PBS grades. Molecular weight and crystallization influence the ability to carry load and deform. The ester linkages also make the material susceptible to chain cleavage under appropriate chemical or biological conditions. A 7.1% strain at break in the cited neat film describes its tested deformation, not a general limit for every PBS article. Orientation, a different molecular weight or an added blend component can change that behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PBS is supplied for packaging films, coated paper, molded coffee capsules and cutlery, and fibers or nonwovens. For a paper coating, adhesion and sealability help the polymer form part of a packaging structure; its function depends on the complete coated article. In one supplier example, BioPBS FZ79AC is intended for extrusion-coated paper cups; its 20 µm film reached a specified seal-strength threshold at 120 °C in a one-second test at 0.2 MPa. The measurement demonstrates a formulation and test condition, not the sealing behavior of every PBS coating. Film extrusion, molding and paper coating place different requirements on flow, sealing and mechanical performance. Some products use PBS blended with other polymers rather than as a neat resin.

Purchasing. PTT MCC lists BioPBS FZ71 grades for injection molding, FZ91 for films, FZ79AC for paper coatings and FZ78TM for fibers. A converter should select a grade for its process and product requirements. The FZ79AC sheet describes 25 kg bags and recommends keeping the material sealed until use; the wider BioPBS portfolio also includes distinct PBSA copolymers.

Scale and evidence limits. The undated supplier brochure states a 20,000-tonnes/year BioPBS capacity at Rayong, Thailand. That figure covers a PBS/PBSA offering and does not separately establish PBS production, sales or current global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Ester bonds in PBS can be cleaved by hydrolysis or by enzymes under suitable conditions. In an intentionally catalyzed methanolysis experiment, the major products were dimethyl succinate and 1,4-butanediol; this chemical-recycling reaction is not a measurement of ambient metabolites.

Timescales: Bionolle 1020MD PBS film, approximately 100 μm thick, showed no visible surface change after one month in nutrient-amended seawater collected from a Japanese harbor and incubated at 23 °C with shaking. In a separate deliberate methanolysis experiment, an organic catalyst gave a reported 93.1% dimethyl-succinate yield at 100 °C in two hours. The controlled reaction conditions and product yield are distinct from the seawater surface observation; neither is a measured environmental mineralization rate.

Environmental persistence: Water access, temperature, microorganisms and article geometry can alter the outcome. No surface change in this laboratory seawater test neither proves permanent persistence nor establishes a general environmental lifetime.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Reprocessing can change PBS even when the material remains usable. In a semi-industrial study of BioPBS FZ71PM, melt flow rate rose from 21.4 to 25.7 g/10 min between the first and fifth extrusion cycles, indicating greater flow under the test conditions; the authors discussed chain scission and branching as possible contributors. This is controlled repeated processing, not a demonstration of postconsumer collection.

In laboratory methanolysis, an organic catalyst gave a 93.1% dimethyl succinate yield by proton NMR at 100 °C after two hours, and recovered products were used to make PBS again. The result demonstrates a chemical route at experimental scale, not a commercial recycling service for mixed products.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: In a study that included PBS raw materials and finished products, methanol-extract bioassays showed that chemical activity varied by product and formulation. These laboratory extracts do not reproduce ordinary food-contact exposure, but demonstrate why biodegradability and resin identity alone cannot establish the safety of additives and other extractable constituents.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Molecular weight, crystallization, orientation and prior heat exposure influence PBS performance. Film measurements cannot be transferred uncritically to molded, chain-extended or filled products, and blends have their own phase structure. Water, temperature and available enzymes can change degradation rates. A result in a controlled reactor does not establish the lifetime of an article in the environment. Product form is also relevant to the reported seawater observation: the tested 100 μm film cannot represent a thick molded article. Hydrolysis of ester bonds, loss of visible film and mineralization to CO₂ are distinct measurements.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Esterification and step-growth polycondensation form PBS. Hydroxyl groups react at carboxyl carbonyls to form ester links. Initial esterification releases water; subsequent ester exchange between hydroxyl-ended species extends the chains. Removal of volatile products favors further condensation, and chains grow through reactions among monomers and oligomers.

steps.title: Build ester links and advance molecular mass
steps.body: Maintain the selected acid/diol functionality balance while removing water from esterification and volatile glycol during the applicable finishing stage. Complementary end groups on oligomers continue reacting; the final chain distribution depends on conversion and end-group control.

steps.title: Form and recover the product
steps.body: Advance under reduced pressure with the selected catalyst while removing volatile diol.

sections.overview: Poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate), or PBAT, is an aliphatic–aromatic copolyester made from 1,4-butanediol, adipic acid and terephthalic acid or their derivatives. Its chains combine flexible aliphatic segments with aromatic-containing segments. The composition and arrangement of these units affect crystallization and mechanical behavior. PBAT is widely used as a flexible component in films and formulated blends.
sections.history: PBAT’s commercial history is anchored by BASF’s introduction of ecoflex in 1998. The aliphatic–aromatic copolyester became a flexible component for compostable films and compounds, including combinations with starch and PLA. Packaging and agricultural films, shopping and organic-waste collection bags, and paper coatings were important application directions. BASF’s later ecovio compounds used PBAT to contribute flexibility and toughness; its 2023 anniversary account describes further paper-packaging grade development. These dates document a commercial product lineage, not the first preparation of every adipate/terephthalate copolyester. They also illustrate that biodegradable performance and renewable feedstock content are separate features of a material.
sections.nomenclature: PBAT is the abbreviation for the butylene adipate/terephthalate copolyester. The record denotes a covalent copolymer, not a physical blend of PBS and another polyester; catalyst package, exact sequence distribution, and a filled or processed formulation are not alternate names for PBAT.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) is an aliphatic–aromatic copolyester built from 1,4-butanediol (BDO), adipic acid (AA), and terephthalic acid (TPA), or the corresponding ester derivatives. Common manufacture is staged melt condensation: direct esterification or transesterification first forms oligomers, then high-temperature, reduced-pressure polycondensation removes water, methanol, or excess diol to raise molar mass. Titanium-, tin-, and zinc-based catalysts are reported examples. The AA:TPA feed, BDO excess, catalyst, temperature, time, and vacuum are synthesis controls; the resulting butylene-adipate and butylene-terephthalate sequences should not be represented as a fixed alternating repeat. A separate patent demonstrates both an acid/BDO/titanium-phosphate esterification route and a route that first prepares butylene terephthalate and butanediol adipate then copolycondenses them. These are synthesis examples, not a claim that all commercial PBAT uses their catalyst package or sequence distribution.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PBAT mechanical response is governed by butylene-adipate/butylene-terephthalate composition, molar mass, crystallinity, thermal and processing history, orientation, and any blend, filler, or degradation exposure. Open reviews specifically identify molecular weight, composition, processing pressure/temperature, and crystallinity as controlling variables, so blend or composite data must not be treated as intrinsic PBAT values.

A bounded film example from one PBS/PBAT-blend study is its neat PBAT control: elastic modulus 81.0 ± 2.5 MPa, stress at break 20.1 ± 2.4 MPa, and strain at break 689.5 ± 110.3%. These tensile values apply to that study's film specimen and reported commercial PBAT; its grade, molecular-weight distribution, film processing, conditioning, and test geometry constrain their use.
sections.processing:
PBAT is chiefly compounded and converted into flexible blown or cast film, bags and coatings, and it is also used in injection molding, extrusion coating, sheet/thermoforming blends, and filament processing. Commercial PBAT frequently appears in blends with starch, PLA, or other biodegradable polyesters. Feed moisture, starch plasticization and dispersion, blend ratio, specific throughput and shear, melt and die temperature, screw speed, residence time, blow-up and draw-down ratios, cooling, winding, and storage humidity influence degradation, gels, gauge, bubble stability, orientation, blocking, and mechanical balance.

Thongkham and co-workers provide a bounded TPS/PBAT film study. They compounded virgin PBAT with 20, 40, or 60 wt% thermoplastic starch at 180 rpm and 120-150 °C, pelletized, dried the blends at 45 °C for one day, and blew films on a 25 mm, L/D 30 single screw. Their formulation-dependent film settings used 150-190 °C extrusion, 35-44 rpm, a 140-160 °C die, 3.0-3.5 blow-up ratio, and 5.0-6.5 draw-down ratio; films were sealed against moisture exchange at 30 °C. These are blend- and equipment-specific settings. The processing review further documents that low specific throughput can overheat/degrade TPS/PBAT even while increasing dispersive shear, so temperature, output, and screw speed must be optimized together.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PBAT chains contain butylene adipate and butylene terephthalate units joined by ester bonds. The aliphatic and aromatic units differ in their ability to pack, and their amounts and sequences influence the crystalline and less ordered regions. Cooling and drawing further affect the structure of a particular film. Blending with PLA or adding fillers introduces interfaces and phases beyond the PBAT chain itself.
sections.properties: PBAT is generally flexible and ductile relative to many packaging polyesters, and it can be blended with more rigid PLA to modify handling. In one melt-blend study, a 90/10 wt% PLA/PBAT specimen reached 136.2 ± 53.4% strain at break, compared with 7.0 ± 1.0% for its neat PLA comparison; its modulus fell from 2.04 to 1.64 GPa. Another study found little increase in ductility while PLA remained the main phase, demonstrating that preparation and morphology matter. These blend observations are not tensile specifications for neat PBAT or every PBAT/PLA product.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PBAT is used in flexible packaging and formulations for shopping bags, organic-waste bags and agricultural mulch films. Its ductility makes it useful alongside a stiffer material such as PLA, where the combination can balance film handling with stiffness. An application or certification concerns the complete formulation and product.

Purchasing. BASF markets ecoflex as PBAT resin for flexible films, while ecovio denotes formulated products rather than neat PBAT alone. Converters select a resin or compound matched to their equipment and end-use requirements.

Scale and evidence limits. A May 2020 BASF/Red Avenue announcement described a planned Shanghai plant with 60,000 tonnes/year PBAT capacity and operation then planned for 2022. It is a historical announced capacity, not verified subsequent output or a global demand estimate.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Enzymes can cleave the ester bonds in PBAT; a laboratory esterase study detected terephthalic acid and terephthalate-containing products. Released compounds and fragments are not themselves proof of complete mineralization. The rate depends on enzyme, formulation and conditions.

Timescales: An approximately 100 μm film of BASF EcoFlex C1200 showed no visible surface change after one month in nutrient-amended seawater collected from a Japanese harbor and incubated at 23 °C with shaking. In a separate soil incubation, 30 μm PBAT film cut into 5 mm squares was buried in sieved Beijing soil at 25 ± 1 °C and maintained at 20% water content. After 180 days the researchers reported 31.86% film mass loss and 16.19% mineralization, based on CO₂ generation compared with the soil control. These are different endpoints for one laboratory soil test, not a time to complete breakdown in every environment.

Environmental persistence: The soil study also detected PBAT microplastics released from the film, showing why loss of retrievable film mass cannot simply be equated with conversion to CO₂. Results obtained with concentrated enzymes in a reactor cannot be substituted for an environmental lifetime: microbial populations, temperature, water availability and film structure all affect breakdown.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
In laboratory research, cutinase hydrolysis of PBAT was followed by acid precipitation to recover terephthalic acid. The recovered acid was used to synthesize PET, demonstrating recovery of a building block into a different polyester rather than closed-loop recycling to PBAT. The recovery and suitability of a monomer depend on the feed and purification.

The laboratory procedure does not establish a commercial recycling stream for mixed or contaminated PBAT-containing products. Collection and treatment must be assessed for the complete article and available local systems.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: In a study that included PBAT raw materials and finished products, methanol-extract bioassays showed that chemical activity varied by product and formulation. These laboratory extracts do not reproduce ordinary food-contact exposure, but demonstrate why biodegradability and resin identity alone cannot establish the safety of additives and other extractable constituents.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Adipate-to-terephthalate ratio, molecular weight, crystallinity and processing history differ between PBAT materials. A film containing PBAT and PLA also depends on blend ratio, phase morphology and compatibility: the reported increase in strain at break in one blend is not guaranteed in another. Specimen preparation, deformation rate and direction matter for comparison. A degradation result belongs to the tested product and conditions, not all PBAT formulations.

sections.overview: Poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate), or PBSA, is an aliphatic copolyester made from 1,4-butanediol with succinate and adipate components. Adding adipate-derived units distinguishes it from PBS homopolymer and changes how the chains crystallize. Composition, molecular weight and fabrication affect the resulting properties. PBSA grades are supplied for films and fibers and studied in coatings and blends.
sections.history: PBSA developed alongside PBS as manufacturers varied aliphatic-polyester composition for flexible materials. Showa Highpolymer’s 1994 polyester-fiber patent includes succinate/adipate chemistry and describes turning such polymers into fibers and nonwoven products. More recent BioPBS literature from PTT MCC Biochem distinguishes PBSA grades from PBS and documents packaging-film, fiber and molded-product development using technology licensed from Mitsubishi Chemical. Biomedical exploration formed a separate branch: Simon Williams and colleagues at Tepha included PBSA among the PBS copolymers in a 2021 patent publication on implant materials. That patent represents an investigated application, not evidence of routine clinical adoption or a first synthesis date.
sections.nomenclature: PBSA is the abbreviation for poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate). The record denotes a covalent succinate/adipate copolymer, not a physical PBS/poly(butylene adipate) blend; PBS homopolymer, PBAT, and modified or filled formulations are separate scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA) is an aliphatic copolyester in which both succinate and adipate residues are incorporated with 1,4-butanediol; it is not a physical blend of PBS and poly(butylene adipate). The cited syntheses charge succinic acid, adipic acid, and 1,4-butanediol to form a prepolymer and then perform condensation poly­merization. The relative diacid feed is a compositional control variable and can change the resulting copolyester, so no single ratio is implied for the entire PBSA name. Additional branching, cross-linking, or chain-extending reactants described in individual sources define modified PBSA variants and are not part of the base copolymer identity.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PBSA is a composition-sensitive aliphatic copolyester. The adipate fraction can lower crystallinity and melting behavior relative to PBS, while molecular weight, film orientation/draw ratio, annealing, filler loading, and environmental exposure further alter tensile response. Independent open studies accordingly describe PBSA as ductile but show that oriented and filled films can be substantially stiffer or less extensible than the neat material.

A bounded neat-PBSA film result from one five-replicate study is Young's modulus 0.29 ± 0.05 GPa, stress at break 21.10 ± 0.50 MPa, and break elongation 400 ± 53%; the same paper reports 32.1% crystallinity for that PBSA. These values are for its particular film and formulation, not for PBSA composites, blends, orientation states, or all succinate/adipate compositions.
sections.processing:
PBSA is a melt-processable aliphatic copolyester used in blown and cast film, extrusion and compounding, injection molding, sheet thermoforming, and blends or composites. Adipate content, molar mass, branching, and blend formulation govern crystallization and melt strength. Pellets and hygroscopic co-components should be dried; melt temperature, shear, residence time, die and chill-roll temperature, draw/blow ratio, cooling and winding must balance homogeneous dispersion against hydrolytic or thermal degradation. Too little melt strength destabilizes film, while repeated heat/shear histories and excessive temperature can lower molar mass.

A bounded cast-film study by Alfano and co-workers used BioPBS FD92PM PBSA in PHBV/PBSA blends. PBSA, PHBV, and compatibilizer were oven-dried at 60 °C for at least 12 h, manually premixed, and fed to an L/D 25 single-screw extruder with a flat die and calender. The profile was 175/175/165/165/165/165 °C at 40 rpm, producing about 500 micrometre sheets. These conditions were selected for those blend compositions and compatibilized films, not neat PBSA generally. The PBS/PBSA review identifies extrusion, injection, casting, and film blowing as established routes and emphasizes that molecular architecture, crystallization, and thermal stability select the suitable process.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PBSA chains contain butylene succinate and butylene adipate units linked by ester bonds. Mixing the two units can interfere with the regular packing seen in the corresponding homopolyesters, producing less crystalline structures at intermediate compositions. The review describes crystallinity and melting temperature decreasing and then increasing across the composition range. Sequence, molecular weight and cooling history also affect the morphology of a particular article.
sections.properties: The balance of succinate and adipate units affects crystallization, melting and mechanical response. In one synthesized PBSA specimen, tensile strength was 21.5 MPa and elongation at break 766.2%, illustrating that the studied material could stretch substantially before failure. Those numbers are specific to the reported specimen and cannot be assigned to every commercial grade or blend. Ester bonds are susceptible to hydrolysis, with the rate dependent on exposure and structure.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PBSA grades are offered for flexible packaging films, fibers and nonwovens; the supplier identifies adipate-containing grades separately from PBS homopolymer. In a research example, lower-molecular-weight PBSA was dispersed in water and applied to kraft paper to create a protective coating. This coating experiment is a formulation study rather than evidence that all PBSA-coated paper behaves identically.

Purchasing. PTT MCC lists BioPBS FD92 grades for extrusion film and FD72 for fibers and spunbond. A buyer specifies the grade and end-use requirements with the producer.

Scale and evidence limits. The producer's undated brochure states 20,000 tonnes/year for its overall BioPBS capacity in Rayong, Thailand. It does not report a separate PBSA allocation, annual PBSA production or consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PBSA ester bonds can be cleaved by enzymes or hydrolytic chemistry under suitable conditions. In a separate deliberate microwave-assisted reaction, propylene glycol shortened PBSA chains and produced hydroxyl-ended oligomers; those reaction products should not be assumed to be ambient metabolites.

Timescales: Bionolle 3001MD PBSA film approximately 100 μm thick showed no visible surface change after one month in nutrient-amended Japanese harbor seawater incubated at 23 °C with shaking. In a different laboratory experiment, 0.3 mm synthesized PBSA film lost mass in Fusarium solani cutinase solution at 37 °C and pH 7.4. The paper reports rapid loss, but its methods state sampling every 24 hours while its results report shorter time points, so the timing is uncertain. The two tests use different materials and conditions; surface change or film mass loss does not establish complete mineralization.

Environmental persistence: Material composition, geometry, temperature and microbial or enzyme activity influence degradation. Neither laboratory result gives a universal lifetime in soil, compost or seawater.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Researchers converted commercial PBSA to shorter chains by microwave-assisted alcoholysis with propylene glycol. At 135 °C for 15 minutes, reducing the PBSA-to-glycol feed ratio from 24:1 to 6:1 by weight reduced the reported NMR-derived molecular weight from roughly half to roughly a quarter of the starting resin. The products were formulated into aqueous coating particles for kraft paper.

The experimental coated paper was repulped; that demonstrates paper recovery and a potential conversion of PBSA, not closed-loop recovery of postconsumer PBSA. The result is specific to the tested coating and repulping procedure.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The supplier sheet for BioPBS FD grades, including FD92PM and FD92PB PBSA, identifies hot-polymer burns, dust-related eye irritation and irritating processing fumes. It recommends ventilation, dust control and prevention of pellet release to waterways. The guidance addresses these industrial grades and does not replace evaluation of a finished food-contact or biomedical formulation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PBSA describes a range of copolymer compositions rather than one fixed succinate-to-adipate ratio. Molecular weight, thermal history, processing and fillers influence both mechanics and water access. An enzyme test on a prepared film can demonstrate susceptibility under that test, but does not establish a rate for all products. PBS homopolymer and PBSA-containing blends should be evaluated separately.

sections.overview: Poly(ethylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate), or PEF, is a polyester made from ethylene glycol and 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid or its ester. The furan ring in its repeat unit distinguishes it from terephthalate-based PET. PEF is being developed for packaging, bottles and fibers, with oxygen-barrier performance motivating packaging research. Molecular weight, crystallization and processing determine the behavior of a particular article. The furan-containing polyester is distinct from a finished bottle or multilayer package: shape, orientation and processing contribute to the properties experienced in use. Controlled chemical or enzymatic treatments can break PEF chains, but bio-based feedstock alone does not establish environmental biodegradation.
sections.history: PEF’s recent development has centered on making its furan-based monomer available at industrial scale. Avantium records proof of its YXY conversion technology in 2006, an FDCA pilot plant and a first PEF bottle in 2011, and the formation of the Synvina venture with BASF in 2016. Avantium regained full ownership in 2019. Led technically by researchers including Gert-Jan Gruter, the program developed partnerships for bottles, films, packaging and textiles. The FDCA flagship plant was inaugurated in October 2024, when Releaf was introduced as the PEF brand. These are scale-up and commercialization milestones, distinct from the first laboratory synthesis of a furan polyester.
sections.nomenclature: PEF abbreviates poly(ethylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate), often shortened to poly(ethylene furanoate). The canonical name specifies the 2,5-furandicarboxylate structure and is not a name for all furan-based polyesters.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(ethylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate) (PEF) is the polyester from 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA), or a diester thereof, and ethylene glycol. FDCA is a furan dicarboxylic-acid feedstock; its use, rather than terephthalic acid, defines the furandicarboxylate repeat unit. Routes first esterify FDCA with ethylene glycol, or transesterify an FDCA diester, then polycondense the oligomer under reduced pressure while removing low-molar-mass products. Titanium alkoxide and antimony- or germanium-based catalysts occur in the cited examples, and solid-state polycondensation may be used for additional molecular-weight build-up. Those catalyst and finishing choices are source-specific, not a single mandatory PEF recipe.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PEF mechanics depend on molar mass, furan-polyester microstructure, crystallinity/polymorph, thermal history and annealing, strain orientation, and any comonomer or diethylene-glycol content. Open studies find that monomer route and intrinsic viscosity change crystallinity and elastic response, while biaxial stretching induces crystallinity and modifies rigidity; therefore amorphous plaques, annealed material, stretched film, and fibers cannot be pooled.

A bounded high-molecular-weight PEF example (Mn 83,000 g/mol, made by melt polymerization followed by solid-state post-condensation) reported Young's modulus 2,450 ± 220 MPa and maximum stress 35 ± 8 MPa. The paper also studied crystallinity effects with temperature, so these results are not a universal PEF datasheet value or directly transferable to lower-molar-mass, copolymer, or oriented PEF.
sections.processing:
Poly(ethylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate) (PEF) can be converted by melt extrusion and extrusion casting, injection molding of preforms and other parts, stretch blow molding, thermoforming, and fiber spinning. Stretching and shear during these operations alter crystallization kinetics and morphology, so melt temperature, residence time, shear history, cooling, and subsequent uniaxial or biaxial orientation must be developed together. A recent open review also identifies high melt viscosity, shear sensitivity, and the proximity of useful melt processing to thermal degradation as practical reasons not to transfer a PET schedule unchanged to PEF.

For one bounded stretch-blow-molding approach, The Coca-Cola Company's EP 3 194 134 B1 discloses water-conditioning an already injection-molded PEF or PEF-copolymer preform, followed by removal of trapped and surface water and stretch blow molding. Claim 1 gives alternative conditioning ranges of room-temperature water for about 3 h to at least 48 h, water at about 80 °C for up to about 15 h, at least about 65% RH air above about 45 °C for about 0.25 h to at least 72 h, or at least about 85% RH air above about 35 °C for about 0.5 h to at least 44 h. The patent warns that excessive moisture together with heat can produce excessive crystallization. These are claimed options for the disclosed preform process, not a general PEF drying or blow-molding window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PEF chains alternate ethylene-derived segments and furan dicarboxylate units connected by ester bonds. Depending on processing and thermal history, material can be largely amorphous or contain ordered crystalline domains. In a study comparing acid- and ester-derived samples, annealing and intrinsic viscosity affected crystallization and the size and number of observable spherulites. Orientation and crystallinity can therefore differ between a laboratory film and a finished bottle. Crystallinity can also influence access to ester bonds: one enzyme study found substantially less mass loss from a 32%-crystalline film than from its largely amorphous comparison under the reported reaction conditions.
sections.properties: PEF is investigated as a barrier polyester because its structure can restrict oxygen transport. For one thermo-compressed film measured at 23 °C, oxygen permeability increased from 3.00 × 10⁻²⁰ to 9.20 × 10⁻²⁰ m³·m/(m²·Pa·s) as relative humidity increased from 0% to 75%. This comparison illustrates a humidity effect for that film; it is not a universal PEF specification. In a separate set of synthesized films, oxygen transmission decreased as intrinsic viscosity increased within each monomer-route series. A separate enzyme study compared approximately 0.2 mm PEF films and reported lower weight loss for the 32%-crystalline specimen than for a largely amorphous film. This affects chemical accessibility under that specific treatment and is not a prediction for all finished containers.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PEF is being developed for beverage bottles, packaging films and fibers. Its oxygen-barrier properties are relevant to packaging where oxygen exposure affects the contents, but finished-container performance also depends on the design and manufacturing process. The company's commercial development includes bottles, fibers and other formats whose geometry and processing alter performance. Avantium's 2026 examples include functional-beverage shot bottles, a PEF-containing cushion and sportswear fibers; they describe partnerships and prototypes rather than market-wide adoption.

Purchasing. Avantium and its conversion partners provide a route for development supply and negotiated offtake. A September 2026 agreement with Sukano reserves future licensed-plant volumes for masterbatch-related uses; reservations do not establish immediate commodity availability.

Scale and evidence limits. In August 2026 Avantium reported 15 capacity reservations covering over 150 kilotonnes of future FDCA and PEF combined, a prospective volume rather than PEF purchases or annual consumption. A September 2026 statement expected first commercial deliveries under existing offtakes at the end of 2026, subject to start-up and qualification; it is a dated expectation.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PEF contains ester bonds that can be deliberately cleaved by glycolysis. In a chemical-recycling study, heated ethylene glycol and an organic catalyst converted PEF film to bis(2-hydroxyethyl) furan-2,5-dicarboxylate (BHEF). A separate study used polyester-hydrolyzing enzymes on PEF films and identified furandicarboxylic acid, ethylene glycol and a hydroxyethyl furanoate intermediate. These controlled-reaction products are not an inventory of compounds released by environmental litter.

Timescales: Researchers treated 1 g of thermo-compressed film with 5 g of glycol and catalyst at 180 °C for two hours, reporting disappearance of residual PEF in that reaction. In an enzyme experiment using 0.2 mm largely amorphous film and repeated additions of leaf compost cutinase, researchers reported up to 98% weight loss after 72 hours at 65 °C. A 32%-crystalline film resisted enzymatic attack more strongly in their comparison. These are laboratory endpoints under specified treatments, not rates of ambient degradation or mineralization.

Environmental persistence: Renewable feedstock origin alone does not establish biodegradability. Film mass loss and recovery of monomers or oligomers do not establish conversion of polymer carbon to carbon dioxide and biomass. Neither the glycolysis reaction nor the controlled enzyme treatment determines a lifetime of PEF articles in soil, freshwater or seawater.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A laboratory study applied catalyst-assisted glycolysis to PEF film and isolated the BHEF product for repolymerization. The subsequent melt and solid-state polymerization steps produced PEF with thermal properties similar to the starting material, demonstrating an experimental closed-loop route.

This does not establish routine collection or recovery of PEF from mixed consumer packaging. Material sorting, contamination and the available local recycling system would affect implementation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The U.S. food-contact assessment for Avantium’s PEF notification 2383 is explicitly use-limited: the July 2024 submission covers specified food-contact articles under room-temperature, refrigerated and frozen-storage conditions and excludes foods above 15% alcohol. It is evidence for that supplier’s notified use and conditions, not unrestricted permission for every PEF grade, hot-fill application or medical device.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Molecular weight, monomer route and crystallization history affect PEF properties. Film thickness, stretching and conditioning also matter, particularly when comparing oxygen transmission or permeability. The reported humidity and molecular-weight comparisons concern specific materials and methods, so neither should be applied directly to every bottle or grade. Feedstock origin does not by itself determine end-of-life behavior. In enzymatic recycling experiments, differences in film crystallinity, enzyme selection, temperature and reaction setup affected mass loss and recovered products. A rate measured for a prepared laboratory film cannot be assumed for an oriented article or for untreated environmental exposure.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Esterification and polycondensation form the furan-containing polyester. Hydroxyl groups react at carboxyl carbonyls to form ester links. Initial esterification releases water; subsequent ester exchange between hydroxyl-ended species extends the chains. Removal of volatile products favors further condensation, and chains grow through reactions among monomers and oligomers.
