sections.overview: Polysulfones are a family of polymers with sulfone-containing backbones, including several aromatic engineering thermoplastics. Distinct members include PSU, PESU and PPSU. Their aromatic structures support use in demanding applications and membranes. The precise backbone and formulation distinguish their properties. PSU, PESU and PPSU contain different aromatic building blocks, even though all are called polysulfones. A dense molded part and a porous filtration membrane also have different architectures and performance requirements.
sections.history:
The commercial polysulfone family grew from work by A. Farnham and R. Johnson at Union Carbide, who obtained high-molecular-weight PSU in 1962. Union Carbide introduced Udel PSU in 1965 and constructed its Marietta, Ohio plant. This is a milestone for bisphenol A polysulfone, not a simultaneous invention of all polyarylsulfones.

The Udel business developed applications in cookware and electrical connectors, followed by plumbing, healthcare, filtration membranes and inkjet cartridges. Amoco acquired it in 1987 and Solvay in 2001. The broader family also includes PESU and PPSU: BASF’s Ultrason portfolio illustrates the distinct sulfone chemistries used in medical technology. Its development therefore combines an early engineering-resin lineage with subsequent diversification into heat-resistant components and separation materials.
sections.nomenclature: Polysulfone is a family-level term and should not be used as a synonym for one named member such as PSU, PESU, or PPSU. The particular bisphenol and dihalodiphenyl-sulfone components identify a specific polymer; a membrane, blend, or reinforced article adds a separate material state.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: The polysulfone family is commonly prepared by step-growth nucleophilic aromatic substitution between a bisphenol and an activated dihalodiphenyl sulfone. Base converts the bisphenol to a phenoxide, which displaces chloride or fluoride from the aryl-sulfone monomer and builds aryl-ether-sulfone chains. Bisphenol A gives the conventional PSU structure; changing the bisphenol produces related members and must not be treated as an interchangeable repeat unit. Polymerization is conducted under dry inert conditions in a high-boiling polar aprotic solvent, with water removed because it limits molar mass. Near-equimolar functional-group balance, monomer purity, a controlled stoichiometric offset, and monofunctional end caps regulate chain length and terminal groups. One cited open study makes a bisphenol-Z polysulfone from 4,4′-dichlorodiphenyl sulfone and potassium carbonate in dimethylacetamide/toluene, then filters and precipitates the polymer. A distinct patent demonstrates a bisphenol-A/4,4′-difluorodiphenyl-sulfone process using carbonate, a composite ionic liquid, an entrainer, and precipitation. Polyethersulfone and polyphenylsulfone have separate monomer-specific records.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
The polysulfone family comprises several amorphous aromatic sulfone thermoplastics—notably bisphenol-A polysulfone (PSU), polyethersulfone (PESU), and polyphenylsulfone (PPSU)—whose repeat-unit structures and mechanical balances are not interchangeable. In dense molded form they are generally glassy, stiff engineering plastics that can yield and deform ductilely, retain useful stiffness at elevated temperature, and resist creep better than many commodity thermoplastics. Toughness remains conditional: notches, thick or highly constrained sections, low temperature, rapid loading, weld lines, residual molding stress, surface damage, and stress-cracking liquids can promote brittle failure. Repeat-unit rigidity and ether-link density, molar mass, residual solvent or moisture, physical aging and annealing, temperature and loading time, specimen geometry and rate, molding or extrusion orientation, additive-manufacturing voids and raster direction, glass or carbon-fiber content and orientation, mineral fillers, lubricants, colorants, thermal or hydrothermal aging, and chemical environment can all change modulus, strength, elongation, impact response, creep, and wear. Porous phase-inversion membranes and hollow fibers add porosity, pore morphology, skin/support architecture, solvent exchange, drying, plasticization, and filler dispersion as dominant variables; their tensile results should not be treated as bulk-resin properties.

A bounded numerical example is Solvay Udel P-1700, an unfilled commercial PSU grade. The supplier's typical-property table reports ASTM D638 tensile strength of 70.3 MPa, tangent tensile modulus of 2.48 GPa, and elongation at break of 50–100%; ASTM D790 flexural strength and modulus are 106 MPa and 2.69 GPa, and ASTM D256 notched Izod impact is 69 J/m. The same guide reports that 30 wt% glass-fiber Udel GF-130 reaches 107.6 MPa tensile strength and 8.69 GPa tensile modulus but only 2% elongation at break, illustrating the stiffness/ductility tradeoff within one supplier system. These are nominal typical values for named formulations; the table warns that batches vary and does not give complete coupon molding, conditioning, tensile-rate, or scatter details. They are not ranges for PESU, PPSU, membranes, printed parts, or the polysulfone family as a whole.
sections.processing:
Polysulfone-family members such as PSU, PESU, and PPSU are amorphous high-temperature thermoplastics converted by injection molding and extrusion, while selected grades are dissolved and cast as flat membranes or spun as hollow fibers before nonsolvent-induced phase inversion. Grade identity must remain explicit because melt viscosity, glass-transition temperature, solvent compatibility, and hydrolysis or impact behavior differ among family members. Pellets should be kept clean and dry; absorbed moisture or other volatiles can create splay, bubbles, hydrolytic loss, or poor surface finish at the high melt temperature, although a properly vented extruder can remove volatiles in some extrusion lines. Melt processing requires sufficient barrel and screw capability, uniform melting with controlled shear, short and stable residence, streamlined nozzles and dies, suitable injection and hold pressure, hot-runner control, mold venting, and uniform mold or roll cooling. Excess time or temperature promotes discoloration and degradation, while high residual stress, sharp temperature gradients, flow orientation, and uneven cooling can cause warpage or later environmental stress cracking. For membrane conversion, a preformed polymer is dissolved with any pore-former or filler, mixed to a homogeneous dope, filtered and degassed, cast or spun at controlled thickness and evaporation history, immersed in a nonsolvent coagulation bath, then washed and dried. Polymer concentration, solvent/nonsolvent exchange, air gap, bath composition and temperature, additives, and post-treatment determine skin formation, pore size, macrovoids, shrinkage, and defects. Aromatic polycondensation remains Synthesis; melt or solution shaping of the finished polymer belongs in Processing.

Solvay's Udel guide gives PSU-grade handling rather than a family window. It targets about 0.05% moisture before molding or extrusion; its oven examples are 3.5 h after pellets reach 135 °C or 2 h at 163 °C, and its hopper example uses about 3.5 h residence at 135 °C with a dew point no warmer than −32 °C. The guide also notes the vented-extruder alternative. A distinct open review documents polysulfone membrane solution preparation, flat-sheet casting or hollow-fiber spinning, evaporation and coagulation-bath phase inversion. Those solution variables are membrane-formulation controls, not melt-molding settings and not a single universal recipe for PSU, PESU, and PPSU.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Aromatic rings and sulfone linkages contribute to the backbone of common polysulfone-family materials. Different linking groups distinguish PSU, PESU and PPSU. Many are amorphous glassy thermoplastics. Membrane fabrication can create pores and asymmetric structures not present in a solid molding. PSU incorporates bisphenol-A-derived segments, whereas PESU and PPSU have different aromatic segments. The differences are visible in the small molecules obtained when a specific backbone is cleaved chemically.
sections.properties: Selected polysulfones offer useful thermal and mechanical performance and can be made into membranes. Membrane permeability and selectivity depend on pore structure and processing. Reinforcement and blends can change stiffness and toughness. Properties of the dense polymer differ from those of a porous membrane. A filtration membrane may use a thin selective region supported by a more porous structure; measured water flow therefore depends on the membrane architecture rather than only the solid polymer’s properties. A review reports that two dense PSU membranes cast from tetrahydrofuran and chloroform had carbon-dioxide permeabilities of 30.0 and 24.8 Barrer, respectively, at 20 °C and 1 bar. This comparison concerns the stated casting conditions and gas, not all polysulfone membranes. A molded heat-resistant component must be evaluated separately.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polysulfone-family materials are used in filtration membranes and heat-resistant fluid-handling components for healthcare, water treatment and food processing. A membrane relies on controlled pores and selectivity, while a molded fitting needs its own mechanical and chemical performance. For example, Toray describes its Toraysulfone TS hemodialyzer as a polysulfone hollow-fiber membrane that removes excess water and dissolved waste from blood; the product line uses fibers with 200-micrometre inside diameter. The membrane is supplied as part of a complete device, with a polypropylene housing and several available membrane areas. PSU, PESU and PPSU have distinct backbones and application requirements.

Purchasing. Supplier portfolios distinguish Udel PSU unfilled or reinforced resin, Veradel PESU powder and compounds, and Radel PPSU color and flow grades. Buyers must specify the polymer, form, process and intended service; a membrane and a molding compound are not interchangeable purchases.

Scale and evidence limits. The catalogs document material choices rather than a combined family purchase tonnage. Device counts or water-treatment capacity cannot be converted directly into resin mass.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A laboratory hydroxylation process cleaves aryl–oxygen links in selected aromatic polysulfones and releases different phenolic compounds according to the backbone. In the study, PSU produced bisphenol A and bisphenol S, while PESU produced bisphenol S. These products belong to a deliberate chemical-recovery reaction, not a list of ambient degradation products. Membranes can also age during repeated cleaning: oxidative agents can attack the polyethersulfone and its hydrophilic additive, changing membrane pores and filtration performance.

Timescales: PESU pellets treated with cesium hydroxide in a polar solvent at 150 °C for four hours gave a reported 92% bisphenol-S yield after extraction in the tested procedure. The reaction temperature, solvent, reagent and feedstock are specific; the duration is not an environmental residence time. Separately, an ultrafiltration membrane made from PESU was soaked for 100 hours at 25 ± 2 °C in 5,000 mg/L oxidant at pH 9 or 11. Hypochlorite exposure increased water permeability and decreased humic-acid retention, whereas peroxide caused little change in those two measures. These accelerated soak results apply to the tested commercial membrane and do not define safe cleaning conditions for every formulation.

Environmental persistence: Controlled solvent treatment does not establish environmental mineralization. The cited work does not determine how long a PSU, PESU or PPSU membrane or molded article persists in soil or water.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A supplier guide discusses regrind for selected sulfone-grade material under controlled processing conditions; grade and prior thermal history influence suitability. Chemical cleavage is a different approach. In a laboratory study, hydroxide treatment of PESU pellets produced bisphenol S, while a PSU example yielded both bisphenol S and bisphenol A.

The reaction recovers small molecules rather than intact polymer, and requires solvent handling and product separation. It does not demonstrate a collection network or a commercial recycling process for mixed polysulfone articles.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation:
The aromatic polysulfone family includes PSU, PESU and PPSU, with grade-dependent handling and application requirements. The following guidance combines family processing precautions with a BPA-based PSU food-contact example.

PSU processing requires protection from hot equipment and molten resin, controlled temperature and residence time, and extraction of processing fumes. BASF’s Ultrason guide, which includes PSU as Ultrason S, warns that excessive thermal exposure produces gaseous decomposition products and can create pressure in a blocked barrel. Its shutdown guidance therefore treats degraded material and hot-machine disassembly as specific equipment hazards.

EU food-contact context, checked 8 September 2026: BPA-based PSU applications require review against Regulation (EU) 2024/3190 and its 2026 correction, including the applicable transitional provisions and derogations. BASF’s March 2026 notice identifies PSU food-contact articles for material requalification and describes an exemption for PSU filtration-membrane assemblies used with food. This is an application-specific restriction; it does not prohibit all industrial PSU uses or establish approval of every alternative resin.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The term polysulfone does not specify a single backbone or grade. Molecular weight, processing, reinforcement and ageing affect material response. Membrane data must retain solvent, preparation and morphology. A PSU datasheet or a particular membrane cannot represent the entire family. Backbone distinctions matter even in recovery: a chemical treatment of PESU can release bisphenol S, while a PSU formulation produces additional bisphenol-A-derived material under the reported conditions.

synthesisRoutes.conditions: Carbonate-mediated reaction in dimethylacetamide and toluene with water removal.
synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Phenolate nucleophilic aromatic substitution forms aryl-ether-sulfone chains. Carbonate base supplies the bisphenolate nucleophile, which displaces halide from the sulfone-activated aromatic carbon to create an ether link. Both monomers carry two reacting groups, allowing repeated end-group coupling and step-growth chain formation.

steps.title: Prepare the reaction
steps.body: Combine bisphenol A and dichlorodiphenyl sulfone with potassium carbonate in dimethylacetamide and toluene; remove water during reaction.

steps.title: Form aromatic ether links
steps.body: Phenolate oxygen replaces chloride on the sulfone-activated aromatic monomer, forming the aryl ether backbone.

steps.title: Form and recover the product
steps.body: Filter out salts, precipitate the oligomer, wash and dry.

sections.overview: Polyisoprene refers to polymers built from isoprene units. Natural rubber is predominantly cis-1,4-polyisoprene and contains additional biological components. Synthetic polyisoprenes can be made with different chain microstructures. Vulcanization and compounding create materials used in tires and other elastomer products. The arrangement of the isoprene units changes material behavior: cis-rich natural rubber can behave as an elastomer, whereas trans-rich polyisoprene has a different chain geometry. A rubber compound also contains curatives and often fillers beyond the polymer itself.
sections.history:
Polyisoprene has both a natural history and a history of chemical synthesis. Natural rubber was used by Indigenous peoples of the Americas before European industrial development; Charles Goodyear’s sulfur-vulcanization work in 1839 helped make rubber goods more durable. Greville Williams isolated and named isoprene in 1860, Gustave Bouchardat produced rubberlike material from it in 1879, and William Tilden pursued isoprene obtained from turpentine in 1882. These early experiments should not be equated with modern stereoregular synthetic rubber manufacture.

The family also encompasses the material lineage represented by gutta-percha. Henry Bewley and Samuel Gurney founded the Gutta Percha Company in 1845; its products moved from molded objects and industrial linings to insulation for the 1850 and 1851 cross-Channel cables. Stereoregular synthetic polyisoprene reached commercial production at Shell in 1960 and Goodyear in 1962, with tires, molded mechanical goods and other rubber products becoming important uses. Natural and synthetic members therefore have related but distinct industrial histories.
sections.nomenclature: Polyisoprene is a family term rather than a single natural-rubber or synthetic-rubber grade. Natural rubber and synthetic IR share the isoprene-polymer boundary but differ in source and composition; a branched polymer, a vulcanizate, or a filled compound requires its own qualifier.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: A cited synthetic route polymerizes isoprene in hydrocarbon solution using a neodymium-based catalyst. The patent prepares the catalyst by reacting a neodymium carboxylate with an organoaluminum compound in the presence of isoprene, then adding a dialkylaluminum chloride. It describes catalyst preparation, polymerization and termination options; the cited example does not specify a cis fraction. A separate laboratory study examined n-butyllithium-initiated isoprene polymerization in n-hexane under high vacuum. Conditions and product microstructure depend on the chosen preparation.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyisoprenes include natural rubber, synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene, trans-rich materials, and formulated/vulcanized elastomers; their mechanics depend on microstructure, molecular weight, nonisoprene components in natural rubber, crosslink system/density, filler and plasticizer package, strain-induced crystallization, temperature, strain rate, aging, and specimen orientation. In a vulcanized natural-rubber versus synthetic-polyisoprene study, strain-induced crystallization began at 250% strain for natural rubber and 350% for synthetic IR; stress upturns occurred at 383% and 450% strain, respectively. Adding liquid-isoprene or naphthenic-oil plasticizers changed crystallinity and tensile strength, with the reported reduction greater for the IR composites. These are specifically formulated and vulcanized rubber-network results, not values for all polyisoprene forms.
sections.processing:
Polyisoprene rubbers are converted through compound preparation followed by shaping and vulcanization. Directly supported operations include internal or Banbury mixing, two-roll milling and sheet formation, press vulcanization, and latex- or solution-dip molding with repeated deposition, drying, leaching, cooling, powdering, and stripping. The choice between dry mixing and solvent-assisted wet mixing affects filler dispersion, dust, energy use, and compound viscosity. For filled compounds, filler moisture and agglomeration, silane or coupling-agent distribution, mixing sequence, rotor or roll shear, dump temperature, solvent recovery, coagulation and drying, sheet gauge, scorch safety, and a rheometer-derived optimum cure time are important. For dipped articles, solution or latex viscosity, degassing, coagulant pickup, withdrawal and form rotation, number of dip/dry cycles, residual-solvent removal, cure heat transfer, cooling, rinsing, and release control thickness and uniformity. Vulcanizing-agent chemistry belongs in Synthesis; compounding, article shaping, and the vulcanization equipment and schedule belong in Processing.

McGlothlin and Schmid disclose several bounded NATSYN 2200 cis-1,4-polyisoprene dip-molding examples. In one, 21 g of the named grade and 0.63 g dicumyl peroxide were dissolved in 700 g tetrahydrofuran, bubbles were allowed to dissipate, a mandrel was dipped and air-dried for 15 min, eight dip/dry cycles were used, the film was finally air-dried 1.5 h, and it was cured for 3 min in a 180 °C molten-salt bath before rinsing, cooling, powdering, and stripping. A separate study by Wang and co-workers used SKI-5 PM cis-1,4-polyisoprene in a wet-mixed silica compound: the silica/TESPT suspension was mixed at 50 °C and 20,000 rpm for 3 min, combined with a 5 wt% IR solution for 30 min at 300 rpm, coagulated in ethanol, micro-extruded, and vacuum-dried at 45 °C. Activators, accelerator, and sulfur were then incorporated on a two-roll mill at 70 °C for 5 min to form about 2.5 mm sheets, which were press-cured at 145 °C and 15 MPa for the formulation's measured t90. Neither schedule is a universal polyisoprene cure.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Isoprene can be incorporated with different configurations and connection patterns, including cis-1,4 and trans-1,4 units. Natural rubber contains a predominantly cis chain structure along with nonisoprene components. Synthetic catalysts influence the distribution of microstructures. Crosslinking connects chains into a network during vulcanization. Cis and trans describe the geometry around retained double bonds in 1,4-linked chains. Their different spatial arrangements influence packing and the accessibility of the double bonds to a particular enzyme.
sections.properties: High-cis polyisoprene can provide elasticity and undergo strain-induced crystallization under suitable conditions. Nonisoprene components and crosslinks affect the response of natural rubber. In one study of unvulcanized natural rubber, the TSR 10 specimen had 33.6% gel and a Mooney viscosity of 108.6, compared with 19.8% gel and 89.8 for the TSR 3CV specimen. The authors linked the higher raw-rubber gel and viscosity to differences in naturally occurring network formation; the comparison is specific to those prepared samples. Fillers and cure change stiffness, strength and fatigue behavior in compounds. Other polyisoprene microstructures can behave differently. The chain’s cis or trans microstructure influences packing, while strain and curing change the structure during use. Results on sulfur-cured natural rubber cannot automatically describe an uncured synthetic grade or a trans-rich material.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Natural and synthetic polyisoprene are used in tires and mechanical rubber goods. Zeon lists its synthetic Nipol IR2200 for tires, conveyor belts, seals and coated fabrics, and says it can be blended with natural rubber, SBR or BR. The supplier lists a lower-viscosity IR2200L variant with a Mooney design value of 70, compared with 82 for IR2200, which gives a raw-material handling distinction when selecting a grade. Elastic recovery is useful in parts that repeatedly deform, but the raw-polymer viscosity values are not cured-product performance measurements. The chosen grade, fillers and cure distinguish a tire compound from a thin latex product.

Purchasing. Synthetic IR is bought by raw-rubber grade for compounding, while natural rubber is traded as technically specified rubber, ribbed smoked sheets or concentrated latex. A buyer selects the material form and specifications for the intended process; raw rubber is not the same product as a cured tire or seal.

Scale and evidence limits. CATAS, citing ANRPC, reports 15.364 million tonnes of natural-rubber consumption worldwide in 2024. That is a natural-rubber supply-stream estimate, not pure-polyisoprene mass or combined natural-plus-synthetic consumption; no combined family total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A purified latex-clearing protein oxidatively cleaves cis-1,4-polyisoprene double bonds, producing smaller chains with aldehyde and ketone ends. The same study did not detect cleavage of trans-polyisoprene under its conditions. This comparison demonstrates enzyme and stereochemistry specificity rather than the full fate of a filled, vulcanized article.

Timescales: For product analysis, researchers incubated a diluted latex emulsion with purified protein in pH 7 buffer for 20 hours at 30 °C. The identified oligomers mark a controlled reaction endpoint; the experiment did not determine complete mineralization or an outdoor lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Chain scission to oligomers is not equivalent to conversion of all material to carbon dioxide. In a separate controlled soil test at 25 ± 2 °C, small pieces of vulcanized natural-rubber formulations produced CO₂ equivalent to about 28% of the theoretical carbon for a highly crosslinked formulation and about 59% for a lightly crosslinked formulation after 365 days. These are formulation-level results for the tested 3 mm pieces, which included curatives; they do not isolate all carbon sources or establish a family-wide mineralization time. Microstructure, crosslinks, formulation and environmental conditions can change an article’s fate.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
A patent describes devulcanization approaches for sulfur-cured isoprene rubber. The objective is to reduce network crosslinks so material can be incorporated into new formulations, but the resulting material is not necessarily identical to the original raw polymer.

The separate latex-clearing enzyme experiment produces oxidized cis-polyisoprene oligomers rather than regenerating intact chains. Neither example establishes a single recycling process for every stereoisomer, formulated rubber or locally collected product.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The source of polyisoprene matters for allergy assessment. Natural-rubber latex contains plant proteins that can cause allergic reactions, while synthetic rubber latex does not supply those proteins. Added processing chemicals can still cause contact rashes. NIOSH’s distinction concerns associated proteins and formulation ingredients, rather than identifying the polyisoprene chain itself as the latex allergen.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Natural and synthetic polyisoprene are not identical materials even when both have high cis content. Source, catalyst, microstructure, additives and cure influence performance. Temperature and strain history affect measured tensile behavior. A natural-rubber result cannot be assigned to every polyisoprene. A purified latex-clearing enzyme cleaved the cis-polyisoprene samples in one comparison but did not cleave trans-polyisoprene under the reported conditions. That is an enzyme- and test-specific distinction, not a guarantee about environmental degradation of every product.

sections.overview: Fluoropolymers are a family of polymers made from fluorinated monomers. The family includes perfluorinated and partially fluorinated structures, as well as thermoplastics and elastomers. Individual members differ in composition and processing. They are used in seals, coatings, electrical insulation and other demanding applications. PTFE is a perfluorinated example, while PVDF retains hydrogen as well as fluorine in its repeat units. Their processing and end-of-life behavior differ; the broad family label does not identify a single resin or treatment.
sections.history:
A central fluoropolymer milestone was Roy Plunkett’s accidental discovery of PTFE at DuPont on 6 April 1938 while investigating tetrafluoroethylene for refrigerant research. Chemours traces an early strategic use to chemically resistant containment during the Manhattan Project. Teflon-branded PTFE entered commercial sale in 1946.

DuPont subsequently broadened this product lineage through FEP in 1960, ETFE in 1970 and PFA in 1972. These dates identify commercial introductions within one supplier’s portfolio, not invention dates for the entire fluoropolymer family. The materials developed roles in chemical equipment, electrical insulation, aerospace and nonstick surfaces. Daikin’s own chronology records DAI-EL fluoroelastomer marketing in 1970 and NEOFLON FEP pellets in 1974, illustrating the expansion of the field beyond PTFE and beyond a single company. Individual fluoroplastics, fluoroelastomers and ionomers retain distinct histories.
sections.nomenclature: Fluoropolymer is a collective family term rather than the name of one repeating-unit structure, grade, or product form. Individual materials such as PTFE, FEP, PVDF, and ETFE require their own names and evidence; their shared fluoropolymer classification does not make them interchangeable.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Fluoropolymers are a broad family defined by fluorine-containing polymer structures, not one polymerization route or one monomer. The family includes fluorinated olefin homopolymers and copolymers (for example materials derived from tetrafluoroethylene, vinylidene fluoride, chlorotrifluoroethylene, hexafluoropropylene, or fluorinated vinyl ethers), as well as side-chain-fluorinated polymers. Free-radical emulsion, suspension, solution, and bulk routes are documented for different members; monomer selection, initiator, medium, surfactant or chain-transfer agent, and feed ratios are therefore subfamily- and grade-specific. An open review covers fluorinated-monomer selection and emulsion-polymerization approaches, while a patent gives a bounded radical ethylene/tetrafluoroethylene example with initiator and chain-transfer-agent control. This family-level account does not treat any one PTFE, PVDF, ETFE, FEP, PFA, or fluoroelastomer recipe as universal, and excludes later compounding or article fabrication.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Fluoropolymers span melt-processable thermoplastics, non-melt-processable PTFE, elastomers, ionomers, and functional materials, so no single tensile strength or modulus represents the family. Mechanical response depends first on chemical identity and molecular architecture, then on crystallinity and thermal history, molecular weight/grade, filler or reinforcement, and finished form such as tube, film, coating, molded part, or elastomeric seal. An open comparative review illustrates the scale of this difference: it lists PTFE with a 550 MPa tensile modulus and 300–550% break elongation, but PVDF with 1,040–2,070 MPa and 50–250%, while ETFE is tabulated at 827 MPa and 150–300%. These are literature summary values for distinct fluoropolymers, not a property range for every commercial grade.

A bounded tubing comparison provides a method-tagged endpoint. Parker lists ASTM D638 tensile-strength ranges of 2,000–7,000 psi for PTFE tubing, 2,800–5,000 psi for FEP tubing, 4,000–4,500 psi for PFA tubing, and 4,500–6,200 psi for PVDF tubing. The values are specifically the supplier's general fluoropolymer-tubing comparison, and should not be transferred to other geometries, grades, or fluoroelastomer compounds.
sections.processing: Fluoropolymer processing is member- and grade-dependent. PTFE's high crystallinity and melt viscosity lead to compression or isostatic molding, ram or paste extrusion, and aqueous-dispersion coating/film casting, whereas melt-processable members such as FEP, PFA, ETFE, ECTFE, and PVDF can use thermoplastic extrusion, injection molding, film or sheet forming, and related operations. The open industry review reports FEP injection molding, extrusion, and film casting, PVDF processing around 200–260 °C, and ECTFE processing around 260–300 °C; it also notes that PTFE properties depend on particle size, sintering temperature, and pressure. For a bounded FEP 100 example, Chemours specifies 3 mm pellets, conventional melt extrusion and injection/compression/blow molding, corrosion-resistant high-nickel equipment, and equipment capability to 400 °C. These settings illustrate the family spread rather than a universal fluoropolymer window; melt viscosity, crystalline morphology, residence time, shear, and corrosive fumes require material-specific design and ventilation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Fluorine may be present along the backbone or in side groups, depending on the polymer. Some fluoropolymers are semicrystalline while others have less ordered structures. Monomer sequence, side groups and thermal history affect chain packing. Fluorinated structure can strongly influence surface and intermolecular behavior. PTFE chains have a carbon backbone surrounded by fluorine, whereas PVDF contains hydrogen-bearing units. These differences affect chemical reactions as well as processing and should be retained when comparing family members.
sections.properties: Selected fluoropolymers provide chemical resistance, low surface energy and electrical insulation. Some also offer low friction or useful thermal stability. These attributes differ among family members and grades. Crystallinity, comonomer content, additives and processing influence the finished material. A European technical report notes that PVDF can be extruded and injection molded, while PTFE needs different forming methods because of its very high melt viscosity. That comparison concerns those polymers and does not assign a single processing route to the whole family. A supplier comparison lists typical melting points of about 327 °C for PTFE and 177 °C for PVDF, illustrating the range within this family. These values are material-selection context, not specified continuous-use temperatures or grade-independent limits.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Fluoropolymers are used in seals, chemical linings, wire insulation, coatings, membranes and semiconductor equipment. The European technical report identifies PVDF in coatings, membranes and batteries, while PTFE is used for applications including electrical insulation and low-friction components. PVDF can also act as a binder within a lithium-ion battery electrode, holding active material in a coated layer; this application uses the polymer as a component of a larger assembly. Chemical resistance or electrical behavior may motivate a choice, but the particular polymer and grade must fit the service.

Purchasing. Buyers specify the chemistry, grade and form. For example, Chemours supplies FEP 100 pellets in 25 kg bags and recommends 1,000 kg pallet shipments; a finished coating or seal is a different purchase from those pellets, and this package does not describe all fluoropolymers.

Scale and evidence limits. An industry-commissioned FPG study estimates EU27 fluoropolymer demand at 56,500 tonnes in 2025 and reports 29,500 tonnes produced domestically, about 15,000 exported and 42,000 imported. These are aggregate regional estimates, not global purchases or a PTFE/PVDF-specific split.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Thermal decomposition depends on fluoropolymer chemistry and treatment conditions. A vacuum study of PTFE at high temperatures reported predominantly tetrafluoroethylene among its volatile products. In the same study, PVDF yielded hydrogen fluoride and wax-like chain fragments, illustrating a different route for a hydrogen-containing fluoropolymer. Separately, researchers treated PVDF concentrate from a photovoltaic backsheet in alkaline solution and recovered fluoride. These treatment-specific products cannot be assumed to describe ordinary outdoor weathering.

Timescales: In the PTFE vacuum study, a 305.7 mg specimen at 423.5 °C lost 0.5% of its mass in 337 minutes. In the separate alkaline study, pulverized PVDF concentrate reached 90.4% defluorination after 600 minutes at 90 °C in 4.0 M sodium hydroxide with tetrabutylammonium bromide. A PVDF powder reached the same defluorination endpoint faster under the reported conditions. Volatile mass loss and fluoride release are different measurements, and neither gives a natural environmental lifetime or a family-wide rate.

Environmental persistence: Fluoropolymers can persist in the environment, but fragmentation, loss of mechanical integrity or release of fluoride does not establish mineralization of all carbon-containing material. Product-specific fate depends on the polymer, additives, article and exposure. These reactor studies do not establish a common soil or aquatic residence time for the family.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Recovery routes differ with the fluoropolymer. A 2021 European technical report describes remelting selected PVDF scrap through extrusion, including production scrap, while PTFE scrap may instead be ground to powder and sintered or used in specialized processing. For PTFE, the report describes shredding and grinding scrap before molding or sintering; the recovered powder may be blended with virgin PTFE where high-purity performance is not required. PVDF production scrap and scrap from customers’ molding processes are identified as feedstocks for specific recycled-content products. Feedstock contamination and output requirements constrain both routes.

A separate PTFE chemical-recovery study uses phosphate-assisted ball milling to release fluorine-containing salts for later reactions. This is a laboratory conversion of selected PTFE materials, not recovery of the original polymer or proof that mixed household waste is accepted. In a separate battery-waste example, PVDF binder makes up only a small fraction of the assembly and is difficult to separate; the report describes metal recovery as the principal recycling incentive. Pyrolysis products and treatment of fluorinated residues require process-specific evaluation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Fluoropolymer handling guidance distinguishes the supplied resin from fumes generated during heating. The Fluoropolymers Product Group guide covers PTFE, FEP, PFA, ETFE, ECTFE and PVDF and warns that overheated fumes can cause polymer fume fever; higher exposure can be more serious. It calls for effective extraction of fumes and dust, protection from molten material, and keeping tobacco away from resin-handling areas because contamination can create hazardous fumes when burned. Fillers and dispersion ingredients need separate assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Fluoropolymers differ substantially in melt behavior, cost and chemical compatibility. Some materials require specialized processing, and some can creep under load. Resistance to one medium does not imply resistance to every chemical or temperature. Comparisons must identify the polymer, grade and service conditions. The European report identifies remelting as a possible route for selected PVDF scrap and grinding and sintering as a different route for PTFE scrap. Recovered feedstock quality and the intended part remain material-specific.

sections.overview: Polyurethanes are a family of polymers containing urethane linkages. Many commercial systems are made by reacting polyols with di- or polyisocyanates. Variations in reactants and processing produce foams, elastomers, coatings and adhesives. A particular material can be thermoplastic or crosslinked. Flexible cushioning foams and rigid insulation foams, for example, use different formulations and cellular structures. Their end-of-life options depend on whether the material is a thermoplastic or a cured network.
sections.history:
Otto Bayer’s 1937 work established the polyurethane development program that became a major part of Bayer’s materials business. Commercial expansion required subsequent work on formulations and machinery. Bayer presented its Moltopren flexible foam for upholstered furniture in 1952; the wider chemistry later supported automotive seating and coatings, including water-based coating raw materials introduced in 1988.

Equipment companies helped turn reactive formulations into large-volume products. Hennecke records flexible-foam block equipment in 1952, high-pressure component metering in 1955, continuous rigid-foam panel equipment in 1966, and automated molded-foam systems in 1971. Furniture cushioning and construction insulation consequently form distinct application histories within the family. The 1937 origin is a chemistry milestone; it does not mean that every polyurethane foam, coating, fiber or elastomer formulation was invented at that time.
sections.nomenclature: PU is a family-level designation, not a single composition, foam density, elastomer, coating, or adhesive. The polyol type, isocyanate, chain extender, crosslinking level, and any blowing formulation distinguish individual polyurethane materials and must remain stated.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyurethanes are produced by polyaddition of compounds bearing hydroxyl groups with di- or polyisocyanates, forming urethane linkages without a small-molecule condensation product. Common soft-segment feedstocks are polyether and polyester polyols; common isocyanates include methylene diphenyl diisocyanate, toluene diisocyanate, hexamethylene diisocyanate, and isophorone diisocyanate. Predominantly difunctional reactants plus short diol chain extenders can give linear thermoplastic polyurethane, whereas polyols or isocyanates with functionality above two create crosslinked foams, coatings, adhesives, and elastomers. A one-shot route mixes the reactive components together; a prepolymer route first reacts excess diisocyanate with a polyol and then chain-extends or crosslinks the isocyanate-terminated intermediate. Tertiary amines and organometallic catalysts such as tin carboxylates accelerate urethane formation. One cited patent documents conventional polyol/polyisocyanate chemistry and preformed tin-complex catalysts. A distinct patent covers water-stable titanium, zirconium, or hafnium catalyst systems, polyether/polyester polyols, polyisocyanates, chain extenders, and prepolymer variants. Water can react with isocyanate to generate urea linkages and carbon dioxide in foamed systems. Formulation-specific blowing, molding, and cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
The polyurethane family covers mechanically dissimilar materials: flexible and rigid cellular foams, rubber-like segmented elastomers, thermoplastic polyurethanes, cast thermoset networks, coatings, and adhesives. In many solid segmented polyurethanes, mobile polyol-derived soft segments provide compliance while hydrogen-bonded or crystalline urethane-rich hard domains provide reinforcing physical crosslinks; covalent crosslinking can add permanent network restraint. Elastomeric grades can show nonlinear viscoelasticity, hysteresis, cyclic softening, and strain hardening, whereas highly crosslinked or rigid grades trade extensibility for stiffness. Cellular foams instead respond through cell-wall bending or stretching, collapse or buckling into a stress plateau, and eventual densification, so apparent density and cell structure can outweigh the neat matrix response. Polyol chemistry and molecular weight, isocyanate symmetry, chain extender, hard-segment fraction and ordering, NCO/OH ratio, crosslink density, hydrogen bonding and microphase separation, fillers or fibers, plasticizers, blowing level, open- versus closed-cell content, cell size and rise-direction anisotropy, cure and post-cure, moisture and hydrolytic history, temperature, loading rate, cyclic history, and specimen geometry are all consequential. Values from foams, elastomers, and coatings must therefore remain separate.

Patel and co-workers provide a bounded cellular example. They tested commercial Sawbones polyurethane foams as 9 mm-diameter cylinders, 3.9 or 7.7 mm long, in unconstrained quasi-static compression at 0.0033 s^-1 with no preload or preconditioning. The 0.09 g/cm^3 open-cell rigid foam gave Young's moduli of 0.08–0.93 MPa and yield strengths of 0.01–0.07 MPa; the 0.16 and 0.32 g/cm^3 closed-cell ASTM Grade 10 and 20 foams together gave moduli of 15.1–151.4 MPa and yield strengths of 0.9–4.5 MPa. Cylinder length affected the apparent result, and cores were taken in a preferred cellular orientation. These measurements demonstrate density-, cell-, orientation-, and geometry-sensitive foam behavior, not intrinsic constants for dense polyurethane or for the family.
sections.processing:
Polyurethane conversion must be organized by material subgroup rather than treated as one melt-processing window. Flexible and rigid foams are shaped by metering and mixing a polyol-side formulation with an isocyanate side, dispensing into an open or closed mold or by spray, and controlling cream, rise, gel, demold, and post-cure. Cast elastomers, coatings, adhesives, and reaction-injection-molded parts likewise use reactive mixing and an article-forming cure, whereas already polymerized thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) is dried and injection molded or extruded into film, sheet, tubing, profiles, cable jackets, and molded parts. For reactive systems, component identity and exact mass or volume ratio, moisture exclusion, preconditioning temperature, filler or pigment agitation, catalyst and blowing-agent distribution, mix quality, degassing, shot size, mold release, tool temperature, pressure, venting, exotherm, and cure/post-cure schedule control bubbles, cells, density, skin, knit lines, shrinkage, scorching, and conversion. Foam lines additionally depend on nucleation, pour pattern, cavity fill and venting, heat removal, and safe control of the rising exotherm. TPU processing depends on desiccant drying, moisture-protected transfer, shear and residence control, melt and mold or die temperature, cooling, drawdown, orientation, annealing, and blocking. Network-forming reaction chemistry and manufacture of polyurethane resin belong in Synthesis; here the reactive operation is included only as the shaping and cure schedule performed in the mold, on the substrate, or in the foam cavity.

The open family review directly documents foam, cast elastomer, coating, adhesive, reaction-injection-molding, and thermoplastic routes and shows why chain extender, catalyst, blowing agent, filler, and crosslinking choices define a formulation rather than a universal process. Two independent supplier examples bound practical settings. Honeywell's hand-mix foam evaluation guide conditions the named polyol premix near 10 °C, calls for 3–10 s mixing after isocyanate addition (5 s in its example), and requires prompt pouring for the rise test. Lubrizol's injection guide covers its Estane, Pearlthane, Isoplast, and Estaloc TPU portfolio from about 70 Shore A to 90 Shore D and advises allowing molded parts to rest 48 h before a 122 °C paint bake to reduce distortion from molded-in stress. The foam and TPU examples describe different polyurethane subgroups and cannot be combined into a family-wide window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Reaction of hydroxyl and isocyanate groups forms urethane linkages. Polyol structure, chain extenders and reactant functionality influence chain architecture and crosslinking. Some formulations contain hard and soft regions, while foams also contain gas-filled cells. Cell structure and density depend on blowing and processing. In a foam the gas-filled cells are part of the article’s structure, so a low-density foam and a solid polyurethane elastomer can respond very differently even when both contain urethane groups.
sections.properties: Polyurethane materials range from flexible foams and elastomers to rigid foams and coatings. Their stiffness, resilience and thermal behavior depend on formulation and morphology. Foam compression is influenced by cell structure, density and test geometry. In a comparison of rigid polyurethane bone-model foams, an open-cell 0.09 g/cm³ foam gave compression moduli of 0.08–0.93 MPa, while the closed-cell 0.16 and 0.32 g/cm³ foams gave 15.1–151.4 MPa across the tested cylinder geometries. Both density and cell structure differed, so this is not a density-only rule or a value for flexible cushioning foam. Additives, ageing and environmental exposure also affect performance. In insulation, trapped gas and the cellular structure are relevant to heat flow; in cushioning, the response of the compressed cells matters. Polyol type, crosslinks and density must be specified before comparing particular foams.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polyurethanes are used in flexible cushioning for mattresses and vehicle seats, rigid foams for building and refrigeration insulation, and elastomers, coatings and adhesives. Foam cells make a material lightweight and affect its compression and heat flow, but a cushioning foam and a rigid insulation board require different formulations. As a specific example, Rogers markets its soft PORON 4701-30 polyurethane foam for gap filling, gasketing and vibration isolation; it compresses to fill a gap and is available in different thicknesses and densities. The supplier lists a typical 25% compression-force deflection of 35 kPa for the 4701-30-20 variant, a material-specific design measure rather than a family-wide property. The family name alone is not a product specification.

Purchasing. A formulator can buy specified polyisocyanates and polyols, such as grades in Covestro’s Desmodur portfolio with companion polyols, then select catalysts, blowing agents and other ingredients for the system. Buyers can instead specify a finished foam, coating or elastomer through a converter; the mass of precursor purchased is not necessarily the mass of finished polymer.

Scale and evidence limits. Plastics Europe reports 413.8 million tonnes of global plastics production in 2023, with fossil-based PUR at 5.3%: a calculated roughly 21.9 million tonnes. That preliminary category excludes quantities used in adhesives, sealants, coatings and several other non-plastic-product applications while including PU fibers; it is not a complete polyurethane-family total or an end-use split.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Polyurethane formulations can contain urethane, urea and, for polyester polyols, ester linkages that react differently with water. Hydrolysis can cleave ester groups to alcohols and acids, while cleavage of urethane linkages yields an alcohol and an unstable carbamic-acid-derived product. Deliberate glycolysis uses a glycol to break a tested rigid foam into a polyol-containing mixture; this reactor treatment is not an environmental-fate measurement.

Timescales: In one laboratory rigid-foam study, waste foam was stirred with ethylene glycol and diethylene glycol at 180 °C for 2.5 hours in the presence of a catalyst. The recovered mixture was used in a new foam formulation. That treatment time does not describe a discarded foam’s natural degradation. In a separate ISO 20200 simulated industrial-compost experiment, selected bioderived polyester-polyurethane foam formulations lost an average 25.4 ± 3.6% of their initial mass after 45 days; two less-disintegrated samples were excluded from that average. A polyether polyurethane control lost much less mass in this comparison, but its solid form and chemistry differed from the foams.

Environmental persistence: Polyester- and polyether-based materials, coatings and foams differ in chemistry and form. Conversion in heated glycol, fragmentation or loss of mechanical integrity does not establish complete mineralization in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill; no single family-wide lifetime follows from these examples. Compost disintegration and mass loss do not establish conversion of polymer carbon to carbon dioxide or biomass, nor do they demonstrate that other polyurethane formulations will behave similarly in soil or water.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Crosslinked polyurethane foam cannot simply be melted into the original precursor. In a laboratory study, rigid-foam waste was glycolyzed with ethylene glycol and diethylene glycol, and the resulting recycled polyol mixture was combined with other ingredients to make new rigid foam. Catalyst choice changed the viscosity and hydroxyl value of the recovered mixture, which affects its suitability as a formulation ingredient.

Mechanical recovery and chemical routes have different feedstock and product requirements; a recovered glycolysate is not necessarily the original pure polyol. Sorting by foam chemistry, managing impurities and qualifying the resulting material are necessary before the results can be applied to a different waste stream.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: During polyurethane manufacture or application, unreacted isocyanate ingredients can irritate skin, eyes and airways and cause sensitization or occupational asthma. NIOSH emphasizes enclosure and ventilation to control vapor or aerosol exposure and protection against skin contact. These ingredient hazards concern reactive formulations and cannot be assigned unchanged to a fully cured article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Polyurethane does not identify one polyol, isocyanate or finished material. Crosslinking, foam density, fillers and cure strongly affect properties. A commercial foam compression result cannot represent a coating or every other foam. Measurements require the grade, specimen, conditioning and test method. Hydrolysis can also affect different linkages: a polyester-based formulation contains ester groups in addition to urethane groups, so its reaction products need not match those of a polyether-based formulation.

sections.overview: Polysiloxanes are a family of polymers with silicon–oxygen backbones and organic groups attached to silicon. They are often called silicones. Different chain structures and degrees of crosslinking produce fluids, elastomers and resins. Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) is a widely used member. PDMS fluid and crosslinked silicone rubber share a siloxane backbone but differ in their ability to flow or recover after deformation. Their applications and environmental behavior therefore cannot be inferred from the word silicone alone.
sections.history:
Frederic Stanley Kipping’s organosilicon research at the beginning of the twentieth century supplied early silicone chemistry. Industrial development accelerated through J. Franklin Hyde’s work at Corning in the 1930s and the formation of Dow Corning in 1943. Eugene Rochow at General Electric developed the direct methylchlorosilane synthesis in 1940; Richard Müller independently developed a related route in Germany. These precursor processes enabled silicone production at industrial scale.

Early uses included electrical protection in aircraft. Subsequent development produced lubricating fluids, caulks, insulating materials and gaskets. Wacker’s history adds a 1949 silane furnace, textile treatments and release agents in 1951, and later heat- and room-temperature-curing rubbers. The family’s progress thus involved precursor manufacture, control of organic substituents, and curing technology, rather than one invention encompassing all polysiloxane fluids, resins and elastomers.
sections.nomenclature: Polysiloxane and silicone-polymer family are collective terms, not one fixed polymer composition. PDMS, fluorosilicones, vinyl-functional materials, and cured silicone elastomers are narrower polymers or networks whose substitution pattern and cure state should be named.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polysiloxanes contain Si–O–Si backbones bearing organic substituents and are commonly built in two stages. Organohalosilanes such as dimethyldichlorosilane are first hydrolyzed to silanols and cyclic or short linear siloxanes, with acid byproduct separated and the hydrolysate washed or neutralized. Those intermediates are then condensed or equilibrated to higher-molar-mass linear, branched, cyclic, or resinous products. Difunctional silanes favor chains, whereas tri- and tetrafunctional silanes introduce branching or networks; monofunctional silanes can cap chains. Ring-opening or redistribution polymerization of cyclic siloxanes is another defining route. One cited patent details controlled organohalosilane hydrolysis and separation of aqueous acid from a polyorganosiloxane hydrolysate. A distinct historical patent polymerizes fully condensed organosiloxanes with sodium- or potassium-alkoxide and alcohol–hydroxide catalysts. Acid or base catalysts, silanolate initiators, water balance, feed functionality, end blockers, and cyclic-monomer/initiator ratio provide architecture and molar-mass control. Subsequent crosslinking of functional polysiloxanes is described in the corresponding silicone-rubber or silicone-resin records.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polysiloxanes include low-molar-mass fluids, crosslinked silicone elastomers, filled rubbers, resins, and functional copolymers, so a PDMS value cannot represent the whole family. Organosilicon substituents, chain length, network/cure chemistry and crosslink density, filler loading and dispersion, temperature, rate, aging, and test geometry govern response. A bounded commercial-elastomer example is Sylgard 184 PDMS tested at room temperature and 500 mm min−1: Young's modulus 3.9 ± 0.2 MPa, tensile strength 10 ± 1 MPa, and break elongation 119 ± 9%. These are one cured PDMS formulation's tensile values; other siloxane fluids, resins, and silicone-rubber grades can differ substantially.
sections.processing:
Polysiloxane processing depends strongly on whether the material is a low-viscosity silicone fluid, a liquid silicone rubber (LSR), a filled high-consistency elastomer, or a silicone-resin/encapsulant formulation; these forms should not be assigned one family-wide processing window. Liquid and resinous formulations are commonly metered, mixed with fillers or the second component, and degassed before casting, coating, encapsulation, or molding. Vacuum degassing reduces bubbles introduced by high-viscosity mixing, but excessive vacuum or residence time can remove volatile solvent and change the formulation; short pot life also limits hold-up in mixers, feed lines, and molds.

For article conversion, pour or inject low-viscosity silicone into an open, closed, or vacuum mold, then cure in the mold and cool before demolding; LSR injection molding uses cooled feed/mixing hardware to delay cure and a heated cavity for rapid crosslinking. Silicone coatings and encapsulants can be spread or cast onto a substrate and then thermally or otherwise cured, while selected polysiloxane precursor systems can be liquid-cast into thin films or patterned parts. Filled high-consistency silicone compounds require more intensive distributive mixing and may be compression-, transfer-, or extrusion-formed before cure. These operations are formulation- and equipment-specific: shear history changes dispersion and viscosity, trapped air causes voids, and premature cure can block a die, gate, or mold before filling. Cooling, post-cure, and controlled demolding are used when needed to complete conversion, reduce residual volatiles or stress, and preserve dimensions; cure shrinkage and exotherm matter particularly in thick castings and optical encapsulants.

A bounded open experiment by Ishikawa et al. used three liquid silicone rubbers with viscosities of 3–20 Pa·s in an in-vacuum molding system. The silicone was mixed and vacuum-defoamed, allowed about 1 min for air escape after transfer to the tank, poured into molds under vacuum, rested for 2 min after filling, and then cured; the method molded cylindrical structures of 1.2–5 mm diameter without bubbles. This is a soft-robotics molding demonstration for those liquid formulations and mold dimensions, not a general polysiloxane cure schedule. A separate silicone-encapsulant study used cast cylindrical specimens and showed why cure temperature, staged heating, room-temperature cooling, exotherm, and approximately 3% complete-cure shrinkage must be considered for a particular resin geometry.

The broad family therefore supports solution or liquid casting, coating, encapsulation, compression/transfer molding, LSR injection molding, and extrusion of suitable uncured compounds where the named formulation and equipment support them. It does not justify transferring silicone-rubber settings to uncured polysiloxane fluids, silicone resins, filled compounds, or already-cured articles; each grade requires its own viscosity, pot-life, shear, mold temperature, cure, cooling, and post-cure controls.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The backbone contains repeating siloxane bonds, with substituents such as methyl or phenyl groups on silicon. Chains can be linear or branched, and reactive groups can form network junctions. Crosslinked silicone elastomers differ from low-molecular-weight silicone fluids. Fillers and formulation add further structural variation. The substituents also affect chain organization: a Gelest guide reports that increasing phenyl substitution raises rigidity and refractive index, and that highly phenyl-substituted examples become solids. These statements concern the described phenylsiloxanes; a cured, filled network has its own morphology.
sections.properties: Selected polysiloxanes have flexible chains and useful surface and thermal properties. Silicone elastomers can remain compliant over a broad temperature range. Their mechanical response depends on crosslinking and filler content. Fluids, elastomers and resins have different physical behavior. As one example, Gelest describes conventional PDMS fluids across a wide range of viscosities and associates their low glass transition with flexible chains. In its rheology guidance, a fluid listed at 12,500 cSt has an apparent viscosity of 4,700 cSt at a shear rate of 10,000 s⁻¹, illustrating shear thinning in that high-viscosity fluid. The response of a fluid does not characterize every silicone resin or crosslinked rubber.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polysiloxanes are supplied as fluids, elastomers and resins for different jobs. Gelest identifies PDMS fluids as engineered liquids for applications including lubrication, heat transfer and damping; viscosity and end-group chemistry help determine which fluid suits a formulation. In a distinct fluid application, Gelest lists low-viscosity phenylsiloxane products PDM-7040 and PDM-7050 as diffusion-pump fluids; these specified examples are trisiloxanes rather than long-chain polymers. The manufacturer also describes phenyl substitution as a way to tune refractive index toward that of silica in optical connections. Cured silicone elastomers and silicone resins are separate material forms, used for example in flexible components and electronics.

Purchasing. Suppliers offer conventional and functional fluids, emulsions, resins and elastomer ingredients. Buyers specify the substituents, viscosity or molecular-weight range, end groups and, for curable products, the intended cure system; a fluid is not interchangeable with a cured rubber.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked supplier portfolio illustrates forms and uses, not the annual volume purchased by each industry. Wet formulations, reactive kits and cured parts cannot be added as though they were the same quantity of polymer.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) fluids, one member of the family, can undergo siloxane-bond cleavage and hydrolysis in soil, forming shorter silanol-containing molecules including dimethylsilanediol. The extent and products depend on the material and exposure; the same behavior should not be assumed for every substituted or crosslinked silicone.

Timescales: A Dutch public-health report reviewing PDMS soil studies describes polymer breakdown half-lives of 4–28 days in seven soils, but much slower breakdown under moist conditions in other studies. These are disappearance or transformation times for the tested PDMS, not complete mineralization times or a prediction for a bulk silicone rubber article.

Environmental persistence: The same report describes a sediment study in which dimethylsilanediol represented 5–10% and carbon dioxide 0.25% of applied radiolabel after one year. Small-molecule formation, volatilization and mineralization are distinct outcomes. Fluid, soil moisture, mineral surfaces and exposure determine the observed fate; the study does not establish a single environmental lifetime for the family.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A patent describes depolymerizing selected silicone wastes with a catalyst and organic polymer to produce volatile siloxanes, which can be separated from nonvolatile fillers and other residue. The recovered cyclic siloxanes are chemical feedstocks rather than the original finished rubber article. The disclosure does not establish collection or commercial recovery for every silicone formulation; fillers and mixed waste can complicate separation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: WACKER’s silicone-elastomer processing guidance identifies flammable low-molecular siloxanes, and sometimes peroxide by-products, in post-cure emissions. A circulating-air oven needs fresh-air supply and effective exhaust to prevent vapor accumulation. Post-cure conditions and contamination control depend on the formulation; the safety of a cured article is not established solely by calling it silicone.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Polysiloxane does not specify the substituents, molecular weight or architecture. Crosslinker, cure, fillers and specimen geometry affect an elastomer measurement. A PDMS result cannot represent all polysiloxanes. Chemical compatibility and service limits require the particular formulation and environment.

sections.overview: Styrenic block copolymers contain polystyrene blocks joined to elastomeric blocks. Examples include SBS, SIS and their hydrogenated relatives such as SEBS. Many act as thermoplastic elastomers because the blocks organize into separate domains. They are used in adhesives, modifiers and flexible products. The glassy styrene-rich domains act as physical junctions in suitable architectures; unlike a permanently vulcanized network, these junctions can soften on heating. Hydrogenating a diene block changes its chemical exposure response as well as its structure.
sections.history:
Styrenic block copolymers emerged from Shell’s elastomer research in the 1950s and early 1960s. Supplier accounts differ on the development date: Kraton’s current corporate history uses 1955, while its 2011 investor presentation identifies Shell’s SBC development in 1961. Both place the commercial footwear introduction in 1964 and the dedicated Belpre, Ohio plant in 1971. These milestones are more specific than attributing the entire block-copolymer concept to one product launch.

The materials combined rubberlike behavior with thermoplastic shaping. Hot-melt adhesives became an early market, followed by roofing and road-bitumen modification. Hydrogenated block polymers supported elastic diaper components and soft-touch molded products. Shell’s commercial work, continued by Kraton after divestment, therefore extended the family from shoe compounds into adhesives, infrastructure and consumer products; different block sequences and hydrogenation states have their own development histories.
sections.nomenclature: SBC abbreviates styrenic block copolymer. The family includes SBS, SIS, SEBS, SEPS, and related architectures; those members are narrower records rather than interchangeable aliases.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrenic block copolymers (SBCs) are sequence-defined polymers containing one or more glassy styrenic blocks and one or more lower-glass-transition blocks. Established thermoplastic-elastomer members include SBS and SIS, made from styrene with 1,3-butadiene or isoprene, and the selectively hydrogenated derivatives SEBS, SEPS, and SEEPS. The principal manufacturing route is living anionic polymerization in a rigorously dry hydrocarbon medium with an organolithium initiator. Sequential monomer charges can build linear A–B–A or multiblock chains; alternatively, living styrene–diene arms are reacted with a di- or multifunctional coupling agent to obtain linear, star, or radial architectures. Initiator amount and block-feed quantities set molar mass and block fraction, while polar modifiers and temperature control diene microstructure. Coupling efficiency sets arm number and residual diblock content. For hydrogenated SBCs, an unsaturated SBS, SIS, or mixed-butadiene/isoprene precursor is contacted with hydrogen and a transition-metal catalyst so that midblock carbon–carbon double bonds are reduced while aromatic styrene rings are largely retained. A cited patent family illustrates sequential and coupling strategies, and a distinct open review places living anionic, controlled radical, and coupling approaches in the broader block-copolymer synthesis landscape. Polymerization is terminated, stabilized, and followed by solvent/catalyst recovery. Polystyrene-rich domains form reversible physical junctions in the finished thermoplastic elastomer; that microphase association is not a covalent cure reaction.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Styrenic block copolymers (SBCs) include SBS, SIS, and hydrogenated derivatives such as SEBS, SEPS, and SEEPS, as well as linear, star, and multiblock architectures; their mechanical properties therefore should not be represented by one family-wide numerical range. In a conventional ABA thermoplastic elastomer, glassy polystyrene-rich end-block domains sit within a continuous low-glass-transition midblock and act as reversible physical cross-links. Between the midblock and polystyrene glass-transition regions, this structure gives a soft rubbery plateau, large extensibility, and recoverable deformation without permanent chemical cross-linking. Loading can also produce hysteresis, stress softening, and residual set as chains and domains rearrange. Failure may involve end-block pullout from the hard domains, hard-domain rupture, or midblock scission. As temperature approaches the polystyrene-domain softening or order–disorder region, the physical network weakens, creep and permanent set increase, and the material ultimately flows; unsaturated SBS and SIS also lose performance through oxidation more readily than hydrogenated analogues.

Styrene fraction, block molecular weights and dispersity, total molecular weight, linear versus radial architecture, coupling efficiency and diblock content, the fraction of bridging versus loop or dangling chains, and sphere/cylinder/lamella morphology control stiffness, strength, toughness, elongation, hysteresis, and set. Midblock chemistry and microstructure, hydrogenation and any crystallinity, domain size and orientation, oils, tackifiers, fillers, reinforcement, polar functionalization, and blending create additional formulation dependence. Melt shear, cooling rate, annealing, molding orientation, service temperature, strain rate, cyclic history, and thermal or oxidative aging can all change the observed response. Neat hydrocarbon SBCs usually have little direct moisture sensitivity, but absorbed water can matter when polar modifications, hygroscopic additives, fillers, or weak interfaces are present.

One bounded family-member example comes from a 2025 review's data for neat commercial SIS (Quintac 3440): 19 wt% polystyrene, number-average molecular mass about 150 kg/mol, and dispersity 1.15. At a nominal tensile strain rate of 0.10 s−1, that material had Young's modulus 2.7 ± 0.03 MPa, maximum tensile stress 9.1 ± 0.2 MPa, reported break strain 29 ± 0.2 as a strain ratio (about 2900 ± 20% elongation), and tensile toughness 110 ± 1 MJ/m3. Dynamic shear on the same named SIS showed a storage-modulus plateau of about 0.8 MPa from −40 to 80 °C before flow associated with the polystyrene end blocks. These are SIS-grade results, not generic SBC values; the review does not provide the full specimen geometry, conditioning history, replicate count, or modern test-standard designation needed to transfer them to another subtype, compound, or process.
sections.processing:
Styrenic block copolymers are thermoplastic elastomers whose polystyrene-rich domains provide reversible physical junctions: heating permits flow and cooling rebuilds the network without a required chemical cure. Commercial SBC compounds can be injection molded, extruded or coextruded into profiles, sheet, film, and wire coatings, and—when melt strength is sufficient—blown as film or hollow articles. Compounding with oils, tackifiers, polyolefins, fillers, pigments, and stabilizers is common; adhesive formulations are also applied by hot-melt or solution coating and lamination. Grade architecture, unsaturated versus hydrogenated midblock, styrene and diblock content, oil and filler loading, feed consistency, melt temperature, screw shear and residence time, gate or die geometry, solvent removal, cooling, and orientation govern flow, recovery, surface quality, and dimensional stability. Excess shear can separate a formulation or create gate splay, soft molded parts need sufficient cooling for clean ejection, high temperature can volatilize oil, and unsaturated SBS/SIS generally tolerate less thermal and oxidative exposure than hydrogenated SEBS/SEPS. Polymerization and selective hydrogenation belong in Synthesis; compounding and article shaping belong here.

Avient's supplier bulletin says its SBC TPEs normally do not require drying, but separates its formulation guidance by chemistry: SBS/SIS-based grades at 290–350 °F (about 143–177 °C), with possible gels and discoloration above 400 °F (about 204 °C), versus harder, at-least-40-Shore-A SEBS/SEPS grades at 350–410 °F (about 177–210 °C), with degradation possible above 460 °F (about 238 °C). These are GLS compound observations, not universal family windows. As a distinct operating example, Ilyin and co-workers compounded a named 44 wt% styrene SIS (Vector 4411A) with specified oil and asphaltene/resin contents in a twin-rotor mixer at 120 °C for 20 min and 60 rpm, then laminated 160 ± 20 µm films between siliconized PET at 120 °C without curing. That demonstration applies to those SIS adhesive formulations and illustrates one conversion path within the wider SBC family.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Block incompatibility can produce polystyrene-rich and rubber-rich domains. In suitable triblock architectures, glassy styrene domains act as physical junctions between elastic segments. Heating softens those domains and permits melt processing. Block identity, proportions and architecture control the morphology. This phase organization depends on both block identity and composition. Heating can allow flow, but added oils, fillers or chemical crosslinking change how a particular compound behaves.
sections.properties: Many styrenic block copolymers combine rubber-like elasticity with thermoplastic processability. Hard-domain content and rubber-block chemistry influence stiffness and deformation. Hydrogenation changes the chemistry of a diene block and its response to exposure. Oils, fillers and blends can substantially change properties. In one laboratory comparison, an SEBS sample showed more consistent differential-scanning-calorimetry curves over five air heating and cooling cycles than the tested SIS and 30%-styrene SBS samples. That comparison concerns thermal behavior of those grades, not unlimited recycling or all mechanical properties.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Styrenic block copolymers are used in shoe soles, adhesives, asphalt modification and resin modification. The ability of suitable grades to combine rubber-like response with melt processability is useful for flexible products and compounding, while the specific rubber block and styrene content determine the achievable balance. Different end uses can require different additives and architectures. ENEOS lists TR 1600 as an oil-containing, 32/68 styrene-to-rubber grade for footwear soles, whereas its TR 2601 has a 31/69 ratio, no listed oil and is sold as crumb or powder for asphalt modification. The comparison illustrates product-specific formulations and supply forms rather than a single recipe for the family.

Purchasing. ENEOS lists TR grades in pellets, crumb or powder depending on the product and application. A buyer should specify the actual block chemistry, grade and formulation rather than treating SBS, SIS and hydrogenated products as interchangeable.

Scale and evidence limits. The portfolio documents material forms and intended applications but does not report a reliable separate annual purchase or consumption tonnage for this family. Package or grade availability does not establish market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Oxygen and heat can attack the rubber-rich portions of styrenic block copolymers, forming oxidation products and changing the response to further heating. A study comparing SBS, SIS and hydrogenated SEBS used chemiluminescence, infrared spectra and calorimetry to track changes; the results depend on the particular block composition. The study observed changes in infrared bands associated with oxidation and concluded that the butadiene-rich chains in its SBS samples degraded before the styrene blocks. This is the authors’ interpretation for the tested materials and heating protocol, not a complete inventory of environmental products.

Timescales: In that laboratory comparison, specimens were heated and cooled in air five times between 30 and 180 °C. The measured calorimetric curves for SEBS remained more consistent across cycles than those of SIS and the tested 30%-styrene SBS. A heating-cycle comparison is not an outdoor residence time.

Environmental persistence: Thermal oxidation or changing calorimetry signals do not demonstrate mineralization. The experiment does not determine how long a shoe, adhesive or modified asphalt containing these materials persists in soil or water.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Many styrenic block copolymers are thermoplastic and can soften when heated, but repeated processing can alter their chemistry. In a laboratory calorimetry study, five heating and cooling cycles produced more stable curves for the tested SEBS than for the tested SIS and 30%-styrene SBS. This measures thermal response rather than demonstrating repeated manufacture of equivalent finished products.

Recovery of a formulated adhesive, asphalt mixture or shoe also depends on sorting and other ingredients. The controlled thermal test does not establish local collection, unlimited reprocessing or recovery of a pure polymer from those products.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: A styrenic-block-copolymer handling example is Kraton SIS: its supplier highlights static-charge accumulation, hot-melt burns and exposure to dust or process fumes. Packaging discharge near flammable vapor requires ignition control, and melt handling needs thermal protection. These are documented SIS-grade precautions; the complete compounded product may introduce different additives or solvents.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: SBS, SIS, SEBS and SEPS are distinct materials, not interchangeable grades. Block molecular weight, styrene fraction and architecture influence domain structure. Compounding and processing alter the measured response. A value for one block copolymer formulation is not a family-wide constant. SBS and SIS retain unsaturation in their diene blocks; hydrogenated SEBS has a different midblock chemistry. The studied grades also differed in composition, so observed oxidation trends cannot be attributed to a single variable without further comparison.
